artigo.texto: Council approves second reading on one-year data center moratorium Jasper County Council passed second reading on a one-year moratorium for data centers in the unincorporated areas of Jasper County. Third reading will be held at the next council meeting. - Jasper County Council is considering a one-year moratorium on new data centers in unincorporated areas. - Officials have cited concerns over the large amounts of water and electricity required by data centers. - The moratorium would allow staff time to study the impacts and develop regulations for these facilities. - During a public hearing, residents and conservation groups spoke in support of the temporary ban. Jasper County Council is working to ensure that the appropriate steps are being taken before it would even consider accepting any future requests from data centers that seek to locate in the unincorporated areas of the county. Council, during its Sept. 21 meeting, unanimously approved the second reading of an ordinance for a one-year moratorium on the centers in unincorporated Jasper County. This ordinance also allows council, if needed, to extend the moratorium for a period of six months at a time. A third and final reading of the ordinance will be required and will take place at the next Jasper County Council meeting. The Sept. 8 approval or first reading of the pending ordinance doctrine gave the county authority to enforce the requirements which are outlined in the ordinance before final reading. Data centers have been topics of numerous discussions among county councils across the Lowcountry as other councils are also considering moratoriums. Leaders have cited concerns over the amount of water and electricity which could be required by the centers. A data center is a facility that houses Information Technology (IT) infrastructure which includes servers, storage systems and networking equipment which stores processes and manages digital data. The centers, according to officials, can significantly increase both electricity and water demand, consuming millions of gallons of water annually and placing a strain on local power grids. Jasper County Director of Planning and Building Services brought the ordinance before council for second reading, explaining staff felt as though a one-year moratorium was needed. “With the increased number of data centers seeking to locate to South Carolina, staff believes it is necessary to ask county council to place a temporary moratorium on the acceptance of any applications for rezoning, site plans, building permits and any type of economic incentives for data centers, data processing facilities, crypto mining operations and any other uses associated with data processing facilities within unincorporated Jasper County,” Wagner said. The moratorium, Wagner said, is proposed for one year and would allow staff time to review and make sure there are adequate provisions with the Jasper County Zoning Ordinance and land development regulations to control the location the design, the size, density, land use, and infrastructure needs for data centers and data processing facilities and cryptocurrency mining operations. “The planning staff intends to have an ordinance regulating data centers, data processing facilities, and crypto mining operations ready for adoption by the time the moratorium expires,” Wagner said. Staff’s plan, Wagner said, includes considering and planning for the potential impacts of data center development, learn how much water and power usage is necessary to support these uses, ensure the county has plans and policies to ensure that the data center development is consistent with the county’s development objectives and that potential negative impacts are prevented or mitigated. The plan, Wagner said, would also identify appropriate locations for data centers within the county, ensuring these locations are identified in the county’s comprehensive plan and permitted by the county zoning and land use ordinances. The plan would also recommend clear standards for data center development within the county. “Article Six of the Jasper County Zoning Ordinance use regulation utilizes the North American Industry Classification System (also known as the NAICS Code), as the basis for determining the use of a property,” Wagner said. “Currently, the NAICS Code within that use table would allow data centers as a use by right in the community commercial, general commercial, industrial development and the mixed business zoning districts.” Wagner said the ordinance was reviewed by the Jasper County Planning Commission during its Aug. 11 meeting and they recommended approval of the one-year ordinance for a moratorium. “This ordinance does invoke the pending ordinance doctrine,” Wagner said. Public hearing held Two people appeared before council during the public hearing to discuss their thoughts about the moratorium with council. Both said they were in support of the one-year moratorium, and no one spoke against the moratorium. “I applaud the council’s vision and wisdom as you consider the proposed one-year moratorium on data processing centers,” Ridgeland resident Nancy Lowther said. “I believe that this time will allow you, as our county leaders, to see the impact that data center construction and operations have on our neighboring counties in which they have already been approved.” Lowther also said she believed the county’s facilities and infrastructure were overburdened with projects already underway. “Even with financial incentives, I believe it would be a mistake to move forward with one of these projects at this time,” Lowther said. Coastal Conservation League South Coast Office Director Grant McClure also commended council for moving forward with a one-year moratorium. “I’m here tonight to express support for the proposed moratorium on data centers in Jasper County,” McClure said. “We are seeing these facilities pop up all across South Carolina and also in Georgia in places like Effingham Cou

artigo.texto: leagend to Showcase Next-Generation Battery and Vehicle Starting Solutions at AAPEX 2026 Meet Leagend at Booth V7315, Venetian Expo Level 2, Nov. 3â5, and explore battery-free SuperCap jump starters, battery testing, monitoring, and more. Visitors can meet the leagend team at Booth V7315, Venetian Expo, Level 2, where the company will present its SuperCap Jump Starter Series, professional battery testers, battery monitors, smart battery chargers and thermal imaging solutions. One of leagend's latest R&D developments, the new leagend SuperCap Battery, will also be on display for visitors to experience at the show. For automotive aftermarket distributors, importers, battery and parts businesses, tool suppliers, service networks, fleet operators and automotive brands, AAPEX provides an opportunity to see how these technologies can fit different vehicle applications and market needs while discussing distribution, private-label and OEM/ODM cooperation with the leagend team. Battery-Free Starting Support Built to Stay with the Vehicle Conventional portable jump starters provide emergency starting assistance, but they depend on an internal battery that must be kept sufficiently charged before it is needed. The leagend SuperCap Jump Starter Series uses supercapacitor technology instead of an internal chemical battery and is designed to remain installed on the vehicle. Once installed, the system functions as on-board starting support rather than a portable booster that must be located and connected after a no-start occurs. Its low-power design allows it to remain connected for long periods, while the battery-free architecture removes the need to periodically recharge an internal lithium battery. The leagend SuperCap Jump Starter Series also incorporates AI self-learning, driving and forced-start modes. Through the companion smart app, users can view battery condition, operating status, starting records and alerts. These functions combine starting assistance with ongoing visibility into vehicle starting behavior rather than limiting the product to one-time emergency use. For workshops, the system can be installed as part of vehicle service. For fleet operators and commercial vehicle users, having starting support already installed on the vehicle can reduce reliance on separately stored portable boosters when additional starting assistance is required. artigo.texto: August 2026 Data Center spending totaled $14.4 billion across 17 projects, lifting the year-to-date (YTD) project count to 153 and the total spent on Data Centers to $98.5 billion. The average Data Center cost $1.18 billion and covers 707,000 square feet YTD, among Data Centers with known prices and square-footage. ConstructConnect Project Intelligence is currently tracking 65 Data Center projects, worth a total $26.1 billion, with start dates before the end of 2026. This exclusive data center report was prepared by ConstructConnect Chief Economist, Michael Guckes, and Associate Economist, Devin Bell. The largest project to break ground for the month was the nearly 300-acre AVAIO Digital Data Center Campus project in Little Rock, Arkansas at $6 billion. Through August 2026, Data Centers accounted for 24% of all Nonresidential Building starts. August 2026 Data Center spending totaled $14.4 billion across 17 projects, lifting the year-to-date (YTD) project count to 153 and the total spent on Data Centers to $98.5 billion. Image and Data: ConstructConnect Data Centers are rising in costs faster than size, pushing cost per square foot prices steeply higher. YTD, among Data Centers with known price and square footage, the average Data Center cost is $1.18 billion and covers 707,000 square feet. The comparable figures for 2025 were $507.4 million and 493,000 square feet. On a per-project basis the Data Center construction cost, per square foot, can range dramatically from less than $300 to more than $2,200 per square foot, depending on the project specifics. After removing the bottom and top 10% of projects by their cost per square foot, the median and average Data Center price, per square foot in the YTD period, is $541 and $867, respectively. Through August 2026, new Data Center builds are moving away from the coasts and towards the Midwest and Southern sections of the country. Image and Data: ConstructConnect From a geographic perspective, new Data Center builds are moving away from the coasts and towards the Midwest and Southern sections of the country. So far in 2026, three particular multi-state areas have reported very high levels of Data Center spending: These include the five contiguous states between Wisconsin and Ohio. Of these five states, four have reported data center starts of $10 billion or more. Additionally, the four states between Texas and Mississippi have reported similarly strong spending with Texas the upward exception at over $22 billion. Finally, along the eastern seaboard the string of states between Georgia and Virigina have seen spending of between $5 billion and over $20 billion. Beyond these tight groupings, only a few individual states have seen spending of $2 billion or more including North Dakota, Arizona, and Pennsylvania. ConstructConnect Project Intelligence is currently tracking 65 data center projects, worth a total $26.1 billion, with start dates before the end of 2026. With the year nearing a close, it looks like much of the planned data center value has reached groundbreaking, with a noticeably smaller planned pool of projects remaining in 2026. These projects remain in various stages of preconstruction, meaning there is no guarantee that any single project reaches groundbreaking. Planned US Data Center construction starts value by US Census Region is shown on a map from September to December 2026. These projects are still in the preconstruction phase and are not guaranteed to break ground. Image and Data: ConstructConnect Geographically, planned data center is heavily concentrated in the South, led by Texas with over $11 billion in planned projects left in 2026. Each of South Carolina, Virginia, Georgia, and West Virginia have $2 billion or more in planned data center projects. The next closest region is the Northeast, though almost all of this value is concentrated in Pennsylvania. Breaking with the year-to-date geographical pattern, the Midwest does not have a significant share of near-term planned data center projects, accounting for just 1.5% of the $26.1 billion total planned spending figure. Power infrastructure has become an increasingly important piece of the construction economy as energy demands increase amid the rapid data center buildout. Year-to-date, Power Infrastructure starts are 119.9% above the comparable period in 2025, largely powered by the $13 billion Catarus Commonwealth LNG project that broke ground in August. Momentum is expected to continue for the subcategory, as Power Infrastructure starts are forecast to rise 30% in 2027 compared to full-year 2026. artigo.texto: - Japan - / - Industrials - / - TSE:6501 Could Modular Data Centers Alter The Investment Case For Hitachi (TSE:6501)? - On 16 September 2026, Hitachi and Mission Critical Group signed an MoU to co-develop solutions for the HMAX Data Center portfolio and jointly sell energy products across modular data center projects. - The focus on factory-built modular data centers aimed at AI workloads highlights how Hitachi is trying to address long equipment lead times and compressed deployment schedules for power hungry digital infrastructure. - We will now look at how Hitachi's investment narrative could be influenced by this modular data center and energy partnership. Scan how Hitachi's AI ready data center push compares with other power hungry digital infrastructure plays by reviewing the hand picked 85 AI infrastructure stocks. Hitachi Investment Narrative Recap To own Hitachi, you need to believe in a long runway for grid upgrades, digital systems and AI heavy infrastructure, supported by disciplined portfolio pruning. The MoU with Mission Critical Group fits this story operationally because it links Hitachi's energy and digital assets to a fast growing, modular data center niche tied to AI demand. The key near term swing factor remains execution in high growth, higher margin segments like Energy and Digital Systems while keeping project costs and capex under control. The biggest risk is that rising input costs, intense IT hardware competition and underperforming legacy units absorb the benefits from these newer, AI ready projects. There are no other fresh announcements listed alongside this MoU, so the most relevant reference point is still the broader push into energy, grid and digital solutions described in Hitachi's recent profile. The HMAX and MCG partnership sits directly on top of that because it tries to bundle grid equipment, power distribution and AI infrastructure into one offering. For you, the interest is in how quickly this kind of modular, factory built approach turns into real orders and recurring digital service revenue, versus simply adding more capital intensity. If tariffs, IT demand softness or weak elevator and construction operations linger, the benefit of this AI focused data center effort could be diluted by the rest of the portfolio. What The Hitachi Consensus Is Pricing In Hitachi's analyst narrative ties this AI ready data center push to a broader set of expectations on revenue, profit margins and capital discipline. Consensus numbers sketch out a picture where grid equipment, digital services and modular data centers are all feeding into a larger earnings pool by the late 2020s, even as the company spends heavily on capacity and software platforms. Hitachi's narrative projects ¥14,366.1b revenue and ¥1,328.2b earnings by 2029. This is based on analysts assuming 9.2% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about ¥528.6b from the current ¥799.6b level. Uncover why Hitachi's fair value indicates a 19% potential upside to its current price that could narrow quickly. Exploring Other Perspectives One alternative view on Hitachi puts far more weight on AI driven data center demand as a long term catalyst. The most optimistic analysts were already penciling in about ¥14,266.5b revenue and ¥1,467.8b earnings by 2029 before this MoU, which could shift expectations further. artigo.texto: The World Trade Organization will examine Russia’s challenge to the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and an alleged export subsidy under its Emissions Trading System (ETS), following a decision by the Dispute Settlement Body on 25 September. The panel’s establishment moves the disagreement into formal examination, with Russia claiming the measures restrict trade and the EU defending their consistency with WTO rules. Russia submitted its second request for a panel after the EU objected to its first request on 24 July. Moscow argued that the CBAM package creates significant barriers for covered goods entering the European market, and that the allocation of emission allowances to certain companies under the ETS amounts to an export subsidy supporting the competitiveness of selected domestic industries. These claims will be examined through the dispute proceedings; the panel’s establishment does not determine their validity. The EU questioned Russia’s reliance on international law to improve export access, pointing to Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine. It said participation in the proceedings reflected its support for the rules-based multilateral trading system and expressed confidence in both measures’ WTO compatibility. Eighteen members reserved third-party participation rights: Argentina, Brazil, Canada, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Malaysia, Norway, Paraguay, Singapore, Switzerland, Chinese Taipei, Thailand, the United Kingdom and the United States. China and Türkiye requested more time to pursue a resolution of their separate dispute over Turkish measures affecting electric vehicles and certain other vehicles originating in China. The panel report in the case was circulated on 28 July 2026, and both governments asked the DSB to postpone consideration of its adoption until 27 October 2026. Members approved the request, allowing further engagement between the two sides. The meeting covered implementation updates in several existing disputes, keeping attention on cases beyond the new carbon measures challenge. The United States reported on Japanese hot-rolled steel, copyright legislation, South Korean residential washers and anti-dumping methodologies involving China. EU updates concerned two palm oil and crop-based biofuel disputes and another involving biotechnology products, and Indonesia reported on its disputes concerning imports of horticultural products, animals and animal products. Colombia, speaking for 130 members, presented the group’s proposal to begin filling Appellate Body vacancies for the 100th time, describing the broad support as evidence of a shared interest in a functioning dispute settlement system. The United States withheld support, saying the proposal did not address its fundamental concerns and that members remained far apart on the reforms needed, leaving the selection process blocked again. More than 20 members voiced support for the proposal and called for the urgent restoration of a fully functioning system. Several encouraged participation in the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement, which allows participating members to use arbitration under Article 25 of the Dispute Settlement Understanding for appeals in disputes between them. Members welcomed Cambodia’s entry into the arrangement, reflecting interest in an available route for handling appeals. Colombia expressed the group’s regret over the repeated failure to launch appointments and said reform discussions should not prevent the Appellate Body from operating or members from meeting their obligations to fill vacancies. DSB Chair Ambassador Guilherme de Aguiar Patriota of Brazil highlighted support expressed on 24 July for sessions preserving institutional memory. The first session, held after the September meeting, covered the dispute system’s history, trends and resolution methods, followed by reform efforts after the 12th and 13th Ministerial Conferences. {{#source}}{{source}} {{/source}}{{#isBlog}} {{disclaimer}} {{/disclaimer}}

artigo.texto: Do ronco ao silêncio: qual a diferença entre dirigir um carro elétrico e um a combustão? César Urnhani, piloto e especialista automotivo, mostra quais são essas diferenças e dá dicas para quem está fazendo essa transição. Crédito: Estadão Na corrida pelos carregadores de carros elétricos mais potentes do mundo, o novo carregador da Geely coloca a fabricante chinesa um passo à frente no mercado global. Batizado de Geely Smart Charging, o dispositivo entrega uma potência de 2.250 kW (2,25 MW) e supera o sistema Flash Charging da BYD. Ele promete elevar o nível da bateria de 10% para 70% em apenas 4 minutos e meio, enquanto a carga completa leva cerca de 8 minutos. Leia também - Preço do seu SUV flex pode derreter enquanto eletrificados usados desvalorizam menos; entenda - Carros PCD: nova lei libera R$ 30 bi para compra e adaptação - Conheça os maiores mitos e verdades sobre a manutenção de carros elétricos Inteligência artificial a serviço da bateria Além do recorde de potência, a inovação do carregador Geely está no gerenciamento térmico com inteligência artificial integrada. O sistema monitora as células do pacote em tempo real para preservar o componente. A IA prevê variações de temperatura com até 30 segundos de antecedência e ajusta a potência preventivamente. O recurso evita o superaquecimento, mantém a média abaixo de 55 °C e garante a máxima eficiência de carregamento. O Smart Charging oferece três modos de operação (Extremo, Inteligente e Automático) e traz a tecnologia de regeneração pulsada. O sistema limpa o acúmulo de íons no eletrodo e pode aumentar a vida útil da bateria em até 20%. Para usar a potência máxima do carregador Geely, o veículo precisa estar preparado. A recarga ultrarrápida estará disponível em estações de quinta geração para modelos equipados com as baterias Ultra Short Blade da própria marca. O dispositivo faz parte do plano de expansão global de infraestrutura de recarga da Geely, focado na China e nos mercados internacionais. Embate contra a BYD O lançamento supera o antigo recordista do setor, o sistema Flash Charging da BYD. Apresentado com 1.500 kW (1,5 MW) de potência, o equipamento da rival recarrega de 10% a 70% em 5 minutos. Com isso, as duas chinesas acirram a disputa pela liderança nas tecnologias de carregamento ultrarrápido. A marca informou que o Smart Charging estará disponível comercialmente a partir de 2027, sem confirmação inicial para o mercado brasileiro. Em contrapartida, a BYD já confirmou a instalação de 1.000 unidades do seu carregador no Brasil. Carregando ofertas... Os comentários são exclusivos para cadastrados.

artigo.texto: - Volkswagen, PowerCo, and Gotion High-Tech will invest €3.22 billion to build a battery-materials facility in Kenitra, Morocco. - The facility will produce up to 100,000 tonnes of LFP cathode material annually, supplying European battery plants in Spain and Slovakia. - Gotion will hold a 51% stake and PowerCo 49%, focusing on supplying cathode materials for electric vehicle battery cells. - The collaboration positions Morocco as a critical upstream supplier in the European EV value chain. Morocco is taking another step up the clean-energy and automotive value chain after Volkswagen Group, its battery subsidiary PowerCo and Chinese battery maker Gotion High-Tech agreed to develop a battery-materials facility in Kenitra as part of a €3.22 billion ($3.7 billion) investment programme spanning Morocco, Spain and Slovakia. The deal puts Morocco upstream in a European electric-vehicle supply chain, with its planned facility producing a critical component for lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries that will be manufactured at the partners’ European plants. The Kenitra joint venture is expected to receive about €480 million ($530 million) in investment and produce up to 100,000 tonnes of LFP cathode material annually. Gotion will hold 51%, while PowerCo will own 49%, with the output intended primarily to supply the partners’ battery-cell operations in Spain and Slovakia. Morocco’s role in the battery chain The two European facilities are planned to have combined annual capacity of 37.5 GWh. The Valencia plant in Spain will account for 29.1 GWh, while the Slovakian facility at Šurany will produce 8.4 GWh. This creates a cross-Mediterranean chain: Morocco produces cathode material, Spain and Slovakia produce battery cells, and Volkswagen’s European vehicle operations provide a major downstream market. The development adds an industrial dimension to Morocco’s long-running renewable-energy strategy. The country is widely recognised as a regional leader in clean-energy deployment, with the Noor Ouarzazate complex having been one of the world's largest concentrated solar-power facilities. DON'T MISS THIS: Morocco to host Africa’s first battery gigafactory with $5.6 billion Chinese investment That combination of renewable-energy ambitions, proximity to Europe and an established automotive manufacturing base has helped Morocco position itself as a bridge between African production and European industrial markets. A strategic shift for Europe’s batteries Volkswagen says LFP batteries are expected to become increasingly important in Europe, with their share of the European battery market projected to rise from about 10% currently to 40–60% by 2030. Europe currently has limited relevant LFP production capacity. The partnership therefore goes beyond a single Moroccan factory. Volkswagen and Gotion are attempting to build a more regionalised European battery supply chain, while using Morocco to diversify the supply of key cathode materials. DON'T MISS THIS: Another Chinese company is set to establish a manufacturing hub in Africa’s most industrialized country, this time for $298 million The partnership also deepens an existing relationship between the German automaker and Chinese battery producer. Volkswagen has worked with Gotion since 2020 and remains a significant shareholder, although it has agreed to sell a 5.3% stake in the Chinese company. For Morocco, the significance is that its role in the European automotive economy is moving further upstream — from vehicle and component manufacturing towards the materials needed to power the next generation of electric vehicles.

artigo.texto: A Weg anunciou dois projetos de expansão, aumentando sua presença em infraestrutura de energia. Na América do Norte, investirá US$ 165 milhões para ampliar a produção de geradores, com conclusão em 2030. No Brasil, ampliará o projeto de baterias BESS, elevando o investimento para R$ 330 milhões e a capacidade para 4GWh. O Citi destaca que a Weg se posiciona para capturar a demanda por energia renovável. A recomendação do Citi é neutra, com preço-alvo de R$ 49, um potencial de alta de 4,22%. A Weg (WEGE3) anunciou dois projetos estratégicos de expansão de capacidade que, segundo o Citi, aumentam a exposição da empresa a temas relevantes de infraestrutura de energia, como data centers (centro de dados) e modernização da rede. Na América do Norte, a companhia vai investir US$ 165 milhões para ampliar a produção de geradores. Com a conclusão prevista para 2030, o banco afirma que a capacidade global de geradores da companhia deve subir de 10 para 50 unidades por dia, com operações no México, nos Estados Unidos, no Brasil e na China. No Brasil, a empresa informou que está ampliando o projeto de baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês para Battery Energy Storage System), elevando o investimento planejado para R$ 330 milhões e a capacidade anual para 4GWh. Os analistas Andre Mazini, Kiepher Kennedy e Piero Trotta observam que o movimento ocorre antes do primeiro leilão de BESS no País, esperado para dezembro de 2026, e avaliam que a Weg se posiciona para capturar a necessidade crescente de integrar geração renovável intermitente. O relatório destaca ainda que o anúncio do projeto de BESS ocorreu apenas sete meses após a primeira divulgação da fábrica em Itajaí (SC). O plano original previa capacidade anual de 2 GWh, mas a revisão dobra o volume para 4 GWh e aumenta o investimento total de R$ 280 milhões para R$ 330 milhões. Na leitura do Citi, a aceleração do plano indica confiança no mercado emergente de armazenamento de energia no Brasil e reforça o posicionamento da empresa em um segmento da cadeia de transição energética. A expectativa é que as operações comecem no segundo semestre de 2027. Para o banco, os dois anúncios reforçam a estratégia da companhia de se aproximar de data centers e armazenamento de energia, apontados como vetores estruturais de crescimento para a próxima década. O Citi também diz ver a WEG negociada a 29 vezes lucro. O Citi tem recomendação neutra para a Weg, com preço-alvo de R$ 49, o que representa um potencial de alta de 4,22% ante o fechamento da ação da empresa na última sexta-feira, 25.

artigo.texto: Monday night in Ashburn, Virginia marked the beginning of a new chapter in the data center debate. Loudoun County is home to 233 data centers at last count, more than anywhere else in the world. Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. Too close, too hot, too noisy, too much water and energy consumption — Those concerns, and others, have been stressed over and over by Loudoun County residents like Anita Selino. “This is what I see from my driveway now, and that is a mile from my house. Then I find out that they're building two more,” she said, showing News4 a picture of a data center on her phone. “I have asthma. I'm very concerned that I will have to move, that I will not be able to live in my house if they're running generators.” The 2000 decision that helped make Loudoun County the original home of AOL into the data center capital of the world is about to be updated. At Broad Run High School in Ashburn Monday night, residents streamed into the first open house where they can give input to county employees on what’s known as “Data Center Standards and Locations Phase 2.” “It's important to have community involvement,” said Broad Run Supervisor Sylvia Glass. “We have a lot of people that are having a lot of questions about what data centers are, you know, where they're going to be built.” Northern Virginia Northern Virginia news, events and updates Chris Bruner, an electrician, said he feels the tax and other economic benefits of data centers must remain part of the discussion going forward. “So the economic boom, a lot of it comes in where they're saying they don't employ a lot of people, but there's been data hall rooms where I've remodeled the room four and five times over over just the past 10 years with 10, 20 electricians working 12-hour days,” he said. There’s a second open house scheduled for Sept. 30 at the Douglas Community Center in Leesburg.

artigo.texto: Uma nova frente de negócios: créditos de carbono Elétricas ampliam a venda de créditos de carbono e miram nova demanda com avanço do mercado regulado Atualizado Com o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono nacional, as empresas do setor de energia passaram a enxergar a comercialização de créditos de carbono como uma extensão de seus negócios. Foi uma evolução natural do setor, uma vez que as fontes renováveis respondem por cerca de 85% da matriz elétrica brasileira e que as reduções de emissões de carbono podem dar origem a créditos. Embora essa frente de negócios não seja relevante em termos de faturamento, integra a sustentabilidade das operações. Trata-se de um negócio complementar, cuja relevância pode aumentar com o mercado regulado de carbono, o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), em implementação. Na Auren Energia, a estratégia ganhou uma área dedicada em 2022 e foi integrada à comercialização. A companhia já vendeu oito milhões de créditos a clientes de mais de 20 países, a maioria deles empresas que precisam neutralizar suas emissões. Ela também mantém o Carbonless, comércio eletrônico para pequenas empresas e pessoas físicas que queiram zerar sua pegada de carbono. Eduardo Diniz, diretor de comercialização, diz que a estratégia da Auren é se tornar um “one-stop-shop” para clientes de energia, de forma que estes possam comprar tanto o fornecimento de energia quanto os créditos para zerar ou compensar as emissões. No momento, a empresa desenvolve um projeto que prevê a restauração de até 2.795 hectares e o plantio de até 5,6 milhões de árvores na bacia do rio Tietê — projetos do tipo geram créditos mais valorizados. Já a Axia Energia comercializou mais de 12 milhões de créditos entre 2013 e 2026. A companhia vê a experiência como credencial para o SBCE, que estabelecerá limites de emissão para agentes regulados e permitirá a negociação de ativos para o cumprimento das metas. A expectativa das empresas é que créditos hoje negociados no mercado voluntário possam, desde que atendam a critérios previstos na regulamentação, ganhar espaço também nesse sistema. “Queremos alcançar empresas que estão começando a jornada de sustentabilidade e empresas maiores com alta demanda de crédito”, diz Cecília Essinger, gerente-executiva de produtos estruturados e ativos ambientais da Axia. Segundo ela, créditos originados em energia renovável são negociados no mercado por cerca de US$ 1 a US$ 3. A Engie atua no mercado de carbono desde 2004. A empresa tem 14 projetos de energia eólica, solar, hidrelétrica e biomassa que geram créditos pela redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa (GEE). Antes registrados no Mecanismo de Desenvolvimento Limpo (MDL), esses projetos estão sendo adaptados às regras do Acordo de Paris. Nos empreendimentos controlados integralmente pela Engie, as reduções de emissões somaram cerca de 6,5 milhões de toneladas de CO2 e até 2020, sendo que 5,3 milhões de créditos já foram usados para compensar emissões e, por isso, saíram de circulação. A empresa também mantém a plataforma Descarbonize, que ajuda clientes a medir e administrar suas emissões e a comprar créditos para compensá-las. Já na EDP, o Parque Eólico Monte Verde, no Rio Grande do Norte, tornou-se em 2025 o primeiro projeto do grupo no mundo certificado para emitir créditos, evitando a emissão de 533 mil toneladas de CO2 por ano. Como o mercado voluntário de créditos de carbono só se sustenta se houver credibilidade e confiança de que os projetos contribuíram para a redução ou remoção das emissões, as empresas têm buscado verificadoras independentes como Verra e Gold Standard, mecanismos vinculados à ONU e o Global Carbon Council. Nem toda redução de emissões entrega o mesmo resultado climático. Daniela Mota, head de meio ambiente e sustentabilidade do escritório Felsberg Advogados, diz que tecnologia, data de geração, metodologia e certificação influenciam qualidade e preço dos créditos. Entre os riscos estão a falta de adicionalidade — quando a redução ocorreria mesmo sem o projeto —, a dupla contagem e benefícios que não se confirmam. “É muito ruim, do ponto de vista reputacional, ter um projeto de carbono que não entrega aquilo que estava prometendo”, afirma. Enquanto alguns monetizam emissões evitadas e projetos de restauração florestal, uma nova fronteira está nas tecnologias de captura, transporte, utilização e armazenamento de CO2, conhecidas pelas siglas CCS e CCUS. O Decreto nº 13.095/2026, publicado em agosto, reconhece o CCS como atividade de redução ou remoção de GEE, que poderá ser considerada no SBCE. A Petrobras informa ter armazenado 86 milhões de toneladas de CO2 em sistemas de CCUS do pré-sal entre 2008 e 2025, sendo 18 milhões no ano passado. Já o piloto Cabiúnas-São Tomé deverá capturar até 100 mil toneladas anuais por três anos a partir de 2028 e armazená-las em reservatório salino profundo no norte fluminense. A licença ambiental integrada foi emitida em agosto. Apesar da escala, a estatal não tem projeto para gerar créditos destinados à venda; suas compras ou compromissos de aquisição são, a princípio, para uso próprio.

artigo.texto: 6abbc8c027f1a373af8e2421 Dreamstime Ai Tetiana Strilchuk 448623057 Energy companies need new solutions to meet rising demand without causing price spikes or slowing the energy transition. On this front, battery storage could help optimize existing power-grid infrastructure — the tools and capital exist; now, resolve and regulation are needed. While this solution is highly relevant to the U.S., where growth and affordability concerns are top of mind, the concept is also applicable globally. Electricity demand is rising fast, driven by electrification, AI, and data centers, as well as expanding access to reliable power globally. Simultaneously, the power sector is facing an affordability crisis. So, how can energy companies serve this new demand and modernize the grid without driving prices higher for consumers? The increasing ubiquity of storage globally provides an unprecedented opportunity to use batteries to optimize existing grid infrastructure to meet this growing demand and place downward pressure on prices. The tools and capital are currently being deployed. Now all we need are the resolve and regulatory structures to act. Kommunalkredit Austria AG’sGareth Foulkes-Jones discusses the growing role of battery storage in European energy markets and considers the commercial and financing factors that sit alongside the technology. An Army veteran, Alix Paultre was a signals intelligence soldier on the East/West German border in the early ‘80s, and eventually wound up helping launch and run a publication on consumer electronics for the US military stationed in Europe. Alix first began in this industry in 1998 at Electronic Products magazine, and since then has worked for a variety of publications in the embedded electronic engineering space. Alix currently lives in Wiesbaden, Germany. Also check out his YouTube watch-collecting channel, Talking Timepieces. Senior Transactor and Director, Project Development and Origination, Renewable Energy,Kommunalkredit Austria AG Gareth Foulkes-Jones is a Senior Transactor and Director, Project Development and Origination, Renewable Energy at Kommunalkredit Austria AG. He brings experience from previous roles at ABO Wind, IGR GREEN, and Suntech. Gareth holds a 2025 - 2025 BatteryMBA.

artigo.texto: BYD Maps Out Solid-State Batteries by 2030 While Scouting a Second European Plant Published on 09/28/2026 at 20:51 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD is pressing ahead on two fronts at once: overhauling the models that drive its sales today and laying the groundwork for the technology it expects to define the next decade. On Monday the Chinese electric-vehicle maker unveiled the exterior design of the second-generation Seal 07 sedan, part of a broader refresh of its highest-volume nameplates. According to media reports, the redesigned sedan will reach customers in both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid form. The reveal follows a similar update to the Seagull, the compact city car sold in export markets as the Atto 1. That model moves to a second-generation platform with rear-wheel drive and a multi-link rear suspension, seats five, and lifts electric motor output to 95 kilowatts, with a launch in China slated before the end of 2026. The new Seal 07 grows noticeably in both length and wheelbase. Buyers will be able to choose a plug-in hybrid variant or a fully electric version whose motor produces up to 300 kilowatts, and the options list includes a roof-mounted LiDAR system for advanced driver-assistance functions. Solid-State Cells Slated for Around 2030 Underpinning the longer-range product plan is a battery roadmap that stretches well past the current lineup. BYD is targeting commercial mass production of solid-state batteries around 2030, leaning heavily on sulfide-based solid electrolytes in their development. Chief scientist Lian Yubo said the new cells will not immediately displace the established Blade battery, which uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry. Instead, the two are expected to be deployed side by side, with solid-state technology reserved for premium models for the time being. That timeline puts BYD alongside international rivals such as Toyota, which is also aiming to bring its first solid-state-equipped vehicles to market in 2027 and 2028. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? Hiring Surge Backs the Production Ramp To keep pace with the wave of new models entering serial output, BYD is expanding its workforce at home. At its Xi'an production site the company is currently recruiting more than 8,000 new employees for its plants and various business units. Reuters, citing the Chinese outlet Yicai, reported that the campaign includes bonuses of up to 6,000 yuan for successful applicants. The staffing push reflects the speed at which the group is moving new model generations onto the line, and the heavy investment in local labor helps secure the ramp-up of forthcoming series such as the revised Seal. Europe: One Plant Opening, Another Being Chosen Beyond China, BYD is deepening its commitment to Europe. Its first European factory, in Hungary, is starting operations, and preparations for further manufacturing steps are already under way. A European adviser to BYD said the company intends to select a location for a second plant by the end of the year, with Spain and France seen as the leading candidates for acquiring and modernizing a facility. Over the long term, the strategy calls for deeper local value creation: the adviser said BYD will eventually need three vehicle assembly plants and its own battery factory on the continent. Executive Vice President Stella Li also announced that BYD plans to introduce its first heavy-duty truck in Europe in 2027 and, in time, to build trucks locally as well. Australia: Fleet Sales Gain Ground The product offensive dovetails with management's efforts to win market share outside China. In Australia, BYD is stepping up its push into the commercial segment. Stephen Collins, chief operating officer of BYD Australia, said the fleet share of the country's sales mix climbed from roughly 8 percent to 20 percent within a year, and the local unit is targeting a figure in the mid-30 percent range over the medium term. Shares Stay Under Pressure None of the operational expansion has been enough to fully lift the stock. The shares slipped on the day, trading at EUR 8.75, a decline of 1.0 percent, and remain 30 percent below their 52-week high of EUR 12.49. Market participants are weighing the ambitious investment and expansion plans against a challenging environment and intensifying competition, while persistent margin pressure in the Chinese home market continues to hold the listing back. artigo.texto: Experts propose 'carbon bank' to monetise Maharashtra's ecological wealth Synopsis Maharashtra plans to create a 'Maharashtra Carbon Bank' to leverage its ecological resources for climate benefit. The proposed initiative aims to integrate carbon credits from bamboo, mangroves, and wetlands. Experts emphasize recognizing the economic value of these natural assets while promoting climate resilience. The initiative aligns with India's efforts to develop its carbon market through the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme. The coalition would identify and map carbon-rich natural assets, quantify their carbon stocks and sequestration potential, verify the data through credible scientific protocols and create a pipeline of certified carbon assets that could participate in emerging carbon markets, he said while presenting the concept at the summit. Kumar said that the idea was to move beyond viewing forests, wetlands, mangroves and bamboo merely as ecological resources and recognise their economic value as climate assets. The proposed carbon bank could also help channel carbon market revenues towards conservation, restoration and local communities, he said. The initiative comes as India develops its domestic carbon market under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme. Kumar said Maharashtra, with its extensive mangroves, wetlands, bamboo resources and green cover, could explore an integrated model, linking nature conservation with the emerging carbon economy. The Green-Blue Carbon Coalition could provide the institutional bridge between nature, science, finance and climate action, he said. (You can now subscribe to our Economic Times WhatsApp channel)

artigo.texto: MIT Leaders for Global Operations, a US-based dual-degree engineering and MBA programme, has published a research brief that puts a cost on mineral supply disruptions for BESS. Its model found that lithium carries the largest exposure, and that complete export restrictions from major producers could raise system costs by more than 20% under baseline assumptions. Copper and aluminum behave differently, because a disruption would lift their commodity prices sharply yet move system costs less. The brief explains that gap by their lower cost share within battery cells. Those results come from a model that turns export concentration, disruption likelihood and price elasticities into post-disruption mineral prices. It then carries the prices through cells and battery packs to full systems. A likelihood-weighted index built on the same model ranks the risks for developers. MIT LGO model finds lithium export curbs could lift BESS costs over 20% Lithium export restrictions could raise BESS system costs by more than 20%, according to a mineral supply risk model from MIT Leaders for Global Operations. artigo.texto: NESTA EDIÇÃO. A disputa do Redata sobre o uso do gás natural abre espaço para tecnologias capazes de reduzir suas emissões. Células a combustível, integração com biometano e captura e armazenamento de carbono estão entre as alternativas. EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: A possibilidade de incluir o gás natural entre as fontes de baixa emissão que os data centers terão que contratar para receber incentivos no Brasil segue indefinida, enquanto o mercado aguarda a regulamentação da política sancionada no dia 15 de setembro. A expectativa era que o decreto fosse assinado nesta segunda (28/9). Com o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), o governo espera atrair investimentos da ordem de R$ 500 bilhões, a partir de benefícios fiscais de até R$ 7,2 bilhões entre 2026 e 2028. Para as isenções de tributos federais, as instalações precisarão comprovar a contratação de energia elétrica 100% renovável ou de baixa emissão. E é este termo que está em disputa no governo. A Fazenda, responsável pelo desenho do programa, tem pressionado para que o presidente Lula (PT) sancione o decreto regulamentador sem incluir o gás natural como fonte energética incentivada, mantendo assim a ênfase em fontes renováveis. A disputa coloca em lados opostos o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), publicamente favorável ao uso do gás natural no programa, e a Fazenda, contrária à inclusão. Na sexta-feira (25/9) à tarde, representantes do setor privado de gás natural se reuniram com interlocutores do Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) para tentar destravar as conversas, que permanecem bloqueadas na Fazenda. Entre as possibilidades discutidas estão excluir o gás, aceitá-lo integralmente ou permitir seu uso condicionado a mecanismos de compensação, como créditos de carbono, uso de biometano e tecnologias de captura e armazenamento de carbono (CCS). Ou, ainda, de que forma será aceita a utilização do gás, a exemplo de backup em situações de queda de energia. Fontes que participaram da reunião afirmaram à agência eixos que, sem o gás natural no decreto, o Redata cria uma espécie de reserva de mercado para as energias renováveis, o que pode trazer desafios para projetos de data centers no Sul e Sudeste do país. Leia na matéria de Gustavo Gaudarde e Gabriel Chiappini Alta demanda, diferentes possibilidades A atração de infraestrutura digital para o Brasil significa uma alavanca da demanda energética e abriu uma frente de disputa sobre quem irá abastecer os centros de dados. O MME contabiliza 38 GW em pedidos de conexão de data centers à rede — o equivalente a quase um terço da capacidade instalada do país. No mundo todo, o consumo de energia por servidores de inteligência artificial deve dobrar até 2030. Estimativas da Kearney apontam que em 2025, os servidores de IA representaram entre 23% e 27% da eletricidade consumida pelos centros de dados. Enquanto o IDTechEx projeta que a capacidade instalada de energia em data centers em todo o mundo ultrapassará 300 GW até 2036, cerca do triplo do valor atual, com a aceleração do crescimento da IA exigindo cada vez mais mais eletricidade. E mesmo com as big techs fechando contratos de longo prazo com parques eólicos e solares, investindo em startups de baterias e apostando nos pequenos reatores nucleares, o gás natural também segue no radar como opção de energia firme — e é aí que diferentes possibilidades começam a se desenhar. Como o gás pode ser baixo carbono A grande crítica de quem é contra o gás natural como “fonte de baixa emissão” no Redata vem do fato de o combustível ser de origem fóssil e liberar emissões de gases de efeito estufa que contribuem com as mudanças climáticas. Mas há caminhos para reduzir esse impacto climático e eles vão desde os mais acessíveis, como substituição de geradores a diesel e a integração com o biometano, até aqueles que ainda precisam ganhar escala e viabilidade econômica, como as células a combustível e o CCS. Ainda de acordo com a recente análise do IDTechEx, o uso de células a combustível abastecidas por gás natural liberam menos CO2 do que os processos de combustão tradicionais e podem, posteriormente, passar a funcionar com 100% de hidrogênio renovável, quando este ganhar escala. Um exemplo dessa aplicação vem da American Electric Power (AEP) que, em janeiro de 2026, fechou um acordo de US$ 2,65 bilhões para implantar até 1 GW de células a combustível de óxido sólido da Bloom Energy em data centers de AI. A captura de carbono é outra solução, com potencial para reduzir as emissões de CO2 de usinas termelétricas convencionais a combustíveis fósseis em mais de 95%, aponta o IDTechEx. Em outubro de 2025, o Google anunciou seu primeiro projeto de captura e armazenamento de carbono, em parceria com a Broadwing Energy, em Decatur, Illinois. A intenção é capturar e armazenar permanentemente aproximadamente 90% de suas emissões de CO2 de geradores a gás. Projetos como esses, no entanto, precisam de precificação do carbono e financiamento para serem competitivos. Além de dependerem de infraestrutura de transporte e armazenamento de CO2, o que pode fazer com que novos projetos de CCS em larga escala levem mais de cinco anos para serem desenvolvidos Segundo a consultoria, na União Europeia e América do Norte, onde há precificação de carbono e políticas de financiamento, esses projetos tendem a se tornar mais atrativos primeiro. O Inmet alerta para uma onda de calor que atinge os estados de Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Minas Gerais, Goiás, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná e Santa Catarina. As temperaturas devem ficar 5°C acima da média nessas localidades nesta segunda-feira (28). (Agência Brasil) Acima de 40ºC. artigo.texto: $1 million investment to make Middle Tennessee facility 1st in world to mass produce ‘breakthrough battery technology’ The goal of the investment is to “advance the push for a zero-emissions, all-electric future,” a press release says. What This Story Is About - A $1 million investment is set to make Middle Tennessee home to the first facility in the world to mass-produce an advanced type of battery cell. Why It Matters - Ultium Cells say the technology boasts 33% greater energy density than than lithium iron phosphate (LFP), the current leading affordable battery chemistry. What Happens Next - Ultium Cells LLC, a joint venture of LG Energy Solution and General Motors (GM), are investing that money into its Spring Hill battery cell manufacturing operations. For Context - The development marks the second major investment by Ultium Cells in Spring Hill, following multi-million dollar investments in 2021 and 2022, the press release notes. Catch Up - General Motors investing $4B in its manufacturing plants in TN, other states - 700 GM employees temporarily laid off in TN SPRING HILL, Tenn. (WSMV) - A $1 million investment is set to make Middle Tennessee home to the first facility in the world to mass-produce “breakthrough battery technology.” Ultium Cells LLC, a joint venture of LG Energy Solution and General Motors (GM), are investing that money into its Spring Hill battery cell manufacturing operations. The goal is to “advance the push for a zero-emissions, all-electric future,” a press release says. The facility will “be the first in the world to produce prismatic lithium manganese-rich (LMR) battery cells in mass production.” Ultium Cells say the technology boasts 33% greater energy density than than lithium iron phosphate (LFP), the current leading affordable battery chemistry. “High-nickel batteries will continue to give customers the highest range in our portfolio, while adding LMR positions us to leapfrog today’s more affordable chemistries and deliver lower costs with better performance,” said Kurt Kelty, vice president of battery and sustainability of GM. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and Deputy Governor and Department of Economic and Community Development Commissioner Stuart McWhorter announced the plans Tuesday. The development marks the second major investment by Ultium Cells in Spring Hill, following multi-million dollar investments in 2021 and 2022, the press release notes. That puts the total investment into the Spring Hill site at $3.5 billion. “When GM and LG Energy Solution announced their joint venture in 2021, we knew it would create new opportunities for more than 1,000 Tennessee families. I’m grateful for Ultium Cells’ continued investment in our state and the confidence they’ve placed in Tennessee’s highly skilled workforce and look forward to building on our partnership in the years ahead,” Lee said. Sen. Joey Hensley (R-Hohenwald) celebrated the investment as an opportunity to support local communities. “Ultium Cells’ $1 billion expansion is a tremendous investment in Spring Hill and a vote of confidence in the skilled Tennesseans who work there,” Hensley said. “Producing this new battery technology here will strengthen our community’s role in automotive manufacturing and help drive Tennessee’s economy forward.” Copyright 2026 WSMV. artigo.texto: Leilão de Transmissão de 2027 marca estreia do armazenamento por baterias na rede elétrica brasileira Crédito: Divulgação Sistema BESS de 100 MW / 200 MWh previsto para o Acre será o primeiro contratado em um leilão de transmissão do Sistema Interligado Nacional e inaugura novo modelo para reforçar a confiabilidade da rede A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) recomendou a adoção de uma solução inédita para aumentar a confiabilidade do fornecimento de energia elétrica em Cruzeiro do Sul e Feijó, no Acre. O estudo técnico propõe a implantação de um sistema de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS) de 100 MW / 200 MWh, equipado com tecnologia grid-forming, aliado à expansão da infraestrutura de transmissão em 230 kV. A contratação do projeto está prevista no Lote 5 do Leilão de Transmissão nº 01/2027, marcado para 30 de abril de 2027, e representa um marco para o setor elétrico nacional. Será o primeiro sistema de armazenamento por baterias contratado por meio de um leilão de transmissão do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), ampliando o papel da tecnologia no planejamento da infraestrutura elétrica brasileira. Além de armazenar energia, o empreendimento utilizará conversores grid-forming, tecnologia capaz de atuar como formadora de rede e contribuir diretamente para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico. Diferentemente dos inversores convencionais, que dependem de uma rede previamente estabilizada para operar, os equipamentos grid-forming conseguem estabelecer referências de tensão e frequência, oferecendo resposta praticamente instantânea em situações de contingência. Na prática, isso permitirá que o sistema combine a energia armazenada nas baterias com serviços de estabilização da rede, resposta rápida a falhas e suporte à operação do sistema elétrico, aumentando a confiabilidade do fornecimento em uma região que ainda apresenta limitações estruturais. O projeto prevê a instalação do BESS na Subestação Cruzeiro do Sul, conectado ao setor de 69 kV, com capacidade para operar durante duas horas em potência máxima. O contrato terá duração de 18 anos, prazo compatível com a vida útil das baterias, e a implantação deverá ocorrer em até 36 meses após sua assinatura. A adoção da tecnologia responde às características do sistema elétrico da região. Embora Cruzeiro do Sul e Feijó tenham sido recentemente integrados ao Sistema Interligado Nacional, o subsistema ainda opera sob critério N, sem redundância suficiente para suportar determinadas contingências na infraestrutura de transmissão. Segundo a EPE, para o horizonte conjuntural, o BESS apresentou a melhor relação técnico-econômica para ampliar a confiabilidade do atendimento. Paralelamente, o planejamento de longo prazo prevê reforços estruturais da transmissão por meio da construção de novos circuitos em 230 kV entre Tucumã, Feijó e Cruzeiro do Sul. O Lote 4 do mesmo leilão contempla uma nova linha de transmissão entre Tucumã e Feijó, com aproximadamente 376 quilômetros, além da implantação do segundo circuito entre Feijó e Cruzeiro do Sul, com cerca de 255 quilômetros. Parte da expansão utilizará estruturas de circuito duplo já existentes, reduzindo impactos ambientais e riscos de implantação. A combinação entre o sistema de armazenamento e as novas linhas de transmissão evidencia uma mudança importante no planejamento da infraestrutura elétrica brasileira. Em vez de substituir a expansão da rede, o BESS passa a atuar como uma solução complementar, aumentando a flexibilidade operacional e a capacidade de resposta diante de falhas ou oscilações no sistema. Para Matheus Teixeira, COO da VOLTXS Energia, a iniciativa demonstra uma mudança importante na forma como o armazenamento por baterias passa a ser visto pelo setor elétrico. "O sistema de armazenamento em baterias está deixando de ser visto apenas como uma ferramenta de gestão energética para o consumidor e passa a integrar também soluções voltadas à confiabilidade da infraestrutura de transmissão do Brasil. Esse movimento demonstra como a tecnologia pode assumir diferentes funções e ganhar relevância na transformação do setor elétrico nos próximos anos." Na avaliação do executivo, o projeto também pode abrir caminho para uma nova geração de investimentos em armazenamento no país. "A decisão de incorporar um sistema BESS ao planejamento da transmissão sinaliza um amadurecimento importante do setor elétrico brasileiro. O armazenamento deixa de ser tratado apenas como uma tecnologia complementar e passa a ocupar espaço em projetos estratégicos de infraestrutura. Esse movimento tende a acelerar novos investimentos e ampliar as aplicações dessa tecnologia, contribuindo para uma rede mais resiliente, flexível e preparada para a expansão das fontes renováveis.", finaliza Matheus Teixeira. Sobre a Voltxs A Voltxs é uma empresa brasileira especializada em soluções para gestão inteligente de energia, digitalização de ativos elétricos e infraestrutura energética. A companhia desenvolve tecnologias voltadas ao monitoramento em tempo real, eficiência energética, automação e integração de sistemas, apoiando empresas na construção de operações mais resilientes, sustentáveis e preparadas para os desafios da transição energética. artigo.texto: Trump diz que empresas farão com que comunidades fiquem "felizes" com data centers Por Courtney Rozen e Steve Holland e Alexandra Alper WASHINGTON, 29 Set (Reuters) - O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta terça-feira que as empresas de tecnologia trabalharão para que as comunidades fiquem “satisfeitas” com a construção de centrais de processamento de dados, em um momento em que o setor enfrenta crescente oposição da população à expansão dessas instalações. Trump fez o comentário após se reunir com executivos do setor de tecnologia na Casa Branca. Os data centers são um componente central do boom da inteligência artificial. A expansão dessa infraestrutura tem gerado oposição em comunidades em todo o país devido a preocupações com a demanda por eletricidade, custos de serviços públicos e outros impactos locais, levando as empresas a oferecerem incentivos com o objetivo de amenizar essas preocupações. Os data centers “vão fazer coisas pela comunidade que serão realmente benéficas financeiramente”, disse ele a jornalistas. Trump praticamente evitou falar sobre a segurança das ferramentas de IA em sua declaração após a reunião, limitando-se a dizer que é “muito importante” que as empresas de IA regulamentem os riscos de sua própria tecnologia. A pressão sobre o governo Trump para lidar com os riscos representados pela IA está aumentando, depois que OpenAI e Anthropic relataram que seus agentes de IA invadiram sistemas de clientes. Os ataques levaram pesquisadores a alertarem que alguns desenvolvedores de IA acreditam que a tecnologia poderá matar seres humanos dentro de uma década, alimentando pedidos de ação tanto de parlamentares democratas quanto republicanos. Entre os executivos presentes na reunião de terça-feira na Casa Branca estavam Dario Amodei, da Anthropic; Mark Zuckerberg, da Meta; Sundar Pichai, do Google; Jensen Huang, da Nvidia; e Alex Karp, da Palantir. Pelo governo Trump, participaram o assessor de tecnologia, Michael Kratsios, e o secretário de Comércio, Howard Lutnick, assim como o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados dos EUA, Mike Johnson. Trump se reuniu com os executivos no mesmo dia em que seus assessores anunciaram uma nova ferramenta de IA que, segundo eles, facilitará o uso de serviços governamentais pelo público. Executivos do Vale do Silício participaram do evento de lançamento na manhã de terça-feira, incluindo Dina Powell McCormick, da Meta, e Shaun Maguire, sócio da Sequoia. O cofundador do Airbnb, Joe Gebbia, liderou o desenvolvimento da nova ferramenta. As empresas do Vale do Silício Google, SpaceX, Meta e 8VC foram listadas no programa do evento de lançamento como patrocinadoras. Trump, no evento de lançamento, disse que não quer trabalhar com o presidente chinês, Xi Jinping, na regulamentação da tecnologia de IA, acrescentando que isso tornará mais difícil para as empresas norte-americanas desenvolverem produtos de IA melhores do que os de suas contrapartes chinesas. Trump também afirmou ter discutido IA com Xi quando este visitou os EUA na semana passada, acrescentando que os EUA já trabalham com o governo de Xi “de muitas maneiras”. “Estamos na liderança agora, à frente da China e de todos os outros, e quero que continue assim”, disse Trump no evento. Os esforços legislativos bipartidários no Senado, centrados na regulamentação da IA, estão paralisados. O senador Ted Cruz, um dos republicanos envolvidos nas discussões, disse na terça-feira que espera “avançar com isso” após as eleições intermediárias de novembro. artigo.texto: Listen to this article in summarized format The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has entered its definitive phase in January 2026. CBAM, essentially, puts a carbon cost on imports into the European Union. It requires EU importers to pay for emissions embedded in select carbon-intensive goods (based on carbon emissions during production) they import. The CBAM obligation is linked to the EU carbon price, while any carbon price already effectively paid on those emissions in the country of production can be deducted. Also Read | On Edge: The Great Nicobar project faces a great engineering question The EU importer pays the border carbon charge, but the economic burden can ultimately be passed back to the Indian exporter through lower margins, higher prices, or reduced competitiveness. The United Kingdom is also preparing to introduce its own mechanism in January 2027. For India, this policy creates a new trade calculation. A factory may meet every conventional requirement for exporting a product, but its emissions could still determine how much more that product costs when it reaches a foreign market. New Delhi is, therefore, trying a new route of its own: putting a price on emissions at home and building a domestic carbon market. Also Read | Beating the Heat: India’s data centre dream and the 50°C reality in its path The question is whether India can make carbon pricing work as an industrial policy—so that money associated with carbon emissions is invested in cleaner electricity, steel, technology and infrastructure inside the country instead of being collected at the borders of its trading partners. The border tax mismatch The stakes are high for India. Carbon-intensive industries such as steel, aluminium, cement and fertiliser are an important part of the country’s export economy. India’s merchandise exports touched $441.78 billion in FY26, with metals remaining a major export category. The exposure to the EU’s CBAM, moreover, is concentrated heavily in metals. The EU’s CBAM currently covers six sectors: iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. According to NITI Aayog’s Trade Watch Quarterly report released this month, annual metals exports stood at about $34.8 billion in 2025, with iron, steel and aluminium accounting for roughly 78% of that trade. Steel, in particular, is seeing strong export growth. India exported 6.94 lakh tonnes of finished steel worth ₹5,541.2 crore in August 2026, up 31.3% in volume and 41.5% in value from August 2025. During April-August, finished-steel exports reached 29.86 lakh tonnes worth ₹23,646.6 crore, rising 34.1% in volume and 32% in value. The challenge is compounded by the carbon intensity of India's metals production. Indian metals have notably higher carbon intensity than the global average, mostly because primary steel production relies heavily on coal-based Blast Furnace–Basic Oxygen Furnace routes and coal-fired Direct Reduced Iron processes, rather than cleaner gas-based or Electric Arc Furnace routes, according to NITI Aayog’s Trade Watch Quarterly (April–June [Q1] FY27). The scale of India's exposure to European markets adds another layer. NITI Aayog estimates that the EU accounts for approximately 22% of India's combined steel and aluminium exports. In the iron and steel sector, India’s trade exposure to the EU stands at 39.3%, meaning nearly two-fifths of its steel exports are destined for the European market. A June 2026 working paper by the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER), titled Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM): Impact on India’s Steel Exports to the EU and Carbon Tax Incidence, estimates that India’s steel exports to the EU could fall by 24% under the CBAM, based on simulations using the ICRIER Samriddhi Model, a GTAP-E-based general-equilibrium model. For India, therefore, the task at hand would be to ensure that the growth of its manufacturing exports is not undermined by a new cost imposed on the carbon content of those goods. The country has stepped up preparations for the EU's CBAM, including the creation of a Committee on Export Preparedness for EU CBAM. Indian verifiers—independent, accredited third-party verifying bodies empanelled under the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)—have begun aligning plant auditing protocols with the EU's carbon registry, ahead of the first annual CBAM declarations due by September 2027 for emissions embedded in 2026 exports. At the same time, Britain has agreed to recognise India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), meaning qualifying carbon payments made in India can be taken into account under the UK's CBAM. The recognition reduces the risk of exporters paying twice, but it does not eliminate the problem: the amount of relief depends on the carbon price actually paid in India. That distinction gets to the heart of India's challenge. Ajay Srivastava, founder of Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), warned that India's carbon price is likely to remain much lower than the price faced by exporters in Europe. “The EU carbon price is currently about €75 per tonne of CO₂, compared with roughly $10 in China (which operates a similar domestic compliance Emissions Trading Scheme), and India’s emissions-trading system will take time to become fully operational,” Srivastava said. Even if India's system is recognised overseas, he added that it “will not remove the border charge...Even after implementation, a large price gap is likely to remain, leaving Indian exporters liable for substantial CBAM payments in the EU and UK.” This creates the central tension for India: a domestic carbon price can keep some carbon-related revenue inside the country, but only rapid decarbonisation can ultimately reduce the carbon bill itself. artigo.texto: I recently attended the ribbon-cutting for a factory expansion. For the event, the workers were gathered outside — hundreds of them. For a company west of the Blue Ridge, where the population is overwhelmingly white (this particular county is 92% white), I was struck by the diversity that I saw gathered in the parking lot and an adjacent hillside — lots of Black and Latino workers. Later, while touring the inside of the plant, I saw several Latino women who were installing some sort of electrical gear on the factory’s product. I asked the company for demographics and was told that 53.3% of the workers were non-white, the biggest group of those being Latino — 41.3%. In short, this seemed the kind of workforce that Democrats usually claim to represent. There’s just one catch, though: These workers at the Munters plant in Botetourt County make heating, ventilation and air-conditioning equipment for data centers. Both parties have been racing to express their concern about data centers, although Democrats have gotten there first and tend to be the most vocal. Beth Macy, the Democratic candidate in the 6th District, has been among the first to call for a moratorium on data center construction. There may well be good reasons for this: Data centers are driving up demand for energy and drinking lots of water. However, for better or for worse, they are also driving the economy. ING Global Market Research, a Dutch financial multinational, issued a report this summer that concluded that AI now represents one-third of the U.S. economic growth in 2026. Likewise, an economic forecast issued recently by the University of Virginia’s Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service also highlighted AI’s role in the economy. “The national economy enters the middle of 2026 with growth and slightly stronger momentum than earlier in the year,” the report said. “The stronger outlook reflects increased artificial intelligence-related investment, particularly in information technology, software, and data centers.” “Economic growth” is often a vague phrase and one that doesn’t always translate into benefiting everyone. The beneficiaries of data center growth are popularly (and not incorrectly) assumed to be tech billionaires. However, there are also lots of working-class tradespeople who are seeing unprecedented growth in their fields due to data centers. In political terms, this is called “cross-pressure,” where political coalitions find themselves pulled in opposite directions. We’ve seen this before: When Virginia was roiled by proposed natural gas pipelines (such as the Mountain Valley Pipeline), environmental groups — a key part of the Democratic coalition — opposed the pipelines. However, many labor unions — another key part of the Democratic coalition — backed them. As politicians, especially Democrats, rush to slow down data center growth, I have to wonder whether they will encounter some of the same cross-pressures — and what the economic implications of slowing down data centers will be. More broadly, I wonder how much of the controversy over data centers is, or will be, a class conflict where Democrats find themselves aligned against the blue-collar workers who are benefiting directly from the data center boom. We may not be at that point yet, and we may never get there. However, it’s demonstrably true that the data center boom is driving employment — and wages — in certain fields and in certain places. That employment is not necessarily with data centers themselves (which average about 50 workers per site, according to a state study) but in the data center supply chain, where the jobs show up in the hundreds and hundreds, such as Munters. Tom Perriello, the Democratic candidate in the 5th District, recently criticized Republican incumbent John McGuire for voting for a particular tax deduction that tech companies have been making use of. Perriello’s campaign cited a Politico story that reported: “ The tech world is pouring oceans of money into chips, data centers, power supplies and other components of the artificial intelligence infrastructure. And that’s eligible for generous tax breaks on investments Republicans included in their 2025 tax cuts.” The Democratic criticism of that vote is that tech companies didn’t need this tax break, that they’d be making these investments anyway, so all the Republicans did was vote for a tax break that has reduced revenue and driven up the deficit. That seems a worthy debate to have, but let’s go back to the first sentence: “The tech world is pouring oceans of money into chips, data centers, power supplies and other components of the artificial intelligence infrastructure …” That’s where the job growth is happening. Data centers themselves generally don’t create a lot of jobs — a 2024 study by the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission put the average employment at about 50 jobs for each 250,000-square-foot facility. By contrast, employment at Munters in Botetourt has tripled over the past four years and now stands at 827. Business is so strong that the company just added a new production building. This is part of a larger ripple effect of job growth emanating from data centers. A study by the consulting firm PwC found that data supply chain jobs in the country add up to about 4.5 million, about 4.5 times as many as employed in data centers themselves. That’s almost the same size as the nation’s hospital workforce and more than the number of truck drivers in the country, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the American Trucking Association. In short, that seems like a lot of people. A report this year by the Randstad human resources company found that an “analysis of over 50 million job postings found that, since late 2022 — marking the mainstream introduction of generative AI and large language models (LLMs) — vacancies for HVAC engineers — critical for installing and maintaining data center cooling systems — have increased by 67%. artigo.texto: BYD's Next-Gen Seagull and Seal 07 Take Shape as Solid-State Battery Timeline Slips to 2030 Published on 09/28/2026 at 18:01 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD is pressing ahead on two fronts at once: refreshing the volume models that carry its home-market sales, and laying out a long-range battery roadmap that won't bear fruit for years. The company unveiled design sketches and specifications for the second-generation Seagull on 22 September, while confirming that commercial mass production of solid-state batteries is targeted for around 2030. A bigger, punchier entry-level hatchback Sketch images of the redesigned Seagull — sold in export markets as the Atto 1 and known in Chinese as Da Haiou, or "Great Seagull" — were released by the head of sales for BYD's Ocean series. The compact EV moves to a rear-wheel-drive platform with a multi-link rear suspension and seating for five, according to media reports. Output from the electric motor climbs to 95 kW (127 PS), a substantial step up from the 55 kW (75 PS) unit in the current car. A market launch in China is slated for before the end of 2026. The Seagull's overhaul follows a string of other additions to the line-up. Earlier in September, BYD launched the Sealion 08, a flagship SUV in the Ocean range offered in both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid form. That rapid cadence of new and updated nameplates is central to the manufacturer's effort to defend its position against cutthroat competition at home. Seal 07 grows, gains LiDAR option Alongside the Seagull, BYD published the first official images and specifications for the second generation of its Seal 07 sedan. The car gains noticeable length and wheelbase, and will be available as a plug-in hybrid or as a pure electric version with a motor producing up to 300 kW. Buyers can also specify a roof-mounted LiDAR system for advanced driver-assistance functions. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? Solid-state cells: 2030, and not a Blade replacement On the technology side, BYD is aiming for large-scale commercial output of solid-state batteries around the end of the decade, leaning heavily on sulfide-based solid electrolytes in its development work. Chief scientist Lian Yubo said the new cells are not intended to immediately displace the established Blade battery, which uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry. The two are expected to be deployed in parallel, with solid-state technology reserved for premium models for the time being. That timeline puts BYD alongside rivals such as Toyota, which is also targeting its first vehicles with solid-state packs in 2027 and 2028. Charging build-out and an Australian fleet push Management is simultaneously pushing harder outside China. The company plans to erect 90,000 fast-charging stations by 2028, with 20,000 in place before the end of 2026, another 30,000 during 2027 and a further 40,000 in 2028. In Australia, BYD is deepening its push into commercial sales. Stephen Collins, chief operating officer of BYD Australia, said the fleet share of the country's sales mix has climbed from roughly 8% to 20% within a year, with a medium-term target of the mid-30% range. First-half profit drop weighs on the shares Heavy spending on products and expansion is colliding with a slowdown in earnings momentum. In the first half of 2026, net profit attributable to shareholders fell 20.54% year on year to RMB 12.33 billion. Revenue for the six months to June slipped 7.13% to RMB 344.82 billion. Second-quarter net profit did rise 30% to RMB 8.2 billion, but that fell short of analyst expectations for growth of around 48%. The stock reflects that caution. BYD shares changed hands at EUR 8.70 on Tuesday, down 1.6%, and at EUR 8.76 in a separate reading, a daily decline of 0.9%. Either way, the equity sits 30% below its 52-week high of EUR 12.49. Whether the coming model launches and higher overseas ambitions can durably support growth momentum should become clearer in the next set of quarterly figures.
