artigo.texto: 247 – Conversas extraídas pela Polícia Federal do celular de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-controlador do Banco Master, registram o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), mencionando um “formato de sociedade” durante as tratativas para a compra de um terreno em João Pessoa (PB) que estava em nome da cunhada do parlamentar. O conteúdo das mensagens foi divulgado nesta segunda-feira (28) pelo site Fatos Online e confirmado pela Folha de São Paulo. Os diálogos começam em março de 2024 e também registram contatos sobre um projeto de lei relacionado ao mercado de carbono, o Fundo Garantidor de Créditos (FGC) e a disponibilização de uma aeronave. Motta afirma que não há ilícito nas conversas e rejeita qualquer relação de favorecimento. Motta menciona “formato de sociedade” Uma das conversas ocorreu em 9 de março de 2024, em meio às negociações para a aquisição de uma área onde funcionava uma fábrica de cimento em João Pessoa. Na mensagem enviada a Vorcaro, Motta tratou diretamente da negociação e mencionou um modelo societário que, segundo ele, já havia sido combinado. “Boa noite amigo! Td bem? Desculpa incomodar no sábado, estou aqui reunido com o pessoal para finalizar a negociação de compra da área aqui de JP. Conforme falamos, já temos os documentos assinados passando a empresa para minha cunhada ela iniciou a negociação com a Adriana mas acredito que ela não tá sabendo do formato de sociedade que ficou combinado”, escreveu Motta. Na sequência, o parlamentar pediu orientação ao então banqueiro: “Quando puder me orienta como devemos proceder pq o prazo é curto para saldar com Intercement [empresa que atua na produção de cimento]”. Segundo a Folha, a cunhada de Motta havia contratado naquele período um empréstimo de pelo menos R$ 22 milhões com o Banco Master. O jornal informou anteriormente que o valor teria sido solicitado diretamente pelo parlamentar. Os recursos foram utilizados na operação de compra do terreno da antiga fábrica de cimento. “Confiança e parceria” Quatro dias depois da primeira mensagem, outro diálogo registra Motta tratando do andamento da operação. Após Vorcaro informar que estava em uma reunião com “nosso amigo”, o deputado respondeu: “Certo, meu sogro está até aqui, queria levar ele pq acabamos agora de desenrolar as assinaturas que faltavam para poder prosseguir o pagamento. Se vc achar conveniente, analisa e me avisa”. Em 15 de março, Motta voltou a procurar Vorcaro. O parlamentar disse que estava “passando para agradecer a confiança e a parceria”. “Deu tudo certo a tempo de cumprir o contrato. Depois vamos marcar uma conversa para traçar os próximos passos, acredito que vamos ter êxito no projeto! Forte abraço!”, afirmou. Vorcaro respondeu: “muito feliz de estarmos juntos! Te admiro muito e esse é o início de uma parceria de vida”. Motta então escreveu: “com certeza meu amigo, a admiração é recíproca!”. Empréstimo de pelo menos R$ 22 milhões O crédito concedido pelo Banco Master serviu para financiar a aquisição, em abril de 2024, de um terreno com mais de 400 hectares pertencente a uma fábrica de cimento desativada em João Pessoa. A área deverá ser loteada para receber um novo bairro da capital paraibana. Segundo a reportagem, Bianca Medeiros, irmã da esposa de Motta, adquiriu em março de 2024 todas as cotas da ETC Participações. Uma semana depois, assinou o contrato de empréstimo com o Master, oferecendo as cotas da empresa como garantia. Bianca afirmou ao jornal que o crédito foi usado na compra do terreno. A área tem dimensão próxima de três vezes a do Parque Ibirapuera, em São Paulo. O preço pago pelo terreno foi de R$ 45 milhões, enquanto o valor fiscal registrado nas matrículas era de R$ 101 milhões. O valor fiscal é calculado pelo poder público municipal e serve, entre outras finalidades, como referência para tributação. Projeto de carbono aparece nas conversas Os diálogos também mostram que a interlocução entre Motta e Vorcaro alcançou um assunto em discussão no Congresso Nacional. Em novembro de 2024, os dois conversaram sobre um projeto de lei relacionado ao mercado de carbono. De acordo com a Folha, Motta encaminhou a Vorcaro mensagens que havia recebido com informações sobre o texto aprovado pelo Senado. No dia 19 daquele mês, Vorcaro perguntou: “consegue encontrar mais tarde hoje”. Motta respondeu: “sim. Pegando o texto aqui para te mandar”. Os trechos publicados registram a interlocução sobre a proposta, mas não demonstram, isoladamente, a ocorrência de favorecimento legislativo. Motta menciona estudo sobre o FGC O Fundo Garantidor de Créditos também aparece nas mensagens recuperadas do celular de Vorcaro. Em 23 de março de 2024, Motta pediu ao então controlador do Master que lembrasse sua equipe de preparar um estudo sobre o fundo. “Quando puder lembra de pedir a seu pessoal o estudo daquele assunto do FGC, se vc for a Brasília essa semana podemos voltar a falar para ver onde podemos tentar encaixar esse assunto”, escreveu o parlamentar. O trecho divulgado não detalha qual era especificamente o assunto relacionado ao FGC nem o que Motta quis dizer com a possibilidade de “encaixar” o tema. Aeronave foi colocada à disposição Outro diálogo, de 27 de abril de 2024, indica que Vorcaro colocou uma aeronave à disposição do deputado. Motta perguntou ao banqueiro de onde partiria o avião que faria seu deslocamento de Guarulhos, em São Paulo, para Brasília. “Já vai estar te esperando”, respondeu Vorcaro. Motta nega ilícito e favorecimento Procurado, o presidente da Câmara afirmou, por meio de sua assessoria, que sempre manteve interlocução com diferentes setores durante sua atuação parlamentar. “Enfatizo que não há nenhum ilícito retratado nos diálogos publicados e repudio a tentativa de atribuir conversas descontextualizadas a qualquer relação de interesse espúrio ou de favorecimento por minha parte. Tenho uma vida limpa, assim como é limpa a minha atuação política nesses 15 anos de vida pública”, declarou. Motta também afirmou que o emprésti

artigo.texto: Decade Energy has signed a Supply Framework Agreement with Sungrow for the supply of up to 200 MWh of battery energy storage equipment for projects across France. The agreement is intended to support Decade Energy’s plans to scale the deployment of battery storage across its growing portfolio of projects in the country. It also establishes a framework for the company to move from developing individual battery storage projects toward a more standardized, repeatable delivery model. Under the agreement, core supply terms will be established in advance, allowing Decade Energy to streamline procurement and reduce project-level complexity. The company said this will enable its teams to focus on site-specific engineering, grid connection and construction requirements across individual projects. Baptiste Perlin, VP of Infrastructure at Decade Energy, said the company’s framework with Sungrow is aimed at building the partnerships and systems required to deploy battery storage at greater speed and scale as France’s electrification progresses. Battery energy storage is gaining importance as power systems integrate increasing levels of renewable generation while electricity demand rises across the transport, buildings and industrial sectors. The agreement is expected to strengthen Decade Energy’s supply chain and delivery capabilities as it expands its project pipeline. Weiyi (Eric) Da, ESS Manager at Sungrow Europe, said the agreement combines Decade Energy’s project pipeline with Sungrow’s energy storage technology and local service capabilities to support the delivery of scalable battery storage projects in France. Sungrow has installed more than 1,000 GW of power electronic converters globally and operates more than 520 service outlets worldwide. The framework agreement forms part of Decade Energy’s broader strategy to establish technology partnerships, infrastructure and delivery capabilities for the faster deployment of battery storage projects in France. artigo.texto: Conheça o novo Jornal do Carro Depois de quase 45 anos, o tradicional Jornal do Carro passa por uma de suas principais reformulações. Confira todos os detalhes!. Crédito: Ricardo Takeuchi A iCaur, submarca de SUVs com pegada off-road, chegará ao Brasil no primeiro semestre de 2027. A estreia no mercado nacional será com o lançamento do V27. O Jornal do Carro apurou que o modelo será vendido por aqui em duas versões, cada uma equipada com um tamanho de bateria diferente. Interlocutores da iCaur contaram à reportagem que o V27 terá opção de entrada com bateria de 20 kWh de capacidade e uma configuração topo de linha com 34 kWh. A informação confirma as expectativas levantadas durante a apresentação do SUV no Festival Interlagos de 2026. Pertencente ao Grupo Chery International, a iCaur chega ao mercado brasileiro para disputar o segmento de SUVs eletrificados de alto padrão com vocação fora de estrada — nicho que vem crescendo no País. A marca se junta à operação da Omoda & Jaecoo, presente no Brasil desde o ano passado. Leia também - Omoda Jaecoo terá carro de R$ 100 mil no Brasil e promete 7 lançamentos - Honda Fit Twist: hatch usado tem espaço de SUV e manutenção barata por menos de R$ 50 mil - Leapmotor B10 agora tem versão Reev, híbrido com sensação de elétrico e autonomia de 900 km V27 não é um híbrido convencional Apesar de utilizar um motor a combustão, o V27 não funciona como um híbrido convencional, no qual os motores elétrico e a gasolina tracionam as rodas juntos ou alternadamente. O modelo utiliza a arquitetura REEV (Range Extended Electric Vehicle), ou veículo elétrico de autonomia estendida. Nesse sistema, a tração é feita exclusivamente pelos motores elétricos, enquanto o motor 1.5 TGDI a gasolina de 156 cv atua apenas como gerador de energia para a bateria. Com a confirmação das duas versões e de suas respectivas baterias, é possível projetar como o V27 chegará ao mercado nacional. A versão de entrada combina a bateria de 20,4 kWh ao motor 1.5 turbo e a um único motor elétrico. Nos mercados asiáticos onde já é comercializado, o V27 entrega 252 cv de potência combinada e 30,5 kgfm de torque nessa configuração. A tração é sempre traseira e a autonomia 100% elétrica fica em torno de 95 km (ciclo europeu NEDC). Já a opção mais cara usa bateria de 34,3 kWh e adiciona um segundo motor elétrico ao sistema, alcançando 455 cv de potência e 51,5 kgfm de torque. Nessa variante, a tração é integral e o alcance elétrico sobe para 150 km. Considerando a autonomia total da arquitetura REEV (combustão + elétrico), o V27 declara até 1.100 km nas versões com tração traseira e 1.000 km na opção com tração integral. O tanque de combustível comporta 60 litros. Quanto ao carregamento, o SUV suporta corrente contínua (DC) de até 100 kW (10% a 80% em 17 minutos) e corrente alternada (AC) de 6,6 kW. No mercado indonésio, o modelo estreou no mês passado como e é vendido em três opções: Standard 2WD, Top 2WD e Top 4WD. Ainda não há confirmação se essa nomenclatura ou divisão será repetida no Brasil. Como é o iCaur V27 A marca já exibiu o modelo no Brasil durante o Festival Interlagos de 2026. Com 5,04 metros de comprimento, 1,97 m de largura, 1,89 m de altura e 2,90 m de entre-eixos, o V27 é um SUV robusto com design reto e clássico, remetendo a modelos como Land Rover Defender e utilitários tradicionais. No visual, o “jipão” chinês destaca para-lamas largos, ampla área envidraçada e faróis circulares de LED com controle automático e função de boas-vindas. O conjunto inclui para-choques proeminentes e estepe pendurado na tampa traseira. A unidade mostrada no Festival Interlagos contava com rodas de liga leve de 21 polegadas, teto panorâmico duplo e rack de teto integrado, misturando a estética fora de estrada com acabamento refinado. Por dentro, o V27 mantém o apelo sofisticado. O modelo conta com vidros acústicos para isolamento de ruído e central multimídia de 15,4 polegadas que reúne o sistema de entretenimento, painel digital, navegação GPS e comandos de voz. O painel oferece espelhamento para smartphones e o sistema de som conta com 15 alto-falantes. O acabamento traz materiais suaves ao toque e revestimentos premium. Na versão topo de linha, os bancos dianteiros oferecem ajustes elétricos e ventilação. Por fim, o porta-malas tem capacidade para 715 litros em posição normal e chega a 1.818 litros com os bancos traseiros rebatidos. A tampa traseira possui abertura elétrica por sensor de movimento, e a cabine traz iluminação ambiente customizável e retrovisor interno eletrocrômico sem moldura. Atualização na China Antes mesmo de sua estreia no mercado brasileiro, o iCaur V27 recebeu uma atualização na China. Por lá, o modelo acaba de ganhar uma nova versão com bateria maior e mais autonomia. A nova variante do SUV passa a vir de série com uma bateria de 51,2 kWh de capacidade, cerca de 49,3% maior que a opção atual de 34,3 kWh. Segundo a marca, esse novo dispositivo permite ao carro rodar no modo totalmente elétrico 300 km (ciclo chinês CLTC). Segundo interlocutores consultados durante apuração, ainda não há confirmação da chegada dessa nova variante de bateria maior ao Brasil. Por enquanto, apenas as versões de 20,4 kWh e 34,3 kWh de capacidade serão vendidas por aqui. Outros modelos da iCaur já confirmados Durante apresentação da marca no Festival Interlagos, a iCaur também já confirmou que vai trazer mais dois SUVs em 2027: o V23 e o V25, utilitários que vêm para brigar por espaço no segmento B e C. Todos eles terão um visual mais quadrado, buscando referências em carros do passado. Ou seja, a marca tem a intenção de resgatar esse visual mais clássico, garantiram os executivos. artigo.texto: New data centers in neighboring Maryland to get additional scrutiny under governor’s order Trending Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore is commissioning a state task force to examine new data center proposals and advise local jurisdictions considering the projects. The final decision on data center projects still rests with local governments, Moore said during a news conference Wednesday morning in Annapolis. "Our administration will always stand with the people, and the state will not go around a local community's 'no,'" Moore said. Moore said he also plans to advocate for the repeal of a state tax exemption for data centers, established in 2020, during the next legislative session, which begins in January. Moore's new task force, which will be staffed by seven state agencies, will evaluate proposals based on whether they align with the state's principles, which include protecting electricity ratepayers from cost burdens, providing sufficient environmental protections and having the support of the community, among other factors. "They need to pay their own way, or they need to go away," Moore said. The task force will decide whether projects are "aligned, conditionally aligned or not aligned" with the state's principles. It will have purview over projects that expect to consume at least 25 megawatts of electricity at their peak demand. The governor also established a public online dashboard, which will be updated monthly and list data center proposals and certain specifications about them, including the name of their developer, expected peak energy demand and anticipated water use. "Any company seeking the state's help will have to make commitments that are specific, that are measurable, and importantly, that are public," Moore said. The task force's determination about a data center project does not have the power to unilaterally sink it, but it could have weighty implications for a data center developer. Moore's executive order calls on his agencies to delay their consideration of permits for data center projects that are considered "not aligned" with the state's principles. "Agencies shall defer substantive review until the developer documents all required local land use approvals," reads the executive order. And in order for a data center developer to receive an incentive, grant, loan or financing from the state, it must be considered aligned or conditionally aligned with the state's principles, per Moore's order. Projects that get a favorable decision from the task force also could get other perks, including letters of support, or advocacy from state officials before other bodies such as regional electric grid operator PJM or the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. Going forward, Moore also commanded his agencies not to enter into any non-disclosure agreements with data center developers, operators, or site-selection agents. The order states that any such agreements already signed will be honored, but not renewed or extended. Moore's executive order stops well short of a ban or pause on data centers. But Moore indicated in a recent interview with Punchbowl News, a Washington, D.C.-based political news site, that if a statewide moratorium bill landed on his desk next year, he would sign it. During Wednesday's news conference at the State House, Moore called moratorium decisions a "local jurisdictional issue." "We don't have that authority, but what we do want to do is making sure that we are clear and transparent with our local jurisdictions about what type of elements need to be in place in order to receive state support," Moore said. Moore's order attracted criticism from groups that have called for him to embrace a ban, including Andy Ellis, the Green Party candidate for governor. "We're demanding a ban," Ellis said in a statement Wednesday. "A moratorium is a half-measure, but a task force is nothing. It's lip service, it's cowardly, and it does nothing to stop extractive corporations." Environmental group Food & Water Watch said in a statement it was "glad the governor is pledging to roll back the tax exemptions and wants to regulate this wild industry," but argued that further steps are needed, including a statewide pause. For instance, Moore should also push to repeal a bill he supported in 2024, which exempted diesel back-up generators at data centers from an approval process at the Maryland Public Service Commission, said Jorge Aguilar, southern regional director with Food & Water Watch, in a statement. "Moore's announcement is a step in the right direction," Aguilar wrote. "It's not the full leap to action Maryland needs." The Chesapeake Climate Action Network is also calling for a statewide pause, and for the legislature to "finish the task" with additional conditions on any future data centers. "Given the deepening climate crisis, Gov. Moore and the General Assembly must explicitly require all new data centers run on 100% clean energy. Period. Full stop," said Brittany Baker, the organization's Maryland director, in a statement. Maryland Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey (R-Upper Shore) argued Moore's plan contradicts his previous statements calling for Maryland to lead on technology, AI and data centers. "You cannot recruit an industry with one hand while taxing it and taking away its incentives with the other," Hershey said. "That kind of inconsistent economic policy makes Maryland less competitive and gives businesses another reason to invest somewhere else." Moore argued on Wednesday that the new state guidelines for data center projects will provide clarity for developers hoping to locate projects in Maryland. Moore's data center task force will be spurred to action when a data center developer makes any new request of the state, such as when a developer applies for a state permit. artigo.texto: Seoul, South Korea – A recent analysis by the Korean Ministry of Intellectual Property shows that South Korea ranked first globally in the number of patent applications for energy storage systems (ESS) for power grids over the past 20 years, totaling 6,030 applications. The analysis was based on data submitted to the five leading global intellectual property organizations (IP5) between 2004 and 2023. This period saw a staggering 125-fold increase in the number of innovations, jumping from just 32 applications in 2004 to 4,010 by the end of the study period. A biotechnology that stores generated electricity Energy storage systems are a vital technology that stores generated electricity for use when needed in homes, industrial facilities, and various power grids. By nationality, South Korea topped the list with 41.3% (6,030 cases). China came in second with 5,176 cases (35.4%), followed by the United States with 1,283 cases (8.8%). Japan had 1,220 cases (8.4%), and Germany 250 cases (1.7%). Extensive Korean dominance among the world’s top companies The analysis confirmed the significant superiority of Korean companies in technological innovation. Four Korean companies secured positions among the top 10 global companies in this sector. LG Energy Solutions topped the list with the most applications, registering 4,605 cases. China’s CATL came in second with 2,653 cases, and Samsung SDI ranked third with 242 cases. LS Electric and Samsung Electronics also stood out, securing seventh and eighth place respectively, with 114 and 78 cases. Safety technologies and long-term storage management In terms of precise technical classification, storage device safety and management technology—which focuses on monitoring device condition and preventing heat and fire hazards—accounted for the largest share with 7,705 cases (52.8%). This was followed by long-term storage technology, designed for storing and supplying energy for extended periods, with 5,338 cases (36.5%). Energy conversion and interconnection technology came in third with 10.7%, representing 1,562 cases. The Korean industry is making progress in the areas of safety assurance Commenting on these results, Park Jae-hoon, director of the Communications Inspection Bureau, affirmed that this significant development reflects the progress of the Korean industry in areas such as safety assurance, long-term storage, and efficient network connectivity. He also emphasized the ministry’s commitment to actively supporting Korean companies in rigorously and promptly protecting their intellectual property rights. This aims to enhance their competitiveness in capturing overseas power grid markets.

artigo.texto: India’s shift towards renewable power is expected to create a major requirement for energy storage, with over Rs 4 lakh crore of storage-related investment estimated to be needed by FY32, according to CareEdge Ratings. The report said India’s power sector is moving from a challenge of adding generation capacity to a new challenge of integrating increasing renewable capacity into the electricity system. While non-fossil sources account for around 50 per cent of India’s installed power generation capacity, they contribute around 29 per cent of actual electricity generation. This gap makes energy storage, transmission infrastructure and flexible generation increasingly important as the share of renewable power rises. The report highlighted that India’s energy storage requirement is expected to reach around 411 GWh by FY32, compared with operational storage capacity of around 54 GWh as of June 2026. It stated, “CareEdge Ratings estimates storage-related capex of over Rs 4 lakh crore to meet FY32 requirements”. It also added that the rise in storage requirements reflects the need to integrate renewable generation into the power system and ensure that electricity produced from variable renewable sources can be managed effectively. Battery and pumped storage gain importance The report also pointed to a sharp increase in standalone storage-based tenders. Such tenders rose to around 21 GW in FY26 from 7 GW in FY25, indicating growing activity in the energy storage segment. The agency highlighted the complementary roles of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Pumped Storage Plants (PSPs) in supporting India’s power transition. Both technologies are expected to have an important role as the country adds more renewable generation capacity. Coal power retains a role in the transition At the same time, CareEdge Ratings said coal-based thermal power is entering a multi-year phase of improved credit stability and renewed investment relevance. Well-contracted coal-based thermal power assets are likely to remain important for meeting growing electricity demand while also providing the flexibility required to integrate increasing renewable capacity, the report said. This indicates that the expansion of renewable energy is likely to be accompanied by investments in other parts of the power system rather than replacing conventional generation immediately. Storage and flexible generation would help manage renewable power, while transmission infrastructure would be required to move electricity across the grid. Transmission investment to rise The transmission sector is also expected to see significant investment. The report estimates a capex outlay of around Rs 5.19 lakh crore during FY27-FY31. However, the agency identified several execution-related challenges for the transmission sector, including right-of-way issues, forest clearances and coordination requirements. Despite these challenges, it said the stable cash flow profile and long concession tenures of operational transmission assets continue to support the sector’s credit profile. Published on September 28, 2026

artigo.texto: A Weg (WEGE3) anunciou dois projetos estratégicos de expansão de capacidade que, segundo o Citi, aumentam a exposição da empresa a temas relevantes de infraestrutura de energia, como data centers (centro de dados) e modernização da rede. Na América do Norte, a companhia vai investir US$ 165 milhões para ampliar a produção de geradores. Com a conclusão prevista para 2030, o banco afirma que a capacidade global de geradores da companhia deve subir de 10 para 50 unidades por dia, com operações no México, nos Estados Unidos, no Brasil e na China. No Brasil, a empresa informou que está ampliando o projeto de baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês para Battery Energy Storage System), elevando o investimento planejado para R$ 330 milhões e a capacidade anual para 4GWh. Os analistas Andre Mazini, Kiepher Kennedy e Piero Trotta observam que o movimento ocorre antes do primeiro leilão de BESS no País, esperado para dezembro de 2026, e avaliam que a Weg se posiciona para capturar a necessidade crescente de integrar geração renovável intermitente. O relatório destaca ainda que o anúncio do projeto de BESS ocorreu apenas sete meses após a primeira divulgação da fábrica em Itajaí (SC). O plano original previa capacidade anual de 2 GWh, mas a revisão dobra o volume para 4 GWh e aumenta o investimento total de R$ 280 milhões para R$ 330 milhões. Na leitura do Citi, a aceleração do plano indica confiança no mercado emergente de armazenamento de energia no Brasil e reforça o posicionamento da empresa em um segmento da cadeia de transição energética. A expectativa é que as operações comecem no segundo semestre de 2027. Para o banco, os dois anúncios reforçam a estratégia da companhia de se aproximar de data centers e armazenamento de energia, apontados como vetores estruturais de crescimento para a próxima década. O Citi também diz ver a WEG negociada a 29 vezes lucro. O Citi tem recomendação neutra para a Weg, com preço-alvo de R$ 49, o que representa um potencial de alta de 4,22% ante o fechamento da ação da empresa na última sexta-feira, 25.

artigo.texto: India to add up to 50 GWh battery storage capacity over next 2 yrs: Crisil Battery storage deployment is set to rise sharply from 1 GWh in FY26 as renewable energy expands and storage-linked projects gain a larger share of government auctions Listen to This Article India’s renewable energy sector is set for a significant surge in battery energy storage system (BESS) deployment, with 45-50 gigawatt-hour (GWh) of capacity expected to be commissioned over the current and next financial year, compared with just 1 GWh as of last fiscal, according to Crisil. The ratings agency said the growth is attributed to a strong pipeline of projects under implementation and continued policy support. Capacity additions could have been even higher, but 8-9 GWh of awarded capacity faces a higher risk of delay, moderating the overall deployment outlook. The analysis covers bids awarded between FY24 and FY26 across 100 renewable energy developers. Crisil said the growing need for storage is a consequence of the rising share of renewable energy (RE) to 39 per cent of India’s installed power generation capacity and 15 per cent of energy generated last fiscal. As RE generation is intermittent, it has increased the need for firm and peak-hour power supply. This has elevated the importance of energy storage solutions, particularly BESS. The requirement is especially acute for solar projects because electricity demand peaks in the evening, when solar generation is negligible and BESS can address this mismatch. In line with its objective of integrating a larger share of RE into the national power grid in a sustainable manner, the government has accelerated storage-linked auctions. Projects incorporating BESS accounted for nearly 40 per cent of total auctioned capacity in FY26, up sharply from about 5 per cent in FY24 and FY25. Also Read “As a result, 50-55 GWh of BESS capacity is scheduled for commissioning across FY27 and FY28. Of this, around 40 GWh has been awarded through government-led auctions, where distribution utilities are the offtakers, while the remaining 10-15 GWh is expected to serve commercial and industrial consumers directly or be deployed in the merchant market,” Crisil said. However, 21 per cent of the under-construction BESS capacity, equivalent to about 12 GWh, faces weak return potential, which may lead to some delays in commissioning. The risk has emerged because battery prices have hardened in 2026, while tariffs bid out for these projects were relatively low. “Developers typically procure batteries about a year after securing project bids. Consequently, most projects awarded in 2025 are now exposed to higher battery prices, which have rebounded from the lows witnessed in 2025. As battery prices were consistently coming down till 2025, developers appeared to have bid aggressively on the assumption that prices would continue their downward trajectory,” said Manish Gupta, senior director and deputy chief ratings officer at Crisil. However, in reality, battery prices have increased and, at these prevailing levels, project returns may be insufficient to achieve a typical target internal rate of return of 12-14 per cent, according to Crisil. Consequently, developers may defer implementation in anticipation of more favourable battery pricing. Further, around 8-9 GWh out of this 12 GWh of planned capacity is exposed to an additional challenge: limited implementation experience among project sponsors. While BESS projects typically face relatively lower land acquisition and connectivity-related challenges compared to conventional renewable energy projects, equipment procurement remains a key risk given the sector’s continued dependence on overseas suppliers for batteries and other critical components. artigo.texto: O mercado offshore vive um superaquecimento na cadeia de fornecedores e que pressiona as decisões finais de investimentos (FIDs, na sigla em inglês) de novos sistemas de produção de óleo e gás. Em entrevista ao estúdio eixos, durante a ROG.e 2026, o consultor Carlos Mastrangelo destacou que o momento pede mais criatividade da indústria na busca por alternativas. Confira na íntegra. Segundo ele, hoje as novas plataformas de óleo e gás competem por equipamentos (como turbogeradores) com o boom de desenvolvimento de projetos de data centers e terminais de gás natural liquefeito (GNL). “As empresas que estão entrando para colocar um projeto novo de desenvolvimento, que são projetos de bilhões, estão tendo que enfrentar preços aquecidos, tendo que enfrentar uma competição que é uma competição quase injusta com vários outros ramos da sociedade, principalmente os grandes data centers”. Nesse contexto, uma tendência, aponta Mastrangelo, é a simplificação e a diversificação na forma de executar projetos. “E até mesmo na forma de você encarar um projeto novo. Não fazer exatamente da mesma forma que foi feito no passado, porque a indústria tem que ter mais robustez de buscar uma forma mais simples de executar”, complementou. A agência eixos entrevista as principais lideranças do setor em um estúdio próprio dentro do evento, que é o maior encontro global da indústria de energia. O estúdio eixos na ROG.e 2026 tem patrocínio de OceanPact, Prio, United Airlines e Vibra. Principais assuntos tratados: - Mercado offshore vive superaquecimento, com preços altos e dificuldade de prever o petróleo, pressionando decisões de FID. - Indústria compete por equipamentos com data centers e terminais de GNL, disputando turbogeradores e chips. - Superaquecimento eleva preços e gera falta de equipamentos e pede mais criatividade da indústria na busca por alternativas. - Tendência é de simplificação e padronização, com unidades menores e reaproveitamento de equipamentos. - Caminho crítico migrou do casco para o topside, e indústria estuda reduzir topside para voltar a conversões. - Inteligência artificial pode aumentar atividades a bordo no curto prazo ao criar backlog de tarefas humanas. - Brasil mantém liderança em FPSOs, e conteúdo local depende de perenização e visão de longo prazo. artigo.texto: -- Kuehne+Nagel and CATL, a global leader in new energy technologies, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a strategic collaboration in battery logistics, transport electrification and emissions reduction initiatives. The partnership will initially focus on practical initiatives including the electrification of CATL transport flows in Europe and a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks provided by Qiji, which is set to launch in China this year. Additional areas of collaboration include battery recycling and aftersales support, as well as energy storage and charging solutions for logistics sites. Together, these activities support both companies' Scope 3 emissions reduction ambitions across their logistics and transportation value chains. "As global leaders in our respective industries, CATL and Kuehne+Nagel share a commitment to accelerating the energy transition and achieving a net-zero emissions future," said Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business. "Our elevated partnership will not only contribute to both parties' sustainability targets, but also help advance a greener future." "Battery-electric vehicles are essential to decarbonising road freight," said Søren Schmidt, Executive Vice President Road Logistics at Kuehne+Nagel. "Accelerating the transition requires solutions that are both high-performing and operationally viable. By combining CATL's battery expertise with our logistics knowhow, we can advance initiatives that help reduce our own emissions and those of our customers." The partnership comes at a time of rapidly growing demand for electric vehicles and energy storage solutions. In 2024, demand for EV batteries increased by more than 75%, while battery manufacturing capacity continues to expand through a growing network of gigafactories worldwide. artigo.texto: BROADCAST-QUALITY VIDEO IS AVAILABLE HERE WASHINGTON – On the floor of the United States Senate today, Sen. Mark R. Warner (D-VA) called on Congress to enact meaningful protections for communities facing the rapid expansion of data centers, arguing that legislation must include enforceable requirements on energy costs, water usage, transparency, and community impacts. The Senate is expected to vote tomorrow on the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would direct states to consider adopting a standard under which certain large data centers would pay for the infrastructure costs associated with their development. States would have two years to consider the standard and would not be required to adopt it. Warner argued that the proposal does not go far enough and urged his colleagues to instead consider his Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act, which would establish mandatory transparency requirements for large data centers and condition valuable federal tax benefits on developers meeting standards related to energy, water, environmental performance, and community impacts. In his speech today, Sen. Warner explained that the Ratepayer Protection Act “could be a starting point, but here’s what the bill does. It says that states can consider adopting a federal standard that would hold data centers responsible for rising electricity bills, and then they get two years to consider that. Candidly, they could do that today. We’ve already taken some action in Virginia. And what happens if nobody takes up that offer? Anything happen to these data centers? Does anything happen to those communities? Well, nothing.” Warner continued, “I think we need real legislation on this. We need legislation that actually has some boundaries. This should not be optional. We have seen communities hit by skyrocketing electrical costs. We’ve seen communities where a lot of their water usage has gone up dramatically. We’ve seen these data centers sometimes literally intrude right into neighborhoods.” Warner’s Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act would require greater public disclosure of data centers’ energy and water consumption, backup power systems, environmental impacts, and other information. It would also condition access to accelerated depreciation tax benefits on developers meeting standards related to energy, water, building efficiency, setbacks, and community transparency. “We need to make sure we’ve got accurate information about power usage, water usage, setbacks, backup power, get rid of non-disclosure agreements,” said Sen. Warner. “My legislation would require, not invite, but require that information to come forward and put a penalty in place.” Warner also emphasized that the legislation would use existing federal tax incentives to encourage better behavior from developers rather than simply relying on voluntary commitments. “If you’re going to do all that and not meet those standards, then you shouldn’t get bonus depreciation,” Sen. Warner said. “We have given these hyperscalers, we’ve given these data center builders, enormous tax benefits and bonus depreciation, where they can write off the cost of these very expensive centers, all in the first year. I don’t want to take that away. I’m not raising anybody’s taxes. But I’m saying, you shouldn’t get all the benefits up front if you don’t provide to the community some guarantees about water, power, setbacks, community involvement.” “Unless we put some consequences, I think we are going to completely miss the boat,” he continued. Warner contrasted that approach with the legislation before the Senate, rejecting the argument that Congress should accept a limited measure now and address the remaining issues later. “I know people will say, and my colleagues may say, well, why don’t you take half a loaf?” said Warner. “But the underlying bill isn’t half a loaf. It’s the promise of maybe one slice of that bread two years down from now.” Sen. Warner said, “I hope that I can encourage my colleagues to join me in passing the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act, one that I’ve already socialized with industry, one that would put some mandatory requirements, but also put some real teeth in this very important issue.” Sen. artigo.texto: Geral Rússia destrói data centers ucranianos e mina potencial militar do país, diz analista Ataques visam prejudicar operações cibernéticas e controle de drones na Ucrânia, aponta especialista. Os ataques diários da Rússia às telecomunicações e aos data centers ucranianos visam minar a capacidade da Ucrânia de travar a guerra, controlar drones e montar operações cibernéticas e fraudulentas dentro da Rússia, afirmou à Sputnik Aleksei Leonkov, analista militar russo. Leonkov apontou que a presença de empresas proeminentes ligadas ao Pentágono, como Blackbird e Palantir, nesses locais não é coincidência, porque elas fornecem o poder de computação para coordenar operações de combate, incluindo o processamento de alvos de drones. "Todos esses centros, especialmente os de Kiev, desempenharam um papel duplo. Oficialmente, forneciam telecomunicações, acesso à internet, conectividade. Extraoficialmente, estavam integrados ao circuito de comando e controle de combate", ressaltou. Na avaliação do especialista, essencialmente, todas as informações sobre o comando das forças ucranianas, dados de inteligência e similares fluíam por esses centros. O analista avalia que a Rússia está interrompendo o componente militar em primeiro lugar, e isso começará a impactar o comando e o controle de combate. Isso afetará também os ataques terroristas da Ucrânia realizados com drones. O especialista não acredita que derrubar os centros levará a um colapso completo das capacidades digitais dos militares ucranianos e dos atores cibernéticos, dado o potencial de explorar data centers em lugares como a Estônia e o sul do Cáucaso, que estão fora do alcance da operação militar especial. No entanto, se os centros fossem fechados, ter que importar esse equipamento incrivelmente caro novamente e ligar tudo de volta seria extremamente caro para a Ucrânia, concluiu. artigo.texto: The project plays an important role in supporting voltage and frequency stability at a key point in Cambodia's central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. Its grid-forming capabilities were put through a series of demanding system-restoration scenarios, demonstrating how energy storage can take on a more active role in supporting the power system. Key highlights include: - Large-scale black start from zero voltage: 516 grid-forming PCS units successfully energized the entire plant from zero voltage, establishing stable voltage and frequency across the system. - Restoration of a 240 km transmission network: The system supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations, while maintaining stable operation as the network was progressively restored. - Support for multiple generation sources: The system supported the start-up and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant, before the restored network was operated together with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, energy storage and loads. - Stable operation under challenging grid conditions: During restoration, the system remained stable through five transformer energization events, including a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stability when synchronizing different power sources under a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees, demonstrating its ability to handle challenging conditions during system recovery. - Extended islanded operation: The system operated independently for 3.5 hours, demonstrating that the energy storage system could continue supporting the local network even when separated from the main grid. - Seamless transitions: The project completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, with voltage deviation kept below 2% and transient frequency fluctuation within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. Reducing Technical Risk and Ensuring Timely Delivery Faced with strict test protocols, complex power system scenarios, a compressed construction schedule and rainy‑season working conditions with ambient temperature up to 40°C, Sungrow's cross‑functional team covering pre-sales, on‑site delivery and R&D collaborated closely to deliver high‑quality project outcomes: - 20-day commissioning and testing: The on‑site team worked relentlessly under hot and humid conditions for two consecutive months. The team wrapped up hot commissioning plus three rounds of performance tests within 20 days to guarantee timely grid‑connection. - End‑to‑End Service Solution: Sungrow provides full‑lifecycle and one‑stop services spanning integrated design of storage and monitoring systems, EPC‑related support, equipment design, commissioning and O&M services, enabling the customer to fulfill customized grid‑level requirements with reduced management overhead. artigo.texto: Oregon’s second largest investor-owned electric utility could soon directly assign the costs of new energy projects and infrastructure needed for data centers to data center operators. Pacific Power last week agreed to the deal following months of negotiations with staff of the Oregon Public Utility Commission, the watchdog Citizens’ Utility Board and a handful of environmental and community advocacy groups. The Citizens’ Utility Board in a news release Tuesday called the agreement “the strongest from a for-profit electric utility yet” under Oregon’s new POWER Act, which mandates the state’s monopoly electric utilities create a separate rate class for data centers to ensure other customers aren’t subsidizing the massive energy demand from the server farms. Both Pacific Power and the state’s largest electric utility, Portland General Electric, have raised customer rates 50% since 2020, while most customer classes became more energy efficient, and data centers grew to make up nearly one-quarter of all retail electricity sales statewide. The three-member Public Utility Commission is expected to approve Pacific Power’s deal on Nov. 13, according to Charlotte Shuff, a spokesperson for the Citizens’ Utility Board. Shuff expects the Data Center Coalition, an industry group representing the tech companies, will attempt to appeal. The coalition also appealed a recent PGE proposal to assign costs based not on how much each rate class is driving “peak demand” on the system, which is moments when usage is at its highest point. The state utility commission rejected the appeal, but the citizens’ board expects the coalition will bring the case to the Oregon Court of Appeals. While Pacific Power’s plan assigns costs based on who is driving overall demand, PGE’s plan assigns costs based on how much each customer class is growing and adding to the system’s highest demand periods. After the state’s Public Utility Commission approved PGE’s proposal in July, the company announced rates for data centers would increase by nearly 30% while residential payers would see their bills decline slightly. Pacific Power’s proposal goes further than PGE’s by requiring new data centers that receive electricity from Pacific Power to cover the costs for all new energy generation and storage projects needed to power them, including new power plants and batteries, even if those additions also benefit other customers. Data centers would also pay for any upgrades that are needed to serve them, even if those same upgrades benefit other customer classes. Data centers would be responsible for the cost of all wires and poles built for them to receive distributed power, and all costs related to energy purchased on the market from other companies to power them. If a 100 megawatt transmission line is needed to serve a 50 megawatt data center as well as other residential and industrial customers, the data center would pay for 50% of the transmission line, directly corresponding with its overall demand, according to the citizens’ board. New transmission lines can cost several million dollars per mile to build, and the West is in need of more than 12,000 miles of new transmission according to one recent estimate. Shuff said Pacific Power’s proposal came a long way in recent months and “to their credit they (Pacific Power) worked really hard to get to this. We’re really pleased with where we landed,” she said. The utility serves more than 650,000 Oregon customers, and has seen energy demand grow by 8% between 2013 and 2023 due to data centers, according to a Sightline Institute analysis of U.S. Energy Information Administration data. PGE is the state’s largest electric utility, serving 930,000 customers, and has absorbed the most data center load growth of any private utility in the state during the last decade, according to that analysis. PGE’s system of charging customers based not on overall demand growth but “peak demand growth” is driven in part by the fact that they serve a higher number of small data centers in densely populated counties, according to Bob Jenks, executive director of the Citizens’ Utilities Board. Pacific Power’s data center customers are mostly large facilities in more rural parts of the state. It’s easier to make the case that building a new transmission line in Washington County could benefit all customer classes, who are all using more air conditioning in the summer, he explained, “whereas if you build a data center in Madras, it’s pretty clear whether or not new energy investments and infrastructure costs associated with that are for the data center or not,” Jenks said. Drew Hanson, a PGE spokesperson, reiterated in an email the different challenges the two utilities face. “(Pacific Power’s) service area is larger and more spread out, so a single data center may require infrastructure built specifically for that customer, such as a new transmission line, substation, or power resource. In those cases, costs can be tied more directly to the customer creating the need,” he said. Pacific Power’s plan applies to future data centers, while PGE’s applies to future and existing data centers. Pacific Power will need to address costs associated with its current data center customers and their demands next spring. The company has just a handful of data center customers at present “but dozens want to get onto their system, and some of them are massive,” Jenks said. artigo.texto: INDIANTOWN – The Village Council here voted unanimously Sept. 10 to direct its legal counsel to began drafting a data center moratorium and transparency ordinance, a week and a half after the recently-elected Board majority fired the village manager and replaced its long-term attorney in a quest to fulfill campaign promises of pausing such applications. In addition to replacing Village Manager Taryn Kryzda with former Stuart City Manager Michael Giardino on Sept. 1, the Council replaced Village Attorney Wade Vose with one of his colleagues because he’d acknowledged his reluctance to recommend Indiantown’s participation in a data center moratorium. Two days afterwards, Community Development Director Deana Freeman tendered her 30-day notice, realizing her work on at least three data center applications had put her in the cross-hairs of an angry group of area residents. Giardino told the Hometown News that he tried to persuade Freeman to stay on, but when she declined, he told her to make her resignation immediate. The interim village manager has now assumed Freeman’s responsibilities as well. Interim Village Attorney Janet Smith launched the moratorium discussion during the latest meeting. “What we would like to proffer to the Council is two ordinances,” she said. “They will both have to go through planning and zoning and come before you on two separate readings. You will have public comment at each of those meetings. The first one is the moratorium that we feel will be legally defensible. The second one is the transparency ordinance.” The last ordinance was in response to public outcry that Freeman had allegedly signed a non-disclosure agreement with a potential data-center developer, which caused much of the opposition to believe it was a common practice in Village Hall in order to keep residents in the dark. Smith admitted that she had not personally seen the NDA in question but had since submitted a public records request for a copy. Around the Sept. 3 date of Freeman’s resignation letter, a purported copy of that NDA began circulating on Indiantown Facebook pages. The Hometown News could not authenticate that document, however. “I’ve only been told that there was one NDA,” she continued. “I’m still waiting to see about getting it, so that’s in the process. I did hear that NDAs were frowned upon by the Council and the community.” Smith acknowledged there were other methods utilized by municipalities to protect industry trade secrets that could still be implemented in the future. “I have statutory exceptions that the Council can use for trade secrets,” she explained. “If someone is bringing forward a proposal considered a trade secret and they’re willing to indemnify the Village while they speak to us so we can protect their records, then we have that opportunity. So, an NDA should not be needed.” The interim attorney hopes to begin the ordinance process with the Planning, Zoning & appeals Board on Oct. 1, followed by the Council’s first reading Oct. 8. “On Oct. 22, we would have it back before you for second reading and adoption,” she concluded as she read her draft language to the Board. “This would become an ordinance for the Village.” Mayor Phyllis Waters Brown was the first to comment afterward, repeating her concerns of potentially clashing with developers over Senate Bill 180 and other Florida statutes. “This is not a surprise to anyone – I do not want wish to go to court,”she said. “What is wrong with having an open house for all of them, [so] we learn what we need to learn. Let them show us and teach us what we’re asking for and do a moratorium on the ones that may come after.” “Nothing in what I’m proposing would stop you from doing that,” Smith responded. “There’s nothing against having a workshop or a town hall. I’m not giving you any solution that can’t be stopped. If you want to do anything in-between working with the interim manager, you still have that opportunity.” After Councilman Anthony Dowling made a motion to follow Smith’s recommendations -- which was seconded by Councilwoman Janet Hernandez -- a handful of public speakers addressed the Board. Clemenstville resident Linda Byczko started them off. Like several others who’ve actively pushed for the moratorium, Byczko does not live within the Indiantown Village limits and could not vote in the last election. Instead, those county residents lobbied Village residents to vote to make a change. “I think you need time to write regulations to protect the Village,” she said. “The land development regulations right now are very weak: They do not address what you have going on here.” Rory Greenberg has submitted a data-center application for the former Florida Steel Corp. site and stressed his desire to collaborate with the community. “This industry’s moving very fast,” he said. “I think working together and being self-regulating is the best approach. We’re not looking to move fast; we’re just looking to move in earnest. You guys pick the expert, I’ll hire them.” The face of the local opposition, Eric Miller, followed Greenberg to the podium. Like Byczko, he couldn’t vote, but it was of his own doing. During the incorporation movement, he successfully lobbied to keep his Little Ranch area outside of the Village limits. “Mr. Greenberg is right,” he said. “What you’re proposing and you’re going to vote on here is what could have started last February had there been open dialogue and everything not kept in dark rooms. We wanted a seat at the table to make sure what was coming in here was going to be safe. This gives us a framework to work in. You’ve been given another opportunity to work with us, the people that live in this area.” The attorney for the Silver Fox 606 data center applicant, Ethan Loeb subsequently advised the Council of potential litigation. “Certain organizations from our perspective have private property rights that are vested,” he said. “My client’s one of them. artigo.texto: New data centers are on hold in Warren County for at least the next six months as officials pause development to study environmental and infrastructure concerns. The Warren County Commissioners unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on data center development in county-controlled areas while local and state zoning codes are reviewed. The pause also allows time for a water impact study by the Ohio EPA and the Ohio-Kentucky-Indiana Regional Council of Governments, expected to be released in November. Some Warren County municipalities, such as Clearcreek and Hamilton townships, already have yearlong moratoriums in place, while other jurisdictions, such as Lebanon, Deerfield Twp. and Mason, are home to small data centers that serve individual businesses. At issue are so-called “hyperscale data centers” that cover 10,000 square feet or more. The centers are integral in cloud computing and the development of artificial intelligence. The centers have become a political hot topic, with both governor candidates Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy proposing conditions on their construction in Ohio. Proponents argue the facilities are essential for keeping businesses and the nation competitive in AI and cloud computing. They also highlight potential boosts to local tax revenue, job creation and economic growth. Opponents to the centers cite a massive increase in demand on utilities leading to higher prices for residential customers, added noise, and the destruction of the environment, including the consumption of massive amounts of water for cooling. Commissioner Tom Grossmann, who is on the ballot for re-election on Nov. 3, said he is neither outright opposed or in favor of data centers, but wants more studies done. “I want to control the size and where they would be located,” Grossmann said. He voted in favor of the moratorium with Commissioners Shannon Jones and Dave Young. Grossmann’s opponents, Libertarian Katherine Bowles and Democrat Ian Logan, both said they would support data centers coming to Warren County as long as they have no impact on the county infrastructure or residents. Deputy County Administrator Susan Walther said there have been no requests from developers to put a data center in Warren County’s unincorporated areas.

artigo.texto: HANGZHOU, China, Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HoyUltra 2000M is Hoymiles' newly launched full-scenario commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage solution, developed around a simple idea: do more in the factory so less efforts will be spent on project site. With integrated system components, flexible electrical configurations and liquid cooling, the MWh-level BESS is built to simplify deployment and operate across different project scenarios. - Simplified deployment through high integration HoyUltra 2000M combines the battery, PCS, thermal management, static transfer switch (STS) and fire protection into a single system. Unlike a conventional solution that uses 10 storage containers in parallel, HoyUltra 2000M reduces the system footprint by approximately 15% with less external equipment and on-site wirings. Based on Hoymiles' estimates, the required on-site work can decrease from 46 hours to 10 hours, promising considerable construction cost savings. - Flexible configuration for different applications HoyUltra 2000M offers a capacity of up to 2.61 MWh. Its AC voltage classes cover 400V, 690V and 800V, enabling adaptation to different electrical conditions. The system also supports integration with PV and diesel generators, providing greater flexibility for C&I and multi-energy applications such as PV + wind. - Built-in STS for seamless switching HoyUltra 2000M has a built-in static transfer switch (STS) to support backup switching in less than 20 ms, maintaining continuous power supply for critical loads. - Reliable operation across challenging environments The system uses liquid cooling for both the PCS and battery, with an operating temperature range from -30°C to 55°C. It maintains rated power output at up to 50°C. HoyUltra 2000M is also equipped with cabinet-level fire protection, including smoke and temperature detection, fire suppression, interlocked ventilation and compartment explosion relief. "As C&I energy storage projects become more diverse, clients need solutions that go beyond storage capacity," said Dr. Rex Zhu, General Manager of Hoymiles' Residential and C&I Storage Business Unit in introducing the design philosophy of HoyUltra 2000M. "Electrical conditions, installation requirements, multi-energy integration, backup power and operating environments all need to be considered." With a focus on integration, flexibility, reliability and safety, HoyUltra 2000M will help more C&I customers improve energy efficiency and maximize the value of energy storage across diverse operating scenarios. Learn more about HoyUltra 2000M SOURCE Hoymiles Power Electronics Inc.

artigo.texto: Falta de baterias faz Stellantis paralisar três fábricas na França por até duas semanas As unidades de Sochaux, de Rennes e de Mulhouse são as atingidas pela decisão A Stellantis vai paralisar a produção em três de suas fábricas na França por pelo menos uma semana, anunciou a montadora, movimento provocado em parte pela escassez de baterias para veículos elétricos. A unidade de Sochaux, no leste francês, responsável pela fabricação dos utilitários esportivos (SUVs) Peugeot 3008 e Peugeot 5008, interromperá as atividades entre 23 e 30 de outubro diante da oferta insuficiente de baterias de longo alcance, informou a companhia, em comunicado. A montadora justificou a decisão afirmando que a demanda por essas configurações segue forte, especialmente entre frotas corporativas, e continua superando a atual capacidade de fornecimento, tornando necessário um ajuste temporário no cronograma fabril para alinhar a produção à demanda do mercado e evitar a formação de estoques descalibrados, classificando a medida como pontual. A fábrica de Rennes também suspenderá as operações de 22 a 30 de outubro pelo mesmo motivo, com o gargalo de suprimentos afetando de forma mais acentuada a produção do Citroën C5 Aircross. A montadora adquire as baterias de longo alcance da Automotive Cells Co (ACC), empresa conjunta mantida em sociedade com a Mercedes-Benz e a TotalEnergies. A fabricante de componentes possui uma instalação na França, mas engavetou projetos para erguer complexos na Itália e na Alemanha nos últimos anos em razão do desaquecimento na procura por elétricos, mercado que voltou a se reaquecer neste ano, impulsionado pelo encarecimento dos combustíveis fósseis após a eclosão do conflito no Irã. Embora um porta-voz da Stellantis tenha afirmado que o ritmo de entrega de baterias ainda é insuficiente, a ACC declarou que o volume produzido em suas linhas em setembro deve se equiparar à produção de todo o ano de 2025, sustentando que os processos de industrialização e ganho de escala estão em andamento e atendem aos compromissos contratados com a montadora. Em paralelo, a fábrica de Mulhouse também interromperá os trabalhos entre 15 e 30 de outubro, por razões não relacionadas à cadeia de baterias. As paralisações nos três locais somam-se a uma suspensão de duas semanas programada para o fim de outubro no complexo fabril de Mirafiori, em Turim (Itália), onde os funcionários entrarão em regime de suspensão temporária de contrato. A unidade italiana já havia enfrentado interrupções operacionais em agosto e setembro, atribuídas formalmente à falta de componentes para motores, embora representações sindicais apontem para um ritmo de vendas inferior ao projetado para o modelo urbano Fiat 500 montado no local.

artigo.texto: NIMBY digital e a conta de energia da inteligÃªncia artificial e datacenters A inteligência artificial não mora na nuvem. Ela ocupa terrenos, usa equipamentos, consome eletricidade, rejeita calor e exige redes de transmissão e fibra ótica. É legítimo perguntar quem pagará por essa infraestrutura e o que receberão as comunidades que a abrigarem. Uma pesquisa divulgada em 22 de setembro pelo Fórum Econômico Mundial registra a expectativa de seus economistas-chefes de que os data centers contribuam para o crescimento, mas também tragam pressão sobre serviços públicos, poucos empregos diretos e resistência local. É um alerta importante. Não é, porém, uma lei da física nem uma sentença para todos os países e projetos. A demanda por energia já cresce por razões muito mais amplas. Queremos casas mais confortáveis, ar-condicionado, mobilidade elétrica, serviços digitais, equipamentos de saúde e processos produtivos mais sofisticados. A Agência Internacional de Energia estima que os data centers responderão por cerca de um décimo do crescimento mundial do consumo elétrico até 2030: uma parcela relevante, mas inferior à de motores industriais, climatização de edifícios e veículos elétricos. Culpar exclusivamente a IA por toda alta da conta de luz seria tão impreciso quanto afirmar que ela não terá impacto algum. Também precisamos distinguir duas coisas que frequentemente aparecem misturadas. Uma família pode pagar mais porque passou a consumir mais eletricidade e, portanto, a usufruir mais serviços e conforto. Pode pagar mais, também, porque subiu o preço de cada quilowatt-hora. Nesse segundo caso, importam os custos da geração, das redes, dos encargos e dos tributos, assim como as decisões sobre quem financia novos investimentos. Chamar tudo isso de “efeito dos data centers” encobre escolhas de política energética e distribuição de custos que devem ser transparentes. Uma grande instalação mal localizada pode, sim, disputar capacidade elétrica e água com a população. Se a rede precisar ser ampliada para atendê-la, não é aceitável simplesmente espalhar a conta entre consumidores residenciais sem demonstrar os benefícios correspondentes. Mas o resultado pode ser diferente quando o empreendedor paga pelas instalações que provoca, contrata geração renovável adicional, ajuda a viabilizar armazenamento e flexibilidade e se instala onde há capacidade ou geração hoje restringida. No Nordeste, essa possibilidade merece estudo projeto a projeto: energia renovável sujeita a curtailment não equivale automaticamente a suprimento firme, disponível 24 horas por dia. O mesmo rigor vale para a água. Um circuito fechado dentro do data center não assegura consumo hídrico próximo de zero: é preciso saber como o calor será finalmente rejeitado. Em regiões de escassez, a localização e a tecnologia de refrigeração devem ser escolhidas antes da licença, com divulgação de captação, consumo efetivo, origem da água e desempenho verificado. Reúso, refrigeração seca e sistemas híbridos são alternativas a comparar, não promessas genéricas. Quanto aos empregos, não devemos vender um data center como uma fábrica que manterá milhares de trabalhadores em seu interior. Seu valor potencial está também na construção, nos serviços especializados e, sobretudo, no que uma região consegue desenvolver ao redor da infraestrutura: pesquisa, formação, computação, aplicações de IA e empresas locais. Esse efeito não nasce sozinho. Requer contratos, investimento em pessoas e instituições capazes de ligar a capacidade computacional à economia regional. A resistência das comunidades tampouco pode ser descartada como medo do futuro. Uma pesquisa da Universidade da Pensilvânia encontrou oposição à instalação de data centers próximos entre 61% dos adultos consultados nos Estados Unidos. Esse dado não descreve automaticamente o Brasil, mas ensina algo: as pessoas percebem quando os custos são locais e os benefícios, distantes. Reprimir ou execrar data centers não resolve a demanda por processamento. Afastá-los sem critério pode apenas transferir consumo de energia, impactos e oportunidades para outros lugares. A resposta é estabelecer condições para recebê-los: conexão planejada; custos de expansão atribuídos com justiça; energia progressivamente menos emissora; metas auditáveis de eficiência elétrica e hídrica; participação das comunidades desde o início; e contrapartidas proporcionais, verificáveis e duradouras. Feito assim, um data center pode deixar de parecer um grande consumidor que chegou para disputar recursos e tornar-se parceiro na expansão da infraestrutura local. As comunidades não têm obrigação de acolher qualquer projeto. Têm o direito de exigir que ele melhore, em vez de encarecer, suas condições de vida. Portanto, a questão é menos sobre quem pagará essa conta, e mais sobre quem colherá os benefícios e quem fará regras impedirão que o futuro dos datacenters seja construído às custas dos seus vizinhos. Jean Paul Prates é advogado e economista com mais de 40 anos de experiência internacional, reconhecido como um dos principais especialistas no setor energético e de recursos naturais. Foi Presidente da Petrobras, Senador da República, Secretário de Estado de Energia e fundador do Centro de Estratégias em Recursos Naturais e Energia – CERNE. Atualmente é sócio da Altiva Inteligência Estratégica, Head do LIDE Energia e conselheiro de empresas e associações setoriais.

artigo.texto: Pune: COEP Technological University and JSW Projects have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to set up what they describe as Indiaâs first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale research and development centre at the universityâs Chikhali Research Park, with an investment of over Rs 800 crore across two phases. The centre will focus on developing and testing lithium-ion battery cells, along with sodium-ion and other advanced battery technologies. The initiative is expected to create over 1,000 jobs linked to the battery ecosystem and provide a platform for students and faculty to work with industry engineers on commercially relevant technologies. In the first phase, the centre will undertake battery-cell design, simulation and prototyping. The second phase will establish a cell validation facility with the capability to manufacture cells with capacities ranging from 100 to 600 Ah. COEP vice-chancellor Prof Sunil Bhirud said the partnership could help develop indigenous alternatives to imported batteries while giving students hands-on exposure to advanced battery technology. JSW Group chairman Sajjan Jindal said the partnership would help develop cells suited to Indian climatic conditions and applications. âCells are the new fuel of this century,â he said, and added that India needed to build domestic capabilities to manufacture them. The project aims to bridge the gap between academic research and industry by enabling joint research, technology development, publications and intellectual property creation. The centre is also expected to support applications in electric vehicles , grid storage and clean energy.

artigo.texto: As large-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in India move into the construction and delivery phase, the country’s domestic storage supply chain is expanding beyond project development into equipment manufacturing. Since the beginning of 2026, companies including JSW Energy, GoodEnough Energy and Waaree have brought GWh-scale BESS manufacturing and system integration capacity online, while Reliance and Vikram Solar are advancing larger battery and energy storage manufacturing projects. The shift is gradually changing India’s BESS supply model. Rather than relying heavily on imported complete systems, the market is increasingly moving toward a model in which cells and some key components are imported, while battery packs and system integration are completed locally. JSW Energy’s 5 GWh battery assembly facility in Pune, Maharashtra, is one of the most prominent examples of this transition. According to the company’s FY2025-26 annual report, its 5 GWh Battery Container Assembly Plant has commenced operations in Pune, marking JSW’s expansion from energy storage project investment and operation into equipment manufacturing. More importantly, the capacity is not being used solely to support JSW’s internal storage portfolio. In July 2026, JSW Energy subsidiary JSW Energy PSP Eleven secured an order from Bondada Renewable Energy to supply a 200 MW/400 MWh BESS together with power conversion systems (PCS). The contract was valued at approximately Rs 4.44 billion. The order indicates that JSW is beginning to compete in the third-party BESS equipment market, with its 5 GWh facility evolving from an internal supply-chain asset into a commercial storage manufacturing platform. Local BESS Integration Capacity Ramps Up JSW is not alone. Several GWh-scale BESS manufacturing and assembly facilities have emerged across India. Tata AutoComp Gotion Green Energy Solutions, the joint venture between Tata AutoComp and Gotion, has established 6 GWh of BESS manufacturing capacity and has begun supplying storage systems to Tata Power. GoodEnough Energy commissioned a 7 GWh BESS manufacturing facility in Noida in January 2026, while Waaree Energy Storage Solutions started operations at a 5.15 GWh automated BESS container manufacturing facility in Gujarat in July. Together with JSW’s 5 GWh plant, these four companies alone represent approximately 23.15 GWh/year of publicly disclosed BESS manufacturing and assembly capacity that has already been commissioned or brought into operation. India’s incumbent battery manufacturers are also expanding into lithium-ion battery packs and stationary storage. Amara Raja has commissioned the first 1.5 GWh phase of its battery pack facility in Telangana, with long-term pack capacity planned at 5 GWh to serve both electric vehicles and stationary energy storage. The company is also developing up to 16 GWh of upstream cell manufacturing capacity. Exide currently operates 1.5 GWh of lithium-ion module and pack capacity and, through Exide Energy Solutions, is developing a lithium-ion cell manufacturing complex in Bengaluru with planned capacity of up to 12 GWh. The prospective capacity pipeline is significantly larger. Reliance has said its BESS Gigafactory in Jamnagar has entered advanced commissioning. The facility is designed for 40 GWh/year of capacity and is expected to begin ramping up in the second half of 2026, with the company’s longer-term roadmap targeting 100 GWh. VSL PowerHive, a subsidiary of Vikram Solar, plans to establish 5 GWh of BESS manufacturing capacity in FY2027 and subsequently expand further into battery cell manufacturing. Powertrac, meanwhile, announced in August 2026 that it would develop a 10 GWh energy storage manufacturing facility in Ahmedabad covering both cell-to-pack and pack-to-container production. These figures should not be added together indiscriminately, as they include operating assembly capacity, projects under construction and longer-term cell manufacturing plans. Nevertheless, the overall direction is clear: India’s BESS manufacturing industry is moving from relatively fragmented project-level integration toward GWh-scale industrial production, with battery packs, containers and system integration currently leading the capacity build-out. “Made in India” BESS Does Not Yet Mean a Fully Localised Supply Chain The rapid expansion in pack and container assembly contrasts with much slower localisation of battery cells and some other critical components. Tata Power has said that India currently imports more than 80% of its battery cells. Until meaningful domestic cell capacity becomes available, the more practical supply-chain model remains importing cells and some key components, including certain BMS products, while completing racks, EMS, containers and system integration in India. The gap is consistent with the progress of India’s domestic cell manufacturing industry. The Indian government’s Advanced Chemistry Cell Production Linked Incentive (ACC PLI) scheme targets 50 GWh of advanced cell manufacturing capacity. By the end of 2025, 40 GWh had been awarded, but relatively little large-scale commercial production had materialised. India’s Ministry of Heavy Industries said in February 2026 that Ola had established approximately 1 GWh of ACC manufacturing capacity by the end of 2025 and was in the process of stabilising production, while other major PLI-backed projects remained under development or in the capacity ramp-up phase. Reliance, Amara Raja and Exide are expected to move progressively into construction, commissioning or commercial production windows during 2026-27. Amara Raja, for example, commissioned its Customer Qualification Plant in July 2026 and plans to establish its first 2 GWh of commercial cell manufacturing capacity in 2027.
