artigo.texto: Self-developed batteries are not a crime On September 7, Li Auto announced that for all orders locked for the new generation MEGA starting from 3 p.m. that day, the battery will be switched from CATL's 5C battery to the 5C battery independently developed by Li Auto. The next day, CATL's market value fell by 3.65%, which was interpreted as car companies' move to "de-CATL-ize". This is not the end. The Li Auto i9 launched on September 16 is initially equipped with CATL batteries. However, the head of Li Auto's product line later stated that all new i9 Home orders placed from September 17 will be equipped with the self-developed 5C battery. According to Li Auto, the material system and structure of the self-developed battery cells are developed in-house, with Sunwoda and CALB responsible for production; the battery packs are developed and manufactured by Li Auto. This September, Li Auto announced a plan to increase its capital contribution to Sunwoda by 2.65 billion yuan. Li Auto New MEGA Launch Event This is not an isolated case. This July, Xiaomi launched the "Dragon Armor Battery": Xiaomi is responsible for product definition, leading the design of the battery pack and participating in the cell design and development, and taking charge of full-process quality management. By September, Xiaomi announced its two strategic partners for the Dragon Armor Battery, CALB and Sunwoda. CALB will develop the electrochemical system and materials as required, while Sunwoda provides cell manufacturing capabilities, and the two sides will build exclusive production lines. On September 4, Xiaomi announced the partnership with Sunwoda and CALB In short, Xiaomi puts forward vehicle-level requirements, leads the definition of battery packs, and participates in cell development and supplier quality management, while battery manufacturers provide cell technology, engineering and manufacturing capabilities. Subsequently, the Pengcheng N70 and N90 series equipped with the Dragon Armor Battery went on the market, and CATL was not included in the list of battery suppliers. In addition, XPeng is also preparing to take similar steps. Also during the interview session at the XPeng G9L launch event this September, He Xiaopeng stated that starting this year, "we will develop all batteries by ourselves", but immediately added "not the battery cells". In other words, all three companies name their products "self-developed batteries", but their specific practices vary: XPeng is currently only prepared to develop battery packs, Xiaomi participates in cell development, while Li Auto has pushed R&D all the way to cell materials and structures. However, the timing when the three car manufacturers "jumped out of the CATL supply system" coincided exactly with CATL's "Global Quality Open Month" event, making it impossible for CATL not to make a statement. Ni Jun, Chief Manufacturing Officer of CATL, said at the event: Those who can make cars may not necessarily make batteries, and professionals should do professional work (BYD: ?). This quiet contest is far more than just the simple trend of "de-CATL-ization". The common question raised by all parties is: who should take control of the design and manufacturing of a battery? Foreshadowed Long Ago Li Auto took the earliest action and moved the fastest in the field of self-developed batteries. The first-generation MEGA launched in 2024 was equipped with the Kirin 5C co-developed by Li Auto and CATL. According to the statement at that time, Li Auto put forward vehicle-level requirements, technical standards and verification methods; CATL was responsible for capabilities in materials, cells, structures and manufacturing processes. From underlying materials to battery pack architecture, the two companies jointly worked out solutions and conducted experiments. Li Auto invested more than 200 people, while CATL invested about 800 people. The scale is 5 to 8 times that of ordinary battery projects[1]. The R&D started in 2020 and took three years to achieve mass production. The changes this year go a step further. According to Li Auto, the company starts with anode and cathode materials, electrolytes and formulas, verifies cell prototypes in its own laboratories, and then cooperates with partner battery manufacturers to turn the solutions into mass-producible engineering designs. At the same time, the battery packs, management systems and vehicle control are also led by Li Auto. Sunwoda and CALB are only responsible for the production of cells and battery packs. Compared with the Kirin 5C back then, the R&D division of labor and cooperation mode between upstream and downstream have all changed. However, there is still no answer to the ownership of intellectual property rights for each specific formula and process, as well as the cost difference when the two factories produce products based on the same solution. Since the timing when new car-making forces turned to self-developed batteries coincided with public opinion that CATL's profitability outperformed all car manufacturers, it is inevitable that the market will speculate on car companies' move to "de-CATL-ize". According to previous supply chain surveys, before Li Auto switched to self-developed batteries, CATL's share in Li Auto's product line was close to 70%, and it is expected to drop to around 50% for the whole year of 2026. Considering Li Auto's strong support for its second supplier Sunwoda, CATL's share may further decline in the future. Together with NCM batteries, CATL's share in Xiaomi's system was close to 70%. artigo.texto: Li wants to learn from Xiaomi to "raise fish", while CATL aims to become the "Huawei" in the battery industry. Li Xiang has finally responded to the "de-CATL" narrative. On September 28, Li Xiang released a public statement addressing external disputes over Li Auto's self-developed batteries. From his perspective, regarding automakers' in-house battery R&D as an attempt to replace CATL is essentially a zero-sum game mindset. Li Auto's drive for in-house battery R&D is not aimed at kicking CATL out of the supply chain, and the truth is even the opposite. Li Xiang specifically thanked CATL and called the company Li Auto's "comrade-in-arms". From the 5C ultra-fast charging battery of Li ONE to MEGA, many originally quite aggressive indicators were first defined by Li Auto for product requirements, then jointly developed with CATL, and finally landed with the support of CATL's engineering and manufacturing capabilities. This statement sounds very sincere, but while denying the "de-CATL" trend, Li Xiang also mentioned three things to explain why Li Auto must continue to adhere to in-house battery R&D: to proactively meet unmet user demands, fully integrate batteries into the entire vehicle system, and open up data across the full life cycle of batteries. In other words, Li Auto can continue to purchase batteries from CATL and is willing to continue cooperating with CATL, but one thing is changing: the capabilities that used to be largely controlled by battery manufacturers will be taken back by Li Auto. It aims to master product definition, system integration and data, and leave the manufacturing work to CATL, Sunwoda or more suppliers. This is no longer a simple matter of "whether to get rid of CATL", but an attempt to turn the power battery industry chain into a white box and turn all battery manufacturers into its own "workers". On the other side, CATL is obviously not satisfied with only being a manufacturer that produces batteries for others. One party wants to white-box the supply chain, while the other wants to become a system-level platform in the battery industry. What Li Auto and CATL are really competing for may never be orders for several batteries, but who will define the batteries of next-generation vehicles. Li Xiang starts to "tame" battery manufacturers Li Xiang's goal may not be to fully develop a battery better than CATL's on his own, but to turn the battery from a "black box" in the hands of suppliers into a "white box" that Li Auto can define, disassemble, and replace suppliers for. Once this goal is achieved, Li Auto's control over the battery industry chain will undergo fundamental changes. After all, as long as the power battery is always a "black box" provided by suppliers, what automakers can truly master will be very limited. What material system the battery needs, how the cell should be designed, what level the fast charging should reach, how to balance service life and safety, and even when the next-generation product will be iterated, all these are largely determined by battery manufacturers. For ordinary automakers, this may not be a problem, but for a company like Li Auto that sells hundreds of thousands of vehicles a year and wants to make smart cars a highly integrated product, this means that one of its most important components with the highest cost proportion is not fully under its own control. What Li Xiang wants to do now is to take back this part of the capability. Judging from this public statement, what Li Auto wants to master in the future is user demands, product definition, vehicle system integration and data across the full battery life cycle, while the actual large-scale manufacturing can still be handed over to CATL, or introduced to other battery enterprises. Li Auto does not necessarily need to become a battery manufacturer itself, but hopes to decide why the battery is designed in this way, what indicators it needs to meet, and how the next-generation product will be upgraded. As for who will produce it in the end, it can be left to the supply chain for full competition. This white-box OEM model is actually not new. In the past decade, one of the most mature companies that played this model well in China's technology industry is Xiaomi. From the very beginning, Xiaomi has not tried to bring the entire industrial chain into its own company. Screens can be purchased, cameras can be purchased, storage can be purchased, structural parts can be purchased, and assembly can be handed over to foundries. What is truly in Xiaomi's hands is product definition. The selling price of a hardware device, what materials to use, what hardware to configure, what screen to choose, how to design the system, and what kind of consumers to target, all these must be decided by Xiaomi itself. The remaining links that can be handed over to the supply chain are handed over to the supply chain as much as possible. Even for the same component, Xiaomi will not only bind one supplier, but introduce as many enterprises as possible to compete. The result of this approach is that suppliers are increasingly like callable modules. Whoever has mature technology will be used, whoever has lower price will get more share, and whoever cannot keep up with the requirements of next-generation products can be replaced by new suppliers. As the industrial chain becomes more mature and standardized, Xiaomi's control over the supply chain has become increasingly strong. By 2025, this model has supported a large-scale hardware ecosystem. The best proof is that the gross profit margin of the mobile phone business, which is restricted by many black-box components such as Qualcomm's products, is only 10.9%, while the gross profit margin of IoT and life consumer products that control the white-box supply chain is as high as 23.1%. artigo.texto: With climate change making headlines almost every day due to devastating fires, extended droughts, record-breaking sea temperatures such as those recently recorded in the Mediterranean, and historically low water levels in rivers and lakes that severely restrict the transport of goods, the need for a more sustainable energy supply has never been more evident. As part of a more renewable energy supply, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are emerging as an essential element of modern energy infrastructure. As renewable energy adoption continues to grow worldwide, utilities, companies, and communities increasingly depend on battery storage to balance fluctuations in power generation and maintain grid stability. BESS are transforming the energy landscape, while the regulatory landscape is evolving just as quickly. At the same time, storage systems are becoming larger, more powerful and increasingly energy dense. This expansion is accompanied by growing attention from regulators, insurers and system operators, all of whom are putting greater emphasis on battery safety. Although developments in cell chemistry, battery management systems, and monitoring technologies have considerably enhanced safety, thermal runaway remains a major design challenge. Consequently, industry focus is increasingly shifting from preventing every potential failure scenario to minimizing the impact when a failure does occur. This article examines how changing safety requirements are influencing battery design and why passive protection solutions are playing a progressively important role in today's BESS architectures. Image Credit: harhar38/Shutterstock.com Why Battery Safety Has Moved Center Stage Around the globe, engineers are developing new battery technologies with remarkable results. Battery energy density has reached unprecedented levels, and further technologies and achievements are already in development. However, these experts are focused not only on maximizing energy density but also on making batteries safer. One of the most important battery safety challenges is thermal runaway events. Battery cells are complex, with each cell engineered to deliver high performance. With today's technology, there is always a residual risk of cell failure. The challenge is that, under certain circumstances, a cell can enter thermal runaway and produce heat that can impact neighboring cells and initiate a propagation event. Since these incidents can be serious, thermal runaway has become a major area of attention. However, the industry's focus is changing from asking, "Can thermal runaway events occur?" to "How can thermal runaway be safely contained when it occurs?" Naturally, the ultimate objective is to avoid cell failure in the first place. However, the industry has not yet reached that point. For this reason, modern battery safety approaches increasingly focus on slowing, isolating, and containing thermal events rather than assuming they can always be avoided. Innovative tape solutions can contribute significantly to this process - but that is a topic for later. As batteries become larger and more valuable, the aim is to restrict thermal events to a specific area, postpone propagation, and stop a failure from spreading across the battery module, pack, or system. To develop safer, more dependable battery systems, new regulations are being introduced, which the following section examines. The Regulatory Landscape is Evolving As BESS installations continue to increase in scale and complexity, safety expectations are developing alongside them. Historically, battery safety discussions largely concentrated on cells, modules, and individual battery components. Today, regulators, insurers, and utilities are increasingly assessing the safety performance of complete energy storage systems. According to Dominique Burgeff, who works closely with Battery Energy Storage Systems at Saint-Gobain® Tape Solutions, this transition is particularly apparent in grid-scale installations. Many contemporary BESS are installed as completely integrated 20-foot container solutions that bring together battery cells, battery management systems, power conversion systems, thermal management, and fire protection systems within a single enclosure. Safety regulations have evolved from cell or module safety toward full container safety. If a thermal runaway event starts inside a container, the resulting fire should be contained within that container and should not propagate to the next one. Dominique Burgeff, Battery Energy Storage Systems, Saint-Gobain® Tape Solutions Although regions pursue different regulatory approaches, a common pattern is emerging: authorities are placing greater importance on thermal runaway containment and system-level safety. In the United States, standards such as UL 9540A and NFPA 855 have established some of the most extensive requirements worldwide for container-level fire resilience. For certain projects, authorities, utilities, and insurers may even demand full-scale fire testing to confirm the safety performance of a BESS installation. Europe is following a somewhat different route. The EU Battery Regulation (2023/1542), CE marking requirements, and the increasing application of IEC 62933 standards are placing greater emphasis on compliance, traceability, lifecycle transparency, and system safety. Battery passports and documentation requirements are becoming increasingly important elements of market access. China is also strengthening its safety requirements. The country's GB 38031-2025 standard introduced considerably more stringent thermal runaway requirements. Although the standard was initially developed for electric vehicle batteries, industry specialists increasingly anticipate these principles could also shape future BESS safety requirements. The focus is moving toward designs that prevent fire propagation beyond the affected battery system and rely on advanced thermal barriers, insulation, and venting concepts.

artigo.texto: My weekend with the tech bros began at Pascal’s Rager, a house party in Washington, DC, cohosted by Micah Bock, who works at the Department of Homeland Security, and Madison Campbell, a flame-throwing, rage-baiting tech influencer with more than 62,000 followers on X. The conversations that night were off the record, but I can tell you there were 500 cigarettes, a tray of Zyns, and a guest list filled with Trump officials and bleach-blonde women in Chanel-esque jackets with impossibly short miniskirts. I can also tell you that MAGA-associated folks are using suspiciously Trumpian accents and slurs I swore were dead and gone. Next up, on Saturday night, I went to a pro-data-center party whose flyer had gone viral the prior week after one of the organizers, Pirate Wires writer Jonas Du, posted about it on X. “In light of the bipartisan psychosis over AI data centers,” the Partiful read, “it’s about time that the people who haven’t lost their minds get together and celebrate the glory of American compute.” It was catnip to MAGA-aligned, Andreessen Horowitz–backed edgelords. After all, wasn’t it silly that, all across the country, congressmen and governors who used to welcome data centers in their state are succumbing to the techno-phobic wokes? According to Data Center Watch, $64 billion of data center projects have already been blocked or delayed. And why? Sure, there’s the holy triptych of problems: 5,000-gallon fuel spills, brown sink water, skyrocketing electricity bills. But also, to hear the party organizers tell it, tech companies have failed to make people understand the benefits, like how one county in Virginia has raked in $1.1 billion in tax revenue from data centers alone. Despite mounting protests from residents, it’s now considered the “data center capital of the world.” One organizer, Casey Given, CEO of libertarian nonprofit Young Voices, said that he wanted to party to counter the “crazy apocalyptic” anti-AI folks, and “shift the Overton window in a more techno-optimist direction.” Enter Data After Dark, tech bros’ attempt at making data centers sexy. With the permission of the organizers, I invited Taylor Frazier McCollum, a newly inspired anti-data-center activist from Prince George’s County, Maryland, to be my date. Last year, when she found out that a hyperscale data center was going to be built one mile from her grandparents’ home, she started researching and learned of a community near Memphis that faced significant air pollution after Elon Musk’s xAI (now called SpaceXAI) built natural gas turbines to power its data center nearby. (Vanity Fair has reached out to SpaceXAI for comment.) She started a petition, which reached over 25,000 signatures, to fight data center construction in her own county and has since quit her job as a cosmetologist to spend more time organizing across the country. I meet up with Frazier McCollum at a bar, and she arrives wearing a T-shirt that reads, “If my mouth doesn’t say it, my face will.” When we enter PubKey, also known as the Bitcoin bar cofounded by crypto enthusiast Thomas Pacchia, we quickly realize that everyone is dressed much better than us, the men in crisp suits with baseball caps that say “Let Data Reign” and the women in slinky silk dresses and kitten heels. We walk past a DJ and a large screen playing an endless loop of Tony Stark, Ana de Armas as the platonic ideal of an AI girlfriend in Blade Runner 2049, and stylized shots of blinking servers. On the dance floor, it’s a ratio of six men to one woman. We duck into a side room—a macho “whiskey bar” with leather couches and a large American flag—and strike up a conversation with Neeraja Deshpande, a conservative writer who tells us she’s concerned by what she sees as the prevailing national sentiment that “growth and human flourishing are at odds with each other.” “It’s not just an imaginary thing that’s happening,” Frazier McCollum responds. She cites studies that show Maryland could face rolling blackouts due to data center energy consumption; she’s watched data centers crop up in the counties around her, and she’s afraid that, if she doesn’t fight these projects, her community won’t have air conditioning, her schools won’t have constant electricity. “But I think that’s a zero-sum vision of energy in general,” Deshpande says. In her eyes, many of the concerns raised by anti-data-center activists are either overblown or solvable, and she points to nuclear reactors as a solution that would address energy issues without increasing emissions. “I would oppose nuclear as well,” Frazier McCollum retorts. Her and Deshpande are arguing on different grounds: Frazier McCollum cares about her immediate access to clean water, pollutant-free air, and affordable electricity, while Deshpande speaks in decades, forgiving the follies of today if they pave the way for future abundance. The conversation is respectful, but it’s clear to me that there is a chasm between their points of view that won’t be bridged today. At 10 p.m. it’s time for speeches, which amount to little more than rally cries. One speaker who runs a pro-AI political firm blames the “Chinese” for convincing us that AI is an energy-guzzling, bill-raising monster. Another speaker, Manhattan Institute fellow Daniel Di Martino, derides the “crazy” and “Luddite” arguments against data centers, before reassuring the crowd that “the good guy with a gun beats the bad guy with a gun.” Frazier McCollum raises her eyebrows as if to say, “Would that make me the bad guy with the gun here?” Then a protester, a young man in a suit, bursts onto the stage and yells something about water usage. I can’t hear him because everyone is already talking over the speeches anyway. But once the crowd registers it’s a protester, they join together in a feral chant: “USA! USA! USA!” The next speaker, Adam Thierer from the R Street Institute, says, “We know who doesn’t believe in freedom. It’s the kind of freaks who were just up here.” By this point, F

artigo.texto: A worker monitors lithium battery cells on a production line at the newly commissioned second phase of CORNEX NEW ENERGY's 80-gigawatt hour battery industrial park in Yichang, Central China's Hubei Province, on August 9, 2026. Photo: VCG China unveiled a new five-year plan for its battery industry on Monday, aiming for the initial large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030 as the country accelerates the transition of next-generation battery technology from research to commercialization. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), together with six other government agencies, jointly issued the new development plan for the battery industry, outlining the sector's development priorities over the 15th Five-Year plan (2026-30) period. The plan comes as China continues to expand its role in the global battery supply chain and seeks to strengthen its leadership in the global energy transition, according to Chinese experts. The country already has strong battery manufacturing capacity, but industry experts said that it still needs to improve basic research and core technologies to maintain long-term competitiveness. To promote the high-quality development of the industry, efforts will be made to accelerate technological innovation, industrial transformation and upgrading, improve the industrial system, enhance the capacity of industrial science and technology services, and raise the quality and level of trade and investment cooperation, according to the document. China will seek steady growth in its new battery industry over the next five years, while making major breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials. It also called for significant progress in new battery systems, with all-solid-state batteries moving toward initial large-scale deployment by 2030. New batteries refer to energy storage and conversion devices built on new mechanisms, materials, structures and manufacturing processes. They include lithium batteries, sodium batteries and flow batteries, which analysts said are becoming key parts of China's push to develop new industrial sectors, build a new energy system and strengthen its manufacturing, energy, transportation and digital capabilities. China's battery industry has strong manufacturing capabilities but still needs to strengthen fundamental research, Sun Xiaohong, former secretary-general of the automotive branch of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, told the Global Times on Monday. All-solid-state batteries are one of the plan's key technological priorities. Compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries, which typically use flammable liquid electrolytes, solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes and are considered safer and potentially capable of offering higher energy density, according to Sun. The plan calls for faster breakthroughs in commercialization technologies, with a focus on improving ionic conductivity, cycle stability and cost efficiency. It also stresses the need to advance key materials and processes, including interface contact technology, high ionic conductivity, long life cycles and engineering pressure system design. China's solid-state battery market is projected to grow from $42.5 million in 2025 to $384.8 million by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 44.4 percent, significantly outpacing the global average of 37.5 percent, according to market research platform MarketsandMarkets. Meanwhile, substantial research and development investments by domestic manufacturers such as CATL and BYD are accelerating solid-state battery commercialization and deployment, according media reports. Sun said that solid-state battery technology worldwide is still in the research and testing stage and has not yet entered large-scale commercial use. He noted that the main challenges remain manufacturing consistency and cost reduction. "Small-scale commercialization is already possible, but large-scale adoption still depends on lowering costs further and improving production processes," Sun said, noting that liquid-electrolyte batteries will still have room to coexist in the market because of their maturity and cost advantages. The plan also highlights the importance of advancing the industrialization of solid-state batteries and laying the groundwork for future battery systems, including new alkali-metal-ion batteries, multivalent-ion batteries, metal-air and sulfur batteries, multifunctional composite structural batteries and nuclear batteries. Beyond the solid-state battery deployment target, the plan sets goals for long-life lithium batteries to reach 15,000 charge-discharge cycles and for leading manufacturers to achieve product defect rates at the parts-per-billion level. To meet the targets, China plans to build a supply system centered on lithium-ion batteries, complemented by sodium and flow batteries, while strengthening its ability to commercialize all-solid-state and ultrafast-charging batteries, according to the document. The document also sets priorities for different application scenarios. These include lighter and more flexible batteries for consumer electronics, safer all-weather power batteries for new-energy vehicles, long-life batteries for grid-scale energy storage, and highly durable batteries for low-altitude aircraft, intelligent robots and equipment used in aviation, deep-sea and polar environments. This plan reflects a clear strategic shift in the battery industry from scale expansion to high-quality development, Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the China Passenger Car Association, told the Global Times on Monday. By emphasizing the balance between development and security, it sets a more sustainable direction for the sector, which prioritizes innovation, safety, efficiency, resilience, and green transformation, Cui noted. artigo.texto: Shinsung E&G said on Sept. 28 that it will unveil its new All In One (AIO) data center cooling platform at Data Center World Asia (DCWA) 2026. DCWA is an event held in Singapore that showcases trends and technologies across the data center industry, including cooling, security and cloud infrastructure. Shinsung E&G will display a model of the AIO at its booth. AIO is an integrated server module combining servers and cooling equipment. The system can significantly reduce space requirements and construction time compared with conventional designs. Conventional data centers separately build data halls for servers, mechanical rooms and air-conditioning systems. For a 2.4-megawatt (MW) data center, AIO can reduce data hall floor space by 22% and floor-to-floor height by 20%. Equipment installation time can also be cut by about half. Each module can accommodate up to eight server racks. It supports power consumption ranging from 16 kilowatts (kW) per rack to as much as 140kW for graphics processing unit (GPU) servers. The system can combine In-Row cooling with direct liquid cooling (DLC), providing cooling performance designed for artificial intelligence (AI) server environments where heat generation is rising sharply. In-Row cooling places cooling units between server racks to remove heat, while DLC places cooling plates directly on heat-generating components and circulates liquid coolant to absorb the heat. The company will also install a kiosk at its booth to help visitors explore its products. It will present detailed specifications and deployment cases for key products including fan wall units (FWUs), which maintain consistent temperature and humidity inside data centers, and fan filter units (FFUs), which filter dust at the ceiling and blow clean air downward. "As the AI industry grows, data centers increasingly require precision cooling solutions optimized for high-heat, high-density environments," said Kim Tae-hyung, vice president at Shinsung E&G. "We will expand our data center business using the precision environmental control technologies we have accumulated in semiconductor and display cleanrooms." Shinsung E&G became the first Korean company to locally develop an FFU in 1991. It supplies equipment to Korean semiconductor and display companies including SK hynix and Samsung Display. More recently, the company has applied its precision cleanroom environmental control technology to data centers and is supplying infrastructure solutions for AI data centers.

artigo.texto: General Motors (GM), the largest U.S. automaker, is making extensive use of Korean companies as it prepares to mass-produce next-generation batteries. Its newly operational Battery Cell Development Center (BCDC), an entirely new battery cell production line, uses equipment from Korean battery equipment makers including PNT, Wonik PNE, Mplus and SEC across key processes ranging from electrode production and assembly to inspection. According to industry sources on Sept. 28, GM is conducting trial operations of battery cell production equipment at the BCDC located at its Technical Center in Warren, Michigan. Battery materials have also been introduced into some processes. GM plans to use the BCDC to develop next-generation battery cells, including lithium manganese-rich (LMR) batteries, and validate their production processes. GM already operates the Wallace Battery Cell Innovation Center (BCIC) at the Warren Technical Center. The BCIC is a research and development (R&D) facility that studies new battery materials and cell designs and produces prototypes. Its cell production capacity, however, is limited, making it difficult to identify process issues that may emerge when production is scaled up ahead of mass production. That is also why GM invested separately in the BCDC. While the BCIC can produce only dozens of prototype battery cells a week, the BCDC can produce thousands. The facility is also about 10 times larger than the BCIC. The BCDC has production capacity of 500 megawatt-hours (MWh), about one-hundredth that of a roughly 50-gigawatt-hour (GWh) Ultium Cells plant, GM's joint venture with LG Energy Solution. The BCDC's role is to conduct final validation of newly developed battery cells and production processes before they are deployed at mass-production plants. The BCDC produces prismatic battery cells. GM will initially validate LMR battery cells that it is developing for mass production in 2028. Sodium-ion batteries could also eventually undergo production-process validation at the BCDC. GM has been developing the technology by producing sodium-ion battery prototypes at the BCIC since June. GM adopted Korean battery equipment for key processes while building the BCDC production line. Korean equipment makers began shipping equipment late last year and installed it at the facility this year. PNT participated in the electrode process. The process involves coating battery materials, including cathode and anode materials, onto metal foil to produce the electrodes that form the basis of a cell. PNT had previously supplied equipment to Ultium Cells, establishing a business relationship with GM. The company is also known to have worked with GM on production equipment for key hydrogen fuel-cell components. Wonik PNE and Mplus supplied equipment for the assembly process, where electrodes are processed and assembled into battery cells. SEC supplied inspection equipment used to check the cells' internal condition and detect defects. In particular, Wonik PNE supplied notching and stacking equipment in addition to its core back-end process equipment. Notching cuts electrodes to a specified size, while stacking layers the cut electrodes. GM marks the first customer for which Wonik PNE has won and fulfilled orders for such equipment. Mplus equipment is used in the subsequent stage, where processed electrodes are inserted into prismatic cases and assembled. Mplus, which had focused primarily on equipment for pouch-type batteries, expanded into prismatic batteries and secured the GM supply deal. The BCDC supply track record could give the Korean equipment makers an advantage when GM invests in mass production of next-generation batteries. Because production processes are validated at the BCDC, the performance of the equipment can also be evaluated there. LMR batteries are likely to be the first target. GM is jointly developing LMR batteries with LG Energy Solution and plans to begin mass production at Ultium Cells in 2028. If the LMR battery production process validated at the BCDC is scaled up to the GWh level, additional investment in new equipment is expected to follow. "In the past, GM focused on researching the batteries themselves, primarily at the Wallace center, but with the BCDC it has moved to the stage of directly validating the actual production process," a source familiar with GM's battery business said. "As it gradually scales up production, it will validate both performance and cost competitiveness."

artigo.texto: The US energy storage system (ESS) market is growing faster than previously expected. The market had been widely expected to slow amid reduced tax incentives and supply-chain uncertainty last year. But rapidly rising power demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers and improving battery supply conditions in the US are lifting the market outlook. Wood Mackenzie said in its recently published US Energy Storage Market Monitor that annual ESS installations in the US are expected to rise more than 50% from current levels on a megawatt (MW) basis over the next five years. The consultancy raised its forecast for cumulative installations through 2031 to 207 gigawatts (GW)/715 gigawatt-hours (GWh). A year ago, the market was expected to slow. In a report published in September last year, Wood Mackenzie forecast a four-year correction in the US ESS market beginning in 2026. It projected cumulative installations of 87.8 GW/281.2 GWh by 2029. Utility-scale ESS installations were expected to fall 10% in 2027 from the previous year. In reality, installations have not declined this year. US ESS installations rose 5% in the first half from a year earlier. Full-year installations are also expected to remain at a similar level to last year. The second quarter saw a record in terms of storage capacity. The US installed 5.4 GW/18.9 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in the second quarter. The increase in storage capacity reflects longer ESS durations. The average duration of ESS installations in the US rose to 3.5 hours in the second quarter from 2.8 hours a year earlier. This means more systems are capable of storing more electricity and supplying it for longer periods at the same power output. The key factor behind the stronger market outlook is AI data centers. As data centers expand rapidly, securing sufficient power on time is becoming a bigger challenge. Building new power plants and transmission networks can take considerable time, while ESS can be installed relatively quickly to respond to rising electricity demand. Wood Mackenzie expects the utility-scale ESS market to grow at an average annual rate of 8% over the next five years, driven by data-center power demand. The consultancy expects more than 130 GW/534 GWh of new utility-scale ESS capacity to be installed from 2026 through 2031. Alison Finney, a researcher at Wood Mackenzie, said, “The expansion of data-center construction is strengthening the outlook across every segment of the US ESS market.” She added that utility-scale ESS could quickly provide the power needed by data centers as hyperscalers face difficulties connecting to the power grid. Slower electric-vehicle demand is also benefiting the US ESS market. As demand for EV batteries falls below expectations, excess production capacity is emerging at local battery plants, prompting battery makers to convert existing EV production lines to ESS applications. LG Energy Solution plans to increase its annual North American production capacity for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for ESS to more than 50 GWh by the end of this year. Its cumulative ESS order backlog has surpassed 140 GWh. Samsung SDI plans to use three of the four production lines at StarPlus Energy (SPE), its joint venture plant with Stellantis, to make LFP batteries for ESS. It also plans to expand production sites to include Synergy Cells, which is being converted into a standalone plant, to increase its US production capacity for LFP batteries for ESS. SK On is using its Georgia plant, SK Battery America (SKBA), to produce LFP batteries for ESS. In August, it signed a supply agreement with US-based NeoVolta Power for 9 GWh from 2027 through 2031 and is pursuing an additional 9 GWh of cooperation. With Samsung SDI and SK On following LG Energy Solution in converting EV production lines to ESS applications, all three Korean battery makers are expected to produce LFP batteries for ESS in North America from the fourth quarter of this year. Their combined US production capacity for LFP batteries for ESS is expected to exceed 100 GWh annually from 2028.

artigo.texto: Doral, Ampa and Nadav Balila plan $325 million data center in Alon Tavor The planned 50 MW facility will be located near major electricity infrastructure, but has not yet secured a grid connection. Renewable energy company Doral, the Ampa Group, and Nadav B. Logistics, controlled by entrepreneur Nadav Balila, are expanding their data center operations with plans to develop an additional facility in the Alon Tavor industrial zone in the Jezreel Valley. The facility is planned to have an IT capacity of approximately 50 megawatts, with an estimated construction cost of more than NIS 1 billion ($325M). The project joins a data center that the three partners are developing in the Har-Tuv industrial zone near Beit Shemesh, which is planned to have an IT capacity of approximately 75 megawatts. If both projects are completed, the partners' combined planned computing capacity will reach approximately 125 megawatts. The land earmarked for the Alon Tavor project is located near electricity generation and transmission infrastructure, with the Alon Tavor power station at the center of the surrounding energy infrastructure. According to the companies, this proximity could provide a significant advantage as access to electricity has become one of the main bottlenecks facing the development of data centers in Israel. The Alon Tavor project, however, has not yet secured a connection to the electricity grid. This contrasts with the Har-Tuv project, for which the partners have already received a commitment from the electricity system operator for a connection. The issue comes as the Electricity Authority and Noga, which manages Israel's electricity system, have imposed restrictions in recent months on new requests to connect data centers to the grid. The restrictions reflect surging electricity demand and concerns about additional loads on the transmission system. The Har-Tuv project, which the companies announced last May, is planned to be built on an area of approximately 27 dunams. It has already received a commitment from the system operator for a 96-megavolt-ampere (MVA) connection. Last week, Doral and Ampa published a forecast stating that the Har-Tuv data center is expected to generate annual revenue of approximately $150 million and EBITDA of approximately $100 million in a full year of operation. Doral says its entry into the data center market is part of an effort to expand its business beyond renewable energy generation and storage into the field of electricity consumption. The company is seeking to leverage its experience in developing energy infrastructure to enter the growing market for high-energy computing facilities, where demand is rising alongside the expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud services. Doral CEO Yoni Hantis said, "the company is working to build a significant activity in the field of server farms, while integrating its capabilities in the production, storage and supply of electricity." Ampa CEO Zohar Levy said the Alon Tavor project is a continuation of the company's expansion strategy in the field. According to Aviv Perianti, deputy CEO of Nadav B. Logistics, "the move is intended to exhaust the potential of the company's land through the development of projects in infrastructure areas that benefit from long-term demand."

artigo.texto: The data center debate Weâve been warned in the past two weeks that artificial intelligence (AI) may kill us all in the next five to 10 years. Industry leaders have suggested there are dangerous developments in the works with AI models and how they are finding ways to self-adapt. Itâs a bit scary, and itâs overshadowing the positives that AI can provide for our personal lives and businesses. Data centers are at the core of this AI revolution, and they are mission-critical to our technological future. If you have a computer or cellphone, youâll be reliant on these new multibillion-dollar data centers to help you search, shop, compare and plan your life. These data centers will also drive business growth in many industries. From banking to manufacturing to healthcare and beyond, data centers will power business to provide the products or services in some sort of fashion. Their processing of data may more quickly identify your health emergency; it could streamline your factory production line; or it could spearhead the security to keep you protected from financial fraud or identity theft. For the data industry, specifically the companies that own and rely on these data centers, a word of caution: You have a huge public perception problem. Data centers are wildly unpopular with the general public. Recent polling conducted by Talk Business & Politics, in conjunction with Hendrix College, revealed that public opinion of data centers is âupside down,â as we say. With over 1,100 respondents, the poll asked: Would you strongly favor, somewhat favor, somewhat oppose, or strongly oppose the construction of a data center in your area to support artificial intelligence, or AI, technology in the U.S.? A little over 7% (7.1%) âstrongly favorâ the building of a data center in their community, while another 12% (11.9%) âsomewhat favor.â Conversely, 19% (18.9%) said they âsomewhat opposeâ the building of a data center in their region, while 51.5% said they âstrongly oppose.â About 10% (10.5%) had no opinion. Citizen concerns range from land and water usage, secrecy of rates and transactions, noise pollution, energy demand and potential rate increases for locals just to name a few. The backlash against data centers has risen quickly and is widespread. When you analyze the polling data, the first takeaway is the size of the âstrongly disapproveâ number. More than 51% is a huge negative number. Also, when a respondent answers a question in the âstronglyâ category, changing their opinion is extremely difficult to do. People donât go from âstrongly approve/disapproveâ in the opposite direction without significant persuasion. Other takeaways in the crosstabs show the strong opposition is found in all age groups, across party lines (Republicans are least strongly opposed), among men and women, and regardless of education levels. The one exception was in the breakdown of ethnicity. Asians, who were a very small sample size, were supportive of data centers. So why is the data center debate raging in Arkansas and America? The opposition is organized and loud and has found a variety of issues that unite opponents to speak out. Supporters of data centers are isolated â they tend to be solo companies â and quite frankly, they havenât been proactive enough in describing the advantages they can bring to communities and how they are mitigating concerns being raised by opponents. Data centers arenât going away. Artificial intelligence isnât going to disappear. The industry and the public are going to have to find some ways to coexist and be OK with their relationships. I donât know what those answers are, and Iâm not sure who or what institution should lead on this. For me, for the time being, Iâm calling on people with concerns to continue to raise them but to also be open-minded enough to have your concerns addressed. For the data center industry, I hope to see a more proactive approach to addressing those concerns and providing the information needed to reduce the skepticism. Finally, I call on all stakeholders in this debate to search for common ground. Data and its power have become an integral part of our lives. We have to find a way to make sure it doesnât kill us, kill progress or kill our hopes for a better future.

artigo.texto: NH Investment & Securities Signs Carbon Credit Cooperation Agreement with Trinity Aviation for Domestic and International Markets Cooperation in Supplying CORSIA Credits and Consignment Trading of Domestic Emission Permits Collaborating to Support Airlines Responding to Carbon Regulations NH Investment & Securities and Trinity Aviation signed a carbon market business agreement on the 21st at Trinity Aviation headquarters located in Gangseo-gu, Seoul. After the signing ceremony, Gunhoo Park, Head of Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities (right), and Dongbin Seo, Executive Director of Management Support at Trinity Aviation (left), took a commemorative photo. Photo by NH Investment & Securities View original image NH Investment & Securities announced on September 28 that it had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Trinity Aviation on September 21 for "mutual cooperation concerning the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) and the Emissions Trading Scheme for greenhouse gases." This agreement marks the first case in which a domestic securities firm and an airline company have established a strategic partnership encompassing the supply of CORSIA credits and consignment trading of domestic greenhouse gas emission permits. Trinity Aviation plans to align with the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport’s aviation sector carbon reduction policy and the implementation direction of CORSIA, by linking NH Investment & Securities’ expertise in the carbon market and financial capacity to its own needs for procurement of emission permits. The company emphasized that the significance of this MOU lies in connecting airlines’ acquisition of emission credits and cost management for procurement to the specialized services of a financial institution. Purchasing emission credits requires not only consideration of the necessary quantity and timing, but also a careful review of market prices and trading conditions. Both companies will collaborate to establish stable and efficient procurement plans based on demand information and market analysis. As part of the collaboration, Trinity Aviation will first secure 20,000 tons of CORSIA credits through NH Investment & Securities, and plans to obtain at least 10% of the emissions that need to be offset, in stages, before the Phase 1 settlement deadline in January 2028. The two companies will use this transaction as a starting point for cooperating on CORSIA credit supply, sharing information such as projected mandatory quantity and procurement timing to strengthen the foundation for mid- to long-term procurement. The companies will also cooperate on establishing and operating a consignment trading framework for the domestic Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS). NH Investment & Securities will support Trinity Aviation’s smooth trading of carbon credits through its proprietary consignment trading system for emission permits, and provide specialized information on market analysis and policy trends. As a result, Trinity Aviation will be able to establish a systematic support system that covers both domestic emissions trading and procurement of CORSIA credits. Gunhoo Park, Head of Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities, stated, "This agreement is meaningful as a strategic collaboration model that connects a securities company’s expertise in carbon finance with the real emission credit needs of airlines. We will support airlines’ stable acquisition of emission credits based on the supply of CORSIA credits and consignment trading of domestic credits, and expand customized carbon finance services that help respond to procurement costs and market fluctuations." artigo.texto: Trinity Air and NH Investment & Securities Collaborate on International Aviation Carbon Reduction Scheme First Korean Airline to Retire 20,000 Tons of CORSIA-Eligible Carbon Credits Trinity Air is strengthening its international carbon regulation response capabilities in collaboration with NH Investment & Securities to address the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). On the 21st, Trinity Air announced that it had signed a “Mutual Cooperation Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on International Aviation CORSIA and Emissions Trading Scheme” with NH Investment & Securities at Sonotrinity Commons in Gangseo-gu, Seoul. On the 21st, at Sonotrinity Commons in Gangseo-gu, Seoul, Dongbin Seo, Executive Vice President of Management Support at Trinity Aviation (left), and Gunhoo Park, Head of Client Solutions at NH Investment & Securities (right), are posing for a commemorative photo. Trinity Aviation View original image The two companies plan to continue multifaceted cooperation, including the exchange of information on CORSIA and the domestic greenhouse gas emissions market and policy, the establishment of a joint response system, jointly pursuing carbon credit–related businesses, and other activities aimed at the development of the carbon market. To proactively prepare for its CORSIA offset obligations, Trinity Air has purchased 20,000 tons of CORSIA-eligible carbon credits and became the first Korean airline to sign a contract for the cancellation of those credits. By the end of this year, the company plans to purchase additional eligible credits, thereby securing more than 10% of the volume that must be offset by January 2028 in phases. CORSIA offset obligations are fulfilled by securing the required amount of eligible credits within the stipulated compliance period and then canceling them in the registry. Trinity Air intends to proactively secure and cancel CORSIA-eligible credits before the specific offset obligations are finalized and executed, thereby ensuring a stable regulatory response. artigo.texto: Impulsionada pela expansão do mercado de data centers e infraestrutura crítica pata TI, uma empresa de Joinville, no Norte catarinense, avança com novos projetos e planos de crescimento. Fundada em 2006, a Novalogic anunciou a assinatura de um contrato com uma gigante global de tecnologia e traçou como meta alcançar R$ 1 bilhão em faturamento até 2030. Atualmente, a receita da Novalogic está concentrada principalmente em três grandes pilares: 50% provenientes de obras para data centers, 30% de projetos de infraestrutura crítica (sistemas essenciais de TI) e 20% de obras verticais de alto padrão. Os data centers são estruturas que abrigam servidores, sistemas de armazenamentos de dados e redes. Este mercado tem crescido principalmente por conta das demandas da inteligência artificial, computação em nuvem, digitalização das empresas e necessidade crescente de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Empresa de Joinville mira expansão; veja fotos: Para sustentar o crescimento, a companhia prepara uma transformação operacional e geográfica. O plano prevê a descentralização da estrutura, com presença física mais próxima das obras e dos grandes projetos, inclusive em regiões consideradas remotas ou de difícil acesso. A estratégia inclui ainda investimentos em novas áreas e unidades operacionais no Nordeste, Sudeste, Centro-Oeste e Norte do Brasil. No Nordeste, a empresa já adquiriu uma área de 50 mil metros quadrados para a construção de uma unidade de grande porte: um novo data center no Ceará que deverá atender a alta demanda de operação no norte e nordeste do país. Em São Paulo, o grupo também ampliará sua presença com uma estrutura física em Alphaville, polo empresarial e tecnológico do país. “Crescer nesta velocidade também traz novos desafios. A expansão geográfica, a ampliação da capacidade operacional e o desenvolvimento de ativos próprios de longo prazo aumentam naturalmente a demanda por capital. O desafio é estruturar esse crescimento com disciplina financeira, preservando a solidez construída pelo nosso grupo e criando as condições para capturar oportunidades cada vez maiores e mais importantes”, afirma o CEO, Felippe Prates. Outra estratégia da Novalogic também é se aproximar mais ativamente em Parcerias Público-Privadas. A companhia identifica oportunidades em projetos de infraestrutura no Brasil e em outros países da América Latina.

artigo.texto: A regional gaúcha da Associação Brasileira da Indústria Elétrica e Eletrônica Regional (Abinee-RS) realizou mais uma edição de sua reunião-almoço nesta terça-feira, em Porto Alegre, abordando as oportunidades a partir da instalação de projetos de data center no Rio Grande do Sul, além de empreendimentos ligados à tecnologia, como o cabo submarino Malbec, cuja chegada ocorre no município de Balneário Pinhal, no litoral Norte. Representantes do segmento industrial e do governo do estado, apresentando números do setor, estiveram presentes no evento. O CEO da Parks, Fabio Cierro, comentou a respeito do andamento do projeto de um data center de R$ 500 milhões no Distrito Industrial de Cachoeirinha, na região Metropolitana. Para o diretor regional e vice-presidente da Abinee, Régis Haubert, as oportunidades tecnológicas têm relação com o momento de transformação digital e inteligência artificial, e o RS pode se beneficiar com isto. “Basicamente, temos aqui no estado um fornecimento e uma capacidade de energia muito boas. Também não nos preocupa a questão da formação técnica, porque temos qualificação e formação profissional muito boa, tanto nos cursos de graduação, quanto nos tecnólogos. O que precisamos é, cada vez mais, agregar a produção local de equipamentos, para que possamos atrair a demanda de nosso próprio mercado”, disse Haubert. Questionado a respeito dos desafios climáticos, o diretor da Abinee disse que eventos naturais como o El Niño são cíclicos. “Precisamos nos adequar às condições e mitigar para evitar problemas”, salientou ele. O vice-prefeito de Balneário Pinhal, Jorge Fonseca, comentou brevemente sobre os bastidores que levaram à construção e implantação da estrutura da V.tal, e que fará a comunicação de dados de milhões de usuários dos serviços da Meta, como WhatsApp, Facebook, Threads e Instagram, aumentando a conectividade e confiabilidade da Internet. Este é o primeiro cabo internacional a atingir diretamente o território gaúcho. “Após esta surpresa inicial, acredito que estamos fazendo a lição de casa, que é entender um pouco de processos, se apropriar de situações e fazer com que Balneário Pinhal não seja apenas um local de passagem do cabo. Já visitamos estruturas semelhantes em Montevidéu a convite da Antel (companhia estatal de telecomunicações do Uruguai) e tivemos bons diálogos com o governo do estado. Temos áreas já com licenciamentos ambientais disponíveis e estamos em uma aproximação com a CEEE Equatorial para analisar a qualidade da energia. São fatores muito significativos para nossas pretensões”, salientou Fonseca.

artigo.texto: Last week, community members made it clear to the City Council at a public hearing that they don’t want more data centers in Denton. The next public hearing on a proposed data center moratorium occurs on Oct. 27 — and a possible moratorium could start in early December. In the midst of the public hearings for a pause on data center development, the council will be voting Oct. 13 on whether to amend the Denton Development Code and tighten restrictions to allow more public input on a project by requiring a specific-use permit. If the City Council approves the development code amendments, all data center developers would need to pursue a specific-use permit regardless of whether the zoning allows the new development by right. Those zoning areas include public facilities, heavy industrial and light industrial, both of which are mostly located on the western part of the city and along the highway, Angie Manglaris, the city’s assistant planning director, pointed out last week at a Planning and Zoning Commission meeting. The commission voted unanimously, 5-0, on Wednesday to offer the council recommendations to amend the city’s development code and strengthen data center regulations. “When it comes to specific-use permits, it’s not prohibited but it’s also not permitted by right,” Manglaris told the commissioners, referring to data center development. “… It requires further scrutiny, specifically as it relates to potential adverse impacts.” Earlier this month, Mayor Pro Tem Nick Stevens, who originally pitched the idea for a moratorium, pointed out while these development changes would be helpful, they’re “more helpful in making it perhaps a little bit more difficult so that there’s more scrutiny.” “I don’t know the last time a council ever denied an SUP,” Stevens said. “Now, historically in the past few years, I just don’t recall the last time an SUP had ever been denied.” Stevens stressed that the purpose of a moratorium is to evaluate whether projected infrastructure demand, environmental impacts and financial returns associated with Denton’s two currently approved data centers align with projections. “The purpose of the moratorium was so that we could study infrastructure demand,” Stevens said. “The development code changes are about planning and zoning ... and say nothing about our grid. They say nothing about water supply because that’s a capacity question, not a zoning question.” Several people spoke on Wednesday at the Planning and Zoning Commission meeting, encouraging city officials “to ensure our development codes protect our community from harmful developments and unsustainable practices,” as Denton resident Rachel Weaver said in her opening remarks. Weaver pointed to the rapid growth of generative AI that “has led to a profusion of new proposed data centers in Texas. “Within two years, our state could become home to more data centers than any other state in the nation,” Weaver said. “This has led to a desperate need for regulation awareness of the environmental impacts of data centers and the AI tools they support. Texans of all political stripes are rightly concerned about water use, electricity use, wastewater, air pollution, noise and loss of working lands that could result.” Weaver also offered solutions including: - Third-party independent studies on the impacts on neighboring communities and local insect and bird populations, especially during migration season. - Power and water usage caps, especially during times of extreme weather. - Disclosure of total water consumption that includes indirect via power consumption. - A notification radius for data centers that equal their impact radius. - A ban on data center development within 5 miles of residential structures and zoning. - Requiring decommissioning bonds, so that developers must pay the teardown costs should the facility be abandoned for any reason in the future. “We’ve had a history of radiopharmaceuticals leaving low-level radioactive waste and contaminated equipment for us to clean up,” Weaver said, referring to the former U.S. Radiopharmaceuticals site on Shady Oaks Drive. “Core Scientific has already gone bankrupt once in crypto mining — what assurances do we have that they won’t go bankrupt again?” Core Scientific originally opened a crypto mining facility in Denton in 2021, only to file for bankruptcy in 2022 and emerge from it in January 2024. In 2024, Core Scientific received council approval to shift from crypto mining to AI data computing, which allowed the company to expand its facility and power usage up to 391 megawatts. The expansion is currently under construction and not at full buildout yet, Denton Municipal Electric General Manager Tony Puente told P&Z commissioners Wednesday. The council approved QumulusAI’s modular 20-megawatt data center in January, but the company still hasn’t broken ground, Puente said. “But for all these facilities, the intent is that we’re going to be managing them as a separate load from the rest of what we consider our native load,” Puente said. “We’re managing them as a separate portfolio, really looking at real-time power, day-ahead power. We’re also buying power well in advance, up to three years through various financial transactions.” Puente said they established a large load energy cost adjustment that’s also separate from the native load that is reflective of the power that DME purchases to serve Core Scientific’s load. This includes a “pretty hefty demand charge base rate [that is] considerably more than what we charge the rest of our native loads,” he said. Neither Core Scientific nor QumulusAI was required to produce water or wastewater impact studies because they aren’t required by ordinance, according to a city spokesperson. artigo.texto: From Isaac Anumihe, Abuja As the world seeks to transit towards climate finance and support greenhouse gas emission reductions as well as accelerate transition to a low-carbon economy, Federal Government has approved the carbon market framework objectives. Speaking at the National Stakeholder Review and Validation Workshop on the draft host country approval criteria for Nigeria’s carbon market operations, in Abuja, Vice Chancellor, University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN), Professor Simon Uchenna Ortuanya, said that the approval represented an important step towards establishing a structured system for carbon market operations in the country. Ortuanya, who was represented by the Director of Resource and Environmental Policy Research Centre, UNN, (REPRC-EfD), Dr Nnaemeka Chukwuone, stated that it’s against this background that the next official task is to ensure that the framework is supported by clear, practical and transparent host country approval criteria. “These criteria will provide guidance on the eligibility, screening and assessment of carbon market projects. They will also clarify institutional responsibilities, approval procedures, measurement, reporting and verification requirements, environmental and social safeguards; alignment with Nigeria’s Nationally -Determined Contribution (NNDC) registry and transparency arrangements, and carbon accounting” he said The criteria, the VC explained, should be sufficiently robust to protect Nigeria’s interests while remaining practical, predictable and responsive to the realities of implementation. “I am glad that the development of the proposed host country approval criteria was guided by sound research” he said. Before she declared the workshop open, the Director General, National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Dr Omotenioye Majekodunmi, said that having approved the carbon market framework, the task before stakeholders is therefore clear — to establish post-country approval criteria that protect Nigeria’s national interests while providing the certainty that credible investors and project developers need. According to her, at the heart of the process is a simple principle that Nigeria must participate in carbon markets on terms that are credible, transparent, equitable and beneficial to the people. “Carbon projects must deliver genuine mitigation outcomes. They must contribute to sustainable development, respect host communities, and promote social inclusion and align with national climate and development priorities” she said. In his remarks, PEP’s Scientific Adviser, Professor Adeola Adenikinju, maintained that the global carbon market presents important opportunities for countries seeking to mobilise climate finance, support greenhouse gas emission reduction and removal, and accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy. For Nigeria, he noted, these opportunities are particularly significant as it has become imperative for Nigeria to pursue economic growth, industrial development, and energy access and poverty reduction while responding to the challenges of climate change. In his opinion, a well-governed carbon market can help mobilise the resources required to support poverty reduction and grow economy.ENDS

artigo.texto: 2026 Fall Homeland | Data centers 101 Sally Scholle Follow The news about rampant data center development in Virginia has made its way across the country, penetrating areas where people never thought such structures would be introduced. Those who learn about what’s happening in those states often adopt one of two views: It won’t happen where I live, or I want to make sure it doesn’t happen where I live. Data center development is exploding in Virginia for several reasons: high quality fiber connectivity, proximity to Washington, D.C., available land and reliable, affordable electricity. These factors provide developers with nearly everything necessary for profitable data centers. At first, those living in western states weren’t too concerned with data center development in the east. However, now that data centers are either under construction or proposed in states including Wyoming, Colorado and Nebraska, new concerns are surfacing. Last year’s announcement regarding construction of a large data center near Cheyenne gained heightened concern with the discovery of an unusual bacteria strain in the wastewater that contaminated the sewer system. Although the bacterium occurs naturally in soil, it poses a threat to immunocompromised individuals. Colorado has numerous smaller-scale data centers, most of which are in the Denver area. As is the case in other states, local government entities are responding to public protest by limiting new construction and passing moratoriums. Nebraska is home to several data centers with more on the way. While Governor Pillen supports data center development, he recently created a task force to set guidelines and signed LB1261, which requires entities to create their own electricity. Most early data center developers kept projects quiet, perhaps because they anticipated public outrage and unified attempts to squash projects. Now that the proverbial feline has exited the bag, there’s widespread interest among rural citizens to make sure data centers don’t become a part of their landscape. The advent and rapid improvement in artificial intelligence (AI) is one a primary reason for data center proliferation. These information hubs have become a necessary evil for a world transfixed with services such as ChatGPT3, launched in November 2022. Insurance, medical facilities, bank fraud protection, rideshare services and even doomscrolling rely on AI, which in turn requires data centers. According to Cleanview (http://www.cleanview.co/data-centers/us), as of August 20206, there were 1,287 data centers currently operating in the U.S. That number might seem high, but there are already more planned. In a recent webinar on data centers, Matt Svetz, Penn State Extension, explained some of the reasons for data center expansion, especially in rural areas. It’s primarily because some data centers don’t require proximity to major population centers because they aren’t sensitive to latency (delays in transmission) in the same way as traditional data centers. “The main thing is access to electrical grid infrastructure,” Svetz said. “This is generally high-voltage transmission lines. They also want space because of the size of the facilities.” Data center developers want access to large land parcels for ease of design and construction. Depending on existing infrastructure, new structures may require a dedicated substation. “They’re generally looking for relatively flat large tracts of land,” Svetz said, “so they can potentially expand operations. They also want less disaster-prone areas. A lot of developers are looking for onsite generation solutions to get around delays in the grid. Data center developers are looking for quicker timelines than grid operators can provide for interconnecting them.” One of the biggest issues in early data center development has been non-disclosure agreements (NDA). These legal contracts are signed by developers and local officials when preliminary deals are made to prevent the public from learning details regarding proposed data centers. From the developer’s perspective, an NDA can prevent land prices from increasing and deter competitors from attempting to purchase land. However, for many communities, learning about data center plans after the fact quickly results in concerns about land, water, noise and electricity; all of which yield strong local opposition. This leads to public distrust, along with highly vocal and even stronger opposition. Michael Helbling, staff attorney, Penn State Center for Energy Law and Policy, explains that for most communities, ordinance provisions are the best way to manage data center development. Such ordinances can address topics such as data center siting, conditional use and special exceptions, land or lot size restrictions, setbacks, building height restrictions and requirements that developers submit plans. Many states’ laws prohibit exclusionary zoning, which means all lawful activities must be allowed – including data centers. However, location and manner of operation can be restricted. When citizens begin to challenge data center development as a unified body, they often lack guidelines. Community members interested in monitoring local data center development should, at the very least, become familiar with state and local permits required for development. Even if the data center is not in your immediate community, it’s worth attending meetings in neighboring communities to gain an understanding of what has been proposed, what local officials have acted on and what can still be done. In many cases, the answer to the last point is ‘a lot.’ “We’re seeing states take action on permitting (data centers),” Helbling said. “How will they be permitted, what kinds of tax breaks and incentives are they getting, and how can they be located? Will municipalities maintain control over siting, or will the state have some centralized ability to determine how they’re located?” Helbling often sees broadly defined goals, but goa

artigo.texto: UK engineers develop dense-fluid energy storage system suitable for low-elevation sites When engineers at RheEnergise popped champagne in January, they were celebrating a milestone most people have never heard of: 500 kilowatts of peak power from a pumped-storage hydroelectricity system. That technology has quietly underpinned the world’s power grids for over a century, accounting for more than 90 percent of global long-duration energy storage. But this version is different in one fundamental way. It contains no water. The fluid needed to be viscous enough to stay put during an accidental spill, yet flow as easily as water through pipes and turbines under normal conditions. The world’s biggest battery — and its biggest limitation Pumped-storage hydroelectricity runs on a beautifully simple principle. During off-peak hours, excess electricity pumps water uphill to a higher reservoir. When demand spikes, gravity pulls that water back down through turbines, generating power on cue. No combustion, no chemical degradation, no exotic materials. That simplicity has made PSH extraordinarily durable. By 2023, global installed capacity reached nearly 200 gigawatts — more than 90 percent of the world’s long-duration energy storage. No other technology comes close at that scale. The technology hits a hard geographic ceiling, though. “You need a suitable mountain, and you need to have a river running along the bottom,” says Tamas Bertenyi, cofounder and CTO of RheEnergise. “You also need an alpine valley you can dam up, and there are just not a lot of sites where you can do that.” Flat countries, rolling hills, densely populated regions — all effectively locked out of the world’s dominant storage technology. That’s the problem RheEnergise set out to solve, according to IEEE Spectrum. A fluid 2.5 times denser than water — and engineered to behave like it The company’s answer is a proprietary substance it calls High-Density Fluid: a mineral-rich suspension 2.5 times denser than water. “It is so dense that if you threw a block of concrete into a pool of the fluid, it would float,” says Bertenyi. That density is the point — more energy potential per unit of height, which means lower hills can do work that mountains once monopolized. Developing the fluid was harder than it sounds. RheEnergise worked with the University of Exeter, where cofounder Richard Cochrane was a professor of renewable energy systems, to engineer something satisfying two almost contradictory requirements. The fluid needed to be viscous enough to stay put during an accidental spill, yet flow as easily as water through pipes and turbines under normal conditions. The solution was a shear-thinning, non-Newtonian formulation. At rest, the fluid is thick; under pumping pressure, its viscosity drops sharply — behaving, hydraulically, much like water. The mixture is 80 percent solid particulates by mass, suspended rather than dissolved. Spill it, and the particles simply dry and settle rather than seeping into soil or groundwater. What the pilot project actually looks like The pilot system, now running in the UK, keeps a deliberately low profile — literally. An upper reservoir sits at 80 meters of elevation. Two-and-a-half-meter fiberglass pipes carry the fluid down to a lower reservoir that Bertenyi describes as “basically a large swimming pool.” Both are buried underground, connected by steel pipe in a closed loop. Above ground, almost nothing is visible. Only the powerhouse — housing the turbine, pump, fluid-management system, and electrical controls — breaks the surface. For communities sensitive to industrial infrastructure, that near-invisibility could matter considerably. In January, the system hit its headline milestone: 500 kW of peak power. Modest, but it proves the concept works at real scale. The commercial ambition is far larger — RheEnergise envisions projects using two to four 5 MW modular turbines each, putting the target operating range at 10 to 20 MW per site. The company aims to deliver its first fully commercial system by the end of 2028. Why gentler slopes could change where energy storage is built The physics are straightforward. Higher fluid density means the same energy output is achievable from lower elevations and shallower gradients than traditional PSH demands, expanding the viable site map dramatically. “Given the system can generate the same energy output from gentler slopes and lower elevations than traditional pumped hydro, it makes far more sites viable worldwide — including low hills and urban fringe areas — not just mountainous regions,” says Professor George Aggidis, emeritus professor of energy engineering at Lancaster University. That matters for the broader grid challenge. Batteries are fast and modular, but cost-effective long-duration storage — the kind needed to balance renewable generation across eight to ten hours or more — remains elusive at scale. “Batteries alone can be expensive” for that role, Aggidis notes. RheEnergise’s target customers reflect the opportunity: independent power producers, utility companies, and energy-project developers all need exactly this kind of flexible, location-independent storage. The road to commercialization — and the competition waiting None of this arrives without friction. Aggidis is direct: “Larger scale deployment will require substantial civil works, permit requirements, and engineering coordination. This is more complex than plug-and-play battery systems.” Capital intensity and long lead times are familiar obstacles for any infrastructure-scale energy project. The competitive field is also crowding fast. Sodium-ion and flow batteries are modular, quick to install, and falling in cost. Compressed-air storage, hydrogen, and thermal storage all compete for the same long-duration market.
