artigo.texto: POSTECH Researchers Uncover Mechanism Behind Manganese-Based Cathode That Gains Capacity With Repeated Charging South Korean researchers at POSTECH have for the first time uncovered the operating principle behind a next-generation battery material that gains usable capacity as it undergoes repeated charge and discharge cycles. The team demonstrated experimentally that internal structural changes—long viewed solely as a culprit in battery degradation—can be precisely controlled to simultaneously boost both performance and lifespan. POSTECH announced on the 28th that a research team led by Professor Hong Ji-hyun of the Department of Battery Engineering and Professor Park Kyu-young of the Department of Battery Engineering and Department of Materials Science and Engineering has identified the structural transformation mechanism of manganese-based cathode materials, which are drawing attention as a next-generation EV battery material. Dr. Lim Guk-hyun of the Department of Battery Engineering and Lee Ho-jun, an integrated program student in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering, also participated in the research. The material at the center of the study is lithium-rich layered oxide (LMRO). This substance has been considered a leading next-generation battery candidate because it can store roughly 20% more energy than conventional nickel-based cathodes while reducing the use of expensive nickel and cobalt. However, it has suffered from a critical weakness: capacity and operating voltage both decline with repeated charge-discharge cycles. Moreover, studies on the underlying cause had produced conflicting findings about the battery's final internal structure, leaving the precise mechanism shrouded in uncertainty. The research team focused on the phenomenon of oxygen escaping from within the cathode during charge-discharge cycles. LMRO originally has a structure in which lithium and metal atoms are arranged in orderly layers, like a brick wall. But with repeated charging, the oxygen that holds this arrangement firmly in place gradually escapes, and the lithium and metal atoms intermix, eventually transforming the material into a disordered rock-salt structure with almost no regularity. The key discovery is that the amount of oxygen released determines the degree of structural change. The higher the voltage to which the battery was charged, the greater the oxygen loss—and correspondingly, the more the internal structure became disordered. The team confirmed that oxygen release can be precisely controlled by adjusting the depth of charge. This is where an unexpected result emerged. While oxygen loss might at first glance appear to damage the battery, when the structure becomes appropriately disordered, the pathways available for lithium transport actually increase, boosting usable capacity. A material with finely tuned oxygen loss demonstrated durability, retaining 98.4% of its initial performance after more than 200 charge-discharge cycles. "By controlling the battery's operating temperature or surface environment, we can regulate oxygen loss and structural change," said Professor Hong. "This can be applied to designing next-generation EV batteries tailored to specific applications." The significance of this research lies in reframing structural change—previously dismissed as an aging phenomenon to be avoided at all costs—as a design tool. By controlling the degree of disorder through either promoting or suppressing oxygen loss, the findings open a path to designing application-specific optimized materials: high-capacity batteries for long-range driving, or long-lifespan batteries for commercial vehicles where durability is paramount. The research was published in Energy & Environmental Science, an international journal in the energy field. The paper was included in the journal's "Hot Articles"—the top 10% of papers selected by the editorial board—and was also selected as a front inside-cover paper. The study was conducted with support from the Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology and the Korea Institute for the Advancement of Technology under South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy; the National Research Foundation of Korea under the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute. The EV battery market is currently being rapidly encroached upon by Chinese-made lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which compete on price. LFP batteries offer low cost, but their lower energy density translates to shorter driving range, and repeated charge-discharge cycles cause permanent loss of available lithium and increased internal resistance, gradually reducing capacity. LMRO is viewed as an alternative that targets both LFP's price competitiveness and nickel-based batteries' performance, as it can achieve higher energy density while reducing nickel and cobalt usage. That said, since this study establishes the principle at the laboratory level, additional validation is needed before commercialization. Long-term reliability at the actual battery cell level, reproducibility in mass-production processes, and integration with thermal management systems remain as follow-up tasks. Nevertheless, as the first study to quantitatively explain the fundamental mechanism of battery degradation and convert it into a design strategy, it is regarded as research that charts the direction for next-generation high-energy-density cathode development. artigo.texto: Raton, New Mexico is among the latest in a line of jurisdictions to consider a moratorium on data centers. In a standing room only meeting last week city commissioners voted down the idea. Resident and business owner Kimberle Burke presented city commissioners with an informal petition signed by hundreds of residents recommending that the city oppose data centers and approve a moratorium. Concerns included environmental impacts and unintentionally influencing the city's efforts to rebrand. “We're hoping that the Raton city commissioners are not simply shining us on at these meetings, that you're truly listening to us and we're not screaming in the dark,” Burke told the commission. Commissioner Daniel Campbell voted against the moratorium and said the city owned utility wouldn't be able to meet the needs of a data center due to its limited energy and water capacities. “I don't believe that it's a necessary step that we need to step out there and be the first municipality in the state (NM) that does it,” he said during the meeting. Other commissioners raised concerns over the legality of the moratorium or how it could affect existing data centers in the city, including one that has been there for 25 years. Currently multiple counties in New Mexico have passed moratoriums on data centers, including Raton's Colfax County. Colfax County passed the moratorium last month, but it doesn't apply to incorporated areas like Raton, a town of 6,000 residents. Across the state line and to the north, the city of Colorado Springs also owns its utilities. A controversial data center was approved by the city planning department. That decision was appealed by residents and is now in the hands of the city council. Earlier this year Raton's city commission signed a preliminary agreement with a company that was considering building a data center in an old K-Mart building in the center of town. “It feels like they tried to slip it in under our nose and didn't say anything about it,” Burke told KRCC. She said shortly after residents found out about the proposal, they started the petition to let local leaders know how the community felt. However, she said the board's decision bucks the will of the people and has shaken her trust in her local government. “The way it feels to all of us here is ‘We don't really care what y'all want. This is going to happen whether you like it or not’.”

artigo.texto: Data centers may provide a major economic development opportunity for local communities in Wisconsin, but concerns around water and energy use and potential costs to residents have made them increasingly controversial. A new report from the Wisconsin Policy Forum aims to put those issues — and Wisconsin’s data center debate — into context. Researchers examined tax incentives supporting those projects as well as their energy and water use. Three major data center projects are in varying stages of development in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington and Beaver Dam. Others have been proposed but canceled in DeForest, Greenleaf and Janesville as polling has shown the issue to be toxically unpopular with the public. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Communities have ‘significant protections’ under data center incentive deals State law allows qualified developers to avoid paying sales and use tax on most purchases supporting the construction and operation of a data center. The Legislative Fiscal Bureau estimates Wisconsin will lose out on $1.5 billion in sales tax revenues related to data center construction between 2024 and 2028, as well as forgo $369 million annually in sales tax revenue related to data center operations. Wisconsin is one of 38 states that offer tax incentives to data centers. Jason Stein, one of the report’s authors, said without its sales tax exemption, Wisconsin might not have attracted the prominent developments. “I think it’s reasonable to think that a lot of this investment — maybe most of this investment — would not have occurred without the incentive,” he said. The report says the state could “recoup a significant portion of the forgone sales tax revenues” if the sales tax exemption helped attract a significant share of data center investment to Wisconsin. That’s through income and sales taxes paid by construction workers and corporate income taxes paid by construction companies, as well as additional taxes paid by utilities serving data centers. Data centers are also expected to generate increased property tax revenues in the communities hosting them. Researchers reviewed local development agreements in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington and Beaver Dam, as well as proposed deals in communities where developments fell through. They found that, in general, local communities were striking “reasonable deals” that included financial safeguards. Those safeguards often included limits on municipal borrowing, guaranteed property values and incentives tied to project performance, the report said. “If the developer and the community follow through on their agreement and it moves forward as laid out, then those agreements offer substantial protections for the communities,” Stein said. “There are significant protections in each of these deals.” Data centers use water, but Wisconsin water use has declined While much of the public debate around data centers in Wisconsin has centered around water use, policy forum researchers found the bigger challenge is meeting the large electricity demands of those projects while protecting existing ratepayers. That’s because water use in Wisconsin has declined over the past generation as some heavy industry left the state, industrial and residential users became more efficient and electric utilities shifted some energy generation from “water-intensive” coal plants to natural gas and renewable energy, the report said. From 2011 to 2024, water withdrawals in the state fell by more than 500 billion gallons, or almost 24 percent, according to the report. The three main data center projects in Wisconsin are projected to use less water than the decline in water withdrawals over that period, the report states. “We were on this track to use less and less water because of changes in our society, and maybe this will slow that down somewhat,” Stein said. “But that is a different thing than saying, ‘Oh my gosh, we’re using more water than ever before.’” For example, Racine Water Works, the utility providing water for Microsoft’s data center campus in Mount Pleasant, saw its annual water sales decline by 2.3 billion gallons from 2000 to 2025, according to the report. That’s “more than 250 times” as much water as the 8.4 million gallons annually Microsoft’s data center will use when fully operational, the report states. Electricity demand expected to rise significantly While long-term declines in water use are expected to help offset demand from data centers, Wisconsin’s electricity demand is expected to grow, in large part driven by demand from data centers. Peak demand from all customers on the grid is expected to rise from 14.6 gigawatts in 2024 to 19.9 gigawatts by 2030, the report states. A recent report from state utility regulators found data centers were driving that projected peak demand growth. The report found that the state Public Service Commission modified proposals from We Energies and Alliant Energy establishing rates for data center-scale customers to shield existing residential customers from costs associated with data centers. But it remains to be seen how data centers will affect transmission rates, which are set at the federal level, said Tyler Byrnes, one of the report’s authors. “It’s a little bit easier to do the math on one power plant for one data center, whereas you’re starting to divide up electrons moving across power lines (and) across state lines, so it’s more complicated,” he said. He also said there is not currently an approved data center rate framework for developments of that scale outside the service territories of Alliant Energy and We Energies. He said policymakers may want to consider adopting a statewide framework for electric rates tied to data centers. The report also notes that there are unresolved questions about whether utilities will be able to bring new energy generation

artigo.texto: A ABINEE (Associação Brasileira da Indústria Elétrica e Eletrônica) decidiu integrar a área de armazenamento de energia à sua estrutura de atuação. A iniciativa, segundo a entidade, amplia as frentes já existentes e busca acompanhar a convergência entre diferentes segmentos tecnológicos ligados à eletrônica, à energia e às novas aplicações de baterias. A primeira reunião do novo grupo responsável pelo tema incluiu discussões sobre os desafios e as oportunidades relacionados às novas tecnologias de armazenamento e às suas aplicações. Nova abordagem A decisão, de acordo com a associação, está relacionada à rápida evolução tecnológica do setor, à diversificação das aplicações e à necessidade de desenvolvimento de um arcabouço técnico e regulatório adequado. A proposta é criar um espaço coordenado para o diálogo técnico e institucional e para a formulação de posicionamentos sobre temas que afetam o mercado. Entre os objetivos estão contribuir para segurança jurídica, competitividade da indústria, inovação e desenvolvimento sustentável do mercado brasileiro. A ideia é reunir diferentes dimensões envolvidas no armazenamento, em vez de tratar a tecnologia de maneira isolada. Da bateria ao BESS A ABINEE relaciona a nova área à própria trajetória de atuação no segmento de baterias. A entidade destaca que sua experiência vai das pilhas e células eletroquímicas aos acumuladores tradicionais e, mais recentemente, aos BESS (Battery Energy Storage Systems) e aos sistemas integrados de armazenamento em larga escala. A abordagem proposta também tem o objetivo de ser transversal. A entidade pretende acompanhar questões industriais, tecnológicas, regulatórias, ambientais, tributárias, de segurança e conformidade, considerando todo o ciclo de vida das baterias — da pesquisa e fabricação à logística reversa. Com a incorporação do armazenamento, a ABINEE destaca ainda que pretende colocar sua experiência em representação institucional e conhecimento técnico a serviço dos associados e do fortalecimento desse mercado. Todo o conteúdo do Canal Solar é resguardado pela lei de direitos autorais, e fica expressamente proibida a reprodução parcial ou total deste site em qualquer meio. Caso tenha interesse em colaborar ou reutilizar parte do nosso material, solicitamos que entre em contato através do e-mail: redacao@canalsolar.com.br.

artigo.texto: A new battery storage facility in Hunts Point is expected to deliver 20 megawatts of power to the neighborhood as the South Bronx continues to transition away from fossil fuel infrastructure that contributes to pollution. NineDot Energy celebrated the ribbon-cutting of the project on Sept. 24, joining city and state officials and community organizations at the site, which the company says is its largest energy storage project to date. The facility is expected to be fully operational ahead of next summer’s heat waves and will be capable of supplying enough energy to power nearly 20,000 homes during peak grid hours, according to NineDot. “We’re honored to bring this battery storage site to the Hunts Point community,” said NineDot’s Chief Technology Officer and co-founder Adam Cohen. “Hunts Point has historically been overburdened by high-emitting fossil fuels, and this battery storage facility marks an inflection point in improving the local environment and grid reliability.” Battery storage systems are increasingly being used as an alternative to “peaker” plants, which operate as a backup during periods of peak energy use, such as the summer months. The New York Power Authority operates two of the most-used peaker plants in the South Bronx, providing New York City with power while the South Bronx bears the brunt of the pollution year-round. Environmental activists have long advocated to phase out the plants, which are one of several sources contributing to the area’s heavy air pollution. The concentration of highways, industrial operations and diesel emissions from the thousands of trucks traveling to and from the Hunts Point Food Distribution Center also contribute to the neighborhood’s pollution burden. Hunts Point residents also face higher rates of health problems associated with fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, a pollutant emitted by vehicles, industrial operations and other sources. Children in Hunts Point visit emergency rooms for asthma-related illnesses at 2.5 times the citywide rate, according to city health data. Located on the site of a former fuel oil trucking company, the project will be part of a neighborhood where the Hunts Point Food Distribution Center is also transitioning toward an electrified market. “Battery storage is foundational to delivering environmental justice: it’s key to retiring peaker plants, allowing for electrification of polluting sources like diesel refrigerators and trucks and ensuring reliable power on hot summer days,” said Assemblymember Amanda Septimo. “Along the way, batteries will help reduce future costs to ratepayers by avoiding expensive utility upgrades. All of these benefits are positive for the residents and businesses in Hunts Point.” According to NineDot energy, their fleet of battery energy storage systems helped reduce stress on the city’s power grid during July’s extreme heat wave, supporting Con Edison’s local distribution system by powering the equivalent of 34,000 households for four hours during peak demand. artigo.texto: SK Telecom's greenhouse gas emission permits are expected to fall short by more than 350,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2-eq, hereafter t) this year. The buffer it had accumulated has run out, while the permits the government allocates free to corporations have been sharply reduced. It has to buy the shortfall, but the price of greenhouse gas permits has roughly tripled this year, adding to the burden. According to the industry on the 30th, SK Telecom estimated its greenhouse gas emissions this year at 1,276,396 t. The company received 918,993 t of free permits from the government this year, leaving a shortfall of 357,403 t. Under the emissions trading scheme, the government allocates an annual greenhouse gas emission cap to corporations that emit above a certain threshold and allows them to trade surpluses or deficits. If a corporation emits less than its allocation, it can sell the surplus on the market. If it emits more than its allocation, it must purchase permits to make up the difference, and if it fails to comply, it pays a penalty surcharge. SK Telecom had surplus permits until two years ago. In 2023, it received 1,327,809 t of free permits and used 1,149,239 t. It sold part of the remaining permits (70,789 t) and carried over the rest. In 2024, it used only 1,166,518 t out of 1,332,500 t allocated free. It sold part of the remainder (63,058 t) and carried over the rest. The buffer disappeared as last year's free allocation decreased. In 2025, SK Telecom's free allocation was 1,021,864 t, down 310,636 t (23.3%) from the previous year (1,332,500 t). As a result, it could not cover the 1,246,142 t of permits it had to submit to the government, and it made up the shortfall with permits carried over from the previous year. This year, with the carryover buffer exhausted and the free allocation reduced further, it needs to purchase permits. As it launched the fourth allocation period (2026–2030) of the emissions trading scheme this year, the government cut the total emissions cap by about 17% from the third period and raised the share of paid allocation for sectors other than power generation from 10% to 15%. As a result, SK Telecom's free allocation fell to 918,993 t this year, down 10.1% from the previous year (1,021,864 t). The free allocation will decrease each year to 877,264 t by 2030. Meanwhile, SK Telecom's greenhouse gas emissions and energy use have been steadily increasing. According to SK Telecom, emissions in 2025 rose about 16.7% from 2019, and energy use rose about 18.6%. Carriers do not have factories, but electricity is needed to run base stations, network equipment and data centers. About 95% of SK Telecom's emissions are Scope 2 (indirect emissions such as electricity), not Scope 1 (direct emissions). The burden could grow going forward. On a consolidation basis including SK Broadband, expected emissions this year will increase to 1,941,339 t, while free allocation stands at 1,399,530 t. SK Telecom has announced plans to gradually build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers totaling up to 15 GW (gigawatts) by 2035, and if power use increases, emissions and the burden of buying permits could rise together. In fact, due to AI data center operations, SK Broadband's greenhouse gas emissions surged 37.7% in one year, from 455,962 t in 2024 to 627,682 t in 2025. SK Broadband completed the Yangju data center in 2025 and acquired the Pangyo data center. In the short term, rising permit prices could also be a burden. According to the Korea Exchange (KRX), the price of permits (KAU26) stood at 30,050 won per ton as of the day, nearly triple from the start of the year (10,400 won). If SK Telecom buys this year's shortfall of 357,403 t at that price, it would cost about 10.7 billion won. SK Telecom says it will respond with energy efficiency. In a climate report published in Jun., SK Telecom said, "Market factors such as increased power demand due to AI data center construction and higher electricity rates will have a very significant impact over the medium to long term," and added, "Rising greenhouse gas permit prices and stronger regulations on energy efficiency are expected to grow more important over the long term." It continued, "Domestic carbon permit prices are expected to rise as greenhouse gas emissions regulations tighten," and said it would respond by improving data center energy efficiency, enhancing energy efficiency at telecom offices, and diversifying renewable energy procurement methods. Fundamentally, the question is whether AI data centers can coexist with the carbon neutrality target. SK Telecom has set a goal of carbon neutrality by 2050. Jung Su-jong, a professor at Seoul National University's Graduate School of Environmental Studies, said, "There is concern as the two major national agendas of industrial green transition and AI transition are colliding," and added, "With the national greenhouse gas reduction target (NDC) far off and AI growth right before us, carbon neutrality is being neglected, so it is time to seriously discuss how to advance both together."

artigo.texto: A Rússia ataca o centro de dados da Vodafone em Kyiv. TPO - O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que suas forças atacaram uma série de alvos de infraestrutura logística, de comunicações e militar na Ucrânia, incluindo um centro de dados da Vodafone em Kiev. O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que, durante a noite, suas forças realizaram ataques com drones contra múltiplos alvos na Ucrânia , incluindo centros de logística, infraestrutura portuária e de transporte, e centros de comunicação. "Na noite passada, as Forças Armadas Russas continuaram a realizar ataques com drones visando centros de logística, infraestrutura portuária e de transporte, centros de comunicação e navios operados pelas forças armadas ucranianas", diz o comunicado. De acordo com a versão russa, um dos alvos do ataque foi um centro de dados da Vodafone em Kiev. Moscou acusa a empresa de ser uma das principais fornecedoras de serviços de telecomunicações móveis e internet para as forças armadas ucranianas, incluindo a transmissão de dados de inteligência. Você também pode gostar O Ministério da Defesa russo afirmou que as tropas russas também atacaram um centro logístico da Zammler na vila de Krasilovka, na região de Kyiv, que armazena e distribui ajuda militar ocidental para a Ucrânia. Na região de Odessa, a Rússia afirma ter atacado o centro logístico de drones Kalinsh em Ilyichovka, que se acredita armazenar drones interceptores FPV. O lado russo também afirmou ter atingido vários alvos no porto de Kiliya, incluindo o quartel-general da base naval de Vostok da Marinha ucraniana, um posto avançado da Guarda de Fronteira ucraniana, quatro depósitos de equipamentos militares e parte da infraestrutura portuária. Segundo um comunicado do Ministério da Defesa russo, os ataques também tiveram como alvo dois armazéns contendo drones e componentes de combate em Nikolayev, bem como um navio cargueiro no mar que, segundo Moscou, transportava equipamentos militares e bens de dupla utilização para o porto de Odessa. artigo.texto: Industry steps up with lithium-ion battery storage guidance Lewis Tyler Share this content UKWA and UKMHA publish guidance to help warehouse operators manage the risks associated with lithium-ion battery storage The UK Warehousing Association (UKWA) and the UK Material Handling Association (UKMHA) have published new guidance to help warehouse operators manage the risks associated with the growing use and storage of lithium-ion batteries. The two trade bodies have worked in parallel to provide practical advice covering both smaller batteries and larger traction batteries used to power warehouse equipment. The guidance was launched at a UKWA Member Connect event in Felixstowe, where Clare Bottle from UKWA and David Goss from UKMHA discussed key highlights for warehouse operators. Lithium-ion batteries are increasingly used across the economy, from laptops, e-bikes and scooters to industrial machinery such as forklifts. While batteries are an important part of the transition away from fossil fuels, the organisations note that unmonitored batteries can, in rare circumstances, enter thermal runaway and cause fire. The new guidance includes recommendations on storing batteries in cool, dry conditions, limiting long-term storage and separating battery types. It also provides advice on monitoring stock, preparing emergency plans and training staff. Clare Bottle, Chief Executive of UKWA, said: “Developments in battery technology are having a huge positive impact, making our lives more convenient, changing the way we move around, and helping the transition away from fossil fuels. All of these batteries move through the supply chain before ending up in businesses or people’s homes, so it is vital we get the storage and handling of them right. “There’s no reason, with proper precautions, that batteries can’t be stored safely. Many warehouses are doing so already. This guidance will help others get to grips with the issue and understand how they can manage the risks. It is a market that will only grow, so it’s important the UK has a wide range of warehouse operators equipped with this knowledge.” David Goss, Technical Director of UKMHA, said: “Lithium-ion batteries have been transformative, not only for consumers but also for powering the equipment essential to today’s fast and efficient logistics sector. “As with any technology, sensible precautions are necessary to minimise the risk of an incident. Whilst lithium-ion batteries have proven safe and reliable, effective risk management requires an understanding of the potential for hazards due to the release of stored energy or chemicals. “Through this collaboration, UKWA and UKMHA have developed complementary guidance addressing the storage of both industrial truck traction batteries and the smaller batteries in warehouse environments.” Both guidance documents are available from UKWA.

artigo.texto: Liftoff: Google is realizing Elon Musk's dream of AI data centers in space Next week, Google will be living out Elon Musk's dream of putting AI data centers in space — and they'll be doing it with help from Musk's space exploration company. On Thursday, October 1, 2026, Google will load an experimental satellite on SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket and launch it in space. The satellite is part of Google's Project Suncatcher initiative, which seeks to set up AI data centers in space. The experimental satellite will be able answer simple A.I. prompts from space, according to the New York Times. In a blog post about Project Suncatcher, Google explained the potential benefits of sending data centers into orbit: You May Also Like Cooling orbital data centers is a crucial research challenge. TPUs generate a large amount of heat in a small area, which needs to be diffused safely or the chips are at risk of overheating. But in space, there’s no airflow. In a vacuum, you can only diffuse heat via radiators, which requires a totally different approach to cooling electronics. As the New York Times reported, Google isn't sending a full-on orbital data center this time; it's sending the potential precursor to one. The satellite, named MVP, contains four “tensor processing units,” which are specialized chips with the computing power of one server in a data center here on Earth. The computer chips will be powered by the satellite's solar panels, which will provide one kilowatt of power to the chips. Google says that this is all it needs for this particular experiment, which will test how the hardware fares in outer space. The satellite is expected to operate in space for a period of one year. While in orbit, the computer chips will be able to process short queries for up to 15 minutes while Google's Gemini AI responds. After a 15-minute period, the chips will need to shut down to cool with a special cooling system, as fans typically used in computer systems don't work in space. After that one-year period, the satellite will stop operating but will continue to orbit the Earth for a total of six years before the planet's gravitational pull brings the satellite down, burning it as it falls through the atmosphere. When Musk's SpaceX acquired Musk's AI company xAI earlier this year, Musk explained that one of the main reasons for the companies to combine was so that they could work on putting AI data centers in space. "Current advances in AI are dependent on large terrestrial data centers, which require immense amounts of power and cooling," Musk said in a statement at the time of the acquisition. "Global electricity demand for AI simply cannot be met with terrestrial solutions, even in the near term, without imposing hardship on communities and the environment." In the long term, space-based AI is obviously the only way to scale," Musk continued. Google seems to agree with Musk. Shortly after Musk shared his orbital AI data center goals, Google announced Project Suncatcher, which the company greenlit in May 2025. It's important to note, however, that these are very early days for the orbital data center ambition. If these experiments prove that the project is at all feasible, it would likely be years, if not decades, before Google and Musk's vision comes to fruition. But Thursday's launch is certainly a first step in potentially building out AI data centers in space. Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? artigo.texto: BYD says it is close to bringing solid-state battery technology to production vehicles, with the Chinese car maker planning to introduce its first model using the technology in 2027. The company believes it holds a strong position in both the development and commercialisation of solid-state batteries, which could eventually offer electric vehicles longer driving ranges, faster charging and improved safety compared with conventional lithium-ion technology. BYD targets 2027 for its first solid-state model BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li confirmed the company’s plans in a recent interview with Carwow’s Spanish outlet. She said BYD was in a “leading position” in solid-state battery development and commercialisation, adding that the company would use a production model to demonstrate the technology. “Talking about solid-state batteries, BYD is in the leading position,” Li said. “We’re in the leading position for commercialisation and technology. So to prove that, next year, we have one model that will be the first one with that technology.” The comments build on plans previously outlined by Sun Huajun, chief technology officer of BYD’s battery subsidiary FinDreams. Speaking at a battery conference in February 2025, Sun said BYD expected to demonstrate and install solid-state batteries in vehicles in 2027, with mass production expected to follow around 2030, according to CarNewsChina. The planned launch does not mean BYD intends to abandon its existing lithium-based batteries. Lian Yubo, BYD’s chief scientist, said at the same conference that solid-state batteries would initially target higher-end vehicles. In contrast, lithium iron phosphate batteries would continue to serve other parts of the market. “Solid-state batteries will be mainly used in high-end models, complementing lithium iron phosphate batteries, and used in vehicles of different levels,” Lian said. This approach would allow BYD to introduce the newer technology without immediately replacing the battery systems already used across its electric vehicle range. Solid-state batteries could improve range and safety Solid-state batteries differ from conventional lithium-ion batteries mainly in the electrolyte that moves ions between the battery’s positive and negative electrodes. Traditional lithium-ion cells use a liquid electrolyte containing dissolved lithium salts, while solid-state designs replace the liquid with a solid material. The solid electrolyte can be made using materials such as oxides, polymers or sulphides. BYD is developing sulphide-based solid-state technology, which could provide higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion cells. Higher energy density could allow manufacturers to build smaller, lighter batteries while maintaining the same amount of stored energy. Alternatively, manufacturers could use a battery of similar size to today’s packs while increasing available energy, potentially extending an electric vehicle’s driving range. Solid-state technology could also offer safety benefits. Conventional lithium-ion batteries use flammable liquid electrolytes and can experience thermal runaway if cells are severely damaged or develop certain faults. Solid electrolytes are less prone to this type of behaviour, although solid-state batteries are not automatically risk-free. Another potential advantage is performance across a wider temperature range. Extreme heat and cold can affect battery performance, and solid-state technology is being developed partly to address these limitations. However, several technical and manufacturing challenges remain before solid-state batteries can be produced at the scale and cost required for mass-market electric vehicles. Manufacturing complexity and material costs remain major barriers, helping explain why early applications are expected to appear in more expensive models. BYD joins growing solid-state battery race BYD is not the only car maker working towards production solid-state batteries. Several major manufacturers have announced plans to introduce the technology in vehicles during the second half of the decade, although development schedules and commercial availability vary between companies. Toyota has previously targeted 2027 or 2028 for vehicles equipped with solid-state batteries. Mercedes-Benz has also been testing solid-state battery technology in an EQS-based vehicle and expects to introduce the technology before the end of the decade. Stellantis has taken another step towards commercialisation by beginning road testing of a solid-state battery-powered Dodge Charger in 2026. The testing is intended to evaluate the technology under real-world driving conditions rather than solely in laboratory environments. Honda has also been developing the technology and announced a partnership with QuantumScape earlier this year. The companies are working on solid-state battery technology as part of Honda’s longer-term efforts towards carbon neutrality by 2050. For BYD, the 2027 vehicle will provide an important step towards determining how its sulphide-based solid-state cells perform in a production car. The company has indicated that wider adoption is likely to follow later, with mass production targeted around 2030. The development could eventually give electric vehicle manufacturers another option to improve range, charging performance, and battery packaging. For now, however, solid-state batteries remain an emerging technology, and manufacturers are still working to overcome the cost and production challenges of bringing them to large-scale vehicle production.

artigo.texto: LG lança chiller centrífugo refrigerado a ar para data centers de IA Equipamento tem capacidade de 480 a 600 toneladas de refrigeração por unidade; segundo a empresa, o sistema pode recuperar a capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos após o retorno da energia. A LG Electronics lançou um chiller centrífugo refrigerado a ar voltado a data centers de inteligência artificial. O equipamento utiliza um compressor com mancal magnético sem óleo e um sistema de free-cooling que aproveita o ar externo frio para reduzir a carga de trabalho do compressor. Segundo uma simulação interna da LG, o free-cooling por refrigerante consumiu aproximadamente 30% menos energia ao longo de um ano que o sistema hidrônico comparado. O cálculo considerou uma unidade de 1.750 kW operando a 100% da capacidade sob as condições climáticas da região metropolitana de Seul. O consumo real pode variar conforme a instalação e a operação. Em caso de queda de energia, uma fonte ininterrupta integrada permite a parada segura do eixo do compressor. Após o restabelecimento da eletricidade, o chiller pode recuperar a capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos, conforme as condições de teste informadas pela empresa. A LG também apresentará uma solução modular de resfriamento hidrônico na Data Centre World Asia 2026, marcada para 29 e 30 de setembro, no Marina Bay Sands, em Singapura. O módulo reúne bombas de água gelada e um tanque de armazenamento térmico e pode ser montado em fábrica para simplificar a instalação no local. James Lee, presidente da LG ES Company, afirmou que a empresa continuará a ampliar seu portfólio de resfriamento diante do aumento da densidade e da geração de calor nos data centers de IA. – Resumen (español) LG Electronics lanzó un chiller centrífugo enfriado por aire para centros de datos de inteligencia artificial. El equipo tiene una capacidad de 480 a 600 toneladas de refrigeración por unidad y utiliza un compresor con cojinete magnético sin aceite. La empresa también presentará una solución modular de enfriamiento hidrónico en la Data Centre World Asia 2026, en Singapur. Summary (English) LG Electronics has launched an air-cooled centrifugal chiller for AI data centers. Each unit has a cooling capacity of 480 to 600 refrigeration tons and uses an oil-free magnetic bearing compressor. The company will also present a modular hydronic cooling solution at Data Centre World Asia 2026 in Singapore.

artigo.texto: This Albertan trades in a murky carbon market crucial to Carney's pipeline deal Everything Ana Avramovic sells sits as numbered entries in a government registry, and none of them are hers. She trades carbon credits, a job so unusual even her mother doesn't fully understand what she does for a living. She came to carbon from power trading, having cut her teeth at Calgary-based TransAlta Corp. Ask her whether leaving a traditional paycheque to build a firm of her own was brave or reckless. The answer depends on the day. "Overall, excited," she says. "And then sometimes like, oh my God, what am I doing? What have I done?" When she traded power, explaining her job took one gesture toward a window. "You see that hotel?" she says. "Somebody has to sell them electricity." Carbon is trickier. You can't see electricity either, but everyone knows what it's for. She founded Carbon Merchant in July 2026 to trade industrial carbon and clean fuel credits. Every big emitter in Alberta, from oilsands operators to power producers and miners, has a limit on what it can release into the atmosphere. Beat the limit and you earn credits for cutting emissions. Miss the benchmark and you buy them from somebody who did. Avramovic is the broker in the middle, helping buyers and sellers find each other. The 42-year-old works in a market so opaque that outsiders can't make sense of it. And, yet the stakes are enormous. The market is one of Canada's biggest levers against climate change. Its design is a signature priority in Ottawa and lies at the centre of Prime Minister Mark Carney's deal with Alberta on a possible West Coast pipeline for oil. But there are flaws, too. Critics worry the market is falling short and flooded with cheap credits, which means that meeting the rules is far less expensive for industry. For Avramovic, it is personal. She has two young children, and they will inherit whatever this market does or fails to do. She chose the work because it was the one place her own effort might count. "I'm just one person. It's not like I can fix it all," she says, "but I can at least do a little part." Location, location, emissions Avramovic rents an office at Pavilion, a coworking space in downtown Calgary. She starts around 7 a.m., and her day is nonstop: ICE chat, where energy traders connect on the Intercontinental Exchange, plus texts, calls, Teams meetings, in-person meetings and coffee, lots of it. "A lot of my day is just communicating with different people and figuring out what are they doing, what are they looking to do," she says. Most of her deals are spot work: one buyer, one seller, done in days. The deal she is building now is slower — a multi-year clean fuel arrangement. She is not matching a buyer to a seller on something that already exists; she is building the deal itself, putting sides together for years rather than for a week. Those are the harder matches. "It's the challenge, the hunt. That's what makes it fun," she says. Avramovic's work is similar to what a real estate agent does, minus the house. A company calls knowing what it needs but not who has it. Avramovic knows who does, and who needs to sell before its deadline. The property just happens to be carbon, so there is nothing to walk through and no keys to hand over, just a line in a registry that moves out of one account and into another. She takes a fee when the deal closes, or a monthly retainer from clients who want to know where prices are heading. Alberta's industrial carbon market is the biggest in Canada, and it exists because the province requires it, and has since 2007, when Ed Stelmach's government put a price on industrial carbon. No one in North America had priced industrial carbon before Alberta did. The European Union got there first. The regulation is meant to be the stick. "But then, within that regulation," Avramovic says, "there's also a carrot that if you do those actions, you can then create credits and monetize them." The actions are emissions cuts. One credit is not the same as another. Each one carries a vintage, like wine, the year it was created. One made in 2024 is good until 2029, then it expires. On the open market, these credits trade for less than $30 a tonne. The alternative is paying $95 a tonne into a government fund. In recent years, big emitters have used as many credits as the rules allow, Avramovic says. Those prices are about to go up. Sarajevo to power trading Avramovic was born in Sarajevo. The family escaped in the early 1990s, when a war started, and moved to the coast of Croatia, where her mother is from, and lived with her maternal grandparents. Her father escaped in the summer of 1994. Her parents applied to immigrate to Canada, and they arrived in June 1995, two weeks after her 11th birthday. She wanted art school. Her parents had crossed an ocean to start over in a new country, and they wanted their daughter to have a profession. She went to the Haskayne School of Business at the University of Calgary, and after graduation took a creative job at Critical Mass, a Calgary agency that was doing some of the first advertising on the internet. On a whim she answered an ad for a real-time power trader at TransAlta. The desk was hiring four new traders for Alberta, she says, two women and two men. "I just put my hand up," she says. She got one of the four. Power is a 24-hour commodity, so the desk ran 12-hour shifts, two days, two nights, then days off, moving power between regions to capture the gap between what it cost to send and what it fetched at the other end. "I was lucky at TransAlta because they were trying to prioritize hiring more women onto a trade floor," she says. "And so, I got my chance that way." Trading is still a man's business, she says, and while there are women across carbon in compliance, greenhouse gas accounting and sustainability, she can only name about a dozen who trade it. artigo.texto: French solid-state battery manufacturer ITEN has produced its one-millionth battery and expanded its Powency range with a 1,500µAh surface-mount device. The new battery is available for sampling and is being evaluated by selected customers. Volume production is planned by the end of 2026. ITEN said the device stores six times more energy than its existing 250µAh Powency battery and offers higher peak-current capability. It is intended for space-constrained Internet of Things and medical applications requiring longer operating or backup times. The battery is designed to support ultra-wideband, LoRa and Bluetooth Low Energy communications. Potential applications include asset trackers, connected healthcare products, smart-building sensors, remote controls and energy-harvesting systems. As an SMD component, the battery can be mounted directly onto an electronic assembly without a separate battery holder. ITEN said this could provide an alternative to larger energy-storage components, including supercapacitors, in highly integrated devices. CEO Vincent Cobée said the one-million-unit milestone demonstrated the company’s accumulated knowledge of solid-state technology, product development and volume manufacturing. “It gives us a strong industrial foundation as we continue to push energy storage towards greater integration, power and safety,” he said. ITEN makes its batteries using proprietary nanomaterials and full-ceramic mesoporous electrodes. The cells contain no liquid electrolyte. The company said its low-temperature sintering process preserves material properties while increasing the electrodes’ specific surface area, supporting high-power performance. The company opened its Dardilly pilot plant near Lyon, France, in April 2024 following an investment of €14 million ($16.4 million). The facility brings together processes ranging from materials chemistry to cell testing and has installed capacity exceeding 30 million devices annually. ITEN claims it is the only company to have reached this level of production maturity for solid-state batteries intended for electronic systems and ready for shipment.

artigo.texto: Russia has continued a bombardment on Ukraine's data centers and communications infrastructure as part of a fresh wave of attacks on the country's capital. Ukraine's air force said Russian forces intensified strikes on Kyiv and other cities overnight by launching a mix of anti-ship and ballistic missiles, as well as dozens of jet-powered drones, which Ukrainian air defenses have struggled to intercept. Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck several targets in Kyiv on Tuesday, including a locomotive depot housing a warehouse of FP-5 Flamingo ground-based missiles and their components. The attacks also hit the Bi-mobile data center, which Russia's Defense Ministry said was one of Kyiv's main internet exchange points, and the Parkovy data center. Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's data centers and internet providers in recent days, seeking to disrupt the flow of information in the country. Ukrainian officials have expressed deep concern over the attacks, saying there is an urgent need for the country to be able to rapidly respond to missile and drone threats. Ukraine, for its part, has sought to raise the cost of Russia's more than four-and-a-half-year war against it, targeting the country's oil refineries and logistics hubs. Meanwhile, NATO on Tuesday denounced Russia's nuclear threats after publicly acknowledging a tense exchange with Moscow. The military alliance said it made clear to Moscow that it is a "defensive alliance" and that none of its activities or exercises "pose a risk to any part of Russia." 'A sign of desperation' NATO was responding to a warning issued by the Russian Embassy in Belgium on Monday that accused the alliance of escalating the situation around Kaliningrad, a small Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea. The embassy said NATO's "reckless and irresponsible" approach regarding the strategic outpost, which is sandwiched between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania, heightens the risk of a direct military confrontation. It added that Moscow was ready to use its entire military arsenal if NATO tried to block the region, according to Russian state news agency Tass. "We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine," a NATO spokesperson said in a statement shared with CNBC. "Russia's use of hybrid tactics is a sign of desperation. But we will not be dissuaded from our support to Ukraine. We have what it takes to defend every inch of Allied territory and remain strong, ready, and able to counter any threat," they added. The exchange reaffirmed the deep tensions in diplomatic relations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.

artigo.texto: Last week, I walked my fields at Trails End Farm in Bradford as the sun came up over the hills. It’s the kind of quiet that reminds you why people move to New Hampshire — and why those of us lucky enough to live here fight so hard to protect it. That’s why I strongly support Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s proposed moratorium on new data centers in New Hampshire. Across the country from Colorado to Virginia, from Texas to right here in New Hampshire, massive new data center facilities are popping up. Recently proposals for new data center projects in Nottingham and Bow have received a lot of attention and public scrutiny — rightfully so. Here’s what the data shows. Data centers are among the most power-intensive facilities ever built. A single large-scale facility can consume as much electricity as a small city. When those facilities plug into New Hampshire’s grid, they drive up demand. When demand outpaces supply, ratepayers pay more. Every family heating their home. Every small business running its equipment. Every farmer keeping the lights on in the barn. They all pay more so that a data center — excuse me, an “innovation hub” — can run its servers around the clock. New Hampshire has a brand. We call it the New Hampshire Advantage. Low taxes. Common sense regulation. A quality of life worth protecting. That advantage doesn’t survive if we allow our energy infrastructure to be overwhelmed by facilities that offer almost nothing to our communities in return — no meaningful jobs, no tax base that justifies the strain, no benefit to the Granite Staters who actually live here. Gov. Ayotte is right to pump the brakes. A moratorium isn’t anti-business. It’s pro-New Hampshire. It says: we will think carefully before we commit our grid, our ratepayers and our communities to something we cannot easily undo. That is conservative governance. That is good stewardship. Any farmer will tell you — you don’t exhaust the land for a single season’s profit. Because apparently, “data center” has become a dirty word — and when a dirty word starts costing you a permit, the instinct in some corners is simple: find a cleaner word. So now, Granite Staters, you may start hearing about proposed “server farms” or “innovation hubs” coming to a town near you. Don’t be fooled. An innovation hub that requires hundreds of megawatts of power, consumes millions of gallons of water for cooling, generates little local employment and plugs directly into our electrical grid is not an innovation hub. It’s a data center. Calling it something else doesn’t change what it draws from our communities — or what it leaves behind. I’ve spent my career in business and academia studying how markets work. I’ve run hotels. I’ve taught marketing. And I know a rebranding campaign when I see one. This is one of the most transparent examples I’ve encountered in public life. The product hasn’t changed. Only the label has. And the label is designed to get past the very guardrails that Gov. Ayotte and this legislature are trying to put in place to protect New Hampshire’s ratepayers and energy grid. My message to those who want to sneak a data center past a moratorium by slapping a new name on it is simple: we see you. The people of New Hampshire see you. And we are not going to let a branding exercise substitute for honest policy. If you have a facility that draws industrial-scale power from our grid, it will be evaluated as what it is — not what you’ve chosen to call it this week. New Hampshire’s energy future is too important to leave to clever marketing. Our ratepayers deserve honesty. Our grid deserves protection. And our communities deserve leaders who won’t be talked out of common sense by people with a thesaurus and a permit application. I’m one of those leaders. And I’m not going anywhere. Sen. Dan Innis, from Bradford, represents District 7 in the New Hampshire Senate.

artigo.texto: Data centers are changing America's landscape, report says The corporate technology giants building data centers to power the artificial intelligence boom are changing America's natural landscape. Although data centers long predate generative AI, hundreds of massive, or "hyperscale," facilities are now sprouting up around the country. Many of these data centers are going up in areas that were once farmland or desert, according to satellite imagery published by the Washington Post. More than 1,300 data centers operate in the U.S. today, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence firm. An additional 2,231 data center projects are planned or in development, according to the group. About 100 facilities already in operation are classified as hyperscale centers that consume at least 100 megawatts of power at peak capacity, according to Cleanview. "Roughly 40 percent of today's hyperscale data centers were built on previously developed land. The rest took over farmland, shrubland and forest," the Washington Post reported. The data centers that power AI have a voracious appetite for electricity. Some companies erecting the facilities are building their own power grids to sidestep criticism that they strain the electric grid and drive up utility costs for residents. "The way that a lot of companies who build data centers are handling this, is they just need so much electricity, and the grid cannot give it. It would take many years to build up that capacity," Washington Post senior graphics reporter Kevin Schaul told CBS News. "And so what they're doing is going off-grid and building their own power plants. They're using repurposed jet engines, whatever they can find to build enough power." The surge in data center construction has sparked significant public backlash, with communities citing concerns about their impact on local water and power supplies, among other issues. Grassroots efforts to block data center development have thwarted some planned projects. In the second quarter of 2026, advocacy groups disrupted at least 45 developments across 27 states, valued at $68 billion, according to a report shared with CBS News by Data Center Watch, which tracks public opposition to the facilities. "Organized opposition became more geographically widespread and visible online, with petition activity expanding significantly and campaigns increasingly addressing statewide policy, utility regulation, and infrastructure," the group said in its report. Thirty states have introduced or adopted legislation or taken other actions to address some of these concerns, including the impact of data centers on utility costs, according to Data Center Watch. Some communities also imposed preemptive moratoriums on data center development, even before builders expressed interest or filed applications, the report notes. Developers have tried to sway local public opinion by offering communities incentives, even promising direct cash payments to residents to facilitate approvals, according to the report.

artigo.texto: Wisconsin Rapids Alder Michael Timm will have to campaign to keep his job after residents forced a recall election over an email he sent a local business. It’s all tied to yard signs showing opposition to a local data center proposal. While data centers have been a contentious issue across Wisconsin, they’re especially so in Wisconsin Rapids where developer wanted to turn the site of a historic paper mill into a data center facility. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. The issue has brought out vocal opposition, large audiences at local meetings and complete changes of data center policies in the small community. Amid the local debate in July, a local hotel bar made available “No Data Center” signs for those who wanted them. In an email, Timm contacted the business and expressed his belief that the signs were unpopular and had led another local business to close down. But in the months that followed, local sentiment swung hard against the proposal. An August forum held by the data center developer and led by former New York City Mayor Eric Adams devolved into heckling and jeering. And this month, the city’s planning commission unanimously recommended denying developers a conditional use permit for the paper mill proposal. When Timm’s email became public, data center opponents called on him to resign and started an effort to recall him. Kaitlyn Federwitz was one of the residents who gathered votes for the recall and is a co-founder of the South Wood County Neighbors for Responsible Development organization. The group has been leading the charge against data center proposals in Wisconsin Rapids. They’re also behind the “No Data Center” signs, which locals can buy to show their opposition. She specifically pointed to Timm’s email to the Hotel Mead as a reason her group started the recall effort. In a statement, Timm said he hasn’t done anything wrong. “There was no threat, no demand, no ultimatum, and no suggestion of any consequence if (Hotel Mead) declined” to stop distributing the signs,” Timm said. “It was simply my opinion. They considered it and voluntarily agreed.” Timm sent the message from his personal email, but in the first two lines identified himself as a city alder and gave his connections to the Chamber of Commerce. The recall effort has two phases: a recall primary on Oct. 27, followed by a recall election on Nov. 24, according to the city. If a primary is not required, local voters in District 7 will decide on Oct. 27 whether Timm will remain in office. Timm responds to claims he ‘pressured’ business In his statement, Timm said he wanted to address claims he had “improperly pressured or threatened the Hotel Mead” over the No Data Center signs. He also released the July email chain at issue. Using a personal email, Timm shared his opinion with Hotel Mead staff that selling the anti-data center signs at the bar could hurt the businesses. “Not sure if you are aware but they tried doing that at 1716 and the bar went out of business,” the email states. Federwitz said that bar closed for personal reasons. “We were working with a local bar, who was holding events for us where we had days where we could sell our signs,” she said. After the closure, the Neighbors group talked with the Hotel Mead bar, who allowed the signs in. “And it came to light that Michael Timm had found out that that was happening, and he sent an email to all the managers at the Hotel Mead,” Federwitz said. “By allowing this, you’re alienating A LOT of people from your establishment,” Timm wrote in the email. “While I remain neutral on the issue, I know several people that won’t be going in there knowing this is going on.” Federwitz said this is not the first time Timm has communicated with locals on data center issues. “He had a very strong stance, not entirely pro-data center, but also definitely speaking in their interest,” Federwitz said. Timm did not respond to a request for comment. The Neighbors group noticed Timm was regularly replying to Facebook comments about local data center topics — according to Federwitz, “in ways that were not necessarily super professional, and really, taking a fighting-back stance against people who were asking questions.” Timm also shared a response email, dated the same day, from Tucker Christensen, the Hotel Mead’s general manager. “Honestly I was opposed to selling the signs here,” Christensen said, adding he did not want the hotel to be part of the data center discussion. Christensen said the decision to sell the signs was made by the hotel’s owners, who thought it would be “harmless.” Timm’s words found support from the general manager, according to the alderman’s Facebook post. “I have spoken to (the owners) regarding your concerns, and I hope they reconsider,” Christensen said, thanking Timm for his opinion. The Hotel Mead went on to host one of the data center developer’s open houses on Sept. 13. “Businesses have every right to decide what they sell on their own property,” Timm wrote later in his statement. “I respected their response then, and I respect it now.” Once locals had the required 252 signatures, the recall was approved by the local council on a vote of 6-0, with one abstention. Timm is a first-time alder, who was elected, running unopposed, in 2025. His term expires in 2027. In his statement, he said he would not resign and said the recall would put “unnecessary costs onto the taxpayers, and I continue to face threats and harassment by people outside my district, I will not abandon my community.”

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution is accelerating technology development to preempt the future battery market despite multiple headwinds, including an electric vehicle chasm (temporary demand slowdown). According to the battery industry on the 28th, LG Energy Solution invested 725.9 billion won in research and development (R&D) expense in the first half of this year. This is the largest amount ever for a half-year period. The number of patents is also increasing significantly. LG Energy Solution holds the most patents among battery makers worldwide, with 62,140 registrations and 105,350 applications. A representative next-generation battery technology held by LG Energy Solution is the solid-state battery. A solid-state battery replaces the liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte, reducing risks that occur when the cathode and anode come into contact and maintaining shape even under external shock, a technology that maximizes safety. "Graphite-based solid-state" is a technology in which LG Energy Solution has strength, and for electric vehicles in 2029 it can maximize energy density per volume by using only the current collector without an anode material. It also announced a battery development roadmap to commercialize "anode-free solid-state" for Humanoid Robot and urban air mobility (UAM) in 2030, pursuing a strategy of differentiating technical approaches to suit market characteristics. To address high manufacturing expense and process complexity, LG Energy Solution has put "dry electrode" technology at the forefront. The dry process that omits the organic solvent drying step is evaluated as a next-generation method that can not only dramatically reduce equipment investment and process expense, but also drive innovation across battery production in terms of manufacturing time and space efficiency. LG Energy Solution is widening the technology gap by filing more than 450 dry electrode–related patents worldwide. It holds key patents such as the "dry electrode fibrillation and tensile strength improvement technology," essential for mass-production-grade dry electrode manufacturing, and has also secured technology applicable to both cathodes and anodes regardless of active material particle size. Sodium batteries are also a technology LG Energy Solution is focusing on. These batteries store and release electricity using sodium instead of lithium ions. They offer price competitiveness due to advantages in materials and supplies procurement and expense, and are known for excellent low-temperature output. LG Energy Solution said in a roadmap released last year that it plans to apply sodium batteries to 12V and 24V automotive lead-acid replacements, energy storage systems (ESS), and small electric vehicles. Prismatic LMR (lithium manganese rich) batteries are another technology drawing attention recently. These batteries significantly reduce cobalt content to boost cost competitiveness while also raising energy density. LG Energy Solution recognized early the potential of combining LMR cathodes with silicon anodes and proactively built a patent foundation. It is also securing competitiveness across materials and processes. In November last year, LG Energy Solution signed a "strategic partnership for aerospace battery cell research and development" with U.S. startup South 8 Technologies (hereafter South 8), which developed the world's first liquefied gas electrolyte for lithium-ion batteries, and agreed to jointly develop next-generation space batteries operable in extreme ultra-low temperatures down to minus 60 degrees. In September last year, the FRL research team, in which LG Energy Solution and KAIST are jointly conducting research, published in the leading journal "Nature Energy" research results on a lithium metal cell that can travel more than 800 km on a single charge, has a lifespan exceeding a cumulative 300,000 km, and can reduce charging time to 12 minutes. In October, through joint research with Pohang University of Science and Technology POSTECH and Sungkyunkwan University, it also developed a core electrolyte technology that can simultaneously improve the low-temperature performance and thermal safety of lithium-ion batteries. An LG Energy Solution official said, "We are continuously expanding R&D investment to secure differentiated technology leadership," adding, "We will not stop at simply developing new technologies, but will introduce technologies with high mass producibility and completeness that can broaden the base of the battery industry."

artigo.texto: Conversas da PF revelam diálogos de Hugo Motta com banqueiro sobre terreno e mercado de carbono Mensagens obtidas pela Polícia Federal (PF) trouxeram à tona uma série de diálogos entre o presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), e o fundador do Banco Master, Daniel Vorcaro. As conversas, que agora são objeto de investigação, abordam temas sensíveis como uma possível “sociedade” para a compra de um terreno em João Pessoa (PB) e discussões sobre um projeto de lei crucial para o mercado de carbono no Brasil. As revelações apontam para uma proximidade entre o parlamentar e o banqueiro, levantando questionamentos sobre a natureza desses contatos em meio a processos legislativos e transações financeiras. A apuração da PF sugere que a relação entre Motta e Vorcaro ia além de meros contatos institucionais. Os detalhes das mensagens indicam um envolvimento em negociações que podem ter implicações tanto no âmbito empresarial quanto no político, especialmente considerando o papel de Motta na Câmara dos Deputados e os interesses comerciais de Vorcaro. Diálogos sobre Negócio Imobiliário em João Pessoa Em 9 de março de 2024, Hugo Motta teria procurado Daniel Vorcaro para discutir a negociação de venda de um terreno situado na capital paraibana. Essa conversa ganha relevância ao ser contextualizada com um empréstimo de R$ 22 milhões, contraído no mesmo mês por Bianca Medeiros, cunhada do presidente da Câmara. O financiamento, concedido pelo Banco Master de Vorcaro, destinou-se justamente à aquisição de um terreno em João Pessoa, o que levanta suspeitas sobre a possível interligação dos eventos. A Polícia Federal investiga se houve algum tipo de facilitação ou influência indevida nas transações, dada a posição de Motta e a simultaneidade dos acontecimentos. A natureza da “sociedade” mencionada nas mensagens é um dos pontos centrais da investigação, buscando esclarecer os termos e os beneficiários de tal arranjo. O Projeto de Lei do Mercado de Carbono em Foco Além das questões imobiliárias, as mensagens revelam que Motta e Vorcaro também discutiram, em 19 de novembro de 2024, o projeto de lei que visa regulamentar o mercado de carbono no Brasil. Trata-se do substitutivo do Senado ao PL 182 de 2024, uma legislação de grande impacto econômico e ambiental. Em uma das mensagens, Motta faz menção a uma questão específica relacionada às seguradoras. A proposta em debate tratava da possibilidade de seguradoras, empresas de previdência e capitalização adquirirem “ativos ambientais” negociados no mercado de carbono para compor suas reservas técnicas e provisões. A versão aprovada pelo Senado previa um mínimo de 0,5% dos recursos para esses ativos, enquanto a Câmara retomou a redação anterior, que estabelecia um percentual de 1% ao ano. Essa alteração é significativa para o setor e para os negócios de Vorcaro. A investigação da PF já havia apontado, em junho de 2026, que Vorcaro teria enviado propostas legislativas diretamente ao gabinete do senador Ciro Nogueira (PP-PI), indicando uma “convergência de interesses ilícitos”. Uma dessas propostas, inclusive, tratava da regulamentação do mercado de carbono, reforçando o interesse do banqueiro na matéria. A Defesa de Hugo Motta e as Implicações Políticas Diante das revelações, a defesa de Daniel Vorcaro foi procurada, mas não se manifestou até o momento. Já Hugo Motta, em nota, defendeu-se afirmando que mantém diálogo com representantes do empresariado e de outros setores da sociedade, e que não há qualquer ilícito nos diálogos divulgados. O parlamentar alegou que as conversas foram descontextualizadas e negou ter atuado em benefício próprio ou de terceiros. Motta também anunciou que pretende apresentar queixa-crime contra o senador Veneziano Vital do Rêgo (MDB-PB), acusando-o de calúnia, difamação e divulgação de fake news com finalidade eleitoral. O contexto político é relevante, uma vez que Veneziano concorre à reeleição e tem como adversário o pai de Motta, Nabor Wanderley (Republicanos-PB). Sobre o empréstimo de R$ 22 milhões contratado por sua cunhada com o Banco Master, Motta esclareceu que a operação ocorreu em um período anterior à divulgação das investigações sobre a instituição financeira e seu proprietário. O presidente da Câmara reiterou sua confiança nos órgãos responsáveis pelas investigações, afirmando que cabe a eles responder pelas apurações. artigo.texto: A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Centers (Redata) marca um novo momento para o país, com regras fiscais que devem apoiar a construção de novas estruturas de processamento de dados, algo que é estratégico para qualquer nação com visão de futuro. Mas, assim como outras infraestruturas críticas, os data centers precisam de energia segura e confiável. E, neste ponto, é preciso encarar as demandas do sistema elétrico com pragmatismo técnico, afastando-se de visões dogmáticas e sem considerar pressões externas que careçam de embasamento adequado. Um data center de grande porte exige suprimento ininterrupto de energia de alta densidade 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Cargas dessa magnitude não toleram oscilações de frequência ou tensão. O processamento de dados em nuvem e o treinamento de modelos complexos de inteligência artificial não podem ser paralisados ou desacelerados quando o vento cessa ou quando a noite cai. Uma carga dessa natureza exige um nível de confiabilidade acima de 99%, requerendo, portanto, a presença de fontes firmes de energia. A aprovação do Redata pelo Senado trouxe a flexibilização necessária ao estabelecer o uso de fontes de baixa emissão, abrindo um espaço legítimo para o gás natural no suporte a essas novas demandas. O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), por exemplo, já sinalizou que a regulamentação precisa contemplar múltiplas fontes de geração para dar viabilidade aos empreendimentos, mas as notícias que vêm de Brasília indicam que outras áreas não estão atentas o suficiente para os problemas que poderão ocorrer caso sejam banidas as fontes movidas a gás natural do suprimento a este tipo de demanda. Tal restrição traz um equívoco conceitual e um risco econômico. As fontes renováveis possuem uma limitação estrutural intrínseca, que é sua intermitência. Sem a presença de geração firme de base para regular o sistema, a conexão de gigawatts adicionais em cargas concentradas pode colocar riscos ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), uma vez que o encargo dessa confiabilidade especificamente recairá no próprio sistema interligado. A aposta em baterias para cobrir esse problema esbarra em limitações de custos, de tecnologias específicas e de maturidade comercial. É nesse cenário que o gás natural se afirma como o vetor indispensável para a transição. Tratando-se de uma fonte de baixa emissão, o gás provê a energia firme e despachável exigida pelos data centers. Países que lideram a corrida dos data centers, como os Estados Unidos, utilizam o gás natural como pilar central de segurança elétrica para viabilizar seus complexos de tecnologia. Impor sobrecustos, condicionalidades punitivas ou exigências de compensação ambiental de carbono trará um efeito adverso. O gás natural brasileiro se tornará menos competitivo, e os investimentos globais serão muito prejudicados em nosso país, e terminarão migrando para países como os Estados Unidos ou a Argentina, onde o suprimento firme a gás é garantido sem amarras regulatórias. O Congresso Nacional agiu com maturidade ao reconhecer a importância das fontes de baixa emissão no Redata. É preciso que o governo federal, respeitando a decisão dos parlamentares, siga pelo mesmo caminho. Xisto Vieira Filho é CEO na Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas (Abraget).

artigo.texto: Trinity Airways(091810) said on the 28th that it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on mutual cooperation regarding the carbon offset and reduction scheme for international aviation (CORSIA) and the emissions trading system with NH Investment & Securities. It is the first business agreement signed in Korea between an airline and a financial company in the fields of CORSIA and the emissions transaction system, and the two companies said they plan to expand cooperation across the entire carbon credit market. The agreement was prepared to proactively strengthen CORSIA response capabilities and establish a cooperation framework for the carbon credit market in line with the carbon reduction policy for the aviation institutional sector promoted by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport and the overall direction of CORSIA implementation. The MOU centers on multifaceted cooperation, including the exchange of information and the establishment of a joint response system for CORSIA and the domestic greenhouse gas carbon credit market and policies; the joint promotion of projects related to carbon credits; and various activities for the development of the carbon market. CORSIA offsetting is carried out by securing eligible carbon credits corresponding to the required offset amount within the set implementation period and then retiring them in the registry. Retiring credits means permanently deleting the secured carbon credits from the registry so the credits cannot be used again. Trinity Airways purchased 20,000 tons (t) of CORSIA-eligible carbon credits and signed a contract to retire those credits to proactively prepare for the obligation. It also plans to gradually secure more than 10% of the Phase 1 volume that must be offset by Jan. 2028 by additionally purchasing eligible credits by the end of this year to ensure stability in complying with greenhouse gas regulations and to ease uncertainties in the supply and demand of carbon credits. The signing ceremony was held on the 21st at Sono Trinity Commons in Gangseo-gu, Seoul, and was attended by Seo Dong-bin, executive in charge of corporate management support at Trinity Airways, Park Geon-hu, head of the Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities, and other key officials from both companies. Seo said, "Through cooperation with NH Investment & Securities, we will strengthen our capabilities in sourcing and managing credits and build an efficient response system from a mid- to long-term perspective."
