artigo.texto: The Pune battery technology centre planned by COEP Technological University and JSW Projects will receive an investment of more than Rs 800 crore and is expected to create over 1,000 jobs across the battery ecosystem, according to the memorandum of understanding signed by the two institutions. The centre will be established at COEP’s Chikhali Research Park in two phases. The partners describe it as India’s first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale research and development centre, with work focused initially on lithium-ion battery cells and later expanding to sodium-ion and other advanced battery technologies. The first phase will cover battery-cell design, simulation and prototyping. The second phase will establish a cell validation facility capable of manufacturing cells with capacities ranging from 100 to 600 Ah. The facility is intended to take technologies beyond laboratory research and towards testing and development at pilot scale. The partnership will bring COEP students and faculty into projects with industry engineers. It will support joint research, technology development, academic publications and intellectual property creation, while providing hands-on exposure to commercially relevant battery technologies. COEP vice-chancellor Prof Sunil Bhirud said the collaboration could help develop indigenous alternatives to imported batteries. The university said the centre would also create an institutional platform for training and research linked to the wider battery ecosystem. JSW Group chairman Sajjan Jindal said the partnership would focus on developing cells suited to Indian climatic conditions and applications. “Cells are the new fuel of this century,” he said, adding that India needed to build domestic capabilities to manufacture them. The proposed centre is expected to support applications in electric vehicles, grid storage and clean energy. Its planned research scope places Pune’s academic and industrial capabilities within a sector that requires cell design, validation and manufacturing expertise, rather than only battery assembly. The MoU does not specify an operational opening date in the information available. The project’s immediate milestones are the rollout of the first phase for design, simulation and prototyping, followed by the planned cell validation and pilot-scale manufacturing facility in the second phase.

artigo.texto: TerraFlow and DG Matrix Pair Flow Battery With Solid-State Transformer for Live AI Compute TerraFlow Energy and DG Matrix plan to combine vanadium flow storage, a programmable solid-state transformer and Dell servers in a live U.S. AI-compute deployment designed to buffer fast-changing electrical loads. Published · 4 min read TerraFlow Energy and DG Matrix announced on September 28 a commercial agreement to deploy a VRFB solid-state transformer system designed to power a live high-performance computing cluster in the United States. The initial installation will combine TerraFlow’s long-duration uninterruptible power system with DG Matrix’s programmable Interport solid-state transformer and Dell PowerEdge servers, creating a test of how long-duration storage and software-defined power conversion can buffer rapidly changing AI computing loads. The companies have not disclosed the deployment location, total megawatt load, battery energy capacity, project cost or commercial-operation date. That makes the announcement a technology-deployment milestone rather than evidence that the architecture has already proven performance at hyperscale. The central claim is narrower: the partners intend to put the combined system against live compute loads and use it to manage power flow between the grid, on-site generation, storage and servers in real time. VRFB solid-state transformer system targets fast-changing compute loads In their September 28 announcement, TerraFlow and DG Matrix said the architecture is intended to absorb rapid changes in computing demand before those changes propagate upstream into electrical infrastructure. TerraFlow’s LDUPS platform combines uninterruptible-power functionality with hours of energy storage, while DG Matrix’s Interport platform performs programmable power conversion and routing among sources, storage and compute loads. The approach addresses a problem that is becoming more important as AI data centers adopt denser computing hardware. Power demand inside an AI facility can change quickly as large GPU clusters move between workload states. Those variations do not automatically translate into a grid reliability event, but sufficiently large and synchronized load changes can complicate planning, protection and operational coordination. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation is already developing dedicated standards for computational loads. NERC’s Project 2026-02 identifies reduced visibility, system-instability risk during disturbances and planning uncertainty among the issues associated with rapidly growing data-center and other computational loads. Long-duration flow storage adds a different role than conventional UPS batteries TerraFlow describes its LDUPS architecture as a long-duration system rather than a conventional short-ride-through UPS. The company’s LDUPS platform supports vanadium or organic electrolyte chemistries and is designed in modular 1.25 MW building blocks with scalable energy duration. In the announced deployment, the vanadium redox flow battery is expected to provide both fast response and multi-hour energy capacity. That combination is important because data-center power systems normally separate several functions. UPS equipment handles very short interruptions and power-quality events, backup generators or other on-site generation provide longer-duration support, and grid-connected batteries may perform peak shaving or other energy-management tasks. TerraFlow and DG Matrix are proposing to coordinate several of those functions through a common power architecture. Microgrid Media has previously examined solid-state transformer testing at UC San Diego, where a California Energy Commission-funded demonstration is designed to connect a 2 MW AI computing load through medium-voltage power electronics and flexible-load controls. The TerraFlow-DG Matrix project is distinct, but both efforts reflect growing interest in replacing static data-center electrical architectures with systems that can actively control how computing loads interact with the grid. DG Matrix is also increasing the power density of its Interport platform DG Matrix said on September 25 that its Interport platform had increased output from 200 kW to 400 kW using silicon-carbide power electronics while maintaining essentially the same power-module footprint. That product update does not establish the size of the TerraFlow deployment, but it provides context for the platform being integrated with the flow-battery system. For the initial project, the companies have not disclosed how many Interport units will be deployed or the voltage architecture feeding the Dell servers. They also have not published a target for round-trip efficiency, load-ramp smoothing, outage duration, grid-services revenue or the amount of utility capacity the system could defer. Those omissions matter because claims about making data centers more flexible need operating evidence. Microgrid Media’s coverage of NERC’s computational-load reliability work has highlighted the need for better modeling, commissioning, telemetry and coordination as large computing facilities connect to the bulk power system. The commercial test will matter more than the first-of-a-kind label TerraFlow and DG Matrix describe the deployment as the first integrated U.S. architecture combining a vanadium redox flow battery with a solid-state transformer to directly power a live high-performance computing cluster. That characterization is a company claim and should be treated as such until independently established across the market. The more consequential question is whether the system can demonstrate measurable performance under real AI workloads. Useful results would include how quickly storage responds to workload transients, how much upstream load variability is reduced, how efficiently power moves through the architecture, and whether the battery can provide meaningful energy duration without compromising UPS-level respons

artigo.texto: Data centers are drawing protests and city hall spats across the country. You wouldn't have known it Saturday night in downtown Washington, DC. When I arrived at Data after Dark, a "pro-data center" party 10 minutes before it was scheduled to start, there were already a few dozen attendees waiting in the rain to get into Pubkey, a bitcoin-themed bar. I was led downstairs, into a VIP room sponsored by AI company Cognitio, where a live jazz trio was playing and drinks were flowing. White gift bags with a black server rack above the words "come and take it" were everywhere. The party hadn't officially started yet, but the room was already full of people. Guests in cocktail dresses and suits (a handful of whom donned the signature of a Hill employee — a pin on their lapel) bounced around the room, pitching themselves and networking. I surprisingly only saw two tech bro vests. The event brought together figures from a trio of tech and free-market organizations. Jonas Du, a journalist at Mike Solana's tech-and-politics media company, Pirate Wires, first posted it on X in August. He organized the event with Casey Given, CEO of Young Voices, a nonprofit talent agency for "classically liberal" writers and commentators, and Ed Tarnowski, a tech fellow at free-market think tank R Street Institute. They were expecting to throw a get-together at his rowhouse in DC, but after more than 300,000 views and hundreds of requests to attend, it became more serious. "We host parties every other month at my rowhouse — it's usually no more than 70 or 80 people, and that's what it was," Du told me. "But we hit 70 within a day." The final Partiful guest list was over 1,000 people, more than double Pubkey's 500-person maximum capacity. The venue was packed, and a security guard told me that if I left, I wouldn't be allowed back in. I wandered upstairs, where I was confronted by flashing lights and a DJ. Behind him, an LED screen showed stock assembly-line footage and the occasional video of Robert Downey Jr., presumably as Tony Stark. The music was loud, but so too were the conversations. The multiple bars never lacked patrons ordering one of the themed cocktails, like a Loudoun County Iced Tea — the county with the most data centers in the world — or an SMRtini, a play on small modular reactors. Around 10 p.m., the music was turned off, but the hum of the crowd stopped for no one. A few weeks before the event, a Partiful blast was sent asking for volunteers for the toast session: that time had come. At least three protesters jumped on the stage separately to hijack the pro-data-center toasts. I couldn't hear them, and the crowd couldn't either, but that didn't stop them from booing and chanting "USA" to get them off stage and out of the bar. "Who believes in freedom?" Adam Thierer, toast-giver and resident senior fellow at the think tank R Street Institute, asked the crowd. "Well, we know who doesn't believe in freedom, it's the kind of freaks that were just up here charging the stage." "All of us need to go out into the world and fight — not for AI, but for America," Manhattan Institute fellow Daniel Di Martino told the crowd during his speech. What was a party quickly turned into a rally as the toasts turned more into battle cries. If you watched the crowd on hand, you'd think a ban on data centers had just been lifted, and a new version of America was on the horizon. The music came back on, and the dance floor was packed, with a few people dancing to the electronic music. Everyone seemed to be on the same page, but I did talk to a couple of guests who were hoping for a little more. One woman who came with her husband from Baltimore — about a 50-minute drive — said she was expecting more technical talk about data centers. She said her icebreaker for entering a conversation was, "Do you have a GPU?" She said only one person knew what that was. (A graphics processing unit is a piece of computing used for graphics and video rendering, a key tool for AI.) She said she'd be back if they hosted another party, though. Another guest didn't expect as many people as there were, and was excited to be among other pro-data-center people, but he didn't really get the chance to talk about them. One attendee, who works for a defense technology company, told me it was refreshing to be in an environment not ruled by "slopulism" (a term he explained to me as a sort of lazy populism). He said that people liked to hate data centers simply because it's popular to do so, but haven't bothered to explore the arguments for them. The audience was thunderous throughout, and the overall mood of the night was optimistic — celebratory even. What exactly they were celebrating is still unclear. They may have just been celebrating the fact that many people felt the same way they did. Du, one of the organizers, said the event wasn't planned to change people's minds — it was promoted widely as pro-data center — but he hopes they won over some skeptics. The main goal, though, was to party. "We want people to have a good time, and I don't know how much actual conversation and debate happens," he said. "I don't know how much appetite there was for that."

artigo.texto: TerraFlow Energy and DG Matrix to Deploy First U.S. VRFB and Solid-State Transformer Architecture to Power Live High-Performance Compute Commercial agreement integrates TerraFlow's LDUPS™ with DG Matrix's Interport™ to create a new power architecture for AI data centers that manages compute loads while protecting the grid HOUSTON, Sept. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TerraFlow Energy and DG Matrix today announced a commercial agreement to deploy the first integrated vanadium redox flow battery (VRFB) and solid-state transformer (SST) architecture in the United States to directly power a live high-performance computing cluster. The initial deployment will integrate TerraFlow's LDUPS™ long-duration uninterruptible power system with DG Matrix's Interport™ solid-state transformer technology and Dell PowerEdge servers, putting a new data center power architecture into operation against real compute loads. The significance goes beyond combining two technologies. AI data centers are introducing enormous new loads to the power system, but the challenge is not only how much electricity they consume. High-performance compute can change power demand rapidly, pushing that volatility back through electrical infrastructure built for more predictable loads. The integrated architecture is designed to manage power between the grid, on-site generation, energy storage, and compute in real time. TerraFlow's LDUPS™ combines the millisecond response required for UPS functionality with hours of energy capacity, allowing it to continuously buffer changes in compute demand. DG Matrix's Interport™ provides programmable solid-state power conversion, routing, and control between power sources and the compute load. Together, the technologies are designed to absorb rapid changes in demand before they reach the grid and other upstream electrical infrastructure. "AI is changing the physics of the power system, and simply adding more generation doesn't solve that problem," said Jon Parrella, CEO of TerraFlow Energy. "We have to change how these enormous loads connect to and interact with the grid. By putting long-duration storage and intelligent power distribution between the grid and the compute, we can give data centers the power performance they need without asking the grid to absorb every movement in demand. That is how we start turning data centers from grid liabilities into grid assets." The commercial agreement establishes a framework for TerraFlow and DG Matrix to bring the integrated LDUPS™ and Interport™ architecture into data center projects beyond the initial deployment. The companies are targeting applications where AI and high-performance computing require greater control over how power is delivered, managed, and exchanged with the grid. "AI infrastructure requires us to rethink power distribution from the grid all the way to the compute," said Haroon Inam, CEO of DG Matrix. "Solid-state transformers allow us to control power dynamically rather than simply move it from one voltage to another. Combining that capability with TerraFlow's LDUPS™ technology creates an architecture that can respond to the compute load in real time while controlling how that load is presented to the grid. This is the direction data center power infrastructure needs to go." The architecture also addresses a growing issue facing utilities and data center developers: how to connect gigawatts of new compute demand without requiring the power system to respond instantaneously to every change occurring inside the data center. By controlling those changes behind the meter, integrated storage and power distribution can help make large loads more predictable, more flexible, and ultimately easier for the grid to serve. For TerraFlow and DG Matrix, the initial deployment is the starting point for a commercial architecture designed to scale with the rapidly growing power requirements of AI infrastructure. "We aren't building another layer of backup power," Parrella said. "We're building the infrastructure that sits between compute and the grid and allows both of them to perform better." About TerraFlow Energy TerraFlow Energy is transforming energy storage from backup equipment into critical power infrastructure. Built on long-duration, non-flammable vanadium flow battery technology, the company's battery-in-building architecture combines uninterrupted power, long-duration energy storage, and controllable load management in a single platform that simplifies electrical infrastructure for AI data centers and other energy-intensive facilities. By turning large electrical loads into flexible grid assets, TerraFlow helps customers improve resilience, reduce operating costs, accelerate deployment, and strengthen the electric grid. Learn more at www.terraflowenergy.com Advertisement About DG Matrix DG Matrix, the global leader in solid-state transformer solutions, is unlocking power as the binding constraint on AI. It is removing this critical bottleneck of stranded power by building the intelligent power fabric of the AI data center. Built on the world's first commercially available, programmable multi-port solid-state transformer, the company's AI-enabled Interport™ platform converts, routes and controls every electron, between the grid, on-site generation, storage and compute loads through a single, software-defined stage. DG Matrix delivers an integrated and simpler solution for faster deployment, lower energy costs, native 800 VDC readiness and protection from GPU pulse loads. Because speed to power is speed to inference, DG Matrix helps hyperscale, neocloud and colocation operators bring AI capacity online in months instead of years — at scale, anywhere in the world. Learn more at https://www.dgmatrix.com/. artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz has secured priority access to ProLogium’s latest Gen4 solid-state battery cells, expanding a partnership that could help bring higher-energy, safer, and more efficient batteries to future electric vehicles. The companies signed a joint testing agreement on September 24, 2026. Mercedes-Benz will test ProLogium’s Gen4 cells for electrical, thermal, and safety performance at its own facilities and at specialist testing centers. One point is important: the official announcement describes “priority access,” not exclusive rights. The agreement gives Mercedes-Benz early access to test the technology, but it does not say that Mercedes has exclusive global rights to the cells. The deal builds on nearly 10 years of cooperation between the two companies. Mercedes-Benz invested in ProLogium in 2022 and joined its board as part of efforts to develop next-generation battery technology. Jörg Burzer, Mercedes‑Benz Group AG, Chief Technology Officer, said: “At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility through technological leadership and innovation. Our long-standing partnership with ProLogium is a strong example of how we bring the best expertise together to advance next-generation battery technologies. By combining ProLogium’s pioneering solid-state battery approach with Mercedes-Benz’s deep battery development, testing, and integration capabilities, we are taking the next step in exploring advanced battery technologies for future electric vehicles.” More Energy, Less Weight: Gen4’s Big Battery Pitch Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion cells with a solid material. The technology can allow manufacturers to use higher-capacity materials while reducing some fire and safety risks linked to liquid electrolytes. ProLogium’s Gen4 lithium ceramic battery uses a fully inorganic electrolyte and ceramic separator. The company says its anode-less version can reach 430–470 Wh/kg and 1,000–1,100 Wh/L at the cell level. These specifications come from the company. They show cell-level performance, not the energy density of a full vehicle battery pack. ProLogium states that Gen4 combines high energy density with fast charging. It also performs well in low temperatures and has better safety features. Its active safety system is intended to help prevent thermal runaway. The potential benefit for EVs is significant. Higher energy density means a battery can store more energy without adding as much weight. That could support longer driving range or allow automakers to use smaller battery packs for the same range. Mercedes Has Already Put Solid-State to the Road Test Mercedes-Benz has been testing solid-state batteries on public roads since 2025. In September 2025, the company reported that a modified EQS test vehicle traveled 1,205 kilometers on a single charge from Stuttgart to Malmö. The vehicle arrived with about 137 kilometers of remaining range. That vehicle used lithium-metal solid-state cells supplied by Factorial Energy, not ProLogium. Mercedes-Benz announced that the new battery boosts usable energy by 25%. It also maintains a weight and size similar to the standard EQS battery. The demonstration showed the potential of solid-state technology, but it was a test vehicle rather than a mass-produced model. The new ProLogium agreement gives Mercedes another route to develop the technology and compare different solid-state battery approaches. The EV Battery Market Is Getting Bigger—Fast The timing is important because global demand for EV batteries is growing rapidly. The International Energy Agency estimates that EV battery deployment hit 1.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025. This is nearly a 30% increase from 2024 and over seven times the level in 2020. EV batteries accounted for more than 70% of total battery deployment during the year. Global electric-car sales also exceeded 20 million units in 2025, up about 20% year over year. One in every four new cars sold worldwide was electric. That is creating strong demand for batteries that can deliver better range, faster charging, and improved safety without sharply increasing vehicle cost. But solid-state technology is entering a market already dominated by conventional lithium-ion batteries. The global battery industry remains heavily concentrated. The IEA says global lithium-ion battery manufacturing capacity exceeded 4 TWh at the end of 2025, up about 30% from 2024. China accounted for more than 80% of global manufacturing capacity and more than 80% of battery-cell production. Chinese battery makers also supplied almost 75% of global EV battery deployment in 2025. This creates a major challenge for European automakers seeking more control over their battery supply chains. Solid-state batteries could offer both a technology advantage and a chance to diversify supply. ProLogium is building its first overseas gigafactory in Dunkirk, France, giving Europe another potential source of advanced battery cells. ProLogium Is Moving Toward Mass Production ProLogium has already moved beyond the laboratory stage. The company began mass production of its Gen3.5 lithium ceramic battery in Taiwan in September 2026. A third-party TÜV test confirmed a 381 Wh/kg gravimetric energy density and 903 Wh/L volumetric energy density for its 185.4-Ah large-format cell. ProLogium says its Taiwan gigafactory had shipped more than 800,000 cells by 2026. It is now preparing to bring Gen4 production to Europe. The Dunkirk factory broke ground in February 2026. ProLogium’s current plan calls for 0.8 GWh of Gen4 production in 2028, with capacity rising to 4 GWh by 2030 and 12 GWh by 2032. The company has also reserved land that could allow the site to expand to as much as 48 GWh in the future. This planned expansion will be important if automakers want solid-state cells at meaningful scale. Europe Wants More Local Battery Production The European link is important for Mercedes-Benz. artigo.texto: With one foot in the Capitol and the other already on the campaign trail, the Senate is poised to consider a bill Wednesday that sounds, at least, like it would shield consumers from rising utility costs tied to data centers. The truth is far more complex — and a lot less consequential. Politically, Republicans are betting that the Ratepayer Protection Act will show voters they care about addressing the cost of living. Crucially, the legislation also would help one of the GOP’s own — Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio — who’s facing a tough re-election fight and has become a prime target for political attacks over data centers. Husted and the GOP claim that the legislation would protect consumers from paying more for electricity as a result of data centers. But, in practice, the legislation is little more than a recommendation. The measure would require state utility regulators to consider adopting new federal standards to ensure data center companies foot their own bill within two years. Because the legislation accomplishes about as much as a press release, Democrats appear poised to oppose it — or, at least, block it from advancing on an expedited timeline before the midterm elections. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called the bill a “fraud, plain and simple.” Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., likened it to a “political act.” Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., said that “it’s clearly designed to help them in campaigns” and not “actually solve any problems, because it does nothing.” And Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told MS NOW that it’s a “a political ploy to enable Husted to go home and boast about getting a bill done when it’s really a fraud on consumers.” While the bill received overwhelming bipartisan support in the House, passing earlier this month in a 417-3 vote, Senate Democrats are instead labeling it a “bait-and-switch.” And some Republicans acknowledge that the bill does more politically than it does practically. “Would I like to do more? Yeah,” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said. “But on the other hand, is it better than nothing? Yeah.” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., agreed that the bill doesn’t accomplish much, noting that most utilities are “managed through local and state decision making.” But he also agreed that it “probably would help” Husted in his re-election efforts. Ohio’s Senate seat — one of a growing number that Republicans are rushing to shore up ahead of November — could be instrumental in determining control of the Senate next year. Husted, who has routinely trailed in the polls in his bid for a full six-year term, has faced an onslaught of ads in Ohio — including from his Democratic rival, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown — casting him as the “face of data centers” that are contributing to higher energy bills. On Tuesday, Husted called his data center legislation “the only bill that has a chance to get to the president’s desk before we get to the election.” Asked why the bill does not make the regulations mandatory, Husted answered that it was because “the states run the grids, and so you have to work with the states to do that.” If Democrats block the bill during a procedural vote on Wednesday, Husted and other Republicans appear eager to cast Democrats as obstructionists. Husted told reporters that it’s up to Democrats “to determine whether or not they want to play politics or they want to solve affordability issues for the American people.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said that voting against the bill “makes it pretty hard for Democrats” to attack Husted over data centers and the cost of living. “It’s a chance to actually make law. It’s not just making a point,” Thune said Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Bruce Lear lives in Sioux City and has been connected to Iowa’s public schools for 38 years. He taught for eleven years and represented educators as an Iowa State Education Association regional director for 27 years until retiring. He can be reached at BruceLear2419@gmail.com Growing up, organized sports consisted of little league, or high school baseball in the spring and summer. Fall and winter meant basketball, since our school was too tiny for football. No adult had yet figured out NBA, and MLB dreams were a sure money maker—so there were no sports academies or traveling leagues. But we did have the town basketball court. It was a kid sanctuary where kid law prevailed. No adult supervision, no minimum or maximum age, and both genders were welcome. The rules were simple and strictly enforced. If you cried, you left. We called our own fouls loosely. If you overshot, and the ball went into the crick, you retrieved it. There were arguments, and fights, but there was urgency to end conflict, because finishing the game was more important than the fight. We needed rules or our game would be swallowed by conflict. Now, like the basketball court, data centers need clear and enforceable rules, or Iowa small towns and rural life will be swallowed just like our basketball games. Currently, Congress seems to lack urgency and understanding on how to catch up to the data center invasion. That sounds like a bad movie, but it’s a serious threat. Even the creators of AI are warning there needs to be a slowdown. That means the urgency to govern is in the hands of local and state lawmakers. It’s time to play catch up. History tells us this happened before during the industrial revolution. As industry grew and became more powerful, there were no laws regulating child labor, worker safety, wages, and other general working conditions. Working class people suffered, while robber barons lived in gilded mansions. I fear the new crop of robber barons are tech billionaires who are quickly trying to build data centers before the laws catch up. They promise high paying jobs but offer no guarantees. They don’t acknowledge their huge consumption of electricity and water, and they ignore the impact these large structures will have on the community. The adage “History may not repeat itself, but it often rhymes” is on target—even if Mark Twain probably never said it. I can hear that haunting rhyme echoing across Iowa corn fields while politicians dither. President Donald Trump said, “Towns that reject data centers risk becoming backwards and poor.” But in a recent Emerson College poll, 60 percent of Iowans believe data centers will negatively impact the environment. Both candidates for governor have proposed new restrictions on data centers. The Iowa legislature needs to act quickly and decisively. Here are my suggestions for regulating data centers in Iowa. In 1991, Iowa lawmakers allowed gambling but also passed strict guidelines. For example, the Iowa Gaming Commission had to approve the location, communities had to vote to see if the majority supported the idea, and each casino was required to provide a percentage of revenue to a separate nonprofit organization for distribution to benefit the community and surrounding area. I’m on one of those boards now. I believe this model would work for data centers, along with five other requirements. 1. Billion-dollar tech companies don’t need tax breaks to locate in Iowa. 2. The tech company must strengthen the electrical grid and pay for its use. 3. The tech company must in writing assure the community there is sufficient water supply and pay for upgrades to the system and water used. 4. The tech company must reduce the noise pollution. 5. The tech company must guarantee the number of permanent jobs. Data centers may be an innovation revolution impossible to prevent, but it should be regulated. No one should ever threaten violence, but we should vote for politicians willing to seriously regulate data centers. Top photo is by Chad Davis, available via Wikimedia Commons.

artigo.texto: Scaling India’s BESS Electronics for Energy Transition ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: India’s energy storage requirement is projected to surge from 82 GWh in 2026-27 to 411.4 GWh by 2031-32, with BESS accounting for 236.22 GWh. - Why it matters: EPCs and developers must look beyond battery cells to the electronics layer—BMS, power conversion, and thermal controls—to ensure system reliability and grid performance. - Watch: The evolution of domestic manufacturing standards for BMS and power electronics as the industry shifts toward larger, multi-hour grid-scale storage. Background and Context As India accelerates its renewable energy transition, the focus on energy storage has intensified. According to the Central Electricity Authority’s (CEA) National Electricity Plan, the nation’s total energy-storage requirement is projected to rise from approximately 82 GWh in 2026-27 to a massive 411.4 GWh by 2031-32. Within this framework, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are expected to contribute 236.22 GWh. To support this trajectory, the government has introduced viability-gap funding mechanisms, incentivizing developers to integrate storage with renewable projects. Key Details While procurement trends show a shift toward larger, multi-hour grid-scale applications, the industry must pivot its focus toward the electronics layer. A modern BESS is a complex integration of cells, battery-management systems (BMS), power-conversion equipment, sensors, and thermal-management systems. The BMS, in particular, is critical; as systems move toward higher voltages and longer durations, the BMS architecture must manage complex parameters including voltage monitoring, cell balancing, and fault detection. The localization conversation in India is expanding beyond simple battery-pack assembly. There is a growing need to domesticate printed circuit board assemblies, control boards, communication modules, and power-management systems. This shift is not merely for import substitution but is essential to customize systems for India’s unique operating conditions, such as extreme temperatures and grid fluctuations. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, reliability is the new benchmark for project success. As BESS installations scale, an electronics failure can compromise system availability and grid performance. Consequently, manufacturing and procurement processes must prioritize inspection, functional testing, and traceability. The ability to track the production history and test results of critical electronic assemblies is becoming a vital component of the broader reliability architecture required for long-term project viability. What Happens Next India’s standards ecosystem is currently evolving to match this market growth. New regulatory frameworks covering electrical energy-storage systems and safety requirements are expected to create greater consistency in system design and performance. As the nation continues to integrate massive amounts of variable renewable energy, the development of a robust domestic electronics supply chain will be the cornerstone of India’s energy security. This transition reflects the broader maturity of the India renewable energy sector as it moves from pilot projects to a sophisticated, grid-integrated ecosystem.

artigo.texto: A Kyivstar, que lidera o mercado de telefonia celular ucraniano, foi atingida por um bombardeio russo no domingo (27), segundo o TecMundo. A companhia informou à agência Interfax que ninguém se feriu. Na mesma ofensiva, um data center da Vodafone teria sido atingido, de acordo com o Ministério da Defesa da Rússia. A Vodafone, dona da segunda maior rede celular da região, não quis se pronunciar. Outro data center na capital ucraniana também foi alvo da ofensiva de domingo, que feriu um adulto e duas crianças, segundo o presidente Volodymyr Zelensky. Conforme a Reuters, estruturas do tipo usadas por operadoras locais estão entre os alvos prioritários. Em um dos episódios, explosões cortaram a conexão de aproximadamente 100 mil residências ao longo da semana, principalmente em Kiev e cidades vizinhas, segundo o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia. Autoridades ucranianas afirmam que os bombardeios comprometeram sistemas críticos de segurança, elevando o risco de mortes durante ataques. O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Andrii Sybha, declarou no X que a Rússia mira centros de dados para interromper o fluxo de informações. Ele também mencionou drones Shahed com propulsão a jato, variante capaz de voar acima de 600 km/h e em altitudes maiores, o que dificulta a defesa aérea. No mês passado, um drone guiado por IA matou três civis no país. Com informações da Reuters.

artigo.texto: NineDot Adds 20 MW Battery Energy Storage Site NineDot Energy has opened its largest battery energy storage site to date in Hunts Point, New York. The new system adds nearly 20 MW of capacity to the local electricity network. NineDot expects it to become fully operational before next summer. The project shows how community scale battery energy storage can help grids handle peak demand. It can also improve grid resilience during heat waves and other periods of high electricity use. Battery Energy Storage Supports Peak Demand The Hunts Point system can deliver nearly 20 MW of power when electricity demand rises. According to NineDot, this is enough to supply nearly 20,000 homes during peak grid hours. The system can also reduce the need for nearby gas fired peaker plants. Utilities typically rely on these plants when electricity demand reaches high levels. Batteries offer another option by storing electricity and returning it to the grid when demand increases. “We’re honored to bring this battery storage site to the Hunts Point community,” said Adam Cohen, NineDot’s Chief Technology Officer and Co-founder. “Hunts Point has historically been overburdened by high-emitting fossil fuels, and this battery storage facility marks an inflection point in improving the local environment and grid reliability.” NineDot built the project on the former site of a fuel oil trucking company. The company expects the battery to support further electrification in Hunts Point. Future demand could include electrified markets and truck fleets. NineDot Targets 400 MW in 2026 NineDot has already used its battery fleet to support the grid during periods of high demand. During New York’s July 1 to 4, 2026 heat wave, nine NineDot projects exported nearly 34 MW at peak times. The batteries supported Con Edison’s local distribution network as well as the wider state transmission system. Currently, NineDot operates 11 projects across six locations in Staten Island and the Bronx. Together, they provide 39 MW of battery capacity. Meanwhile, the company continues to expand its battery energy storage portfolio. More than 60 additional projects are now in development. Its total project pipeline exceeds 1 GW. By the end of 2026, NineDot aims to have 400 MW of battery storage in operation, under construction or in development. Electricity networks face growing demand from electrification and renewable energy deployment. Distributed battery storage can help networks respond to those changes. In particular, batteries can supply power during peak periods and reduce pressure on existing grid infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Stakeholders call for carbon trading framework reforms DAR ES SALAAM: CARBON trading stakeholders have called for reforms to carbon trading framework after Carbon Tanzania temporarily halted its YaedaEyasi Landscape Project due to shifting global market demands and rising compliance costs. The suspension comes as international buyers increasingly favour carbon credits certified under the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market’s (ICVCM) Core Carbon Principles (CCP), while existing domestic regulations make it costly for local projects to meet the new standards. Speaking to the Daily News recently, Carbon Tanzania Chief Executive Officer, Ms Sally Capper said the project had suffered a sharp decline in funding as buyers shifted away from traditional REDD+ forest protection credits. “The decision comes as the project faces a sharp decline in funding as a result of global demand that is prioritising Core Carbon Principles (CCPs)-labelled carbon credits, which entail high costs to upgrade projects to new methodologies and a prohibitive domestic regulatory framework,” Ms Capper said. She said the temporary suspension would allow stakeholders to address the challenges and identify solutions that would enable the project to transition to CCPlabelled standards and secure long-term funding. The Yaeda-Eyasi Landscape Project protects about 108,000 hectares of dryland forest in northern Tanzania, the ancestral homeland of the Hadza hunter-gatherers who have lived in the area for thousands of years. Implemented since 2013 through a partnership between Carbon Tanzania and Hadza and Datooga communities, the project works with 11 villages involving about 63,000 people across Manyara and Arusha regions. Ms Capper said the changing voluntary carbon market had significantly reduced demand for conventional REDD+ credits, with many buyers now preferring carbon removal projects over emission reduction initiatives. She said Tanzania also lacks some of the national datasets required under the new CCP methodologies, making it difficult for local project developers to transition their credits quickly to meet emerging global standards. According to her, the combination of changing market expectations and regulatory costs has disrupted revenues earned by communities participating in carbon projects. “Funds are actively being sought to bridge the gap until the project can upgrade,” she said. While reaffirming Carbon Tanzania’s commitment to its community partners, Ms Capper said the current framework places an unsustainable financial burden on project developers. “Our primary duty is to ensure they continue to receive the financial benefits of their stewardship. To do that, we need to bridge this funding gap and work alongside other stakeholders to build a regulatory framework in Tanzania that actually enables high-quality carbon projects to succeed,” she said. She said similar regulatory challenges had also forced Carbon Tanzania to pause development of another project covering the Tongwe and Masito forests in western Tanzania. The company is evaluating how that initiative can achieve long-term success for local district councils, surrounding communities and the company within the existing regulatory framework. Ms Capper said the experience highlighted the importance of transparent and supportive policies in unlocking both the economic and ecological value of Tanzania’s forest resources. “To make nature-based carbon projects viable in Tanzania over the long term, the national carbon trading regulatory framework needs to be reformed,” she said. She warned that without regulatory changes, high investment and compliance costs could threaten the viability of community-based carbon projects across the country. According to 2024 Uongozi Institute report, Carbon Trading in Tanzania, also calls for stronger regulatory and institutional frameworks, improved coordination across the sector and benchmarking Tanzania’s carbon trading system against more developed regional and international markets.

artigo.texto: The Baltimore Banner’s annual innovation conference returns for a second year with a program focused on the infrastructure supporting digital businesses and the research institutions helping develop new products and companies. BannerX will be Sept. 30, in Columbia, Maryland. The event launched last year to explore how organizations could navigate the intersection of AI and cybersecurity. This year, the conversation shifts to what it takes to build and sustain the foundation in this space through four main discussions: - Data center development - The risks of adopting AI - Collaboration in the life sciences - How tech intersects with economic policy The program also includes a conversation on Maryland’s innovation future, bringing technology, public policy, workforce development and economic strategy into one discussion. It will explore how those areas intersect and the role of partnerships across government, industry and the broader business community. Speakers leading the conversations represent a range of perspectives from academia, government and industry. They include W. Mason Emnet, senior vice president of public policy at Constellation; Jason Michael Perry, founder and chief AI officer at PerryLabs; and Monica Lopez, privacy officer at VHC Health and cofounder and CEO of Cognitive Insights for AI. Also slated to participate is Bezawit Sumner, chief information security officer and senior director of security and compliance at CRISP Shared Services; Mary Morris, director of innovation initiatives at the University of Maryland, Baltimore; and Bret Schreiber, senior vice president of life sciences and technology at Fulton Financial Corp. Together, the sessions aim to help answer questions like: “Who is prepared to use a new technology?” “What infrastructure does it require?” “Which organizations need to work together to put it into practice?” With the central discussions plus space for networking, the event creates a venue for conversation between the people and institutions involved in turning technological capability into everyday use. BannerX takes place Sept. 30, 2026, on the first floor of 10285 Lakefront at 10285 Little Patuxent Parkway in Columbia, MD. Doors open at 8:30 a.m., and the program runs from 9 to 11:30 a.m. Tickets are $45 and include the discussions, networking and breakfast. The full agenda and registration are available online.

Gotion is expected to invest about €1.59bn, while PowerCo – Volkswagen’s battery manufacturing subsidiary – will contribute approximately €1.62bn. The ventures are planned to produce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells and cathode materials in Valencia, Šurany and Kenitra. Volkswagen Group technology management board member and PowerCo supervisory board chairman Thomas Schmall said: “This marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility. “Volkswagen is the first European automotive manufacturer to cover the entire battery value chain, from development and cathode materials through to production.” In Valencia, PowerCo’s under-construction gigafactory is expected to transfer into a joint venture producing LFP cells, with an annual capacity of 29.1GWh. PowerCo will hold 51% and Gotion 49%, making the venture a controlled PowerCo subsidiary. Gotion is expected to invest about €1.1bn for its stake. The Valencia facility is intended to serve as a European production hub for Volkswagen’s LFP-based Unified Cells. Gotion’s planned cell factory in Šurany will also transfer into a joint venture. The facility will have an annual capacity of 8.4GWh and produce LFP cells for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Gotion will own 51%, with PowerCo holding 49%. In Kenitra, the companies plan to establish a facility producing 100,000t of LFP cathode material annually. Gotion will retain a 51% stake, while PowerCo will own 49%. The project is intended to diversify supply sources for key cathode active materials. PowerCo is expected to contribute approximately €470m to the Šurany and Kenitra projects by 2030 for its 49% stake in each project. The agreement extends a partnership that began in 2020 and covers joint procurement and sales activities in Europe. The transactions remain subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions, including approval from Gotion shareholders and governmental approvals in China and overseas. Gotion said implementation would take place in phases. Volkswagen Group, through its subsidiary Volkswagen (China) Investment, has also entered definitive agreements to sell a 5.3% equity stake in Gotion. The company said its voting rights, board representation, nomination rights and position as a strategic investor would remain unchanged after completion. Gotion chairman Li Zhen added: “Through cross-shareholdings and three joint sites, we are anchoring our shared strategy to localise battery production in Europe, racing to seize the opportunities of global electric mobility, and jointly forging a new paradigm of world-class, win-win cooperation in the lithium battery industry.”

artigo.texto: A U.K. lab test detected only trace lithium in battery material provided by Finnish startup Donut Lab, and the company has cited the result as support for its argument that the much-discussed cell is not lithium-ion. Even so, the test left major questions unanswered — Donut Lab disassembled the sample before analysis, and, as Electrek reported on Sept. 23, no production vehicle used the battery. Here's what to know Intertek's lab in Wilton, U.K., reported 3.4 ppm lithium by weight and 632 ppm sodium in a small amount of material identified as the anode, cathode, and current collector, per Electrek. "We wanted to put this speculation to rest with an independent test demonstrating that it is neither a lithium-ion nor a sodium battery," Donut Lab CEO Marko Lehtimäki explained. Lithium-ion cells typically contain lithium at much higher levels. If the tested material truly came from a functioning Donut Lab cell, the result would seem to rule out the battery chemistry most commonly used in the market. Intertek did not attempt to determine the battery's complete chemistry and was asked only to measure lithium and sodium. The material also reached the lab in "tear down condition" from Donut Lab, so Intertek was not the party that opened a sealed cell. Electrek noted that the published report labeled the material only as "Pouchcell – Cell 1." It said nothing in the document clearly connected that sample to the Donut "V1.5" unit VTT used in energy-density testing. More background Better batteries can help cut EV charging time, extend driving range, strengthen backup power during blackouts and storms, and eventually lower costs for drivers, fleets, and cities transitioning away from fuel-burning vehicles. That promise helped Donut Lab attract significant attention at CES in January, when it said it had the "world's first solid state battery that is ready for use in OEM vehicle manufacturing." But the company's timeline has since come under greater scrutiny as independent testing has slowly emerged. Questions about Donut Lab's claims intensified in June, when Electrek reported that battery researcher Ziroth and more than 20 experts reviewed the voltage curve and swelling data from a Donut Lab cell sent to VTT. They said it behaved like a high-nickel lithium-ion battery with a graphite anode. VTT also measured 185.7 watt-hours per pound (409.3 watt-hours per kilogram) on a Donut cell cycled between 2.3 and 4.25 volts — numbers that fit familiar lithium-ion territory. What's being done? Companies including Toyota, Samsung SDI, Factorial, and QuantumScape have solid-state cells working in lab settings and prototype vehicles, even if large-scale production remains a difficult step. Lehtimäki admitted that the battery was "already in production," but also acknowledged that the 185.5 watt-hours per pound (409 Wh/kg) cell "is not even the cell that's going to be shipped to customers." Where can I learn more? Questions about Donut Lab's battery underscore a broader push to improve chemistry, safety, and real-world EV performance. These stories explore battery advances aimed at extending range and reducing reliance on conventional materials. • Researchers found lithium titanium phosphate could ease range limits that still worry EV buyers. • Engineers are testing long-range lithium-ion batteries with potential for EVs and airplanes. • At the University of Hong Kong, a high-temperature design could open new battery paths. artigo.texto: AI cloud company plans data center in Mayes County CHOUTEAU, Okla. (KOKH) — Cloud computing company Lambda plans to build a data center in Mayes County, a project the company said could generate $500 million in tax revenue over the next decade. The facility will be built in the industrial park’s southern section within the Chouteau-Mazie Public Schools tax boundary, according to Lambda and MidAmerica Industrial Park. Lambda said the project could create up to 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent jobs. The company did not announce a construction start date, completion date or total project cost. The company said its tax projection is based on current rates. “This project will bring an estimated $500 million in tax revenue to our county over the next decade,” Chouteau Mayor Brenda Cunningham said. Lambda said it will use closed-loop cooling technology to recycle water and reduce water use. The company also said it will pay its full electricity costs and fund infrastructure needed for the facility, rather than passing those costs to other Grand River Dam Authority customers. “Lambda will fund the upfront infrastructure costs required to serve the project, ensuring those expenses are not passed on to other GRDA customers,” Grand River Dam Authority CEO Dan Sullivan said. Cloverleaf Infrastructure was selected by GRDA and MidAmerica to prepare the site for Lambda’s development. Lambda and MidAmerica said they will continue meeting with local leaders and residents in the coming weeks.

artigo.texto: A carbon credit may be traded as a single unit, but its value is shaped long before it reaches a buyer. Decisions about project ownership, finance, data, verification and benefit-sharing determine who participates, who carries the risk and who ultimately benefits. As new regulations and international partnerships expand market access, these questions are becoming increasingly important across Africa. They will be central to the Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026, taking place from 13 to 15 October at the Kigali Convention Centre in Rwanda. The summit will convene African governments, project developers, investors, buyers and technical experts involved in decisions across the carbon-market value chain. Countries are approaching these decisions from different regulatory, economic and environmental positions. While recent developments in East Africa demonstrate growing market activity, questions concerning international requirements, technical capacity, investment and benefit-sharing are relevant across Africa. Ousmane Fall SARR, Coordinator of the West African Alliance on Carbon Markets and Climate Finance, says: “African countries are developing carbon markets from different starting points. Stronger African expertise and regional cooperation will be important if the continent is to contribute to the standards and market practices that determine how its projects compete, attract investment and create value.” Against this continental backdrop, East Africa provides a timely example of how the market is developing. In January 2026, Rwanda and Singapore invited applications for carbon-credit projects under their bilateral Implementation Agreement, aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Credits from authorised projects may be used by eligible Singapore-based carbon tax-liable companies to offset up to 5% of their taxable emissions, subject to both governments’ requirements. Across the continent, carbon market frameworks are rapidly taking shape. Kenya and Uganda are strengthening regulatory oversight, regional partnerships are helping governments build market capacity and infrastructure, and South Africa is advancing reforms to modernise its carbon-credit ecosystem and attract investment. Together, these developments are bringing greater focus to questions of authorisation, project ownership, verification, pricing and access to international buyers, while also raising expectations that carbon finance should deliver sustainable economic and development value beyond the credit itself. Emmanuelle Nicholls, Portfolio Director for CMAS, says: “A carbon credit may be the final product, but behind it are decisions about ownership, data, risk, pricing and who ultimately benefits. The conversations in Kigali will examine what credible participation looks like across the full carbon-market value chain.” These decisions have consequences beyond individual transactions. Carbon finance is increasingly connected to conservation, agriculture, soil restoration, food security, clean energy and waste management. Its success will therefore also be judged by whether projects produce credible environmental outcomes and lasting benefits for African economies and communities. A practical example comes from the Chinko Conservation Area in the Central African Republic, where revenue from the Chinko Carbon Project is channelled through a community fund that supports locally selected initiatives, including the expansion of a medical centre in Agoumar. At CMAS 2026, African Parks and Welthungerhilfe, both Bronze Sponsors, will share perspectives on how carbon finance can support conservation, climate resilience, food systems and community development, while highlighting broader questions around project governance, impact and the distribution of value. From project-level impact to market-wide structures, these questions will underpin discussions at CMAS 2026. The programme will address government authorisation, buyer requirements, pricing and offtake, investment risk, early-stage finance, registries and African measurement, reporting and verification capacity. It will connect the question of who sets the terms with the practical requirements for building credible, investment-ready projects and transactions. CMAS 2026 is hosted by the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda, with UNDP and the African Development Bank as host organisations, the Development Bank of Southern Africa as host partner and AUDA-NEPAD as strategic institutional partner. Taking place ahead of COP31, CMAS will focus attention on the decisions behind every carbon credit and what they mean for African governments, projects, investors and communities.

artigo.texto: This Albertan trades in a murky carbon market crucial to Carney's pipeline deal When Ana Avramovic was young, art school was her plan. She landed a job trading power instead, and 20 years later runs her own Calgary firm, dealing in something you can’t see or touch. And the stakes are enormous Article content Everything Ana Avramovic sells sits as numbered entries in a government registry, and none of them are hers. She trades carbon credits, a job so unusual even her mother doesn’t fully understand what she does for a living. She came to carbon from power trading, having cut her teeth at Calgary-based TransAlta Corp. Ask her whether leaving a traditional paycheque to build a firm of her own was brave or reckless. The answer depends on the day. “Overall, excited,” she says. “And then sometimes like, oh my God, what am I doing? What have I done?” When she traded power, explaining her job took one gesture toward a window. “You see that hotel?” she says. “Somebody has to sell them electricity.” Carbon is trickier. You can’t see electricity either, but everyone knows what it’s for. She founded Carbon Merchant in July 2026 to trade industrial carbon and clean fuel credits. Every big emitter in Alberta, from oilsands operators to power producers and miners, has a limit on what it can release into the atmosphere. Beat the limit and you earn credits for cutting emissions. Miss the benchmark and you buy them from somebody who did. Avramovic is the broker in the middle, helping buyers and sellers find each other. The 42-year-old works in a market so opaque that outsiders can’t make sense of it. And, yet the stakes are enormous. The market is one of Canada’s biggest levers against climate change. Its design is a signature priority in Ottawa and lies at the centre of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s deal with Alberta on a possible West Coast pipeline for oil. But there are flaws, too. Critics worry the market is falling short and flooded with cheap credits, which means that meeting the rules is far less expensive for industry. For Avramovic, it is personal. She has two young children, and they will inherit whatever this market does or fails to do. She chose the work because it was the one place her own effort might count. “I’m just one person. It’s not like I can fix it all,” she says, “but I can at least do a little part.” Location, location, emissions Avramovic rents an office at Pavilion, a coworking space in downtown Calgary. She starts around 7 a.m., and her day is nonstop: ICE chat, where energy traders connect on the Intercontinental Exchange, plus texts, calls, Teams meetings, in-person meetings and coffee, lots of it. “A lot of my day is just communicating with different people and figuring out what are they doing, what are they looking to do,” she says. Most of her deals are spot work: one buyer, one seller, done in days. The deal she is building now is slower — a multi-year clean fuel arrangement. She is not matching a buyer to a seller on something that already exists; she is building the deal itself, putting sides together for years rather than for a week. Those are the harder matches. “It’s the challenge, the hunt. That’s what makes it fun,” she says. Avramovic’s work is similar to what a real estate agent does, minus the house. A company calls knowing what it needs but not who has it. Avramovic knows who does, and who needs to sell before its deadline. The property just happens to be carbon, so there is nothing to walk through and no keys to hand over, just a line in a registry that moves out of one account and into another. She takes a fee when the deal closes, or a monthly retainer from clients who want to know where prices are heading. Alberta’s industrial carbon market is the biggest in Canada, and it exists because the province requires it, and has since 2007, when Ed Stelmach’s government put a price on industrial carbon. No one in North America had priced industrial carbon before Alberta did. The European Union got there first. The regulation is meant to be the stick. “But then, within that regulation,” Avramovic says, “there’s also a carrot that if you do those actions, you can then create credits and monetize them.” The actions are emissions cuts. One credit is not the same as another. Each one carries a vintage, like wine, the year it was created. One made in 2024 is good until 2029, then it expires. On the open market, these credits trade for less than $30 a tonne. The alternative is paying $95 a tonne into a government fund. In recent years, big emitters have used as many credits as the rules allow, Avramovic says. Those prices are about to go up. Sarajevo to power trading Avramovic was born in Sarajevo. The family escaped in the early 1990s, when a war started, and moved to the coast of Croatia, where her mother is from, and lived with her maternal grandparents. Her father escaped in the summer of 1994. Her parents applied to immigrate to Canada, and they arrived in June 1995, two weeks after her 11th birthday. She wanted art school. Her parents had crossed an ocean to start over in a new country, and they wanted their daughter to have a profession. She went to the Haskayne School of Business at the University of Calgary, and after graduation took a creative job at Critical Mass, a Calgary agency that was doing some of the first advertising on the internet. On a whim she answered an ad for a real-time power trader at TransAlta. The desk was hiring four new traders for Alberta, she says, two women and two men. “I just put my hand up,” she says. She got one of the four. Power is a 24-hour commodity, so the desk ran 12-hour shifts, two days, two nights, then days off, moving power between regions to capture the gap between what it cost to send and what it fetched at the other end. “I was lucky at TransAlta because they were trying to prioritize hiring more women onto a trade floor,” she says. “And so, I got my chance that way.” Trading is still a man’s business, she says, and whi

artigo.texto: The Tribune and Illinois Answers Project’s recent investigation into tax incentives and assessment reductions for data centers performed a public service by putting real numbers into an important debate. Tax policy should be transparent, and every incentive should be open to scrutiny. But the investigation captures only one side of the ledger. As mayor of a community that has hosted data centers for more than 25 years, I also have seen what those investments produce: Substantial revenue for schools and local governments, private investment in aging industrial areas and family-sustaining union construction jobs. Data centers in Elk Grove Village collectively generated approximately $60 million in property taxes for the 2025 tax year. Over the past year, they also generated $11.1 million in building permit fees, $4.5 million in electric utility tax revenue and more than $1 million in sales tax revenue. Some of those revenues are recurring and some are to construction, but all of them support real public needs. The Tribune calculated that incentives on five Elk Grove Village data center complexes saved their owners about $14.5 million in 2025 and concluded that, without those property tax incentives, the average village homeowner’s property tax bill would have been roughly $33 lower — but that calculation is misleading. The reporting would lead you to believe that Elk Grove Village residents are paying more because data centers are here. In actuality, the projects in question received the Cook County Class 6B property tax incentive, a temporary tax reduction designed to encourage new or substantially rehabilitated industrial development and the reoccupation of abandoned industrial property. Even with the temporary 6B property tax incentive, all of these data centers are generating significantly more property tax revenue than the industrial properties did before they became data centers. The 6B incentive does not erase the additional tax base created by the development; it just temporarily reduces the amount of new property tax revenue collected during the temporary incentive period. And when the incentive expires after 12 years, that additional property tax revenue remains part of the village’s tax base for decades to come. The 6B is a temporary form of tax relief that allows communities such as Elk Grove, located on the Cook County border, to compete with communities in neighboring counties where the taxes are lower. Elk Grove Village is home to the largest industrial park in North America, and we have decades of experience using the tax incentive to attract development, including data centers, that delivers a net benefit to the community. Data centers pay millions of dollars to school districts without adding students to classrooms. They require inspections, infrastructure and public safety planning, much like any other development, but they do not create the daily traffic, school enrollment, or service demands associated with a large residential development, warehouse or office campus. That makes them unusually valuable contributors to the local tax base. Additionally, data centers are recession-proof businesses that will continue to produce revenue during periods of economic downturn. The impact of data centers also reaches beyond property taxes. In 2024, when data center construction projects generated more than $3 million in permit fees, we returned that money directly to residents by sending a $200 Visa gift card to each of approximately 14,000 households. That was only possible because major data center investment generated revenue beyond what was needed to cover the village’s planned expenses during that fiscal year. In fiscal year 2026, Elk Grove Village permitted approximately $1.2 billion in private-sector construction. Data center construction, expansion and interior buildouts were the primary contributors. That investment supports contractors, suppliers, skilled tradespeople and other businesses throughout the region. On average, more than 1,000 people are working on data center construction in Elk Grove Village on a given day, many in high-paying union careers. Illinois should insist that data center developers pay the infrastructure costs they create, protect ratepayers and natural resources, use strong labor standards and deliver measurable community benefits. But we should not mistake accountability for hostility to investment. That is why I welcome the work of the Coalition for Responsible Data Centers, which is bringing together municipal leaders, labor, businesses and community voices to pursue responsible, pro-growth policy. State leaders should listen to communities with real experience, not only abstract projections or worst-case assumptions. In Elk Grove Village, data centers are not theoretical. Neither are the revenue, jobs and investments they generate. Craig B. Johnson is the mayor of Elk Grove Village. Submit a letter, of no more than 400 words, to the editor here or email letters@chicagotribune.com.

artigo.texto: Planejando, a forte demanda dos data centers pode ser atendida com segurança energética Para isso, a rede de transmissão precisa ser expandida para dar conta da alta demanda de energia dos, cada vez mais gigantescos, centros de dados A expansão dos data centers para atender o processamento de grandes volumes de dados e imagens — resultante do crescente uso da computação em nuvem e da inteligência artificial (IA) — acende um sinal de alerta de como os recursos energéticos exigidos por esses empreendimentos serão administrados. Um dos desafios é garantir que a segurança do sistema elétrico não seja comprometida, o que significa que a rede de transmissão também deve se expandir para dar conta da nova demanda de energia dos centros de dados. Há também desafios ambientais, como a demanda por água para resfriar equipamentos, e o ruído produzido por eles — questões que, no exterior, levantam oposição. Mas, por aqui, a visão que prevalece é a de que os data centers são importantes para a soberania digital, além de uma boa oportunidade para atrair investimentos. A matriz elétrica limpa e as fontes renováveis, ou de baixa emissão, são um dos apelos do país e um dos requisitos do Redata, regime de benefícios fiscais recentemente aprovado pelo Senado Federal para incentivar o segmento. “Como a energia elétrica pesa entre 40% e 60% no custo operacional de um data center, ter acesso a fontes de geração renovável com preços competitivos e fornecimento estável faz diferença na viabilidade econômica desses empreendimentos e ajuda a atrair investimentos para o país”, afirma Carlos Fogarolli, sócio-líder para a indústria de tecnologia, mídia e telecomunicações da Deloitte. Mas o ritmo da demanda por data centers tem crescido mais rápido do que a capacidade da rede de transmissão de energia consegue acompanhar, considera Fogarolli. Ele informa que, para reduzir essa distância, a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) estima em R$ 128,6 bilhões o investimento necessário até 2034 para viabilizar 30 mil quilômetros de novas linhas de transmissão e 82 mil megavolt-ampère (MVA) em novas subestações. Um data center leva, em média, de 18 a 24 meses para ser implantado no Brasil, prazo mais curto do que o de uma obra de transmissão de grande porte. “Isso ajuda a explicar por que a entrada em operação de novos data centers antes da conclusão dessas obras é vista como um risco concreto, com reflexo direto na segurança do fornecimento e nos custos de energia da região”, afirma Fogarolli. Na opinião do diretor-presidente da ISA Energia, Rui Chammas, o atual sistema de transmissão do país tem condições de acompanhar o crescimento da demanda energética, desde que haja planejamento e coordenação entre as novas unidades e a expansão da rede elétrica. “Como os data centers preveem expansões futuras de carga, é fundamental que essa demanda seja informada aos agentes envolvidos no planejamento setorial para dimensionar os investimentos necessários na infraestrutura de transmissão.” A Associação Brasileira de Data Centers (ABDC) aponta que o Brasil tem 162 data centers em operação, a maior parte no Sudeste, seguido pelo Sul e pelo Nordeste, região que mais vem atraindo unidades por oferecer energia eólica e solar, terrenos e conexões com os cabos submarinos de comunicação. E há uma forte tendência de expansão. A capacidade de data centers no país deve quadruplicar nos próximos cinco anos, passando de cerca de 1 gigawatt (GW) em 2025 para mais de 4 GW no início da década de 2030, segundo o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). “Os números mais recentes já incluem 27 contratos de conexão assinados e 30 solicitações de acesso à Rede Interligada Nacional com parecer favorável, indicando que grande parte dos projetos está avançando em paralelo aos investimentos em infraestrutura de transmissão planejados para os próximos anos”, opina Rodrigo Borges, diretor-executivo da Aurora Energy Research. Parcerias com fornecedores de energia renovável estão entre as estratégias para viabilizar projetos. É o caso da Omnia Data Centers, que está construindo um data center localizado no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém (CE), com investimentos de R$ 12 bilhões e voltado para um único cliente, a ByteDance, controladora da rede social TikTok. “A disponibilidade de energia renovável foi um dos fatores estratégicos considerados na escolha da localização da unidade, com capacidade de 200 megawatts (MW) e que será abastecida pelos parques eólicos no Ceará e no Piauí a partir de um contrato com a Casa dos Ventos”, afirma Rodrigo Abreu, CEO da Omnia Data Centers. Para se ter uma ideia da magnitude desses projetos, o Estado de Sergipe consome entre 150 MW e 200 MW de energia com carga constante, segundo a EPE. A estratégia da Scala, que conta com 13 data centers em operação e outros sete em desenvolvimento, é contar com infraestrutura elétrica própria, com a construção de três subestações. Além de uma unidade em Tamboré, na Grande São Paulo, que teve investimentos de US$ 10 bilhões e que chegará a 20 data centers quando concluída, vai inaugurar um segundo data center de larga escala (“hyperscale”), chamado de AI City, localizado no Rio Grande do Sul, voltado para IA, e que aproveita a infraestrutura elétrica já existente. “O clima mais ameno da região reduzirá o consumo de energia destinado à refrigeração e vai operar com PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness, ou Eficácia no Uso de Energia) de 1,2, métrica usada para definir a eficiência energética do data center, além de dispensar uso contínuo de água durante a operação”, afirma Fabio Yanaguita, diretor de energia da Scala. artigo.texto: Segundo o InvestNews, análise da The Economist divulgada neste domingo (27) mostra que a indústria europeia vive crise concentrada, não generalizada. Montadoras e químicas perdem terreno, enquanto fabricantes de equipamentos para data centers e empresas de defesa ampliam atividades. A produção de veículos da União Europeia está 17% menor que antes da pandemia. A China, que já rendia lucros às montadoras europeias, agora lança carros mais rápido e com custos menores. Em 2025, a UE importou € 559,4 bilhões em mercadorias chinesas e exportou € 199,6 bilhões, com déficit de quase € 360 bilhões, segundo o Eurostat. Antes de subsídios, a eletricidade industrial na França e na Alemanha custa cerca do dobro da registrada nos EUA ou na China, conforme a Economist. Desde o começo de 2023, o emprego na manufatura da UE caiu cerca de 2%, para 28 milhões, e quatro quintos dessa perda vieram da Alemanha. No mesmo período, vagas para engenheiros e técnicos cresceram 7%. Empresas buscam novas receitas: Vestas e MTU Aero Engines vendem manutenção; Siemens comprou empresas de software; Solvay e K+S buscaram reduzir exposição à oscilação dos preços de energia. Componentes chineses podem baratear a produção europeia, e estudo do Banco Central Europeu associou essas importações ao avanço da produção. Para a análise, os problemas de algumas grandes companhias não decretam crise de todo o setor.
