artigo.texto: A LG anunciou um novo Chiller Centrífugo Refrigerado a Ar (ACC) desenvolvido para atender à demanda de resfriamento de data centers voltados à inteligência artificial. O equipamento combina tecnologias proprietárias da empresa para aumentar a eficiência energética e manter a operação do sistema de refrigeração em ambientes que exigem disponibilidade contínua. O novo chiller possui capacidade de 480 a 600 toneladas de refrigeração (RT) por unidade e pode ser configurado de acordo com as necessidades de diferentes data centers de IA (AIDCs). Entre os principais recursos estão um compressor centrífugo com mancal magnético livre de óleo, tecnologia de free-cooling por refrigerante, sistema de alimentação ininterrupta (UPS) e recuperação da capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos após o restabelecimento da energia. Compressor com mancal magnético elimina o uso de óleo O compressor centrífugo utiliza um sistema de mancal magnético para suspender o eixo rotativo sem contato físico. Com isso, o projeto dispensa óleo lubrificante e reduz perdas associadas ao atrito mecânico. A tecnologia faz parte do conjunto de soluções proprietárias Core Tech da LG, que também inclui componentes como motores, inversores e outros elementos utilizados nos sistemas de refrigeração. A empresa afirma que desenvolve e fabrica internamente esses componentes antes de integrá-los aos sistemas completos. Segundo a LG, essa estratégia também busca melhorar a disponibilidade de peças e reduzir o tempo necessário para manutenção. Free-cooling por refrigerante reduz consumo de energia Outro recurso utilizado pelo novo chiller é o free-cooling por refrigerante. A tecnologia utiliza o ar externo quando as condições climáticas permitem reduzir a carga sobre o compressor. A solução se diferencia de sistemas convencionais de free-cooling hidrônico porque o refrigerante circula diretamente, sem a utilização de um trocador de calor intermediário. O sistema também não exige glicol, segundo a LG. Com base em uma simulação interna da empresa, o free-cooling por refrigerante apresentou consumo anual aproximadamente 30% menor do que uma solução de free-cooling hidrônico. A comparação foi feita pela LG considerando uma unidade de 1.750 kW operando com 100% da capacidade de resfriamento nas condições climáticas da região metropolitana de Seul. Nesse cenário, a empresa calculou consumo de 1.479.655 kWh para o free-cooling hidrônico e 1.044.824 kWh para o sistema por refrigerante. A LG ressalta que o consumo real pode variar de acordo com as condições de instalação e operação. O chiller também utiliza a tecnologia SCF (fluxo contracorrente em série), desenvolvida pela empresa para distribuir a carga de resfriamento entre os compressores. Sistema pode recuperar capacidade em até três minutos A continuidade do resfriamento é outro ponto destacado pela LG. O chiller possui sensores integrados ao sistema de mancal magnético para monitorar a posição do eixo rotativo e permitir um controle mais preciso. Recursos de machine learning também são utilizados para adaptar o funcionamento do equipamento aos padrões de operação e auxiliar na redução de instabilidades. Em caso de interrupção de energia, um UPS integrado fornece energia de emergência. A solução permite que o eixo do compressor seja parado de maneira controlada, reduzindo o risco de danos ao mancal. Depois que a energia é restabelecida, o sistema conta com uma função de recuperação rápida que pode retornar à capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos. O resultado, entretanto, pode variar conforme as condições de teste. LG oferece software para gerenciamento do resfriamento O novo chiller também pode ser integrado ao Data Center Cooling Management (DCCM), plataforma da LG voltada ao monitoramento e controle de infraestruturas de resfriamento. O sistema pode trabalhar com diferentes equipamentos, incluindo Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs), Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAHs) e chillers centrífugos refrigerados a ar. Entre os recursos estão detecção antecipada de anomalias, diagnósticos baseados em sensores virtuais e manutenção preditiva. A plataforma também permite otimização em tempo real de acordo com as cargas de trabalho de TI. A proposta é centralizar informações dos equipamentos de refrigeração para auxiliar no gerenciamento de instalações mais complexas. Solução modular busca facilitar expansão de data centers Além do novo chiller, a LG apresentará uma solução modular de resfriamento hidrônico durante a Data Centre World Asia 2026, que acontece entre 29 e 30 de setembro no Marina Bay Sands, em Singapura. A solução reúne componentes como bombas de água gelada e um tanque-pulmão para armazenamento térmico de energia (TES) em um módulo padronizado. A empresa afirma que a pré-fabricação e a montagem em fábrica podem simplificar a instalação no local. O projeto modular também permite ampliar a infraestrutura conforme o data center aumenta sua capacidade. A abordagem é particularmente voltada para instalações de inteligência artificial, que podem exigir expansão da capacidade computacional e, consequentemente, da infraestrutura necessária para remover o calor gerado pelos equipamentos. Chillers da LG possuem certificações internacionais Segundo a empresa, os chillers e as instalações de teste da LG seguem padrões do Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI). Os chillers refrigerados a ar da companhia também receberam o AHRI Performance Award por nove anos consecutivos. A linha atende ainda a requisitos relacionados a diferentes mercados, incluindo normas da ASME para vasos de pressão, certificação ETL para segurança elétrica na América do Norte e requisitos CE de segurança, saúde e meio ambiente na Europa. Com o novo chiller centrífugo refrigerado a ar, a LG amplia seu portfólio de soluções destinadas à infraestrutura térmica de data centers de IA, combinando sistemas de refrigeração, gerenciamento e arquitetura modular para instalações que precisa

artigo.texto: Quarta-feira, 30 de setembro de 2026 Por Redação O Sul | 29 de setembro de 2026 A instalação de grandes centros de processamento pode representar aumento significativo da demanda local por eletricidade. Foto: Reprodução O crescimento dos data centers e da demanda por infraestrutura para inteligência artificial abriu uma discussão sobre o impacto que o aumento do consumo de energia pode provocar no sistema elétrico brasileiro. A expansão desses centros de processamento exige grandes quantidades de eletricidade e levou o governo e especialistas a discutir como os custos adicionais deverão ser distribuídos entre empresas, consumidores e demais usuários da rede. Os data centers são estruturas utilizadas para armazenar e processar grandes volumes de informações. Com a expansão da inteligência artificial, a necessidade de capacidade computacional aumentou e empresas de tecnologia passaram a buscar locais com disponibilidade de energia, infraestrutura de transmissão e condições para ampliar suas operações. O aumento da demanda ocorre em um momento em que o sistema elétrico brasileiro já enfrenta desafios relacionados ao equilíbrio entre oferta e consumo. O país ampliou significativamente a geração de fontes renováveis, especialmente solar e eólica, mas enfrenta limitações na transmissão e períodos em que parte da energia disponível não consegue ser aproveitada. Em artigo publicado pela CNN Brasil, o ex-presidente da Petrobras e ex-ministro Jean Paul Prates afirmou que é legítimo discutir quem deverá pagar os custos associados à energia necessária para abastecer os novos data centers. Segundo ele, a expansão dessas estruturas pode pressionar os sistemas elétricos e elevar custos em determinadas regiões. A discussão ocorre em meio à expectativa de novos investimentos em infraestrutura digital no País. A instalação de grandes centros de processamento pode representar aumento significativo da demanda local por eletricidade, exigindo reforços em linhas de transmissão, subestações e equipamentos. O impacto sobre as tarifas depende, entre outros fatores, de como esses investimentos serão estruturados e de quem ficará responsável pelos custos de expansão da rede. Uma parte das despesas pode estar associada diretamente aos empreendimentos, enquanto outros investimentos podem integrar a infraestrutura compartilhada do sistema. O tema ganhou importância também porque o Brasil tenta utilizar a disponibilidade de fontes renováveis como um diferencial para atrair investimentos ligados à tecnologia. A oferta de energia de menor intensidade de carbono é apontada como uma das vantagens para empresas que precisam abastecer instalações de grande consumo. Ao mesmo tempo, especialistas têm alertado para o risco de uma expansão sem planejamento integrado. O setor elétrico brasileiro convive com momentos de excesso de geração renovável em determinadas regiões e horários, enquanto enfrenta restrições para transportar essa energia até os locais de consumo. A discussão sobre os data centers se soma, portanto, a um problema mais amplo do setor elétrico. Segundo especialistas, o país precisa ampliar o planejamento da transmissão e da capacidade de armazenamento para lidar com o crescimento da demanda e com a variabilidade das fontes renováveis. Outro ponto envolve o custo da energia para consumidores e empresas. Dados mostram que o preço da eletricidade para o setor produtivo brasileiro, em valores em dólar, acumulou alta de 327,7% entre 2000 e junho de 2026. No mesmo período, a alta foi de 145,3% nos Estados Unidos e de 12,5% na União Europeia.

artigo.texto: Data centers may be the sleeper issue of the midterm elections. Fox News reported that Senate candidates are confronting growing voter anger over the electricity costs, water consumption, and sprawling developments associated with artificial intelligence. One recent Gallup survey found that 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of new AI data centers in their own communities. Politicians are paying attention. Some are calling for moratoriums. Others are targeting tax incentives or demanding that projects generate their own power. The political temptation is obvious: When voters are worried about higher utility bills and rapid changes in their communities, blaming large technology companies is easier than explaining a complicated energy and infrastructure problem. ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER The concerns are real. They should not be dismissed by industry, and they cannot be ignored by elected officials. No family should be forced to subsidize the grid upgrades required by one of the world’s wealthiest companies. Communities deserve honest answers about water use, noise, land, electricity demand, tax incentives, and who will pay for new infrastructure. But, legitimate concerns are quickly hardening into something far more dangerous: a political campaign against the physical infrastructure of American artificial intelligence. If that happens, we will repeat one of the most damaging patterns in modern American history. For decades, the United States surrendered factories, critical supply chains, mineral production, and industrial capacity to foreign competitors. Communities lost jobs, our national security became dependent on adversaries, and Washington eventually spent billions trying to rebuild industries that should never have left. THE AI REVOLUTION COULD BECOME A NATIONAL SECURITY DISASTER IF WE AREN'T CAREFUL We cannot make the same mistake with AI. Artificial intelligence does not exist somewhere in the cloud. It requires chips, servers, power plants, transmission lines, cooling systems, construction workers, electricians, pipefitters, engineers, and data centers. These facilities are not incidental to the AI economy. They are the factories of the next industrial age. AMERICA RUNS ON DATA. IF WE DON’T BUILD THE INFRASTRUCTURE, CHINA WILL China understands this. Beijing is not debating whether it should possess the energy and computing infrastructure necessary to dominate artificial intelligence. It is building. The International Energy Agency projects that data-center electricity consumption will increase substantially in both China and the United States through 2030. If America decides that data centers are too politically difficult to construct, the demand for AI will not disappear. The investment, jobs, technical expertise, and strategic advantage will simply move elsewhere. That would be a profound failure of American competitiveness. It would also create a serious political problem for Democrats. Data-center construction has become an important source of work for the building trades. The Associated Press recently reported that data centers account for at least 40 percent of the work hours performed by members of the Columbus-Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council and at least 50 percent for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 26 in the Washington metropolitan area. WELDER TURNED LAWMAKER SEES A ‘NUCLEAR BOMB FOR WORK’ — AND A CHANCE TO HELP BLUE COLLAR AMERICANS Those are not theoretical jobs promised years from now. They are jobs for electricians, laborers, operating engineers, pipefitters, and other skilled workers today. Democrats cannot claim to represent organized labor while allowing progressive activists to shut down the projects employing union members. Republicans should resist a similar temptation. Conservatives have spent years arguing for reshoring, energy dominance, permitting reform, American manufacturing, and competition with China. Those commitments mean very little if they disappear when building the next American industry becomes locally controversial. The answer is not to wave every project through without conditions. It is to build responsibly and communicate honestly. Data-center developers should be expected to explain what they are building, how much electricity and water it will require, how they will protect residential ratepayers, and what the surrounding community will receive in return. Utilities and regulators should ensure that large customers pay the costs created by their demand. Projects should pursue closed-loop cooling, on-site generation, long-term power agreements, and other options that reduce pressure on local systems. TO BEAT CHINA IN AI, AMERICA MUST WORK WITH COMMUNITIES — NOT AROUND THEM Most importantly, America needs more energy. Data centers are exposing a problem that existed before the AI boom. Electricity demand from data centers has tripled over the past decade and could double or triple again by 2028. Electricity demand is rising after years of stagnant generation, premature plant retirements, congested transmission systems, and permitting processes that make major infrastructure nearly impossible to build on time. Stopping data centers will not modernize the grid. Building more reliable generation, accelerating transmission, preserving existing nuclear capacity, expanding natural gas infrastructure, and deploying advanced nuclear power will. Industry also needs to recognize that silence is no longer a strategy. As Sen. Jon Husted told Fox News, data-center companies have not done a good enough job explaining why they should be allowed to develop in communities. He is right. Americans hear about enormous power consumption, water use, and tax incentives. They need to hear, in plain language, what data centers make possible, which jobs they create, how they support national security, and why domestic computing capacity matters i

artigo.texto: Data centers are powering your chat ramblings — and the growth in the American construction industry. AI buildouts are set to become the largest capital expenditure project in US history, per a Brookings Institution analysis, outpacing spending on highways and railroads as a share of GDP. That massive spending and construction boom needs workers to — literally — prop it up. And blue-collar employment for data centers is booming, with the number of nonresidential specialty trade contractors — workers like electricians in non-residential buildings, which includes data centers— growing by 86,000 in the past year. "I think it's fair to say that a very large portion of construction labor demand right now is being driven by increasing data center construction activity," said Zach Fritz, an economist at Associated Builders and Contractors. The American Institute of Architects found, based on multiple forecasts of nonresidential construction, that data center construction spending is set to climb more than other kinds and account for about 8% of nonresidential building spending by 2027. But the sustainability of that jobs boom could be precarious. Construction spending on the whole has fallen 3.8% year-over-year as of July, according to the Census Bureau, and KPMG finds that data centers are a "structural growth driver" for spending. Year-over-year spending on data centers has grown by just over 57%, a sharp contrast to both residential and non-residential private spending growth since early 2025. For now, the data center boom is good news for construction workers and larger industry spending. Guy Berger, a senior fellow at the research organization Burning Glass Institute, said one concern is if the data center boom cycle ends up being shorter than anticipated: "And all of a sudden, we trained a lot of electricians, people like that, to do stuff that is no longer needed," Berger said. Data center workers are in demand Job postings on Indeed for data center-related roles have skyrocketed, up almost 130% from about two years ago, while overall postings are down compared with the same period. About half of the data-center demand this year came from the IT infrastructure, operations, and support occupational group and the installation and maintenance occupational group. A job-posting analysis from Lightcast, a job market intelligence company, showed a rise in demand for some data-center-related jobs. Based on growth in average monthly job postings from January to August 2022 and the same period this year, postings for electrical engineers within the utilities sector have increased 34%, and 22% for project management specialists. Within commercial and institutional building construction, there's been a rise in demand for construction managers, project management specialists, cost estimators, and civil engineers. And so, in the short term, the data center boom will likely remain a workhouse for the construction industry. What's more unclear is the longer-term prognosis, especially since AI infrastructure is still reliant on a slice of hardcore spenders to keep it afloat. "The next few years, it's stable. It's going to keep growing. We're going to keep building data centers," Fritz said. But rising community opposition could eventually limit the rate of growth, he said, or technological advancements might require smaller footprints. "There's all kinds of things that could happen here," he said. "They're not going to happen anytime soon." It's unclear how permanent data center jobs will ultimately be, especially after data center construction, but listings on Indeed at least suggest firms are advertising them as long-term. Aubrey Woessner, an economist at Indeed Hiring Lab, said only about two in every 1,000 data center postings are temporary. "'Permanent' is a label the employer chooses, and there's reason to think it may overstate how durable these roles really are: Local incentive agreements often require a project to create a set number of permanent positions, which gives employers a reason to post that way regardless of how long a given build-out job actually lasts," Woessner said. Are you in a data center-related job? Reach out to these reporters to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com and jkaplan@businessinsider.com.

artigo.texto: ROME, Sept 29 (Reuters) - Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her Czech counterpart Andrej Babiš will agree joint proposals to curb energy costs and overhaul the European Union's carbon market, officials from Rome said ahead of their meeting on Tuesday. The two leaders aim to present the reform package at the October 15-16 EU summit, the Italian officials said. Meloni and Babiš are focusing on easing European Union rules that could trigger energy supply disruptions while also reforming the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a regulation forcing power plants and industries to buy CO2 permits when they pollute. As part of the package, Rome and Prague are calling on the EU to temporarily suspend a regulation on methane which, according to the officials, could make it more difficult to rely on alternative gas suppliers from January, potentially increasing energy costs and threatening security of supply. The two governments also want the EU to postpone ETS2 regulation, currently scheduled to come into force in 2028, arguing it could further increase energy costs in some sectors including road transport and housing. (Reporting by Giuseppe Fonte; Editing by Alvise Armellini and Kirsten Donovan)

artigo.texto: - The companies plan battery projects in Spain and Slovakia with combined annual capacity of 37.5 GWh, alongside a cathode materials project in Morocco. - Gotion plans to invest about €1.598 billion, while Volkswagen's PowerCo plans to contribute about €1.62 billion. Gotion High-tech (SZSE: 002074) and Volkswagen Group plan to jointly invest about €3.22 billion ($3.67 billion) in battery and materials production projects in Europe and North Africa, deepening supply chain cooperation to serve Volkswagen's European market. The companies plan to establish 3 joint ventures through their subsidiaries in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco, Gotion said in a stock exchange filing on Monday. Gotion plans to invest about €1.6 billion in total, while Volkswagen's PowerCo plans to contribute about €1.62 billion, with funding to be provided in stages. The largest project, in Valencia, Spain, calls for an investment of about €2.26 billion to build annual lithium-ion battery production capacity of 29.1 GWh. Gotion plans to acquire a 49% stake in the existing PowerCo Spain through a capital increase. PowerCo will retain control with a 51% stake after the transaction. The project in Šurany, Slovakia, involves a planned investment of about €480 million for annual lithium-ion battery production capacity of 8.4 GWh. Gotion will hold 51% and PowerCo 49%. Cells produced by the 2 European projects will prioritize Volkswagen's demand in Europe. Specific purchase volumes and supply assurance arrangements remain subject to subsequent definitive agreements. The companies also plan to invest about €480 million in Kenitra, Morocco, to build a lithium iron phosphate cathode materials project with annual capacity of 100,000 metric tons, prioritizing supplies to the 2 battery joint ventures. Gotion will also control the Moroccan joint venture with a 51% stake, while PowerCo will hold the remaining 49%. The construction scope specified in the filing for all 3 projects excludes land and factory buildings. Each project is expected to take no more than 5 years to build, subject to actual construction progress. The cooperation will further strengthen the companies' equity and business ties. Volkswagen (China) Investment Co held a 24.28% stake in Gotion as of September 20, making it the battery maker's largest shareholder. Gotion said it will participate in the development of Volkswagen's key European cell production base, while PowerCo will take stakes in Gotion's battery and materials projects in Europe and Africa to jointly build a localized battery supply network for Europe. Gotion's board approved the proposal on September 28, but the companies have yet to sign the investment agreement. The transaction still requires shareholder approval and government clearances in China and overseas. The projects will increase capital expenditure in the near term, Gotion said, adding that financing, approvals and market changes could affect construction progress and expected returns. The investment plan comes as Gotion gains share in the global battery market. Its global EV battery installations totaled 34.0 GWh in the first 7 months of 2026, up 44.2% from a year earlier, according to South Korean market research firm SNE Research. Gotion High-tech ranked fifth globally during the period, with its market share rising to 4.7% from 3.9% a year earlier. ($1 = €0.8783)

artigo.texto: Last Tuesday, there was a large turnout at a Bow Selectmen meeting, preceded by a rally with residents from Bow and nearby towns that will be affected by the pollution of air, water and noise from a possible AI data center, particularly one fast-tracked without input from stakeholders. I am a longtime resident of Bow with a background as an environmental science educator and advocate for climate justice. I was one of many who raised major concerns about the environmental and health risks of data centers and requested a moratorium on these data centers until these problems are addressed. I was part of the long struggle to close down the dangerous coal-fired power plant, and had hoped with many others that the site would be used to support affordable renewable energy. I am a co-leader of the Concord Chapter of Climate Hope Affiliates, a faith-based advocacy group for climate justice, and several of our chapters across the country have been successful in advocating for members of Congress to support bipartisan legislation to examine and regulate AI data centers. Data centers consume enormous amounts of energy and water at a financial and environmental cost borne by residents. The United States has more than 3,000 data centers. Of particular concern are “hyperscale” data centers that demand at least 50 MW of power — enough electricity for a small city. Sixty-eight hyperscale facilities operate today, and 267 more are planned. Nationwide, communities are protesting existing and proposed data centers. A local ban might protect one community from data center pollution, but it cannot protect all communities across the country. Two bills before Congress offer a national response. Reps. Rob Menendez (D-NJ) and Greg Casar (D-TX) have introduced the Preventing Rate Inflation in Consumer Energy (PRICE) Act (HR 6983) and the Data Center Transparency Act (HR 6984). The PRICE Act would require large data centers to generate the electricity they consume and transition to 100% clean energy by 2040. The Data Center Transparency Act would require federal agencies to report regularly on data centers’ air pollution, water use, energy consumption and effects on household utility bills. Our representatives in Congress should cosponsor these bills if they have not already done so, or explain what other action they will take to protect our communities and state. Our senators should introduce companion legislation. The PRICE Act applies to data centers with a power demand of at least 50 MW. It provides a timetable for transitioning to clean energy. A data center’s energy would need to be 75% clean by 2035 and 100% clean by 2040. Failure to comply would result in a civil penalty that could be as high as $100,000 per day until the requirement is met. To establish a more comprehensive approach, the Data Center Transparency Act would make the broader environmental and consumer impacts of data centers transparent to the public. It would require the EPA to collect data every three months on impacts related to water, local utilities, greenhouse gas emissions and the cumulative impact of emissions on overburdened communities. It would additionally require the Energy Information Administration to collect data every six months on both a data center’s energy consumption and any impacts on household energy bills. With more and more massive data centers being built, the question is where they will land. Local bans and moratoriums are effective, but we need a unified movement across the United States to protect all of us and the environment. Climate Hope Affiliates is highlighting one particularly egregious data center in Memphis. Local chapters are hosting community discussions and postcard-writing parties in towns and cities across the U.S. Attendees watch a 17-minute video about a predominantly Black community in Memphis that has been struggling to address the pollution from an XAI data center that, at the time of filming, was the world’s largest supercomputer. The video illustrates a familiar pattern of environmental injustice: a powerful corporation adds pollution to an already overburdened, predominantly Black community, while the concerns of residents are discounted and environmental protection laws are blatantly disregarded. A number of solutions are needed, but for starters, no one should have to live near the gas turbines or diesel generators that help power some data centers. The fossil fuels that generate the energy cause air and water pollution which causes a myriad of heart and lung problems as well as problems for the animal life in the water. The low-frequency noise pollution sounds like jet engines 24/7, causing ringing of the ears, tinnitus and stress, which causes heart problems. No one should have those in their backyard. This is why the two bills are currently being championed by Climate Hope Affiliates and Creation Justice Ministries, an ecumenical organization that brings more than 35 different denominations together in common cause for environmental stewardship. The Rev. Dr. Brooks Berndt, who directs Climate Hope Affiliates and serves as the Environmental Justice Minister, explains this broad approach by saying, “Ultimately, the key to bringing about the needed solutions is for members of communities across the country to come together to build a bigger ‘we,’ so that when we say not in ‘our’ backyard, we mean everyone’s backyard.” Several New England Conferences have resolutions about a moratorium on data centers. Please urge all four of our Congresspeople and Senators to support these two important bills. We are taking care of business in our back yard, but the urgent need to address AI data centers is a nationwide issue that demands our action. It’s a matter of money versus morals, greed versus health. Sue Moore, from Bow, is co-Leader of the Concord Climate Hope Affiliates with an MS in Environmental Health Science, a Teacher/Naturalist with Audubon and an environment/climate activist.

artigo.texto: Conhecida por ser a fábrica de bilionários, a empresa WEG anunciou que vai investir US$ 165 milhões, aproximadamente R$ 840 milhões, para expandir sua capacidade de produção de geradores na América do Norte. O projeto será realizado em duas fases e tem como objetivo atender à crescente demanda por soluções de geração de energia para aplicações críticas nos EUA, especialmente impulsionada pela expansão dos data centers. A iniciativa representa mais um passo na estratégia de crescimento dos negócios incorporados à companhia por meio da aquisição da Marathon. A WEG, que tem sede e nasceu em Jaraguá do Sul, no Norte de SC, tem operações em diversas partes do mundo e vai continuar expandindo. A primeira fase do projeto anunciado para a América do Norte contempla investimentos de 24 milhões de dólares para aquisição e adequação de um prédio industrial localizado ao lado do atual Parque Industrial de Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula, no México. A unidade será destinada à montagem de geradores e contribuirá para a expansão da capacidade produtiva da companhia, com início das operações previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Na segunda fase, em local ainda a ser definido na América do Norte, a WEG investirá 141 milhões dólares na construção de duas novas instalações industriais. O projeto prevê a implantação de uma estrutura produtiva verticalizada que abrangerá processos estratégicos como fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças, aumentando a eficiência operacional e a competitividade da operação. Ao fim da segunda fase, prevista para ser concluída em 2030, a companhia terá capacidade global de fabricar cerca de 50 geradores por dia em suas fábricas no México, EUA, Brasil e China, frente a atual capacidade de 10 geradores por dia. “Este investimento representa mais um passo importante na consolidação da nossa estratégia para o negócio de geradores na América do Norte. Além de ampliar nossa capacidade de produção, o projeto fortalece a integração das operações incorporadas com a Marathon e nos prepara para acompanhar a evolução de mercados que demandam infraestrutura crítica cada vez mais robusta, como o de data centers”, afirma João Paulo Gualberto da Silva, vice‑presidente da Unidade de Energia da WEG.

artigo.texto: O candidato ao Governo do Rio Grande do Norte Robério Paulino (PSOL) afirmou que apoiará Cadu de Lula (PT) caso o petista dispute o segundo turno contra Allyson Bezerra (União). A declaração foi feita durante sabatina promovida pelo Grupo Dial Natal, a seis dias do primeiro turno, marcado para 4 de outubro. Questionado se Cadu seria seu candidato numa segunda etapa do pleito, Robério respondeu: “Sem dúvida. Se o Cadu for para o segundo turno, o Psol vai apoiar o Cadu contra o Allyson, indiscutivelmente“. O apoio veio acompanhado de ressalvas. Robério descreveu Cadu como “um homem da área fiscal” e “uma pessoa de esquerda há pouco tempo“. “Respeito muito o Cadu, mas a visão dele é uma visão muito gerencialista“, afirmou, acrescentando que o petista tem “menos visão social” do que a dele. Data centers Na mesma sabatina, o candidato do PSOL disse não se opor à instalação de data centers no estado, desde que gerem empregos. “Eu, a priori, não estou contra“, afirmou. Robério, porém, apontou o impacto ambiental desses empreendimentos, em especial o alto consumo de água, e defendeu que cada projeto seja avaliado considerando os efeitos ambientais e o número de empregos gerados. “Não vejo que essa é a grande saída para o Estado“, disse sem detalhar qual seria a alternativa. A posição contrasta com a de Cadu, que em sabatina na mesma série, citou a resolução do Conselho Estadual de Meio Ambiente (Conema) que abriu caminho para data centers no RN. O petista apresentou os empreendimentos como parte de sua estratégia para agregar valor à energia renovável produzida no estado.

artigo.texto: Center point considers rules for possible data center City and county leaders discuss ordinance before any proposal is submitted CENTER POINT, Iowa (KCRG) - Center Point leaders are considering what to do if a data center wants to come to town, even before there is a proposal on the table. The city council teamed up with Center Point’s planning and zoning commission. They met with County Supervisor Brandi Meisheid to review the county’s rules. Using Linn and Johnson counties as models, leaders zeroed in on power grid demands, cooling systems, and requiring utility impact studies. No data center has approached Center Point yet, but the mayor says they want to set the rules before developers come knocking. “I think it’s important to be proactive about having an ordinance so this way when or if we are ever approached by a data center, we have a path forward,” Mayor Traer Morgan said. Public comment raises questions During public comment, people questioned whether the city is prepared for the long-term impact of a data center. Some people thanked the city for getting ahead on a proposed ordinance. The council says after this discussion they now believe they have enough information to draft a data center ordinance. artigo.texto: - Virginia’s return to RGGI has coincided with a sharp rise in carbon allowance prices, with the latest auction clearing at $37.65 per allowance. - Dominion Energy is seeking to recover higher RGGI costs from customers through a proposed monthly charge of roughly $10 to $13. - RGGI is entering a tighter phase as participating states reduce emissions caps through 2033, while Virginia prepares to align with the updated rules. Virginia’s return to the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, or Virginia RGGI, has pushed carbon allowance prices sharply higher, while Dominion Energy seeks approval to recover the cost from customers through a proposed monthly charge. The development, reported by the Virginian Pilot, puts Dominion Energy and Virginia electricity customers at the center of a renewed debate over the cost of the regional carbon market. Virginia resumed participation in RGGI on July 1 after leaving the program in 2023 under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin. The state had originally joined in 2021. Under the system, covered power plants must acquire an allowance for each metric ton of carbon dioxide they emit. The first auction following Virginia’s return cleared at $37.65 per allowance on Sept. 9, according to RGGI. That was up from $35 in June and $24.99 in March. The September auction generated more than $1.07 billion across the 11-state market. Why electricity bills are in focus Dominion has asked Virginia regulators to reinstate its RGGI rate adjustment mechanism. The company estimates it will need roughly 51 million allowances between July 2026 and the end of 2028, with its filing assuming allowance prices between $37.04 and $38.32. Its filing projects a Virginia jurisdictional revenue requirement of about $1.18 billion tied to RGGI costs over that period. A Virginia Mercury report said Dominion’s proposed RGGI charge could amount to roughly $10 to $13 a month beginning in spring 2027, compared with about $4 a month during the state’s earlier participation. The State Corporation Commission is considering Dominion’s petition, with public comments currently scheduled through Oct. 21. The potential increase comes as Virginia households are already facing other electricity-cost pressures. Dominion says an approved 2026 rate adjustment is expected to raise the average residential bill by $11.24, with another $2.36 increase scheduled for 2027. RGGI’s next phase The financial picture is also changing because Virginia’s law directs 45% of RGGI revenue toward credits for eligible residential and other customers, with the remaining 55% distributed under the state’s existing framework. Meanwhile, RGGI’s broader program is becoming more restrictive. Participating states agreed in their third program review to lower the regional emissions cap beginning in 2027, with allowances declining through 2033. The updated rules also expand cost-containment reserves intended to provide additional allowances when prices rise sharply. Virginia is expected to align its program with those updated rules by Jan. 1, 2027, meaning the state’s return to RGGI is only the beginning of a broader regulatory transition. artigo.texto: BYD says its new solid-state EV battery tech is nearly ready for the open road The Chinese company is one of several car makers expected to adopt solid-state batteries in the next few years. Switching from lithium-ion to solid-state batteries promises to extend the range and charging speeds of electric vehicles, and Chinese car maker BYD believes it's in a "leading position" to commercialize the technology. BYD's Executive Vice President Stella Li shared the claim in a recent interview with Carwow's Spanish outlet, alongside the news that BYD would release its first car with a solid-state battery in 2027. "Talking about solid-state batteries, BYD is in the leading position," Li said. "We're in the leading position for commercialization and technology. So to prove that, next year, we have one model that will be the first one with that technology." Li's comments further confirm plans shared by Sun Huajun, the Chief Technology Officer of BYD's battery subsidiary FinDreams, at a battery conference in February 2025. At the time, Sun said BYD would offer its first demonstration and installation of solid-state batteries in 2027 before the technology enters mass production around 2030, CarNewsChina reports. While that means people will be able to buy cars with the company's sulfide solid-state batteries, that doesn't mean its traditional lithium batteries will be phased out, BYD Chief Scientist Lian Yubo shared at the same conference. "Solid-state batteries will be mainly used in high-end models, empowering each other with lithium iron phosphate batteries, and used in vehicles of different levels," Lian said. In comparison to lithium-ion batteries, which move ions between positive and negative terminals through a liquid solution of dissolved lithium salts, solid-state batteries replace the liquid with solid electrolytes made from oxides, polymers or sulfides (the kind BYD is developing). Solid electrolytes give solid-state batteries higher energy density, which opens up the possibility of smaller, lighter batteries and a longer range on a single charge. Solid-state batteries are also theoretically safer because they're far less prone to catching fire and they're able to operate at extreme temperatures, an issue current lithium-ion batteries struggle with. The problem with using the battery technology as it exists now is cost, which is why BYD suggests you'll see its solid-state batteries on more expensive models first, like possibly a future version of its Denza Z. The company is one of several car makers planning to ship a vehicle with solid-state batteries in the next few years. For example, Toyota committed to offering cars with solid-state batteries by 2027 or 2028; Mercedes-Benz began testing a solid-state EQS model and shared that it would ship the technology before the end of the decade; and Stellantis began road testing a solid-state Dodge Charger in 2026. Earlier this year, Honda struck up a new partnership with QuantumScape to develop solid-state batteries it hopes will help it reach carbon neutrality by 2050. The potential for solid-state battery technology is exciting, but most car makers are only in the first leg of the race.

artigo.texto: Weg investirá R$ 840 milhões para ampliar capacidade de produção na América do Norte com avanço de data centers Multinacional brasileira informou em comunicado que investimento será feito primeiro no México; duas novas unidades serão construídas na região Atualizado A multinacional brasileira Weg, fabricante de motores elétricos e equipamentos eletroeletrônicos, anunciou nesta segunda-feira um plano de investimento de US$ 165 milhões, aproximadamente R$ 840 milhões, para expandir sua produção de geradores na América do Norte. A Weg conta com três unidades industriais nos Estados Unidos focadas em equipamentos elétricos, tintas ou suporte produtivo. No México, a empresa tem quatro unidades industriais, com destaque para a operação em Atotonilco de Tula (Parque Quma) e a unidade em Monterrey, voltada para motores, geradores e pesquisa e desenvolvimento. O investimento tem como objetivo atender o aumento da demanda por soluções de geração de energia impulsionada pela expansão dos data centers. A iniciativa representa mais um passo na estratégia de crescimento dos negócios incorporados à companhia por meio da aquisição da Marathon. Em 2023, a Weg adquiriu os negócios de motores elétricos industriais e geradores da americana Regal Rexnord Corporation, incluindo a tradicional marca Marathon. O valor do negócio, à época, foi de cerca de US$ 400 milhões. O novo investimento na região será realizado em duas fases. A primeira contempla US$ 24 milhões para aquisição e adequação de um prédio industrial localizado ao lado do atual Parque Industrial de Quma I. A unidade será destinada à montagem de geradores e tem início das operações previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Na segunda fase, em local ainda a ser definido na América do Norte, a WEG investirá US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais. O projeto prevê a implantação de uma estrutura produtiva verticalizada que abrangerá processos estratégicos como fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças, aumentando a eficiência operacional e a competitividade da operação. De dez para cinquenta Ao fim da segunda fase, prevista para ser concluída em 2030, a companhia terá capacidade global de fabricar cerca de cinquenta geradores por dia em suas fábricas no México, EUA, Brasil e China, frente a atual capacidade de dez geradores por dia. "Este investimento representa mais um passo importante na consolidação da nossa estratégia para o negócio de geradores na América do Norte. Além de ampliar nossa capacidade de produção, o projeto fortalece a integração das operações incorporadas com a Marathon e nos prepara para acompanhar a evolução de mercados que demandam infraestrutura crítica cada vez mais robusta, como o de data centers", afirmou em nota João Paulo Gualberto da Silva, vice‑presidente da unidade de Energia da WEG. A WEG estima que as atuais tarifas dos Estados Unidos devem pressionar sua margem consolidada caso permaneçam em vigor, mas avalia que sua presença global e a diversificação da produção podem ajudar a reduzir os impactos das medidas comerciais, segundo a agência Bloomberg. Atualmente, 21% da produção no Brasil é destinada aos Estados Unidos, percentual inferior ao registrado em 2024, quando cerca de um terço da produção brasileira era exportada ao mercado americano. O México passou a ser o principal centro de produção da companhia para atender os EUA, com 41% da produção das operações mexicanas destinada ao país.

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA Entidades do setor de gás natural e geração termelétrica defendem a inclusão do gás natural entre as fontes de energia elegíveis ao Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Centers) e manifestam preocupação com a possibilidade de a regulamentação do programa excluir a fonte. A Abraget (Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas) e a Abegás (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado) argumentam que o gás pode complementar as fontes renováveis e contribuir para o fornecimento contínuo de energia aos empreendimentos. A Abraget afirma que a eventual exclusão do gás natural pode aumentar os custos do sistema elétrico e estima um impacto de aproximadamente R$ 7 bilhões na conta de luz dos consumidores. Segundo a entidade, além da necessidade de recorrer ao gás e a outras fontes nos períodos de menor geração renovável, a expansão de fontes intermitentes não garantiria, sozinha, o fornecimento firme exigido pelos data centers. “Quem pagará a conta será o consumidor brasileiro”, afirma a associação. A entidade também argumenta que a concentração da geração renovável no Nordeste pode exigir investimentos adicionais em transmissão para atender data centers instalados no Sul e no Sudeste, com possibilidade de repasse dos custos aos consumidores. Para a Abraget, o gás natural oferece geração firme e pode contribuir para a segurança e a viabilidade desses projetos. A Abegás também defende a presença do gás no Redata e sustenta que a fonte deve ser utilizada de forma complementar às renováveis. A associação afirma que a geração a gás pode permitir a implantação descentralizada dos data centers e reduzir a necessidade de novos investimentos em linhas de transmissão. “Defender a neutralidade tecnológica é permitir que esses projetos avancem sem sobrecarregar o sistema de transmissão nem encarecer a conta de energia para os demais consumidores”, afirmou o diretor-executivo da Abegás, Marcelo Mendonça. As duas entidades alertam ainda para o risco de insegurança jurídica caso a regulamentação, na avaliação delas, ultrapasse os limites definidos pelo Congresso Nacional. A Abraget afirma que isso pode provocar questionamentos legislativos e afetar investimentos. A Abegás acrescenta que medidas que excedam o escopo da lei aprovada podem levar à apresentação de PDLs (Projetos de Decreto Legislativo), o que, segundo a associação, poderia dificultar a implementação do regime.

artigo.texto: Vena Energy Wins 46.8 MW Battery Storage Contract in Japan Vena Energy's NRE Nakagawa 2 project in Nagano Prefecture has been selected in Japan's FY2025 auction for long-term decarbonised power sources. Vena Energy, the renewable energy arm of Vena Group and a provider of green energy solutions across the Asia-Pacific region, announced the selection of its NRE Nakagawa 2 Battery Storage project in Japan's FY2025 Long-Term Decarbonised Power Source Auction (LTDA), conducted by the Organisation for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO). The project, currently under development in Japan, was awarded a capacity of 46,828 kW, according to the company. This type of battery storage deployment reflects a broader trend of similar infrastructure being rolled out, such as the 210 MWh battery storage system installed in Nickelsdorf, Austria. An auction mechanism to support carbon neutrality Introduced in fiscal year 2023, the LTDA scheme is designed to support Japan's ambition to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. The programme encourages investment in decarbonised power generation by providing long-term revenue certainty, thereby helping developers recover their development and capital costs, according to OCCTO. The NRE Nakagawa 2 project adds to the battery storage portfolio that Vena Energy is developing in Japan. It follows the Hikone Battery Storage project, which began commercial operations last year, according to the company. This new asset confirms Vena Energy's strategy in energy storage within the Japanese market. Company Vena Group: company profile A grid-connected site near Matsumoto The grid-connected battery storage system is located near Matsumoto City, in Nagano Prefecture. Raul Rienda, Head of Japan at Vena Energy, said that deploying battery storage systems is necessary to address the intermittency of renewable energy and enable more efficient use of electricity. According to Mr. Rienda, the project's selection in the FY2025 auction should help strengthen the reliability and resilience of Japan's power system. The company said it will continue to engage with local communities throughout the project's development, with careful attention paid to the surrounding environment. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 %

artigo.texto: Germany could need 10 GW to 14 GW of bankable BESS tolling capacity by the mid-2030s, according to a PwC and FfE whitepaper As of May 2026, independent developers accounted for 69% of the country’s installed BESS capacity, increasing the importance of debt financing and predictable revenues Authors recommend that higher fixed tolling payments, a greater share of capacity under contract and longer agreement terms can improve the cash flow certainty Germany could require 10 GW to 14 GW of battery energy storage system (BESS) tolling capacity by the mid-2030s to support the financing of its growing storage pipeline, according to a joint white paper by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) and the Research Centre for Energy Economics (FfE). The whitepaper titled Challenges in Financing and De-Risking BESS Projects, highlights the growing importance of tolling agreements as battery storage developers increasingly depend on debt financing. Germany’s large-scale BESS capacity is expected to expand significantly. The country’s current grid development plan assumes installed capacity will reach 40 GW by 2037, while FfE expects expansion to up to 28 GW by the mid-2030s. The report also anticipates a shift in storage duration: while installations in the coming years are likely to have durations of around two hours, new projects from the 2030s onwards are expected to increasingly feature around four hours of storage, reflecting changing flexibility requirements. Much of this expansion is driven by independent project developers, according to the whitepaper. Referring to Germany’s Market Data Register, the analysts believe only 31% of the installed capacity of the existing BESS portfolio in Germany was covered by energy supply companies till May 2026, while 69% was realized by independent project developers. The latter rely on debt financing having limited financing capacities of their own, which the report says is difficult to secure based solely on merchant revenues. Tolling models can help address this financing gap by providing more predictable income, recommend the authors. “Tolling makes volatile storage revenues more predictable, thus creating an essential prerequisite for bankable financing of BESS projects,” reads the whitepaper. A recent example of the model’s use in the Asia-Pacific region is Amazon’s tolling agreement with Anza Power for the 50 MW/200 MWh Bairnsdale battery in Australia. The agreement gives Amazon access to the battery’s storage capacity and flexibility without requiring it to own the asset (see Amazon Signs First Battery Storage Tolling Deal In Asia Pacific). However, the availability of bankable tollers is a key challenge, as they need to offer operational expertise, sufficient risk capital and creditworthiness, points out the whitepaper. Additionally, flexible connection agreements, changes to network charges and co-location with renewable energy projects could affect battery operations and revenues. Germany’s proposed AgNes reform of electricity network charges may also have significant implication for project revenues in the future. The reform will require BESS projects commissioned after August 4, 2029 with no qualifying FID, to contribute to network costs (see Germany's AgNes Draft Draws Industry Concerns On Storage FID Timeline). Such factors and uncertainties could lead tollers to demand higher risk premiums, offer lower payments or impose shorter and more restrictive contract terms. The authors of the whitepaper explain how tolling terms can affect the debt available to a BESS project. For instance, a higher fixed tolling payment or a larger share of battery capacity covered by the agreement can increase the cash flow available for loan repayments. A longer contract can also give lenders greater certainty over revenues. The report emphasizes that the tolling agreement, financing terms, manufacturer warranties and technical design must therefore be structured together. Florian Mayr, Partner, Strategy & Germany, PwC said, “The BESS market not only needs more projects and more capital. It also needs a scalable market for bankable tolling capacity and structures that allow risk to be sensibly distributed between asset owners, tollers and capital providers.” The authors therefore highlight the need for project-specific financing and tolling arrangements that account for grid connection conditions, technical design and the project’s marketing strategy. The white paper also identifies potential demand for tolling beyond standalone storage developers. This includes unsubsidized wind and solar plants, large electricity consumers such as data centers and electrolyzers, and certain must-run power plants as market participants that could use tolling structures to manage exposure to volatile electricity prices. The complete white paper in German is available for free download on FfE’s website.

artigo.texto: Pro-data center party interrupted by protesters in D.C. A pro-data center party took place in Washington D.C. on Saturday night, as opposition to data center construction has intensified across the country. An invitation to the event on Partiful said: "In light of the bipartisan psychosis over AI data centers, it's about time that the people who haven't lost their minds get together and celebrate the glory of American compute." Videos posted on social media showed the party in full swing, complete with a DJ booth and dance floor. One X user wrote that the event had "a generative AI photo booth, AI themed cocktails." At one point, protesters appeared to crash the party. One female protester took to the stage and shouted to the crowd "thank you for using all the water" and "you're killing the world," as party-goers chanted "USA!" The protester was eventually seen being removed from the stage. As data center construction accelerates, the debate over how and where the facilities should be built is expected to remain a growing political and environmental issue. After the disruption, Adam Thierer from the R Street Institute took to the stage to say: "You know who doesn't believe in freedom, is the freaks who were just up here charging the stage," the Washington Sun reported. As demand for AI computing has boomed, data centers have become a growing source of tension over their enormous demands for power, water and land. Newsweek contacted Jonas Du and Young Voices via email on Monday, outside of regular working hours. The Party "Data After Dark: A Pro-Data Center Party" was held at the self-described "Bitcoin bar," PubKey in D.C. More than a thousand people had signed up to attend through the Partiful invitation, though it is not clear how many ultimately attended. Young Voices, Pirate Wires and The Compute Optimist were listed on a flyer as the organizations behind the party. The event was sponsored by several think tanks, technology advocacy groups and organizations promoting the expansion of computing infrastructure. The event featured themed cocktails with names inspired by the data center industry, one of the organizers wrote on X. These included the Loudoun County Iced Tea, a reference to the Virginia county at the heart of the region's "Data Center Alley," as well as the SMRtini and the Closed-loop Spritz. Who Were the Event Organizers? The event was organized by Ed Tarnowski, a technology policy fellow at the free-market R Street Institute who has launched the Substack publication The Compute Optimist; Jonas Du, a writer at technology and politics publication Pirate Wires; and Casey Given, the CEO of Young Voices, a nonprofit that trains and promotes young pro-liberty commentators. Tarnowski and Du appeared in a video filmed at the event, in which a reporter asked attendees why they loved data centers. "This is our industrial revolution," Tarnowski said. "AI is poised to deliver benefits that we couldn't imagine," he said, adding that technological progress was reliant on American "dominance of data centers." He also touted the "national security benefits" of data centers, particularly their importance to the U.S. in maintaining a technological edge over China. Du also appeared in the video, and said: "The only way we can get young people and everyday Americans feeling more optimistic about the economy and the future of the country and the American dream is by growing our economy and increasing our innovation rate. And data centers power AI, which is the number one thing driving that right now." "We should use common sense as to where we built them and how we build them, but no question we need to build more," he added. Along with the protesters who expressed their displeasure in person, the event also sparked backlash on social media. While one X user went so far as to say they wished the party would be set on fire with attendees inside, others expressed more temperate criticisms that hosting a glitzy D.C. cocktail party in support of data centers would not help ordinary Americans get on board. Data Center Debate Heats Up The U.S. is in the midst of a boom of data centers, which are large facilities that house the computer servers and other equipment needed to store and process vast amounts of digital information. There are at least 4,000 operational facilities nationwide and some 3,000 more planned or under construction. But the expansion has faced growing opposition over the facilities' demands for resources and their proximity to residential areas. A Gallup poll found that around 70 percent of Americans are opposed to data centers being built in their area. The issue has increasingly become a political flashpoint, as opposition to data centers has spread across party lines, even as the Trump administration promotes their expansion as essential to the U.S. race for AI dominance. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Cristina Diciu. Related Articles

artigo.texto: What leaders are arguing about According to diplomats familiar with the talks, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis intend to reopen the carbon-market dispute during a Tuesday meeting in Prague. Their ask is to put off the 2028 step that would bring heating and road transport fuels into the EU's Emissions Trading System, the add-on commonly referred to as ETS2. Their rationale, per those diplomats: with prices still elevated, expanding the market now would hit the buildings and transport sectors and strain people's purchasing power. Who wants the plan to proceed A group of six countries is pushing back on another delay after the expansion had already slipped by a year. Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg warned in a document shared with other EU governments, "We are concerned by recent calls for further amendments to and postponement of ETS2." They added, "Going forward, EU businesses and households need political stability and predictability." That split captures the EU's balancing act. The bloc wants to stay on track for net zero by 2050 without undercutting its competitiveness with the US and China or prompting voter blowback over higher costs. Elections next year in France, Italy, Spain and Poland only raise the political temperature. Prices, policy and the market Since the war started, the price of gas in Europe has climbed to over twice its earlier level, and earlier in September it reached the highest point since late 2022. Power has jumped too, with prices up around 77% in France and roughly 60% in Germany. To ease concerns about adding ETS2 on top of that, the European Commission has outlined tools to prevent sharp price moves and soften energy cost worries. EU ministers are expected to sign off on those tweaks on Oct. 9 in Luxembourg. Beyond the ETS2 timing fight, Meloni and Babis also plan to discuss a wider revamp of ETS1, the current carbon market, put forward by the commission in July. Policy debates remind investors to keep long term goals and risk plans aligned. They want measures to shield European companies from new costs by temporarily allowing rules that loosen how free emission permits are used in energy‑intensive industries like ceramics, steel and cement. They also want to lessen how carbon prices affect electricity by, for a limited period, capping the degree to which emission costs are passed into wholesale power prices. And they favor tighter transparency and oversight, with closer monitoring by the European Commission, the European Securities and Markets Authority and the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators. Established in 2005, the EU's cap-and-trade system sets progressively tighter emission caps for more than 10,000 installations across industries such as steel, cement and chemicals. Across the bloc, carbon charges make up about 11% of the average electricity bill, with a bigger effect where fossil fuels dominate. In Poland, that share can reach as high as 24%. What this means for your portfolio Whether ETS2 stays on schedule, slips again, or gets paired with stronger buffers will ripple into energy bills and industrial margins, which eventually feed into consumer prices and earnings. With politics heating up and climate targets fixed, watch for signals on price safeguards, free permit flexibility and how much of carbon costs power producers can pass through. artigo.texto: FMC pede registro do herbicida rimisoxafen no Brasil Ingrediente ativo atua nos Grupos 12 e 32 e mira plantas daninhas resistentes em soja e milho O Brasil reúne 20 projetos de carbono agrícola e manejo do solo desenvolvidos com a metodologia VM0042, da Verra. O volume representa cerca de 8% dos 264 projetos desse tipo registrados na base global da certificadora. O pipeline nacional supera 10 milhões de créditos de carbono potenciais por ano. O levantamento consta em relatório da RaboResearch. A escala da agropecuária brasileira amplia o potencial desse mercado. Segundo os dados apresentados pela RaboResearch, com base na Embrapa, o país possui 177 milhões de hectares de pastagens. Desse total, cerca de 28 milhões de hectares, ou 15%, apresentam algum nível de degradação. Essas áreas poderiam passar por processos de recuperação com práticas regenerativas. A proposta associa a melhoria do manejo ao aumento dos estoques de carbono no solo. Entre as práticas citadas aparecem plantio direto, culturas de cobertura, rotação de culturas, integração lavoura-pecuária, manejo regenerativo das pastagens, menor revolvimento do solo e otimização do uso de insumos. O processo também pode gerar efeitos agronômicos. O relatório cita aumento da matéria orgânica, maior retenção de água, redução da erosão, melhoria da fertilidade, ganhos de produtividade e maior resiliência diante de secas e eventos climáticos extremos. A adoção, porém, exige investimento inicial, mudanças operacionais e período de adaptação. Os créditos de carbono podem funcionar como uma fonte adicional de remuneração nesse processo. O produtor adota práticas capazes de elevar os estoques de carbono. O projeto mede e monitora os resultados. Uma entidade independente realiza a validação e a verificação. Após essa etapa, o padrão de certificação pode emitir os créditos. A metodologia VM0042, denominada Improved Agricultural Land Management, concentra boa parte dos projetos analisados. A base pública da Verra reunia 264 projetos de carbono agrícola e manejo do solo na data considerada pelo estudo. A Ásia concentrava 119 projetos. A Europa somava 45. A América Latina tinha 40 e a África, 26. O Brasil respondia por 20 iniciativas, metade do total latino-americano. A maior parte dos projetos brasileiros ainda percorre fases anteriores à emissão. O relatório identificou sete projetos em pipeline aprovado, quatro em pipeline solicitado, um em pipeline solicitado já em validação, três em validação, dois em processo de registro e verificação, dois aguardando registro e apenas um projeto registrado com créditos emitidos. O quadro indica um mercado ainda em consolidação. A entrada de uma propriedade em um projeto agrupado de carbono no solo começa pela análise de elegibilidade. O processo considera histórico de uso da terra, práticas de manejo, localização, disponibilidade de dados e potencial de remoção de carbono. Depois da adesão, o projeto realiza um diagnóstico da propriedade. Essa avaliação estabelece a linha de base. A referência reúne as condições produtivas e os estoques de carbono existentes antes da implantação das novas práticas. O projeto define então o plano de manejo. Durante o período de creditação, o produtor precisa manter as práticas acordadas e fornecer dados operacionais. Também precisa permitir auditorias e participar do monitoramento. Esse acompanhamento pode envolver registros de manejo, imagens de satélite, análises de solo, visitas de campo e modelos científicos. O desenvolvedor consolida os dados. Entidades independentes fazem a validação e a verificação. Após a confirmação das remoções, o padrão aplicável emite os créditos. A comercialização gera receita. O produtor recebe uma parcela conforme as condições previstas em contrato. A RaboResearch ressalta o horizonte longo desses projetos. A implantação das práticas, o monitoramento, a verificação e a emissão dos créditos ocorrem ao longo dos anos. O retorno financeiro não ocorre de forma imediata. Entre as iniciativas citadas aparece o ReTerra, parceria entre Rabobank Brasil, Ruuts by Ovis 21 e Anthesis Group. O projeto pretende ampliar a integração lavoura-pecuária e o pastejo regenerativo adaptativo. A meta envolve pelo menos 350 mil hectares nos próximos cinco anos. O relatório também apresenta o Programa de Agricultura Regenerativa da América do Sul, conhecido como SARA. A iniciativa concluiu sua primeira emissão em fevereiro de 2026. Foram gerados 210 mil créditos sob a metodologia VM0042 para o período de monitoramento de 2019 a 2023. Mais de um quarto desse volume já havia sido comercializado na data do relatório. A receita alcançou cerca de 1,2 milhão de dólares. O valor implica preço médio próximo de 21,80 dólares por tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente. O programa atende mais de 130 fazendas em 150 mil hectares na Argentina, Chile e Paraguai. A meta prevê alcançar 500 mil hectares e superar um milhão de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente em remoções anuais a partir de 2028, condicionadas às verificações e à expansão do programa. Outra iniciativa reúne AMAGGI e NaturAll Carbon em Rondônia. A primeira etapa abrange cerca de 25 mil hectares na Fazenda Carolinas. O manejo previsto inclui plantio direto, rotação de culturas, culturas de cobertura e maior uso de insumos biológicos. O projeto prevê certificação pela metodologia VM0042. A quantificação do carbono aparece entre os principais desafios. Os projetos precisam demonstrar remoções mensuráveis e associadas às mudanças de manejo. Também precisam comprovar a manutenção dos ganhos ao longo do período definido. O relatório aponta necessidade de sistemas robustos de monitoramento, amostragem e verificação. Os resultados ainda podem sofrer influência da variabilidade climática, de eventos meteorológicos extremos, dos preços dos créditos e da demanda dos compradores. A regulamentação brasileira também integra esse cenário. A Lei número 15.042, de 2024, instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissõ

artigo.texto: A produção tropicalizada de baterias garantirá a segurança da matriz energética brasileira De olho no potencial do país, fabricantes traçam planos de longo prazo para suprir o mercado de armazenamento de energia Atualizado Mercado ainda incipiente no país, as soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias, essenciais para garantir flexibilidade e segurança às redes elétricas, ganham um novo impulso com a queda no custo das baterias de íon-lítio no mercado internacional, com a maior facilidade de negociação nos contratos de energia e com a perspectiva de avanços no ambiente regulatório — inclusive com o esperado Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade destinado a sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, agendado para dezembro. As ações dos fabricantes de tecnologia no mercado brasileiro focam estratégias de longo prazo, visando consolidar uma produção tropicalizada, como avalia Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da multinacional chinesa BYD no Brasil, que anunciou em fevereiro deste ano um investimento de R$ 500 milhões para a fabricação de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias — em inglês, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) — no país. “Estamos falando de uma decisão de longo prazo”, define. “É um movimento baseado na confiança que temos no potencial desse mercado e na importância que o armazenamento terá para o futuro da matriz energética brasileira”, diz. Segundo Baldy, a estratégia visa desenvolver capacidade industrial local e, ao mesmo tempo, criar condições para que uma cadeia brasileira de fornecedores cresça junto com esse mercado. “Esse processo de nacionalização também permitirá atender aos requisitos previstos pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia para o Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade, ampliando o acesso dos investidores a linhas de financiamento do banco, tanto para projetos ligados ao leilão quanto para outras aplicações”, afirma. No leilão, há dois segmentos: armazenamento nacional, com exigência de, no mínimo, 15% de componentes locais, e geral, sem requisitos de nacionalização. A Contemporary Amperey Technology Co., Limited (CATL), outro superfabricante chinês de tecnologia, pretende fornecer para os dois. Para participar do leilão nacional, a CATL anunciou uma parceria estratégica com o Grupo Moura, um dos principais fabricantes de baterias do país, sediado no município de Belo Jardim (PE). “Para maximizar nosso impacto, estamos nos preparando ativamente, em conjunto com parceiros nacionais, para fornecer equipamentos credenciados, implementando plataformas avançadas de armazenamento com capacidade nativa de frid-forming [seguidores de redes]”, explica Ray See, vice-presidente de negócios para as Américas da CATL. Ele diz que, além de fornecer equipamentos, a parceria com o Grupo Moura visa integrar os sistemas de baterias localmente com um fabricante nacional e cumprir as regras de nacionalização previstas pelo governo federal. Para suprir o leilão de armazenamento geral, a CATL vai importar os equipamentos. Nos últimos anos, as vendas acumuladas de soluções BESS no Brasil somaram somente 1,9 GWh, dos quais 730 MWh foram comercializados em 2025, especialmente nos setores comercial e industrial. Nesse ano, os financiamentos registrados em BESS atingiram R$ 126 milhões. É um volume maior que o registrado em 2024 (R$ 117 milhões), mas que não reflete a real expansão da tecnologia no país, aponta levantamento do Clean Energy Latin America (Cela), uma boutique de investimentos do setor de energia renovável da região. “A expectativa é que os primeiros leilões dedicados exclusivamente ao armazenamento, previstos para 2026, marquem uma nova fase de escala para o segmento, com impacto direto nos volumes de financiamento”, confia Camila Ramos, diretora-executiva do Cela. “Podemos ter até um crescimento explosivo dos sistemas de armazenamento por baterias no Brasil nos próximos oito anos”, acredita Markus Vlasits, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). “A corrida das empresas estrangeiras e brasileiras por esse mercado deve movimentar mais de R$ 80 bilhões em investimentos até 2034”, diz. Só o leilão previsto para este ano deve destravar R$ 10 bilhões em projetos, estima Vlasits. Segundo ele, esse aumento dos negócios no setor de armazenamento de energia em baterias é movido pela redução de quase 70% no custo das baterias de lítio nos últimos três anos e a necessidade crescente de flexibilidade no sistema elétrico do país para gerenciar as diversas fontes de energias renováveis, como a solar e eólica. “Teremos muitos projetos dos fabricantes voltados para atender o setor comercial e industrial, além de projetos de descarbonização na região amazônica”, destaca. A WEG avalia que o potencial de negócios não se restringe apenas a grandes projetos. “Acreditamos muito também nas aplicações de médio porte, principalmente soluções BESS junto à carga e combinado com geração distribuída”, diz Manfred Peter Johann, vice-presidente de automação e sistemas da WEG. “A bateria pode ajudar a superar gargalos de fornecimento de energia e limitações da rede, garantir backup e maior confiabilidade para o consumidor e permitir arbitragem de energia entre diferentes horários.” No início deste ano, a WEG anunciou a construção de uma nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em Itajaí (SC), com financiamento de R$ 280 milhões do programa BNDES Mais Inovação. A nova unidade ampliará capacidade produtiva para até 2 GWh ao ano e deverá entrar em operação no segundo semestre de 2027, informa Johann. “Praticamente todo o sistema pode ser industrializado no país”, indica. “O principal componente que ainda depende de importação é a célula da bateria, cuja fabricação exige uma escala muito maior para se tornar economicamente competitiva.” Praticamente dominado por fabricantes de tecnologia de ponta e gigantes industriais, o mercado de BESS movimenta t
