artigo.texto: The New Economics of Enterprise AI AI costs stop being about tokens once it hits production — the real question is whether you own or just rent the economics. September 28, 2026 Sponsored by HPE Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from "can we use it?" to "how efficiently are we using it?" Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes. That's the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow. Three ways to run AI Utilization is central to this economics. Directing more work to paid-for capacity lowers effective unit cost; idle GPUs, fragmented workloads, and oversized models all raise the cost of every useful result. Enterprises generally choose among three models: A bespoke stack — procuring infrastructure and controls in-house. Flexible, but it creates a continuing burden, since teams must revalidate the environment as models and policies change. On-demand consumption — hyperscalers reduce the assembly burden and suit low or uncertain demand, but charges rise with every prompt or agent action. An integrated private AI platform — owned or dedicated capacity paired with a validated stack. The advantage isn't free inference; it's control over efficiency levers like scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management. The right model depends on the workload. APIs can be rational for experimentation or variable demand. As workloads become sustained and business-critical, enterprises need to weigh not just what they consume, but how efficiently they operate the system. Ownership is an operating discipline Buying a Formula 1 race car and parking it in your garage means owning one of the most sophisticated vehicles ever built — but ownership alone doesn't make you competitive; you still need drivers, mechanics, and track time to justify it. AI infrastructure works the same way. One of the biggest misconceptions in enterprise AI is that owning infrastructure automatically improves economics. Owning GPUs creates the opportunity for better economics, but only if the organization has sufficient demand and operational discipline to keep resources productive. The infrastructure that returns the best ROI isn't a reference architecture or a bespoke build-out — it's a fully integrated, qualified stack that lets teams route tasks to the least costly model that meets quality requirements and reuse context through techniques such as KV-cache management, reducing wasted capacity while maintaining responsiveness. Without these practices, committed infrastructure can become stranded capital. With them, rising demand improves economics as fixed costs are amortized across more useful work — increasingly important in agentic systems, where economics are shaped less by any single prompt than by the efficiency of the complete environment. From deployment to value HPE Private Cloud AI is a production-ready foundation combining infrastructure, software, models, tools, governance, and services, reducing the integration burden of operating private AI at scale. Its architecture lets teams manage scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management as operational levers, aligning capacity and service levels with each workload's requirements. It also includes a 90-day engagement with forward-deployed engineers who help customer teams deploy initial use cases and establish repeatable operating practices. In independent testing commissioned by HPE, an integrated platform serving multiple workloads at high utilization delivered a lower effective cost per token than repeatedly renting equivalent capacity. Actual results will vary based on workload mix and utilization. Measure what matters Token consumption remains useful, but it isn't a complete measure of AI economics. A fuller enterprise view tracks cost per business-relevant outcome, accelerator utilization, and model choice relative to task complexity. Enterprises already operating private AI should ask how mature their utilization is, and how workload volume will change over the next 12 to 18 months. Those earlier in the journey should build these practices in from the first deployment, so strategy anticipates growth before demand becomes a bottleneck. For low-volume, unpredictable demand, an API or hyperscaler may remain sensible. But as AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises have a growing incentive to control utilization, amortize fixed costs, and manage the environment as a long-term operating asset. The strategic question isn't whether enterprises will pay for AI — it's whether they will understand, and ultimately own, the economics behind it. For the past 15 years, his focus has been on bridging the gap between cutting-edge research and enterprise-scale deployment for Machine Learning and AI. His passion is turning the art of the possible into operational reality. artigo.texto: Key points: Solid-state batteries will not see PV-style industry-wide involution in the short term: unconverged technology routes, high capital thresholds, and yields of only 50%-60% form a firewall. There are phased risks in 2027-2029, with surplus pilot lines and localized price wars on the equipment side; after 2030, if technology routes converge, leading capacity is released, and demand growth slows, industry-wide involution could occur, with intensity likely lower than in PV but with slower market exit. Given the lessons from PV, the solid-state battery industry is fully capable of avoiding involution. SMM has recently reviewed the future of solid-state batteries and compiled a ten-year series. Using the current development of the lithium battery industry as a reference, especially the intertwined history of the LFP and ternary routes, which has written an epic chapter over time. In the long history of conventional liquid lithium batteries, semi-solid and solid-state batteries will take the stage, outlining a new generation of high-specific-energy battery world. artigo.texto: SMT Energy Secures $268 Million for Battery Storage Expansion ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: SMT Energy secured an equity investment of up to $268 million from Climate Adaptive Infrastructure (CAI) to scale its battery energy storage project portfolio. - Why it matters: This capital infusion highlights the growing institutional appetite for BESS assets, providing a roadmap for similar financing structures in the Indian market. - Watch: The deployment of these funds into utility-scale storage projects and the potential for similar cross-border infrastructure investments. Background and Context SMT Energy, a developer, owner, and operator of critical energy infrastructure, has successfully closed an equity partnership with Climate Adaptive Infrastructure (CAI) to secure up to $268 million in funding. This significant capital injection is earmarked for the development, construction, and operation of battery energy storage projects across the United States. The partnership builds upon a prior $32 million investment by CAI, signaling strong investor confidence in SMT Energy’s operational model and the broader energy storage sector. Key Details The funding is structured at the parent-company level, providing SMT Energy with the necessary liquidity to expand its development platform. According to the company, the capital will be used alongside tax equity and project-level debt to execute its pipeline of distributed generation and utility-scale storage assets. This follows a successful financing round in February 2025, where the company secured $135 million to develop a 160 MW/320 MWh battery energy storage project in Houston, Texas. Macquarie and KeyBanc served as joint lead arrangers for that specific project financing. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, this deal underscores the increasing importance of grid stabilization as renewable energy penetration grows. As wind and solar capacity continues to scale globally, battery storage is becoming the primary solution for managing intermittency. The ability to secure large-scale equity partnerships is a critical differentiator for developers. Furthermore, the involvement of specialized infrastructure firms like CAI demonstrates that institutional investors are moving beyond simple project-level debt, opting instead for platform-level investments to capture long-term value in the energy transition. What Happens Next The energy storage market continues to see robust capital flows, with Mercom reporting $8.9 billion in corporate funding across 73 deals in the first half of 2026. As the India renewable energy sector matures, the demand for sophisticated storage solutions is expected to mirror global trends. Developers in India should monitor such international financing models, as they provide a blueprint for securing the capital-intensive backing required for large-scale BESS and pumped hydro projects. The focus will now shift to how effectively SMT Energy deploys this capital to meet the rising demand for grid-scale storage capacity.

artigo.texto: Crusoe, a company building AI factories, has announced that it is the developer of Google’s new data center campus being built in Armstrong County outside of Amarillo, Texas. The campus is Crusoe’s latest in West Texas, joining two others under development in Abilene. Construction of the data center campus began in June 2025 and connects directly to Serena’s Goodnight 1 wind farm, which is operational and generates 265.5 MW. It is also adjacent to the Goodnight 2 wind farm ,which is under construction and will generate the same 265.5 MW. Surplus power from the wind farms will be fed back to the grid, in line with Crusoe’s efforts to support the buildout of clean, affordable energy in the region. “Building the future of AI requires a new kind of infrastructure, starting with energy. Crusoe’s strategy is to build AI factories directly at the source of abundant, low-cost energy – to both improve utilization of existing assets as well as catalyze new energy generation,” said Chase Lochmiller, Crusoe Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer. “The Armstrong County campus is a prime example of this energy-first strategy. We’re bringing new, affordable clean energy online. We broke ground in June 2025 and are building at the same swift pace we set in Abilene.” In addition to the power supplied by the wind farms, the campus is designed to be water efficient. It will utilize a closed-loop, non-evaporative liquid cooling system. According to the press release, this will limit the facility’s water consumption to domestic uses such as kitchens. Crusoe has not said how much IT capacity the campus will support, nor how much it intends to invest in the development. Power has become the great decider for projects in Texas. In August, governor Greg Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to conduct a verification audit of all data center projects moving through ERCOT’s interconnection process. ERCOT was considering 474 GW in grid connection requests at the time, 90 percent of which were for data centers. Since then several projects have been granted conditional base load status including the 2 GW Sweetwater Hub in West Texas being constructed by IREN. CleanSpark, Hut 8, and Galaxy Digital were granted the same status in ERCOT’s Batch Zero process in September, as w.media reported.

artigo.texto: The global artificial intelligence industry needs to earn $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed to build data centers around the world, Bain & Co. said. Existing consumer and enterprise AI services may generate as much as $1.8 trillion of that sum, leaving $4.2 trillion in new revenue that needs to be created, the consulting firm said Tuesday in its annual global technology report. The shortfall likely will come from nascent segments ranging from autonomous machines to robotics, as well as emerging fields such as drug discovery, mental health and energy generation, it said. “What the industry needs is a wave of innovation that will dwarf what mobile and cloud unlocked,” said David Crawford, the report’s lead author and chair of Bain’s Global Technology, Media, and Telecommunications practice. “AI infrastructure is being built well ahead of the demand curve, and funding it sustainably will require adding approximately 1% to the annual global GDP growth rate,” he said. Bain’s report highlights the hurdles ahead to make the current pace of AI development sustainable. Companies led by Microsoft, Alphabet’s Google, Amazon.com, Meta Platforms and Oracle are investing trillions of dollars in data centers to quench AI’s demand for computational resources. Data center sizes and costs are doubling roughly every 12 to 16 months, in part due to surging prices of chips from the likes of Nvidia and SK Hynix, networking equipment and other components. The report comes as debate intensifies around the as-yet elusive returns for AI service providers. Critics worry about an increasingly interconnected web of dependencies between technology manufacturers and AI developers that help to propel lofty expectations that in turn require bigger sums of money. While discussions today are fixated on employee productivity, the economics of AI infrastructure will demand trillions in new revenue beyond productivity gains, Bain said. The consultancy projects $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion of data-center spending by 2030, adding at least 150 gigawatts of capacity that will further strain countries’ energy resources. Annual spending on AI infrastructure — spanning data centers, computing capacity and upgrades in accelerators and memory chips — may reach as much as $1.5 trillion by 2031, it said. Data center developers already face shortages in transformers and water and power supplies, as well as fierce local opposition that’s blocked or delayed $68 billion worth of projects in the June quarter in the United States.

artigo.texto: Advait Energy’s arm signed a supply deal with HiTHIUM for up to 1 GWh of battery cells to feed its upcoming storage plant in Gujarat. Advait Battery Ecosystem, a step-down subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions Ltd, signed a Master Supply Agreement with HiTHIUM on 18 September, the company said in an exchange filing. HiTHIUM is a global energy storage manufacturer, listed as a BloombergNEF Tier 1 supplier. Battery energy storage systems, called BESS, hold power so it can be used later, on power grids and in factories. Advait plans to assemble them in Gujarat, and it needs battery cells to do that. This deal covers the need. The plant needs cells first. HiTHIUM will supply 314 Ah lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic cells, with up to 1 GWh of purchases over the next 12 months. GWh is a measure of stored energy capacity. LFP cells are widely used in stationary storage because of their long life and stability. The contract price is $49.5 per kWh for up to 350 MWh of cells. Pricing beyond that will depend on future project orders. The cells will go to a planned assembly plant at Gangad in Gujarat, with a capacity of 2.5 GWh a year. It will put together modules and packs, fit them into containers and commission the systems for utility, commercial and industrial customers. The company says commercial production should begin soon. Bhushan Shahane, chief operating officer of Advait Battery Ecosystem, said a dependable, world-class cell supply is central to delivering cost-efficient storage systems as the plant scales up. The 1 GWh covers about 40% of the plant’s yearly capacity. It is a supply framework, not a firm order for the whole amount, and actual use will depend on production schedules and customer demand. For HiTHIUM, the deal opens a supply link with an Indian storage manufacturer. The listed parent is also widening its business. artigo.texto: A LG anunciou nesta segunda-feira (28) que passou a integrar a NVIDIA Partner Network (NPN) como Parceira Preferencial em Soluções de Energia e Resfriamento. A colaboração amplia a atuação da companhia no desenvolvimento de infraestrutura para data centers voltados a cargas de trabalho de inteligência artificial. Segundo a LG, o aumento da densidade computacional dos data centers de IA exige sistemas capazes de lidar com cargas térmicas maiores. Nesse cenário, a empresa está ampliando seu portfólio de soluções de resfriamento líquido, voltadas principalmente para infraestruturas de alta densidade. A companhia também destaca a integração das soluções de resfriamento desde os estágios iniciais do planejamento dos data centers, permitindo considerar as necessidades térmicas e de energia na própria concepção da infraestrutura. LG tem CDU de 2,6 MW qualificada pela NVIDIA Entre os principais produtos apresentados pela LG está uma Unidade de Distribuição de Fluido de Resfriamento (CDU) de 2,6 MW. Segundo a empresa, o equipamento foi qualificado como NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU e atualmente possui a maior capacidade de resfriamento entre as soluções que receberam essa qualificação. A LG também concluiu a qualificação de infraestrutura de IA para modelos de 600 kW e 1 MW. De acordo com a companhia, o processo de avaliação considerou critérios técnicos relacionados ao desempenho de resfriamento, recursos de failover e confiabilidade. As qualificações fazem parte da estratégia da LG para atuar em diferentes etapas da infraestrutura térmica necessária para data centers de IA de alta densidade. Resfriamento líquido direto ao chip As CDUs desenvolvidas pela LG utilizam uma arquitetura de resfriamento líquido direto ao chip (DTC, Direct-to-Chip). Nesse sistema, o fluido de resfriamento é direcionado diretamente para componentes que geram grande quantidade de calor, incluindo CPUs e GPUs. A solução pode trabalhar em conjunto com sistemas tradicionais de resfriamento a ar já instalados no data center. A combinação permite criar uma arquitetura híbrida, utilizando o resfriamento líquido nos componentes de maior demanda térmica enquanto mantém parte da infraestrutura convencional para outras áreas do ambiente. O avanço desse tipo de tecnologia está relacionado ao aumento das cargas de processamento utilizadas por sistemas de inteligência artificial. A LG afirma que suas CDUs foram desenvolvidas para lidar com essas demandas térmicas em infraestruturas de alta densidade. LG prepara CDU de 4 MW para qualificação A empresa também revelou planos de ampliar sua linha de soluções. Até o final de 2026, a LG pretende buscar a qualificação da NVIDIA para uma CDU com capacidade de 4,0 MW. A iniciativa deve ampliar a capacidade do portfólio voltado a data centers de IA e complementar os modelos de 600 kW, 1 MW e 2,6 MW já mencionados pela companhia. A LG não divulgou, no anúncio, uma previsão de conclusão do processo de qualificação do modelo de 4 MW além da indicação de que pretende buscá-la até o fim deste ano. Soluções serão apresentadas em evento em Singapura As CDUs da LG que concluíram a qualificação de infraestrutura de IA da NVIDIA serão apresentadas na Data Centre World Asia 2026 (DCWA 2026). O evento está programado para acontecer entre 29 e 30 de setembro, no Marina Bay Sands, em Singapura. A participação permitirá à LG apresentar suas soluções de resfriamento líquido para data centers e os modelos que já passaram pelos processos de qualificação relacionados à infraestrutura de IA da NVIDIA. Parceria mira expansão da infraestrutura de IA A entrada da LG na NVIDIA Partner Network como Parceira Preferencial em Soluções de Energia e Resfriamento coloca as soluções de gerenciamento térmico da companhia dentro do ecossistema de parceiros da NVIDIA voltado à infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. “Integrar a NVIDIA Partner Network como Parceira Preferencial em Energia e Resfriamento é um passo importante em nossa estratégia para apoiar a expansão do ecossistema global de IA”, afirmou James Lee, presidente da LG ES Company. Segundo o executivo, a LG pretende trabalhar com a NVIDIA no desenvolvimento de soluções de resfriamento destinadas aos desafios térmicos dos data centers de IA. Com as CDUs de 600 kW, 1 MW e 2,6 MW já qualificadas e o plano de buscar a qualificação de um modelo de 4 MW, a empresa pretende ampliar sua presença no segmento de infraestrutura térmica para data centers de alta densidade. - Categorias Participe do grupo de ofertas do Mundo Conectado Confira as principais ofertas de Smartphones, TVs e outros eletrônicos que encontramos pela internet. artigo.texto: While President Trump was holding a press conference at the White House this morning and extolling the AI-related work of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and a promo for Wednesday night’s South Park episode dropped. It was less salutary. Here’s the logline for Episode 6 of Season 29: “Butters is unhappy with the data centers that the billionaires are building in our backyards.” The clip opens with an X-Pest exterminator guy ringing the doorbell at Butters’ home. Watch on Deadline “I understand you’ve got some billionaires in your backyard,” he says. “Yeah, there’s more of these stupid billionaires every day!” replies Butters. The first image from the episode (see it above) shows Butters in what appears to be his backyard with the X-Pest exterminator guy, who has strapped on his tank of poison and has his sprayer wand at the ready. The topic of data centers is a hot one across the country and especially in Hollywood, where unions and workers worry about job displacement and writers and directors express concern over what it might do to their art. Among the biggest players in the data center land rush is, of course, Oracle CEO and Paramount-WBD deal financier Larry Ellison. South Park airs on Comedy Central, which is owned by Paramount. As in the past, the show’s creators are seemingly not afraid to bite the hand that feeds them. Mark Ruffalo and others have decried the introduction of “really profoundly scary technology” into Hollywood and how AI might impact media outlets soon to be owned by Ellison and his son David. “Larry is a classic oligarch,” wrote Ruffalo. “They are crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.” Paramount, for its part, responded by accusing Ruffalo of using “antisemitic tropes” in his argument, especially when linking the Ellisons’ studio acquisition to Oracle’s work with the Israeli military.

artigo.texto: A WEG (WEGE3) anunciou nesta segunda-feira (28) um investimento de US$ 165 milhões (R$ 840 milhões) para ampliar sua capacidade de produção de geradores na América do Norte. O plano busca atender à crescente demanda por geração de energia para aplicações críticas nos Estados Unidos, impulsionada especialmente pela expansão dos data centers. Segundo comunicado ao mercado, o projeto será executado em duas fases. Ao fim da expansão, prevista para 2030, a capacidade global da companhia chegará a cerca de 50 geradores por dia. Atualmente, a empresa pode produzir 10 unidades diárias. WEG terá nova operação de geradores no México A primeira etapa prevê investimento de US$ 24 milhões na compra e adequação de um prédio industrial no México, destinado à montagem de geradores. O início das operações está previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Na segunda fase, a WEG investirá US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais. A localização ainda será definida, mas ambas ficarão na América do Norte. Com a conclusão do projeto, a capacidade global de produção será cinco vezes a atual, considerando as fábricas da companhia no México, nos Estados Unidos, no Brasil e na China.

artigo.texto: Larsen fights for guardrails on data centers Published 1:30 am Tuesday, September 29, 2026 Submitted by the Office of Rep. Rick Larsen. U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen (WA-02) joined 110 House Democrats in a letter to tech industry leaders last Friday, demanding that all data center construction follow strict guardrails to protect consumers from electricity and water price hikes. “Data center projects and the energy systems and infrastructure that support them must be built and operated responsibly with a commitment to high-quality construction, good jobs, strong environmental stewardship, and strong partnerships with the communities they serve,” wrote the Members. The lawmakers stated that they would oppose new data center construction projects that failed to incorporate strong labor standards, negotiate community benefits agreements with local leaders and mitigate impacts on local air quality, drinking water and utilities costs for residents. “At a time when the nation’s power grid, roads, bridges, schools, and other public infrastructure require significant investment, data center development must strengthen rather than strain, these systems,” the Members continued. “Developers must also invest responsibly in grid infrastructure, including new generation and grid upgrades, to protect ratepayers from bearing the costs of data center projects’ energy needs.” The full text of the letter to tech industry leaders can be read at https://larsen.house.gov/uploadedfiles/final_open_letter_to_tech_industry_leaders_9.18.26.pdf. Larsen holds data centers accountable Last week, Larsen voted for legislation to protect families from higher electricity bills because of data centers in their communities (Ratepayers Protection Act). Larsen also cosponsors the Big Ugly Tax Breaks for Data Centers Act to roll back tax breaks for large artificial intelligence data centers in Republicans’ Big Ugly Law. Larsen supports tough, upfront restrictions on data centers: • No high electric bills for local families and small businesses. • No federal tax breaks. • No construction without community approval and union labor. • Data centers must pay their fair share to connect to and use the grid. • Data centers must use closed-loop water systems. A one-pager on Rep. Larsen’s work to hold data centers accountable can be found at https://larsen.house.gov/uploadedfiles/data_centers_one_pager_1.pdf.

artigo.texto: Bangor City Council votes to extend data center moratorium Published: Sep. 28, 2026 at 11:27 PM EDT|Updated: 7 hours ago BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Bangor City Council has unanimously voted to extend a freeze on new data centers. Councilors voted 8-0 Monday night to add another 180 days to the city’s data center moratorium. Officials say Bangor faces growing interest from developers looking to build data centers, which take up large tracts of land and require massive amounts of power and water for cooling. Because city ordinances weren’t designed for facilities of this scale, councilors say the extra six months will give them time to draft zoning rules that protect local infrastructure, the environment, and neighboring property owners. artigo.texto: Portugal-headquartered Greenvolt Group has started construction of its 600 MW/2.4 GWh Siedlce battery energy storage system (BESS) in Poland through its utility-scale renewable energy business, Greenvolt Power. The project, expected to begin commercial operation by the end of 2027, will be Poland’s largest battery storage facility and one of Europe’s largest, it claims. BYD Energy Storage will supply the battery technology, with the project comprising 210 battery containers and 105 transformer containers equipped with power conversion systems. Siedlce is part of Greenvolt’s approximately 4.6 GW probability-weighted BESS pipeline, including around 2.4 GW in Poland. South Korean battery manufacturer LG Energy Solution has entered a strategic partnership with B2U Storage Solutions which is a US-based battery energy storage systems (BESS) manufacturer that works with repurposed EV batteries. Under the agreement, B2U will receive priority access to LG Energy Solution battery capacity and use its patented technologies to repurpose the batteries for grid-scale storage before recycling. The companies say their aim is to extend battery lifetimes and develop cost-competitive storage solutions for utilities, developers and large commercial users, including data centers. InoBat, a Slovakia-based BESS manufacturer and integrator is moving forward on its plans to list on the Nasdaq. The company along with Cartesian Growth Corporation II, a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), recently filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Their business combination agreement (BCA) values InoBat at $1.265 billion on a pre-money, pre-merger basis. Following completion, the combined company is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol INBT. InoBat counts Volkswagen Group-backed Gotion High-Tech, mining giant Rio Tinto, and Indian battery maker Amara Raja Energy & Mobility Limited among its strategic shareholders and partners. Alongside the transaction, InoBat is expanding its European manufacturing footprint in Slovakia. At its Voderady site, the company is developing a BESS module, pack and container assembly facility with a targeted annual capacity of 5 GWh. Meanwhile, GIB EnergyX Slovakia, its gigafactory investment with Gotion in Šurany, is developing a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cell facility with an initial planned capacity of 20 GWh and targeted production start in 2027. The company is also advancing a sodium-ion battery roadmap in collaboration with Clarios and Altris. Decade Energy, a European developer of energy infrastructure for truck electrification, has signed a two-year supply framework agreement with Sungrow. The China-headquartered energy storage technology company will provide Decade Energy with up to 200 MWh of battery storage equipment in France. Decade Energy says this agreement is intended to support its growing French project pipeline. It will also enable the company to reduce complexity between projects and create a ‘repeatable’ delivery model across multiple sites. US-based SMT Energy has entered into an equity partnership with Climate Adaptive Infrastructure (CAI) for up to $268 million at the parent-company level. The investment, in addition to $32 million previously deployed by CAI into SMT assets, will support the development, construction and operation of battery storage projects across the US. SMT says the funding will enable it to develop and build energy infrastructure with an aggregate value significantly exceeding the equity investment. Its portfolio includes distributed-generation and utility-scale battery storage projects. Singapore-based renewable energy developer Vena Energy has secured a contract for its NRE Nakagawa 2 Battery Storage Project in Japan. The 46.8 MW grid-connected battery energy storage system (BESS), under development near Matsumoto City in Nagano Prefecture, was selected in Japan’s FY2025 Long-Term Decarbonised Power Source Auction (LTDA) conducted by the Organisation for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO). Vena Energy says the LTDA provides long-term revenue certainty to support investment in decarbonized power infrastructure. Nordic Solar, a Danish renewable energy company, has started commercial operation of a 20 MW/40 MWh BESS at its Moletai site in Lithuania. The battery is now integrated with the company’s existing 100 MW solar park, with hybrid trading now underway. The integration of solar generation and battery storage is expected to improve operational flexibility and enable the company to better utilize renewable power generation and market opportunities, stated Nordic Solar. The company switched on the 100 MW Moletai Solar Park in 2024 calling it the country’s largest back then (see Lithuania’s ‘Largest’ Solar Power Station Commissioned).

artigo.texto: During a recent trip to Sichuan Province in China, we got a chance to see BYD’s Flash Chargers up close. For those unfamiliar with the brand’s Flash Charging technology, these T-shaped structures provide EV charging at a rapid pace—around 9.7% charge per minute. According to BYD Philippines’ Adam Hu, these chargers are expected to arrive on our shores by 2027. The BYD Flash Chargers were first launched in China this year, with global rollouts expected for next year. The brand states that it can achieve charging times from 10% to 70% in only five minutes, and 10% to 97% in just nine minutes. During a live demonstration, the charging connector was plugged into a Denza Z9 GT, and while charging, a cup of pour-over coffee was being made on the side. The coffee was served in a cup just before the Z9’s battery topped off, achieving 97% from 33% in just seven minutes. What cars can use these chargers, you ask? Technically, anything with a CCS2 DC charging port can top up at these stations, but the Flash Charging feature is specific to cars with second-generation BYD Blade Batteries. In the Philippines, there are currently no cars equipped with the Blade Battery 2.0. However, the Denza Z9 GT and BYD Ti 7, which are both expected to come to the Philippines, are equipped with these batteries. The rest of the CCS2-equipped vehicles can charge at these stations but are limited to their maximum charging speed. OTHER STORIES YOU MIGHT HAVE MISSED: Fare hikes for jeepneys, buses, taxis, and TNVS take effect today Geely’s AI-powered EV charger will do sub-5min top-ups from 10% to 70% Even though most cars can’t take advantage of Flash Charging right now, it’s still a good thing that the infrastructure will be available. BYD and Denza’s future models will certainly feature Blade Battery 2.0 and later versions, so it shouldn’t be long before more consumers can use these ultra-fast chargers for their EVs.

artigo.texto: WTO to Review EU's Carbon Border Mechanism Challenged by Russia The WTO's Dispute Settlement Body has decided to establish a panel to examine the European Union's carbon border mechanism, which Russia has been challenging since May 2025. The World Trade Organization's (WTO) Dispute Settlement Body decided on Friday, September 25, to establish a panel to examine the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) as well as the European Union's Emissions Trading System for CO2. The decision follows a renewed request from Russia as part of the trade dispute it opened against the EU. The case had already faced an initial block from Brussels before the panel was ultimately established. A Mechanism in Force Since January 2026 The proceedings concern the European scheme applied since January 1, 2026, to imports of certain carbon-intensive products. According to the WTO, Russia had formally requested, on July 10, 2026, the establishment of a panel, after having sought consultations with the European Union and its member states as early as May 12, 2025. CBAM, known as MACF in French, aims to align the carbon cost borne by certain importers with that paid by European producers covered by the EU's carbon market. Its initial scope covers steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen. The European Commission publishes a CBAM certificate price based on auctions under the European Emissions Trading System. This price stood at â¬75.36/tCO2e for the first quarter of 2026, then at â¬75.28/tCO2e for the second quarter of 2026, according to data released by the Commission. Russia Invokes International Trade Rules Moscow contests the European mechanism, arguing it violates the principles of international trade. In the proceedings registered with the WTO, Russia targets both the CBAM regulatory package and what it describes as an export subsidy linked to the European Emissions Trading System. Russia's complaint cites several provisions of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1994, as well as the Agreement on Import Licensing Procedures and the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures. Russia also challenges the treatment of free allowances granted to certain European industries under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), which has been in force since 2005. Brussels Limits Dialogue with Moscow The European Union had rejected, on May 22, 2025, Russia's request for consultations. Brussels had then argued that such talks "could not be fruitful and could not lead to a mutually satisfactory resolution of the matter," citing the "extraordinary circumstances" created by the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Following Russia's request on July 10, 2026, the EU had blocked an initial establishment of the panel, an option available upon the first presentation before the Dispute Settlement Body. In practice, WTO rules subsequently lead to acceptance of a second panel request. In a communication to the WTO, the European Union states it will engage with the panel but not directly with Russia. Brussels stated: "As long as the Russian Federation continues its war of aggression against Ukraine, it cannot expect to be able to invoke WTO rules to improve access for its exports to the European Union market."

artigo.texto: Estudo do Rabobank destaca o potencial do Brasil para se tornar líder no mercado de créditos de carbono. O mercado de créditos de carbono no solo apresenta-se como uma nova oportunidade de financiamento para a agricultura regenerativa no Brasil. O país, com seu vasto potencial agrícola e áreas disponíveis para recuperação, pode remunerar produtores que adotem práticas que aumentem o estoque de carbono no solo. Uma análise do Rabobank enfatiza que o Brasil possui as condições necessárias para se tornar um dos principais mercados de créditos de carbono no solo globalmente. Dados da Embrapa indicam que dos 177 milhões de hectares de pastagens no país, cerca de 28 milhões, ou 15%, estão degradados e têm potencial para serem restaurados com práticas regenerativas. ✨ Essa transição, embora promissora, requer investimentos iniciais, modificações no manejo e um período de adaptação. Entre os benefícios da agricultura regenerativa estão o aumento da matéria orgânica no solo, maiores índices de produtividade, melhor retenção de água e a mitigação de riscos climáticos. O Rabobank ressalta que é necessário expandir os mecanismos de financiamento e remuneração ambiental, como prêmios em cadeias de suprimento sustentáveis e linhas de crédito favoráveis, incluindo créditos de carbono. O mercado já desenvolveu metodologias para medir e monitorar o aumento de carbono armazenado no solo, e os primeiros projetos no Brasil estão avançando nas fases de validação, monitoramento e emissão de créditos. Segundo o estudo de Andrés Padilla, Fernanda Casagrande e Roberto Strumpf, a expansão desse mercado dependerá do avanço desses projetos, da adesão dos produtores, do aumento da demanda, da segurança regulatória e da preservação da integridade ambiental. artigo.texto: Why the rush to build data centers? Let’s ignore all the technology chatter for now. Forget the debates about the infrastructure demands of these massive computing sites. And we’ll also sidestep the big question marks about artificial intelligence – the key driver of data center demand. If you follow the money, however, you see a major force behind developers’ thirst to construct data centers: They’ve been one of the nation’s hottest real estate investments. That’s what my trusty spreadsheet found when looking at Nareit indexes tracking values of real estate investment trusts owning properties across 15 key categories. These benchmarks calculate price swings and dividends paid. The value of trusts that own data centers rose 33% so far in 2026, the second-best performance in the REIT industry, and more than double a 15% gain for all trust assets. What’s performing better in 2026? Trusts that own lodging and resort properties are up 37% on a strong year for tourism. No. 3 is healthcare properties, up 23% as an aging population needs more medical services. Remember, real estate sectors like data centers often heat up when there’s a shortage of specific assets. Big gains in value, plus perceptions of high demand, often get developers in a construction mood. Not just this year Note that the investment buzz for data centers isn’t just a 2026 story. Data center values are up 43% from the start of 2024 through August 2026, the industry’s third-best result, and nearly double the 23% gain for all assets. The gains were only topped by healthcare properties, up 96%, and regional malls, up 69%. Shopping hubs are enjoying a go-out-to-shop renaissance. Trailing the pack So, what properties will developers avoid? Well, look at which property trusts trail the pack. In 2026, the worst places to be are casinos, down 5% as in-person gambling wanes; telecommunications properties, down 2% as cell phone growth ebbs; and timberland, down 1% amid weak construction demand for lumber. Looking longer-term, back to 2024, the trust laggards have been timberland, down 25%; telecommunications, down 16%; and owning single-family rentals, down 4%, as the housing market weakens and regulatory concerns grow. artigo.texto: Gerando resumo No Brasil, um maço de cigarros carrega 83% de tributos. Um casaco de pele, 81%. Já as baterias que armazenam energia limpa e garantem a confiabilidade do sistema elétrico pagam 84%. Tributamos como supérfluo, ou como vício, um equipamento que se tornou infraestrutura essencial no mundo inteiro e que, no Brasil, poderia ajudar a reduzir a conta de luz. A distorção ganha urgência às vésperas das eleições. Com eventos climáticos extremos e mais frequentes, decisões sobre o setor elétrico dizem respeito à segurança energética e à competitividade da indústria nacional. O Brasil reúne condições únicas para liderar essa transformação: um dos melhores recursos solares do mundo e uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável. A energia solar já é a segunda maior fonte da matriz, fruto de uma década que mobilizou mais de R$ 320 bilhões em investimentos. Mas o sistema não foi projetado para essa velocidade. Cortes de geração renovável, inversões de fluxo nas redes e pressões tarifárias mostram que desperdiçamos energia limpa e barata enquanto o consumidor paga uma conta de luz que sobe acima da inflação. É exatamente esse o problema que as baterias ajudam a resolver. Elas armazenam energia nos momentos de maior geração e a devolvem quando o sistema mais precisa, aumentando a confiabilidade, reduzindo desperdícios e custos sistêmicos e diminuindo a dependência de combustíveis fósseis nos horários de pico. Segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), o armazenamento pode atrair mais de R$ 200 bilhões em investimentos na próxima década. O que trava esse potencial é, em boa medida, a tributação. Corrigi-la não é conceder subsídio: é dar às baterias tratamento isonômico em relação às demais tecnologias do setor elétrico. Enquanto essa distorção persistir, a sociedade seguirá exposta a riscos operacionais e custos desnecessários. O próximo governo também precisará evitar retrocessos. A inclusão recorrente de “jabutis” em projetos de lei para privilegiar combustíveis fósseis aumenta a conta dos consumidores e indica ao mercado uma direção na contramão do mundo. Cada política pública deve ser guiada pela eficiência e pelo interesse coletivo. A transição energética precisa ser política de Estado, com planejamento, estabilidade regulatória e visão de longo prazo. Aos candidatos deste ano, fica uma pergunta: por que o Brasil ainda cobra mais imposto da bateria do que do cigarro? Quem tiver a melhor resposta estará mais preparado para decidir o futuro energético do País.

artigo.texto: BUFFALO, N.Y. (WBEN).....The Buffalo Common Council has taken the first - and expected step - towards creating a two year moratorium on data center development projects within the city. Next up: A local law, crafted by the city's Corporation Counsel office, that prevents any new data center construction and development while the moratorium is in place. That law is expected to be before the council by early October, with a formal vote to follow. Buffalo is now joined the growing list of municipalities and larger governments that have hot the pause button when it comes to data center development. Mayor Sean Ryan said he supports the council vote. "We need clear safeguards that put Buffalo residents first," Ryan said. New York, this summer, at the urging of Gov. Kathy Hochul put a one-year moratorium on data center developments. The Buffalo data center ordinance will be created by a nine--person task force that includes public and private sector interests. "There is a lot of misinformation on both sides," said Ellicott District Councilwoman and Council Majority Leader Leah Halton-Pope. "Hopefully, the task force cam work its way through all that." The moratorium was crafted by North District Councilman Joseph Golembek Jr., who said he has concerns about projects that may be developed near residential neighborhoods. "It could destroy a neighborhood's quality of life," Golembek said. Data centers are coming under fire - mostly for environmental reasons including noise, heavy drains on power supplies and on water supplies. When Buffalo developed its Green Code development blueprint a decade ago, data centers did not figure into economic landscape. Golembek said he hopes the moratorium will address that development void. "Just like what we did 15 years ago with food truck regulations, we want to address this new form of development," Golembek said. "My sole mission is to protect the interests of the residents of the City of Buffalo." Moratorium is the first step; local law still needed

artigo.texto: Policy Considerations for Orbital Data Centers Orbital data centers could complement terrestrial infrastructure by processing selected workloads in space, particularly where data is generated in orbit. Their value will depend on technical performance, life cycle economics, market demand, and a regulatory environment that does not hinder testing and deployment. KEY TAKEAWAYS Key Takeaways Contents Why Orbital Data Centers Are Gaining Relevance 3 Advantages of Orbital Computing. 3 Technical and Economic Challenges for Orbital Data Centers 4 Policy Challenges and Recommendations for Orbital Data Centers 6 Introduction Orbital data centers are specialized satellites that support computing functions by processing data in space.[1] This emerging technology is attracting growing attention amid both rising demand for computing capacity and advances in commercial space capabilities.[2] As the global space economy continues to grow and more digital services rely on space-based infrastructure, orbital computing may become useful for selected space-based workloads. Government assessments, technical research, and industry feasibility studies are currently examining whether selected computing functions could be performed in orbit for specialized applications, although significant engineering and economic questions remain.[3] Today’s orbital data center concepts should not be understood as near-term substitutes for terrestrial cloud infrastructure.[4] Data centers on Earth benefit from mature supply chains, easier repair and upgrade cycles, and lower operating complexity. Orbital systems, by contrast, must operate in a harsher environment that includes radiation exposure, thermal management challenges, communications constraints, and high deployment and replacement costs.[5] If orbital compute clears current technical and economic hurdles, then the central policy consideration is whether orbital systems can perform specialized computing functions well enough to justify their operational complexity rather than whether they can replace terrestrial hyperscale data centers. Orbital computing can reduce bandwidth demands and improve operational responsiveness, particularly where decisions must be made in orbit rather than on the ground. The strongest near-term opportunity for orbital computing lies in workloads that benefit from processing data where it is generated in space. These include Earth observation, remote sensing, and onboard spacecraft autonomy.[6] Over a longer time horizon, onboard or distributed computing could also become useful for certain lunar and cislunar missions, particularly where communications architecture or operational requirements favor local processing. In such settings, orbital computing may reduce bandwidth demands and improve operational responsiveness, particularly where decisions must be made in orbit rather than on the ground.[7] For that reason, orbital data centers are best treated as a complementary layer of digital infrastructure rather than a wholesale replacement for terrestrial systems.[8] Public policy should focus on ensuring that existing regulatory frameworks allow markets to identify and develop those applications for which orbital computing offers genuine comparative advantages, which could lead to orbital systems becoming a meaningful complement to the broader digital infrastructure ecosystem. Why Orbital Data Centers Are Gaining Relevance The simultaneous increase in demand for compute-intensive services alongside the improvement of commercial space capabilities is generating interest in orbital data centers. The Government Accountability Office’s (GAO’s) April 2026 “Science & Tech Spotlight” describes space-based data centers as “satellites that would house data processing and storage systems for AI and other computing needs,” potentially reducing the land, electricity, and water required by terrestrial facilities.[9] This framing, in the context of resistance to expanding terrestrial data center infrastructure, helps explain why the concept is now receiving policy attention, even though the underlying technology remains in an early stage.[10] Orbital data centers may eventually complement terrestrial infrastructure in specialized use cases. Private-sector research has reinforced that interest. Google's Project Suncatcher is an exploratory initiative that examines the feasibility of scaling machine-learning compute in space using solar-powered satellite constellations, special processors, and free-space optical communications links.[11] Thales Alenia Space’s ASCEND project likewise presents space-based data centers as a feasibility question, indicating that orbital computing has become the subject of structured technical and commercial investigation.[12] The broader relevance is that orbital computing may become a useful layer of digital infrastructure for specific workloads before it becomes competitive with terrestrial cloud infrastructure.[13] A space-based architecture that is appropriate for one mission class may still be uneconomical for general-purpose computing, particularly where latency, maintenance, replacement, and scale economies continue to favor Earth-based facilities. Therefore, the current evidence supports measured attention rather than exaggerated expectations. Orbital data centers may eventually complement terrestrial infrastructure in specialized use cases, but their near-term significance will depend on whether the technical and economic constraints can be managed at acceptable costs. The role for policymakers is to create a regulatory environment that minimizes unnecessary barriers to testing and deploying this new technology. The true value of orbital data centers will be easier to assess once these regulatory barriers are reduced. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Submer Group lança Corenix, empresa de data center modular para IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Submer Group anunciou em 28 de setembro de 2026 o lançamento da Corenix, uma empresa de infraestrutura de data center modular que atende neoclouds, hyperscalers e operadores de IA, e nomeou o ex‑executivo da Johnson Controls, Martin Renkis, como seu diretor executivo. A Corenix oferece plataformas de data center modular projetadas sob medida, baseadas em designs de referência da NVIDIA, que o Submer Group descreve como industrializados para IA em escala e entregues desde a construção e teste em fábrica até o comissionamento no local. A nova empresa tem sede em Houston, Texas, e foca na camada de implantação da infraestrutura de IA, reunindo energia de rack, refrigeração, rede e TI em um único sistema integrado, testado em fábrica, destinado a colocar capacidade de IA em operação em uma data fixa. Modelo de entrega fábrica‑para‑site De acordo com o modelo de entrega descrito pela empresa, a Corenix projeta, constrói, integra e testa em fábrica módulos completos e funcionais de data center — abrangendo TI, energia, refrigeração e rede — nas instalações de produção antes de entregá‑los aos locais dos projetos. A instalação, conexão à infraestrutura do site, teste de aceitação no local, comissionamento e preparação operacional ocorrem então no site do cliente. A Corenix gerencia o escopo do projeto acordado em ambas as etapas, combinando engenharia, manufatura, coordenação da cadeia de suprimentos e implantação no local em um único modelo de entrega. O Submer Group afirmou que as construções tradicionais de data center não conseguem acompanhar as demandas de energia, rede, refrigeração e capacidade de serviço da computação acelerada, nem a necessidade de suportar gerações sucessivas de computação de alta densidade, e que a Corenix foi criada para fechar essa lacuna. O grupo descreve a abordagem modular como oferecendo aos clientes um caminho repetível de uma arquitetura técnica aprovada até a capacidade operacional no local necessário, com cada plataforma baseada em um design de referência da NVIDIA e projetada sob medida para os requisitos específicos do cliente. Renkis afirmou que os clientes precisam de clareza antes de se comprometerem sobre o que deve ser construído, como será testado, quem é responsável e quando entrará em operação. “A Corenix coloca um programa datado e uma data de início em produção na mesa antes mesmo de existir um contrato”, disse ele. Ele acrescentou que uma equipe permanece responsável desde a integração e teste na fábrica até o comissionamento no local e a preparação operacional, com flexibilidade para suportar sistemas de computação acelerada atuais e futuros. Liderança Renkis chega à Corenix vindo da Johnson Controls, onde atuou como diretor executivo de Serviços de Infraestrutura de Data Center e desenvolveu ofertas de infraestrutura de IA que abrangem energia, refrigeração, recuperação de calor, operações e financiamento. Anteriormente, foi fundador e CEO da Smartvue, uma empresa de plataforma de hardware e software IoT adquirida pela Johnson Controls, e da Trainersoft, uma empresa de software corporativo de e‑learning adquirida pela OutStart, agora IBM. Patrick Smets, CEO do Submer Group, afirmou que as fábricas de IA estão gerando uma demanda sem precedentes por nova capacidade de data center e que o mercado precisa de uma forma mais rápida e previsível de construí‑la. “Estamos trazendo essa experiência para um negócio dedicado, criado para fornecer infraestrutura de IA em escala”, disse Smets, referindo‑se ao histórico do grupo na entrega modular de data centers e à expertise em engenharia, térmica e de infraestrutura que desenvolveu ao resolver desafios de computação de alta densidade. Estrutura e escala do Submer Group A Corenix baseia‑-se na experiência do Submer Group em engenharia térmica de alta densidade, implantação global de infraestrutura e operações. O grupo afirma que essa experiência foi comprovada em escala por um campus com centenas de megawatts de capacidade entregue como uma construção totalmente modular de computação em nove meses, desde o pedido até a entrega, juntamente com mais de uma década de engenharia de refrigeração líquida. A Corenix trabalha ao lado de duas empresas irmãs cujas capacidades apoiam os requisitos de implantação de infraestrutura de IA de ponta a ponta de um cliente: Rubix Data Centers, que desenvolve e opera campuses de data center de IA, e Radian Arc, que oferece GPU‑as‑a‑Service e AI‑as‑a‑Service. O Submer Group, que se descreve como uma empresa de infraestrutura de IA de pilha completa, reúne empresas operacionais especializadas ao longo da pilha de infraestrutura de IA, abrangendo terra e energia até nuvem e edge. O grupo afirma ter implantado mais de 500 MW de infraestrutura refrigerada a líquido e possuir mais de 8 GW de terreno energizado nas Américas, EMEA e APAC. Fundado em Barcelona em 2015, o grupo opera globalmente com centros em Houston e Taipei. O site do grupo apresenta quatro camadas de capacidade: GPU‑as‑a‑Service e AI‑as‑a‑Service, alimentados pela Radian Arc; desenvolvimento e operações de data center, alimentados pela Rubix; soluções de data center modular; e arquitetura térmica. O site também cita três laboratórios globais de P&D e mais de 90 redes de parceiros de telecomunicações em todo o mundo.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Facilities seeking backup power will help boost annual installations in the commercial-sector energy storage market 27% in megawatt terms through 2031, according to an estimate by the American Clean Power Association and renewable power data firm Wood MacKenzie. - Data centers facing grid-connection bottlenecks are a big driver of the growth. “Storage can provide needed capacity faster, cheaper and more reliably than gas alone," Allison Feeney, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie, says in a summary of the U.S. Energy Storage Monitor that the firm puts out with ACP, released this week for the third quarter of 2026. - When utility-scale and residential sectors are factored in, annual installations of energy storage are expected to grow more than 50% in megawatt terms through 2031. Utility-scale storage will see 8% average annual growth, and residential storage 9% average annual growth, over the next five years, the report says. Dive Insight: Energy storage encompasses several technologies, but most commercial applications are battery systems, and about 90% of those are lithium-ion, the International Energy Agency says based on 2025 data. Hydroelectric, thermal and compressed air are among the other types of systems. Those are generally utility-scale applications, EIA says. Innovation in the battery space is giving facilities options in addition to lithium-ion. Google, for instance, closed a deal earlier this year with Form Energy and utility Xcel Energy to install 30 GWh of battery storage at one of its data centers in the form of iron-air batteries, which engineers tout for their duration. “By … pioneering long-duration storage … we are helping to build a more resilient system,” Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s head of data center energy, said when the deal was announced. Form Energy says on its website that its batteries can release energy for up to 100 hours, delivering power “for multiple days at a time.” In the ACP-Wood Mackenzie analysis, improving durations, particularly in utility-scale and residential applications, is one reason the sector saw an increase in megawatt hours even though the number of installations dipped in the second quarter. “Longer duration … systems drove MWh growth,” the report said. The average duration of U.S. energy storage systems increased from 2.8 hours to 3.5 hours, the report said. Changes in public policy priorities are supporting storage growth, too. In addition to states and municipalities requiring data centers and other large load users to bring their own power, which in many cases include a storage component, public entities at local, state and federal levels are pushing virtual power plants. VPPs are programs in which utilities leverage excess capacity in commercial facilities, homes and other sources to support grid power. Storage is a frequent component of VPPs. “Distributed storage's value proposition is broadening beyond customer-centric benefits to include grid services, as the industry seeks to position virtual power plants … as a key enabler of load growth,” the report says. Looking at second-quarter data, the ACP-Wood Mackenzie analysis says 48 MW of energy storage was installed in the commercial property segment. That’s down from the first quarter, which was unusually high, it says, because of a rush in California by facilities and households installing storage before state tax incentives dropped. Although the reduced incentives took effect in 2023, the state’s top court didn’t settle questions about their legality until June, spurring the rush. As a result, while the storage installed in the second quarter is lower than in the first quarter, it’s in line with historic norms, the report says. Utility-scale deployments for the quarter totaled 4.7 GW/17.6 GWh, down 8% year-over-year in MW terms, which the report attributes to market saturation. Residential deployments also declined, falling 15%, to 676 MW, which the report attributes in part to the federal clean energy and energy efficiency tax credits eliminated in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Despite the quarterly drop among the segments, the outlook is bright for the next five years because of the broader trends favoring energy storage, the report says. “With a strong pipeline and continued technology improvements, the outlook for storage remains exceptionally strong,” John Hensley, ACP’s senior vice president of markets and policy analysis, said in a statement.

artigo.texto: Advait Battery Ecosystem, a subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions, signed a Master Supply Agreement with energy storage manufacturer HiTHIUM for the supply of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells. Under the agreement, HiTHIUM will supply its 314 Ah LFP battery cells to support Advait’s upcoming battery energy storage system (BESS) assembly plant in India. 1 GWh Cell Supply to Support BESS Production Advait plans to procure up to 1 GWh of battery cells from HiTHIUM over the next 12 months. The supply arrangement will support the company as it moves towards commercial production and scales its domestic BESS assembly capabilities. Advait is developing a BESS assembly facility with an annual capacity of 2.5 GWh. The company plans to build capabilities across battery module and pack assembly as it expands its presence in India’s energy storage market. Securing a reliable battery cell supply is therefore an important part of Advait’s manufacturing strategy and will help establish a sourcing base for its initial production phase. 314 Ah LFP Cells for Energy Storage Systems The 314 Ah prismatic LFP cells will serve as the core energy storage component for BESS units assembled at Advait’s facility. LFP chemistry is widely used in stationary energy storage applications because of its combination of cycle life and thermal stability. Consequently, the cells are suited to applications requiring reliable and durable energy storage. Supporting India’s Battery Storage Supply Chain Advait’s planned 2.5 GWh facility forms part of its broader expansion into battery energy storage systems. The company is developing domestic assembly capabilities as demand for energy storage infrastructure increases alongside renewable power generation and grid modernisation. The company’s manufacturing strategy will integrate imported battery cells into locally assembled battery modules and packs. Over time, this approach could help strengthen domestic capabilities across the BESS value chain. HiTHIUM Expands Presence in India’s BESS Market For HiTHIUM, the agreement establishes a supply relationship with an Indian BESS manufacturer and expands the deployment of its 314 Ah LFP cell technology in India. Meanwhile, Advait will gain a defined cell supply base as it moves towards higher-volume commercial production. The planned offtake of up to 1 GWh over 12 months represents a significant portion of the facility’s 2.5 GWh annual assembly capacity, although actual utilisation will depend on production schedules and customer demand. Building Domestic BESS Manufacturing Capabilities The partnership will support Advait’s efforts to develop an integrated battery assembly ecosystem in India. By securing battery cells and combining them with domestic module and pack assembly capabilities, the company aims to establish a foundation for commercial BESS production. As India continues to expand renewable energy and modernise its power grid, battery energy storage systems are expected to play an increasingly important role in balancing electricity supply and demand. As reported by manufacturingtodayindia.com, Advait’s planned facility and its agreement with HiTHIUM position the company to participate in this growing energy storage market.

artigo.texto: ‘Cannot Give Up’: Hyundai’s R&D Boss On The Solid-State Battery Bet Hyundai's head of R&D expects that small-volume cars with solid-state batteries will hit the market within five years. Startups and big-time automakers alike continue to dump resources into solid-state batteries in the hope that this so-called "holy grail" technology will deliver blazing-fast EV charging and longer range. At the same time, conventional lithium-ion batteries now perform better than ever and continue to make strides. Just consider that Geely's latest technology allows for a 10-97% charge in under nine minutes. So is solid-state still worth chasing? According to Hyundai Motor Group research and development chief Manfred Harrer, the answer is a firm yes. "You cannot give up right now on that. That's clear," he told reporters last week. "You must be in the game." The batteries in today's EVs use a liquid electrolyte to transport lithium ions between a cell's anode and cathode. Solid-state batteries substitute that solution for a solid, often a ceramic or polymer, potentially bringing both safety and performance benefits. But nobody has cracked producing solid-state cells at automotive scale yet. Read Up On Solid-State Harrer said the potential advantages—a smaller battery, better fast-charging capability, and longer range—are hard to ignore. Within the next five years, he believes, there will be small-volume halo cars on the market with solid-state packs. That tracks with the timelines laid out by some other industry players; QuantumScape, for instance, expects its batteries to hit high-performance vehicles by the end of the decade. But the raw material costs will remain extraordinarily high for many years as the technology scales up, Harrer said, keeping the batteries out of the mass market. "You can solve, in the end, everything, but it comes with cost, tremendous cost," he said. Hyundai is developing solid-state batteries internally and alongside partners, like Solid Power. It's far from the only automaker investing in the technology, which Harrer calls "the big bet in the industry right now." Toyota has been working on solid-state for at least two decades and aims to put it in production in the next few years. Volkswagen is a big backer of QuantumScape. BMW is working with Solid Power. General Motors, Ford, Honda, and Nissan, among others, are working on it too. While some have trotted out demonstration prototypes—like a Ducati packed with QuantumScape cells or a Mercedes with Factorial's tech—none have put solid-state batteries into a car you can actually buy. Once the technology is mature, Harrer wants Hyundai to be there with its own supply chain and know-how. "We want to be the owner of this core technology, and that's the reason why we're also investing in our own battery manufacturing," he said. Harrer said the company sees a lot of value in deeply understanding what it takes to make batteries and the costs associated with that—because batteries are the most expensive part of an EV and because they also go into other electrified vehicles. Hyundai plans to put in-house nickel manganese cobalt cells in the Santa Fe extended-range EV that hits the market early next year. But it will be a considerably longer wait before solid-state makes its way into the mainstream, Harrer told reporters: "I am not believing you can solve the raw material cost problem in five years from now." artigo.texto: The backlash against data centers is growing, driven by concerns about their environmental impact, effects on local communities, and demands on public infrastructure. But the backlash is also developing a partisan dimension. Recent polling shows that Democrats are substantially more likely than Republicans to oppose data centers and that support has fallen sharply over the past year, particularly among Democrats. Much of that shift reflects growing concerns about the resources data centers consume. The risk is that legitimate concerns about particular projects become absorbed into a broader partisan narrative in which data centers are treated as inherently harmful. Those concerns deserve serious attention, but Democrats should be wary of allowing opposition to data centers to become an ideological reflex. The campaign against data centers increasingly resembles the opposition that wind and solar projects have faced for years. Large infrastructure projects create real local impacts, but those impacts can often be managed without abandoning investments that serve broader economic and environmental goals. Democrats once made that case in support of clean energy. They should be careful not to abandon it now that the infrastructure in question is data centers. Indeed, many objections to data centers closely resemble objections to clean energy projects. Some residents simply do not want large industrial facilities in their communities, whether that means wind turbines altering the landscape, solar farms replacing open land, or massive data centers appearing in rural areas. Others object to noise, whether from wind turbines or the backup generators and cooling equipment associated with data centers. Similar disputes arise over who bears the costs and who receives the benefits. Private landowners may profit directly by selling or leasing their property, while neighboring residents worry about effects on property values or quality of life. Infrastructure presents another source of tension. Both clean energy projects and data centers require substantial investments in transmission lines, substations, roads, and other supporting infrastructure. Residents understandably worry that public resources or utility customers will ultimately bear costs associated with a private company’s investment, particularly if a developer abandons a project. The concerns about data centers are not frivolous, but neither were the concerns raised about wind and solar development. The appropriate response was not to halt clean energy construction altogether. Policymakers instead sought ways to reduce conflicts and distribute benefits more broadly. Developers and communities experimented with approaches such as agrivoltaics, which allows solar generation and agricultural production to coexist on the same land. The broader lesson is not that every concern about new infrastructure proves unfounded. Some problems are real and require meaningful safeguards, while others reflect uncertainty, exaggerated claims, or resistance to development itself. Policymakers should distinguish among them rather than treating every objection as equally persuasive. The same approach should guide data center development, with practical solutions to genuine concerns about water use, electricity costs, noise, land use, and community impacts. For years, Democrats were among the strongest advocates for deploying clean energy despite local opposition. They correctly recognized that building wind and solar capacity could create jobs, generate local tax revenue, and help build the industries that would underpin the future American economy. That basic judgment remains sound. Clean energy projects are worth pursuing even when individual projects generate controversy and when some of the companies developing them are large, profitable corporations. The same principle should apply to data centers. The United States is in the midst of a major technological transformation driven by artificial intelligence. Data centers are the physical infrastructure supporting that transformation. They also represent a significant source of construction and investment, often in communities seeking new economic opportunities. Data center growth can also support clean energy expansion. Major technology companies have made substantial commitments to reduce the carbon intensity of their operations and are investing in new sources of electricity, including wind, solar, and nuclear power. Microsoft’s agreement to support the restart of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant illustrates the scale of investment that growing demand for computing is helping mobilize. Some communities will reasonably decide that a particular data center proposal is not appropriate for a particular location. Others may demand changes to address concerns about water, electricity, noise, or local infrastructure. Policymakers should take those concerns seriously and ensure that their communities benefit from these infrastructure investments. But blanket moratoriums and reflexive opposition to data center development treat complex and often addressable challenges as reasons to stop building altogether. The United States does not need to choose between technological progress and protecting communities. Policymakers can establish rules that mitigate genuine harms and fairly allocate costs while allowing investment to proceed. Democrats understood that approach when the infrastructure at issue was wind turbines and solar panels. They should apply the same judgment to the infrastructure powering the next generation of the American economy. Image credit: Chad Davis/Flickr

BYD also uses Yangwang to showcase its breakthrough technologies. In the past, Yangwang vehicles have debuted with disruptive new tech, including BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its Disus Intelligent Body Control System. A new Yangwang model was recently spotted testing in China that, according to local reports, will push the brand further into the elite segment. New images of the vehicle surfaced online, revealing a nearly identical design to the Rolls-Royce Phantom. It will even be BYD’s first vehicle with rear-hinged coach doors. Hu Xiaoqing, Yangwang’s general manager, shared a few images of the flagship sedan on Weibo and confirmed that the car’s name has yet to be finalized. Internally, BYD is calling it “HU” for now. The new model is “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.” No other details were revealed, but one image shows the vehicle at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it can support megawatt fast charging. According to China’s Autohome, Yangwang’s executive-class EV sedan will be BYD’s first EV to use solid-state batteries among other new technologies. Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, confirmed the new model will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” but didn’t reveal specifics. The sedan measures about 5.5 meters in length, or about the size of the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class. BYD executive vice president Stella Li confirmed in an exclusive interview with Carwow.es earlier this month that the company is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery tech and its commercialization. Li said that BYD will “prove it” with its first vehicle equipped with solid-state batteries set to debut in 2027. BYD’s battery R&D team is “very strong,” Li said, adding that they are studying the battery chemistry as well as the manufacturing and equipment needed for mass production. FinDreams, BYD’s battery business, aims to begin producing sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in limited batches in 2027, scaling up to mass production by 2030. Will Yangwang’s ultra-luxe sedan be the first to showcase BYD’s solid-state batteries? If it does, it will likely be offered on higher-priced variants, while standard models could still use BYD’s latest Blade LFP batteries. Top comment by Blake I expect this will have sold state batteries. The huge sales price means they can afford to ‘hand make’ the batteries and have a high failure rate. Solid state batteries will matter more when it comes to the inherent complexities of mass production Outside of that, the flagship model is expected to feature BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering over 1,000 hp combined. BYD has yet to announce prices or any details, but reports estimate the Yangwang sedan will cost over 2 million yuan, or nearly $300,000. The Yangwang U7, the brand’s current luxury electric sedan, starts at just 658,000 yuan ($98,000). According to Autohome, the new executive-class sedan is expected to make its official debut in October, so we should learn more shortly. Check back soon. We’ll keep you updated.
