artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Lambda planeja novo data center no MidAmerica Industrial Park de Oklahoma Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Lambda anunciou planos em 27 de setembro de 2026 para construir um novo data center no MidAmerica Industrial Park, no condado de Mayes, Oklahoma, um projeto que a empresa disse que deve pagar cerca de $500 million em impostos nos próximos 10 anos, com base nas tarifas atuais. Receita Fiscal Projetada e Empregos Espera‑se que o projeto crie até 1.000 empregos de construção e até 100 cargos permanentes, de acordo com o anúncio da empresa. A instalação ficará localizada na seção sul do parque industrial e estará dentro da zona fiscal do Chouteau-Mazie Public School District. A prefeita de Chouteau, Brenda Cunningham, disse que o projeto traria uma receita fiscal estimada em $500 million para o condado ao longo da próxima década, financiamento que, segundo ela, seria destinado ao apoio de escolas, serviços públicos e prioridades locais. O comissário do condado de Mayes, Steve Grossman, afirmou que o investimento fortaleceria a base tributária local e criaria novos recursos para apoiar escolas, infraestrutura e outras prioridades da comunidade. O superintendente da Chouteau-Mazie Public School, Josh Gwartney, declarou que a receita permitiria ao distrito investir em instalações melhores, salários competitivos para professores, programas avançados e mais oportunidades de educação profissional e técnica. Proteção dos Consumidores de Energia e Compromissos de Recursos A Lambda afirmou que, em conformidade com a Oklahoma’s Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act, assumirá total responsabilidade pelos recursos e infraestrutura necessários para operar a instalação, incluindo o pagamento de 100 % dos custos de energia. A empresa disse que está projetando o projeto para ser um cliente de rede mais flexível, com a capacidade de deslocar ou reduzir determinadas cargas de computação durante períodos de pico de demanda. A instalação utilizará tecnologia de refrigeração de circuito fechado, que a Lambda afirmou reduzir drasticamente o consumo de água em comparação com a refrigeração tradicional de data centers, e a empresa disse que otimizará a eficiência energética. O projeto está sendo construído no parque industrial existente, com infraestrutura projetada para minimizar impactos nas áreas residenciais circundantes. O governador Kevin Stitt afirmou que os compromissos refletem o tipo de investimento responsável que ele deseja ver em Oklahoma. “A Lambda se comprometeu a assumir a responsabilidade pelos custos de energia associados à sua instalação, garantindo que esses custos não sejam repassados aos consumidores residenciais, ao mesmo tempo em que gera centenas de milhões em receita fiscal e crescimento econômico aqui em Oklahoma”, disse Stitt. O CEO do Departamento de Comércio de Oklahoma, John Budd, chamou a decisão da Lambda de construir no estado de um voto de confiança na força de trabalho, na infraestrutura e no ambiente favorável aos negócios de Oklahoma. O CEO da Grand River Dam Authority, Dan Sullivan, declarou que a Lambda financiará os custos iniciais de infraestrutura necessários para atender ao projeto, garantindo que essas despesas não sejam repassadas a outros clientes da GRDA. Sullivan afirmou que a concessionária criou um processo de planejamento focado e abrangente ao avaliar projetos potenciais dessa magnitude e fez os investimentos necessários na última década para estar preparada para projetos dessa escala. O projeto segue o anúncio de 14 de setembro de 2026 da Lambda, que havia assinado o White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Naquela declaração, a empresa afirmou que apoia políticas de proteção dos consumidores que exigem que os desenvolvedores de data centers paguem pela energia que suas instalações utilizam, e que apoia a expansão da capacidade de geração, o fortalecimento da rede elétrica, a manutenção de um serviço confiável e a proteção dos consumidores à medida que a demanda por infraestrutura de IA cresce. Processo de Seleção e Próximas Etapas A MidAmerica selecionou a Lambda dentre uma variedade de parceiros potenciais com base na abordagem da empresa ao desenvolvimento responsável e aos padrões de construção. David Stewart, CEO e membro do Board of Trustees do MidAmerica Industrial Park, afirmou que a MidAmerica e a GRDA adotaram uma abordagem deliberada para encontrar o parceiro certo. “Por meio do que chamamos de reverse RFP, começamos com os pontos fortes deste local e procuramos um desenvolvedor cujos planos entregariam valor duradouro à região”, disse Stewart. Ele afirmou que, à medida que a construção avançar, o projeto deverá criar aproximadamente 1.000 empregos e gerar oportunidades para fornecedores, empreiteiros e fornecedores locais. A Cloverleaf Infrastructure foi selecionada pela GRDA e pela MidAmerica para preparar o local no condado de Mayes para o desenvolvimento pela Lambda. Aaron Bilyeu, chief development officer da Cloverleaf, afirmou que o trabalho será orientado pelo Cloverleaf Standard, que ele descreveu como o compromisso da empresa de desenvolver infraestrutura crítica de forma responsável, transparente e em parceria com as comunidades que atende. O cofundador da Lambda e Chief Technology Officer, Stephen Balaban, disse que a empresa tem se reunido com líderes locais em Chouteau e no condado de Mayes para entender suas prioridades e ajudar a moldar seus investimentos de longo prazo na comunidade. O CEO da Lambda, Michel Combes, afirmou que a responsabilidade da empresa é garantir que o projeto entregue valor ao condado de Mayes, respeitando os recursos, a infraestrutura e as prioridades da comunidade. Lambda e MidAmerica disseram que, nas próximas semanas, continuarão se reunindo com líderes locais e residentes para ouvir e coletar sugestões que orientem o investimento na comunidade, e que mais informações sobre o cronograma do projeto e seu impacto econômico esperado serão compartilhada

artigo.texto: Volkswagen battery unit PowerCo and Chinese battery maker Gotion have announced joint plans to invest around €3.22bn (US$3.68bn) in three battery and materials joint ventures across Spain, Slovakia and Morocco. Gotion’s board approved the proposal the same day, though the companies have yet to sign a formal investment agreement, and the deal still requires shareholder approval and government clearances in both China and Europe. The largest project in Valencia, Spain, calls for a €2.26bn investment to build 29.1 GWh of annual lithium-ion battery capacity. Gotion will acquire a 49% stake in the existing PowerCo Spain entity through a capital increase, with PowerCo retaining 51% control. That structure follows local media reporting in July that the two companies were in advanced talks over a Gotion stake in the Valencia plant specifically. Visits were made by Gotion Chief Executive Li Zhen to evaluate the site, and PowerCo said at the time it had no plan to cede control. With a 51% stake, this remains the case—albeit only just. A second project in Šurany, Slovakia, involves a €480m investment for 8.4 GWh of annual capacity and will see this ownership structure put in reverse: Gotion takes 51% and PowerCo 49%. A third joint venture, also split 51-49 in Gotion’s favour, will invest €480m in a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials plant in Kenitra, Morocco. The companies expect 100,000 metric tons of annual capacity from the plant, which will supply the two European battery projects. Cells from the Spanish and Slovakian plants will prioritise Volkswagen’s own European demand, though specific purchase volumes remain subject to separate definitive agreements. The expansion deepens an already substantial equity relationship: Volkswagen’s Chinese investment arm held a 24.28% stake in Gotion as of 20 September, making it the battery maker’s largest shareholder. While small compared to giants CATL and BYD, Gotion’s global electric vehicle battery installations reached 34.0 GWh over the first seven months of 2026, up 44.2% year-on-year. The company ranked fifth globally with its market share rising from 3.9% to 4.7%, according to SNE Research. The Gotion partnership is one piece of a substantially larger battery strategy Volkswagen has been building since founding PowerCo in 2022. At the core of this strategy is a standardised prismatic ‘Unified Cell’ architecture, designed to power more than 80% of future vehicles across the Group’s sprawling brand portfolio. The battery’s external cell dimensions stay identical regardless of application, but the internal chemistry varies depending on the segment’s needs. Low-cost LFP and eventual sodium-ion are intended for the entry-level offerings, while high-nickel, nickel-manganese-cobalt and eventual solid-state technology are reserved for the premium end. PowerCo operates its own gigafactories on a ‘Standard Factory’ blueprint, using identical building layouts, machinery and IT systems across sites specifically to speed deployment and reduce capital expenditure, with plants in Valencia; Salzgitter, Germany; and St. Thomas, Ontario together targeting up to 200 GWh of annual capacity. Upstream, the unit’s Ionway joint venture with Umicore, is building a cathode and precursor materials facility in Nysa, Poland aimed at supplying enough material for roughly 2.2 million electric vehicles a year by 2030. PowerCo has a stated goal of reducing battery pack costs to less than US$100 per kWh. This will depend on running a standardised architecture across every partner simultaneously: Gotion for LFP engineering and Asian volume, QuantumScape for solid-state licensing, CATL and LG Energy Solution for current MEB-platform demand. Thus, the Gotion joint ventures function less as standalone deals than as one component of a supply network in which the automaker is deliberately remaining technology-agnostic and geographically diversified. Reversing the ownership split between the Spanish project, where PowerCo retains control, and the Slovak and Moroccan projects, where Gotion holds the majority stake, suggests Volkswagen is calibrating how much operational control it cedes to its Chinese partner by asset type. It is keeping its most strategically important European cell plant under direct control while relying on Gotion’s expertise for smaller, more specialised capacity.

artigo.texto: Parcerias Crusoe Revela Papel de Desenvolvedor no Campus de Data Center de IA da Google no Texas Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Crusoe anunciou em 28 de setembro de 2026 que é a desenvolvedora do campus de data center da Google em construção no Condado de Armstrong, nos arredores de Amarillo, Texas, um projeto que a empresa disse ser projetado para fornecer capacidade para alimentar IA avançada e onde mais de 5.500 trabalhadores qualificados estão no local diariamente. “Construir o futuro da IA requer um novo tipo de infraestrutura, começando pela energia. A estratégia da Crusoe é construir fábricas de IA diretamente na fonte de energia abundante e de baixo custo – tanto para melhorar a utilização dos ativos existentes quanto para catalisar a geração de nova energia”, disse Chase Lochmiller, CEO e cofundador da Crusoe, em o anúncio da empresa. Lochmiller descreveu o campus do Condado de Armstrong como um exemplo dessa estratégia centrada na energia e afirmou que a empresa está colocando energia limpa, nova e acessível em operação no local. A construção começou em junho de 2025 e continua em andamento, de acordo com o anúncio, que afirmou que o projeto está trazendo investimento significativo e empregos para a comunidade local. Lochmiller disse que a Crusoe está construindo no mesmo ritmo acelerado que estabeleceu em Abilene. Conexão Direta ao Vento e Projeto de Resfriamento O campus tem uma conexão direta com o parque eólico Goodnight 1 adjacente a Serena, uma instalação de 265,5 MW que está operacional, e o parque eólico Goodnight 2, também de 265,5 MW, que está em construção e foi catalisado pelo desenvolvimento da Crusoe no local. Quando a geração eólica excede a demanda do campus, o excedente de energia é devolvido à rede, um arranjo que Crusoe disse beneficiar os consumidores locais e reduzir a limitação da energia eólica do oeste do Texas. O projeto utilizará um sistema de resfriamento líquido de circuito fechado e não evaporativo que a Crusoe afirmou ser projetado para limitar significativamente a pegada hídrica da instalação, destinando-a principalmente a usos domésticos, como cozinhas. O Modelo de Energia Across the Meter Em uma postagem no blog publicada no mesmo dia, a Crusoe descreveu o modelo “across the meter” por trás do design do campus: co‑locar data centers de IA na fonte de geração para capturar energia que de outra forma seria limitada ou abandonada. A postagem afirmou que as áreas mais ventosas e as mais adequadas para produção solar costumam estar em locais remotos com demanda local limitada, o que pode levar os preços da energia a valores negativos quando a geração excede o consumo local, uma dinâmica agravada pela congestão de transmissão, já que muitas usinas enviam energia pelas mesmas linhas para mercados urbanos distantes. O post da Crusoe cita o Independent Market Monitor para o Relatório Estado do Mercado 2025 da ERCOT, que constatou que aproximadamente 4,7% da geração eólica foi reduzida em 2025, e uma estimativa da U.S. Energy Information Administration de que aproximadamente 5% da eletricidade é perdida durante a transmissão e distribuição. A empresa afirmou que seu modelo de negócios original levou data centers modulares a locais remotos de produção de petróleo para capturar gás que, de outra forma, seria queimado, e que a mesma lógica agora se aplica à energia renovável encalhada. Sob o design across-the-meter, um campus extrai energia incremental da rede quando a geração local é insuficiente e envia energia excedente para a rede quando a geração local supera a carga do campus. A Crusoe disse que a carga co‑locada também oferece aos desenvolvedores de renováveis um incentivo orientado pelo mercado para repotenciar e atualizar turbinas envelhecidas, porque os sites eólicos e solares existentes já possuem terras permitidas, acordos de interconexão e relacionamentos comunitários. Investimento na Comunidade e Portfólio do Oeste do Texas O anúncio informou que o investimento local na comunidade também inclui o Texas Energy Impact Fund da Google, que recentemente anunciou apoio a melhorias de eficiência em edifícios públicos e residências no Condado de Armstrong. A Google divulgou os primeiros beneficiários do fundo em 21 de maio de 2026, como parte de um compromisso de US$ 30 milhões com a resiliência e a acessibilidade energética no Texas. A postagem da Google informou que os beneficiários inaugurais incluem a Energy Management Alliance, financiada para expandir o treinamento de gestores de energia para comunidades rurais e financiar melhorias de eficiência em edifícios públicos nos Condados de Armstrong, Ellis, Haskell e Wilbarger, juntamente com reparos residenciais pré‑climatização nesses quatro condados por meio da Solar United Neighbors, do Texas Energy Poverty Research Institute e da aliança, e na região de Houston por meio do Houston Advanced Research Center. As bolsas do Texas Energy Poverty Research Institute financiam desafios de inovação focados em resiliência, acessibilidade e eficiência energética para edifícios multifamiliares e cooperativas elétricas, enquanto a Solar United Neighbors implantará energia solar, baterias e bombas de calor em residências de baixa renda e como centros de resiliência comunitária no Condado de Ellis, segundo a postagem. A Crusoe afirmou que seu portfólio em expansão no oeste do Texas reforça ainda mais a região como crítica para o futuro da infraestrutura digital americana. Juntamente com o campus do Condado de Armstrong, o portfólio inclui dois campuses em desenvolvimento em Abilene.

artigo.texto: German carmaker Volkswagen and Chinese battery manufacturer Gotion plan to invest some €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion) to expand their partnership, the companies said on Monday. Volkswagen and Gotion aim to set up three joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco to "accelerate the development of a regional battery supply chain for Europe." Under the plans, which are dependent on regulatory approval, a gigafactory currently being built by Volkswagen's battery division PowerCo in Valencia is to be transferred into a joint venture, alongside Gotion's plant in Surany, Slovakia. Volkswagen and Gotion also aim to set up a new production facility in Kenitra, Morocco, "to produce cathode material for LFP batteries." All three ventures are to be managed jointly, the companies said. Volkswagen subsidiary PowerCo is to invest some €470 million by 2030 to acquire a 49% stake each in the Slovakian and Moroccan sites. In return, Gotion is to spend some €1.1 billion to acquire a 49% stake in the Valencia factory. Volkswagen's battery division PowerCo, which was established in 2022, is responsible for the development and production of battery cells. Its first factory in Germany's Salzgitter began production at the end of 2025, with another plant under construction in St. Thomas, Canada.

artigo.texto: Fox ESS has unveiled Power Beast, its new commercial and industrial energy storage system, at the company’s first large-scale APAC product launch. Held in Wenzhou, China, on 21 September 2026, the Fox ESS New Product Launch Event welcomed more than 200 customers from around the world. The open-air event marked a significant step in Fox ESS’s expansion into advanced commercial and industrial (C&I) battery energy storage. Power Beast combines the 125 kW H3 Plus hybrid inverter with Fox ESS’s high-voltage CQ series batteries. The CQ20 is described as the industry’s first modular C&I energy storage system with a fully integrated hybrid inverter. This integrated design allows businesses and installers to deploy a flexible, all-in-one commercial energy storage solution. Michael Zhu, CEO of Fox ESS, said: “Today, we are not only launching a product, we are demonstrating our capability as an integrated energy storage provider. Power Beast reflects our commitment to global clients by delivering higher efficiency, lighter weight, and smarter energy management.” Fox ESS puts Power Beast installation to the test The Power Beast launch went beyond a traditional product presentation. Lyren Liu, CCO of Fox ESS, shared insights into market growth and his perspective on battery storage. He then revealed a Cybertruck loaded with CQ batteries from behind a black curtain on stage. An installation team was invited to assemble a complete system live, with a timer displayed on the main screen. The team assembled battery packs comprising: - eight modules of CQ20; - 12 modules of CQ7; and - 12 modules of CQ6. Together, the system provided 316 kWh of energy storage capacity. The completed battery system was then connected to charging piles, a diesel generator, and a motor. Fox ESS completed the entire live demonstration in under 30 minutes. Power Beast offers scalable C&I battery storage Power Beast has been designed around modular expansion, allowing system capacity to grow alongside a business’s energy requirements. With one H3 Plus hybrid inverter, Power Beast can support capacities ranging from 28 kWh to nearly 1,000 kWh. The system supports several installation environments, including rooftop, outdoor, and indoor applications. For larger projects, multiple Power Beast systems can operate in parallel. In grid-connected mode, the system supports up to 100 units in parallel, providing total capacity of up to 96 MWh. In off-grid mode, Power Beast supports up to 30 units in parallel, reaching a total capacity of 28.8 MWh. Modular design simplifies commercial battery installation Fox ESS has also focused on reducing installation complexity. Power Beast’s modular architecture is designed to improve deployment efficiency and accommodate challenging or irregular installation environments. According to Fox ESS, the system’s design can reduce total installation time by 90 per cent. This modular approach gives installers greater flexibility when configuring commercial energy storage systems across different sites. Lighter C&I battery storage with integrated energy management Power Beast has been designed to integrate with multiple energy sources and loads. The CQ20 series batteries achieve a unit energy weight of 7 kg per kWh. This helps reduce the system’s physical footprint while maintaining energy output. Fox ESS has also incorporated a five-layer, end-to-end safety approach. This covers: - cell-level protection; - electrical design; - structural design; - active detection; and - emergency response. The system connects with FoxCloud 2.0, Fox ESS’s proprietary smart energy management platform. FoxCloud 2.0 provides real-time monitoring and visibility of energy flows, alongside detailed performance analysis. The platform also supports scheduling across up to 96 time slots, providing centralised smart energy management for Power Beast installations. Fox ESS introduces AI energy management agent Maimai Alongside Power Beast, Fox ESS introduced its AI agent, Maimai. Maimai provides product, installation, and usage information through natural dialogue. Using large-model conversational capabilities, the AI agent can interpret user requirements and provide relevant information at any time. Maimai can also generate optimised energy strategies using historical energy consumption patterns and real-time dynamic electricity prices. The technology adds another layer of intelligent energy management to Fox ESS’s growing commercial energy storage ecosystem. Michael Zhu said Fox ESS remains focused on creating products that deliver measurable value for customers. “We believe a great product speaks louder than marketing. That is why we aim to make our products the best kind of promotion, by delivering real value every single day,” Michael Zhu said. With scalable storage from 28 kWh through to multi-megawatt-hour deployments, Power Beast expands Fox ESS’s offering for businesses seeking flexible commercial battery storage. The combination of the H3 Plus hybrid inverter, CQ series batteries, FoxCloud 2.0, and Maimai also brings hardware, monitoring, and intelligent energy management into one C&I energy storage ecosystem.

artigo.texto: BYD, Batteries, and the Architecture of Dependence Dateline, Canberra, Austrlia I have just arrived in Canberra for the October 1 seminar hosted by the Sir Richard Williams Foundation. So no place better to start than by focusing on one of the themes in my latest book with Kenneth Maxwell on China’s informal empire. BYD is not simply a car company that got good. It is the clearest automotive expression yet of what I have called, with Kenneth Maxwell, the “Architecture of Dependency”: a strategy that pursues vertical integration of an entire value chain — from mineral extraction through midstream processing to the logistics that move finished goods to market — rather than conventional market access. In The Australian, Brazilian, and Chinese Dynamic, we traced this architecture through lithium refining, rare-earth processing, and port infrastructure such as Chancay. The global automobile is now a fourth front in the same campaign. BYD’s pricing is not merely competitive; it is engineered to convert every vehicle sold abroad into a node in a Chinese-controlled battery and software supply chain. A car buyer in São Paulo, Bangkok, or Budapest who chooses a BYD is not just choosing a product. They are choosing a dependency relationship whose terms were set upstream, in cell chemistry and mineral processing capacity that China already dominates. Toyota’s solid-state battery program in progress for launch projected within the next five years is the most credible industrial counter to this dynamic now on the table, not because it beats BYD on price, but because it proposes an entirely different chemistry, supply chain, and manufacturing geography. This article examines both halves of that contest: how BYD builds dependence, and Toyota’s bet to break it. BYD’s Global Expansion Strategy: Asymmetrical Market Penetration BYD’s rise has been startling in its speed. In April 2026 alone the company exported 135,098 vehicles worldwide, every one fully electric or plug-in hybrid, a figure that by some analyst estimates exceeded Tesla’s global monthly deliveries for the same month. SNE Research put BYD’s non-China deliveries at roughly 497,000 units in the first half of 2026, up 81 percent year on year, placing it third worldwide behind Volkswagen and Tesla in overseas volume. BYD’s own target is 1.6 million overseas sales in 2026, backed by new or expanding plants in Hungary, Brazil, Thailand, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Turkey, with Spain under consideration. The strategy behind these numbers is not a frontal assault on the most fortified Western markets. It is what one industry analysis calls “asymmetrical market penetration”: BYD largely avoided the politically hardened U.S. market where tariffs and political resistance keep it effectively locked out and instead targeted the Global South and secondary Western markets where legacy automakers had grown complacent. Thailand became a regional hub and template for ASEAN expansion; Brazil, Hungary, and Turkey became manufacturing footholds that double as tariff workarounds and in June 2026 Canada cut its tariff on Chinese EVs from 100 percent to 6.1 percent as part of a broader energy and climate partnership with Beijing, opening a new North American corridor. What makes this expansion durable rather than opportunistic is BYD’s unparalleled vertical integration. Unlike Western automakers, which depend heavily on third-party suppliers for battery cells, semiconductors, and software, BYD manufactures nearly everything in-house, an inheritance from its origins as a battery maker before it built a single car. That integration is precisely why the company can build factories concurrently across continents while still undercutting incumbents on price: it is not buying components at a margin, it is capturing the margin at every stage of the chain. Chinese EV factories capable of producing more than 200,000 vehicles a year have sprung up in Indonesia, Thailand, Pakistan, Turkey, Hungary, and Brazil, offering vehicles that are, on average, around 20 percent cheaper than their Western counterparts even before subsidies are considered. Domestically, this expansion is not evidence of strength alone. BYD’s first-quarter 2026 net profit fell 55 percent, its worst showing in three years, as a brutal domestic price war and thinning subsidies compressed sector-wide margins to an average of 3.2 percent. Exports abroad, where BYD can command significantly higher average selling prices, have become less a growth option than a financial necessity which only sharpens the incentive to keep undercutting Western rivals in every market it can reach. The Battery Dependency Mechanism BYD began life as a battery manufacturer, and that lineage is the key to understanding its strategy. Its battery subsidiary, FinDreams, is one of the largest EV battery producers on earth, second only to CATL, and together the two Chinese firms anchor a domestic battery-cell industry that supplies the overwhelming majority of the world’s electric and plug-in-hybrid vehicles. This is where the automotive story connects directly to the argument Kenneth Maxwell and I made in The Australian, Brazilian, and Chinese Dynamic. China today controls 57 percent of global lithium refining and 85 percent of global rare-earth processing, even though Australia alone produces 45 percent of the world’s raw lithium. A nation can extract the resource from its own soil and remain, in our phrase, a “feeder economy” so long as it lacks the midstream processing capacity to break the refining monopoly. The battery pack under a BYD Seal or a Dolphin is that same architecture, miniaturized and rolling on four wheels: raw lithium, cobalt, and rare-earth inputs processed almost entirely within Chinese-controlled facilities, assembled into cells by Chinese battery makers, and sold into foreign markets as a finished vehicle whose entire value chain, mine to midstream to cell to car, never leaves Beijing’s sphere of control. artigo.texto: BSES holds industry workshop on BESS safety As battery energy storage becomes an increasingly important part of India’s clean-energy transition, BSES recently organised a three-day workshop on the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Safety Framework, bringing together power-sector leaders, global safety experts, utilities, fire and emergency services and industry professionals. The workshop focused on a priority: ensuring battery storage scales up safely, responsibly, and with the right level of preparedness. Discussions covered safety-by-design, early warning and detection, thermal runaway, recognised testing, emergency preparedness, evacuation protocols and first-responder readiness. The inaugural session was addressed by Ghanshyam Prasad (Chairperson, CEA); Amal Sinha (Director & Group CEO, BSES); Abhishek Ranjan (CEO, BRPL); Sunil Kumar Jha (Director General, FS, CD & HG); Santosh Kumar (COO, BYPL); Alok Kumar (Director General, AIDA); Asko Rajput (Chairman, Standards Committee, BIS); Tanya Singhal (Vice President & Country Head, GEAPP); and Dr Rashi Gupta (MD, Vision Mechatronics Pvt Ltd). The workshop moved beyond discussions to practical preparedness. A major highlight was a live thermal runaway demonstration in a battery module, followed by firefighting intervention by Delhi Fire Service personnel. The exercise helped participants understand how battery failures can develop and the challenges emergency responders may face. Global experts Richie Stephen (Senior Standards Project Manager, UL Standards & Engagement), Kurt Vollmacher (Director, Intotech & Fire Safety Trainer) and Dr Judy Jeevarajan (UL Standards & Engagement) shared insights on system testing, failure modes, manufacturing defects, battery ageing, fire safety and emergency response, drawing on experience. The workshop concluded with nine multidisciplinary teams working through emergency scenarios involving smoke at a BESS site, flooding at an installation, and post-fire dismantling and waste management. The exercise helped participants identify priorities, responsibilities and the safest course of action. The programme also drew on BSES’ experience with its pioneering 20 MW/40 MWh Kilokri BESS, reinforcing the need to keep safety at the heart of storage growth.

artigo.texto: Pennsylvania’s legislators return to the capitol Monday following a 10-week recess, with several unresolved issues awaiting action, including the future of skill games, regulation of data centers, rising utility costs and restrictions on cell phone use in schools. Skill Games Following a Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling in June that determined skill games are slot machines, the legislature was given 120 days to establish a law to keep the industry alive. Advocates for skill games have encouraged Pennsylvanians to call their representatives to ask them to support bills that would regulate the machines. HB2213 and SB1079 are bipartisan measures. Rep. Danilo Burgos (D-197) is prime sponsor of the house bill. “This is about job security for community members across Pennsylvania,” he said. “And helping keep doors open at VA clubs, at VFWs, and a slew of other community groups that benefit.” Republican Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) is prime sponsor of the Senate bill. “It’s going to be a tremendous hit to a significant number of Pennsylvanians if we don’t address it,” Yaw said. “I can’t remember anything that I have been involved in in the Senate that would affect so many people negatively in one instant happening.” The Senate only has six session days to address it before the deadline, but Yaw says lawmakers could reach an agreement. Last week, Rep. Brad Roae (R-6) proposed legislation to extend the deadline by six months. The House unanimously passed the bill in June, and Fiedler is hopeful for a Senate vote soon. Cell phone ban in schools There are two bills that would ban cell phone use in schools waiting to be voted on. HB1814 passed the house in June, while SB1014 was passed in the Senate in February. Polls show the majority of Pennsylvania voters support leaving cell phones out of the classroom. Shapiro called on the General Assembly to pass legislation during his February budget address, but a ban did not end up in the approved budget. “Students need to spend less time focused on their phones and more time focused on learning, on talking to their friends face to face, and on developing the critical skills they’ll need later in life,” he said. “I know there are bills in both chambers to do this — come together and send a bill to my desk.”

artigo.texto: Protests against data centers have exploded across the US, with communities revolting against a multitude of proven damaging effects on energy prices, clean air and water – and the devastation of tens of thousands of acres of agricultural land. Recent headlines in national publications report that farmers and rural communities are rejecting multimillion-dollar bids from institutional investors and tech companies to buy their farmland to build data centers. A farmer in Kentucky rejected $33 million for her farmland; another in Pennsylvania turned down a $15 million offer; and one farmer in Wisconsin even reportedly refused a whopping $70+ million bid. Land has become the next big asset class for investors, especially billionaires and private equity firms, to hide and protect their wealth. It is seen as a safe, low-risk way to park money to hedge against inflation – at the expense of farmers and local communities alike. These investors aren’t just seeking out farmland to build data centers. Just like they’re targeting housing, investment firms are buying up land and renting it back to farmers for a hefty profit. The 2024 Tenure, Ownership, and Transition of Agricultural Land (TOTAL) Survey, released this March, shows that 87% of the more than 2 million landowners renting out farmland are non-operators – that is, they are not actively farming, and the majority of these landowners never have. While these landlords raked in more than $34 billion in rent combined, the total value of farmland held for rent is $1.7 trillion – up 47% since 2014. We are watching in real time the emergence of a long-term, non-farming rural landlord class. While the TOTAL survey provides a useful indicator of farmland ownership trends, it doesn’t give us the full picture. Farmland ownership has never been effectively tracked in the US with regularity, and what limited data exists is difficult to find. The data we do have shows that investment in farmland has risen dramatically over the past two decades. Companies like AcreTrader, Farmland Partners, and others that allow individuals to invest in farmland have become increasingly popular. The most alarming growth has come from institutional investors, like pension funds, private equity firms, and wealth management groups. The value of farmland held by institutional investors has more than doubled over the past three years up to $16.6 billion dollars by 2024, an eightfold rise since 2008. Based on publicly available data alone, the largest corporate owners of US farmland control more than 2 million acres. But why are farmers selling their land in the first place? The hard truth is that farming just isn’t working as a viable livelihood anymore, and hasn’t for years. In just five years from 2017-2022, we lost 159,000 US family farms. The Farm Crisis didn’t go away in the 1980s – it’s just become quieter and less visible to most. Chronic low and volatile prices across sectors, coupled with a handful of multinational corporations tightening their iron grip over global agriculture, have pushed farmers to the brink of existence. With farm debt at an all-time high, selling the farm for the best offer possible is often the only feasible way to escape dire financial straits. And when the farm is for sale, companies with billions in assets are primed to outbid new and beginning farmers seeking land to start their own businesses. The best opportunity we have to protect farmland comes from strong federal policies that safeguard land for multiple generations of working farms and ensure farmers make a living wage. Right now, the Farmland for Farmers Act is one of the boldest pieces of federal legislation to combat this worrying trend. Modeled after anti-corporate farming laws in Midwestern states, the bill would stop large corporate entities from being able to purchase farmland only to let it lie fallow in the hopes that its value will skyrocket over time, or to rent it back to farmers at a premium price. With policies like it, coupled with a Farm Bill that allows farmers to pay their bills and sustainably grow their businesses, farmers might stand a chance. It’s long overdue for policy solutions championed by federal representatives not afraid to stand up against deep pocketed special interests. We need Congress to enact policies like the Farmland for Farmers Act that fight back against the profiteering on the backs of farmers, communities, and our natural resources. The first step in protecting farmland means supporting the next generation of farmers to enter the business with confidence and without having to compete with billionaires. We need to ensure that farmers now and in the future actually have the land they need to feed us all. Tim Gibbons is the Executive Director of the National Family Farm Coalition, a national coalition representing 30 grassroots farm, ranch, and fishing organizations in Washington, DC. A life-long Missourian, Tim has spent decades organizing family farmers, ranchers, and rural residents in support of fair, healthy and thriving rural economies, fair markets, and clean water and air. Dena Hoff represents the Northern Plains Resource Council on the NFFC Board. Since 1979, she’s raised sheep, cattle, alfalfa, corn, and edible dry beans, among other crops, on her farm in Glendive, Montana. She is an active member of and advocate for her rural community.

artigo.texto: LG Electronics apresenta soluções “Chip-to-Chiller” para resfriamento de data centers de IA na Data Center World Asia 2026 AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 29 de setembro de 2026 Empresa destaca infraestrutura integrada para fábricas de IA e portfólio completo de soluções de resfriamento para data centers de IA Resumo da notícia - A LG Electronics apresenta suas soluções de resfriamento “Chip-to-Chiller” na Data Center World Asia 2026, ao mesmo tempo em que demonstra sua abordagem “One LG” para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA, em conjunto com a LG CNS e a LG Energy Solution. - O portfólio da LG inclui soluções hidrônicas pré-fabricadas, chillers centrífugos refrigerados a ar, Unidades de Distribuição de Líquido Refrigerante (CDUs) qualificadas pela NVIDIA, resfriamento por imersão, Fan Wall Units (FWUs) e o Data Center Cooling Management (DCCM), apoiando uma implementação mais rápida, operação confiável e expansão eficiente da infraestrutura de data centers de IA. - As soluções modulares de resfriamento da LG são projetadas para reduzir o tempo de construção no local, diminuir o investimento inicial e apoiar os operadores de data centers na expansão eficiente de seus ambientes de servidores de IA. - A LG Energy Solution apresenta soluções de baterias otimizadas para data centers de IA, incluindo Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), Battery Backup Unit (BBU) e Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). - A LG CNS apresenta o “Prefabricated Modular Data Center”, com módulos padronizados e pré-fabricados de GPUs, servidores e energia. SÃO PAULO, 29 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A LG Electronics (LG) apresenta suas soluções de resfriamento “Chip-to-Chiller” para servidores de Inteligência Artificial (IA) na Data Center World Asia 2026 (DCWA 2026), realizada de 29 a 30 de setembro no Marina Bay Sands Expo & Convention Center, em Singapura. A exposição destaca a abordagem integrada da LG para atender às crescentes demandas de gerenciamento térmico e energia do setor de data centers de IA. Uma parceira de ponta a ponta para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA com o “One LG” Participando da DCWA pelo segundo ano consecutivo, a LG demonstra suas capacidades como parceira de ponta a ponta para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA em um espaço de exposição com mais de três vezes o tamanho de seu estande de 2025. A empresa apresenta uma solução integrada de infraestrutura baseada na estratégia “One LG”, que reúne as tecnologias de climatização/HVAC da LG com a expertise da LG CNS em projeto, construção e operação (DBO) de data centers e os equipamentos de energia da LG Energy Solution. A LG Energy Solution apresenta soluções de baterias desenvolvidas para apoiar o fornecimento confiável de energia para data centers de IA incluindo Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), Battery Backup Unit (BBU) e Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). Implementação acelerada com soluções modulares pré-fabricadas As soluções hidrônicas pré-fabricadas e os chillers centrífugos refrigerados a ar da LG contribuem para uma implementação e expansão mais rápidas da infraestrutura de data centers de IA. A solução hidrônica incorpora equipamentos de resfriamento, equipamentos de energia e sistemas de controle em um único módulo pré-fabricado, reduzindo o trabalho de engenharia no local e encurtando o tempo de implementação. O chiller centrífugo refrigerado a ar da LG incorpora um compressor centrífugo com mancal magnético sem óleo, que minimiza as perdas por atrito mecânico e melhora a eficiência energética. Além disso, o chiller utiliza a tecnologia free-cooling por refrigerante da empresa, que aproveita as baixas temperaturas externas para reduzir a carga sobre o compressor e ajudar a diminuir o consumo de energia do data center. Tecnologias especializadas de resfriamento para servidores de IA de alta densidade A exposição também apresenta as mais recentes soluções de resfriamento líquido da LG para servidores de IA, incluindo suas avançadas Unidades de Distribuição de Líquido Refrigerante (CDUs). Uma CDU é um componente essencial de um sistema de resfriamento líquido direto para o chip (DTC), que fornece e circula o líquido refrigerante para placas frias (cold plates), instaladas diretamente sobre CPUs e GPUs para absorver seu calor. As CDUs de 1 megawatt (MW), 2,6 megawatts (MW) e 600 quilowatts (kW) da LG concluíram a qualificação de infraestrutura da NVIDIA neste ano, atendendo a critérios técnicos que abrangem desempenho de resfriamento, capacidades de failover e confiabilidade do sistema. Além disso, a CDU de 2,6 megawatts (MW) da LG foi qualificada como NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU, atendendo aos requisitos aplicáveis do projeto de referência NVIDIA DSX para soluções de resfriamento líquido da AI Factory Platform. Na DCWA 2026, a LG demonstra uma solução de resfriamento por imersão que remove o calor de forma eficiente ao submergir os servidores em um fluido de resfriamento não condutivo. Paralelamente, a empresa apresenta sua Fan Wall Unit (FWU), uma solução de resfriamento a ar que incorpora ventiladores EC de alta eficiência e serpentinas ovais de baixa perda de pressão para fornecer um fluxo de ar energeticamente eficiente e estável aos racks de servidores. Soluções integradas de gerenciamento e energia A LG apresenta seu Data Center Cooling Management (DCCM), que permite o gerenciamento integrado dos principais equipamentos de resfriamento, incluindo CDUs, FWUs e chillers. Utilizando tecnologia de IA, o DCCM pode prever a carga de resfriamento e otimizar os sistemas de resfriamento para possibilitar uma operação mais eficiente do data center. Como parte da oferta “One LG”, a LG CNS e a LG Energy Solution também apresentam suas soluções para data centers na DCWA deste ano. artigo.texto: The CEO of T5 , a development company set to build what could eventually become the second largest data center in Illinois by square footage, spoke exclusively to NBC 5 Monday amid an outcry of opposition from local residents. "We haven't hidden behind anything," Peter Marin said. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. A group of residents called the Lake County Data Center Opposition Coalition has sued to block the project, claiming the village wasn't transparent about the project during public meetings. "it wasn't out in public. It wasn't open," said coalition leader Morgan Coghill. "It wasn't on the agenda of the Grayslake like town meeting. And because they knew it was going to be a problem." In a statement, Grayslake mayor Elizabeth Davies says there were 18 public meetings and “Every one of those meetings and hearings was open to the public, publicly noticed, and on the record.” The village has put out a fact sheet online assuring residents the project won’t increase power bills, and will bring in $1.4 billion in tax revenue over the next 20 years. Martin says the company has communicated directly with residents through public meetings, as well as pamphlets and billboards. Local "We did everything by the book," he says. The Grayslake facility will be large enough to house companies that build generative AI, but activists opposed to the project say there has been a lack of specifics. "Who's the tenant? Is it Anthropic? Is it OpenAI? Is it going to be a swarm of AI agents pouring out from this data center to attack our government websites?" Coghill asked NBC 5. Martin says the Grayslake data center will operate on a closed-loop system, which means it will rely more on power than water to cool the computer servers inside. The project is slated to consume up to 1.2 gigawatts of energy once all phases are complete, which is the equivalent to powering a city of about one million residents. Marin says T5 has a separate rate agreement with ComEd, and will be effectively paying for all the power it consumes, but coalition members say they aren't buying that argument. "All they do is tap into the same grid we're all using, and they're getting their electricity," said Coalition member Michael Smith. "And we're being told, 'hey, throttle down your electricity use during hot summers because we're taxing the grids.'" Martin says the Chicago region is attractive because Illinois is a high power-producing state and he believes the grid can easily handle the influx of data centers. And he says if communities here say no, data centers will just go somewhere else. "Data centers are in every part of your life from, you know, from 911 to the grocery store to shopping online, whatever you interact with, everybody touches a data center every day," he said. The two sides are set to meet in court in November, but preliminary site-evaluation has already begun on the land. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has urged Illinois lawmakers to pass the so-called "POWER Act" when they return for their fall veto session that month. The legislation would put strict new limits on a data center's water and power usage. The coalition members were unswayed by Marin's explanations, but told NBC 5 they had one remaining question for him: would he personally want a data center of this size in his community? "Yeah I'd be fine with it," he said. "You're not going to see the building. You're not going to hear anything that's going on."

artigo.texto: Kozlowski and Savela discuss data centers, mining at forum Incumbent Liish Kozlowski and challenger Shawn Savela addressed the Hermantown data center, downtown Duluth and mining DULUTH, Minn. (Northern News Now) - District 8B incumbent Liish Kozlowski and Republican candidate Shawn Savela took the stage Tuesday for a candidate forum hosted by the Duluth News Tribune and Duluth Area Chamber of Commerce, the second of a two-day series of forums. The candidates addressed the proposed Hermantown data center, downtown Duluth, and the economy and mining. Savela said the Hermantown data center project is “a blueprint for how to do things wrong.” He said public officials signing non-disclosure agreements have caused chaos and mistrust for the project. Kozlowski called for more research. “We’re asking for a pause; we’re asking for a comprehensive regulatory framework to look at air, noise, groundwater,” Kozlowski said. Savela said increasing county jails and services would help clean up the streets and increase public safety. “Fund our jails and make them bigger so that we can take people in who are violent offenders, people that need to get off the street,” Savela said. Kozlowski said they want to see Duluth residents receive basic necessities to afford to live. “Basic needs, thrivable wage, access to childcare, good education, housing, all of it to live your best life,” Kozlowski said. Savela spoke about his desire to see copper-nickel mining in Minnesota. “We need these resources, copper and nickel. We need it for your phones, we need it for your cars, we need it for everything,” Savela said. Kozlowski said they are against copper-nickel mining. “We are now in what the international climate community has identified as a water bankruptcy,” Kozlowski said. Kozlowski also brought up the need for the top 1% to be taxed at a higher rate, while Savela called for more republican representation in the state. The two-day forum series also included debates between Sen. Grant Hauschild and challenger Andrea Zupancich, Rep. Pete Johnson and Allan Kehr, and Rep. Natalie Zeleznikar and Aaron Schweiger. artigo.texto: AI data centers erupt as major battleground in Florida governor’s race The three alarms of the AI boom Big picture view: TAMPA, Fla. - The nationwide boom in artificial intelligence is raising three distinct levels of concern among policymakers and the public: - Existential risk: Warnings from tech leaders that advanced AI could eventually escape human control. - Workforce disruption: The potential for rapid automation to eliminate millions of traditional jobs. - Physical infrastructure demands: The immediate environmental, energy and land-use impacts of industrial-scale data centers. While the first two alarms involve national and global debates, the third alarm has arrived directly in Florida, making the state's election a key factor in where these massive facilities go—or don't go. Loudoun County’s $1.2 billion trade-off The backstory: To examine what a data center boom looks like on the ground, Democratic candidate David Jolly traveled to Loudoun County, Virginia—commonly known as "Data Center Alley." While Loudoun County has been a tech hub since the late 1990s, rapid expansion over the past decade has steadily converted open land and wooded parcels near residential neighborhoods into industrial campuses. Today, Loudoun County hosts roughly 230 existing data center buildings, with another 100 facilities in the pipeline. The Virginia experience highlights the trade-offs facing local communities: - Community strain: Residents express concerns about noise and air pollution, industrial views replacing natural woods, and concerns over declining property values. - Massive tax revenue: Loudoun County Economic Development Director Buddy Rizer notes that data centers deliver approximately $1.2 billion in annual local tax revenue—an asset class unmatched by any other industry. That tax base funds local public schools, roads, and community projects, including a local recreation center featuring pools, weightlifting rooms and amenities built largely from data center revenue. Whether Florida should embrace Virginia's high-revenue, high-density model or block it at the state line, has become a core issue between the candidates. Jolly’s plan: A statewide pause, environmental review, and potential ban Democrat David Jolly argues that the state must step in to protect communities, public health, and natural resources before data centers proliferate across Florida. Jolly proposes a one-year statewide moratorium on new data center construction to study their impacts on Florida's air, water systems, energy grid, real estate values, and overall economy. Key pillars of Jolly's position include: - State jurisdiction & permanent ban potential: Jolly asserts that the state has a clear duty to intervene on environmental and health grounds. If research shows severe negative impacts, Jolly says he would extend the temporary moratorium into a permanent statewide ban. - Economic skepticism: While acknowledging short-term construction jobs, Jolly questions the long-term economic value of data centers relative to their resource consumption, raising concerns about the "functional obsolescence" of these massive structures 5 to 10 years down the road. - Quality of life and AI anxieties: Beyond noise pollution and real estate devaluation, Jolly notes that data centers have become a physical symbol of broader public anxieties regarding job loss, wage disruption, privacy, and security. - Clean energy contrast: Jolly strongly supports expanding solar, wind, and renewable technologies, stating that clean energy can lower utility bills, create jobs, and protect Florida's natural environment. Donalds’ plan: Local control, ratepayer safeguards Republican Byron Donalds strongly opposes a statewide pause, arguing that banning or stalling data center construction sends a dangerous signal to the business community that Florida is closed to capital investment. Donalds' strategy relies on local government authority and legislative ratepayer protections: - A departure on local preemption: In recent years, Florida's Republican-led state government has preempted local municipalities on a range of issues. However, on data centers, Donalds explicitly opposes state preemption, arguing that cities and counties should retain full authority to decide whether a facility belongs in their community. - Current ratepayer protection law & caveats: Donalds points to current state law—enacted through legislation sponsored by his running mate, Representative Bryan Avila—which requires large data centers to pay their full energy and water infrastructure costs, so traditional utility bills do not increase. However, that law applies specifically to Florida's four major investor-owned utilities (leaving municipal utilities and rural electric co-ops exempt) and relies on the Public Service Commission (PSC) for enforcement. - Transparency vs. past legislation: Donalds calls for full transparency for local data center proposals, stating there should be "no more NDAs" (non-disclosure agreements). Earlier legislative efforts sponsored by Avila sought to exempt data center plans from public records laws, but that transparency exemption failed to pass. Donalds emphasizes the consumer-protection provisions that did become law. - Replacing solar arrays with nuclear reactors: Skeptical of solar power—which he argues takes large tracts of land out of productive use for relatively low power output—Donalds states he is "dovish on solar and wind power." Instead, Donalds proposes placing four data centers on the footprint of a single solar array and powering them with an SMR (Small Modular Reactor)—a small nuclear fission reactor. Any excess electricity generated by the SMR would be fed back into the public power grid. - Protecting pristine land and tourism: Donalds argues Florida has available interior land to accommodate high-tech development without building next to residential homes or harming core tourism hubs like Disney, Universal, and state beaches. artigo.texto: Georgetown council votes to draft ordinance banning data centers Council members raise concerns over water, land and infrastructure GEORGETOWN, Ky. (WKYT) - The Georgetown City Council voted Tuesday night unanimously to ask legal counsel to prepare an ordinance banning data centers. The ordinance would also define what a hyperscale data center is. The action comes as council members shared their concerns about the possibility of a data center in Georgetown. Council members said they also want to be cautious of the impact a ban could have. “I think most of us are talking about the mega ones is what the issue and just making sure that were not trying to take out somebody who has a small one that needs for processing for the facility,” said Mayor Burney Jenkins. Councilmember Karen Tingle-Sames said that the city can’t support a data center. “If you look at the things as we know about data centers as of today, the city of Georgetown can’t handle a data center. We don’t have the water for it, we don’t have the land for it, we don’t have the infrastructure for it,” she said. Jenkins said he also wants to be prepared if a total ban faces legal challenges. The ordinance to completely ban data centers would also need approval from the Planning and Zoning Commission. The Scott County Fiscal Court extended its data center moratorium last week. artigo.texto: Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) is facing growing scrutiny over the financing of its AI infrastructure after about $18 billion of loans tied to its Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico were quoted at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar, according to the Financial Times, as reported by Reuters. The project is part of Oracle's AI infrastructure expansion with OpenAI, but local opposition over water and air-quality concerns and a regulatory setback involving a proposed natural-gas pipeline have raised questions about its development. Banks have also struggled to distribute the debt to other investors as concerns about Oracle's leverage have increased. Reuters noted that S&P downgraded Oracle in July to one notch above junk. Photo from Oracle website Oracle's AI Backlog Could Provide a Cushion for Rising Financing Needs The debt pressure is occurring alongside exceptionally strong demand for Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL)'s cloud infrastructure. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, cloud revenue rose 62% to $11.6 billion, while cloud infrastructure revenue increased 121% to $7.4 billion. Oracle's remaining performance obligations also reached $664 billion, up $209 billion year over year, providing substantial contracted demand to support continued infrastructure investment. The financing model is also becoming less dependent on Oracle funding every dollar itself. Oracle said $75 billion of its large AI contracts involved customers prepaying for GPUs or supplying the GPUs themselves, substantially reducing the capital it needs to raise for AI data centers. Oracle raised $43 billion of debt and $5 billion of equity in fiscal 2026, while expecting about $40 billion of additional debt and equity financing in fiscal 2027. If customer-backed contracts continue expanding, the revenue generated from infrastructure could increasingly offset the financing burden. Rising Infrastructure Costs Could Test Oracle's AI Investment Strategy The immediate concern is that Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) is committing capital faster than its infrastructure generates cash. Capital expenditures jumped to $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026 from $21.2 billion a year earlier, producing negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027 alone, capital expenditures reached $28.5 billion, and Oracle expects fiscal 2027 spending to exceed the prior year. The balance sheet leaves less room for execution problems. As of August 31, Oracle had $125.3 billion of notes payable and other borrowings, compared with $37.1 billion of cash and marketable securities. It also had $34.6 billion of recognized operating lease liabilities and another $288 billion of additional data-center lease commitments expected to begin between fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2029.

HOPKINSVILLE, Ky. (WBKO) - The City of Hopkinsville has announced Community and Development Services will hold a public hearing Monday evening to gather public input on proposed zoning regulations for commercial data centers. The hearing is scheduled for 6 p.m. in the Lecture Hall of the Hopkinsville Community College Auditorium Building, 720 North Drive. The proposed amendment to the Hopkinsville Zoning Ordinance outlines how data centers are defined locally, establishes siting and operational standards, and determines which zoning districts would permit such facilities. artigo.texto: Battery maker Eve Energy says it signed deals covering more than 30 GW/h at IAA Transportation 2026, where it showed its Open Source Battery 4.0: AI Battery in Europe for the first time. Named buyers include WEG, BMZ, Sunswap, Janus Electric and Morris Commercial, though Eve gave no split by customer or delivery date. It says both meet European market access rules and suit harsh operating conditions. The AI Battery adds a custom AI chip that, according to Eve, enables cell-level sensing and real-time diagnostics. That would shift battery management from passive monitoring towards active control, although the release offered no test data. Commercial vehicle OEMs including BAIC, Sany and Nivalis visited the stand, the company said. Eve argues that tough regulation and extreme conditions are raising the bar for traction batteries in Europe, a market where the IAA deals give it a firmer foothold. Source: Eve Energy

artigo.texto: Buffalo, NY (WBEN) The Buffalo Common Council will vote Tuesday on whether to impose a two year moratorium on data centers in the city. Mayor Sean Ryan says the city previously looked at a moratorium. "We had been working on a one-year moratorium as an executive order, and then we kept in close contact with the state legislature and the governor, and so the state came in with a one-year moratorium. So we pulled back our executive order; it wasn't necessary anymore. Now the council has a two-year moratorium that differs significantly from the states, so we're going to take a look at that," says Ryan. But while the concern is companies coming in and buying land, he has a caveat. "We have to make sure that we don't inadvertently sweep up Roswell Park's computers, M&T Banks computers, Kaleida's computers, so we're going to be checking with all the University of Buffalo. So we're going to be checking with all these institutions that have rather large computer storage facilities to make sure that this somehow doesn't affect them," warns Ryan. Count Councilmember Mitch Nowakowski among those willing to vote for the moratorium. "I believe that a moratorium will allow the city of Buffalo to get in conjunction with the state of New York, with an ability to be able to better get ahead of data centers that are being proposed through you know the region, but also the country," says Nowakowski, who would like to take it from an urban planning standpoint. "I believe that a moratorium would allow the city of Buffalo planners to get ahead of if a data center was proposed in the city, where would it be most applicable or not? What environmental impacts would transpire if this happened? So we really have to take this from a planning perspective, but ultimately from an environment standpoint as well, to because of the the amount of water and electricity, and can the grid handle this? And ultimately, where would this, you know, where would a proposal go? I mean, we're we're a city of a quarter of a million people, and you know, we we hit with the vacant land that we do have. We would like it to be used for housing, and and and where in this city would this even be proposed? And even if it was appropriate, where where would this be? So taking this from a municipal planning perspective is not only the right thing to do, but it's it's the appropriate thing to also do for our city, our built environment, and for our residents." Leah Halton-Pope says she wants to make sure the city has the right infrastructure when it's ready. "A lot of people have an issue with environmental hazards and what it does to communities around it," she says. She notes underprivileged communities tend to be most affected. She says a moratorium allows to make sure the Green Code is up to date. The Council votes this afternoon at 2pm. Lawmakers to decide on two year moratorium Lawmakers to decide on two year moratorium

artigo.texto: Capacidade de data centers em São Paulo cresce 91% em um ano Região do entorno da capital já é o principal parque de dados da América Latina, de acordo com levantamento da Cushman & Wakefield A capacidade operacional de data centers no eixo São Paulo–Campinas cresceu 91% em um ano, passando de 346 megawatts no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 661 megawatts no mesmo período de 2026, segundo levantamento da Cushman & Wakefield, empresa global especializada em serviços imobiliários corporativos. O resultado consolida a região como o principal mercado de data centers da América Latina. Além da capacidade já em operação, o eixo composto pelas duas cidades paulistas possui 250 megawatts em projetos em construção e outros 2.066 megawatts planejados. O volume planejado equivale a mais de três vezes a capacidade operacional atual e supera, somados, os projetos previstos em Querétaro, no México, Santiago, no Chile, e Bogotá, na Colômbia, que totalizam cerca de 1.47o megawatts. Apesar da expansão da oferta, a consultoria destaca que a vacância dos projetos que já estão em operação permaneceu baixa, ficando 4,1% no primeiro semestre no eixo de São Paulo, indicando a alta demanda por esse tipo de infraestrutura. A Cushman & Wakefield também destaca os novos impulsos que o Brasil deve receber com o Redata, novo regime de incentivos tributários aprovado em setembro. O Redata prevê a suspensão de tributos federais sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, ampliação e modernização desses empreendimentos. “O mercado brasileiro já vinha apresentando crescimento consistente antes da sanção do Redata”, disse Dennys Andrade, chefe de pesquisa e intligência de mercado da Cushman & Wakefield no Brasil. “A redução dos custos de implantação pode favorecer o avanço dos projetos, mas sua viabilidade continuará dependendo de fatores como disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, terrenos adequados, licenciamento e segurança regulatória.” Com 661 megawatts em operação, o hub de São Paulo tem quase o dobro da capacidade de Querétaro, que registra 336 megawatts, e supera Santiago, com 272 megawatts, e Bogotá, com 58 megawatts. Consideradas todas as Américas, contudo, os Estados Unidos continuam sendo o principal centro deste mercado: o estado da Virgínia, por exemplo, seu maior parque, tem 12.338 megawatts em operação, enquanto a cidade de Atlanta possui 3.488 megawatts. Além disso, dos 38 gigawatts que já estão em construção em todo o continente (equivalente a 38.000 megawatts), 92% estão nos Estados Unidos.

artigo.texto: A restauração florestal após a exploração mineral abre oportunidades no mercado de carbono. A extração mineral contribui significativamente para o desenvolvimento econômico, mas também exerce pressão sobre os recursos florestais, a terra e os ecossistemas. Com a demanda por minerais para impulsionar a transição energética projetada para continuar aumentando acentuadamente, o controle do desmatamento e a restauração de ecossistemas após a mineração estão se tornando uma necessidade urgente. Especialistas acreditam que, se feita corretamente, a restauração florestal pós-mineração não só ajudará a restaurar as funções ecológicas, como também abrirá oportunidades para gerar financiamento adicional a partir de projetos de carbono. Na manhã de 29 de setembro, em Hanói, o Centro de Certificação de Florestas Sustentáveis da Academia Vietnamita de Ciências Florestais, em colaboração com a organização Forest Trends, realizou um workshop de consulta sobre "Soluções baseadas na natureza para a restauração florestal após a exploração mineral e oportunidades de participação no futuro mercado de carbono". Segundo To Xuan Phuc, Diretor do Programa de Política Florestal, Comércio e Finanças da Forest Trends, a mineração é a quarta maior causa de desmatamento no mundo, sendo responsável por aproximadamente 7% do desmatamento em regiões tropicais. Ao mesmo tempo, a demanda por minerais poderá quintuplicar até 2050 devido ao desenvolvimento de tecnologias de transição energética, como painéis solares, energia eólica, veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Isso exige um equilíbrio entre o desenvolvimento econômico e a proteção das florestas e dos ecossistemas. Sem um controle adequado desde as fases de planejamento, licenciamento e operação, o impacto sobre as florestas pode persistir mesmo após o fechamento da mina. No Vietnã, segundo o Sr. Vu Tan Phuong, Diretor do Escritório de Certificação de Gestão Florestal do Vietnã (VFCO), o país possui mais de 5.000 áreas de mineração com cerca de 60 tipos de minerais, incluindo bauxita, apatita, titânio, carvão, elementos de terras raras e granito. A exploração mineral (excluindo petróleo e gás) contribui com cerca de 4 a 5% do PIB anualmente, impulsionando o desenvolvimento econômico local. No entanto, a mineração a céu aberto pode fragmentar a paisagem, destruir a vegetação florestal, perturbar as camadas do solo, poluir as fontes de água e degradar a qualidade do solo. Esses impactos dificultam a restauração da floresta após a exploração madeireira, especialmente em áreas de rejeitos. Você também pode gostar Segundo o Sr. Vu Tan Phuong, a mineração a céu aberto de carvão, apatita e bauxita tem um forte impacto na cobertura vegetal, na topografia e nas camadas do solo. As condições do solo e do local nas áreas de rejeitos de carvão e apatita representam muitos desafios para a restauração florestal. Portanto, a restauração não pode se limitar ao simples plantio de árvores para arborizar a área, mas precisa ser realizada de forma contínua, formando gradualmente um ecossistema florestal estável. As soluções baseadas na natureza devem ser escolhidas de acordo com as condições específicas de cada área após a mineração. A restauração deve ser baseada nas características do local para determinar as espécies de árvores apropriadas, a densidade e os métodos de intervenção. Para depósitos de rejeitos de carvão e apatita, o objetivo principal é restaurar a função ambiental, estabilizar o solo, limitar a erosão e estabelecer gradualmente um ecossistema florestal, gerando simultaneamente benefícios de carbono. Em áreas com condições mais favoráveis após a extração de bauxita, a regeneração florestal pode ser orientada para objetivos econômicos, combinada com a geração de créditos de carbono. Essa abordagem contribui para a restauração da terra e da paisagem, além de criar valor econômico adicional a partir da área florestal após a mineração. No entanto, para traduzir esse potencial em resultados tangíveis, especialistas acreditam ser necessário abordar as lacunas na gestão da extração mineral e da conversão florestal. De acordo com o Dr. Nguyen Thanh Long, membro da equipe de pesquisa apoiada pelo projeto "Apoio Técnico para Atividades no Vietnã com o Apoio do Programa de Governança Florestal, de Mercado e Climática (FGMC)", as lacunas existem desde as fases de planejamento e licenciamento. O planejamento de recursos minerais e o planejamento florestal são desenvolvidos dentro de sistemas de gestão diferentes, o que pode levar a sobreposições entre áreas com potencial mineral e áreas florestais. Outra questão é a avaliação do impacto ambiental de projetos de mineração. Os relatórios precisam considerar de forma mais completa os impactos cumulativos, a fragmentação de habitats, a perda de biodiversidade e os efeitos de instalações auxiliares, como depósitos de rejeitos, rotas de transporte e plantas de processamento. Além disso, a gestão pós-licenciamento precisa ser fortalecida. O monitoramento dos limites da mineração, a expansão dos depósitos de rejeitos, a restauração ambiental e o reflorestamento após a mineração não foram implementados de forma sincronizada em todos os setores, o que dificulta a inspeção, a supervisão e a determinação da responsabilidade pelas áreas florestais após o encerramento do projeto. O Dr. Nguyen Thanh Long sugeriu que os critérios de proteção florestal sejam integrados desde a fase de planejamento da exploração mineral; que a qualidade das avaliações de impacto ambiental para projetos que se sobrepõem ou são adjacentes a áreas florestais seja aprimorada; que o monitoramento pós-licenciamento seja fortalecido; e que a coordenação entre as agências de gestão mineral, fundiária e florestal seja reforçada. artigo.texto: Amazon Taps Prysmian and Rio Tinto for Low-Carbon Data Center Cables. What Does it Mean for Investors? Prysmian is finding another way into the data-center buildout, and this time the story isn't about fiber. The Italian cable maker has partnered with Rio Tinto (NYSE:RIO) to supply electrical cables made with low-carbon aluminum for an Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) data center in Ohio. The cables will use aluminum produced with ELYSIS inert-anode technology, which Prysmian says eliminates direct greenhouse-gas emissions from the aluminum-smelting process and releases pure oxygen instead. For Prysmian investors, the project's significance lies in the fact that the technology Prysmian and Rio Tinto were developing earlier this year is now being put to use in a data-center project for Amazon. Bull Case The Amazon project gives Prysmian's work with ELYSIS something it didn't have when the company announced its expanded collaboration with Rio Tinto in March, which is a specific data-center application. Prysmian says this will be the first known use of aluminum produced through inert-anode smelting in a data center, and the cables will be manufactured at its Sedalia, Missouri facility. The project didn't emerge from a new supplier relationship either, as Prysmian and Rio Tinto (NYSE:RIO) signed a five-year supply agreement in 2023 for low-carbon aluminum produced using renewable hydropower from Rio Tinto's Canadian operations. They later strengthened the relationship through a joint development agreement before announcing their work with ELYSIS-produced aluminum in March 2026. Data centers were already part of the thinking at that point, as Prysmian said in March that its customers, particularly those in the data-center sector, shared similar sustainability commitments, while Rio Tinto specifically identified the rapidly expanding data-center sector as an area where lower-carbon aluminum could support decarbonization efforts. Amazon has now provided a concrete example, with AWS Vice President of Data Center Engineering Joern Tinnemeyer linking the Ohio initiative to Amazon's target of reaching net-zero carbon emissions across its operations by 2040. The project also fits with targets Prysmian has set for its own business. The company is targeting Net Zero by 2035 and has said it wants sustainability-linked solutions to account for 55% of revenue by 2028. Bear Case There is an obvious reason not to get carried away with the announcement, as Prysmian has not provided a contract value or expected revenue contribution of the Amazon project. Without a contract value, volume figure, or expected revenue contribution, there is no basis for arguing that the Ohio data center will materially change Prysmian's financial performance.

artigo.texto: Brasil deve dobrar capacidade de data centers até 2030, diz Kanamaru Em entrevista, Senior advisor do BCG relaciona expansão da infraestrutura ao ReData, à soberania digital e demanda por processamento no País. O Brasil deve duplicar sua capacidade instalada de data centers até 2030, na avaliação de Márcio Kanamaru, senior advisor do Boston Consulting Group (BCG) para telecomunicações, mídia e tecnologia (TMT). Em entrevista ao Tele.Síntese, ele associou a expansão aos investimentos em infraestrutura digital e às políticas voltadas ao setor, entre elas o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (ReData). “Então o Brasil deve, até 2030, duplicar a sua capacidade em data center”, afirmou Kanamaru. Segundo ele, grandes projetos de investimento em andamento no País estão relacionados à construção dessa infraestrutura. O executivo também relacionou o cenário à aprovação do ReData e a outros estímulos tributários. Para ele, essas medidas deverão acelerar investimentos e projetos de data centers no mercado brasileiro. Acompanhe a entrevista: Soberania passa pela infraestrutura instalada no Brasil A disponibilidade de capacidade computacional no território nacional também aparece, na avaliação de Kanamaru, como parte da discussão sobre soberania digital. Ele citou empresas interessadas em manter no País dados de clientes e parceiros e o treinamento de modelos. “É importante a gente ter uma capacidade instalada aqui de data centers para que isso possa ser feito”, afirmou. Para Kanamaru, porém, a instalação de data centers não encerra a discussão. Ele defendeu que as políticas públicas considerem uma cadeia tecnológica mais ampla, chegando à capacidade nacional relacionada aos semicondutores. “O Brasil tem que buscar, através dessas políticas públicas, a construção de uma soberania mais verticalizada”, disse. Como horizonte para os próximos anos, ele cita “inclusive a construção e desenho de semicondutores no país”. Futurecom terá casos de uso com retorno sobre investimento Kanamaru também antecipou alguns dos temas que estarão em discussão na Futurecom 2026. A 31ª edição terá cinco eixos: inteligência artificial e economia de dados; infraestrutura digital; regulação e soberania; indústrias digitais; e uma arena dedicada a entretenimento e esportes. Na área de IA, a mudança apontada pelo executivo é a passagem da discussão sobre possibilidades da tecnologia para aplicações empresariais já implementadas. “Nas últimas edições a gente estava falando muito sobre perspectivas, oportunidades que a IA poderia propiciar. Nós veremos aqui casos de uso já materializados, com retorno sobre investimento”, afirmou. Segundo Kanamaru, a programação deverá apresentar business cases já construídos pelas empresas. Ele também destacou a evolução dos modelos generativos em áreas como ciência, matemática, física e saúde, além do avanço dos modelos abertos. Empresas poderão desenvolver modelos próprios baseados em open source, tema que também deverá aparecer nos debates do evento. BCG discutirá agentes e integração com redes orbitais O BCG participará de dois painéis na Futurecom, nos dias 6 e 7 de outubro. O primeiro tratará da utilização de agentes de IA no Brasil, com foco nos casos de uso e em como essas aplicações estão sendo implementadas. No segundo, o debate avançará sobre a integração das redes terrestres com redes orbitais. Kanamaru citou o uso dessas redes para ampliar a conectividade em áreas de difícil atendimento e em situações de missão crítica, onde a disponibilidade de infraestrutura por cabo, fibra ou redes móveis é mais limitada. Segundo ele, a discussão contará com a Anatel e outros participantes do ecossistema e abordará a integração entre diferentes infraestruturas de conectividade.
