artigo.texto: Google aims to answer questions on Pine Island Data Center project (ABC 6 News) — Pine Island residents are still pushing back against the prospect of a Google-based data center project. Google and partner companies attempted to address some of the main concerns expressed to the residents. One of the main concerns surrounded Google’s water use, with residents expressing worries about discharge and usage. Presenters at the webinar attempted to assure that the center would not overuse water at a more-than-necessary level. “Overall, the water strategy is focused on safe and sustainable construction process, reducing ongoing demand and relying on public infrastructure in a planned and regulated way,” Dave Meadows of Kimley-Horn said. “ Some residents were skeptical about the center’s plan, wondering if they will commit to their goal of limiting water usage. “My biggest concern is the water,” resident Lee Ondler said. “They won’t tell you how they’re going to dispose of it.” Another major concern for residents surrounded the rural land that would be repurposed for the center. “What makes me worry about the idea is it’s taking up farmland,” resident Calob Darci said. The webinar presenters spent time focused on the water conversation, as it is a common concern among communities in the early stages of data center development. “People care deeply, deeply about the quality of water in this state,” said John Wade of Rochester Area Economic Development, Inc. Construction is currently halted on this project as it navigates a temporary restraining order and court proceedings. Other data centers The city of Harmony is continuing progress on the creation of a new ordinance related to data centers. The ordinance draft will now go to the Planning and Zoning Commission on Oct. 14. They will determine whether it will go to the council for approval. In Hancock County, the board discussed a resolution that could have put a moratorium on data centers for six months. However, the motion died from the board’s desire to study the public health effects and concerns, along with building an ordinance to create guidelines for prospective companies.

artigo.texto: Data centers não podem virar mais um encargo na conta de luz Em artigo à CNN Infra, Lino Cançado argumenta que restringir o Redata às energias renováveis pode gerar encargos bilionários aos consumidores O Brasil encontra-se diante de uma oportunidade histórica com o avanço da demanda global por novos data centers, impulsionada sobretudo pelas soluções de inteligência artificial. A atração desses investimentos trará inovação, geração de empregos e desenvolvimento tecnológico para quem souber aproveitar essa janela. Nesse sentido, o Redata (Regime Especial de Incentivos para o Desenvolvimento de Infraestrutura de Data Centers) é uma oportunidade fundamental para garantir que não fiquemos para trás nessa corrida. No entanto, o debate atual sobre a regulamentação desses incentivos fiscais tem girado em torno das fontes de energia que irão abastecer as estruturas de processamento de dados, em especial na questão de incluir apenas fontes intermitentes para atender à grande demanda energética dos data centers. A consequência direta de preterir fontes seguras e de baixa emissão pode ter um impacto preocupante: o aumento da conta de luz do consumidor comum. Data centers são instalações que funcionam sem parar. Por isso exigem energia contínua, estável e segura, 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana. Embora o Brasil tenha uma matriz elétrica invejável e predominantemente renovável, sabemos que as fontes eólica e solar são intermitentes. Quando o sol se põe e os ventos cessam, coincidindo com o horário de ponta de consumo, eles não são capazes de sustentar o fornecimento constante que esses centros de processamento exigem. Se o modelo não for bem estruturado, a expansão acelerada sobrecarregará o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) na ponta, exigindo uma contratação massiva de reserva de capacidade. Esse encargo de potência tem um alto custo, que acaba sendo rateado e repassado para a conta de luz de todos os brasileiros. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) já realizou uma segunda revisão do plano de carga para o horizonte 2026-2030, saltando a previsão da carga de data centers de 2.157 MW para alarmantes 5.653 MW. É uma diferença repentina de 3.496 MW. Para garantir que essa demanda seja atendida com segurança dia a dia no horário de pico, o sistema terá um custo de capacidade adicional de R$ 7 bilhões ao ano. Isso equivale a 13,35% de todo o orçamento previsto para a Conta de Desenvolvimento Energético (CDE) em 2026 (orçada em R$ 52,7 bilhões) e a 17,95% do LRCAP. Em outras palavras, seria um encargo severo imposto à tarifa de cidadãos e indústrias, que não têm relação nenhuma com a operação desses centros de dados. A saída para evitar essa penalização social não é frear o desenvolvimento, mas adotar uma política pragmática. O ideal é condicionar a instalação de novos data centers à autoprodução de energia. Esse é um modelo internacional já testado, que vem sendo aplicado de maneira eficiente nos Estados Unidos. Na definição do conteúdo do decreto do Redata, o poder público deve focar em estabelecer as regras de atendimento e deixar que o próprio empreendedor decida como supri-las da forma mais competitiva e eficiente. A melhor equação para esses complexos é a combinação inteligente de matrizes: aliar a energia limpa das renováveis ao atributo da confiabilidade e firmeza do gás natural. Dessa forma, os data centers não demandam do grid na hora da ponta, o que evita a criação de custos adicionais para o restante dos consumidores. O gás natural, como combustível da transição energética, viabiliza uma solução de baixíssima emissão para suprir essa intermitência, garantindo a resiliência operacional do investidor sem onerar os demais usuários da rede. A transição energética e a digitalização não podem ser desenhadas de costas para a realidade sistêmica do país. Restringir o Redata exclusivamente à energia renovável forçará o sistema a prover uma reserva artificial bilionária paga pela sociedade. Precisamos criar um marco legal que incentive a autoprodução e reconheça a importância da flexibilidade do gás natural, assegurando que o Brasil avance rumo à liderança digital sem transferir o custo dessa modernização para o bolso do cidadão. * Lino Cançado é CEO da Eneva

artigo.texto: DE PERE, Wis. — De Pere, Wis., and Milwaukee are moving toward one-year moratoriums on large-scale data center development, as Wisconsin communities consider how to address potential impacts on land use, utilities and local infrastructure. Planning bodies in both communities approved proposed moratoriums Monday night. Both measures still need final approval from their respective common councils. De Pere Mayor James Boyd said the moratorium would give the city time to review its local rules. “The City of De Pere doesn’t have any of them in the works. We don’t have the land for it, most likely. That said, you just never know,” Boyd said. “The moratorium gives you a chance to pause and get your code up to date regarding the hyper-scale centers.” Boyd said local officials are seeking more direction as data center proposals become a larger issue across Wisconsin. “What’s most likely going to happen is you’re going to see legislation at the state and federal level that will give us guidance,” Boyd said. “That’s really what we’re hoping for. I don’t know of any municipality that cherishes this moment where they’re handling this by themselves.” The issue has drawn attention from residents concerned about how large developments could change the landscape. Lauren French lives in Denmark, Wis., and drives through rural Brown County to her downtown De Pere business: Idolscape. “Driving here, there’s so much open space,” she said. “I don’t want that leveled. I don’t want to look and see this big, huge building and big, huge parking lot, and it’s just another concrete thing. We don’t need that.” Concerns about data center development also extend to utility costs and infrastructure needs. Tom Content, executive director of the Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, said part of the organization’s work is making sure data centers pay their own way for needed infrastructure. “Communities want to be ready,” Content said. “If a data center comes, they want to be ready to make sure the community impacts are talked about. The energy costs are talked about. The water issues are addressed, and the community needs are part of the conversation.” Boyd said the scale of large data centers became clearer to him after seeing one of them near Port Washington, Wis. “I didn’t really realize the size and scope of it until you drive down 43 and go toward Milwaukee and back,” Boyd said. “Then you really get a handle on what you’re looking at. The magnitude. The size. And the usage those things need to survive.”

artigo.texto: Talbot County considers zoning rules for battery storage facilities Planning commission holds first public hearing on proposed regulations TALBOT COUNTY, Ga. (WTVM) - Talbot County leaders are looking at new rules to prepare for large battery storage facilities, the kind often used to power heavy developments like data centers. The planning commission held its first public hearing Monday on how to zone for them. County says current rules don’t cover private systems County leaders say their rules currently don’t cover private battery systems, which store extra electricity and pump it back out when the grid is strained. No developer has applied to build one yet, but neighbors and local planners are already weighing in. Clarence Napier said he believes more work needs to be done on the plan. “I think more work needs to be done with developing the plan,” Napier said. “Like I asked the question this plan came from a template and maybe the plan needs to be designed or scaled down or maybe even elevated for just this town.” Allison Slocum, assistant planning director for the River Valley Regional Commission, said the facilities could benefit the grid. “This is really going to help make our energy grid more resilient by taking power off the grid when it’s not being used, storing it and then releasing it when it’s most needed,” Slocum said. Existing facility not subject to local zoning Talbot County already has one battery storage facility, built by Georgia Power in North Talbot. Because Georgia Power operates as a utility, it was not required to follow local zoning rules. A private developer would be. The Board of Commissioners will hold a second public hearing next Monday at 6 p.m. Copyright 2026 WTVM. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority on Wednesday selected eight bulk energy storage and 13 large-scale renewable projects to receive financial support, totaling almost 1.7 GW of clean energy resources expected to be online by the end of 2030. - The state’s first bulk energy storage awards went to 950 MW of lithium batteries ranging from four to eight hours in duration. Renewables awards will go to solar, wind and hydroelectric projects totaling 719 MW of capacity. - The state has fallen behind its clean energy goals and earlier this year made changes to the greenhouse gas reduction targets laid out in its Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act. “This announcement couldn’t come at a better time,” Amisha Rai, Advanced Energy United’s senior vice president of advocacy, said in a statement. Dive Insight: New York pushed back its emissions targets this year, but officials say the state remains committed to clean energy and has not adjusted its procurement goals. The state’s target of 70% renewable energy by 2030, set when the CLCPA was passed in 2019, is unchanged. New York doubled its storage target in 2022 to have 6 GW of storage online by 2030. NYSERDA plans to issue a second annual bulk energy storage request for proposals by the end of this year and said it intends to select 3 GW of energy storage procurement over its first three solicitations. The newly contracted large-scale energy projects “not only further the growth of clean energy and more than double the utility-scale energy storage that exists currently statewide – but they contribute to New York’s comprehensive, all of the above energy strategy,” NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris said in a statement. The selected projects in New York range in size from a 4-hour, 94-MW facility being developed by Key Capture Energy in Ulster County; to a similar 150-MW facility in Suffolk County, also developed by KCE; to the 8-hour, 140-MW Lighthouse Energy Storage project in Chautauqua County, proposed by Grid Connected Infrastructure LLC and Neoen US. The projects will more than double the utility-scale energy storage that has been awarded, contracted, and installed in New York to date, “making meaningful progress toward 6 gigawatts by 2030,” NYSERDA said. “Bringing new renewable energy and storage projects online means more homegrown power, more flexibility for the grid, and more investment in communities across the state,” AEU’s Rai said. The projects announced last week are expected to support 1,000 jobs and generate over $3.7 billion in private investment, NYSERDA said. Payments to the contracted projects will only begin once projects are operational.

artigo.texto: Nebraska data center growth raises questions for host counties NORTH PLATTE, Neb. (KNOP) - Nebraska’s push to attract data centers is facing questions from the counties that would host them. Lincoln County commissioners met last Tuesday in Grand Island with power companies, water districts and Gov. Pillen for the first meeting of Nebraska’s Data Center Task Force. Task force reviews power, water strain The group is looking at how the state should handle the rapid growth of data centers and the strain they could put on power and water supplies. Lincoln County Commissioner Kent Weems said the county is not against the idea but wants any deal to come with benefits for taxpayers. “If we’re going to be the ones taking the heat for these, whatever they evolve into, if they evolve at all, which apparently there’s something and it works locally. It’s my hope and prayer that this community can, in fact, have substantial beneficial results and be mandated in the agreement so that the county can see property tax relief,” Weems said. Not all data centers are the same, commissioner says Lincoln County Commissioner Micaela Wuehler said data centers vary in scale and impact. “It’s important for people to remember: not all data centers are created equal. They’re not all hyperscale... they may not all be appropriate for Lincoln County. That’s where our good planning and zoning regulations come in,” Wuehler said. artigo.texto: Trending PARKERSBURG, W.Va. -- The Democratic challenger for one of West Virginia's congressional seats pitched legislation Friday to place a two-year moratorium on new, large data centers and to give local communities a say in whether they're built. Ace Parsi, a Morgantown community organizer running for U.S. House of Representatives 2nd District seat occupied by Rep. Riley Moore, said the proposed "Neighbors, Not Servers Act" would be "the very first piece of legislation that I would introduce as a member of Congress." Moore said Friday, "West Virginians need a voice in this important debate," and he has co-sponsored legislation to that effect. Parsi said the impact of data centers on the environment, communities and utility costs is an issue he's heard about from Democratic, Republican and independent voters alike. "Our communities do not have a say in whether these things go in our backyards," he said, referencing transmission lines as well. The legislation would pause new construction of data centers using 20 megawatts or more of power, according to a news release from Parsi. During that time, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine would conduct studies into the effects of such facilities on public health, water, jobs, utility bills, property values and the power grid. It proposes a fine of up to $1 million a day for developers who break the pause. The bill also would ban nondisclosure agreements between developers and public officials, including those already in place. NDAs signed by Washington County, Ohio, officials for a proposed data center in the Waterford area have ignited debate. Commissioners have said such agreements are standard for preliminary conversations about potential development and signing allowed them to enter into conversations with the developers. Parsi's proposed bill also would establish a referendum process so community members could seek a vote on approving construction of a data center. Before a vote, developers would be required to disclose information such as who is behind the project, who will use it, how much power and water it will use, noise levels, tax breaks sought and number of jobs it will create, the release states. Parsi said during an online news conference Friday that a public vote would not be mandatory, as local bodies like county commissions could make the call as representatives of residents. "We would direct those (federal) agencies to not give those permits (for data center construction) until they made sure the community" had a voice in the process through one of those mechanisms, he said. "The local people need to be able to determine this," Parsi said. "This bill is not about big government." Moore said "it is critical that America wins the AI race against countries like China, but we must do so responsibly. "I'm for local control. Local communities need to have a say about whether to build data centers in their backyard, and we need to ensure that Americans are not being forced to foot the bill for increased energy demands and water usage," he said. "That's why I proudly cosponsored and voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act in the House to ensure that local communities have a voice in these important decisions and ensure that West Virginians are not being forced to foot the bill for data center development." Moore announced in an Aug. 31 news release he was co-sponsoring that bill, which would "require state public utility commissions to consider standards ensuring that large data centers pay the full incremental costs associated with generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades needed to serve their electricity demand." It adds that the bill would protect ratepayers while preserving the authority of state regulators to determine how its standards were implemented. OHIO ELECTION TOPIC Data centers are also a topic of interest in Ohio's gubernatorial election. Democratic nominee Dr. Amy Acton this week called for the state Legislature to enact a conditional moratorium on data centers, including prohibiting data centers and investors from passing along costs to ratepayers, banning their use of NDAs and requiring them to be built with union labor, maintain zero environmental impact and prioritize the use of brownfield sites. In the release, she also criticized Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's investments in data centers. "I am calling on lawmakers from across the aisle to come together and fight against the unchecked development of data centers driving up costs in our communities," Acton said. "I will always put the needs of working families over the wants of billionaires, corporations and special interests." Ramaswamy's campaign website lists three "non-negotiable" requirements for companies wanting to build data centers in Ohio: Ensure nearby families receive free electricity by providing power or compensation, pay their full property taxes so revenue can be used to provide relief for homeowners, and comply with strict air and water quality standards while minimizing water use and prioritizing brownfield and industrial sites over farmland.

artigo.texto: “A fraction of proposed data centers will get built. Utilities are wising up.” That was the headline on a May 2025 Utility Dive article that explored the conundrum speculative data center requests pose for U.S. electric utilities. More than a year later, it’s unclear how much has changed. Community opposition has emerged as a major barrier to data center development, with other challenges including construction labor shortages, long lead times for critical electrical equipment, limited power availability in key markets and uncertainty around consumer demand for artificial intelligence tools. More than $170 billion in AI data center capacity has been “blocked, withdrawn, or stalled” by community opposition since January 2024, the energy advisory company Relae, formerly Carbon Direct, said in June. That’s a sizable chunk of the roughly $581 billion Goldman Sachs expects the big tech companies known as hyperscalers to spend in the U.S. on AI infrastructure, including data center construction, this year. Yet market analysts see no sign that the AI-driven construction boom will disappear anytime soon, despite challenges. Goldman Sachs said in May it sees U.S. data center power demand more than doubling from its 2025 levels to reach 66 GW in 2027. Only about half of data center capacity scheduled for the next one to two years is expected to come online on time amid delays and cancellations, it said. The Electric Power Research Institute, a research nonprofit, said in February that data centers will represent 9% to 17% of U.S. electricity demand in 2030 and up to 20% by 2035. Questions persist around the scale, timing and location of new data center load. If anything, the uncertainty is growing amid public backlash to data centers that is fueling state-led efforts to impose stricter rules on data center development, up to and including moratoriums on new facilities in some places. Firmer answers would benefit not only the utility planners and regulators ensuring that the electric grid is neither over- nor under-built, but also the millions of other customers who could bear the consequences of a disorderly buildout, industry experts say. Texas hits the brakes on large loads as states assert control Many utilities and their regulators have turned to large-load tariffs to try and weed out speculative load by requiring minimum contract durations, minimum billing demand and collateral requirements, upfront payments for impact studies, exit fees and specific ramp schedules. Some states have also introduced incentives for developers that bring their own capacity, agree to be flexible in their energy use or commit to state clean energy or economic development goals. The question of just how much data center capacity is going to come online, and when, is particularly urgent in Texas, which has paused new data center interconnections pending an audit of its 474-GW queue. That’s more than five times the Texas grid’s recent all-time peak demand record of a little over 90 GW set this summer. Few experts expect all that load to materialize. Pablo Vegas, president and CEO of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, is among the skeptics. “We believe this forecast to be higher than expected future load growth,” Vegas said in an April statement, citing uncertainty around protocols for identifying, verifying and incorporating large load demand into long-range planning. Vegas said ERCOT would work with the Public Utilities Commission of Texas to adjust its forecasting methodology. Thomas Gleeson, the PUCT’s chairman, was more blunt in an appearance on the Energy Capital podcast in June. “The projections are extremely high, and what we know is that a lot of that load will not actually come here. A lot of it is speculative,” Gleeson said in comments made before the interconnection pause. The sheer number of large-load interconnection requests compounds the state’s challenge. Texas’s load growth — not only from large computing and industrial loads, but also garden-variety residential and commercial demand — is leading to congestion in load pockets that previously had capacity to spare, Gleeson said. That creates unwelcome uncertainty for large-load customers eager to put steel in the ground. “That has been the problem we have been trying to solve for the past eight or so months — that when [a customer has] an interconnection agreement and they are ready to move forward, they know that the capacity will be there to serve them so they can make proper business decisions,” Gleeson said. Texas has developed “gating” conditions to discourage speculative interconnection requests, balance load and capacity and “make sure that no one is harmed by these large loads,” Gleeson said. Last summer, Gov. Greg Abbott, R, signed Senate Bill 6, a sweeping measure requiring prospective large-load customers to demonstrate site control, substantially cover necessary grid upgrades, disclose duplicative interconnection requests elsewhere in Texas and accept curtailment during firm load shed events, among other provisions. On June 18, the PUCT adopted a cluster study framework for prospective loads larger than 75 MW that officials said would streamline a “lengthy and repetitive” sequential study process as ERCOT stakeholders work to develop a comprehensive transmission planning framework later this year. ERCOT said at the time that it expected to publish a final transmission plan for the first study cluster, known as “Batch Zero,” in late 2027. Gleeson said on the podcast that the cluster study and transmission planning frameworks will mitigate uncertainty for large loads, grid operators and generation owners across Texas. Together, they assure loads that “once they interconnect, they will get the electricity they need to fully energize,” and they assure other stakeholders that “all the loads coming here are real and will stay,” he said. artigo.texto: CATL, the world’s largest EV battery and energy storage manufacturer, began trial production at its newly built cell manufacturing gigafactory in Debrecen, Hungary, towards the end of September, 2026. This means the Chinese manufacturing giant has met all necessary preconditions and regulatory requirements for what is essentially a trial period, where equipment is optimised and validated ahead of full-scale series production. The €7.3 billion facility’s first two production lines are now operational for testing and are operating at a capacity of 34 GWh. As of autumn 2024, CATL’s Debrecen site has built over 537,000 battery modules. Since the firm’s foundation in 2011, CATL batteries have been fitted to more than 17 million vehicles globally. CATL-using manufacturers include Tesla, Volkswagen, Porsche, Audi, Kia, Changan, and Stellantis. With a 100 gigawatt-hour (GWh) capacity, the Debrecen plant will be CATL’s largest outside China. For context, a 1 GWh capacity factory can make enough batteries for some 17,000 vehicles. Earlier this year, local authorities from Debrecen’s surrounding Hajdu-Bihar county ordered a temporary shutdown of certain zones of the factory due to safety concerns when nine employees were exposed to nickel. CATL then implemented several health and safety changes, which the authorities confirmed met the correct regulatory frameworks. CATL is the latest EV player to join what appears to be a gold rush for manufacturing and production space in the Central and Eastern European (CEE) region. Also in Debrecen, Chinese battery specialists, EVE, have confirmed it will build a 30GWh factory next to the BMW plant where the new BMW iX3 is built. By the end of this year, BYD has promised to open a production site in the Hungarian town of Szeged to circumnavigate European Union tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles. Meanwhile, Toyota promises to build its next EV at its Kolín factory in the Czech Republic. In 2008, Ford built a factory in Craiova, Romania. At present, the facility manufactures the all-electric Puma Gen-E, E-Tourneo Courier, and E-Transit Courier. The Mercedes-Benz GLC’s electric drive system is also Romanian-made.

artigo.texto: Medford council, planning commission to discuss data centers Published 4:26 pm Tuesday, September 29, 2026 Medford man launches online petition urging city officials to prohibit the facilities, which have been a subject of extensive environmental concerns A Medford man is urging residents to tune in for a planned discussion of data centers by Medford city officials on Wednesday night. The joint study session, which will include Medford City Council and the city’s Planning Commission, is set for 6 p.m. Sept. 30 in the Medford Police Department’s Prescott Room. The agenda for the meeting — residents can attend in person or via Zoom — is posted to the city website. Discussion of data centers comes amid ongoing conversations around the state and nation as community leaders grapple with how to navigate a growing number of the facilities. While data centers provide technology for artificial intelligence, data storage and other online services, concerns range from heavy electricity usage, large consumption of water for equipment cooling purposes and environmental impacts. Land use considerations range from the amount and cost of available land to demands on water, sewer, transportation and stormwater infrastructure. Large facilities may require 50 to 150 acres. City and county municipalities tout economic development, with the facilities projected to create millions in tax revenues and thousands of jobs. Medford city officials report no existing applications have been submitted and no decisions will be made during the study session. Online petition Medford resident Matthew Damigos expressed concern that consideration of data centers by city officials could mean proposed data centers could soon be under consideration. Damigos has launched an online petition on Change.Org titled, “Prevent the construction of an AI data center in Medford, Oregon.” Damigos told the Rogue Valley Times he was “deeply concerned about the potential implications for our city and our way of life” if a data center should be constructed, and he said he felt the topic warranted a community conversation “and not just a discussion between the council and planning commission.” Damigos expressed concern about the council’s “willingness to take citizen input,” pointing to a recent back-and-forth involving changes to downtown Main Street, where traffic pattern changes were made and then changed again. Damigos said he hoped citizens would weigh in on the topic of data centers. “Public comment is absolutely necessary regarding an AI data center. AI data centers simply have shown negative effects on communities, and (there are) long-term effects that are unknown,” he told the Times. “This is not a political matter. This is a public health matter, and the Medford and nearby communities in Jackson County should be heard,” Damigos said. Damigos said notice of the study session posted Friday did not allow for enough time for residents to plan to attend. “I just think it’s odd to announce they’re having this discussion and then, ‘Oh, by the way, you have only two business days for the public to even see it.’ Everything the city of Medford does is quite questionable in my opinion. This is an important issue for our community,” he said. “I was concerned they were entertaining the discussion, and I wanted to make sure people were aware because not everyone is going to go to the city of Medford website to see that this discussion is happening.” Currently, Medford Land Development Code Section 10.337 allows data centers in all commercial zones as well as the Light Industrial zone. They are not permitted in the General or Heavy Industrial zones, and the city has no special design or location standards established for data centers. Council and planning commission members will discuss whether to make changes to city land-use regulations pbefore any future proposals for data centers. State and national date center headlines Following concerns raised by a large coalition of environmental, farm and social advocacy groups, and the urging of a moratorium of data centers, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek earlier this month ordered a pause on data centers on state lands, effective through July 2027. A report this week by the Oregon Capital Chronicle detailed plans for a data center proposed on 100 acres of BLM land near Hermiston — the project would be the first on federal public land in Oregon and one of a dozen proposed in six western states. Reach reporter Buffy Pollock at 458-488-2029 or buffy.pollock@rv-times.com. Follow her on Twitter @orwritergal.

artigo.texto: Battery storage (BESS) financing in the Netherlands In the Netherlands, several reports were published in 2026 predicting growth of battery energy storage systems (BESS) located in the Netherlands in terms of both Dutch GWh capacity and Dutch market share in Europe. For lenders, investors and developers, this expansion presents opportunities. However, financing, regulatory and business-case challenges require careful navigation. In this blog, we highlight some key developments and considerations for the financing of BESS projects. The Dutch BESS market The Netherlands is fast developing into a more attractive jurisdiction for BESS projects. Whereas other countries took an early lead in BESS project development, the Dutch market was behind the curve due to limitations in supporting legal infrastructure for BESS development, grid capacity and connection issues, high grid fees and limited bankability of the business case. However, this has changed as a result of various initiatives yielding results starting from 2025. In various market reports published in 2026, the Dutch BESS market is predicted to grow into a major European BESS jurisdiction. Opportunities for BESS in the Netherlands - Dutch government priorities for BESS In the Dutch state budget for 2027, published on 15 September 2026, the Dutch government announced further support for energy storage, in the form of enhanced tax advantages for companies investing in innovative energy storage systems. In the updated National Energy System Plan, also published on 15 September 2026, the Dutch government acknowledged the need for risk-sharing to facilitate the scale-up of energy infrastructure and storage.From 2027, the Netherlands must establish goals for non-fossil flexibility to stabilise the electricity grid pursuant to the EU Electricity Regulation, on the basis of assessments determining how much clean flexibility electricity systems require and identifying existing barriers. Although the outcomes of the Dutch assessment and the Dutch goals are not yet known, these may encourage BESS projects further. These developments follow earlier initiatives that have mitigated and supported the business case for Dutch BESS projects. - The Dutch grid operator reduced grid rates The Dutch grid operator TenneT published a position paper on BESS in 2024 to clarify its position regarding the application of large batteries (>70MW) by market parties to the grid, which served as guidance to the market and public authorities. TenneT also started offering new flexible contract forms with lower transport rates for batteries and other flexible capacity: TenneT now offers time-based transmission rights for high-voltage grids and transmission rights of at least 85% availability. By leveraging time-based rights, flexible grid users like batteries can achieve significant discounts. - Improved bankability for debt and equity funding The willingness of debt and equity investors and financiers to fund BESS projects in the Netherlands has traditionally been undermined by uncertainty around cash flows and floor prices of BESS projects. These days, the Dutch government’s subsidies mitigate the floor price risk and the measures taken by TenneT help reduce the cost and risk elements, improving the cash flows in relation to BESS projects. The new developments described above may improve the bankability of BESS projects further.The bankability of a BESS project could require both debt and equity funding, with alternative lenders and investors providing a mix of both. The Netherlands is known for its flexible legal framework in respect of corporate and finance laws. This effectively provides access to corporate and project-based debt and equity funding solutions, allowing capital flows into and within the Netherlands. BESS projects in the Netherlands have been financed through corporate financings or project financings. Other forms of BESS financing – already applied internationally and depending on the BESS project involved – could also include innovative forms of securitisation, green bonds, possibly in combination with corporate or project financing. Legal expertise of the Stibbe team We are a multidisciplinary team of professionals who are top-ranked practitioners in projects, energy, administrative law, corporate law and debt finance, with expertise in BESS projects. The Stibbe team has market-leading expertise in the Benelux in respect of the full development and financing life-cycle of utility-scale BESS projects, from advising on site acquisition, zoning & permitting, energy regulatory matters, procurement structure and supplier contracts, to FDI, competition, corporate and project financing expertise. We have been involved in various roles (as developers’, equity investors’ and lenders’ counsel) in many of the utility-scale projects to have achieved financial close in the Benelux to date. Through our experience in working with investors, lenders, developers, contractors and other key players in these areas, we have an excellent understanding of the objectives and challenges facing this fast-developing critical segment of the energy industry. If you have any questions, please contact Marieke Driessen or Ellen Vintges from Stibbe’s Financial Markets team.

artigo.texto: Six major financiers signed on to fund Nvidia's AI build-out. Buried in the deal: Nvidia's promise to cover up to 25% of losses if the hardware loses value, a guarantee that could hit $125 billion, with much of that risk headed for insurers' balance sheets. On August 10, Nvidia announced memorandums of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to build financing platforms meant to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure, according to Axios. The pitch to these firms was straightforward: raise money from pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and insurers, use it to buy Nvidia chips and build data centers, then lease the capacity to AI companies for years of steady payments. To make that pitch land with investors who don't normally gamble on chip depreciation, Nvidia added a sweetener. It said it "may provide a residual-value support mechanism for up to 25% of an opportunity, assessed carefully on a project-by-project basis." That covers part of the gap if hardware turns out to be worth less than expected when a lease ends. Do the math across every deal Nvidia is courting, and that backstop could total $125 billion in exposure, per Axios's reporting on the plan. That's Nvidia, the company selling the shovels in this gold rush, agreeing to personally guarantee that the shovels won't rust. Here's the part that should catch your attention: none of that $500 billion sits on Nvidia's own balance sheet, and neither does most of the credit risk behind it. The GPUs get bought by special purpose vehicles. The vehicles issue debt. And increasingly, according to CNBC's reporting from April 2026, that debt gets placed with insurance and retirement capital managed by firms like Apollo and KKR. Data centers are expensive, decades-spanning projects, and they happen to match the long-dated liabilities insurers already carry - things like annuities and pension obligations. The risk doesn't disappear. It just changes owners, and it arrives on an insurer's books relabeled as investment-grade fixed income. CNBC's April reporting quotes the phrase "GPU debt treadmill," coined by AI commentator Dave Friedman, to describe the core mismatch driving this whole structure. GPUs have a useful life of roughly seven years. The data centers housing them are built to last 20 to 30. Lenders and insurers underwriting a 20-year facility are implicitly betting that today's Nvidia chips, or their replacements, will still be worth something in year fifteen, even though the hardware itself will have been swapped out two or three times by then. Nvidia's $108 billion fiscal third-quarter forecast assumes it sells zero AI data center chips to China, even though analysts peg potential Chinese demand at $30 billion. Trump hosts Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24, with Jensen Huang expected at the state dinner and chip access on the agenda. - Nvidia China AI chip sales forecast outlook - state dinner Xi Jinping impact on Nvidia revenue Capacity is also a live problem. One insurance executive told CNBC that insuring a single $20 billion data center campus was nearly impossible to price in 2023. By 2026, it's become, in that executive's words, a weekly conversation. Insurers have responded with new products built for this exposure: cover for credit losses, cover for declines in chip resale value, and cover for contract breaches tied to power outages or cooling failures at the facilities themselves, according to the same CNBC report. The scale of the debt underneath all of this has grown fast. Incremental borrowing funded about 9% of hyperscaler capital spending in fiscal 2024. By mid-2026 that figure had climbed to roughly 32% on a trailing basis, and U.S. data-center debt issuance roughly doubled to about $182 billion in 2025, per the reporting Axios cited in its financing coverage. Frankly, that's the kind of growth curve that makes credit analysts nervous even when the underlying business is healthy. Why the timing matters Nvidia isn't doing this in a vacuum. Bain & Company said this week that the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion a year in new revenue by 2031 just to justify the data center spending already committed. Existing AI services might cover $1.8 trillion of that, leaving a $4.2 trillion gap to fill from businesses that barely exist yet, like autonomous robotics and AI-driven drug discovery. Bain separately projects $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion in data center spending through 2030. Those are the numbers Wall Street is holding up against Nvidia's financing push. They explain why insurers are being asked to carry so much of the weight: the traditional lenders and Nvidia's own balance sheet can't absorb spending at that scale alone. Nvidia's arrangement doesn't eliminate risk. It reroutes it, from Nvidia's income statement and from the banks that might otherwise hold this debt, into the reserves of companies whose entire business model depends on correctly pricing tail risk decades in advance. If AI demand keeps compounding the way Nvidia's revenue guidance assumes, the residual-value guarantee mostly sits unused, a marketing device that made institutional capital comfortable enough to write the check. But if a major AI lab pulls back capacity, or a cheaper chip generation arrives faster than expected and strands the current fleet, the 25% backstop gets tested for real. Insurers holding the debt behind it find out how much of that "investment-grade fixed income" was actually GPU depreciation risk wearing a different label. None of the six firms named in the MOUs have disclosed how much capital they've actually committed, or whether the residual-value terms are even finalized. Nvidia's own release says the partnerships remain subject to final agreements. artigo.texto: A startup wants to build a massive nuclear-powered data center on public land in Utah A startup whose founder has vowed to "make nuclear great again" is planning to place hundreds of reactors on federal land in Utah, according to documents reviewed by NPR. Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah. The facility would include data centers and some 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and others for storing nuclear waste, according to a proposal from the company to federal regulators. In aggregate, the reactors would produce around 9.6 gigawatts of power for the data centers and even more thermal heat for other industrial applications. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces only around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average (though its peak capacity in summer can reach around 10 gigawatts). The project's timeline calls for nonnuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028. Loading... Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records. The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands. The project has raised alarm among local activists, who are already facing a slew of data center proposals in the state. "It's concerning to see that the Trump administration, with the support of the state of Utah, is pushing this forward on significant acreage of public lands," said Neal Clark, wildlands director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, a Utah-based nonprofit that seeks to protect public lands. "The coalition of people who are concerned about these things completely transcends political lines," added Lexi Tuddenham, the executive director of the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, which has tracked nuclear-related industries in the state. Tuddenham said that at the moment her primary goal is to raise awareness. "The biggest thing we can do right now is to let people know about it." In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company. "We are currently reviewing the application for completeness," it told NPR in an email. As the application moves through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, "we will make sure the public has meaningful opportunities to provide input," it added. Valar did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment. In an interview with NPR in July, Valar CEO Isaiah Taylor said his company was committed to safety and community engagement. "We're doing it responsibly and accountably to this community," he said of a smaller test reactor that the company was operating in a neighboring county. Small reactors, big plan Project Beehive reveals the scale of the ambitions held by a new generation of companies planning a comeback for nuclear power. The companies are backed by the Trump administration, which has enacted a slew of regulatory reforms over the past year and a half to make their "small modular reactors" easier to test and build. Valar has been both closely involved with those reforms and a beneficiary of them. Taylor was in the room when President Trump signed a series of executive orders last year designed to accelerate the development of nuclear power, and his company was accepted into the Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025. This past February, the U.S. military flew Valar's test reactor from California to Utah aboard a C-17 transport aircraft. The reactor, known as Ward 250, received rapid approval this year after the Department of Energy conducted a quiet overhaul of its internal safety and security regulations for nuclear reactors. It achieved criticality by reaching a self-sustaining nuclear reaction in June, in a tentlike structure in the Utah desert about 30 miles from the site of Project Beehive. At a press event on July 1, the company marked another milestone when it used Ward 250 to produce electricity. Taylor powered up the test reactor and used a simple thermoelectric system to run a single Nvidia microchip. "Ladies and gentlemen, Valar Atomics just became the first startup in history to make nuclear electricity right here," he told the crowd. The scale of Project Beehive vastly outstrips that July demonstration. Since the turn of the century, the U.S. has switched on just three new nuclear power plants, producing a total of around 3.4 gigawatts of electricity. Those reactors are far larger than the small modular reactors that Valar plans to use, and each costs many billions of dollars to build. Valar and other companies are hoping to upend the nuclear business model because small reactors can be mass-produced and placed in series, like a set of nuclear batteries. Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years. That in turn would reduce the cost and allow the site to enter operation relatively quickly. According to a document reviewed by NPR, the full site could be completed by 2032. Tuddenham said she thinks the use of federal lands for such a project is unprecedented. "In this case, I think it's bigger than the local community," she said. "If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers, that's going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used." NPR's Shannon Bond contributed to this report. Contact Geoff Brumfiel on Signal at gbrumfiel.13

artigo.texto: Advait Energy Signs Cell Supply Deal With HiTHIUM; Shares Fall 1.79% Authored By HDFC SKY | Published at: Sep 28, 2026 03:07 PM IST Advait Energy Transitions signs a 1 GWh cell supply agreement with HiTHIUM for its planned 2.5 GWh BESS assembly facility, while shares fall 1.79%. Open Free Demat Account Open Free Demat Account Mumbai, September 28: Advait Energy Transitions has entered into a Master Supply Agreement with HiTHIUM for the purchase of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells, covering cell supply of up to 1 GWh over the next year. Advait Energy Signs 1 GWh Battery Cell Supply Agreement According to the company’s exchange filing, the agreement was executed on September 18, 2026, with HiTHIUM, a global energy storage manufacturer and BloombergNEF Tier 1 supplier. Under the arrangement, HiTHIUM will supply 314 Ah LFP prismatic battery cells to Advait Battery Ecosystems Private Limited. The agreement is structured to support cell offtake of up to 1 GWh over the next year. The supply will be used for Advait’s upcoming cell-to-container Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly facility. The arrangement is linked to Advait’s planned 2.5 GWh annual-capacity BESS assembly facility, which is being developed for utility-scale, commercial and industrial energy storage as well as renewable energy integration applications. Stock Market Snapshot The Advait Energy share price stood at ₹1,871.80 as of 2:28:37 PM IST on September 28, 2026, down ₹34.20 or 1.79% from the previous close. The stock traded lower during the session, while the company disclosed its battery cell supply arrangement with HiTHIUM. The announcement comes as Advait continues to build out its domestic BESS manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities. HiTHIUM Deal Supports Advait’s BESS Manufacturing Plans The company said the cell supply arrangement is intended to support the planned scale-up of its domestic BESS assembly operations. Advait’s facility is being developed with capabilities spanning cell sourcing, module and pack assembly, container integration and system commissioning. The company said the HiTHIUM agreement will provide a structured supply framework as the facility moves towards commercial production. The upcoming assembly capacity is aimed at applications across utility-scale energy storage, commercial and industrial users, and renewable energy integration. HiTHIUM will supply 314 Ah LFP prismatic cells under the agreement. The company is described in the release as a BloombergNEF Tier 1 global energy storage manufacturer supplying battery cells and energy storage systems across international markets. Advait Energy Expands Domestic Energy Storage Business Advait Energy Transitions is developing an integrated energy storage platform around its planned BESS manufacturing capabilities. The company is also building capabilities across battery module and pack assembly, container integration and related system commissioning. Its broader energy transition portfolio includes power transmission infrastructure, renewable energy, green hydrogen, electrolyser manufacturing, fuel cell manufacturing and clean energy EPC activities. About Advait Energy Transitions Advait Energy Transitions Limited, formerly known as Advait Infratech Limited, is an energy transition and infrastructure company based in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. The company operates across power transmission, renewable energy, BESS and other clean energy technologies. Its business portfolio includes battery energy storage manufacturing, green hydrogen projects, electrolyser manufacturing, fuel cells and clean energy infrastructure solutions. artigo.texto: The construction industry accounted for around half of the non-farm job growth in Wisconsin over the last year, as a few high-profile data center projects moved forward in the state. Wisconsin added 10,500 construction jobs from August 2025 to August 2026, more than half of the 19,400 total non-farm jobs added over that period, according to data from the state Department of Workforce Development. The industry accounted for 156,500 jobs as of August, the most recent month with available data. That growth has come in a year in which Microsoft completed the first phase of its data center campus in Mount Pleasant, while construction continued on other campuses in Port Washington and Beaver Dam. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Scott Hodek, an economist at the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development, said there’s a variety of factors contributing to the sector’s growth statewide and the agency did not have the “specificity of data” to break out construction jobs tied to data centers. Hodek said there was demand coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic, and — as inflation has remained high — more companies are deciding to move forward with building projects in hopes of beating future cost increases. “We’re seeing a lot of growth in construction in general, and that’s all across the board,” he said. “Honestly, that’s generally a good sign when you’re still seeing construction, even though materials and labor costs are up.” Data center development is widely unpopular with the public in Wisconsin. In a Marquette Law School Poll of Wisconsin residents released in August, 67 percent of respondents said they would like to ban data center development for at least a year. For voters questioned for the poll, data centers were a bigger issue than abortion policy, public schools and crime in their communities. Despite pushback from the public, the industry has been growing fast in the state. Especially in southeast Wisconsin — home to two of the three major data center projects under construction in the state — business and labor leaders say data centers are driving growth in both the construction and manufacturing industries, though manufacturing job growth has been weaker statewide. Union construction industry views data centers as ‘decade-long runway’ for growth Chris Mambu Rasch is the executive director of Building Advantage, a labor management association for the union construction industry in southeast Wisconsin. He said both data center campuses being developed in southeast Wisconsin “are essentially 100 percent union construction” projects. The Microsoft development in Mount Pleasant completed its first phase earlier this year. Mambu Rasch said the phase had around 3,000 union construction workers at peak construction, while roughly 10,000 workers cycled through the site over a two-year period. He said phase two is expected to “see similar numbers” and is already “pretty heavy” into construction, with one union sending 600 workers to that project alone. In Port Washington, he said there are between 2,500 and 2,800 union construction workers at the data center site. He said he expects “well over 4,000” union jobs on that project during peak construction. “Data centers have created an extraordinary amount of work related to the projects in Mount Pleasant and in Port Washington,” he said. Meanwhile, social media giant Meta, the company behind the data center being developed in Beaver Dam, has said its project would support “approximately 1,000 construction jobs.” Mambu Rasch said he believes there’s a “decade-long runway” where union construction could see strong growth tied to data centers. He said Microsoft plans to build 15 more in Mount Pleasant, while the Port Washington project is in the first phase of development. He said data center developers are interested in other sites in Wisconsin. “This is sustained, long-term employment,” Mambu Rasch said. “We have the utmost confidence that this work is going to be there for the next decade, and that shows because our contractors are bringing on a record number of apprentices.” Data centers help spur construction of power facilities Aside from building data centers themselves, the projects are also spurring construction of new power plants and electric infrastructure to help meet an expected spike in power demands. Mambu Rasch said union workers generally build Wisconsin’s power infrastructure, from natural gas power plants to solar and wind farms. “The energy infrastructure buildout to supply the energy for the data centers is certainly having a positive impact on our industry,” he said. A recent draft report from state regulators found peak electricity demand in Wisconsin could increase by more than 40 percent by 2032, with more than 70 percent of that increase tied to data centers. The Port Washington and Mount Pleasant data centers are in We Energies’ service territory. artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA O Copergs (Comitê de Planejamento Energético do Rio Grande do Sul) defendeu que a regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) permita o uso de gás natural em projetos de data centers no estado como fonte para “soluções eficientes de geração dedicada, potência firme, flexibilidade operativa e segurança de suprimento”. Em manifestação institucional enviada ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nesta terça-feira (29), o comitê, vinculado à Sema (Secretaria do Meio Ambiente e Infraestrutura), afirma que a elegibilidade dos projetos deve ser definida por critérios de desempenho, como eficiência energética e hídrica, intensidade de emissões, confiabilidade, rastreabilidade dos combustíveis e trajetória de descarbonização. O Copergs argumenta que “a exclusão prévia do gás natural reduziria as alternativas de engenharia disponíveis e poderia impedir que os estados transformem vantagens concretas de energia e conectividade em investimento produtivo” e afirma que conectividade e energia precisam avançar de forma integrada. Segundo o documento, data centers operam de forma contínua e exigem estabilidade, redundância e potência firme, condições que não seriam garantidas apenas por contratos de energia renovável ou por baterias. “Contratos de energia renovável são fundamentais para reduzir emissões e assegurar lastro comercial, mas não garantem, isoladamente, que a potência estará fisicamente disponível no local e no instante da necessidade. Sistemas de alimentação ininterrupta e baterias respondem por milissegundos, minutos ou poucas horas. Contingências prolongadas, restrições de rede e recomposição do sistema exigem recursos controláveis de maior duração.” O comitê destaca que a matriz gaúcha tem elevada participação de fontes renováveis, mas sustenta que isso não elimina a necessidade de recursos despacháveis. Nesse contexto, o gás natural é apontado como alternativa para reserva, ponta, acompanhamento de carga ou operação contínua, conforme os critérios técnicos e ambientais de cada projeto. Para o Copergs, excluir previamente o gás natural do Redata poderia reduzir a capacidade do Rio Grande do Sul de transformar conectividade internacional e infraestrutura energética em desenvolvimento econômico. “O gás natural não substitui a vocação renovável local. Ele assegura que ela possa sustentar cargas digitais críticas sem comprometer confiabilidade, resiliência e competitividade. Excluí-lo previamente do Redata significaria reduzir a capacidade de converter infraestrutura energética e conectividade internacional em desenvolvimento econômico”, afirma o posicionamento.

artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment. International experience suggests that as the data center industry scales up, tensions emerge. In Ireland, data centers accounted for 21% of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023 and could reach 32% this year. In the U.S., their share of demand is expected to triple from 4% in 2023 to a projected 12% by 2028. No surprise, then, that this is a source of growing political and public concern. A Gallup poll found that 71% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local community. Researchers at Cambridge University have identified what they call a “data heat island effect,” whereby large facilities can raise temperatures in surrounding areas. And a recent study by researchers from Yale and the University of Chicago found that the development of a new data center is associated with an increase in nearby housing prices. The question isn’t whether data centers are needed — they are — but how they are developed. What type of data centers do we need? And who will govern their expansion? Economic experience teaches a simple lesson: that proactive regulation is more effective than reactive intervention. And it’s certainly much better than no intervention at all. Having clear rules from the start makes it possible to separate responsible projects from unsustainable ones, align private incentives with public interests and ensure that investment and growth go hand in hand with protecting critical resources and communities. International experience is, again, instructive. Ireland tightened its rules only after data centers became a major source of pressure on the electricity grid. In the US, the state of New York has adopted a temporary moratorium, and a growing number of projects have faced delays or cancellation as local resistance intensified. The lesson could not be plainer: Failing to plan and regulate up front ends up being costlier and less effective. Spain is still a long way from facing that kind of pressure. And yet, our healthy economy and renewable capacity has sparked huge investor interest in building data centers. Current estimates of electricity demand for computing power run as high as 4 gigawatts by 2030, but requests and permits granted for this type of facility exceed that target several times over. We are approaching a tipping point, and we must act to stay ahead. In August, my government launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework designed to do exactly that. The proposal starts from a straightforward principle: Access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset and should not be held up by projects that lack credibility, viability or a meaningful contribution to the economy and society. Our proposal introduces energy- and water-efficiency standards. Data centers will have to disclose key performance indicators, letting us assess and compare their resource use and discourage waste. Any increase in electricity demand must also be accompanied by additional renewable capacity. The framework includes requirements to make sure that a significant portion of data center consumption is supported by newly built clean-energy projects. The regulation recognizes, too, that data centers are a strategic asset. In a world where Europe still relies heavily on non-European digital capabilities, the framework combines safeguards on how data is controlled — and how the infrastructure is managed — with incentives designed to expand Europe’s technology sector and strengthen the continent’s sovereignty. Our objective must be to trade in bytes, not in watts. The challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically. The goal is not to slow down growth or constrain innovation. Quite the opposite: It is to ensure that they remain economically sustainable, and environmentally and socially fair. Countries that understand this will be the ones best positioned to lead the next phase of the digital economy. Pedro Sanchez is the prime minister of Spain. He wrote this for Bloomberg Opinion.

(WRDW/WAGT) - South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews is calling for a two-year moratorium on new data center projects in the state. Andrews said large data centers are receiving billions of dollars in tax breaks while local families deal with high gas, diesel and living costs. She said local officials are outmatched by the corporations building the projects. “We have incredibly wealthy, powerful companies coming into these rural communities in South Carolina, dangling a few carrots, and then the communities are getting steamrolled,” Andrews said. “I’ve been really heartened to see people from both sides of the political spectrum joined together to fight back against these large corporation.” Andrews said the proposed moratorium would give communities more protection from the projects. artigo.texto: Minister Lecce, IESO and more recognized at 2026 Energy Storage Canada Awards Awards presented Sept. 22-23 at ESC Conference in Toronto. Talking Points Energy Storage Canada (ESC) honoured leaders in the energy storage sector at its 2026 Awards, held September 22-23 in Toronto. The awards recognized achievements across seven categories, including the Energy Storage Trailblazer Award, which went to Lesley Gallinger for his role in advancing utility-scale storage in Ontario. - Gallinger emphasized the importance of energy storage for Ontario’s electricity future. - The In Memoriam Trailblazer Award was awarded to Jim Fonger, a former ESC chair. - Stephen Lecce, Ontario’s Minister of Energy and Mines, received the Friend of Energy Storage Award for his support of energy storage initiatives. This recognition highlights the critical role of energy storage in enhancing grid reliability and supporting Canada’s transition to sustainable energy solutions. Energy Storage Canada (ESC) recognized outstanding examples of leadership, innovation, and research at its 2026 Energy Storage Canada Awards, taking place September 22 and 23 at the Energy Storage Canada Conference in Toronto. The awards program is a technology-agnostic showcase of accomplishments from across the sector, recognizing generators, developers, utilities, regulators, researchers, manufacturers, and service providers across seven categories. Categories include the Grid Management Storage Award, the Foundational Research in Energy Storage Award, the Landmark Application of Energy Storage Award, the Energy Storage Milestone Award, the Friend of Energy Storage Award, and the Energy Storage Trailblazer Award, which is presented both as a standard award to an active member of the industry and as an “In Memoriam” tribute to a recently deceased industry leader. The Energy Storage Trailblazer Award is presented to individuals selected by the ESC’s board of directors who has demonstrated exceptional leadership and contributed to the development of energy storage that serves the overall needs of the industry at large. Lesley Gallinger, past president and CEO of the Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO), received the 2026 Energy Storage Trailblazer Award for his contributions toward the procurement of more than three gigawatts of utility-scale storage projects in the province during his tenure with the IESO. “I am honoured to receive the 2026 Energy Storage Trailblazer Award. Energy storage has moved from the technology of tomorrow to an essential part of Ontario’s grid and Canada’s electricity future. I am grateful to have contributed to this remarkable journey,” Gallinger said. The In Memoriam Trailblazer Award was presented to Jim Fonger, who once served as chair of ESC and held roles with Rodan Energy Solutions and Ameresco. Fonger passed away in July 2026. “Jim Fonger was a true trailblazer whose vision and leadership helped lay the foundation for Energy Storage Canada and the growth of the sector nationwide,” said Justin Rangooni, president and CEO of ESC. “His legacy lives on in the momentum he helped create and in all of us who continue advancing the storage advantage.” Ontario’s Minister of Energy and Mines, Stephen Lecce, received the Friend of Energy Storage Award, which recognizes individuals from outside of the energy storage sector selected by ESC’s board of directors as a supporter of the industry. Minster Lecce was recognized for his continued commitment to the role of energy storage through the launch of initiatives such as Long Lead-Time Procurement and the modernization of the province’s electricity system. “From nuclear and hydro to battery storage, we are harnessing every resource to keep the lights on and our economy moving. This work has seen over 1,200 MW of battery storage capacity come online to help offset peak demand times, and I am proud to champion the technologies that continue to deliver reliable, affordable electricity to Ontario,” said Minister Lecce. BluWave-ai became the ESC Awards’ first consecutive winner after being recognized with the Grid Management Storage Award for the second year in a row. The award recognized a project that leveraged BluWave-ai’s artificial intelligence-driven platforms to coordinate stationary energy storage and electric vehicles as a single, grid-aware flexible resource. IESO’s Mohamad Shamelstein was presented with the Foundational Research in Energy Storage Award for his demonstration of how energy storage assets supporting large data centres can provide services to the broader electricity system without compromising essential IT infrastructure. The Landmark Application of Energy Storage Award, which recognizes new energy storage technologies or innovations in existing technology, was presented to AlumaPower Corporation. AlumaPower was recognized for its off-grid microgrid demonstration that showed solutions beyond the traditional single-use model of aluminum-air energy storage through its usage of solid recycled aluminum. The Energy Milestone Award was presented to NextStar Energy in honour of the grand opening of its battery manufacturing facility in Windsor, Ont., and the benefits this development is set to bring to Canada’s domestic battery supply chain and the North American energy ecosystem at large.

artigo.texto: 29 de set, 2026 A descarbonização da economia brasileira pode ser não apenas uma resposta às mudanças climáticas, mas também uma estratégia para reduzir custos e aumentar a competitividade das empresas. “Usar formas de energia mais limpa, renovável, já é uma estratégia de negócio,” Grazielle Parenti, vice-presidente de Sustentabilidade da Vale, disse em um debate promovido pelo Brazil Journal durante a Climate Week, em Nova York. A executiva destacou ainda que o Brasil tem alternativas próprias para a transição, como a biomassa, e que grandes empresas precisam trabalhar em conjunto com fornecedores e outras companhias para desenvolver tecnologias em escala. Já Paulo Skaf Filho, CEO da ComBio, empresa de energia térmica renovável para a indústria, lembrou que o custo de capital influencia muito nos projetos de transição energética. “Não é um problema de tecnologia, é um problema de capital e de demanda.” Como os projetos de transição são intensivos em capital e exigem investimentos altos e compromissos de longo prazo, disse Skaf Filho, a incerteza sobre o custo de capital e a falta de previsibilidade regulatória podem dificultar a tomada de decisão das empresas. Roberto Waack, presidente do Comitê de Sustentabilidade da MBRF, chamou atenção para outro desafio: adaptar as metodologias internacionais de mensuração de carbono à realidade brasileira. “Nós estamos num ambiente tropical e a maior parte das metodologias de mensuração de carbono não capturam as características da agricultura e dos ecossistemas brasileiros.” Waack também defendeu o reconhecimento econômico do capital natural brasileiro e afirmou que o mercado de carbono será um dos temas centrais para a transição no país. Para os três executivos, a agenda de descarbonização avançará apenas se o Brasil conseguir transformar soluções que miram uma economia de baixo carbono em negócios.

artigo.texto: NANTICOKE — Newport Twp. residents gathered Sunday at West Side Park in Nanticoke to begin rallying against a developer who seeks to build 15 data centers in the township. The meeting, organized through a Facebook event, served as a preliminary step to gather interested residents and supporters and voice their opposition to the project. The packed field house was standing room only that spilled out into the park. Brenda Grabowski, who helped organize the meeting and started the Facebook event, said she did so after going to the previous commissioners’ meeting looking for answers and receiving none. “I don’t know a lot about data centers; I’m learning myself now. But I want to know what’s going to happen in my backyard,” said Grabowski. Fern Leard, who is running to capture a seat in the state House 120th District, spoke at the meeting, telling residents, “This is where it starts.” Leard, who is not running to represent Newport Twp., said she showed up and spoke to show support. “The fact that you guys organized this so quickly is amazing,” said Leard. “It just showcases how when communities come together and work together we can get it done.” Newport commissioners were asked about a rumored data center coming to the township at a meeting earlier this month. In response, Township Manager Joe Hillian issued a prepared statement that left residents with more questions than answers. Hillian said a developer seeks to build three gas generation facilities and 15 closed-loop data centers — seven in the mixed-use zone and eight in the industrial zone. The township’s zoning ordinance, drafted earlier this year, allows data centers by right in mixed-use zoning districts and permits them in industrial districts. Derek Sutcliffe, who has been fighting data center development in Lackawanna County, urged residents to think about how these facilities will be powered and what that will do to their community. “You are not defeated,” Sutcliffe told residents. “Where you are in your process is the beginning. If you think you’re going to lose, you’re going to lose. Don’t think that. You can beat this.” The next Newport Twp. commissioners meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. on Oct. 5.

artigo.texto: Tecnologia: novo plano divulgado na China prevê baterias de estado sólido em larga escala até 2030 e modelos com vida útil de até 15 mil ciclos (Imagem gerada por IA) Agência Publicado em 28 de setembro de 2026 às 15h45. A China quer levar as baterias totalmente de estado sólido a uma fase inicial de aplicação em larga escala até 2030. O país também estabeleceu como meta que baterias de lítio de longa duração cheguem a uma vida útil de até 15 mil ciclos. As metas fazem parte de um novo plano para a indústria de baterias divulgado nesta segunda-feira (28) pelo Ministério da Indústria e Tecnologia da Informação e outros seis órgãos do governo chinês. O documento prevê avanços em diferentes tecnologias, incluindo baterias de lítio, sódio e fluxo. A estratégia também envolve o desenvolvimento de novos materiais para eletrodos, eletrólitos e outros componentes usados na fabricação. Uma das prioridades será ampliar o uso dessas baterias para além dos veículos elétricos e produtos eletrônicos. O plano prevê aplicações em embarcações, aviação, robôs inteligentes, máquinas de engenharia e equipamentos agrícolas. A expansão também deve alcançar sistemas de armazenamento de energia. As novas baterias poderão ser utilizadas junto à geração de energia, em redes elétricas, parques industriais e data centers. Outros formatos também aparecem no planejamento. Baterias flexíveis e de formatos especiais deverão ter aplicações ampliadas em dispositivos vestíveis, casas inteligentes e equipamentos médicos móveis. O plano inclui ainda medidas para aumentar a coleta, reciclagem e reutilização de baterias usadas. As empresas deverão participar da estruturação desses sistemas, diretamente ou por meio de terceiros, de acordo com o volume de produtos colocados no mercado. Fonte: China news
