artigo.texto: CATL Leading global battery maker, launched first-gen sodium-ion battery in 2021 A new life cycle assessment from China, drawing on factory data, has concluded that layered-oxide sodium-ion battery packs carry a lower production footprint than lithium iron phosphate packs, even as recent European research points the other way for cells. The findings, reported by ESS News, indicate that making a one kilowatt-hour sodium-ion pack in China emits 56.8 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent, which is 24.9 percent below the 75.5 kilograms attributed to an LFP pack. The researchers gathered inventory data directly from Chinese battery manufacturers operating at gigawatt-hour scale. For both chemistries, the assessment attributes the bulk of emissions to the electricity used in manufacturing, a pattern the authors link to China's coal-heavy grid. They suggest sodium-ion's footprint could decline further through process optimization and cleaner power supplies, while LFP producers would need to pursue raw-material substitution and reduce material intensity. The study's authors note that earlier work, including research by Peters and colleagues in 2016 and by Guo and colleagues in 2023, placed sodium-ion's footprint slightly above that of lithium-ion, a result they attribute to reliance on lab-scale data and default European databases. A 2025 study by researchers at Fraunhofer and RWTH Aachen University, also built on primary factory data, reached the opposite conclusion. That work put cradle-to-gate emissions for layered-oxide sodium-ion cells at 75 to 87 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour, compared with 59 to 70 kilograms for LFP cells. Because the European study measured cells rather than packs, the two sets of figures are not directly comparable. Both assessments stop at the factory gate, so neither incorporates cycle life, meaning they compare manufacturing impacts rather than emissions per unit of lifetime energy delivered. Both also cover only layered-oxide cathodes. HiNa Battery, for instance, uses layered oxides, while Hithium's 785 Ah storage cell relies on a sodium iron pyrophosphate cathode. The Chinese researchers additionally modeled a scenario in which broader sodium-ion adoption avoids 147 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2035. Using a cradle-to-gate boundary spanning raw materials through manufacturing, they determined that the total environmental impact of sodium-ion packs is 27.3 percent lower than that of LFP packs. The scientists set out their findings in a paper titled Comparative life cycle assessment and carbon footprint of sodium-ion and Lithium Iron phosphate batteries, recently published in Environmental Impact Assessment Review. artigo.texto: Macurco Introduces 10-Year Hydrogen Detector for BESS and Data Center Applications UL 2075-Listed HD-6 offers early fault detection with minimal maintenance SIOUX FALLS, S.D., September 29, 2026 (Newswire.com) - Macurco Inc., a DwyerOmega brand and a leader in fixed gas detection solutions, announces the launch of the new HD-6 Hydrogen Gas Detector, designed specifically for continuous hydrogen monitoring in Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) applications and other critical environments where hydrogen detection is essential. Hydrogen detection in BESS applications is vital for safety and monitoring normal equipment operation. When a battery begins to malfunction, it can emit hydrogen gas, which may create explosive and dangerous conditions. Early detection can help identify fault events, prevent further equipment damage, and keep personnel informed of potentially hazardous environments. The new HD-6 provides reliable, continuous hydrogen monitoring and early warning to help protect personnel, equipment, and facilities. The detector features two configurable alarm levels with relay activation, allowing facilities to automate responses such as activating fans, valves, louvers, horns, and strobes. Standard features also include local audible alarms, bright visual indicators, and analog communication for seamless integration with Building Management Systems (BMS). The HD-6 is UL Listed to UL 2075 and CAN/ULC 588 and is CE marked. These listings and the CE marking reflect rigorous electrical safety, performance, and gas detection requirements, demonstrating the detector's electrical integrity, accurate response to hydrogen gas, and reliable operation. CE marking supports the HD-6's availability in the European market. The detector is engineered for long-term performance with a robust, low-maintenance design ideal for demanding applications, including data centers, BESS facilities, and industrial hydrogen monitoring "The Macurco HD-6 is an iteration and upgrade of our current flagship hydrogen detector, the GD-6," said Jonathon DeKam, Macurco Line Product Manager for DwyerOmega. "The new HD-6 includes many significant upgrades - minimal maintenance, resistance to silicone poisoning, additional alarm setpoints, and a generous 10-year lifespan. Macurco developed the HD-6 to address ongoing customer requests for a hydrogen detector that is more robust, more reliable, and lasts longer in the field. "With a UL 2075 listing for hydrogen gas detection, customers can be confident in relying on the HD-6 to monitor their data centers, BESS facilities, or any application where hydrogen detection is imperative. We are eager to get the HD-6 into our customers' hands and begin collecting feedback for future product improvements." Key Features and Benefits of the HD-6: - 10-year sensor life - UL 2075 & CAN/ULC 588 Listed - Minimal maintenance requirements - Resistance to silicone poisoning - Two configurable alarm levels - Sensor range: 0-50% LEL Hydrogen - 5A SPDT fan relay and 0.5A alarm relay - LED display for easy gas concentration monitoring - 4-20mA output for VFD control and BMS integration - End-of-life notification - Compatible with Macurco digital control panels - Easy installation to standard 4×4 electrical boxes - Operates on 12 to 24 VAC or 12 to 32 VDC power Availability & Contact To learn more about the HD-6, visit www.macurco.com or contact Macurco_info@dwyeromega.com. About DwyerOmega DwyerOmega is a leading global manufacturer of precision measurement and control solutions, trusted across a diverse range of industrial and controlled environment applications to monitor, manage, and optimize critical processes with confidence. Serving customers worldwide with a portfolio of industry-leading brands, including Macurco, DwyerOmega has a legacy of, and ongoing commitment to, innovation and quality. The Macurco product line designs, develops, and manufactures a full set of fixed and portable gas detection monitors for the protection of workers, responders, and the community. Macurco has 50 years of proven gas detection experience in residential, commercial, and industrial gas monitoring. Macurco gas detection systems (HVAC, Fire & Security, AimSafety, and TracXP) are widely recognized by distributors and users for their high performance and consistent reliability. artigo.texto: CHEYENNE — City officials are considering leasing a portion of Belvoir Ranch for a proposed 140-megawatt solar project and battery storage facility. Representatives from Hanwha Renewables, a Korean utility-scale solar and energy storage developer, presented a preliminary proposal, called Project Wrangler, to members of the Cheyenne City Council at a work session Friday. The company is seeking to lease approximately 3,300 acres of the 18,800-acre ranch while it conducts environmental, engineering and other feasibility studies. The project is expected to eventually occupy 1,200 to 1,400 acres. Councilman Tom Segrave said the city has been exploring ways to generate additional revenue from portions of Belvoir Ranch that aren’t reserved for the city’s planned landfill and water development. “(Hanwha has) been working with the city and me, specifically, on a proposed solar development on the Belvoir Ranch,” Segrave said. “This has been a council goal for, I don’t know, four or five years. … We have areas that we’ve been leasing for grazing, and we’ve been looking for opportunities to increase the revenue off of those lands that are not set aside for the original purposes.” Tyler Nokleby, Hanwha project developer, said the company isn’t looking to gain formal project approval yet. Instead, he wants to enter an option-to-lease agreement that would allow it to conduct necessary studies. “We’re not asking for a permit, we’re not asking to annex,” Nokleby said. “We are hoping to engage with the city, to be the land owner in this process, so that we can kick off everything.” The agreement would last up to four years, although Nokleby said the company hopes to complete its studies within two. During that period, Hanwha would conduct environmental and wildlife studies, geotechnical work, topographical surveys and other assessments. Existing uses of the land, including grazing, would not be affected, Nokleby said. Lida Jauregui-Rivera, Hanwha project engineer, said the solar panels would be around 4 to 5 feet above the ground, but the final design is subject to change based on study results. The battery storage facility would be located near the project’s substation and would occupy around five acres of large, container-like battery units, Jauregui-Rivera said. Hanwha is considering connecting the project to Black Hills Energy’s West Cheyenne substation, which is located a mile from the proposed project area. Council members questioned how the facility would withstand severe weather conditions like hail, and Jauregui-Rivera said the company would consider thicker-glass solar panels and tracking systems that would automatically reposition panels during hailstorms. She estimated crews could inspect the facility and return it to operational condition within four to eight hours after a significant storm, if panels become damaged. The proposed agreement also includes a $50,000 one-time payment to the city for future development at Belvoir Ranch. Payment would occur within 30 days of signing the option-to-lease. “If the project falls through, that $50,000 is the city’s to keep,” Nokleby said. “So that’s kind of a no-strings-attached payment there, as well — a good-faith payment, we’ll say.” Additionally, if the project falls through after the four-year agreement period, Nokleby said the city would also receive $912,160 in option payments, which includes the $50,000. But the larger financial benefit would come if the project becomes operational. Nokleby said projected lease revenue could range from $30 million to $60 million, depending on the project’s final size and how long the lease remains in effect. The currently proposed lease has a 30-year operating term with four potential five-year extensions. While Hanwha is the proposed developer of the project, Nokleby said it would not own or operate the solar farm long term. Southern Power, which owns South Cheyenne Solar, could potentially become the owner. Hanwha developed the 150 megawatt South Cheyenne Solar project off South Greeley Highway in unincorporated Laramie County under its former name, Qcells Development. Black Hills Energy is also interested in purchasing the electricity, he said, but neither arrangement has been finalized. Because the land is widely known for its wildlife inhabitants, Nokleby said the proposed agreement also includes protections similar to those used at South Cheyenne Solar, including dividing the solar facility into separately fenced sections to preserve wildlife migration corridors. “We did not get into the sustainable energy industry to destroy the environment,” Nokleby said. “These projects are obviously very large and impactful, so we do everything we can to mitigate those impacts.” Nokleby further clarified that signing the option agreement is not a guarantee that the project will be constructed. “Not every lease or option-to-lease turns into a project,” Nokleby said. “If we run our studies and they come back with a very rare type of butterfly that only lives in this one specific spot on Earth, we’re not in the business of putting solar over that. … We won’t be cutting corners. We’re not asking for rubber stamps on any approvals.” The developer’s option-to-lease agreement is planned to be introduced at the City Council meeting for consideration Oct. 12.

artigo.texto: On September 10, 2026, Reuters reported that Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) plans to expand its global data center capacity to more than 38 gigawatts by 2032, more than tripling its current roughly 12-gigawatt footprint, according to Bloomberg News reporting that cited people familiar with the plans. Only about 2 gigawatts of Microsoft's current capacity is dedicated to AI-specific chips, a share the company expects to grow to roughly one-third of the much larger 38-gigawatt total by 2032, though Microsoft has not confirmed the target in any public filing or statement. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) already has strong cloud demand to support a major expansion of its data center footprint. Azure and other cloud services revenue increased 43% year over year in fiscal Q4. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $59.3 billion for the quarter and $214.4 billion for fiscal 2026. Microsoft also said capacity constraints have limited its ability to satisfy some demand, so expanding from roughly 12 gigawatts toward the reported 38-gigawatt target could allow the company to capture cloud and AI business that its existing infrastructure cannot currently support. Microsoft's massive contracted backlog gives management substantial revenue visibility as it adds new computing capacity. Commercial remaining performance obligations increased 84% year over year to $678 billion, while Microsoft expects to recognize roughly 30% of that amount as revenue during the next 12 months. The large backlog gives Microsoft a significant pool of committed business that can help support the economics of its aggressive infrastructure expansion as new capacity comes online. Microsoft has already shown that it can add capacity quickly while securing long-term power for its expanding data center network. The company added another gigawatt of capacity in fiscal Q4 and remains on track to roughly double its overall capacity within two years. Microsoft has also signed a 20-year agreement with Constellation Energy linked to the restart of the 835-megawatt Three Mile Island Unit 1. It gives the firm another long-term electricity source as AI workloads drive sharply higher power requirements. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)'s data center expansion requires enormous capital commitments that could continue weighing on free cash flow. Microsoft expects more than $50 billion of capital expenditures in fiscal Q1 2027 and about $175 billion during calendar 2026 under its broader capex definition, which includes finance leases. Microsoft reported roughly $145 billion of capital expenditures in fiscal 2026, while cash additions to property and equipment totaled about $116 billion. Power availability and growing political resistance could make a 38-gigawatt network harder to build on schedule. Texas temporarily halted approvals for new data center grid connections as officials reviewed the industry's electricity and water demands. New York imposed a moratorium on large new data centers amid concerns about electricity costs. Microsoft needs to secure enormous amounts of power, land and regulatory approval across multiple jurisdictions as it more than triples its reported footprint. The 38-gigawatt figure remains a reported internal roadmap rather than formal Microsoft guidance. It adds uncertainty to the long-term investment case. Bloomberg reported the target through people familiar with Microsoft's plans. Reuters said Microsoft did not immediately comment on the figure. Multi-year construction timelines, changing customer demand and improvements in computing efficiency could alter how much physical capacity Microsoft ultimately needs. So investors should treat the 2032 target as a planning framework rather than a guaranteed outcome. Azure's 43% growth, Microsoft's $678 billion commercial backlog and management's progress toward doubling capacity within two years give the company strong commercial support for further infrastructure investment. However, Microsoft must commit enormous amounts of capital, secure enough electricity, and navigate growing regulatory resistance to execute the roadmap. artigo.texto: Samsung SDI's (006400.KS) lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) have passed a global fire safety test. The company said on Sept. 28 that its integrated ESS product, the SBB 2.0, met all evaluation criteria in a large-scale fire test conducted by UL Solutions, a global safety certification body. The SBB 2.0 is the first Samsung SDI energy storage solution to use LFP batteries. It will be produced at StarPlus Energy (SPE), the company's joint venture with Stellantis in Indiana. The test involved deliberately igniting a fire inside an SBB 2.0 container and checking whether the flames spread to adjacent containers. No fire spread occurred, and there was no gas venting, explosion or overheating. Samsung SDI attributed the result to the structural advantages of its prismatic batteries and to technology built up over many years. In July, the company also passed a large-scale fire test and won certification for an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) unit equipped with nickel-cobalt-manganese batteries. "Prismatic cells use a rigid aluminum can structure that withstands heat, impact and pressure, and they allow various safety devices to be added, which makes them superior to batteries in other form factors," a Samsung SDI official said.

artigo.texto: A second Alachua City Commission meeting confused residents Monday after the meeting was abruptly cancelled because three commission members, including Mayor Walter Welch, weren’t present. Vice Mayor Jennifer Ringersen and Commissioner Shirley Green Brown were also absent, while commissioners Jacob Fletcher and Jackson Youmas attended. The city’s ordinance doesn’t allow business to be conducted at commission meetings without at least three commissioners present. The no-shows come just two weeks after a Sept. 14 city commission meeting in which Welch abruptly killed Fletcher’s motion to revisit a moratorium, or pause, on data center development. The pause was proposed by Ringersen earlier that night, and Fletcher was unable to get specifics from the rest of the commission. He moved for the board to further hash them out at Monday’s meeting. However, when Fletcher reminded Welch a few minutes later that he had to second the motion to delay the vote to Monday’s meeting, Welch replied with, “It died.” Welch’s response garnered reactions from residents and Fletcher because the mayor doesn’t have the power to deny a motion before it’s seconded and voted on. During an interview Sept. 15, Commissioner Jacob Fletcher said many Alachua residents have called moratoriums “a good step to figuring out the next step.” The Sept. 14 data center discussion resembled one step in a long process requiring community participation, he said. “I think there [are] more conversations to be had,” Fletcher said. “A moratorium, again, is only a Band-Aid.” He said the next step will require the commission to listen to Alachua residents and ensure the city’s regulations align with their concerns. Following the Sept. 14 meeting, attendees expressed confusion over whether the data center moratorium would be further discussed at Monday’s meeting. It was on the agenda leading up to the meeting. Zoe King, a transit maintenance manager for Gainesville’s Regional Transit System, stayed over an hour after the meeting’s cancellation Monday to speak with Fletcher, Youmas and fellow residents. More than 70 people attended the meeting, and King said most had come to comment on data centers. “We were told that the draft for the moratorium would be presented today to the commissioners,” King said. Following its cancelation, the meeting was rescheduled to Oct. 5, when the commission plans to discuss and vote on the meeting’s agenda items. The city’s budget, a data center moratorium and a contract between the city and Duke Energy were among items on the agenda. “This is becoming a game,” she said. To King, it feels like every time an important topic is scheduled to be discussed, something pushes it back. It’s caused residents to lose faith in the city, she added. On Sept. 8, a planning and zoning board committee meeting, during which data centers were set to be discussed, was canceled for the same reason: a lack of board attendance. Fletcher and Youmas met with citizens outside Alachua City Hall on Monday to discuss the meeting's cancellation, its rescheduling and to catch up with supporters. Deborah Bagley, a 60-year-old Alachua resident, questioned the qualifications of some of Alachua’s public officials, including Matthew Webster, who was appointed to the planning and zoning board in August. Webster is the son-in-law of Virginia Johns, a former planning and zoning board member whose term expired a month before Webster assumed the role, according to Bagley and a Facebook post by Our Alachua Water. “[Webster] has monetary gain, so they knew that he would vote yes on things related to development,” said Bagley, adding that Webster’s construction company, Sterling Builders Group, would benefit from more development. A special planning and zoning board meeting is scheduled for Oct. 6 at 6 p.m., where the board is scheduled to discuss permits, site plan proposals and the city’s comprehensive plan. He is a fourth-year student who prefers to spend his free time trying new and random things, cooking, reading, watching TV, or hiking.

artigo.texto: Nova Gales do Sul aprova projeto de armazenamento por bateria Deniliquin East de 100MW/200MWh O governo de Nova Gales do Sul deu sinal verde para o sistema de armazenamento de energia por bateria de Deniliquin East, um empreendimento de 100MW/200MWh na região australiana de Riverina apresentado pela BESS Arctic Pty Ltd. A BESS Arctic está levando o projeto adiante por meio da Gransolar Development Australia, subsidiária local do grupo espanhol Gransolar Group. A instalação está prevista para a Riverina Highway, na área do governo local de Edward River, situada a cerca de 7km a sudeste de Deniliquin. Depois de construída, a instalação será conectada ao Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade e ocupará um terreno de 3,53 hectares que historicamente serviu para pastoreio de ovelhas. O consentimento foi emitido pelo Diretor Executivo Interino de Avaliações de Energia, Recursos e Indústria, no exercício de autoridade delegada pelo Ministro de Planejamento e Espaços Públicos. Durante a avaliação, foram apresentadas 71 objeções públicas, além de uma única manifestação de apoio. Pela aprovação, o sistema de baterias fica limitado a uma potência máxima de 100MW e a uma capacidade máxima de armazenamento de energia de 240MWh no local. As condicionantes exigem um Estudo de Segurança contra Incêndio antes da construção, um Plano de Emergência antes do comissionamento e uma faixa corta-fogo trafegável de pelo menos 10 metros ao redor da área de armazenamento de baterias. O Departamento de Planejamento, Habitação e Infraestrutura concluiu que as vantagens do projeto superavam seus efeitos adversos, destacando sua capacidade de armazenar energia renovável para despacho nos picos de demanda e sua consonância com o Marco de Política de Mudança Climática de Nova Gales do Sul, a Estratégia de Eletricidade de Nova Gales do Sul e o Roteiro de Infraestrutura Elétrica de Nova Gales do Sul. Segundo o departamento, o risco de contaminação no local era baixo, conforme estabelecido por uma Investigação Preliminar e Detalhada do Local, e a perda de área agrícola seria insignificante, afetando menos de 0,0004% das terras agrícolas da área do governo local de Edward River. Risco de incêndio e perigos, os méritos da energia renovável e a compatibilidade do uso do solo formaram o núcleo das 71 objeções, enquanto várias manifestações também apontaram preocupações com o abastecimento de água para combate a incêndios, a garantia de descomissionamento e a contaminação por PFAS. O departamento determinou que essas questões poderiam ser adequadamente tratadas pelas condicionantes do consentimento, observando que nem o órgão do governo de Nova Gales do Sul nem o Conselho de Edward River apresentaram objeções ao projeto. O aviso de decisão avalia o investimento de capital do projeto em cerca de AU$ 118 milhões, ou US$ 82,6 milhões, e projeta até 52 empregos na construção e dois cargos operacionais. A BESS Arctic também se comprometeu com um Acordo Voluntário de Planejamento com o Conselho de Edward River que prevê AU$ 600.000 em contribuições de benefício comunitário. Essa aprovação insere um projeto regional em um pipeline estadual que vem se expandindo muito além da escala de qualquer empreendimento isolado. A AEMO registrou que 9,1GW de nova capacidade de geração e armazenamento atingiram plena produção no NEM durante o ano fiscal de 2026, um número recorde que mais que dobrou o volume do ano anterior, enquanto o pipeline mais amplo de conexões cresceu 42%, para 75,4GW. Outros projetos em estágio comparável ao de Deniliquin East estão avançando pelo processo de registro da AEMO. Vena Energy, o Tailem Bend BESS 3, na Austrália do Sul, e o Wooreen BESS, em Victoria, desenvolvido pela EnergyAustralia e pela Banpu Energy Australia, ambos entraram no Sistema de Gestão de Mercado da AEMO no início deste mês, contribuindo com 554MW de capacidade combinada enquanto avançam rumo à operação comercial. O próprio histórico de contratações de Nova Gales do Sul ilustra como um projeto como o de Deniliquin East poderia, em última análise, obter certeza de receita. Todos os projetos de armazenamento por bateria e resposta à demanda selecionados no leilão de firming de 2023 do estado já estão operacionais, proporcionando cerca de 1GW/3GWh de capacidade despachável e mais de AU$ 1,8 bilhão em investimento por meio de Acordos de Serviço de Energia de Longo Prazo concedidos à AGL Energy, à Akaysha Energy, à Iberdrola Australia e à Enel X. O órgão responsável pelos leilões do estado indicou que pretende continuar usando essa abordagem de contratação para ajudar projetos de alto valor a alcançar o fechamento financeiro mais rapidamente. artigo.texto: Saginaw approves new rules for future data centers as moratorium nears end The ordinance sets rules for water and energy use, noise, residential buffers and neighborhood meetings before any data center can set up shop in the city. SAGINAW, Mich. (WNEM) - Saginaw now has a rule book in place for data centers before any come to town. The Saginaw City Council approved a new ordinance Monday night setting regulations for any future data center development in the city. The ordinance comes ahead of Saginaw’s data center moratorium ending at the close of 2026. There are currently no data centers in development in the city. Under the new rules, data centers would only be allowed as special land uses in light industrial and general industrial districts. Developers would have to provide information on expected water and energy use, wastewater and noise. Data centers and most related equipment would generally have to stay at least 500 feet from homes and residential districts, with noise near residential areas capped at 55 decibels. Developers would also have to hold at least two neighborhood meetings before moving forward with a project. The moratorium remains in place through the end of the year. The new ordinance is expected to be added to Saginaw’s code of ordinances Oct. 9. Subscribe to the WNEM TV5 newsletter and receive the latest local news and weather straight to your email every day. artigo.texto: OCP, Envision power up first phase of BESS at Morocco mining site OCP Green Energy, a subsidiary of Morocco’s OCP Group, signed a contract in 2025 with Chinese technology supplier Envision Energy to supply and commission a storage system based on LFP (lithium iron phosphate) technology. OCP Green Energy, the OCP Group subsidiary dedicated to generating and storing electricity from renewable sources, has installed its first BESS (Phase I) at the Benguerir mining site in Morocco. This comes just a few months after Phase I of OCP Green Energy’s solar PV program entered service, with a total capacity of 202 MWp across the solar plants at Benguerir (67 MWp), Foum Tizi (30 MWp) and Oulad Farès in Khouribga (105 MWp), OCP said in a press release. OCP Green Energy signed a contract in 2025 with Chinese technology supplier Envision Energy to supply and commission a storage system based on LFP (lithium iron phosphate) technology. With a capacity of 25 MW / 125 MWh, equivalent to five hours of storage, the system is coupled with the existing solar plant at the Benguerir mining site. This investment of close to 170 million dirhams (approximately USD 17.5 million) covered the acquisition of BESS equipment and batteries, together with the full scope of integration works, including civil and electrical engineering, as well as studies and project management, OCP said. The project also benefits from USD 20 million in financing from the Clean Technology Fund (CTF), a program led by the African Development Bank. “As we announced last year when our first solar PV projects were commissioned, storage is the natural extension of our energy strategy,” Omar Kadir, General Manager of OCP Green Energy, said. “It allows us to reconcile the variable output of renewable energy with the continuous needs of our industrial platforms, while strengthening the reliability of our energy supply.” Envision Energy said that it provided the full storage system and led the commissioning work, integrating the BESS with the site's solar generation, grid conditions and industrial load profile. “The successful energisation of Morocco’s first large-scale battery storage project demonstrates the reliability, flexibility and cost-effectiveness of integrated renewable-plus-storage solutions in industrial applications,” said John Lee, General Manager of Envision Energy for the Middle East and Africa, according to a press release issued by Envision.

artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment. International experience suggests that as the data center industry scales up, tensions emerge. In Ireland, data centers accounted for 21% of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023 and could reach 32% this year. In the U.S., their share of demand is expected to triple from 4% in 2023 to a projected 12% by 2028. No surprise, then, that this is a source of growing political and public concern. A Gallup poll found that 71% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local community. Researchers at Cambridge University have identified what they call a “data heat island effect,” whereby large facilities can raise temperatures in surrounding areas. And a recent study by researchers from Yale and the University of Chicago found that the development of a new data center is associated with an increase in nearby housing prices. The question isn’t whether data centers are needed — they are — but how they are developed. What type of data centers do we need? And who will govern their expansion? Economic experience teaches a simple lesson: that proactive regulation is more effective than reactive intervention. And it’s certainly much better than no intervention at all. Having clear rules from the start makes it possible to separate responsible projects from unsustainable ones, align private incentives with public interests and ensure that investment and growth go hand in hand with protecting critical resources and communities. International experience is, again, instructive. Ireland tightened its rules only after data centers became a major source of pressure on the electricity grid. In the US, the state of New York has adopted a temporary moratorium, and a growing number of projects have faced delays or cancellation as local resistance intensified. The lesson could not be plainer: Failing to plan and regulate up front ends up being costlier and less effective. Spain is still a long way from facing that kind of pressure. And yet, our healthy economy and renewable capacity has sparked huge investor interest in building data centers. Current estimates of electricity demand for computing power run as high as 4 gigawatts by 2030, but requests and permits granted for this type of facility exceed that target several times over. We are approaching a tipping point, and we must act to stay ahead. In August, my government launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework designed to do exactly that. The proposal starts from a straightforward principle: Access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset and should not be held up by projects that lack credibility, viability or a meaningful contribution to the economy and society. Our proposal introduces energy- and water-efficiency standards. Data centers will have to disclose key performance indicators, letting us assess and compare their resource use and discourage waste. Any increase in electricity demand must also be accompanied by additional renewable capacity. The framework includes requirements to make sure that a significant portion of data center consumption is supported by newly built clean-energy projects. The regulation recognizes, too, that data centers are a strategic asset. In a world where Europe still relies heavily on non-European digital capabilities, the framework combines safeguards on how data is controlled — and how the infrastructure is managed — with incentives designed to expand Europe’s technology sector and strengthen the continent’s sovereignty. Our objective must be to trade in bytes, not in watts. The challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically. The goal is not to slow down growth or constrain innovation. Quite the opposite: It is to ensure that they remain economically sustainable, and environmentally and socially fair. Countries that understand this will be the ones best positioned to lead the next phase of the digital economy. Pedro Sanchez is the prime minister of Spain. He wrote this for Bloomberg Opinion.

artigo.texto: Vaisala Indigo Supervisor Vaisala Indigo Supervisor helps data centers scale environmental monitoring by enabling up to 100 measurement points to be managed as a single system. As monitoring requirements grow, the challenge is shifting from measurement coverage to operational scalability. Environmental monitoring must scale with AI infrastructure As data centers scale to support growing AI workloads, environmental monitoring infrastructure must keep pace. Higher computing densities and accelerated construction schedules are increasing the need for environmental measurements throughout data centers, including data halls, technical spaces, support areas, and other critical locations, while leaving less time for installation, commissioning, and maintenance. As monitoring requirements grow and measurement networks expand, operators need ways to deploy, standardize, and maintain environmental monitoring across facilities without adding complexity or slowing project timelines. From sensors to systems: a new approach to environmental monitoring To address this need, Vaisala today introduced the Vaisala Indigo Supervisor, a solution designed to simplify environmental monitoring in data centers by shifting from managing individual sensors to managing measurement networks as a unified system. The solution enables up to 100 measurement points to be managed as a single system through a local touchscreen interface and integrated into a building management system (BMS) through a single standardized connection. The Indigo Supervisor reflects a broader industry shift toward modularity and system-level environmental monitoring. As data center infrastructure expands, operators increasingly need solutions that can be deployed consistently across sites, scaled over time, integrated into building management systems, and managed efficiently throughout their lifecycle. Designing infrastructure for the next generation of data centers "AI is accelerating data center growth at a pace that is changing how supporting infrastructure is deployed, managed, and scaled," said Anu Kätkä, Product Line Manager for HVAC and Critical Buildings at Vaisala. "When a facility contains dozens or hundreds of measurement points, environmental monitoring can no longer be managed one sensor at a time. Operators need a system-level approach to environmental monitoring that can be commissioned efficiently, maintained without disrupting operations, and scaled consistently as capacity expands." artigo.texto: Loudoun County hosts open house as debate over data center growth continues ASHBURN, Va. - Loudoun County held the first in a series of community open houses in Ashburn Monday to give residents a chance to weigh in on the future of data center development in the community. What we know: The event, held at Broad Run High School, allowed community members to speak directly with county staff, take surveys and view noise-monitoring demonstrations. Similar open houses for tech infrastructure have taken place in Loudoun County and across the region, including in Prince William County. The feedback gathered from the sessions will help shape recommendations that are expected to go before the planning commission in 2027. The open house comes amid public debates and community pushback over rapid infrastructure expansion. Neighbors have expressed concerns over noise levels, power consumption, power substations and the proximity of data centers to surrounding neighborhoods. "I think they need some guidelines, especially for controlling some emissions and the noise. And too close to where people live... yeah, they need some standards," said Loudoun County residents Kathy and Paul Wagner, who noted they live just 500 feet away from existing infrastructure. In response to growing community concerns, Loudoun County supervisors recently approved a one-year pause on certain new AI data centers and substation applications, giving officials time to review standards for future projects. However, supporters of data center infrastructure emphasize the economic benefits, pointing to substantial local revenue and employment opportunities for workers like contractors and electricians. Don Slaiman, political coordinator for the IBW Local 26 electricians union, highlighted the financial and labor impact of the industry in the region. "That is a lot of revenue coming to this state, that is a lot of great jobs," Slaiman said. "I have 1,018 members who live in the richest county in the country right here in Loudoun... we have 17,500 members... we have doubled our membership in the last 9 years." The Source: information in this article is from a Loudoun County open house and previous FOX 5 DC reporting.

artigo.texto: Gov. Abigail Spanberger dropped a few hints Tuesday about what will be in the energy plan she’s releasing on Thursday. She said she backs more on-site electricity generation for data centers so they’re not pulling power from the grid. She also said her energy plan will lay out multiple options for Virginia to meet its power needs in the years ahead. “What are the gives and takes?” Spanberger asked. “What are you sacrificing? What are you getting from the different energy mix choices? And so we modeled out and actually pushed out a variety of different examples where we show these different types of plants have various different localized pollutant risks with these types of energy generation. We have this amount of CO2 emissions. And what is the ultimate cost to the user? So that really anyone who chooses to read a 100-page report on Virginia’s energy plan has a good sense of what all the options are. “And importantly, I think as you’ll see when we release it, there’s not one single right path because there’s something you give up with every choice that you make. When you forego one option, you’re giving something up even when you’re gaining something. And so, making sure that people have a clear understanding of the push and pull as we create the right energy mix into the future is something that very intentionally will be including in the plan we’re going to be releasing later this week.” She said one goal of the energy plan is “making sure that people have a clear understanding of the push and pull as we create the right energy mix into the future.” Spanberger’s hints about the energy plan came at an event in Danville sponsored by Cardinal News and the Institute for Advanced Learning and Research where the governor was invited to speak about economic development and then took questions from the audience. I served as moderator to read those audience questions. (Cardinal sponsored a similar event during then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s first year in office; the event was held in Bristol.) Those remarks came in the context of a question about data centers and their energy requirements. While data centers have become pariahs in many localities, political and business leaders in Danville and Pittsylvania County have embraced a large-scale data center coming to the Southern Virginia Megasite at Berry Hill. The developer, Stack Infrastructure, has signed a performance agreement that calls for creating 2,500 permanent jobs over the next 20 years at the site. The Stack project prompted several questions from the audience about how Virginia can guarantee that localities that want data centers can still host them — and about on-site power generation. She enthusiastically backed on-site power — “It’s incredibly important that we have on-site generation” — but did not specifically address natural gas, something that environmental groups oppose. “This is a place where I’ll go back to the word that I mentioned before, innovation,” she said. “Here is a lot of work being done as it relates to fuel cell, other types of noncombustion natural gas types of energy generation, where we can really ensure that we are meeting long-term the Virginia Clean Economy Act goals into the future, and also ensuring that we’re adding greater stability and reliability to the grid by having a behind-the-meter work, the bring-your-own generation.” She also mentioned the prospect of small nuclear reactors and fusion technology, the latter of which is being developed by Commonwealth Fusion Technology in Chesterfield County. “There are, on the path outside of Richmond, the potential, there are deals in place with data centers to develop small modular reactors,” the governor said. artigo.texto: Can Supercapacitors Smooth AI’s Power Swings? Supercapacitors promise millisecond response for AI-induced power transients, but most experts see them complementing, not replacing, UPS systems and batteries. AI workloads can create load swings far sharper than steady-state compute, producing hard power spikes that conventional architectures struggle to absorb. Supercapacitors, also called ultracapacitors, sit between conventional capacitors and batteries. They store energy as a surface charge rather than through a battery’s chemical reaction, which gives them higher power density than batteries but lower energy density. That trade-off suits short, frequent bursts rather than sustained runtime. Operators are testing supercapacitors alongside batteries and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems rather than replacing them. Batteries and UPS systems still support the sustained load and provide a longer backup window. A September 2026 report from IDTechEx identifies three roles for supercapacitors in data centers: voltage stabilization, peak shaving, and short-term backup power. Supercapacitors charge and discharge in milliseconds to seconds – fast enough to track AI training cycles and recharge before the next spike. Market Outlook: Small Today, Growing Fast IDTechEx projects the data center supercapacitor market will reach $950 million by 2037, a 40.9% compound annual growth rate from 2026. That growth rate stands out against the wider category. A separate IDTechEx report from August 2025 puts total global supercapacitor revenue across automotive, grid, and industrial uses at $4.86 billion by 2036, growing 15.3% annually. Three Designs Vying for the Rack Slot IDTechEx groups data center supercapacitors into three categories, based on how they store charge and where they fit: - EDLCs (electric double-layer capacitors). The most commercially mature of the three, EDLCs store charge electrostatically at the electrode surface, much like a conventional capacitor. - Hybrid capacitors. These are usually lithium-ion (Li-ion) hybrids, combining an EDLC’s surface charge storage with the “rocking chair” lithium-ion chemistry in which ions shuttle back and forth between electrodes during charge and discharge. - Pseudocapacitors. These store charge through fast, reversible chemical reactions at the electrode surface rather than purely by electrostatic storage, delivering higher energy density than an EDLC but lower power density. Backup power is the narrowest application across all three. Typical EDLC deployments sustain output for approximately 2 minutes, while some hybrids can last up to 10 minutes – enough to prevent data corruption during brief outages but not enough to replace a UPS system. IDTechEx frames supercapacitors as a complement to backup infrastructure, not a substitute. From Pilots to Deployment: Pace and Roadblocks The market for supercapacitors in data centers is still in its early stages, but growing. “The market is transitioning from early evaluation to meaningful deployment, although adoption rates vary by technology type and supply chain maturity,” said Chris Butler, president of embedded and critical power at Flex, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. “Instantaneous load transients can reach more than 150% of a power shelf’s rated capacity during certain AI compute events.” Rack designers are building in flexibility rather than committing to one architecture. “Rack designs typically include dedicated slots that can accommodate BBUs (battery backup units), CBUs (capacitor backup units), or mixed configurations, providing deployment flexibility,” Butler said. “Supply chain concerns remain a major hurdle, particularly for newer hybrid supercapacitor technologies with limited qualified suppliers.” Parag Nathaney, principal quantitative engineer for energy policy and power markets at Exelon, tied the pace of adoption to the reliability bar data centers operate under. He told Data Center Knowledge that the technology must meet 99.999% reliability for the power supply, which is why he sees the market as in its early stages. “Supercapacitors are advancing toward greater deployment, but the current state is characterized by pilot and early commercialization,” Nathaney said. Ian Wright, chief technology officer at DIMAAG, which builds battery systems designed to avoid supercapacitors, argued that the DC-to-DC conversion stage determines the response time, not the device alone. “The response speed to load changes is then determined by the DC/DC, which will be slower than either caps or batteries,” Wright told Data Center Knowledge. “If supercaps have been tried and not observed to get hot, that’s probably because they are not actually absorbing the cyclic loads.” What’s Next and How Operators Decide Whether IDTechEx’s forecast for supercapacitors plays out remains to be seen. Wright expects directly connected batteries, not supercapacitors, to become the primary tool for smoothing AI power swings. Nathaney reached a different conclusion, tied to reliability rather than economics. “I think the application of supercapacitors for data centers is novel, but the long track record of the technology in other applications could lower the barrier for adoption by data centers,” he said. Butler is somewhat more optimistic. As rack power levels scale from hundreds of kilowatts toward multi-megawatt designs, he expects CBUs to see growing use in managing transient peak demands. Over time, he anticipates workload-driven optimization will determine the mix of batteries and capacitors, with supercapacitors playing an increasingly important role in handling high-cycle, peak-power events. “I expect capacitor-based energy storage to become a mainstream element of next-generation AI power architectures,” Butler said.

artigo.texto: B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution Partner to Repurpose Batteries B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution announce a strategic partnership giving B2U priority access to the South Korean firm's batteries to develop large-scale stationary storage solutions in the United States. B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution have announced a strategic partnership aimed at developing battery energy storage system (BESS) solutions across the United States. The agreement gives B2U Storage Solutions priority access to LG Energy Solution's battery capacity and allows both companies to jointly explore business opportunities in this market. The partners plan to use B2U Storage Solutions' patented repurposing technologies to give LG Energy Solution batteries a second life in grid-scale storage applications. Extending battery life before recycling The joint initiative aims to extend batteries' service life through repurposing, keeping them in operation longer while deferring the costs and environmental impacts associated with recycling. Once integrated into BESS systems, these batteries could continue generating value for several years, according to both companies. "This partnership advances our strategy to extend the value of our batteries beyond their original applications," said Seung Tak Joo, leader of the Energy as a Service (EaaS) business department at LG Energy Solution. "By repurposing batteries for grid-scale energy storage, we can lengthen their useful life and create new growth opportunities that deliver long-term economic returns." Company LG Energy Solution: company profile Targeting data centers and grid operators The partnership intends to make BESS more accessible by offering cost-competitive storage solutions to utilities, energy storage developers, and large commercial energy users, including data centers. Both companies are working to expand energy storage infrastructure and strengthen the stability of the U.S. electrical grid by leveraging repurposed batteries, with the ambition of delivering storage capacity measured in gigawatt-hours. "We are committed to driving down the cost of energy storage by unlocking the inherent value of repurposed batteries. The alliance unites proven technology with a reliable supply of batteries, making energy storage more cost-effective and bankable," said Freeman Hall, founder and chief executive officer of B2U Storage Solutions. A response to mounting pressure on the U.S. grid The announcement comes as rising electricity demand and the growing integration of intermittent renewable energy sources place increasing pressure on the U.S. electrical grid. By storing electricity for use when needed, BESS systems help balance supply and demand, ease strain on the grid, and improve energy resilience for communities across the country. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 %

artigo.texto: Jesup advances data center regulations despite pushback from packed crowd SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - Following hours of fierce public debate inside a packed Cracker Williams Recreation Center, Jesup city officials voted Tuesday night to advance proposed regulations governing data centers. In a 4-2 vote, commissioners approved the first reading of an ordinance that formally defines data centers and permits them as a “conditional use” in light industrial zoning districts. Because Tuesday’s vote was only a preliminary step, the measure must pass additional readings before taking final effect. Dozens of residents lined up at the microphone to voice concern, urging leaders to enact a complete moratorium rather than moving ahead with regulations. Opponents argued a temporary freeze on new applications would allow the city adequate time to study potential impacts on local water resources and the power grid. “My concern is that commissioners are talking about — we need the ordinance because if the moratorium doesn’t go through, then we’re not protected,” said Jesup resident Erin Wallace. “But then the others are saying they don’t want the ordinance because the moratorium will give us time to make the ordinance stronger. It just seems disingenuous to me that we don’t do both.” City officials have not yet announced the date for the ordinance’s second reading. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Pune, 28th September 2026: COEP Technological University is set to establish India's first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale research and development centre at its Research Park in Chikhali, with an investment of over ₹800 crore. The university has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with JSW Projects, part of the JSW Group, to develop the facility in two phases. The proposed centre will focus on developing indigenous lithium-ion, sodium-ion and other advanced battery technologies. It will support battery cell design, simulation, prototyping and testing, providing a platform for research and innovation in India. The project is expected to strengthen the country's battery manufacturing ecosystem and reduce dependence on imported technologies. The project will be developed in two phases, with a combined investment of more than ₹800 crore. The first phase will focus on establishing a cell research and development centre to design, simulate and prototype lithium-ion, sodium-ion and other advanced chemistry-based battery cells. The second phase will establish a cell validation facility capable of developing battery cells with capacities ranging from 100 to 600 ampere-hours (Ah). The facility will support testing and validation, helping develop battery technologies suited to Indian conditions. The partnership is expected to create more than 1,000 employment opportunities across the battery technology ecosystem. The centre will also provide students with access to advanced battery research and practical training, strengthening industry-academia collaboration. The project is expected to support the development of electric vehicles, grid-scale energy storage and clean energy solutions. It will also contribute to India's long-term goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2070. JSW Group Chairman Sajjan Jindal said, "Battery cells will become the new fuel of this century, and the time has come to manufacture them in India. Our partnership with COEP, which has a 172-year legacy in engineering, will bring a new dimension to industry-academia collaboration. It will also help design, test and validate battery cells suited to Indian climatic conditions." COEP Vice-Chancellor Dr Sunil Bhirud said, "This project has the potential to develop indigenous alternatives for battery manufacturing. It will give students an opportunity to learn advanced battery technologies while providing a platform for research, innovation and technological development." The MoU was signed by COEP Registrar Dr D. N. Sonawane and JSW Group Executive Vice-President Naresh Lalwani. Vice-Chancellor Dr Sunil Bhirud, RIIL Director Dr S. P. Mahajan, Dean Dr P. A. Sadgir, Dr Ranjit Date, Dr Sarika Kelkar, Mandar Bhatwadekar and Officer on Special Duty Dr Avinash Joshi were among those present.

artigo.texto: Trinity Airways (091810) will work with NH Investment & Securities to prepare for the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Trinity Airways said on the 28th that it signed a memorandum of understanding on CORSIA and emissions trading with NH Investment & Securities on the 21st at Sono Trinity Commons in Seoul's Gangseo District. It is the first such agreement between a Korean airline and a financial firm in the areas of CORSIA and emissions trading. The two companies plan to cooperate on exchanging information and building a joint response system for CORSIA and the domestic greenhouse gas emissions market and related policies, jointly pursuing emissions credit projects, and carrying out activities to develop the carbon market. As a first step toward meeting its CORSIA offset obligations, Trinity Airways purchased 20,000 tons of CORSIA-eligible carbon credits and signed a contract to retire them, becoming the first Korean airline to do so. The company plans to buy additional eligible credits by the end of this year, gradually securing more than 10% of the volume it must offset by January 2028. "Through this partnership with NH Investment & Securities, we have laid the groundwork to secure emissions credits at home and abroad on a stable basis and to respond systematically to carbon regulations," said Seo Dong-bin, head of management support at Trinity Airways. "We will strengthen our capabilities in sourcing and managing credits and build an efficient response system from a medium- to long-term perspective."

artigo.texto: Hobart residents opposing the Amazon Web Services data center project are pursuing a legal strategy to hopefully hit the reset button on the city’s site plan approval process. The plaintiff’s petition, filed in Lake Superior Court, seeks injunctive relief over procedural matters involving the city’s plat and zoning approval process. However, the lawsuit experienced another delay when one of the plaintiff’s attorneys was unable to make a September 22 court appearance due to personal reasons, according to Hobart resident Barbara Koteles. Koteles is one of the plaintiffs in the case and a resident of the Eagle Creek subdivision, which is located directly across the street for the data center along 61st Avenue. An attorney conference is scheduled for Sept. 30. Koteles is joined in the complaint by fellow Hobart residents Joe Conn, Angelita Soriano and Albina Venegas-Roman. The complaint, filed against the Hobart Plan Commission and the Hobart Common Council, seeks a preliminary injunction to nullify a fill permit allowing mass grading on the property, according to court documents. Earlier this year, Hobart Plan Commission voted to treat the project’s site plan application as an application for a fill permit, the court filing states. Furthermore, “the Plan Commission voted (without findings of fact) to approve the morphed fill permit for mass construction grading activities in preparation for the project …”. The plaintiffs are challenging the fill permit solely on legal grounds, contending that the Plan Commission had no power to authorize it because it failed to provide all of the information required for a such an application nor did it produce the required findings of fact required for issuance of the permit. In series of court filings over the past several months, including motions by the city to dismiss the case, the matter reached a possible ruling on September 22. But as the case has dragged out in court, the city of Hobart has allowed grading and fill work on the 723-acre site to proceed. The Plan Commission granted the data center preliminary plat approval at a highly-charged five-hour meeting in May, but tabled final plat approval at its September 4 meeting. Final plat approval concerns two separate parcels of land. One area is 555-acre parcel, located south of 61st, east of Colorado Street and north of 69th Avenue, known as Hobart Tech Park and is owned by Amazon Web Services. The other parcel, described as the Ewen Farm property, encompasses 168 acres and is located southeast of 61st and Arizona Street. That parcel will be leased by Amazon Web Services from the current owner Meanwhile, the plaintiffs are hopeful that their legal strategy can turn back the clock and re-start the plat approval process, as well as reexamine the site plan altogether. By seeking to invalidate the fill permit, which concerns only grading of the land, the plaintiffs hope they can win new concessions, such as air and truck traffic monitoring, if not permanently halt the project. Koteles said that a judge’s order to re-start the planning process could trigger a review of the community benefits agreement signed between Amazon and the city of Hobart. She also hoped the city would develop a comprehensive ordinance governing data center development and operations. “The ordinances the city has passed, such as the one involving noise, have been done rather piecemeal,” Koteles said. She added that there has not been so much work done on the site yet, primarily grading of the land, over which the project could not be reasonably halted without a detrimental financial impact to either Amazon or the city. The plaintiffs also contend in the court filing that the data center development is negatively impacting their property values (within Eagle Creek), and will do so in the future. The city argues in court documents that the plaintiffs have failed to meet the requirements for a preliminary injunction. “I wish it (the data center) was just half the size and farther away from residents,” Koteles said. “I’ve been saying that from day one, and if that were the case it wouldn’t even be an issue.” Soriano said she is concerned about air quality in the neighborhood from the ongoing site work. “We have asked the city to measure particulate matter and monitor the air quality to make sure that all the dust blowing around is not harmful to residents,” she said, adding that she received a portable air purifier and gift cards for car washes from Amazon. The city is already spending direct payments from Amazon, having granted tax abatement on the development. Hobart Mayor Josh Huddelston explained that the city negotiated a plan for direct payments, thus granting Amazon a 35-year tax abatement on personal property (equipment on site) and a 10-year abatement on real property (buildings). The city has already received $47 million, with another $10 million arriving in September, according to Huddleston. He expects a $45 million payment in-hand by the end of 2026, with a $43 million coming in 2027. The city will receive approximately $40 million in both 2028 and 2029 and approximately $52 million in 2030 when the project is expected to be completed. Then, Hobart will receive approximately $52 million per year over the next 35 years. The data center will have 26 buildings spread out across the two sites, with six buildings at the 61st Avenue location and 20 at the Colorado Street location. Amazon is planning 170 emergency backup diesel generators at the location on 61st, and 612 emergency backup generators along Colorado, enabling a combined power capacity of 2,119 megawatts. Attempts to reach Hobart City Attorney Heather McCarthy by phone at the city’s Law Department on Thursday and Friday for comment were unsuccessful. Jim Masters is a freelance reporter for the Post-Tribune.

artigo.texto: Q3 Executive Roundtable Recap For Data Center Frontier’s Q3 2026 Executive Roundtable, three industry leaders examined a question increasingly central to the AI infrastructure buildout: What happens when data centers are asked to become larger, denser and faster at the same time? Across three discussions, a consistent theme emerged. AI is not simply increasing the amount of infrastructure required to support the modern data center. It is exposing assumptions that were easier to tolerate at lower densities, expanding the boundaries of what operators must consider mission-critical, and making the interaction between systems increasingly important to overall resilience. That begins with density. As the value and power concentrated in individual racks rises, traditional approaches to redundancy, monitoring and risk mitigation can leave less room for error. Resilience can no longer be measured simply by installed capacity or the presence of backup equipment. Operators increasingly need to understand how electrical, thermal and control systems behave together under dynamic AI workloads — and how quickly the facility can respond and recover when something goes wrong. The same shift is broadening the definition of critical infrastructure. Power generation, UPS systems and network connectivity remain fundamental, but energy storage, liquid cooling, leak detection, controls, monitoring and the interfaces connecting them are becoming part of the same reliability equation. A component can perform exactly as designed while the larger system still fails if coordination, communications or control logic break down. And all of this is happening while the market is demanding faster deployment. Standardization, modular construction, factory integration and earlier modeling can legitimately compress project schedules. But the Q3 panelists drew a clear distinction between eliminating unnecessary time and eliminating rigor. As infrastructure becomes more tightly coupled, commissioning, integrated systems testing, operational visibility and system-level validation may need to become more thorough precisely because projects are moving faster. Taken together, the Q3 discussion points toward a broader change in how AI data center resilience must be understood. The challenge is no longer simply designing enough redundancy, specifying reliable equipment or reaching first power quickly. It is building an increasingly complex infrastructure system whose components, controls and operators can perform together — under load, under stress and at the speed the AI market now demands. Here's the full question-and-answer session, organized by topic: - Roundtable: AI Infrastructure Under Pressure - Roundtable: Redefining Critical Infrastructure - Roundtable: Speed Without Compromise Here are links to the individual Q&A summaries for each of our panelists: - Chrissy Olsen, Vice President of Critical Power Solutions, MPI Energy - David Shepard, Global Head of Data Center Business, Chemelex-Raychem - Pierre-Adrien Bel, Product Manager, EMEA, Rehlko The conversation is moderated by Data Center Frontier Editor in Chief Matt Vincent. Thanks to all of our executive participants for sharing their time and insights! About the Author Matt Vincent Matt Vincent is Editor in Chief of Data Center Frontier, where he leads editorial strategy and coverage focused on the infrastructure powering cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and the digital economy. A veteran B2B technology journalist with more than two decades of experience, Vincent specializes in the intersection of data centers, power, cooling, and emerging AI-era infrastructure. Since assuming the EIC role in 2023, he has helped guide Data Center Frontier’s coverage of the industry’s transition into the gigawatt-scale AI era, with a focus on hyperscale development, behind-the-meter power strategies, liquid cooling architectures, and the evolving energy demands of high-density compute, while working closely with the Digital Infrastructure Group at Endeavor Business Media to expand the brand’s analytical and multimedia footprint. Vincent also hosts The Data Center Frontier Show podcast, where he interviews industry leaders across hyperscale, colocation, utilities, and the data center supply chain to examine the technologies and business models reshaping digital infrastructure. Since its inception he serves as Head of Content for the Data Center Frontier Trends Summit. Before becoming Editor in Chief, he served in multiple senior editorial roles across Endeavor Business Media’s digital infrastructure portfolio, with coverage spanning data centers and hyperscale infrastructure, structured cabling and networking, telecom and datacom, IP physical security, and wireless and Pro AV markets. He began his career in 2005 within PennWell’s Advanced Technology Division and later held senior editorial positions supporting brands such as Cabling Installation & Maintenance, Lightwave Online, Broadband Technology Report, and Smart Buildings Technology. Vincent is a frequent moderator, interviewer, and keynote speaker at industry events including the HPC Forum, where he delivers forward-looking analysis on how AI and high-performance computing are reshaping digital infrastructure. He graduated with honors from Indiana University Bloomington with a B.A. in English Literature and Creative Writing and lives in southern New Hampshire with his family, remaining an active musician in his spare time.

artigo.texto: Brasil amplia infraestrutura de inteligência artificial enquanto gigantes da tecnologia aceleram construção de data centers pelo mundo Por Sandro Felix Publicado em 27/09/26 às 07:24 A corrida pela inteligência artificial está transformando a infraestrutura digital global, com investimentos bilionários em data centers, chips especializados e energia elétrica. No Brasil, novos projetos buscam ampliar a capacidade de processamento e reduzir a dependência de estruturas instaladas no exterior, enquanto Estados Unidos, China e países europeus disputam espaço na expansão dessa tecnologia. A mudança vai muito além dos chatbots. Para treinar e operar modelos avançados de IA, empresas precisam de instalações capazes de abrigar milhares de processadores, sistemas de refrigeração e redes de alta velocidade. Quanto maior a demanda por serviços como ChatGPT, Gemini e Copilot, maior a necessidade de infraestrutura para sustentar essas operações. O Brasil participa desse movimento com projetos concentrados principalmente nas regiões Sudeste, Sul e Nordeste. A disponibilidade de energia renovável, a conectividade internacional e a possibilidade de atender empresas locais estão entre os fatores que atraem investimentos. Brasil já ultrapassa 1 GW de infraestrutura de data centers O mercado brasileiro atingiu 1 gigawatt (GW) de capacidade de TI comissionada no primeiro trimestre de 2026, segundo dados da datacenterHawk divulgados pela Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). O indicador considera a capacidade de equipamentos de tecnologia já comissionada e não deve ser confundido com a potência total anunciada para empreendimentos ainda em construção. Outro levantamento, realizado pela consultoria JLL e divulgado pela Exame em 16 de setembro, apontou 706 megawatts (MW) de capacidade instalada no primeiro semestre, com previsão de entrega de mais 134 MW até dezembro. As diferenças entre os números refletem metodologias e recortes distintos de acompanhamento do setor. O crescimento ocorre em um mercado que já concentra aproximadamente 48% da capacidade instalada de data centers da América Latina, conforme relatório publicado pelo GRI Institute em julho. Entretanto, nem toda essa infraestrutura é dedicada à inteligência artificial. Parte dos equipamentos atende serviços tradicionais de nuvem, armazenamento, aplicações corporativas e plataformas digitais. Ceará receberá data center do TikTok com investimento superior a R$ 200 bilhões Um dos maiores empreendimentos anunciados no país está no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, no Ceará. O TikTok confirmou um investimento estimado em mais de R$ 200 bilhões para instalar seu primeiro data center na América Latina, com início da operação previsto para 2027. O projeto envolve a Omnia, operadora de data centers do grupo Pátria Investimentos, e a Casa dos Ventos, responsável pela parceria energética. Do investimento anunciado, R$ 108 bilhões estão previstos para equipamentos de alta tecnologia até 2035, enquanto o restante contempla expansões e atualizações ao longo dos anos seguintes. A primeira etapa prevê aproximadamente 200 MW de capacidade de TI e demanda energética próxima de 300 MW. A expansão poderá levar o complexo a uma potência de até 900 MW, conforme informações divulgadas sobre o empreendimento. A empresa afirma que a instalação utilizará energia renovável proveniente de novos parques eólicos dedicados ao projeto. O sistema de refrigeração terá circuito fechado, com recirculação de água e resfriamento por ar. Embora a instalação represente uma expansão expressiva da infraestrutura digital brasileira, não se trata de uma confirmação de que toda sua capacidade será destinada ao treinamento de modelos de IA. O complexo foi anunciado para atender operações do TikTok. Rio Grande do Sul e Rio de Janeiro apostam em grandes complexos de IA No Rio Grande do Sul, a Scala Data Centers desenvolve o projeto Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul, na Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre. A primeira fase prevê investimento de R$ 3 bilhões e capacidade de 54 MW, com infraestrutura voltada ao processamento de inteligência artificial. O empreendimento foi concebido para permitir ampliações conforme a demanda e a viabilidade das próximas etapas. Em maio de 2026, o projeto avançava na elaboração do plano de negócios e na preparação para o licenciamento, segundo informações divulgadas pela GaúchaZH. A proposta de longo prazo contempla a formação de uma cidade de data centers, mas as dimensões futuras dependem da concretização das expansões planejadas. O Rio de Janeiro também participa dessa disputa com o Rio AI City, da Elea Data Centers, que combina infraestrutura existente com planos de ampliação voltados à computação de alto desempenho. Em São Paulo, a concentração de clientes corporativos e de infraestrutura de conectividade continua atraindo operadores. A Scala mantém operações e projetos em Barueri, Campinas e Jundiaí, enquanto a Tecto, do grupo V.tal, anunciou um empreendimento de 200 MW em Santana de Parnaíba. Estados Unidos concentram megaprojetos de IA Fora do Brasil, os Estados Unidos continuam no centro da expansão das instalações destinadas aos modelos mais avançados de inteligência artificial. O projeto Stargate, liderado pela OpenAI em parceria com outras empresas, tem como objetivo desenvolver uma ampla rede de infraestrutura computacional no país. Em abril de 2026, a OpenAI informou que havia superado o marco de 10 GW de capacidade de infraestrutura assegurada, inicialmente estabelecido para 2029. Segundo a companhia, mais de 3 GW foram adicionados nos 90 dias anteriores ao anúncio. O número representa compromissos de capacidade e não significa que toda essa potência já esteja em funcionamento. Entre os locais associados à expansão estão Abilene, no Texas, e outros campi norte-americanos desenvolvidos por diferentes operadores. artigo.texto: Data centers in Alaska: Fairbanks leaders weigh in on controversial issue FAIRBANKS, Alaska (KTUU/KTVF) - Candidates running for seats on the Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly have weighed in on whether they support the building of data centers in the borough. The issue garnered attention earlier this year, when the U.S. Department of Defense announced potential data centers housing artificial intelligence servers to be constructed near three installations in Alaska, including Eielson Air Force Base. On Aug. 27, the Assembly voted 6-1 in favor of adopting a set of legislative priorities for 2027 which includes a moratorium on commercial data centers on municipal or state-owned lands in Alaska, pending the creation of standards for addressing community concerns. Alexis Howell, who is running for the open Assembly seat D, agreed with the idea of a moratorium in the borough. “There is a lot of interest and excitement in this idea that we’re going to move these data centers forward, that they’re going to create jobs. I think they might do that for a month or two while they’re being built,” she said. Arguing that the borough’s grid is currently struggling, Howell said, “I would hate to see us dump a data center on top of that.” “I think that at the end of the day, a lot more analysis needs to go into that. A lot more processes should be in place before a data center just gets built,” she said. Her opponent Miguel Ramirez said there should be a study on these centers’ environmental impact before they are built. “I think we should, you know, do a study where we can all agree and see the, work with the environmental folks and find out where the goods are, where the pros are, where the cons are, if it’s good, if it’s not, but I can’t really say ‘yay’ or ‘nay’ because I think there need to be more studies done,” he explained. Nick LaJiness, running for reelection to seat E, didn’t mince words on his opinion on data centers. “I don’t think that data centers are good for any community, to be honest with you,” LaJinness said. Shelly Shupe, meanwhile, who is running for the same seat, divided public opinion on data centers into three groups: those who are concerned about environmental impacts from data centers, those who support them, and those who are not discounting them but need more information. “I’m somewhere in between the ‘I’m worried about what it might bring’ and ‘I don’t want to discount it’ groups,” she said. Scott Crass, who is running to retain seat H on the Assembly, defended his vote in favor of the moratorium. “I think that’s important that we understand the potential impacts that come from these large data centers,” Crass said. “Energy costs in our community have skyrocketed. They’re incredibly high, some of the highest in the nation, and grappling with that while thinking about a project that would consume more energy than our entire town is absolutely terrifying at first blush.” Adding that a data center which supplied its own power might be a different conversation, Crass discussed the advantages to data centers of Fairbanks’ cold climate. “That moratorium would allow us to find some time to figure out if our community is ready to accommodate those sorts of large-scale projects,” he said. Joshua Leaders, who hopes to unseat Crass from seat H, said he likes the idea of data centers as long as their presence benefits the community. “We need to take a serious look at the impact on the infrastructure, the power grid, the water and how that’s affected, and we need to see if that benefit outweighs the cost,” Leaders explained, adding that he supports a temporary moratorium while data is collected. Election Day in Fairbanks is Oct. 6, and early voting has already begun. See a spelling or grammar error? Report it to web@ktuu.com Copyright 2026 KTUU. All rights reserved.
