artigo.texto: Volkswagen and Gotion expand partnership in LFP batteries — InsideEVs Volkswagen is expanding its partnership with Chinese battery manufacturer Gotion through three joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco. As InsideEVs reports, the agreements are intended to develop a manufacturing base for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for the mass-market electric vehicle segment. Investment in Valencia Gotion will pay $1.25 billion for a 49% stake in PowerCo's plant in Valencia, Spain. The facility will be jointly managed by PowerCo and Gotion. Volkswagen said the plant is to become a European production hub for unified LFP cells. According to financial documents, its production capacity will amount to 29.1 GWh. The unified prismatic battery cell is being developed by Volkswagen subsidiary PowerCo. The group plans to use this platform for different battery chemistries, including potentially solid-state batteries, in models of various brands, from Volkswagen to Porsche. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Projects in Slovakia and Morocco Volkswagen also plans to spend about $535 million by 2030 to acquire a 49% stake in a Gotion plant in Slovakia and establish a facility in Morocco. The Slovak plant, with a capacity of 8.4 GWh, is expected to produce LFP cells for electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems. The Moroccan facility will manufacture cathode materials for such batteries. Volkswagen called LFP batteries a key technology for affordable electric mobility in the mass-market segment. The company expects their share of the European market to increase from the current 10% to 40–60% by 2030. At the same time, the automaker noted that Europe currently lacks significant LFP battery production capacity.

artigo.texto: Many gather to discuss proposed Newport Township data centers NANTICOKE — A standing-room crowd filled the hall at West Side Park Sunday as Newport Township residents gathered to learn more about proposed data center development and hear from activists, residents, and others who have been following similar projects across Northeast Pennsylvania. The roughly hourlong community meeting came less than two weeks after residents learned that zoning permits had been issued for 15 data centers and three natural gas generation facilities proposed in Newport Township. For Jennifer Lobb, a Newport Township resident and one of the meeting’s organizers, the goal Sunday was less about providing residents with all the answers and more about making sure they knew questions remained to be asked. “We’re just here to let people know about what’s going on, to encourage them to get involved with our local government, to attend the commissioners meetings, to let them know how they feel, and to bring the power back to the people who have to live with these decisions,” Lobb said in an interview before the meeting. Lobb said residents began organizing after learning about the scope of the proposed development earlier this month. “A lot of us woke up in the morning to a newspaper article about 15 data centers and three new gas power plants that were permitted for our township,” she said. Sunday’s turnout suggested the issue has gotten residents’ attention. Chairs filled the hall, while others stood along the perimeter as speakers discussed potential effects of large-scale data center development, including water and electricity use, noise, pollution, emergency response, and changes to surrounding communities. Much of the meeting also focused on encouraging residents to attend the Newport Township commissioners meeting Oct. 5 and press township officials for additional information. Luzerne County resident Nate Eachus, who said he has spent about a year attending municipal meetings throughout the region and researching environmental issues associated with data center development, urged residents to ask detailed questions about water, wastewater, diesel fuel, and power generation. “Everybody needs to show up at this October 5 meeting,” Eachus told the crowd. “Ask good, hard questions.” Eachus pointed to data center development elsewhere in Luzerne County as examples residents could study as they consider what may come to Newport Township. Jeremy Benscoter, a candidate for the Pennsylvania House’s 117th District who described himself as having a background in information technology, told residents the scale and demands of newer hyperscale data centers distinguish them from traditional facilities used to host websites and other internet services. Benscoter focused much of his remarks on the complexity of regulating the facilities, particularly when it comes to water use, electricity demand, and municipal zoning. “We have to basically decide, as a community, what you think is the best option for you,” Benscoter said. He also encouraged residents to consider effects beyond Newport Township, arguing that the rapid development of data centers throughout the region could have implications for the electrical grid and other infrastructure shared across municipal boundaries. Fern Leard, a candidate for the state House’s 120th District, focused on community organization and emergency preparedness, telling residents that first responders could require additional equipment and training to respond to emergencies at large data center facilities. “What I see in this room is people taking the time to listen to one another,” Leard said. She encouraged residents to continue attending municipal meetings and participating in the public process. Paul Shiptuski, who said he has lived in Newport Township’s Lee section for 42 years, spoke about changes his neighborhood has already experienced from nearby industrial activity. Shiptuski said residents contend with truck traffic, dust, noise, and blasting associated with a quarry near his home. He questioned what additional development could mean for residents who rely on wells and value the area’s rural surroundings. “How does that benefit us in the long run?” Shiptuski asked. Other speakers brought perspectives from neighboring communities. Derek Sutcliffe, a Moosic resident involved in opposition to a proposed data center development in Archbald, discussed the substantial electrical infrastructure required by hyperscale facilities and encouraged Newport Township residents to scrutinize how proposed facilities would be powered. Dr. Gere Reisinger, who spoke as a representative of the Seneca Nation and local Native American historian, emphasized the cultural and environmental importance of the Susquehanna River and Wyoming Valley. Lauren McCurdy, a candidate for the Pennsylvania House’s 119th District who attended Sunday’s meeting, said she sees the issue as one that extends beyond individual municipal boundaries. McCurdy, who did not address the crowd, said in an interview that she is concerned about the potential long-term environmental effects of rapid data center development throughout Northeast Pennsylvania. “We have an obligation to protect our communities from interests that are not coming here to improve the quality of life for people in Northeastern Pennsylvania,” McCurdy said. For Lobb, Sunday’s meeting was a starting point. She said residents have not yet formed a formal organization but came together quickly after learning about the permits and are encouraging neighbors to educate themselves and become involved. “They just really need to stay informed,” Lobb said. Residents were repeatedly encouraged Sunday to attend the next Newport Township commissioners meeting, scheduled for 6 p.m. Oct. 5 in the Nanticoke Area High School auditorium. artigo.texto: Lowndes County residents continue to oppose proposed data center project LOWNDES COUNTY, Ala. (WSFA) -Lowndes County residents continue their fight against the so-called red clay project as they packed out another county commission meeting. “The truth does not fear light or hard questions,” said Lowndes County resident Dennis Blair. Opponents of a proposed data center in Lowndes County say a majority of residents have been against the project for months. What’s unclear to some, like Marie Barnes, is the current status of the project, known as “red clay.” “We live here. This is our world, this is our property, this is our land, and we don’t want a data center here because we don’t want to look like a Silicon Valley,” said Barnes. So far, residents say they only know the name of the developer, Cloverleaf Infrastructure, and the proposed site, a piece of farmland along Highway 80 near Highway 21. This is about 6 miles southwest of Montgomery. “I think anyone with common sense would say this is not a part of the county that’s economically distressed, so why here? It looks like they gerrymandered pretty good to get enough undeserved people in it to qualify for an opportunity zone,” said Blair. “It’s not in the right place. Within 2 and a half miles of this data center, there are 276-something families right around it,” said Elder Tom Gardner III of Beulah Primitive Baptist Church. “It shouldn’t be that these residents have to show up week after week after week after week and not get answers, said Alabama state Rep. Phillip Ensler. This is the third commission meeting Ensler attended. He says he’s not against data centers as a rule, but says transparency is key. “We have to do it in a way that is smart and responsible. We have to do it in a way that if the community really doesn’t want it or it’s going to hurt the community, we shouldn’t have it. And this here in Lowndes County, it feels like and seems like to a lot of residents that it’s being forced on them. And we first need answers before it goes to those.” “No matter what they do, how they do it, when they do it. We’re still going to be here until this is done,” said Barnes. artigo.texto: Data centers powering AI have rapidly become a new layer of critical infrastructure worldwide that are central to technology innovation, economic growth, and national sovereignty. US capital investment in data centers as a share of GDP now rivals what it spent building its railroads, telecom networks, and electrical grid: generational projects. The data center boom is moving faster. Five years ago, a 50-megawatt (MW) facility was considered large. Now, hyperscalers are planning to build data center campuses 100 times bigger: 5 gigawatts (GW) or more, costing $150 billion to $200 billion each. AI compute demand is already outrunning supply, and the shortage is intensifying. To overcome it, the tech industry is planning investments at unprecedented scale and speed. In a base case, Bain’s Data Center Model projects approximately $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion of spending to build nearly 150 GW of new compute capacity by 2030 (see Figure 1), almost tripling global capacity in just five years. Most of the growth will come from the US, but compute capacity will grow by double digits across regions. What many business leaders are missing is that the AI compute shortage is unlikely to resolve on its own. The usual assumption that supply chains respond to demand and that they’ll eventually balance doesn’t hold here. Power, hardware, and skilled labor are simultaneously constrained (see Figure 2), and public approvals are increasingly difficult to secure. Lead times are long enough that decisions made today determine capacity several years from now. - Power: Grid connection is delaying and freezing projects. Adding grid capacity takes four-plus years, and critical equipment inventory (e.g., transformers, etc.) is scarce. Onsite, behind-the-meter power relieves some of the bottleneck, but it adds regulatory exposure, longer equipment lead times, and more project complexity. - Semiconductors: GPUs, memory, optical networking, and other components are being locked in years ahead. Operators without long-term supply agreements are effectively out of the queue. - Labor: Skilled trades are the human version of the same problem, with too few electrical workers, mechanical tradespeople, and cooling specialists. Meeting demand means recruiting, training, and retaining talent far above historical rates. - Regulations and public opinion: Complex permitting rules across local, state, and national levels add time and uncertainty, even when primary inputs are secured. Citizens and politicians are increasingly pushing back regarding water use, energy prices, and noise. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 projects worth $130 billion in the first quarter of this year alone, nearly matching the $156 billion worth of projects disrupted in all of 2025. In July, New York became the first US state to pause construction of the largest data centers; 14 others have introduced similar legislation. Countries including Ireland, the Netherlands, and Denmark have restricted or paused new grid connections, at least temporarily. Structural solutions are required Individual projects are finding workarounds, but they can’t be replicated at scale, and some are controversial. Colossus (from xAI, now part of SpaceXAI) was built in under a year by repurposing a factory and leasing dozens of gas turbines without federal clean air permits, drawing a lawsuit. Constructing a 1 GW data center typically takes one to four years, even on sites with existing power (see Figure 3), and it can take longer when new generation and transmission infrastructure is needed. Meeting the global ambition instead will require system-level fixes outside the usual free-market playbook. A grand challenge on this scale demands grand solutions, and executives planning on business as usual will get blindsided. The forces below are deliberately provocative and mostly long term, and some will create new challenges, even as they mitigate others. But overcoming the shortage will take at least one of the following forces: consolidation, new power at scale, orbital data centers, government investment, and social license. Consolidation: Consolidation could occur as capital requirements grow so large that only a handful of companies survive. Hyperscalers’ data center capex could top $1 trillion by 2028. Semiconductors provide a useful corollary. Staying at the leading edge grew so costly (tens of billions of dollars per generation) that missing one generation made catching up effectively impossible. Companies exited, were acquired, or retreated to older nodes (see Figure 4). Facing unsustainable costs, data center providers may also turn to once-unthinkable solutions: shared power procurement, colocated servers, and jointly funded grid upgrades. New power at scale: Power is one of the most challenging, multidimensional bottlenecks, and no single source solves it. The realistic path combines near-term options that could come online this decade with long-term ones that are scheduled to pay off in the 2030s. Near term, behind-the-meter generation (mostly natural gas today) is one of the few ways to add large blocks of power on data center timelines. Pairing it with carbon capture, utilization, and storage could make it cleaner, but that’s unproven at scale. Tech companies are also turning to renewables, storage, and virtual power plants (VPPs) that use software to aggregate and redirect power in real time from distributed sources such as batteries and smart thermostats. Google, for instance, is funding 1.6 GW of renewables (mostly wind) and 300 MW of storage alongside a new Minnesota data center. North America’s VPP market grew by 13.7% last year, to 37.5 GW, per Wood Mackenzie. Novel VPP agreements are emerging, such as the Google-Voltus deal that would aggregate up to 100 MW annually over three years in the PJM grid. Nuclear is another clean source that could eventually help, but new, large-scale capacity realistically won’t arrive until the mid-2030s. Recommissi

artigo.texto: Das ‘baterias de água’ às novas soluções de armazenamento de energia Em artigo à CNN Infra, Fernanda Genova Martins, da CTG, afirma que o leilão de baterias dará mais flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico, mas será apenas parte da solução Antes das baterias de lítio, o Brasil já contava com armazenamento de energia em larga escala. Por décadas, os reservatórios das usinas hidrelétricas funcionaram como “baterias de água”: deslocaram a disponibilidade hídrica entre períodos chuvosos e secos e ofereceram flexibilidade para atender às variações sazonais da demanda. Essa capacidade foi um diferencial estratégico da matriz elétrica brasileira. O país construiu um sistema renovável, integrado e capaz de aproveitar a complementaridade entre regiões. Mas essa característica já não responde sozinha à complexidade da operação. A expansão hidrelétrica ocorreu com maior participação de empreendimentos a fio d’água, com menor capacidade de regularização, enquanto a geração eólica e solar avançou rapidamente. Em 2025, as fontes renováveis responderam por 86,8% da oferta interna de eletricidade. Eólica e solar, somadas, já representam 26,4%, ante 10,9% em 2020, segundo a EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética). Esses resultados ampliam a necessidade de recursos capazes de oferecer flexibilidade, potência, controle e deslocamento temporal de energia. Mais renováveis exigem novas formas de flexibilidade Solar e eólica apresentam perfis variáveis de geração: a produção solar se altera ao longo do dia, enquanto a eólica depende dos ventos. Em determinados momentos, restrições elétricas, energéticas ou operativas exigem reduzir parte da produção renovável porque o sistema não consegue absorvê-la ou transportá-la. Em 2025, o corte de geração eólica e solar (curtailment) chegou a 20,6%, mais que o dobro de 2024, com prejuízo estimado acima de R$ 6 bilhões, segundo a Volt Robotics. O desafio é ajustar oferta e demanda, armazenando o excedente e disponibilizando energia quando ela gera mais valor ao sistema. Essa flexibilidade pode vir de baterias, reservatórios, usinas reversíveis, transmissão, resposta da demanda e gestão inteligente da geração distribuída. As usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis merecem atenção especial. Ao combinar armazenamento em grande escala e maior duração com resposta às necessidades de potência e flexibilidade, elas podem aproveitar a experiência hidrelétrica do Brasil e complementar as baterias em serviços de maior duração. O debate deve incluir soluções capazes de sustentar a expansão renovável nas próximas décadas. Já as baterias ganharam protagonismo pela rapidez de implantação, capacidade de resposta e queda de custos. Em 2025, foram instalados 108 GW de novos sistemas no mundo, avanço de 40%, segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia. Já não é uma tecnologia experimental. No Brasil, o ambiente econômico e regulatório precisa direcioná-la aos pontos e serviços em que o benefício para o sistema seja maior. Leilão será um teste para o desenho do mercado Os primeiros leilões no Brasil voltados ao armazenamento em baterias, previstos para dezembro, marcam a passagem dos projetos-piloto para uma nova escala. O desenho prevê contratos de 15 anos, início do fornecimento em 2028 e entrega de energia por pelo menos quatro horas. O interesse foi imediato: a EPE recebeu 6.091 projetos, que somam 296.807 MW. O número é expressivo, mas o cadastro não equivale a projeto habilitado, investimento contratado ou necessidade do sistema. Avaliação técnica, capacidade de conexão e volume demandado ainda funcionarão como filtros. Essa diferença entre intenção e execução é central. Para atrair capital de longo prazo, o marco regulatório deverá oferecer previsibilidade sobre remuneração, alocação de riscos, medição do desempenho e tratamento das limitações da rede. Será preciso, ainda, evitar que a competição pelo menor preço produza ativos incapazes de sustentar o desempenho por 15 anos. Baterias perdem capacidade com o tempo, e conexão, software, manutenção e destinação final fazem parte da conta. Escala depende de uma combinação de soluções O primeiro leilão é voltado a baterias com ciclos de quatro horas de duração. Esse produto pode contribuir para o deslocamento intradiário de energia, a gestão de rampas e a resposta rápida a necessidades operativas. Sua contribuição, contudo, deve ser avaliada com outros recursos de flexibilidade, porque nenhuma tecnologia de armazenamento atende isoladamente a todos os requisitos do sistema elétrico brasileiro, por isso a importância da diversificação e complementariedade. Nesse contexto, as usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis podem ocupar posição estratégica. Esses empreendimentos utilizam energia para bombear água a um reservatório superior e voltam a gerar quando o sistema requer energia, potência ou outros serviços de flexibilidade. O Brasil reúne experiência hidrelétrica e condições naturais favoráveis; sua inserção dependerá de inventários, licenciamento, conexão e mecanismos de remuneração compatíveis com os serviços prestados. As tecnologias devem ser comparadas conforme o serviço requerido. Duração, tempo de resposta, localização, disponibilidade, prazo de implantação, conexão, impacto ambiental, usos múltiplos do reservatório e custo total são atributos relevantes. Conforme a necessidade, a alternativa poderá ser bateria, usina reversível, transmissão, participação da demanda ou uma combinação desses recursos. Projetos-piloto ajudam a converter hipóteses em evidências. Em janeiro, a CTG Brasil inaugurou, na Usina Hidrelétrica Ilha Solteira (SP), o FlexBess, laboratório que combina geração solar e baterias para avaliar desempenho, segurança e modelos de operação. A experiência reforça que armazenar energia exige inteligência operacional, qualificação técnica e regras que reconheçam o valor entregue ao sistema. artigo.texto: UL Solutions Launches Certification for Direct-to-Chip Liquid Cooling Equipment Used in AI Data Centers Certification evaluates liquid cooling subassemblies for safety, performance, leak integrity and interoperability, helping support reliable AI infrastructure. - AI chips generate intense heat, making effective cooling essential to data center performance and reliability. - The certification provides a consistent way to assess critical cooling components before deployment in AI data centers. - Certification can help manufacturers demonstrate product readiness and help data center customers make informed purchasing and integration decisions. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260929465054/en/ UL Solutions today launched a certification program for liquid cooling subassemblies that target powerful chips directly, providing more effective cooling in AI data centers and other high-density computing systems. AI computers use chips that produce a large amount of heat. If that heat is not removed, equipment may slow down, shut off or become damaged, but traditional air cooling, such as fans or chilled air, may not be enough for today’s most powerful computing systems. With direct-to-chip liquid cooling, coolant flows through a cold plate that is attached to the chip. The coolant absorbs heat from the chip and carries it away, much like water flowing through a radiator. “As AI data centers handle more powerful computing, they depend on even more advanced cooling systems to operate safely and reliably,” said AI and other high-performance computing systems are increasing energy use and heat in data centers. Global data center electricity use is expected to more than double between 2024 and 2030. Cooling can account for up to 40% of a data center’s energy use. Liquid cooling can improve heat control, but it also brings risks. Leaks, corrosion, contamination or parts that do not work well together can affect system safety, performance and reliability. Connecting parts from different suppliers can also be a challenge. Parts may fit together but require different coolants, pressure levels or operating conditions. Industry observers have identified integration problems and limited standards as barriers to wider use of liquid cooling. The UL Solutions certification program covers eligible liquid-filled parts and subassemblies that move coolant through information and communication technology equipment. These may include: - Cold plates, which absorb heat directly from computer chips - Manifolds, which send coolant to servers and equipment racks - Quick disconnects, which allow equipment to be serviced without draining the full cooling system UL Solutions uses UL 4501, the Outline of Investigation for Safety, Performance and Interoperability of Liquid-Filled Components and Assemblies Used in Liquid Cooling Systems, to evaluate eligible liquid cooling subassemblies. The evaluation covers coolant compatibility, pressure and leak integrity, durability, liquid flow, interoperability, production controls and installation requirements. Evaluating these parts before adding them to a complete cooling system can help identify problems earlier and reduce the need for repeated testing. Independent certification demonstrates that an eligible product meets applicable requirements. This helps manufacturers support their product claims and helps data center customers make informed buying and integration decisions. “AI infrastructure must scale without sacrificing safety or reliability,” said UL Solutions can also evaluate other data center cooling equipment under applicable UL Standards. This equipment includes coolant distribution units, self-contained liquid-filled systems, liquid-cooled busways, cables, connectors, power whips, gaskets, O-rings and hoses. Requirements depend on each product’s design, function and intended use. Learn more about UL Solutions services that support data center development and operations. About UL Solutions A global leader in applied safety science, UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS) transforms safety, security and sustainability challenges into opportunities for customers in more than 110 countries. UL Solutions delivers testing, inspection and certification services, advisory offerings and software solutions that support our customers’ product innovation and business growth. The UL Mark serves as a recognized symbol of trust in our customers’ products and reflects an unwavering commitment to advancing our safety mission. We help our customers innovate, launch new products and services, navigate global markets and complex supply chains, and grow sustainably and responsibly into the future. Our science is your advantage. Learn more about UL Solutions. artigo.texto: Business Follow Us on Google September 29, 2026 by Franca Ochigbo, Abuja FG approves carbon market framework, moves to establish approval criteria The Federal Government has taken steps to institutionalise Nigeria’s carbon market by approving a framework for its operation, the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Nigeria, Prof. Simon Uchenna Ortuanya, has said. Ortuanya, represented by Prof. Nnaemeka Chukwuone, spoke at the National Stakeholders Review and Validation Workshop on the draft Host Country Approval Criteria for Nigeria’s Carbon Market Operations, organised by the National Council on Climate Change in Abuja. He said the global carbon market offered countries opportunities to mobilise climate finance for greenhouse gas emission reduction and removal while supporting the transition to a low-carbon economy. According to him, the opportunities are particularly important for Nigeria as the country seeks to pursue economic growth, industrial development, energy access and poverty reduction while responding to climate change. “The approval represents an important step towards establishing a structured system for carbon market operations in the country. The next critical task is the reason why we are in this meeting, which is to ensure that the framework is supported by clear, practical and transparent host country approval criteria,” he said. Ortuanya said the criteria would guide the eligibility and assessment of carbon market projects while clarifying institutional responsibilities, measurement and reporting procedures, verification requirements, environmental and social safeguards, alignment with Nigeria’s nationally determined contributions, registry and transparency arrangements, and carbon accounting. He stressed the need for the criteria to protect Nigeria’s interests while remaining practical and predictable within the country’s regulatory environment. He said the proposed criteria were developed with research input from the University of Nigeria, adding that effective public policy should be based on credible research, evidence and stakeholder engagement. The Vice Chancellor said the participatory approach adopted for the workshop included technical sessions, stakeholder group discussions and plenary deliberations aimed at generating recommendations for refining and finalising the Host Country Approval criteria. He urged participants to examine the proposed project eligibility and assessment requirements and determine whether institutional roles and coordination arrangements were sufficiently clear. artigo.texto: PJM to Data Centers: Stop Bailing on the Grid Every Time It Blips Remember that July morning when 4,000 megawatts (MW) of Northern Virginia data centers yanked themselves off the PJM grid because of a routine, properly cleared fault on a single transmission line (see PJM: Data Centers Panicked, Nearly Crashed the Grid on Purpose)? PJM hasn't forgotten either. On Sept. 8, PJM's Planning Committee got its first look at proposed "ride-through" standards that would require big data centers and crypto mines to stay connected and keep drawing power when the grid wobbles — instead of hitting the eject button and running for their diesel generators. And PJM isn't easing into it: new facilities entering the study process would have to demonstrate compliance starting Nov. 1, 2026 — about five weeks from now. artigo.texto: Volkswagen Group, its battery subsidiary PowerCo SE and Gotion High-tech have expanded their battery production partnership, with an agreement to establish joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco. The agreement will see facilities covering lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery-cell production developed in Valencia, Spain and Šurany, Slovakia, while Kenitra, Morocco will house a cathode-material operation. It also includes joint procurement and sales activities in Europe. The moves form part of a wider strategy by the groups to ‘jointly accelerate the development of a regional battery supply chain for Europe’. ‘Major breakthrough’ “I am delighted that we are expanding our long-standing partnership with Gotion into the joint industrial production of LFP batteries to strengthen Europe’s battery industry,” commented Thomas Schmall, member of the board of management of Volkswagen Group for technology and chairman of the supervisory board of PowerCo SE. “This marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility. Volkswagen is the first European automotive manufacturer to cover the entire battery value chain, from development and cathode materials through to production.” As the groups noted, the market share of LFP batteries is expected to rise from around 10% today to between 40% and 60% by 2030, with Europe currently lacking LFP battery production capacity. Project structure The largest project under the partnership, in Valencia, is being positioned as a future ‘European production hub for unified LFP battery cells’, and will be 51% owned by PowerCo and 49% by Gotion. The companies also plan a joint venture around Gotion’s battery project in Šurany, Slovakia, with Gotion holding a 51% majority stake, to PowerCo’s 49%, while a similar structure will be maintained at Kentira. The Morocco project will supply cathode material to the two European battery operations. Li Zhen, chairman of Gotion Hith-tech said that the latest announcement follows “six years of close collaboration” between Volkswagen and Gotion. “Through cross-shareholdings and three joint sites, we are anchoring our shared strategy to localise battery production in Europe, racing to seize the opportunities of global electric mobility, and jointly forging a new paradigm of world-class, win-win cooperation in the lithium battery industry,” he commented. artigo.texto: O workshop contou com a presença de especialistas, palestrantes, parceiros nas áreas de energia solar e armazenamento de energia, bem como empresas e investidores atuantes no setor. Soluções integradas de energia solar e armazenamento para uso comercial e industrial. No dia 29 de setembro, em Dak Lak, a Unitek, a Uhome e a Usolution organizaram em conjunto o seminário ALL-IN-ONE ENERGY TOUR 2026 com o tema "Soluções Integradas de Energia Solar + Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias - Liderando o Mercado". Segundo avaliações, o mercado de energia do Vietnã está entrando em um período de transformação significativa, o que impõe novas exigências em termos de gestão e otimização dos custos de eletricidade. Juntamente com as regulamentações do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio sobre horários de pico, o Decreto nº 243/2026/ND-CP, de 26 de junho de 2026, do Governo, ampliou o mecanismo de venda do excedente de energia elétrica proveniente de sistemas solares fotovoltaicos instalados em telhados. Essas mudanças criaram novas exigências, que incluem não apenas a geração de energia, mas também a otimização do fornecimento no momento adequado. Segundo os organizadores, a energia solar gera a maior parte da eletricidade durante o dia, enquanto a demanda e os custos de energia elétrica podem aumentar à noite. Portanto, a combinação de energia solar com sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) é considerada uma solução para armazenar o excedente de eletricidade, utilizando-o em momentos oportunos, otimizando custos e melhorando a eficiência do investimento. O mercado atual oferece diversas tendências, tecnologias de armazenamento e soluções Solar + BESS para atender a diferentes necessidades. Para que um sistema seja eficaz, a questão reside não apenas na seleção de dispositivos individuais, mas também na capacidade de conectar, sincronizar e otimizar os componentes em uma solução completa que atenda às reais necessidades do negócio. No workshop, o Comitê Organizador atualizou os participantes sobre as mudanças do mercado e apresentou soluções práticas, tais como: sincronização e otimização da eficiência do investimento; modelos e soluções adaptados às necessidades de negócios; operação, manutenção, teste e melhoria do desempenho e estabilidade do sistema… fornecidas pela Pylontech, Fox Ess, Fluke e Goneo. Durante o programa, palestrantes e parceiros também discutiram diretamente e responderam a perguntas de empresas e investidores sobre a implementação de sistemas de energia solar combinados com armazenamento de energia. O conteúdo focou na seleção da capacidade adequada, na capacidade de suprir a demanda, nas opções de armazenamento e na utilização eficiente da eletricidade em diferentes momentos. Portanto, o workshop contribuiu para fornecer mais informações e soluções tecnológicas para empresas em processo de transição para modelos de uso de energia mais eficientes, tornando-se mais proativas no fornecimento de eletricidade e reduzindo gradualmente os custos operacionais. artigo.texto: O relatório Flexera State of the Cloud 2026 indica que 73% das organizações operam com um modelo de Nuvem Híbrida (essa taxa sobe para 78% em empresas com mais de 5.000 funcionários). Notavelmente, a taxa de migração de cargas de trabalho e dados da Nuvem Pública para outros ambientes também aumentou 2% em comparação com o ano anterior. Essa mudança reflete uma tendência real: as empresas estão cada vez mais posicionando suas cargas de trabalho de forma proativa onde alcançam a máxima eficiência operacional. Isso não significa que as empresas estejam "abandonando a nuvem". Pelo contrário, os gastos com a nuvem continuam a crescer. A realidade é que, quanto mais disseminada for a adoção da nuvem, mais clara ficará para as empresas a compreensão de quais cargas de trabalho podem aproveitar o ambiente da nuvem e quais exigem uma arquitetura especializada. Essa necessidade de diferenciação clara redefiniu o papel do Data Center na arquitetura híbrida. Quando uma arquitetura simplesmente não consegue "se adequar" a todas as cargas de trabalho. Uma aplicação digital que exige escalabilidade rápida para atender às demandas de tráfego certamente terá requisitos de infraestrutura diferentes de um sistema central que necessita de estabilidade 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Da mesma forma, uma carga de trabalho de análise de dados pode exigir poder computacional flexível, enquanto um sistema de segurança demanda hardware dedicado, arquitetura de armazenamento ou uma arquitetura independente de rede. Este é o grande diferencial da Nuvem Híbrida: liberar as empresas da pressão de ter que "amontoar" todas as cargas de trabalho em um único ambiente. Embora as nuvens públicas ofereçam um vasto ecossistema de serviços com recursos de alocação instantânea, para componentes que exigem um nível mais profundo de personalização, as empresas ainda precisam de "espaço" para projetar proativamente sua infraestrutura de acordo com suas necessidades. É essa lacuna que os data centers preenchem na arquitetura híbrida. Em vez de ser apenas um "local de hospedagem" para servidores, um data center (DC) é uma plataforma de lançamento para que as empresas implementem sua própria infraestrutura: desde computação e armazenamento até redes e segurança. As empresas podem ajustar a configuração para cada carga de trabalho principal, aproveitando ao máximo o poder da nuvem para os demais componentes. Em outras palavras, as soluções híbridas ampliam as opções, enquanto os data centers ajudam as empresas a manter o controle sobre essa personalização. Quanto mais nos aprofundamos na computação em nuvem, mais importante se torna o papel dos centros de dados. No entanto, uma infraestrutura perfeitamente "sob medida" não tem significado algum se se transformar em um oásis isolado. As aplicações em nuvem ainda precisam extrair dados de bancos de dados localizados em infraestrutura privada. O sistema central deve sincronizar-se continuamente com as plataformas digitais na nuvem. E, à medida que o negócio se expande, a arquitetura atual precisa ser flexível o suficiente para se conectar com outras nuvens, plataformas ou parceiros. É aqui que entra em jogo o segundo papel do Data Center: a infraestrutura dedicada não só precisa estar operacional, como também precisa estabelecer uma "via expressa" perfeita que a conecte à parte da Nuvem da arquitetura híbrida. O estudo de caso da Equinix e do Credit Saison no Japão é um exemplo claro. Essa instituição financeira migrou aproximadamente 80% de seus sistemas para a nuvem. Com o aumento do uso da nuvem, o Credit Saison precisava resolver o problema de conectar seus sistemas internos aos serviços em nuvem. Por meio da infraestrutura de data center da Equinix e da solução de interconexão direta, a largura de banda do Credit Saison para a AWS saltou de 10 Mbps para 10 Gbps. Ainda mais impressionante, o tempo para ativar uma nova conexão foi reduzido de vários meses para apenas 3 dias úteis. Esta história oferece uma nova perspectiva: o fato de 80% dos sistemas serem baseados em nuvem não significa que os data centers estejam se tornando infraestrutura "obsoleta". Pelo contrário, o uso em larga escala da nuvem gerou uma nova tarefa para os data centers: garantir que a infraestrutura privada e a nuvem se comuniquem na velocidade desejada pelos negócios. Portanto, à medida que a presença da nuvem se expande, a questão central não é mais "Qual é o volume de trabalho da empresa em seu data center?". Uma pergunta mais prática deveria ser: "A partir desse data center, qual o alcance da arquitetura híbrida da empresa em termos de conectividade e escalabilidade?". De "Estação de Armazenamento" a "Camada de Suporte" para a Nuvem Essa mudança não diminui o valor de padrões tradicionais como fornecimento de energia, capacidade, segurança ou disponibilidade do data center. No entanto, a arquitetura híbrida impõe uma camada adicional de requisitos. As empresas precisam conhecer o grau máximo de personalização de sua própria infraestrutura; como conectar essa parte à nuvem; e a adaptabilidade do sistema atual quando uma nova carga de trabalho ou plataforma é adicionada. Isso é especialmente crucial à medida que a arquitetura de TI se torna cada vez mais complexa. O relatório da Flexera para 2026 aponta para um crescimento contínuo do modelo de Nuvem Híbrida, com um crescimento de 2% em Multicloud; simultaneamente, fluxos de migração e repatriação para a Nuvem ocorrem de forma concomitante. artigo.texto: Crusoe Developing Data Center Campus in Armstrong County, Texas Data center to be built at the source of West Texas clean energy CLAUDE, TX – September 28, 2026 – Crusoe, the AI factory company, today announced it is the developer of Google’s data center campus under construction in Armstrong County outside of Amarillo. The campus is engineered to provide capacity to power advanced AI. “Building the future of AI requires a new kind of infrastructure, starting with energy. Crusoe’s strategy is to build AI factories directly at the source of abundant, low-cost energy – to both improve utilization of existing assets as well as catalyze new energy generation,” said Chase Lochmiller, CEO and Co-founder of Crusoe. “The Armstrong County campus is a prime example of this energy-first strategy. We're bringing new, affordable clean energy online. We broke ground in June 2025 and are building at the same swift pace we set in Abilene.” The campus has a direct connection to Serena's adjacent Goodnight 1 (265.5 MW) wind farm, which is operational, and Goodnight 2 (265.5 MW) wind farm, which is currently under construction and was catalyzed by Crusoe’s development at the site. When wind generation exceeds campus demand, surplus power is supplied back to the grid – benefiting local ratepayers and reducing curtailment of West Texas wind energy. By co-locating directly at the source of West Texas wind energy, Crusoe’s approach actively supports the region's buildout of clean, affordable energy. In addition to its innovative energy sources, the campus is designed for water efficiency. The project will utilize a closed-loop, non-evaporative liquid cooling system, which is designed to significantly limit the facility's water footprint to primarily domestic uses such as kitchens. Construction broke ground in June 2025 and is underway, with more than 5,500 skilled laborers on-site daily, bringing significant investment and employment to the local community. Local investment in the community also includes Google’s Energy Impact Fund, which recently announced support for efficiency upgrades in public buildings and homes in Armstrong County. The campus is part of Crusoe's growing West Texas portfolio, which includes two campuses under development in Abilene, further establishing West Texas as a critical region for the future of American digital infrastructure. Read more about Crusoe's energy approach here: www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/co-located-power-for-ai-data-centers. About Crusoe As the AI factory company, Crusoe is on a mission to accelerate the abundance of energy and intelligence. The company provides a reliable, scalable, cost-effective, energy-first solution for AI infrastructure. By harnessing large-scale energy sources, building AI-optimized data centers, and delivering a powerful AI cloud platform, Crusoe empowers its customers and partners to build the future faster. artigo.texto: Securing the energy storage surge This article is authored by Arun Goyal, former CERC member and senior advisor, MSL, and Jaisal Sarma, public policy professional, MSL. India’s ambitious commitment to establish 500 GW of non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030 marks one of the most dramatic clean energy expansions. Achieving this goal, however, hinges on an operational reality: solar and wind power are inherently variable, requiring massive utility-scale energy storage capacity to keep the electric grid balanced, stable, resilient, and reliable. The Central Electricity Authority’s National Generation Adequacy Plan estimates that India will need the energy storage installed capacity of 174 GW/888 GWh including Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) of 80 GW/321 GWh by the year 2035-36 to effectively manage this clean power transition. Yet, as the nation accelerates its energy transition, it faces a new and complex strategic vulnerability. Clean energy technology is no longer simply an environmental and economic transaction; it is fundamentally a global contest for critical raw materials. Without secure, cost-effective access to key battery inputs, such as lithium, graphite, cobalt, and nickel, India’s energy storage deployment remains deeply exposed to global price volatility, unilateral export restrictions, and geopolitical disruption across international supply corridors. To build energy sovereignty in an increasingly fractured global order, India cannot rely on conventional market imports alone. It must instead execute a thoughtful, dual-track strategy that pairs strategic international technology alliances with a robust domestic circular economy. Across the globe, clean energy supply chains are re-aligning along geopolitical lines as major economies seek to de-risk their manufacturing hubs and secure raw material inputs. Multilateral frameworks like the US-led Pax Silica initiative, designed to build resilient supply chains across semiconductors, critical minerals, and advanced technologies, alongside the Minerals Security Partnership, reflect a historic shift towards friend-shoring. For India, active participation in these technological coalitions offers vital strategic advantages. It provides access to international co-investment mechanisms for overseas mineral processing, technology sharing for next-generation battery chemistries like sodium-ion and helps diversify raw material inputs away from single-country concentrations. However, foreign alliances, no matter how well-negotiated, are an incomplete shield against supply chain volatility. Diplomatic access to minerals extracted or refined abroad does not fully eliminate risks of long maritime shipping routes, foreign exchange volatility, or international refining bottlenecks during global crises. To turn global partnerships into lasting national resilience, India requires a strong domestic anchor. Through the National Critical Mineral Mission, supported by a ₹16,300 crore central outlay up to 2030-31, the Indian government has formally elevated secondary mineral recovery to a cornerstone of national economic policy. The mission’s dedicated ₹1,500 crore incentive scheme for critical mineral recycling explicitly targets the extraction of battery-grade minerals from e-waste, manufacturing scrap, and end-of-life electric vehicles. This strategy complements domestic exploration by focusing on urban mining that converts domestic waste into high-value strategic mineral reserves. From an economic perspective, establishing a closed-loop domestic recycling ecosystem fundamentally improves the financial viability of clean energy infrastructure over its entire operational lifecycle. Processing secondary battery scrap inside India creates an immediate buffer against wild fluctuations in global critical mineral spot prices, thereby stabilizing long-term power purchase agreements and lowering the overall lifetime cost of storage systems. At the same time, implementing clear Extended Producer Responsibility guidelines ensures that valuable battery materials remain within the domestic industrial ecosystem rather than moving overseas as unprocessed scrap. A predictable stream of recycled secondary feedstocks lowers raw material costs for domestic cell manufacturers, creating a self-sustaining feedback loop that supports long-term industrial competitiveness. By recovering these critical inputs locally, India can expand its energy storage capacity while significantly reducing the net capital outlay required for fresh critical mineral imports. Translating this strategic blueprint into an operational reality requires pragmatic policy execution, cluster-based industrial infrastructure, and aligned fiscal structures. Foremost among these is updating tax policy to support new clean technologies. Lowering the GST on standalone energy storage systems and specialised recycling machinery to a uniform 5% can immediately lower upfront capital barriers and attract private investment. Simultaneously, regulatory bodies can establish clear, standardised quality and safety benchmarks for battery state-of-health diagnostics, enabling second-life electric vehicle batteries to be safely repurposed for stationary grid storage applications. Furthermore, public procurement agencies and energy developers should modernize their evaluation frameworks to assess storage projects based on full lifecycle economic value, factoring in secondary material recovery and recycling buybacks, rather than relying strictly on initial capital expenditure. Ultimately, India’s clean energy sovereign future cannot be built on import dependencies or uncoordinated execution. International technology blocs like Pax Silica open vital doors to global capital and advanced research, but internal administrative execution will decide whether India achieves true energy independence. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage: 6 security questions operators should be asking Tue, 29th Sep 2026 (Today) Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) play a critical role in grid stability and renewable energy utilisation. But as these infrastructures become more sophisticated, the risk of cyberattacks grows, potentially compromising operations, safety and energy reliability. In Centrii's recently published GRIDLOCK report, using risk modelling to analyse what an attack on BESS would cost the grid, it put the chance of a major coordinated attack on the UK's battery storage fleet at 92% within the next five years. The estimated financial cost is between £2 billion and £10 billion. But what's interesting from our analysis is that the probability of an attack falls as the security investment and enhancements increase. For example, under voluntary improvements adopted gradually and unevenly across the sector, the probability falls to 78%. With mandatory IEC 62443 certification and attack-readiness drills, it fall to just 61%. BESS are not passive assets. They are software-controlled, grid-interactive systems that directly influence frequency, load balancing and stability. The integration of IT and OT in energy storage systems increases their vulnerability. As more countries shift toward long-duration energy storage, these systems could face more frequent attacks. The issue is whether operators and asset owners are prioritising security. These are the questions every operator should be asking: 1. Do I have visibility into my distributed assets? When operators lose visibility into distributed assets, whether that's down to communication failures, misconfigurations, or malicious interference, the response becomes reactive rather than coordinated. Unlike centralised generation, battery assets are often remote and dispersed, and heavily dependent on real-time telemetry. Last year's attacks on Poland's power grid show just how threat actors understand how to manipulate remote locations simultaneously to destabilise critical power networks. Without continuous, validated visibility into operational states, operators are managing blind. 2. What happens if dispatch signals are manipulated? Battery systems do not just store energy; they respond to it. Charging and discharging decisions are driven by automated signals tied to grid frequency, market conditions, and control system inputs. If signals are altered, delayed, or spoofed, the behaviour of the battery changes accordingly. A coordinated manipulation of dispatch signals could cause batteries to discharge during peak stress or charge when supply is already constrained. At scale, this could become a major grid stability event. 3. How secure is my remote access infrastructure? Remote access is critical to today's energy operations. But it's also one of the most consistently exploited pathways into operational environments. The challenge is not just whether remote access exists, but whether it is continuously monitored, authenticated and segmented. One example of a UK battery facility revealed remote connectivity and VPN management as key vulnerabilities before security improvements were made. Without robust controls these pathways could directly access systems responsible for charging discharging and grid interaction. Remote access must be treated as a critical control point, or it becomes an attacker's shortcut. 4. Are my OT systems designed for today's threat environment? Many battery installations rely on industrial control systems (ICS) originally designed for isolated environments. But in today's environment, SCADA platforms, battery management systems and programmable logic controllers are connected to external networks. While this enables efficiency and scalability, it also exposes them. Advisories by CISA in the US have highlighted vulnerabilities in widely used ICS components, including unauthorised command execution, denial-of-service conditions, or system manipulation. In the UK BESS example, outdated firewalls, irregular patching and poor segmentation led to exploitable conditions within the operational environment. 5. Is cybersecurity being managed at the speed of deployment? The simple fact is that battery storage is being deployed faster than many operators can secure it. According to the IEA, global energy storage capacity is expected to grow more than six-fold by 2030. As growth accelerates, it creates a gap between what is operationally critical and what is operationally secured. In practice, this gap shows up in incomplete asset inventories, delayed patch cycles and limited monitoring of newly deployed systems. When basic vulnerabilities exist, attackers will always sense an opportunity. 6. Do I understand how cyber risk translates into financial impact? Cybersecurity in energy is often framed as a data protection issue. In BESS environments, it is an operational and financial issue. The GRIDLOCK report backs this up. It estimates that bringing the UK's battery storage infrastructure up to IEC 62443 Security Level 2 – the standard the modelling shows meaningfully reduces attack probability – would cost between £400m and £1bn across the national fleet. This is a return on proactive security investment of roughly 5x to 25x. The earliest likely attack window also changes, from 2027–28 under a baseline posture to 2029–31 under the most rigorous one. What's clear is that security investment reduces risk, but also buys time The grid is becoming far more distributed, connected and automated – and BESS is at the heart of this energy transformation. Distributed control without distributed visibility creates fragility rather than resilience. For operators the question is not whether cybersecurity matters, but why it matters.

artigo.texto: Mercado de carbono abre espaço para o agro regenerativo A transição, porém, exige investimentos iniciais O mercado de créditos de carbono no solo pode se tornar uma fonte adicional de financiamento para a expansão da agricultura regenerativa no Brasil. A combinação entre o potencial agrícola do país, a disponibilidade de áreas para recuperação e a busca por sistemas produtivos de baixo carbono abre espaço para remunerar produtores pela adoção de práticas que aumentem o estoque de carbono e melhorem a qualidade do solo. Análise do Rabobank aponta que o Brasil reúne condições para se tornar um dos principais mercados de créditos de carbono no solo do mundo. Dados da Embrapa citados pelo banco mostram que, dos 177 milhões de hectares de pastagens existentes no país, cerca de 28 milhões de hectares, equivalentes a 15% do total, apresentam algum nível de degradação e poderiam ser restaurados com práticas regenerativas. A transição, porém, exige investimentos iniciais, mudanças no manejo e um período de adaptação. Entre os benefícios associados à agricultura regenerativa estão o aumento da matéria orgânica do solo, ganhos de produtividade, maior retenção de água e redução dos riscos relacionados ao clima. Nesse cenário, o Rabobank avalia que será necessário ampliar os mecanismos de financiamento e remuneração ambiental. Entre as alternativas estão prêmios em cadeias de suprimento sustentáveis, linhas de crédito com condições preferenciais e pagamentos por serviços ambientais, incluindo os créditos de carbono. O mercado já conta com metodologias para medir e monitorar o aumento do carbono armazenado no solo. No Brasil, os primeiros projetos avançam pelas etapas de validação, monitoramento e emissão de créditos. Segundo a análise elaborada por Andrés Padilla, Fernanda Casagrande e Roberto Strumpf, do Rabobank, a expansão dependerá do avanço dos projetos, da adesão dos produtores, do crescimento da demanda, da segurança regulatória e da manutenção da integridade ambiental.

artigo.texto: How Data Center Growth Is Reshaping Facility Design Rapid demand, AI workloads and power constraints are pushing developers into new markets while changing how data centers are designed and operated. September 28, 2026 By Jeff Wardon, Jr., Assistant Editor Key Takeaways: - Data center demand is pushing developers beyond traditional markets as they seek available power, land, connectivity and workforce capacity in emerging locations. - AI workloads are increasing power density and driving greater adoption of liquid cooling, adaptive reuse and other approaches to meet growing capacity needs. - Rapid growth is accelerating changes in data center mechanical and electrical design as operators seek new ways to overcome power and capacity constraints. North American data center demand reached 25 gigawatts (GW) of absorption in the first half of 2026, while vacancy has fallen to 1 percent or below, according to JLL’s North America Data Center Report Midyear 2026. However, this rapid growth isn’t due to AI alone. Society continues to create and consume more data, with data creation growing at roughly 23 to 25 percent annually, says Sean Farney, vice president of data center strategy at JLL. The bigger picture is that data center development is basically responding to the increasing demand for and dependence on digital services. “This is similar to what happened 100 years ago or so with the introduction of electricity,” Farney says. “Once people saw the benefits of electricity, they wanted to have electrical devices and they consumed more electricity. So, we’re dealing with a very similar kind of societal force. The industry is positioned well to take advantage of this new paradigm and the way we operate as humans.” Changes in site selection The ongoing shortage of land and power in traditional data center markets is changing how developers select sites. Historically, development was clustered around major metropolitan or telecommunications hubs such as Chicago, Dallas, Atlanta, Washington, New York and Los Angeles. Farney describes this as a shift towards what he calls a “de-marketization” of data center site selection. “So, it’s forced this new, what I call this new de-marketization of data center site selection,” Farney says. “It used to be there were things like markets, a real estate topic. Now the data center developers are simply going to where they can get to revenue fastest.” Factors influencing site selection now include power availability, fiber and network connectivity, land, taxes and regulations and workforce availability. New areas for data centers are being considered as well, including West Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana and Wisconsin. Moreover, developers are becoming more willing to solve individual site constraints rather than limiting development to established markets. However, this geographic shift poses a second issue: What happens when major infrastructure projects enter communities that haven’t traditionally hosted them? “When a data center comes into town, a whole bunch of jobs are created,” Farney says. “I built a data center in suburban Chicago years ago, and I kept 600 union electricians busy for more than nine months working triple shifts. That supported a lot of families, putting a lot of meals on tables.” Similarly, he points to large multi-gigawatt developments in West Texas as examples where entire towns are being employed for development projects. “JLL hired more than a couple of 100 people to staff a large project in Abilene over the last few years,” Farney says. “We work with local trades, local colleges and so on, to find, train and hire folks.” AI and changing data center requirements While AI is the fastest-growing segment, Farney cautions against treating it as the only source of growth. Traditional cloud-service-provider data centers continue to be built as well. AI facilities can operate at 50+ kilowatts (kW) per cabinet, he says. They also require much higher power density, and liquid cooling is becoming increasingly important for those environments. Farney adds that liquid cooling can be about 40 percent more efficient than moving air around in a closed-loop system. The bigger idea is that the basis of design for data centers is changing rapidly, as mechanical and electrical technologies have evolved significantly in just the past few years. Additionally, enterprises are reconsidering older on-premises data centers that had previously been emptied in favor of cloud computing. Some of these facilities may be retrofitted to support higher-density AI workloads. “It generally saves money over the long term for the enterprises,” Farney says. “It’s an adaptive reuse project. It’s not going out and trying to build a new data center. You don’t have to compete with the big guys. So that’s a great solution to some of this low vacancy that we’re seeing across the US.” Another consistent constraint is utility power availability. Developers are increasingly exploring their own power generation, including natural-gas generation, rather than waiting on traditional utility connections. This further illustrates how the industry is adapting its infrastructure strategy to keep pace with demand. Overall, the industry has historically been relatively conservative about mechanical and electrical systems because reliability is paramount, says Farney. However, pressure to bring capacity online is accelerating the adoption of cutting-edge technologies. “I really like to emphasize the massive change in data center basis of design,” Farney says. “We’ve experienced more change in the last three years from a tech perspective, the mechanical and electrical tech that runs data centers than we saw in the prior 20 years. I see all kinds of fascinating new technologies as part of this creative destruction as we move faster.” Jeff Wardon, Jr., is the assistant editor for the facilities market. artigo.texto: Projeto de níquel na Indonésia avança com plano híbrido de solar e armazenamento A Indonésia avançou com um projeto híbrido de energia solar fotovoltaica e armazenamento de energia em baterias desenvolvido pela PT. Kolaka Nickel Indonesia, segundo comunicado da fonte. A instalação fica em Oko Oko, Pomalaa, na Regência de Kolaka, no Sudeste de Sulawesi, e combina um parque solar de 20 MWp com um sistema de armazenamento de energia de 20 MW / 30 MWh. O projeto representa um investimento corporativo em energia limpa autogerada, destinado a apoiar operações industriais. O financiamento foi obtido em janeiro de 2026 por meio de financiamento sem recurso de três bancos: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (Indonesia) Limited, também conhecido como ICBC Indonesia; Standard Chartered Bank Indonesia; e China CITIC Bank International Limited, ou CNCBI. A contratante de engenharia, aquisição e construção é a The 11th Design & Research Institute of Electronics Industry Co., Ltd., referida como EDRI. Essa empresa supervisionará o projeto, a aquisição e a construção da instalação de solar com armazenamento. Os módulos fotovoltaicos de alta eficiência da usina estão sendo fornecidos pela fabricante ZNSHINE SOLAR. Os módulos foram selecionados por sua durabilidade e desempenho e são projetados para resistir às condições tropicais da Indonésia, ao mesmo tempo que sustentam a confiabilidade de longo prazo do sistema. A entrada em operação está prevista para março de 2027. Uma vez em operação, espera-se que a instalação proporcione benefícios de descarbonização para as operações locais do setor de níquel. O projeto é apresentado como evidência de que a colaboração entre o desenvolvedor, a contratante de EPC e os credores internacionais pode apoiar tanto a gestão ambiental quanto a competitividade industrial. Seu desenvolvimento é descrito como um marco no caminho da Indonésia rumo a maior sustentabilidade e autossuficiência energética, à medida que o país continua a expandir a infraestrutura de energia renovável para a descarbonização industrial. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Daily presents a selection of the latest developments from China's automotive industry. Here are the key stories in this edition. FAW Group, GAIG Automobile Form Alliance FAW Group and Guangzhou Automobile Industry Group ("GAIG Automobile"), the controlling shareholder of GAC Group, signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement on September 29. The two state-owned automakers plan to strengthen coordination in assets and capital, technological innovation, and cross-regional industrial resources, drawing on their respective strengths in manufacturing, brands, global operations, and key automotive technologies. The agreement comes as GAC Group advances a major asset restructuring. Under a proposal disclosed on September 28, the listed automaker plans to acquire a 50% stake in FAW Toyota through a share issuance. The strategic partnership and the proposed transaction will move forward in parallel. China Unveils 2026-2030 Battery Plan China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and six other government departments have jointly released a plan for the new-type battery industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030), setting out development goals and key priorities. A key target is to achieve initial large-scale commercialization of all-solid-state batteries by 2030. The plan also calls for major advances in next-generation battery technologies, while targeting a cycle life of 15,000 cycles for long-life lithium batteries and product defect rates at the parts-per-billion level for leading manufacturers. The plan outlines 19 key tasks across five areas, including breakthroughs in all-solid-state battery industrialization, development of next-generation battery chemistries and a supply system centered on lithium-ion batteries alongside sodium-ion and flow batteries. It also calls for stronger battery recycling and the development of standards for emerging technologies. Beyond technology, China plans to promote the digital and green transformation of battery manufacturing and support battery companies expanding overseas. The policy also calls for international cooperation and measures to address overseas technical trade barriers, signaling an effort to strengthen China's battery industry across both technology development and global markets. XPeng's Carbon Credit Revenue Tops RMB 1 Billion XPeng has reportedly reached carbon credit deals with Porsche and several other international automakers covering emissions regulations in the EU, UK and Australia, generating more than RMB 1 billion ($140 million) in total revenue. XPeng's vice president confirmed that the reports were accurate, with the company expected to generate more than RMB 500 million in carbon credit revenue in 2026. The deals come as automakers face increasingly stringent emissions requirements in overseas markets. According to European Commission documents, Porsche has opted out of Volkswagen Group's internal CO₂ emissions pool and plans to form an independent open compliance pool for 2026–2027, with XPeng identified as a key partner. Under EU rules, automakers can form emissions pools and use surplus credits from low-emission manufacturers to offset excess emissions. XPeng's growing overseas sales are helping build its position as a potential carbon credit supplier. Its overseas deliveries topped 20,000 units in the second quarter, up 81% year on year, while overseas business accounted for more than 25% of revenue in the first half. From January to July, XPeng ranked first among Chinese new-energy brands in pure-electric sales in several European markets, including Norway, Denmark, France and Portugal. The development highlights a potential new revenue stream for Chinese automakers expanding overseas. As emissions regulations tighten globally, carbon credits are becoming an increasingly strategic asset, allowing automakers with strong EV sales to monetize their regulatory compliance advantages beyond vehicle sales themselves.

artigo.texto: Kandi Technologies’ China Battery Exchange Secures Follow-On Order for CATL Heavy-Truck Battery Swap Stations Second Batch Order in Two Months Underscores Growing Value of CATL Partnership Jinhua, China, Sept. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Kandi Technologies Group, Inc. ("Kandi" or the "Company") (NASDAQ GS: KNDI), a global innovator in intelligent equipment and a technology-driven platform company, today announced that its wholly-owned subsidiary, China Battery Exchange (Zhejiang) Technology Co., Ltd. ("China Battery Exchange"), has secured a second batch procurement order for heavy-truck battery swap station equipment from QIJI Energy, a subsidiary of Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited ("CATL"). The order follows just two months after the initial batch order placed in July 2026, highlighting the continued commercial development of the Company's relationship with CATL. China Battery Exchange's cooperation with CATL began in August 2025, when the two companies signed a Framework Procurement Contract under which China Battery Exchange became part of CATL's global supplier network and began coordinating CATL's first order for a heavy-truck battery swap station, which was secured later that month. In January 2026, China Battery Exchange entered into a three-year strategic cooperation agreement to serve as a designated equipment supplier for QIJI Energy's heavy-truck battery-swapping program. In July 2026, QIJI Energy placed its first batch procurement order under the strategic cooperation agreement, marking China Battery Exchange's transition from product validation to commercial deployment. With its supplier relationship with CATL and approved-supplier status with QIJI Energy, China Battery Exchange is positioned to pursue additional equipment orders in connection with CATL's heavy-truck battery-swapping program . China Battery Exchange's Lin'an intelligent manufacturing facility commenced production in July 2026. With an expected annual production capacity of up to 200 battery swap stations, the facility is intended to support China Battery Exchange's ability to fulfill existing and potential future orders from CATL and serve additional battery swap equipment customers. Feng Chen, CEO of Kandi, commented, "We have received two batch orders within eight months of signing the QIJI Energy agreement, reflecting CATL's continued confidence in our products and delivery capabilities as well as the commercial potential of this partnership. We will continue to advance product development, expand production capacity and improve delivery efficiency to capture opportunities in the emerging heavy-truck battery swap market and establish battery swap equipment as a new growth engine for Kandi."

artigo.texto: Marisa Wanzeller, da Agência iNFRA A Echoenergia, braço de geração renovável do grupo Equatorial, defende que o leilão de baterias, agendado para dezembro deste ano, seja adiado caso a regra de custeio não mude. Atualmente, a legislação atribui aos geradores o pagamento dos encargos de contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. “A gente entende que um adiamento de dois a quatro meses, se necessário, é pouco relevante para efeitos do sistema elétrico e é um tempo suficiente para que a gente discuta e resolva o problema”, apontou o CEO da companhia, Liu Aquino, em entrevista à Agência iNFRA. Ele minimizou o risco de uma possível mudança de rota na política energética em 2027: “ninguém vai ser contra uma solução de menor custo marginal para o consumidor”. O executivo afirmou que o modelo vigente gera insegurança jurídica e levará a um leilão pouco competitivo, com custos altos de contratação devido aos riscos. Isso, na sua avaliação, prejudicaria a expansão das baterias no país. Medida Provisória Mesmo que o tema ainda passe por regulamentação na ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), a agência não poderá ultrapassar o dispositivo legal nos seus normativos. Dessa forma, torna-se necessária uma alteração da lei, aponta o CEO da Echoenergia. Para evitar que o certame seja postergado, ele sugere que o governo edite uma MP (Medida Provisória), diante da improbabilidade de o Congresso votar um projeto de lei antes de dezembro. Para ele, apesar da incerteza sobre a aprovação da medida e de sua transformação em lei posteriormente, realizar o leilão durante a vigência da MP daria mais segurança para o investidor do que o cenário atual. “O ideal era que houvesse um projeto de lei aprovado no Congresso. Agora, entre o cenário atual, que não tem nada, e o cenário de ter uma MP que vai ser discutida junto ao legislativo, a gente entende que o cenário da MP é de menor risco.” O deputado federal Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) apresentou, ainda em julho, o PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, que revoga o trecho da Lei 15.269/2025 que é considerado ruim pelos geradores. A matéria, contudo, ainda está parada e – em meio às eleições – tem poucas chances de tramitar nas duas casas legislativas a tempo da realização do certame. Custos O CEO da Echoenergia entende que os geradores vão subsidiar o leilão de baterias, uma vez que o benefício financeiro a eles será menor que o custo dos sistemas de armazenamento. Segundo levantamento da empresa, caso a alternativa de rateio entre todos os geradores conforme a flexibilidade da fonte prevaleça, o custo da contratação para os agentes eólicos e solares ficará em cerca de R$ 10,8 por MWh (megawatt-hora) a cada 5 GW (gigawatts) de potência. Considerando que toda a potência contratada seja utilizada para evitar curtailment, o benefício seria de R$ 2,6/MWh e R$ 4,7/MWh para os geradores eólicos e solares, respectivamente. “O leilão de bateria não está com propósito ou com racional econômico de atender os geradores e eles estariam pagando por isso. Na prática, o leilão de bateria estaria sendo subsidiado por investimentos que já foram feitos, por contratos e outorgas que estão no sistema há alguns anos e estariam pagando esta compra”, avalia Liu Aquino. Dessa forma, o executivo entende que a contratação deve ser bancada pelo consumidor, uma vez que o principal objetivo do leilão seria atender à demanda nos horários de “ponta”, quando a carga aumenta e a geração renovável cai. Na visão do CEO, a contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento irá reduzir a necessidade de contratação de térmicas, levando a um benefício econômico. Enquanto as baterias custariam entre R$ 600/MWh e R$ 800/MWh, as termelétricas seriam cerca de R$ 2.300/MWh. Acesso à transmissão Outro ponto que preocupa os agentes, segundo Liu Aquino, é a falta de regulamentação da Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) antes da realização do leilão de baterias. Isso porque, sem uma especificação, os sistemas de armazenamento terão que concorrer por espaço na rede durante as temporadas de acesso. O ideal, do ponto de vista da Echoenergia, seria o espaço na rede garantido para os lotes que ganharem o certame. “Esse processo de aprovação de conexão do sistema de bateria precisa ser sujeito somente a questões técnicas, e não a fluxo de potência. A restrição do fluxo de potência já tem que ser definida no leilão, porque não dá para o empreendedor entrar lá no leilão e assumir todos os compromissos para ver se vai poder conectar depois”, apontou.
