artigo.texto: Candidates in 5th Congressional District race discuss AI and data centers at forum Republican and Democratic candidates weigh in on energy production and environmental concerns MONROE, La. (KNOE) - A forum was held Tuesday night for the 5th Congressional District race, featuring candidates from both major parties. Republican candidates Stewart Cathey, Misti Cordell, Michael Echols, Gabe Firment and Austin Magee attended the forum. On the Democratic side, Dan McKay and Pat Moore also weighed in. One topic at the forefront of the forum was artificial intelligence and data centers. When asked about energy production and environmental concerns surrounding the growing industry, Republican candidates Magee, Firment and Cathey said there needs to be some oversight. “What frustrates me is seeing that all of this red tape being cut for AI companies when the people need more power, we need better infrastructure, we can’t seem to get it. But the second that a small group of elites want to build God in a box and build these massive AI data centers, all red tape is immediately cut for them and they can have whatever they want,” Magee said. “The first thing that Congress needs to do is pass Ratepayer Protection Act which will ensure that as we see this growth of energy resources being spent here in this country that the companies that are actually using the energy are the ones that are paying it, not passing it on to the rate payer,” Cathey said. “You have to protect the consumer. It’s also absolutely imperative that we take care of our water and our natural resources. I passed House Resolution 374 last session to instruct the state to do just that, to study the use of one of our most precious natural resources, our water,” Firment said. Two Republicans, Cordell and Echols, said they see the lack of infrastructure for data centers as an opportunity to grow. “Nuclear is something that’s very effective and it’s also clean. Also hardening our grids. That’s something we have not done since the 70s. And the pellet technology. Part of this district is loggers, so any of the pellet technology could be a new version of energy,” Cordell said. “I passed a resolution that would encourage more nuclear, small nuclear reactor, and other types of fuels. I think Louisiana is a fuel-rich state. We just have to use the resources we’ve got to produce that,” Echols said. The Democratic candidates agreed with Magee, Cathey and Firment, saying there needs to be more regulations and laws placed on this type of growth. “I just believe that they have a lot of constitutional power. We’re going to have to look to make sure that we exercise that. And anything that is not healthy, not for the best interests of the people, then they’re going to have to make that decision,” Moore said. “We need some rules. And I say we get together in Congress and we make some rules to control the haphazard growth of these types of things,” McKay said. Republican Oscar “Omar” Dantzler and Democrat Antonio Wilson were not in attendance. The deadline to register to vote in the November election is Oct. 5, by mail or in person. If you would like to register to vote, you can visit the Secretary of State’s website here. The full forum can be found on under the streaming tab of our website. Copyright 2026 KNOE. artigo.texto: Volkswagen slows gigafactory battery manufacturing plans in Ontario Subscribe to our free newsletter today to keep up to date with the latest manufacturing news. Volkswagen’s battery subsidiary PowerCo is pushing back the start of operations at its St. Thomas, Ontario, gigafactory to 2029, extending a timetable that had originally targeted the first battery cells for 2027 and giving the company more time to align production with changing market conditions. The shift adds two years to the schedule for one of Canada’s largest electric vehicle manufacturing investments, but it does not represent a retreat from the project because construction is continuing and the planned industrial scale remains largely unchanged. Volkswagen has said the plant could represent an investment of as much as C$7 billion, or about US$4.9 billion, by 2030, with annual production capacity eventually reaching up to 90 GWh and as many as 3000 direct skilled jobs supported at full development, alongside additional employment across the regional supply chain. The revised timetable matters beyond St. Thomas because battery manufacturers are trying to build factories that will operate for decades while the market they are designed to serve is evolving far more quickly, particularly as EV demand, vehicle platforms, battery chemistry and manufacturing economics continue to change. The two-year extension could strengthen the factory’s production ramp St. Thomas holds an important position in PowerCo’s global manufacturing network because Volkswagen has described the Ontario facility as the company’s first overseas gigafactory and its largest planned battery cell factory. At full expansion, the plant’s potential annual capacity of 90 GWh would make it a significant supplier to Volkswagen Group electric vehicle production in North America, giving the company a large regional source of battery cells while reducing dependence on longer and more complex international supply chains. The plant is based on PowerCo’s standardized factory concept and Unified Cell strategy, which are designed to create greater manufacturing consistency across several locations while still allowing battery cells to be adapted to different vehicle requirements and market conditions. Moving the start of operations from 2027 to 2029 changes the economics of the production ramp because a battery factory does not create value simply by having its equipment installed and its production lines available. Its financial performance depends heavily on utilization rates, production yields, material costs, customer demand and the ability to operate complex equipment at a sufficiently high volume to spread fixed costs across a large number of cells. Bringing major production capacity online before vehicle manufacturers are ready to absorb it can create an expensive mismatch between supply and demand, leaving costly machinery operating below its intended utilization rate while manufacturers continue to carry significant fixed operating expenses. A more gradual commissioning schedule gives battery producers more room to align cell output with vehicle programs, supplier contracts and regional demand rather than bringing large volumes online before the market can consistently support them. This approach has become more relevant as automakers reassess the pace of their electric vehicle investments and reconsider how quickly new platforms, factories and battery programs should be introduced across North America. The shift does not suggest that electrification has stopped, but it does show that manufacturers are becoming more selective about when individual factories should reach full production and how quickly capital-intensive capacity should be brought into service. For suppliers, logistics operators and industrial service providers, a two-year change to battery production can affect warehouse planning, inbound material contracts, equipment commissioning, workforce requirements, transport volumes and the timing of supplier investments tied to the plant. PowerCo can use the extra time to transfer technology from Europe The revised schedule could have another important consequence because the St. Thomas factory that begins producing batteries in 2029 may benefit from substantially more manufacturing experience than the plant that was originally expected to begin operations two years earlier. PowerCo began cell production at its Salzgitter gigafactory in Germany in late 2025, and Volkswagen has positioned that facility as the lead plant for subsequent battery operations in Valencia, Spain, and St. Thomas. That structure gives the Canadian operation more time to absorb production knowledge developed elsewhere in the network before it moves into high-volume manufacturing, which could influence how equipment is configured, how quality is managed and how operating procedures are designed. Battery manufacturing is particularly sensitive to this type of learning because improvements in production yield, quality control, energy consumption, material handling and equipment reliability can materially change the cost of every cell leaving a factory. Experience accumulated during the ramp-up of earlier plants can therefore affect the performance of later facilities, particularly when production teams are able to identify recurring problems before new factories reach commercial scale. Battery chemistry is evolving at the same time, creating another reason why a later production date could materially affect how the St. Thomas operation is configured when it begins manufacturing cells. Volkswagen, PowerCo and Chinese battery producer Gotion expanded their partnership in September 2026 to cover industrial production of lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, cells and cathode active materials in Europe, with Valencia expected to become an important European production hub for LFP technology. artigo.texto: Democrats See Opening In Long-Red Seat Over Data Center Tax Breaks Rally in River Falls spotlights anger over a $1.6 billion exemption and its GOP author, Shannon Zimmerman. Democrats trying to flip a Wisconsin Assembly seat long held by Republicans are hoping anti-data center sentiment will help them oust a GOP incumbent they call the “architect” of tax breaks helping drive a data center building boom in Wisconsin. Republican Assemblyman Shannon Zimmerman has held the 30th District for a decade. He says Democrats are trying to mislead voters, but Democratic challenger Kevin Knoke says Zimmerman is an AI executive with a conflict of interest. The sounds of speeches and the occasional chants of opposition to AI data center development and the state tax break for the industry echoed from the small Veterans Park in Downtown River Falls on a warm, sunny Wednesday evening. The 50 or so people were members of the western Wisconsin grassroots activism group called GROWW and they held signs that read “No Blank Checks For Big Tech” and “No Deals Behind Closed Doors.” The rally was aimed squarely at Zimmerman, R-River Falls, who authored legislation resulting in a tax exemption for the data center equipment and software. The Wisconsin Department of Revenue has estimated the tax exemption would cut an estimated $1.6 billion from the state’s coffers. “AI data centers are not only extracting water, but they’re also extracting wealth from our communities that could be invested into the things that real people need in their lives,” GROWW co-executive Director Bill Hogseth told the crowd before encouraging them to support Zimmerman’s Democratic challenger, Knoke, who was standing in the audience. Zimmerman’s 2023 bill had backing from Microsoft, business groups and several utilities that would be selling massive amounts of electricity to data centers. It even garnered some Democratic votes, but it never cleared the Legislature. Instead, the bill’s language was included in that year’s state budget, which was signed by Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Wisconsin has seen a data center building boom since the tax breaks were enacted, which has given rise to a surge of opposition from communities around the state. In an interview with WPR, Knoke said the high cost of gas, groceries and housing are top of mind for voters he’s talked to, but they’re also concerned about data centers looking to build in the 30th District. “One thing I can tell you right away is, I am not interested in tax giveaways to corporations,” said Knoke. “They need to pay their fair share.” Knoke has been accusing Zimmerman of having a data center conflict of interest because the lawmaker’s job history shows he’s held two executive positions with AI companies that could benefit from the tax breaks. Knoke said he’s not proposing an outright data center ban, but the state has to be careful. “We’ve got to move incredibly slow,” said Knoke. “I want to see that there’s ratepayer protections. I want to see that there are environmental protections. I want to see that there’s transparency, and most importantly, I want to see that there’s accountability. I want to know that these places are going to be held accountable for everything that they do.” In an emailed statement sent to WPR, Zimmerman said the criticisms from Knoke and fellow Democrats are “political fodder in a desperate act to mislead voters on a topic that is hyper political.” He said he started a tech business in River Falls 20 years ago and Knoke can’t prove a conflict of interest “because it simply is not true.” “My opponent is losing so he must now invent a narrative to scare voters,” Zimmerman wrote. “The original sales and use tax exemption is a long-standing economic practice used to drive major investment into WI. Gov Evers signed it. It was bipartisan. Evolving from that, for those who expressed concerns, I responded as the author of AB840. It specifically addresses energy, water, land and taxpayer concerns.” Zimmerman’s bill sought to require the Wisconsin Public Service Commission to ensure costs of upgrading electrical grids were not passed on to residential customers and require data centers to report how much water they use and set money aside for reclaiming land after the facilities close. The bill passed the Assembly with the help of just three Democrats, but died in the Senate. This year, the Public Service Commission took matters into its own hands by modifying a proposal from We Energies setting electric rates for data center-scale customers. At the time, the commission said the changes were meant to protect residential ratepayers and ensure data centers pay their own way. As public opposition to data centers has grown, Republican and Democratic candidates have been accusing each other of cozying up to big tech. Whether that line of attack on Zimmerman will help Knoke flip the Assembly seat is an open question, as Democrats have been unable to win the 30th District since 1977. artigo.texto: Alberto Kuba, CEO da WEG: 'não imaginávamos que teria esse boom' (Leandro Fonseca/Exame) Repórter Publicado em 30 de setembro de 2026 às 05h00. A multinacional fabricante de equipamentos elétricos WEG anunciou, entre sexta-feira, 25, e segunda-feira, 28, novos investimentos em baterias e geradores para atender à expansão de data centers e redes elétricas. BTG Pactual, Ativa Investimentos e Citi veem potencial de crescimento nos projetos, embora o impacto sobre os resultados deva ocorrer de forma gradual. A WEG (WEGE3) não esperava o ritmo que os data centers imprimiriam ao negócio de geradores. "Não imaginávamos que teria esse boom", afirmou Alberto Kuba, CEO da companhia, em entrevista para a edição 2026 do prêmio Maiores e Melhores, da Revista EXAME. Segundo o executivo, a demanda pelo equipamento ganhou força com a expansão dos data centers, que precisam de grupos geradores para garantir o fornecimento de energia em caso de interrupções. E a reação da companhia a esse movimento vem aparecendo cada vez mais nos investimentos.Na última sexta-feira, 25, a multinacional que fabrica equipamentos elétricos anunciou a ampliação da fábrica de baterias em Santa Catarina e, três dias depois, na segunda, 28, divulgou um investimento de US$ 165 milhões, cerca de R$ 869 milhões, para aumentar a produção de geradores na América do Norte. Os dois movimentos colocam a WEG em uma frente que combina geração, armazenamento e infraestrutura elétrica — e que ganhou força com o avanço dos data centers e a necessidade de redes mais robustas. Para o BTG Pactual (do mesmo grupo controlador da EXAME), Ativa Investimentos e Citi, os movimentos colocam a WEG em segmentos que podem sustentar o crescimento da companhia nos próximos anos, embora os efeitos dos novos investimentos sobre os resultados devam aparecer de forma gradual. No caso da iniciativa para ampliar a capacidade de produção de geradores na América do Norte, o projeto será dividido em duas fases e foi anunciado com foco na crescente demanda por soluções de geração de energia para aplicações críticas nos Estados Unidos, especialmente para atender à expansão dos data centers. A primeira fase receberá US$ 24 milhões para a aquisição e adequação de um prédio industrial próximo ao atual Parque Industrial Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula, no México. A unidade será destinada à montagem de geradores e tem início de operação previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Na segunda etapa, a WEG pretende investir US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais, em local ainda a ser definido na América do Norte. A estrutura terá produção verticalizada, incluindo a fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças. Com a conclusão da segunda fase, prevista para 2030, a capacidade global da WEG para fabricar geradores deverá passar das atuais 10 unidades por dia para cerca de 50. A produção será distribuída entre as fábricas da companhia no México, EUA, Brasil e China. O movimento amplia uma operação que já vem se beneficiando da expansão dos data centers. "O negócio de alternadores, sob a marca Marathon, tem apresentado um forte desempenho, apoiado pela robusta demanda por energia de reserva por parte dos data centers", escreveu o BTG em relatório nesta terça-feira, 29. Para o banco, o novo investimento aumenta a capacidade da WEG de atender a uma demanda que tende a exigir cada vez mais equipamentos para garantir o fornecimento de energia. O BTG considera o anúncio positivo e afirma que a expansão cria uma plataforma para o crescimento do negócio de geração de energia da companhia na América do Norte no médio prazo. O banco, porém, ressalta que o investimento não deve trazer uma contribuição relevante para o lucro imediatamente. Mas ressalta que "embora os gastos de capital iniciais impliquem uma contribuição limitada para os lucros no curto prazo, a adição de capacidade deve proporcionar uma plataforma para um maior crescimento dos negócios de geração de energia da WEG na América do Norte no médio prazo", afirmou. "A WEG realizará seu Investor Day nesta semana, onde esperamos mais detalhes sobre sua estratégia para aproveitar as oportunidades de crescimento no mercado norte-americano", acrescentou o banco sobre o evento que ocorre nesta sexta-feira, 2. O investimento em geradores veio três dias depois de outro anúncio relacionado à infraestrutura de energia. Na sexta-feira, 25, a WEG ampliou o projeto de sua fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, os BESS, em Itajaí, no litoral norte catarinense. O investimento previsto para a unidade passou de R$ 280 milhões para R$ 330 milhões, enquanto a capacidade anual de produção foi dobrada, de 2 para 4 gigawatts-hora (GWh). O início das operações está previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027. A expansão ocorre às vésperas do primeiro leilão de armazenamento de energia do país, previsto para dezembro de 2026. A expectativa é de crescimento da demanda por baterias para integrar fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica, ao sistema elétrico. Na avaliação da Ativa Investimentos, há aí uma oportunidade para a WEG. "Como temos discutido, as iniciativas de BESS e o crescimento de data centers são os principais gatilhos para destravar valor para a companhia", disse o analista da casa, Lucas Dias. O Citi também coloca os dois anúncios dentro de uma mesma tese. Para o banco, geradores para data centers e sistemas de armazenamento aumentam a exposição da WEG a dois segmentos ligados à expansão da infraestrutura energética. No caso dos geradores, o Citi destaca que a capacidade global da companhia deverá passar de 10 para 50 unidades por dia após a conclusão do projeto em 2030. Já no BESS, chama atenção para a velocidade da expansão: em sete meses, a WEG dobrou a capacidade planejada da fábrica e aumentou o investimento em R$ 50 milhões. artigo.texto: Anju Singh served as the host for a community forum in Cumberland County about data centers on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. Haley O'Brien / WITF Curious and concerned residents heard from experts, officials and organizers about data center development — and efforts to challenge it — during a community forum in Cumberland County on Tuesday. Environmental lawyers discussed the developments’ potential effect on the region’s water and power grid while organizers of local grassroots groups shared tips for residents concerned about proposed projects. John Werner is a member of Stewards of Cumberland County, an advocacy group that formed in response to data center developments. “We were one of the first organizations that formed locally, and we formed because people were not getting off Facebook,” he said. Werner spoke about what he called “the importance of people power.” “There are residents who have mounted robust challenges in municipalities all over the place and beat these data centers,” Werner said. “And our strongest weapon in this fight is one another.” Michael Ewall, founder of the Energy Justice Network, shared how the developments are projected to strain the power grid. “By 2030, we need about 60% increase in electric generation to meet the demand… which is largely being driven by the data center boom,” he said. Residents concerned about potential data center developments in their neighborhoods also asked what they can do to challenge the projects. “I feel very tiny in a very big space,” said Harrisburg resident Amara Nazario, who is in the early stages of forming a community group to advocate against proposed developments in Swatara Twp., Dauphin County. “I’m still just wrapping my head around everything and jumping into a fight,” she said. Werner recommended those who live in a community with a project in the works to find a way to slow down the process. “The more hurdles that you can throw up, the more inconvenient it is for the developers,” he said. Amy Zeigler, from the group Protect South Hanover PA, had flyers and a presentation prepared to show the impact of a proposed data center on surrounding communities. She suggested groups work together and share each other’s strengths, including graphic design, public speaking and organizational skills. Dauphin County Commissioner Justin Douglas did not say he supports data centers. But he said municipalities are struggling to balance budgets and these expensive developments can provide significant revenue. artigo.texto: A expansão da inteligência artificial no mundo inteiro tem levado à corrida pela construção de data centers para suprir as necessidades de processamento desta tecnologia, e o Brasil é um palco importante para este desenvolvimento. Ao mesmo tempo que as empresas querem expandir os seus negócios, crescem as notícias sobre o impacto da construção de data centers nas cidades. Um exemplo é a cidade de Paracatu, em Minas Gerais, onde vereadores da Câmara Municipal descobriram que em breve a obra de um data center começará na região. O site O Eco fez uma reportagem sobre a referida obra, mostrando que não se trata de um data center qualquer: o equipamento terá a potência de 1 gigawatt, “maior que a soma total de todos os data centers atualmente instalados no país, que consomem cerca de 800 megawatts”. Só que a construção de data centers pode provocar danos ambientais, alto consumo de água e aumento do custo de energia para o consumidor, sem trazer benefícios reais para a população e para o país. Este assunto foi discutido em audiência pública no Senado em 4 de agosto na Comissão de Ciência e Tecnologia (CCT). O diretor-executivo do Instituto de Defesa do Consumidor (Idec), Igor Britto, ressalta que os data centers de inteligência artificial representam um alto consumo de energia elétrica sem capacidade de adaptação horária das atividades. “Temos empreendimentos de vários setores produtivos que já são organizados e se controlam para, por exemplo, evitar operar e consumir energia nos horários de maior pico. Isso não acontece com os data centers, que vão acabar sobrecarregando o sistema nesses horários. Todos nós pagamos. É necessário ter infraestrutura para mais geração, para mais distribuição, e o pior é que todos esses custos também são bancados pela tarifa. Cidades onde existem data centers tiveram aumento considerável na conta de energia e, quanto ao consumo de água, algumas residências chegam a ficar sem o abastecimento. As cooperativas nas diversas regiões do país precisam ficar atentas aos projetos vindouros, principalmente após a sanção da Lei 15.504, que cria incentivos fiscais para estimular a instalação de data centers, os centros de processamento de dados, e favorecer investimentos em inteligência artificial (IA) no Brasil. Apesar das preocupações com geração de energia e consumo de água, os data centers podem também ser uma forma de expansão tecnológica das cooperativas. Oportunidades No Paraná, um grupo de investidores apresentou em julho, ao Governo do Estado e a instituições paranaenses, a proposta de implantação de um super data center no município de Pinhais, na Região Metropolitana de Curitiba. Na oportunidade, os investidores informaram que têm interesse em realizar negócios com produtos do agronegócio das cooperativas paranaenses, contemplando especialmente soja, milho e proteínas animais. Segundo eles, o grupo projeta movimentar grandes volumes de exportação e conta com estrutura logística própria, incluindo frota e terminais portuários. Foi ainda mencionada a possibilidade de facilitar a aquisição de matérias-primas para a produção de fertilizantes e o fomento na região. Apesar de acreditarem ser um projeto promissor, seguir compromissos de sustentabilidade é necessário para o avanço do projeto.

artigo.texto: Setor de gás natural teme exclusão do Redata e se mobiliza por decreto Regime especial para datacenters prevê incentivos ao uso de fonte de "baixa emissão" para abastecer projetos, mas Fazenda quer limitar incentivos O setor de gás natural iniciou uma ofensiva junto ao governo para evitar que o insumo seja excluído do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center) como fonte de suprimento energético. Conforme relatos feitos à CNN, o decreto de regulamentação da nova lei está perto de sair. Hoje, segundo fontes, a tendência é que prevaleça um entendimento do Ministério da Fazenda de que o gás natural não se enquadra nos critérios para receber os incentivos do Redata. Na reta final de tramitação do projeto, aprovado neste mês pelo Senado, uma emenda de redação substituiu a exigência de uso de energias renováveis e limpas por fontes de "baixa emissão". Entre os combustíveis fósseis, o gás natural é o que menos emite gases-estufa e visto como uma fonte complementar à matriz elétrica, assegurando energia firme de menor geração das renováveis (como solar e eólica). O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) já se posicionou favoravelmente à inclusão do gás na regulamentação do Redata, mas a Fazenda é contra. Diante da indefinição, o setor foi na sexta-feira (25) ao MDIC (Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços), encarado como um possível aliado no impasse entre Fazenda e MME. Representantes do IBP (Instituto Brasileiro do Petróleo), da Abegás (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado) e da Abraget (Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas) estiveram com o secretário-adjunto de Desenvolvimento Industrial do MDIC, Luis Felipe Giesteira. Quatro possibilidades estão sendo aventadas: - Liberação do gás natural como fonte de suprimento energético - Liberação do gás natural com compensação das emissões geradas - Incentivos somente para fontes renováveis (energia nova ou existente) - Incentivos somente para investimentos novos em fontes renováveis (critério de adicionalidade) Para o diretor-executivo da Abegás, Marcelo Mendonça, a característica de renováveis como solar e eólica é a intermitência, o que comprometeria a estabilidade necessária para o investimento em data centers. O uso de térmicas a gás natural, segundo ele, possibilitaria oferecer uma energia "competitiva e firme" para atrair projetos no setor tecnológico. O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), no entanto, tem dado sinais na direção contrária. "Não vamos deixar que a energia produzida vá somente para o data center. Quem quiser vir para cá terá que investir na construção em energia renovável", disse o petista, no dia 19, em campanha em Santa Catarina. A fala foi interpretada como uma tendência de que o governo optará pelo critério de adicionalidade em fontes limpas como habilitação para o Redata. A iniciativa privada e setores na Esplanada dos Ministérios que discordam disso tentam, nos bastidores, ganhar tempo para discutir melhor a regulamentação antes do decreto presidencial.

artigo.texto: Community voices concerns ahead of new AI data center in Jefferson Davis County JEFFERSON DAVIS COUNTY, Miss. (WDAM) - A digital infrastructure campus is coming to Jefferson Davis County. The developer, Eagle Rock Partners, held a public hearing Tuesday evening to address concerns. Some residents worry about water usage, power rates and the amount of noise the campus will cause, while others want to have a say in whether they build it or not. “We’re concerned about how the traffic for them trying to build this is going to affect our daily lives,” Bassfield Resident Patti Warren said. “There’s a lot involved in all of this, and we just think that the community should have a right to be able to vote.” The campus will cover 800 acres of land near Gum Swamp Road and the Covington County line. Eagle Rock Members say it will offer a projected 200 full-time operational jobs and over 1,000 construction jobs. Economic Development Association Executive Director Gary Russell Bass understands the negative feelings surrounding AI data centers, but he wants the public to understand the opportunities this will bring to the county. “I’ve done a lot of research on this company, I’ve done a lot of research on what they’re saying, and I think that the information that they’re trying to provide the community is a step in the right direction,” Bass said. “I just hope that everybody would come with an open mind, and get all of their questions answered.” Ken Lober with Eagle Rock Partners wanted the meeting to leave no box unchecked. With a project like this already in motion, Lober wanted the community to be involved and know the “why” behind the project. “We aspire to be completely transparent, and this is a big step towards that,” Lober said. “To have the community come out, ask any questions they want, walk through the facts of what this project is, then work with the economic development agency, the county supervisors, and to be able to make sure that the county engineer and everybody validate what we’re saying we’re going to do, and that we do it.” This campus is an estimated $6 billion capital investment. artigo.texto: Gotion High-Tech has secured 6 GWh of battery energy storage capacity under Saudi Arabia’s first utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) procurement program, representing around 75% of the total capacity awarded in the first phase. The award was made by Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) as part of the Kingdom’s efforts to expand energy storage alongside renewable energy deployment. The G1 project has a total capacity of 2 GW/8 GWh and an estimated value of $1.16 billion. Gotion has been selected for three sites: Al Muwayah, Haden, and Al Kahafa. Each site will have a capacity of 500 MW/2 GWh. The award makes Gotion the largest single technology supplier in the first phase of Saudi Arabia’s utility-scale storage program. The projects will deploy Gotion Grid, marking the first international large-scale deployment of the company’s utility-scale energy storage system. According to Gotion, the system is designed for harsh desert conditions and can operate between -30°C and 55°C. The company said its thermal management system is optimized for high-temperature and dusty environments, allowing the batteries to maintain output during sandstorms and reducing high-temperature degradation by 40% compared with conventional systems. The system has a stated design life of 25 years, compared with an industry average of 15–20 years. Gotion Grid also incorporates an artificial intelligence-powered battery management system for intelligent dispatch, safety monitoring, and lifecycle diagnostics. The three projects will be remotely operated and connected to Saudi Arabia’s 380 kV transmission network. The award strengthens Gotion’s presence in the Middle East and North Africa energy storage market. The company said its regional pipeline and projects total around 9 GWh, including a 1.5 GWh BESS project in Egypt and a 1.2 GWh project in Morocco with ACWA Power. In Egypt, Gotion is also planning a 3 GWh local manufacturing facility. Globally, the company said its cumulative system-level energy storage projects have exceeded 10 GWh. Its international portfolio includes a 281 MW/843 MWh solar-plus-storage project in Australia, which is under construction and expected to achieve commercial operation in the first half of 2027. Saudi Arabia has already started the next stage of its storage procurement program, with G2 underway. The G1 award is therefore expected to provide an important reference for future utility-scale BESS tenders as the Kingdom increases renewable energy capacity and strengthens grid flexibility. artigo.texto: ORANGEBURG- Congressman Mike Lawler (R, NY-17) is demanding that Governor Kathy Hochul and the New York Power Authority disclose the value of discounted electricity being provided to data centers in Orangeburg. Lawler’s action follows reporting that three of the four data centers in the Orangeburg section of Orangetown receive discounted hydropower through NYPA’s ReCharge NY program. NYPA has declined to disclose the rates individual facilities pay or the value of their discounts, saying the information is proprietary and protected by contracts. Lawler is calling on the state to at least disclose the total annual cost of the discounts and the average subsidy provided to participating businesses. ReCharge NY is a statewide economic-development program that provides qualifying businesses and nonprofits access to lower-cost hydropower through long-term contracts. NYPA says the program is intended to support business growth and job retention across the state. The issue comes as data centers face increased scrutiny in New York because of their electricity demands. Hochul announced a one-year moratorium on certain new large-scale data center projects in July and said the state would pursue additional protections for ratepayers. Lawler said greater transparency is needed as New York weighs the economic benefits and infrastructure demands associated with data center development. “Transparency has to apply to government too,” Lawler said. “If New York is going to use public power to attract data centers, it should be able to tell the public what the deal is and what taxpayers get in return.”

artigo.texto: Motta conversou com Vorcaro sobre “sociedade” e PL sobre carbono Presidente da Câmara diz que não há ilícito nas conversas e que os diálogos foram descontextualizados Mensagens obtidas pela Polícia Federal mostram que o presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), manteve conversas com o fundador do Banco Master, Daniel Vorcaro, sobre uma “sociedade” relacionada à compra de um terreno em João Pessoa (PB) e sobre um projeto de lei que trata do mercado de carbono. Em 9 de março de 2024, Motta procurou Vorcaro para tratar da negociação de venda de um terreno na capital paraibana. A conversa se deu no mesmo mês em que Bianca Medeiros, cunhada do presidente da Câmara, contraiu um empréstimo de R$ 22 milhões com o Banco Master para a compra de um terreno em João Pessoa. Mercado de carbono Motta e Vorcaro também conversaram em 19 de novembro de 2024 sobre o projeto de lei que regulamenta o mercado de carbono no Brasil. Trata-se do substitutivo do Senado ao PL 182 de 2024. Na mensagem, Motta menciona uma questão relacionada às seguradoras. A alteração feita pelo Senado e posteriormente modificada na Câmara tratava da possibilidade de seguradoras, além de algumas empresas de previdência e capitalização, comprarem “ativos ambientais” negociados no mercado para compor suas reservas técnicas e provisões. A versão aprovada pelo Senado estipulava que essas empresas destinassem, no mínimo, 0,5% dos recursos a esses ativos. A Câmara retomou a redação anterior, que estabelecia percentual de 1% ao ano. O tema interessava aos negócios de Vorcaro. Em junho de 2026, a PF afirmou que o então banqueiro havia enviado textos de propostas legislativas diretamente ao gabinete do senador Ciro Nogueira (PP-PI). Segundo a investigação, os 2 tinham uma “convergência de interesses ilícitos”. Uma das propostas encaminhadas por Vorcaro ao gabinete do senador tratava justamente da regulamentação do mercado de carbono no país. Outro lado O Poder360 entrou em contato com a defesa de Daniel Vorcaro para saber se gostaria de se manifestar sobre o assunto, mas não teve resposta. A reportagem será atualizada caso a parte envie manifestações a este jornal digital. Procurado pelo Poder360, Motta afirmou, em nota, que mantém diálogo com representantes do empresariado e de outros setores da sociedade e disse não haver ilícito nos diálogos divulgados. O presidente da Câmara também afirmou que as conversas foram descontextualizadas e negou ter atuado em benefício próprio ou de terceiros. Motta informou que pretende apresentar queixa-crime contra o senador Veneziano Vital do Rêgo (MDB-PB). Disse que Veneziano promove calúnia, difamação e divulgação de fake news com finalidade eleitoral. O senador concorre à reeleição e tem como adversário na disputa o pai de Motta, Nabor Wanderley (Republicanos-PB). Sobre o empréstimo contratado com o Banco Master, Motta afirmou que a operação ocorreu quando ainda não eram conhecidas as investigações posteriormente divulgadas sobre a instituição financeira e seu proprietário. Leia a nota de Hugo Motta na íntegra: “Enquanto parlamentar em meu quarto mandato na Câmara dos Deputados, sempre mantive diálogo com os diversos segmentos do empresariado e representantes da sociedade brasileira. Enfatizo que não há nenhum ilícito retratado nos diálogos publicados e repudio a tentativa de atribuir conversas descontextualizadas a qualquer relação de interesse espúrio ou de favorecimento por minha parte. Tenho uma vida limpa, assim como é limpa a minha atuação política nesses 15 anos de vida pública. Informo que estou protocolando queixa-crime contra o senador Veneziano Vital do Rego, diante da série de calúnias, de difamação e produção de fake news que ele tem efetivado contra mim neste período eleitoral. Não permitirei a suspeição de ilícitos promovidos por ele, especialmente com fins eleitoreiros. Como já explicitei anteriormente, o contrato de empréstimo realizado por empresa privada com um banco privado se deu quando não se tinha conhecimento dos fatos e investigações que posteriormente vieram a público sobre o Master e o seu dono. Reitero que confio nos órgãos responsáveis pelas investigações, a quem cabe responder pelas apurações.”

artigo.texto: Suntech has showcased its latest N-type PV and energy storage solutions at the 2026 edition of Solar & Storage Live UK in Birmingham, highlighting advances in quarter-cut cell technology, high-efficiency modules and integrated solar-storage applications. The UK solar market continues to expand, driven by strong growth in rooftop installations and the growing integration of solar and battery storage. With solar becoming increasingly important across residential, commercial and utility-scale applications, the market is placing greater emphasis on technologies that can make effective use of available space while delivering reliable energy generation. As solar-storage integration gains momentum, demand for high-efficiency and reliable PV technologies continues to grow across utility-scale projects, industrial and commercial rooftops and residential applications, making module efficiency, energy yield and long-term performance increasingly important considerations for projects in the UK. Against this backdrop, the exhibition featured Suntech’s products across key stages of PV manufacturing, from silicon wafers and solar cells to modules. It also highlighted the continued refinement of N-type quarter-cut cell technology, with a focus on optimizing cell architecture and current distribution to reduce energy losses and improve power generation. By carrying these cell-level advances into module design, the company is further developing high-efficiency module solutions for a range of applications. This approach is particularly relevant to projects where making the most of available installation space and maximizing energy yield are important considerations, including residential and commercial rooftops. This technology is further demonstrated in its Ultra T 3.0 quarter-cut modules, a key highlight of the exhibition. Built on Suntech’s proprietary TOPCon 3.0 cell technology, Ultra T 3.0 combines an optimized quarter-cut cell architecture with advanced high-density encapsulation. The module achieves a cell conversion efficiency of up to 27.5% and a module efficiency of more than 25.2%, enabling higher power output while supporting long-term reliability, its high-efficiency design helping make effective use of available rooftop and project space. Also featured at the exhibition was the Ultra T 2.0, a 520W half-cell N-type TOPCon module, further extending Suntech’s module offering for commercial and residential applications. In addition to its PV portfolio, the company also showcased its self-developed SunStorage energy storage systems for commercial and residential applications. Featuring a modular design, high-voltage architecture and flexible expansion capability, the systems can be combined with Suntech PV modules to provide integrated solutions for households and small businesses, enabling daytime solar generation, energy storage, night time power supply and backup electricity during outages. SunStorage offers both AC-coupled and DC-coupled solutions, providing flexibility for different system configurations and application needs. The combination of PV modules and energy storage enables a more coordinated approach to solar generation, storage and power consumption, supporting the growing demand for integrated solar-storage solutions across the UK market.

artigo.texto: The argument over data centers should include access to the internet. I am not sure to what extent data centers should include the internet, but I do know the internet is a connection of provider servers that are interconnected, and I have little doubt the data centers will be connected to the internet. If you want to slow the internet down, by all means, work to stop data centers. ADVERTISEMENT On the other hand, if your only problem is change and you do not like change, then you have a problem. For better or worse, change, by any definition, is going to happen, and you won't stop it. In my opinion, the only thing you could accomplish during change is to make it work to your advantage. artigo.texto: BYD says it will have an electric vehicle with a solid-state battery in 2027 — InsideEVs Chinese company BYD plans to have its first electric vehicle model with a solid-state battery in 2027. BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li said this in an interview with Carwow.es, InsideEVs reports. First model with the new technology According to Li, the company will “have one model” with this technology next year. She also said that BYD holds a leading position in the development of solid-state batteries. At the same time, the top manager did not specify which model would be equipped with the new battery or when it would appear. It is also unclear whether this refers to a full market launch of the vehicle or a demonstration prototype. The publication notes that Chinese automakers, including BYD, are rapidly introducing new technologies into production models. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Possible Yangwang flagship CarNewsChina sources claim that the solid-state battery may be used in the recently teased flagship sedan of the Yangwang brand. BYD has not confirmed this information. The InsideEVs author suggests that the expensive technology at an early stage could first be used in a premium model, such as the Denza Z9 or BYD Great Tang. Solid-state batteries are considered a promising technology for electric vehicles: they may be lighter and safer, have higher energy density, and support faster charging. At the same time, automakers are still working to resolve technological issues and establish mass production of such batteries. Toyota plans to launch an electric vehicle with this technology in 2027 or 2028, while Honda and Mercedes are targeting a period closer to 2030.

artigo.texto: The Elements of Innovation Discovered Metal Tech News - September 29, 2026 An up to $75 million Pentagon grant awarded to Amprius Technologies to reconfigure an electric vehicle battery production line to one that produces high-energy-density silicon-anode lithium-ion cells for drones highlights an emerging shift in the battery market. Since the introduction of the Nissan LEAF and Chevrolet Volt in 2010, electric vehicles have increasingly driven lithium-ion battery demand. Automakers have shifted among cathode chemistries to balance cost, range, safety, and performance, including the growing use of lower-cost but less energy-dense lithium iron phosphate. Graphite, however, has remained the predominant material on the anode side of both battery types. Drones, robotics, and more compact transportation such as e-bikes are changing the battery equation. Unlike passenger EVs, where cost per kilowatt-hour is a major consideration, drones and other weight-sensitive technologies place a premium on packing more energy into every kilogram and cubic inch of battery. Amprius Technologies is targeting that market with lithium-ion batteries that replace much of the graphite traditionally used on the anode side with silicon, an abundant element capable of storing substantially more lithium than graphite. The challenge is that silicon expands dramatically as it absorbs lithium during charging, which can cause conventional silicon particles to crack and degrade after repeated cycles. Amprius has developed two primary battery platforms to overcome this problem. Designed to deliver maximum energy density, its SiMaxx technology uses a high-purity silicon nanowire anode that provides room for the silicon to expand and contract during charging and discharging while maintaining electrical contact. The company's SiCore platform uses a proprietary silicon-carbon anode material designed to balance high energy density with power, cycle life, manufacturability, and cost. Amprius introduced a second-generation SiCore cell in September capable of being manufactured on conventional lithium-ion battery production equipment. This ability to produce high-energy silicon-anode batteries on existing equipment is central to the Pentagon-backed project. To explain the energy-density advantage in an easy-to-visualize way, Amprius CEO Tom Stepien compares conventional graphite batteries with drip coffee and the company's silicon-anode batteries with espresso. Both can provide roughly the same caffeine, but espresso fits that dose into a much smaller volume. Likewise, an Amprius battery can provide a similar amount of energy in a smaller and lighter package, or significantly more energy within the same weight and space constraints. For a drone, that can mean longer flight time, greater range, or room for additional payload. The U.S. Department of War's Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program has awarded Amprius up to $75 million to bring that technology into high-volume domestic production. Under what the company calls Project acCELLerate, Amprius plans to reconfigure an existing U.S.-based EV battery production line operated by an unnamed major South Korean battery manufacturer to produce advanced silicon-anode pouch cells for unmanned aerial systems. The converted line is expected to be operating by early 2028 with capacity to produce 12 million Amprius cells annually. Amprius estimates the conversion will cost roughly $100 million, including in-kind investments from the company and its South Korean manufacturing partner. "Our technology, combined with the U.S. manufacturing prowess of our South Korean manufacturing partner, positions us to accelerate adoption of standardized, high-performance pouch cells in a fast-growing market," said Stepien. The decision to convert an EV battery production line to manufacture cells for military drones also underscores a changing lithium-ion battery market. EVs created enormous demand for batteries that balance range, longevity, safety, and affordability. Drones, advanced aviation, robotics, light electric vehicles, and other mobile technologies are creating markets where reducing battery weight and volume can be worth paying a premium. This is particularly true for aircraft, where every pound devoted to batteries is a pound that cannot be used for payload, and every improvement in energy density can translate directly into longer flight times. The Pentagon-backed production line could also provide Amprius with the manufacturing scale needed to expand further into commercial drones, robots, e-bikes, electric aviation, and other applications where packing more energy into a smaller space carries a premium. And if higher production volumes and manufacturing efficiencies lower the cost of silicon-anode batteries, the market for the technology could broaden further. That could eventually open the door for EVs and other transportation systems capable of carrying drip-coffee-sized energy in an espresso-sized package.

artigo.texto: Curso abre 35 vagas para segunda turma gratuita de Data Center Programa intensivo da Generation Brasil de 14 semanas prepara pessoas sem experiência para iniciar carreira em tecnologia; iniciativa reúne gigantes do setor como Equinix, Cisco Foundation, ODATA, Vertiv e Cummins. Redes sociais, serviços bancários, streaming, computação em nuvem e ferramentas de inteligência artificial dependem de uma infraestrutura que funciona 24 horas por dia nos bastidores: os data centers. Com a digitalização da economia e o avanço da IA, essa infraestrutura cresce e amplia também a demanda por profissionais preparados para operar, monitorar e dar suporte a esses ambientes. O Brasil já conta com cerca de 163 data centers em operação e ocupa a 11ª posição mundial em número de instalações, reforçando a expansão do setor e a necessidade de formação de novos profissionais. Para ampliar o acesso a essas oportunidades, a Generation Brasil está com inscrições abertas para a segunda turma do Programa de Empregabilidade em Data Center e Suporte de TI, formação 100% gratuita voltada a pessoas que desejam começar uma carreira em tecnologia, mesmo sem experiência prévia, você pode conferir as informações aqui. São 35 vagas para moradores de São Paulo e região. Ao longo de 14 semanas, os participantes terão uma formação intensiva que combina conhecimentos técnicos, desenvolvimento de habilidades comportamentais, preparação para processos seletivos e experiências práticas relacionadas ao dia a dia da profissão. Entre os conteúdos estão fundamentos de data center, servidores, racks e cabeamento, redes, Windows e Linux, ambientes em nuvem, suporte técnico, monitoramento de sistemas, gestão de incidentes, segurança da informação e configuração básica de redes. Formação com dupla certificação amplia possibilidades de carreira Um dos diferenciais desta turma é a dupla certificação em Data Center e Suporte de TI, permitindo que os participantes desenvolvam competências para diferentes posições de entrada na área de tecnologia. Entre as possibilidades profissionais estão cargos como Operador de Data Center, Data Center Technician, Técnico de Infraestrutura, Técnico de Operações, Analista de NOC, Técnico de Suporte, Help Desk e Service Desk Analyst. A formação é híbrida e combina aulas online ao vivo com uma semana de atividades presenciais obrigatórias, aproximando os participantes de ambientes e situações práticas da profissão. Além da formação técnica, os alunos desenvolvem competências como comunicação profissional, trabalho em equipe, organização, resolução de problemas, atenção aos detalhes, adaptabilidade e proatividade. Formação conectada ao setor O programa integra uma iniciativa global liderada pela Equinix, em parceria com Generation, Cisco Foundation, ODATA, Vertiv e Cummins para ampliar a formação de talentos para o setor de data centers. A colaboração aproxima a formação das necessidades encontradas no mercado e proporciona aos participantes contato com empresas e profissionais que atuam diretamente no ecossistema de infraestrutura digital. Mais do que ensinar conteúdos técnicos, a proposta da Generation é apoiar a entrada dos participantes no mercado de trabalho. Durante a jornada, os alunos contam com mentoria de carreira, preparação para processos seletivos e conexão com oportunidades em empresas parceiras. Participantes elegíveis também poderão receber apoios de permanência, como empréstimo de notebook, auxílio para internet e outros recursos, conforme critérios e disponibilidade do programa. “Além de desenvolver conhecimentos técnicos, queremos que os participantes terminem o programa preparados para disputar oportunidades reais no mercado. Nosso papel na Generation é construir essa ponte entre pessoas que buscam uma nova carreira e empresas que precisam de profissionais qualificados, oferecendo formação, preparação para processos seletivos e acompanhamento ao longo dessa jornada”, afirma Andrea Matsui, CEO da Generation Brasil. Quem pode participar O programa é destinado a pessoas com 18 anos ou mais, ensino médio completo, residentes em São Paulo ou região e atualmente sem vínculo empregatício. Não é necessário ter experiência anterior em tecnologia. Também é necessário ter disponibilidade integral para participar da formação de segunda a sexta-feira, das 9h às 17h, durante as 14 semanas, incluindo os momentos presenciais obrigatórios. A Generation incentiva especialmente a participação de mulheres, pessoas pretas e pardas e pessoas LGBTQIAP+, grupos historicamente sub-representados no setor de tecnologia.

artigo.texto: Redata aproxima o Brasil da soberania na infraestrutura digital A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, o Redata, criou condições para acelerar projetos represados e ampliar a capacidade brasileira de processamento. Essa medida gerou uma oportunidade industrial de alcance. Chegou no momento em que a inteligência artificial exige mais servidores, memória, energia e capacidade de rede. O novo modelo tributário destrava bilhões em aportes paralisados diante da corrida pela computação de alto desempenho. Mais de 106 megawatts foram entregues no primeiro semestre de 2026 e outros 134 megawatts estão previstos até dezembro. Cerca de 56% do estoque de data centers em construção no país já apresentava contratos de pré-locação consolidados antes mesmo da aprovação parlamentar e da sanção presidencial. Havia uma demanda latente. O Redata catalisou um mercado preexistente ao eliminar a trava tributária que adiava decisões urgentes. O marco regulatório canaliza e multiplica essa força. A norma alcança dois atores fundamentais. Um deles é a empresa habilitada, responsável por operar o data center. O outro é a coabilitada, que fabrica os equipamentos para essa infraestrutura de TI. Em troca das isenções federais, o operador reserva ao menos 10% da capacidade instalada ao mercado interno e aplica 2% do valor dos equipamentos adquiridos em inovação. O formato operacional dessas contrapartidas, os critérios de sustentabilidade e os trâmites de coabilitação ainda dependem de regulamentação complementar do Executivo. A direção estratégica, contudo, já está dada. Esse percentual ganha corpo ao lado dos 5% injetados compulsoriamente pelas fabricantes de servidores por meio da Lei de Informática. Essa união de cifras constrói a maior transferência de recursos já destinada à pesquisa e desenvolvimento no país. O ponto central do marco legal, previsto no artigo 11-C da Lei 11.196/2005, com redação dada pela Lei nº 15.504/2026 e que instituiu o Redata, revela uma engenharia regulatória inteligentíssima. A desoneração da contribuição ao PIS-Pasep e da Cofins alcança de forma horizontal toda cadeia produtiva. A manutenção da cobrança do Imposto de Importação para equipamentos com produção nacional equivalente e do IPI para os equipamentos produzidos na Zona Franca de Manaus, cria as travas de proteção essenciais. Incentivo fiscal para tecnologias inexistentes no país constitui política industrial coerente e responsável. Desonerar importações predatórias de máquinas já fabricadas internamente causa desindustrialização subsidiada. A regra atual protege quem produz no Brasil, seja qual for a origem do capital investido. Empresas globais de hardware mantêm fábricas aqui ao lado de companhias brasileiras, sob o mesmo rigoroso critério. O mercado nacional de servidores ganha uma expansão sem precedentes com essa barreira inteligente. Permitir a importação isenta de um equipamento pronto anularia a competitividade das operações industriais instaladas no país e destruiria cadeias inteiras de fornecedores. O Redata evitou essa armadilha. A legislação assegura a previsibilidade necessária para as fábricas investirem pesado em novas linhas de produção e contratarem mais talentos para a engenharia local. O parque fabril no nosso país superou, definitivamente, a fase de mera linha de montagem. A realidade das fábricas expõe uma maturidade densa e o domínio prático de uma etapa decisiva. Engenharia de ponta, arquitetura térmica, integração complexa, testes exaustivos e suporte contínuo ocorrem no território nacional. Fabricar a infraestrutura da inteligência artificial exige calibração milimétrica de energia e certificações rigorosas que consomem meses de dedicação exclusiva de times altamente especializados. Nos últimos anos, a título de exemplo, entregamos sucessivos sistemas de supercomputação para o setor de óleo e gás, com integração nacional completa. Construímos sólida tradição tecnológica nesse segmento, e essas máquinas operam hoje entre as maiores do mundo em capacidade de processamento de dados. As placas aceleradoras vêm de fora, mas toda a inteligência da integração ganha forma, escala e excelência aqui. A repatriação veloz de cargas de trabalho tem impulsionado a demanda por hardware local. Em paralelo, os custos financeiros para treinar modelos computacionais aumentaram exponencialmente. Faturas forçam as organizações a transferir operações complexas das nuvens públicas para ambientes locais blindados. Diretores de tecnologia encontram na escolha de um servidor nacional a convergência exata entre eficiência de custos e segurança de dados. Esses líderes corporativos valorizam a vantagem estratégica de ter o fabricante do hardware fisicamente próximo. Essa proximidade garante a customização ágil da arquitetura, viabiliza manutenções críticas em tempo recorde e assegura a continuidade das operações sem o risco atrelado à dependência de um suporte técnico estrangeiro distante. A soberania digital do Brasil ganha uma dimensão muito concreta com o Redata. O país dispensa a fantasia da autossuficiência em semicondutores para desenvolver uma indústria real de inteligência artificial. artigo.texto: The Aurora City Council on Monday faced a chamber packed with residents opposed to a data center that is proposed to go up next to their neighborhoods, even as the city attorney reiterated that the site is an industrial zone district where data centers are permitted. The city attorney also noted that, if an application meets zoning standards, Aurora could face potential liability if administrative officials denied it. Recommended Stories The council heard from about 40 Aurora and Denver residents who are upset about the plans for Trident Data Center, which would go up near Green Valley Ranch if approved. Before the public comment period began, City Attorney Pete Schulte asked everyone attending who opposed the Trident Data Center to stand up. Almost everyone in the room did so. When Schulte asked if anyone in the room supported the data center, nobody stood. Broadly speaking, supporters have argued that data centers bring jobs and investment to local communities as well as new tax revenues. They have also insisted that cultivating and growing data centers in America has positive repercussions for national security. Meanwhile, a political split is emerging in how cities and counties deal with data centers: The Colorado counties that recently approved data center construction are conservative-leaning, while cities calling for or imposing moratoriums lean progressive. Plans for the new data center, which is proposed to sit at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue, have already been through two formal city reviews and a third is underway, an Aurora spokesperson told The Denver Gazette. Vantage Data Centers submitted the application for Trident to the city on Aug. 25, 2025. If built, the data center would be two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by Vantage through the city’s development portal. Residents said they feel “totally blindsided” by the proposal. The Aurora residents opposed to the data center claimed that, until early September, they had not heard a word about the plan from the city or Oakwood Homes, the real estate developer for the community. The property where Trident is proposed is in an industrial zone district, where data centers are a permitted use and can be approved administratively as long as no major adjustments are requested, a city spokesperson said. Residents from both Aurora and Denver spoke at the meeting, with those in Denver saying they are close to the data center’s location but have no say in its location. Bre Kennedy, 16, told council members that the data center plan is “ridiculous,” asking councilmembers to raise their hands if they would want to live next to a data center. None of the councilmembers did. “You don’t want this near your neighborhood, so why is it OK for it to be near others’?” Kennedy said. “When you’re writing new regulations, please think about the people who are actually going to have to live next to these facilities.” “We the residents of The Reserve and the groups impacted by this were never informed,” added Dan Bergander, who has lived at The Reserve 55+ community since 2021. In fact, Aurora officials were not required to notify area residents of the plans for a data center because of the land’s zoning, according to Schulte, the city attorney. When applications go to the city for use of land that’s zoned for that use, it goes to administrative approval. “If the council had to approve every project that had to go through, our meetings would be two days long,” Schulte said. “That’s why we have zoning laws.” If an application meets the zoning standards, the city is subject to potential liability if administrative officials deny it, he said. Development and zoning information is public record, Schulte added. “We’re not in the game of hiding the ball,” he said. “Everything we do is open, on our website and can be searched. I encourage any homeowner with parcels of land by their neighborhood to figure out what the land is zoned for.”

artigo.texto: A Rússia atingiu neste domingo (27) a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, e um data center da Vodafone Ukraine, a segunda maior. Zelensky disse que um data center em Kiev foi atingido duas vezes, ferindo duas crianças e um adulto. Os ataques a data centers não são um caso isolado. Na semana anterior, a Rússia já havia atingido centros de dados de provedores de internet, deixando cerca de 100 mil residências de Kiev e região sem conexão ou com internet degradada. A Rússia tem como alvo os principais data centers ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais — eles salvam vidas. Por que a Rússia mudou de alvo agora? Segundo o instituto de pesquisa ISW, o Kremlin amplia o conjunto de alvos em busca de "mecanismos alternativos de derrota", porque as ofensivas russas em 2026 não avançaram no campo de batalha, enquanto a Ucrânia registrou ganhos que o próprio instituto chama de estrategicamente significativos. Entre 23 e 25 de setembro, ataques russos danificaram pelo menos quatro data centers em Kiev: os operados pela UTELS e pela Pavutyna, e depois os da Cosmonova e da Datagroup. Um representante do ponto de troca de tráfego de internet 1-IX resumiu a mudança de padrão: os ataques a data centers passaram a ser sistemáticos desde setembro, e não mais esporádicos. O Ministério da Defesa russo afirma que o alvo são sistemas de comunicação militares. O governo ucraniano diz não ter encontrado dano a redes militares ou institucionais. A diferença separa dois tipos de guerra: uma contra alvos militares, outra contra a vida civil. Especialistas ouvidos pela imprensa ucraniana avaliam que um apagão nacional completo de internet é improvável, graças a sistemas de backup e à distribuição da infraestrutura entre fronteiras. O ataque a data centers é parte de um padrão mais amplo: dias antes, a Rússia já havia mirado a maior siderúrgica da Ucrânia, forçando a parada da produção. O contexto de fundo é um front que praticamente não se move: Zelensky recorreu recentemente a uma métrica pouco usual para mostrar o custo do imobilismo russo, contando baixas do Exército russo por quilômetro quadrado conquistado. A resposta ucraniana também mira infraestrutura: em setembro, drones atingiram uma refinaria em Moscou no dia da eleição russa. O episódio mostra que ataques a infraestrutura estratégica correm nos dois sentidos da guerra. O ponto em aberto Se a mudança de alvo é resposta a um impasse militar, a pergunta é até quando a Rússia sustenta essa estratégia sem conseguir travar de fato o funcionamento da internet ucraniana, dada a infraestrutura de backup já existente no país. O que acontece agora Zelensky anunciou a decisão de reforçar a proteção física de data centers e instalações de comunicação no país. Não há, porém, prazo definido para a conclusão dessas medidas.

artigo.texto: How Carbon-Aware Scheduling Can Cut Data Center Emissions Aligning flexible workloads to cleaner hours and locations turns variability into measurable Scope 2 reductions. Data centers are often described as having fixed carbon footprints tied to their size and grid mix. In practice, operators can lower emissions by aligning flexible workloads with periods and locations where electricity is cleaner. This “carbon-aware” approach complements long-term renewable procurement and efficiency programs, creating a practical pathway to reduce Scope 2 emissions and to demonstrate progress toward 24/7 carbon-free energy objectives. It also helps address growing regulatory expectations and stakeholder scrutiny of digital infrastructure’s electricity demand. What Is Carbon-Aware Computing? Carbon-aware computing is the practice of scheduling compute-intensive but time-flexible tasks – such as data backups, batch analytics, AI model training, report generation, and non-urgent patching – during windows when grid carbon intensity is lower or when on-site renewable or stored energy is available. The core idea is to compare the emissions profile of running a workload at one time or place versus another, and then choose execution options that minimize emissions within operational constraints. How Carbon-Aware Scheduling Works Electricity grids are dynamic. Solar production peaks during daylight, wind output varies seasonally and hourly, and some regions benefit from geothermal, hydro, or nuclear baseload. Grid conditions change by the hour based on demand, transmission constraints, and market dispatch. As a result, the emissions intensity of a kilowatt-hour can swing significantly across a single day. Carbon-aware computing takes advantage of this variability by aligning flexible workloads with periods when low-carbon energy is most available. Operators assess which workloads can shift in time or location without violating service-level agreements (SLAs), latency requirements, data residency constraints, or change-control policies. The outcome is a set of scheduling policies that favor cleaner windows while maintaining service objectives. That way, compute-hungry tasks can run without forcing incremental demand at higher-emitting hours. Implementation Realities: Data, Forecasts, and Constraints The principles behind carbon-aware computing are simple enough. In a data center context, however, implementing carbon-aware strategies can be challenging for a few key reasons. Common hurdles include limited observability into tenant workloads (particularly in colocation facilities), difficulty predicting workload power draw due to dynamic CPU/GPU utilization and I/O patterns, and uncertainty in renewable forecasts. Additionally, not all workloads are flexible. Mission-critical, latency-sensitive applications may be fixed in time and location. A practical approach starts with cataloging workloads by flexibility class, power profile, and compliance constraints. From there, operators can pilot carbon-aware scheduling on clearly deferrable tasks. What Operators Can Do Today Effective carbon-aware programs typically include: - Instrumentation and metering. Enhance power telemetry at the rack and cluster level to identify high-draw, schedulable workloads and measure realized emissions impacts. - Behind-the-meter resources. On-site renewables improve certainty that incremental workload energy is low-carbon. Generic utility grids typically can’t guarantee that the energy they supply comes from any particular source. However, data centers with their own solar, wind, or geothermal energy supplies can do this. When paired with batteries, operators can time-shift energy and shave peaks. While few sites can economically size batteries to cover full facility load, modest storage can be sufficient to power energy-intensive, deferrable tasks during clean windows. Reduce Emissions, Keep Reliability Perfect optimization is unrealistic for most data center environments. Even so, carbon-aware computing can deliver real reductions by capturing the “clean hours” that already exist on many grids. Over time, it becomes another reliability-minded tool – one that lowers emissions while respecting the operational realities that keep data centers running.

artigo.texto: Abbott says data center permits frozen until power, water concerns addressed HEMPHILL, Texas (KTRE) - Two AI data centers, AmpZ and Hyper Data Grid, are targeting Angelina County, but state permits for the facilities remain on hold. Governor Greg Abbott placed a moratorium on new data centers statewide earlier this month to assess their strain on local resources. During a stop in Hemphill, Abbott drew a hard line on electricity. “They must provide their own power as opposed to taking power off the Texas power grid,” Abbott said. Utility costs and firm purchase agreements Abbott said new facilities must prove they will drive down utility costs for neighboring residents. “Firm purchase agreements for buying a certain amount of electricity. Knowing full well they will not all the time buy that electricity, and that additional supply on the marketplace will then drive down the cost of electricity rates,” Abbott said. Abbott also said cities and counties need more control over where these facilities build, a power local leaders currently lack. Local control over land use Without tax abatement agreements, county leaders have no say on land use. That prompted both Angelina County commissioners and the Lufkin City Council to lobby state lawmakers for regulatory oversight. “And the reason we’re doing this - if we can’t get an abatement, if there’s not going to be an abatement, then there are zero control that we have over these data centers,” said Keith Wright, Angelina County judge. Abbott said he supports giving communities that authority. “Local communities should have the authority and the independence to make their own decision about whether they do or do not want data centers,” Abbott said. Abbott said the state Legislature and the Texas Water Development Board are drafting new rules to prevent data centers from draining local water supplies. The Texas Legislature’s next regular session begins Jan. 12, 2027. Copyright 2026 KTRE. All rights reserved.

Those and other discoveries will be used to eventually craft zoning laws to regulate data centers should one ever want to locate in Sheboygan.

artigo.texto: Building Resilience Into Digital Infrastructure As infrastructure expands beyond traditional regions, organizations will be better positioned by using a lifecycle approach to network resiliency. September 28, 2026 Sponsored by SES AI Growth Is Changing Infrastructure Assumptions Major hyperscale cloud providers have launched over 50 cloud regions in the past five years, and the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure is forcing data center operators to rethink long-standing assumptions about site selection and deployment. Growth in cloud services and AI workloads is pushing infrastructure into a wider range of geographies, exposing operators to new risks as facilities move beyond traditional connectivity hubs. While considerations of power, land acquisition, cooling, and permitting all remain important, connectivity readiness in some geographies can be just as consequential as power readiness. Connectivity Risk Is Changing Beyond well-documented financial impacts of outages, operators must also consider the potential cost to customer trust. If a fiber or power cable is cut, can you answer questions about the security systems in the data center? Can you tell a customer if their cage door was recently opened? Operators must also account for disruptions that occur well beyond the data center itself. As AI infrastructure footprints expand into new regions, connectivity can be affected by subsea cable failures, natural disasters, regional infrastructure disruptions, geopolitical events, civil instability, and other factors out of a facility operator’s control. For example, in 2024, a rockslide off the coast of West Africa caused multiple subsea cable breaks, disrupting service in West Africa. The Red Sea has experienced two incidents of simultaneous fiber cuts. As operators expand into new geographies and new risk environments, connectivity resilience is becoming a core design consideration. From the operator perspective, the question isn't whether connectivity outages occur but how critical management systems will remain reachable when those outages occur. Resilience Beyond Redundancy Traditional planning suggests that multiple fiber providers deliver resilience. But subsea routes and regional infrastructure concentration can create hidden dependencies. Resilient designs will look at carrier, path, and infrastructure diversity. Operators should consider if their resiliency plans provide: - Guaranteed capacity to help avoid consumer-grade congestion concerns. - Private routing options to avoid public internet exposure. - Flexible traffic routing that can support in-country routing, specific cloud destinations, and recovery sites outside a potential disruption zone. - Meaningful upload throughput for continuous support and visibility of operational systems, infrastructure management, and security platforms. Sovereign Infrastructure Is Raising the Stakes As both governments and enterprises place more emphasis on compliance, data control, and transparency, connectivity decisions now extend beyond uptime and resilience. During outages or failover events, organizations may also need visibility into where traffic is routed and how network paths align with jurisdictional requirements. This is driving interest in network designs that combine resilience with greater visibility into routing decisions. One Planned Connectivity Lifecycle Joining Construction, Commissioning, and Operational Resilience Resilience is most effective and cost-efficient in the long term when it is designed into a facility from the outset. By viewing connectivity as a lifecycle consideration rather than a series of point solutions, operators can take a more consistent approach to ensuring critical management, monitoring, and security systems remain accessible throughout the life of the facility. For example, a facility’s connectivity requirements may evolve like this as it moves from construction to operations: - During construction, delivering communications, site monitoring, security support, and temporary operational access before permanent infrastructure is in place. - As the facility approaches launch, enabling initial network access, testing, commissioning, and operational readiness. - Once the facility enters production, a shift from enablement to resilience with satellite serving as an independent management path, operational backup, and recovery communications channel. Conclusion Old connectivity assumptions are becoming harder to sustain as operators expand into new geographies and face new sources of infrastructure risk. In the AI era, the impact of lost connectivity grows, and connectivity resilience is a design decision that should be made well before a facility's first workload goes live. Successful infrastructure projects will evaluate connectivity with the same rigor applied to power, land, and cooling infrastructure. About the Author: Robert Hegblom is Sr. Principal Product Manager for Land and Sovereign Enterprise at SES, where he builds multi-orbit satellite connectivity offerings for global businesses and telco partners. He also has a decade of experience expanding data centers to underserved locations for hyperscale cloud providers, content delivery networks.
