artigo.texto: A primeira etapa do plano prevê US$ 24 milhões para a aquisição e adequação de um prédio industrial localizado ao lado do atual parque fabril da WEG em Atotonilco de Tula, no México. A unidade será destinada à montagem de geradores e tem início das operações previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. A WEG já tem outras operações industriais no México. Além de Atotonilco de Tula, onde mantém atividades relacionadas à fundição e revestimentos, a companhia tem uma unidade em Huehuetoca voltada à produção de motores de baixa e média tensão, geradores, painéis, transformadores e subestações. Também mantém, em Monterrey, a operação incorporada com a aquisição da Marathon, que produz motores e geradores e realiza atividades de pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Na segunda fase, a companhia investirá os US$ 141 milhões restantes na construção de duas instalações industriais em local ainda a ser definido na América do Norte. A nova estrutura terá produção verticalizada, com processos como fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças. Segundo a WEG, a segunda etapa do projeto deverá ser concluída em 2030. A expansão ocorre em um momento de aumento da demanda por infraestrutura de energia nos Estados Unidos. A WEG encerrou 2025 com receita líquida de R$ 40,8 bilhões. A companhia possui unidades industriais em 18 países, presença comercial em mais de 135 países e mais de 49 mil funcionários. Cerca de 59% da receita de 2025 veio de vendas realizadas fora do Brasil. Data centers O movimento anunciado nesta segunda-feira reforça uma frente de negócios que vem ganhando importância para a WEG: o fornecimento de equipamentos para a infraestrutura elétrica dos data centers. Um relatório do BTG Pactual aponta que a exposição da companhia ao setor não se limita aos geradores. Cerca de 20% da receita de transmissão e distribuição (T&D) da WEG nos Estados Unidos já está relacionada a clientes de data centers, segundo informações da própria empresa. Os geradores são outro ponto dessa exposição. Data centers precisam de sistemas de geração de energia de emergência para manter suas operações em caso de interrupções no fornecimento da rede elétrica. A WEG atua nesse mercado por meio de suas próprias operações e da Marathon Electric. Juntas, as duas marcas têm cerca de 10% do mercado global de alternadores e grupos geradores, de acordo com o BTG. A companhia também fornece outros equipamentos utilizados nesses empreendimentos. Entre eles estão sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias, conhecidos como BESS, além de motores industriais e inversores de frequência usados nos sistemas de refrigeração dos data centers. A demanda por esses equipamentos ocorre ao mesmo tempo em que a WEG amplia sua capacidade de produção de transformadores, outro negócio ligado à infraestrutura elétrica necessária para esses empreendimentos. A companhia tem projetos de expansão nos Estados Unidos, México, Colômbia e Brasil. Nos EUA, uma nova unidade de transformadores especiais receberá US$ 77 milhões, com conclusão prevista entre 2027 e 2028. No México, uma nova fábrica está prevista para o fim de 2026 ou início de 2027. Em conjunto, os projetos devem aproximadamente dobrar a capacidade de produção de transformadores da WEG em relação ao fim de 2023. Segundo o BTG, a capacidade adicional deve entrar nos resultados de forma gradual, à medida que as novas fábricas comecem a operar. A utilização total da estrutura ampliada é esperada apenas para o fim de 2027. O tema deve estar entre os assuntos discutidos no WEG Day, evento anual da companhia marcado para sexta-feira (2), em Jaraguá do Sul (SC). Além da expansão de transformadores e da exposição aos data centers, o BTG espera informações sobre o impacto das tarifas de importação nos Estados Unidos e os próximos passos da estratégia de crescimento da companhia. A WEG vem adaptando sua produção para o mercado americano em resposta às mudanças tarifárias. Segundo o BTG, aproximadamente 41% do fornecimento relacionado às vendas nos EUA vem do México, 33% da produção doméstica americana e entre 20% e 21% do Brasil. O que o investidor deve acompanhar Apesar do aumento da demanda por equipamentos elétricos, a expansão da WEG também traz pontos de atenção. Um deles é a possibilidade de aumento da oferta nos próximos anos. WEG e outros fabricantes estão ampliando a produção para atender ao aumento da demanda por eletricidade, transformadores e equipamentos para data centers. O BTG Pactual avalia que a entrada simultânea de novas fábricas em 2027 e 2028 pode aumentar a oferta e pressionar os preços em alguns segmentos. O risco, segundo o banco, é maior nos produtos em que novos concorrentes conseguem adicionar capacidade com mais facilidade. As tarifas americanas também continuam no radar. A WEG vem compensando parte dos custos com reajustes de preços e mudanças na origem da produção, mas uma alteração nas tarifas ou na capacidade de repasse para os clientes pode afetar as margens. Outro ponto é o tempo necessário para que os novos investimentos se transformem em receita. Parte relevante da capacidade adicional de transformadores e geradores só estará disponível nos próximos anos, enquanto os desembolsos começam antes. A exposição aos data centers também merece acompanhamento. A WEG tem diferentes linhas de produtos relacionadas a esse mercado, mas o ritmo de expansão desses projetos será importante para determinar a velocidade com que a nova capacidade instalada será absorvida.

artigo.texto: Publicidade A Samsung concordou em investir US$ 1 bilhão na Helix Digital Infrastructure, empresa de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial (IA) apoiada por KKR e Nvidia, em mais um aporte na corrida global por data centers, energia e redes capazes de sustentar a demanda por IA. O investimento eleva o capital já assegurado pela Helix para mais de US$ 11 bilhões, a ser usado na estratégia de entregar uma nova geração de data centers, geração de energia e transmissão. A Helix foi criada em junho por um consórcio liderado pela KKR, com investidores-âncora que incluem Nvidia, a Kuwait Investment Authority e a Vistra, empresa de geração e varejo de eletricidade. Leia também: OpenAI segura lançamento de novo modelo de IA após falhas em testes de segurança O CEO e cofundador da Helix, Adam Selipsky, disse que o compromisso da Samsung é um “voto de confiança” na estratégia da companhia para atender a uma demanda sem precedentes de grandes provedoras de nuvem por infraestrutura de IA cada vez mais complexa e em alta velocidade. Gigantes como Microsoft (MSFT34), Amazon (AMZO34), Meta (M1TA34) e Alphabet (GOGL34) vêm gastando centenas de bilhões de dólares para expandir infraestrutura de IA. O gasto de capital das quatro empresas chegou a US$ 410 bilhões no ano passado, quase o triplo do nível de 2022. Estimativas do economista Stijn van Nieuwerburgh, publicadas pela Brookings Institution, projetam US$ 10,3 trilhões em investimentos em data centers e infraestrutura relacionada entre 2025 e 2032. Leia também: AMD compra startup de pioneira da IA por US$ 8,2 bilhões Continua depois da publicidade A Helix afirma que, além do papel da Nvidia em tecnologia e infraestrutura de ponta e da Vistra em energia, pretende aproveitar capacidades da Samsung em tecnologia avançada, construção, armazenamento de energia e refrigeração para desenvolver infraestrutura em escala. A Samsung disse que o aporte ajudará suas afiliadas a avançar de fornecedoras de componentes para funções de maior valor em sistemas e infraestrutura de IA. O movimento também ocorre enquanto empresas sul-coreanas ampliam investimentos para capturar o boom de IA. Samsung Electronics e SK Hynix planejam investir mais de US$ 520 bilhões em um polo de semicondutores no sudoeste do país, como parte de uma iniciativa liderada pelo governo estimada em US$ 2 trilhões para desenvolver capacidades domésticas completas em IA. Analistas da BMI, da Fitch Solutions, apontam que a competição deve se intensificar e que projetos maiores podem pressionar preços. Eles também alertam que a rede elétrica pode não acompanhar o ritmo e que regras recentes de licenciamento exigem padrões de eficiência energética, elevando as dificuldades para garantir energia para instalações de IA, intensivas em consumo. Fonte: Dow Jones Newswires. artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – San Antonio leaders are looking at whether data centers should be required to use recycled water instead of drinking water as concerns grow about the potential impact of future artificial intelligence facilities. San Antonio’s District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan filed a council consideration request (CCR) almost a year ago to have city staff look into the impact data centers have on city resources and look at the possibility of requiring data centers to use recycled water. Water is used to cool down the industrial servers that data centers use for extended periods of time. Water is also used to produce power for the facilities. KSAT attempted to speak to Galvan about the recycled water proposal, but his office sent a statement. In it, Galvan said he wants to keep data centers from using any drinking water, and in order for a mandate on recycled water usage by data centers can move forward, San Antonio Water System (SAWS) must adopt a policy first, specifically outlining that that is what data centers must do. Donovan Burton, the senior vice president of water resources and governmental relations for SAWS, said when talking about data centers in the city, there must be a distinction made between existing data centers and future AI data centers and their water consumption. He said 23 of the existing data centers in the city account for a very small amount of the water pulled from the city’s water supply. “The existing data centers are very small (and have a) very, very small footprint. In fact, they’re using about .1% of our potable water supply,” Burton said. He said it is the future AI data centers that could potentially use a lot more water, and added SAWS’ Recycled Water Network could help data centers comply if the recycled water use became an official requirement. “Our Recycle Water Network has been in place for over 20 years,” he said. He explained that it is 130 miles of purple pipeline that specifically carries recycled water that is used and paid for by contracted, non-residential customers. “The recycle water programs, after (water) has been used, we treat it and put it into a purple pipe network that goes around ... a good portion of the entire city,” Burton said. “That network then takes it from three different plants, and we can move water back and forth.” SAWS headquarters, CPS Energy, Toyota, the San Antonio Zoo and the River Walk are among the multiple big entities and attractions that are connected in part or entirely to SAWS’ Recycled Water Network, and you can tell by the designated purple pipes present on or near the respective properties. Burton said if a recycled water use restriction is implemented, data center owners would have to choose to obtain a permit from SAWS and enter into a contract for a specific amount of water to connect to the purple pipeline. But he shared there is another option data centers have that can be a conservative measure. “Some of them are going to a closed loop (water) system, which will end up using a lot less water,” Burton said. An internet search on what a closed loop water system is yielded a general definition, describing how data center use the same water or a cooling liquid through sealed pipes to absorb heat and as it moves along the pipe path it removes heat from servers over and over again without pulling in or using fresh water. Until further notice, Burton said SAWS will continue its forward strategy. “It’s a matter of making sure that that works for all future customers, not just a very few one or two or five data centers or anything else,” he said. In the statement sent to KSAT, Galvan said he asked SAWS leadership to come up with a possible plan to move forward with the water usage restriction for new data centers. The statement went on to say he is interested in hearing from SAWS this week as to whether or not the board has made any movement on the proposal over the summer.

artigo.texto: Lexington residents rally against proposed data center near Green Acres Park Neighbors cite water, utility bills, and traffic concerns as city leaders urge public turnout ahead of an Oct. 6 meeting LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) — Residents gathered Sunday near Green Acres Park to voice sharp opposition to a proposed Lexington data center, just weeks before the city’s development moratorium is set to expire. The pushback centers on Texas-based developer DartPoints, which recently purchased a portion of the former Lexmark campus off New Circle Road. The company plans to use 20 to 30 megawatts of power initially, with capacity to expand up to 70 megawatts. For neighbors living less than two miles from the site, the proposal sparked serious concerns over water usage, rising utility bills, and increased traffic. “I am here today to say no to the data center,” one young resident said from the podium during Sunday’s community meeting. Officials urge public turnout ahead of key meeting Lexington Mayor Linda Gorton joined residents at Sunday’s meeting, reiterating that city officials were never given advance notice of the private real estate transaction. “What happened downtown that day, when we read it, we all said, ‘Did you know about this? Did you know about this?’” Gorton told the crowd. “No one knew about this.” Gorton said the Urban County Council should not rush to a decision and urged the public to attend an upcoming special hearing to voice their concerns. The council’s Committee of the Whole will hold a public input session at 5:30 p.m. on Oct. 6 at City Hall (200 E. Main St.) — weeks before the city’s current moratorium expires on Oct. 31. Vice Mayor Dan Wu, Councilmember Tyler Morton, and Fayette County Public Schools Board Chair Tyler Murphy also attended Sunday’s meeting and addressed the crowd. Mayoral candidate Raquel Carter spoke to WKYT following the event, arguing that concern over the project reaches well beyond the immediate neighborhood. “I think it’s clear no one wants them. There is no place for them here,” Carter said. “Large-scale data centers are just concerning to everyone.” Neighbors lean on ‘people power’ Community organizers say public turnout at City Hall is their strongest leverage against the developer heading into October. “It’s people power. That is the power that we have,” organizer Katie Dapkus said. “We don’t have the financial resources to advocate for our position, but what we do have is community. And I think now more than ever we need reminded of how powerful that can be.” WKYT reached out to DartPoints for comment regarding Sunday’s meeting and is waiting to hear back. Copyright 2026 WKYT. artigo.texto: Granbury residents stage walkout during city council meeting amid data center controversy GRANBURY, Texas - Dozens of Granbury residents walked out of Monday night's city council meeting as city leaders pushed back on petitions for their removal over alleged plans to build a data center in the city. Granbury data center concept Granbury data center concept What we know: Earlier in 2026, Granbury City Council voted to annex 2,200 acres of land near Meadow Wood Road. Now, there are plans for a data center to be built on the land. The city says it has received concept plans for the center, which is called Project Patriot. Project Patriot's website says the data center is being planned as a "self-sufficient campus with on-site power generation and privately funded infrastructure designed to minimize impacts on local utilities, public services, and taxpayers." Recall petition Local perspective: Some Granbury residents believe their city's leaders didn't disclose enough information about the potential data center before the land was annexed. Those concerns led to 15% of the city's population signing a petition to recall Granbury Mayor Jim Jarratt and four city council members, with over 1,300 signatures on the petition. "They tend to do this. We speak, they don’t hear what we’re saying," Rachael Jacobson, a resident, tells FOX 4's David Sentendrey. "Maybe they hear it, but they don’t hear what we’re saying — and then the rest of this show goes on and they just do whatever they want." "The city council, whatever their intentions may be, neglected to listen to the citizens and the citizens have decided they’re not going to tolerate than anymore — to the tune of over 1,300 signatures on multiple recall petitions," said Alex Wolf, a Granbury resident and Granbury City Council-elect. Granbury Mayor Jim Jarratt "A circus" The other side: "I will not resign." At Monday's Granbury City Council meeting, Jarratt and city council members defended themselves. Jarratt said he believes there are procedural issues with the recall petition. "The petition against me does not explain any substance whatsoever, which makes it impossible for me to defend my public record against a generic accusation that could potentially span over the past five-and-a-half years. That’s how long I’ve been your mayor." When Granbury City Councilman Skip Overdier began speaking against the recall petition, dozens of Granbury residents walked out of the meeting. Rachael Jacobson described the meeting as "a circus." "You could tell they weren’t listening when we spoke during public comment." What's next: Petitioners are hoping to get the recall on the November ballot. A court battle over the proposed data center is also looming. City officials say any official development plans for the data center would go through the city's normal review process, and would need to meet zoning and development standards before approval. The Source: Information in this story comes from a Granbury City Council meeting.

artigo.texto: Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia is offering carbon market incentive schemes to global business leaders investing in green projects across the archipelago, Coordinating Minister for Food Zulkifli Hasan announced during the 81st UN General Assembly and Climate Week NYC 2026. Addressing more than 20 global corporate executives at the High-Level and CEO Forum on Low-Emission Rice and Sustainable Agriculture in New York, the minister emphasized that carbon pricing mechanisms would allow investors to unlock additional financial value from verifiable emissions reductions in Indonesia. "Indonesia is facing a waste emergency that must be addressed immediately, one of which is through waste-to-energy. Therefore, the government is encouraging green investment in the waste sector as a priority," Zulkifli said in a statement on Tuesday (September 29). Zulkifli outlined three primary sectors open to green investment: sustainable agriculture through low-emission rice cultivation, waste-to-energy processing, and marine conservation through blue carbon development. As chair of the Carbon Economic Value (NEK) Steering Committee, he said Jakarta is streamlining regulatory frameworks and strengthening carbon trading governance to ensure high-credibility carbon assets. A key step came on July 6, 2026, when the Financial Services Authority (OJK) enacted POJK No. 10/2026, mandating that all exchange-traded carbon units be formally registered under the Carbon Unit Registry System (SRUK). OJK data as of August 31, 2026, revealed that 159 service users have registered on the Indonesian Carbon Exchange since its inception on September 26, 2023. Total transaction volume reached 1.98 million tons of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e), with a cumulative value of Rp93.90 billion (approximately US$5.24 million). Government projections indicate that the carbon pricing framework could mobilize up to US$5.80 billion in green investment while reducing greenhouse gas emissions by roughly 570 million tCO2e. Beyond waste management, Indonesia is seeking various international partners to scale up low-emission rice production to strengthen domestic food security while reducing agricultural methane emissions. Zulkifli noted that implementing low-emission rice cultivation on a large scale requires technological support, financing, market certainty, and clear economic benefits for farmers. He added that climate action must translate into concrete, field-level projects that directly benefit farmers and coastal communities. artigo.texto: By Daniel Swinney A loud humming noise interrupted a Louisville Metro Council meeting on Sept. 15. A video of the disruption went viral on social media. The noise was an audio recording of generators and cooling fans used by data centers. It was being played in protest of a hyperscale data center proposal to be built on a 154-acre lot on Campground Road. A member of the local organization No Data Center 502 played the noise to protest the 1.8 million square foot data center, replicating what they say residents would hear at all hours from their homes. “We’re against the construction of hyperscale AI data centers because the people of Louisville are against the construction of hyperscale AI data centers,” said Danielle Ray, one of the lead organizers for No Data Center 502. The fight The grassroots organization was founded in October 2025 after the city announced developer Steve Poe’s data center plans. Since then, the group of residents has made progress toward preventing it from being built. “We’ve won a six-month moratorium and finally have updated zoning legislation making its way through Metro Council to stop future hyperscale data centers from stealing from the community,” said Ray. Many are already aware of rising water and electric costs for those living near hyperscale data centers. But Ray specifically cited Kentucky House Bill 775, a bill that granted 50-year tax breaks to data centers built in Kentucky, as an example of how Poe and other developers take from the community. “We’re talking billions of dollars stolen from working people across Kentucky whilst our elected officials in Frankfort slash public funding for education, Medicare and Medicaid, SNAP and TARC,” said Ray. Poe Companies, along with Powerhouse Data Centers, plans to build Kentucky’s first hyperscale data center in Rubbertown, located in West Louisville. Ray and many Rubbertown residents see this as the latest in a series of environmentally harmful decisions that have affected the predominantly Black community for decades. A recent report by the Kapor Foundation suggests data centers are primarily being built in impoverished and largely Black communities. Many of these communities already suffer from degraded air quality and health concerns due to local industry and lack of regulations. “It’s no coincidence that the West and Southwest parts of the city are overindustrialized,” said Ray. “All of our struggles are connected. As such, we express solidarity and extend support to various fights against environmental racism and injustice.” Ideology No Data Center 502’s collectivist and social ideals have drawn criticism from opponents. Metro Councilor Anthony Piagentini, seen in the viral video asking the protester to stop playing the data center noise, referred to the organization as the ‘Marxist Mob’ during the moratorium hearing in August. “Unironically, I would say this is a fairly accurate description of the politics of myself as well as our organization,” said Ray. Ray stressed that No Data Center 502 is open to all Louisville residents, not just leftists, as long as they are there in good faith. “We are a mixed bag of folks from all over the city when it comes to politics! We have people of all ages and backgrounds in our organization,” Ray said. Ray believes the issues surrounding data centers are inextricable from what leftists call a class struggle against U.S. imperialism, overpolicing and AI-driven surveillance. For Ray, building Poe’s hyperscale data center would exploit the working class people of Rubbertown, while the land could instead enrich the community. “There are so many other positive alternatives to build on the 154 acres that are being occupied by Steve Poe,” said Ray. “Reforesting, grocery stores, community centers, new schools, housing, doctor’s offices, the options are endless.” The Louisville moratorium on data centers will end in February 2027. This will give Louisville Metro Council time to decide on zoning amendments and other associated regulations for future data center proposals. The council could also debate a proposed ban on all data centers in Louisville. The moratorium and potential regulations do not impact the Campground Road hyperscale data center, as the construction was approved and began before the moratorium was voted on. Despite the setback, No Data Center 502 remains committed to preventing its construction and achieving a total ban on data centers in the city. “Ultimately, the way to prevent hyperscale data centers from being built in Louisville is through regulations and policy,” said Ray. artigo.texto: ABEGÁS DEFENDE GÁS NATURAL NO REDATA E ALERTA PARA RISCO DE INSEGURANÇA JURÍDICA A Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado (Abegás) defende a inclusão do gás natural na regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), argumentando que o combustível pode desempenhar papel complementar às fontes renováveis na garantia da segurança energética necessária à operação dos data centers no Brasil. Segundo o diretor executivo da Abegás, Marcelo Mendonça, o gás natural não deve ser tratado como concorrente das fontes renováveis, mas como uma alternativa complementar diante da necessidade de fornecimento contínuo de energia. “Ele atua de forma complementar para garantir a segurança energética indispensável à viabilização dos data centers. Defender a neutralidade tecnológica é permitir que esses projetos avancem sem sobrecarregar o sistema de transmissão nem encarecer a conta de energia para os demais consumidores”, afirmou. A entidade argumenta que a característica intermitente de parte das fontes renováveis reforça a necessidade de alternativas capazes de assegurar o fornecimento contínuo exigido pela operação dos centros de processamento de dados. Para a Abegás, a geração a gás pode contribuir para a implantação de projetos de forma mais descentralizada, especialmente nas regiões Sudeste e Sul, onde a expansão dos data centers poderia exigir investimentos elevados em transmissão de energia devido à concentração de parte da geração renovável no Nordeste. Na avaliação da associação, a possibilidade de utilizar geração a gás próxima aos centros de consumo também pode reduzir a necessidade de novos investimentos em linhas de transmissão e evitar a transferência de custos adicionais para os demais consumidores de energia elétrica. A entidade defende, assim, que a regulamentação do Redata adote o princípio da neutralidade tecnológica e considere as diferentes alternativas disponíveis para garantir a segurança energética dos empreendimentos. Ao mesmo tempo, a Abegás manifesta preocupação com a possibilidade de a regulamentação do regime ultrapassar os limites estabelecidos pelo Congresso Nacional. Segundo a associação, a inclusão de medidas que extrapolem o escopo da legislação aprovada poderia provocar questionamentos por meio de Projetos de Decreto Legislativo (PDLs), aumentando a insegurança jurídica e dificultando a implementação dos projetos de data centers. “Contudo, nos preocupa que uma regulamentação que extrapole o que foi decidido pelo Congresso crie insegurança jurídica e trave esses investimentos essenciais para o país. Reiteramos nosso compromisso com o desenvolvimento do setor e com a construção de um ambiente regulatório que reconheça os benefícios e as externalidades positivas do gás natural para a infraestrutura digital do país”, declarou Mendonça.

artigo.texto: MAHOMET — When you ask communities if they’re interested in data-center development, responses can vary, says Clean Cloud Energy CEO Raj Keswani. “You have some communities that say, ‘Yes, absolutely. This solves a lot of problems for us. The tax revenue’s important. We really welcome you,’” he told The News-Gazette. “Other times, communities say, ‘We want to hear what you have to say, no promises. We’re willing to listen.’ And then there are other communities that say, ‘You’re the 15th data center. We have no interest in anything more than the 14 we already have. No, thank you.’” Keswani said that when the company started to gauge interest in Champaign County, the response was in the middle: “No promises, willing to listen.” The village of Mahomet announced Monday that it has been in preliminary talks with Clean Cloud Energy, which is interested in potentially building a data-center campus “in a rural area west of Champaign.” This has included discussions around language for a possible development agreement. The company referred to the potential project as the Rising Edge Data Center. The area being considered by the company is outside of village limits but within Mahomet’s extraterritorial jurisdiction, which grants the village “certain planning and subdivision authority involving the property,” Mahomet officials said. “The Village has a responsibility to consider economic-development opportunities that could strengthen our tax base and support the long-term financial health of our community,” said Mayor Jason Tompkins. “At the same time, the size and nature of this proposal require careful and thoughtful evaluation. We must fully understand its infrastructure needs, financial benefits, environmental considerations and effects on residents before making any decision.” Tompkins added that the public will have the opportunity to review “any officially submitted proposal,” as well as to submit questions and comments to the planning and zoning commission and the village board. Village officials emphasized that, at this point, all conversations have been “strictly preliminary and exploratory,” with no formal proposal submitted to the village board at this time. Clean Cloud Energy likewise said in a statement Monday that it is “in the early stages of clarifying whether a data center is possible.” The company added that, if approved and built, the project would be expected to generate millions of tax dollars annually “to support schools, emergency services, and community infrastructure.” Maggie Bruns, executive director of the Prairie Rivers Network, said that the environmental nonprofit has been aware of Clean Cloud Energy’s past interest in developing a data center in the area. “We were surprised to learn today about the steps being taken by the Village of Mahomet to further explore the development of a data center just outside village limits,” she said. “We are, of course, concerned by this possibility and are seeking more information as we assess its potential impacts. Their interest underscores the simultaneous need for strong protections locally as we work to pass statewide protections in Springfield.” When asked about the size of the potential project, Clean Cloud Energy Director of Development Clark Bixler said that Ameren is studying the transmission system to determine what size of project could be supported at this location. According to the company’s website, Clean Cloud Energy develops campuses for hyperscale data centers. Bixler said that, in addition to being within the village of Mahomet’s extraterritorial jurisdiction, the potential project area is also within Champaign County’s jurisdiction. The county currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with “at least 10,000 square feet of processing area”; the ban is currently set to end in April. The county has also created a data-center activities task force to draft planning and zoning regulations for such developments. According to Bixler, the timing of the project also will depend on the company’s work with Ameren, though he said that Clean Cloud Energy would like to see the first phase online in late 2028, with construction starting in late 2027 to early 2028. “Data centers are built in phases based on the amount of power that’s available and the amount of infrastructure they can construct in a year,” he explained. “So depending on what’s available to be delivered through Ameren’s Rising substation, there could be more than one stage that’s built. We’ll still ultimately be talking about the total project in terms of one size, but it may be more than what could be built in a particular, individual phase.” Clean Cloud Energy said in its announcement that the project’s energy usage would not affect “the price or availability of power to the community.” “The project would pay for any needed upgrades and bear the full burden of any improvements to the local energy and transmission infrastructure,” the company said. “The energy that we’re talking about is coming from the grid. It’s not energy consumed by the county now; it’s coming from beyond the county along transmission lines,” Keswani said. “And all that is being studied as we speak. So our power and energy needs are not cannibalizing anything the county is using now.” “In order to support a data center, you need a strong grid infrastructure,” Bixler said. “So this area has that through the Rising substation.” The company also said that it will use “zero water” to cool the project. “The coolant is an engineered solution that will be trucked on-site with a small amount of water that may be used during the initial fill,” company officials said. “The only potable water used would be for the needs of the employees in the building — sinks, bathrooms, and canteen — just like any other business or manufacturing facility. American Battery Technology entered the present session with a clear catalyst: small speculative companies are attracting selective interest where financing visibility or a tangible commercial milestone supports the story. Investors now have to separate a tradeable reaction from a development that changes how the business should be understood. That distinction depends on company evidence, not on the direction of the broader tape. Readers tracking Penny Stocks can use this development as a starting point while keeping the analysis tied to American Battery Technology and its own disclosures. A fresh signal with conditions attached At its heart, American Battery Technology is exposed to battery materials and recycling. The market will want a direct link between todays attention and the operating model. That link could appear in customer activity, a clearer product cycle, stronger execution or more disciplined use of capital. Where execution becomes decisive For American Battery Technology, proof should arrive through repeatable operations rather than a single announcement. Readers should listen for specific explanations of demand, delivery and spending. Consistency across several updates would show that the company is building a pattern instead of benefiting from one favorable moment. The sector comparison The comparison with other penny stocks names is useful but limited. Businesses in the same category can face very different funding needs, customer cycles and competitive pressures. American Battery Technology must earn its own valuation through evidence that fits its model. What could reverse sentiment For American Battery Technology, the cautious view starts with timing. A sound strategy can still disappoint when adoption, delivery or approvals take longer than investors expect. Any shift in priorities or unexplained change in language would make the current case harder to defend. Evidence to seek next For American Battery Technology, a practical watchlist includes customer activity, competitive responses, capital allocation and the reliability of management guidance. No single item settles the case, but together they reveal whether the company is creating a repeatable advantage. What the setup means For now, American Battery Technology offers a credible watch item rather than a settled verdict. The decisive issue is whether management can turn attention around battery materials and recycling into consistent delivery. The next disclosure should make that judgment easier. How to read the next update For American Battery Technology, investors can keep the review grounded by separating fresh information from the share-price reaction. The useful questions are straightforward: did management clarify the source of demand, explain the resources needed to deliver, and identify the risks that could interrupt progress? Answers supported by operating detail deserve more weight than broad optimism. If the next update connects those points to battery materials and recycling, the thesis may become easier to defend. If the discussion stays general, the market may continue to debate the quality and durability of the opportunity. A closer company-level reading A useful reading of American Battery Technology begins with the mechanics of battery materials and recycling, not with the popularity of the wider theme. The company has its own customer mix, execution history and set of constraints. Those features determine how quickly an opportunity can become a repeatable business result. The next update should therefore be judged for specificity: who is responding, which priority comes first and what could still interrupt delivery.

artigo.texto: St. Louis officials say they will analyze financial estimates for a data center that is projected to generate millions in tax revenue for the city and impose fines on the project if it doesn’t meet them. Development group TerraWatt has told the city that its planned $3 billion data center in Midtown near the historic Armory building will generate $445 million in tax revenue over the next 10 years. A 120-megawatt data center will be built in the old Famous-Barr warehouse on Market Street as part of the campus. The tax revenue estimate comes from the developer and its consultant, Steadfast City, which provided the numbers to the city’s Land Clearance for Redevelopment Authority earlier this month. But Mayor Cara Spencer and other city officials say they want to ensure the city receives the tax revenue developers have promised from the project. They plan to do so through a recently agreed-upon community benefit agreement and financial analysis from the city’s development arm. “This was a first of its kind for the city, so it was important to set a strong precedent for accountability and enforcement for environmental, workforce and revenue,” said Casey Millburg, Spencer’s chief of staff, of the agreement. “It was negotiated over many months.” The data center has been a focal point of conflict among anti-data center groups, concerned residents and city leaders over the past year as the project has slowly grown from proposal to reality. Previously, Spencer and other city leaders have said the project’s revenue could have significant benefits for the city, St. Louis Public Schools and other local taxing authorities that would receive revenue from it. “I think where we need to land here — where I want us to land as a city — is recognizing the economic benefit and protecting the community to the best of our ability,” Spencer said in July. City spokeswoman told St. Louis Public Radio that Spencer believes the city needs to keep a “keen eye” on the project. As a result, the project will undergo a financial analysis by St. Louis Development Corporation, the city’s development arm. Typically, SLDC conducts analysis only if developers seek tax incentives. In a statement, Steadfast City CEO Cecilia Dvorak said an independent assessment by the city would be welcomed. Jamboretz said city officials believe the project will be the first to undergo an analysis by SLDC while not seeking incentives. Per the recently agreed-upon community benefit agreement between the data center’s developers and city officials, it may not seek tax incentives from the city. The city sometimes uses tax incentives to attract developers to build, often delaying the city’s ability to see the full impact of a development for years. The agreement guarantees the city’s coffers will see an immediate impact from the project. The community benefit agreement also provides for the city to seek damages if the project fails to meet its annual tax revenue projections, Millburg said. She said fees will enforce the economic promises made by TerraWatt. For instance, the city will charge the developer $15,000 in damages for every $100,000 by which annual tax revenues fall short of the project’s projections. In a larger example, the city stated that if the actual tax revenue reported by the project in the first full year of operations is $60 million — nearly $3.1 million short of its goal — the developer will pay the city $476,249, or roughly 31 additional payments of $15,000 each. That amount must be paid within 60 days of reporting the shortfall. The community benefit plan also calls for TerraWatt to pay the city $15.7 million, with nearly $9 million of that paid by spring 2027, according to the agreement. Regarding jobs, the developers have agreed that by July 30 of the year in which the project’s building permit is issued, the center must employ at least 25 people. The center must employ at least 50 people by the second year, eventually increasing to at least 100. Millburg said the city will assess a $2,000 penalty for every job below the required target. The city also has the power to revoke the data center’s permits for uncorrected noncompliance on jobs, noise, utility and renewable energy requirements. Construction on the project, colloquially known as the Armory data center, is expected to begin next August. However, last week, David Daneshforooz, CEO and co-founder of TerraWatt, filed suit against the city, arguing that the city’s requirements exceed its powers and would make construction of the project impossible. Additionally, several data center opponents recently filed suit against the city to stop the development.

artigo.texto: A expansão da inteligência artificial, da computação em nuvem e da digitalização das empresas está acelerando a demanda por infraestrutura de processamento de dados no Brasil. No eixo São Paulo–Campinas, esse movimento já aparece nos números: a capacidade operacional de data centers cresceu 91% em apenas um ano, passando de 346 megawatts (MW) no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 661 MW no mesmo período de 2026. O avanço coloca São Paulo como o terceiro mercado primário das Américas com maior crescimento percentual no período, atrás apenas de Atlanta e Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos, segundo levantamento da Cushman & Wakefield. A perspectiva é de uma nova rodada de investimentos. Atualmente, o corredor São Paulo–Campinas possui 250 MW em construção e outros 2.066 MW planejados. Redata pode acelerar novos projetos O crescimento ganha um novo componente com o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado em 15 de setembro. O regime prevê a suspensão de tributos federais sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, ampliação e modernização de data centers, incluindo Imposto de Importação, PIS/Cofins, PIS/Cofins-Importação e IPI sobre itens elegíveis. O incentivo contempla estruturas direcionadas à computação em nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e inteligência artificial. “O mercado brasileiro já vinha apresentando crescimento consistente antes da sanção do Redata. A redução dos custos de implantação pode favorecer o avanço dos projetos, mas sua viabilidade continuará dependendo de fatores como disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, terrenos adequados, licenciamento e segurança regulatória”, afirma Dennys Andrade, Head de Market Research & Business Intelligence da Cushman & Wakefield. 96% da capacidade está ocupada A expansão ocorre em um mercado com pouca capacidade disponível. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a capacidade operacional avançou 6%, de 623 MW para 661 MW. Ao mesmo tempo, o volume em construção saltou 69%, passando de 148 MW para 250 MW. Mesmo com a ampliação da oferta, a vacância ficou em apenas 4,1%, o que significa que aproximadamente 96% da capacidade de colocation estava ocupada. Os 2.066 MW atualmente planejados representam mais de três vezes a capacidade operacional do eixo São Paulo–Campinas. O pipeline brasileiro também supera a soma dos projetos previstos em Querétaro, Santiago e Bogotá, que alcança aproximadamente 1,47 GW. O volume planejado, porém, não significa que todos os projetos serão efetivamente construídos. Além do capital necessário, a expansão depende de disponibilidade de energia e acesso à rede de transmissão, conectividade, equipamentos especializados, licenciamento e demanda contratada. “O impacto do Redata será medido pela capacidade de transformar projetos planejados em infraestrutura operacional. O Brasil reúne demanda e potencial de expansão, mas energia, conectividade e velocidade de execução determinarão quais empreendimentos efetivamente sairão do papel”, acrescenta Dennys Andrade. São Paulo lidera infraestrutura na América Latina Com 661 MW operacionais, o eixo São Paulo–Campinas possui quase o dobro da capacidade de Querétaro, no México, que registra 336 MW. Santiago, no Chile, aparece com 272 MW, enquanto Bogotá, na Colômbia, possui 58 MW. A escala ainda é distante dos principais polos norte-americanos. A Virgínia soma 12.338 MW em operação e Atlanta, 3.488 MW. Em velocidade de crescimento, porém, São Paulo se aproxima desses mercados: enquanto o corredor brasileiro avançou 91% em um ano, Virgínia cresceu 97% e Atlanta, 106%. Energia pode definir próximo mapa dos data centers Embora São Paulo e Campinas concentrem a maior infraestrutura do setor no Brasil, a próxima etapa de crescimento pode abrir espaço para outras regiões. Locais com disponibilidade de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão, conectividade de alta capacidade e terrenos adequados tendem a entrar no radar dos novos projetos. Segundo o estudo da Cushman & Wakefield, a capacidade paulista poderá atingir aproximadamente 1,6 vez o volume atual até 2036. Mais do que incentivos tributários, a capacidade de transformar o volume recorde de projetos anunciados em data centers efetivamente operacionais dependerá, portanto, de uma combinação entre energia, conectividade, licenciamento e velocidade de implantação. Com IA e nuvem aumentando a necessidade de processamento, esses fatores tendem a ganhar peso na disputa pelos próximos investimentos do setor.

artigo.texto: A autonomia da bateria é uma queixa comum entre os utilizadores de iPhone, que reportam sobretudo que a capacidade de armazenamento de energia vai reduzindo progressivamente ao longo dos anos. Lembrar que este tipo de degradação é normal em baterias de telemóveis e é também normal que, caso queira manter o seu dispositivo durante mais tempo, tenha de considerar a hipótese de trocar este componente se quer manter uma autonomia semelhante à que tinha quando o comprou. Mas como saber se a bateria do seu iPhone está de tal forma degradada que a substituição deve ser considerada? Para começar, deverá basear-se sobretudo na sua utilização do equipamento. A bateria ficar sem energia demasiado rápido é um sinal evidente que uma troca pode ser necessária, mas há outras “pistas” em que se pode basear. Uma maior lentidão em tarefas mais exigentes ou enquanto joga, por exemplo, é um sinal que o telemóvel está a evitar um encerramento, sendo que um sobreaquecimento da bateria quando esta não está a ser carregada também deve servir como um sinal de alerta. Felizmente, o iPhone conta com uma forma de saber o estado da sua bateria e pode ter acesso a esta informação diretamente a partir das definições do telemóvel. Para tal, só terá de entrar nas Definições e ir até à área dedicada à Bateria. Uma vez aqui, vá até ao Estado da bateria, onde poderá encontrar mais informações sobre a degradação da sua bateria. Se não tiver problemas, o estado da bateria aparecerá como Normal, com a Apple a apresentar uma mensagem onde indica que “a bateria deste iPhone está a funcionar como esperado”. Contudo, se aparecer outra mensagem, significa que está na hora de trocar a bateria para obter um melhor desempenho. Esta área dedicada à bateria conta ainda com outras informações e que lhe permite ver a Capacidade máxima de armazenamento de energia (com 100% a ser capacidade original com que adquiriu o telemóvel) e também poderá ver a Contagem de ciclos (que lhe permite saber quantos ciclos de carregamento já completou desde que adquiriu o telemóvel). Uma vez reunidos todos estes dados e se decidir proceder com a substituição da bateria, recomenda-se então que vá até uma loja da Apple ou a uma loja de reparações autorizadas para que o componente seja trocado. Leia Também: Ecrã partido ou bateria fraca? Eis quando vale a pena trocar de telemóvel

artigo.texto: Key takeaway:In the third quarter of 2026, the solid-state battery industry is at a critical stage of transition from “pilot-scale validation” to “the eve of mass production.” National-level special plans have been implemented, and the standards system is being accelerated and improved. On the materials side, sulfide electrolytes are seeing “rising volume and falling prices,” entering a transition period of ton-level volume ramp-up. On the technology side, solid-liquid (semi-solid) batteries are the first to be deployed in scenarios such as commercial vehicles, energy storage, and eVTOL, while pilot lines for all-solid-state batteries are being built intensively. Capital and industry are collaborating deeply, equipment orders continue to be secured, and downstream application scenarios are flourishing in multiple areas. At the same time, however, risks such as insufficient capacity utilization, lagging orders, and interface and manufacturing bottlenecks remain, requiring a rational view of the pace of industrialization. Foreword: Material Price Analysis—Policy Side Hot, Spot Side Cold, Sulfide “Rising Volume, Falling Prices” In Q3 2026, the solid-state battery sector showed a striking divergence: “hot on the policy side, cold on the materials spot side.” On September 28, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and six other departments issued the “15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the New Battery Industry,” clarifying preliminary large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, which drove the battery sector and solid-state battery sector stronger on September 29. However, on the materials spot side, the pricing anchor centered on lithium salts declined unilaterally, and sulfide electrolytes showed a typical pattern of “rising volume, falling prices.” On lithium salts, the average spot price of battery-grade lithium carbonate in Q3 was about RMB 148,000/ton. At the end of the quarter, the quotation on September 29 for battery-grade lithium carbonate was RMB 123,000/ton, with a Q3 cumulative decline of -22.9%. On solid-state-battery-specific materials, sulfide electrolytes were the segment with the most obvious “price collapse” this quarter. From January to August 2026, China’s cumulative output of sulfide electrolytes was 70 tons, up 119.7% year-on-year, already exceeding the full-year 2025 output of 58.29 tons, but only 19.6% of the annual forecast target of 360 tons was completed. In August, capacity utilization was only 5.82%, product prices continued to plummet, and LPSC fell by more than 24% in a single month. Lithium sulfide also ramped up simultaneously: in August, China’s battery-grade lithium sulfide output was 7.79 tons, up 3.6% month-on-month and up 143% year-on-year; the January-August cumulative total was 52.9 tons, already exceeding the global full-year 2025 output of 34 tons. China’s output accounts for about 95% of the world total. It is expected that monthly output in Q4 will rise to 9–10 tons, with full-year output of 85–95 tons. On the supply side, Q3 saw the concentrated landing of “hundred-ton-level” production lines: Tinci Materials’ hundred-ton-level lithium sulfide and solid electrolyte pilot line was completed and put into production in Q3; Shandong Chuanglu’s 150-ton/year solid electrolyte production line completed installation and commissioning; Capchem’s oxide electrolyte will put thousand-ton-level capacity into operation in 2026. However, in the first half of the year, both supply and demand for lithium sulfide and sulfide electrolytes were weak, and price pressure was the main theme of Q3. Anode materials were relatively resistant to decline, and additives were structurally strong. Overall, the solid-state battery materials sector has entered a transition stage from “kilogram-level transactions” to “ton-level transactions,” with the price center moving downward. Q4 needs to verify the quality of ton-level volume ramp-up. I. Solid-State Battery Materials - Electrolytes: Sulfide Upstream Volume Rises but Prices Remain Under Pressure; Oxide Capacity Takes the Lead in Scaling; Halides Accelerate Reserve The sulfide route was the most intensively expanded direction on the materials side in Q3. The high-purity lithium sulfide pilot line of a subsidiary controlled by Semcorp has been completed, with plans to achieve thousand-ton-level mass production of sulfur-halide solid electrolytes in 2026–2027. Tinci Materials’ hundred-ton-level lithium sulfide and solid electrolyte pilot line was completed and entered trial production in Q3, using a self-developed liquid-phase method with costs 30%–40% lower than the mainstream solid-phase method. XTC New Energy’s high-purity lithium sulfide entered trial production. Yahua Group’s lithium sulfide pilot line entered the demonstration and design stage and has been sent to customers for samples. Tianqi Lithium’s 50-ton lithium sulfide pilot project is under construction and is expected to be completed in the second half of the year; most processes for argyrodite-type sulfide electrolyte preparation have been removed from glove boxes. Gotion Holding’s world’s first ten-thousand-ton-level high-purity lithium sulfide line started in Anqing, with plans to complete pilot testing by the end of 2026 and full mass production in 2027, with purity reaching 99.99%. Qinghai Weixiang’s 3,000-ton lithium sulfide project completed filing, with Phase I of 500 tons and Phase II of 2,500 tons, planned for completion in July 2027. Easpring’s sulfide electrolyte has entered small-scale validation with leading solid-state battery customers and has scalable supply capability. Guoci Materials’ sulfide solid electrolyte automated production line was completed, with a strategic focus on sulfides. Langu New Energy’s sulfide and halide solid electrolytes have achieved hundred-ton-level capacity, with the next step planned to expand to thousand-ton or even ten-thousand-ton levels. artigo.texto: A expansão de data centers no Brasil abriu uma discussão sobre o risco de pressão na conta de luz, conforme indica reportagem do Valor Econômico. O governo federal avalia como atender ao consumo dessas cargas, aproveitando a oferta de energia renovável do país, sem elevar os custos para os demais consumidores, e discute alternativas como o uso de gás natural e de baterias para armazenar energia nos momentos de maior geração. No setor, há divergências, entretanto, sobre o impacto desses investimentos sobre as tarifas de energia. Nos Estados Unidos, onde esses empreendimentos avançaram em escala muito maior, os preços da energia estão entre os fatores que alimentam a resistência de comunidades. No Brasil, cálculos de agentes do setor apontam para um custo adicional de cerca de R$ 7 bilhões por ano na conta de luz. O cenário considera um crescimento de 3,5 mil megawatts no consumo de energia causado pelos data centers em 2026 e parte da premissa de que a demanda será atendida pela expansão da matriz, com novas usinas eólicas e solares. A regulamentação, porém, ainda não definiu se será exigida nova geração ou se poderá ser utilizada a oferta renovável que já atende ao sistema elétrico. Setor de gás entra em alerta com possível decreto do Redata sem o insumo Reportagem da Agência Infra indica que o setor de gás natural entrou em alerta com a possível publicação de decreto nesta segunda-feira (28) para a regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) sem a inclusão do insumo como fonte de suprimento energético. Segundo interlocutores do governo, o Ministério da Fazenda está articulando a edição do normativo com o entendimento de que o gás não atende à exigência de “baixa emissão de carbono”. Do outro lado, agentes do setor se apoiam no MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), que já fez a defesa pública da inclusão da molécula na lista de fontes para atendimento dos data centers. A pasta estaria tentando segurar a publicação do decreto e ganhar tempo para que o insumo seja contemplado, disseram fontes da Esplanada. Marcelo Mendonça, diretor executivo da Abegás (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado), disse à Agência Infra que os “rumores” de que o gás não será contemplado no Redata preocupam. “Existe uma falta de sintonia nesse discurso entre os ministérios, têm chegado informações equivocadas em relação ao tratamento do gás natural”, aponta. EPP pede que a Aneel retire documentos da Eneva e Global em leilão A CNN Brasil informa que a disputa sobre quem vai levar quase 2 GW em termelétricas do leilão de reserva de capacidade ganhou um novo capítulo. A EPP (Evolution Power Partners) pediu à diretoria da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) que desconsidere e retire dos autos os memoriais e documentos apresentados por Eneva e Global Participações em Energia na disputa pela habilitação dos consórcios ION. Para a EPP, a Eneva e a Global manifestaram fora do prazo previsto para responder ao recurso contra a inabilitação de seus projetos. A EPP lidera os consórcios ION que ganharam projetos termelétricos que somam 1.685 MW. Total Energies apresenta plano de crescimento até 2035 A TotalEnergies apresentou seus objetivos de crescimento para ampliar sua capacidade de energia após 2030, apoiada por bilhões de dólares em investimentos anuais. A companhia francesa de energia afirmou que pretende investir entre US$ 14 bilhões e US$ 17 bilhões por ano entre 2027 e 2032. A empresa espera que seu segmento de petróleo e gás registre crescimento de produção de cerca de 2% a 3% ao ano entre 2030 e 2035, sustentado por seu portfólio de projetos orgânicos. Para o segmento de eletricidade, a companhia prevê geração líquida de energia de 10 a 12 terawatts-hora por ano entre 2030 e 2035. A TotalEnergies espera que a eletricidade represente cerca de um quarto de sua matriz energética — que também inclui petróleo e gás — até o fim desse período. (Valor Econômico – por Dow Jones) Proposta para novas regras de transmissão pode beneficiar data center O diretor-geral da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, propôs uma regra de transição na Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) para atender cargas como data centers. A proposta teria alcance até 2029 e beneficiaria os centros de processamento de dados que têm implementação por etapas, o que levaria ao aumento do consumo de energia nos próximos anos. Conforme voto-vista apresentado na quinta-feira (24), o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) deverá priorizar, no acesso ao sistema de transmissão de energia, os empreendimentos que já tinham parecer positivo de viabilidade técnica emitido antes das novas regras, que começaram a valer em dezembro de 2025. Sandoval argumenta que o decreto que criou a Pnast, ao ter vigência imediata, impediu a “adoção de providências prévias” por consumidores como data centers, que têm previsão de acesso escalonada à carga. Ou seja, aqueles que já tinham acesso ao sistema e estavam aumentando o seu montante de uso de energia ano a ano teriam sido prejudicados pela criação da política, que substituiu a análise dos pedidos de forma cronológica pelas Temporadas de Acesso. O processo era relatado pelo ex-diretor Fernando Mosna, que apresentou voto em julho deste ano, quando Sandoval pediu vista. O assunto está na pauta do circuito deliberativo da Aneel, marcado para amanhã (29). Se aprovado, será iniciada consulta pública de 45 dias. artigo.texto: Elsewedy Electric has connected a 50 MW / 100 MWh battery energy storage system to Greece’s transmission grid, marking a step toward the national goal of between 5 GW and 7 GW by 2030. The government is also providing support for batteries for small and mid-sized firms, to be integrated with solar panels. In addition, deadlines for BESS investments in coal regions are set to be extended. While its neighbor Bulgaria is at the top of the chart on a global scale in battery energy storage systems, Greece is rushing to become a major player itself. The country has some 600 MW of operating power from the 13 active facilities in the system controlled by Independent Transmission System Operator (IPTO or Admie). The goal is 5 GW to 7 GW by 2030. In 2027, the total would need to reach 1.5 GW. Elsewedy adds 100 MWh to Greece’s battery storage fleet Elsewedy Electric energized a standalone BESS early this month. The project was developed by Elsewedy Energy and EPC and implemented by Elsewedy Electric Power Systems Projects and BMS. The battery facility has 50 MW in capability and a two-hour duration, which translates to 100 MWh in storage capacity. It is the Egypt-based firm’s first BESS in Europe. Elsewedy won government support three years ago at the country’s first auction for standalone energy storage, in the form of a contract for difference (CfD). Connected to the 150 kV network and a new 33/150 kV substation, the facility is located in Oinofyta in the municipality of Tanagra, part of the regional unit of Viotia in Central Greece. The investment was worth EUR 41.9 million. In early 2025, Elsewedy obtained a EUR 18.2 financing package from the National Bank of Greece. It also benefits from a EUR 10 million grant and EUR 5.5 loan, both from the European Union’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). SMEs win subsidies for BESS backup for solar power Expansion is underway in other segments of battery storage as well. The ministry recently published the provisional list of beneficiaries of the support program for small and mid-sized enterprises. The subsidies total EUR 8.15 million. Overall operating power for 209 firms is 28.2 MW, with 49.3 MWh of storage. BESS facilities will support 30.8 MW of photovoltaics altogether. It took almost eleven months since the applications deadline for the first list. The package was intended to cover 333 MW of battery capability with EUR 153 million. More time for projects in coal regions in transition Futhermore, the Ministry of Environment and Energy is prolonging a deadline for the winners of the third auction. The beneficiaries would be able to submit the so-called declarations of readiness to the Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO or ADMIE) by mid-December, according to a bill of law, Energypress reported. The procedure is for four-hour BESS projects in the coal regions of Western Macedonia and the Peloponnese. HELLENiQ Renewables and government-controlled Public Power Corp. (PPC) were the biggest winners, with two plants of 25 MW and one 50 MW system, respectively. The rest of the list comprises Amber Energy (18 MW), Plain Solar (7.9 MW), Enercoplan (25 MW), Eunice Group’s Arkadia Storage (10 MW), EDF’s subsidiary Heliothema (10 MW) and Ardassa Energy (18 MW). The three standalone energy storage tenders resulted in contracts for 900 MW overall.

artigo.texto: Crestview bans large-scale data centers, but mayor says decision could be revisited CRESTVIEW, Fla. -- The City of Crestview voted to ban large-scale data centers Monday evening. They aren't the first municipal government in the region to pass a similar law. Escambia and Walton County commissioners have also passed bans. The City of Pensacola has said there's no place for them in the city's plans. And Okaloosa County commissioners voted to regulate data centers rather than ban them. RELATED STORIES - Escambia County moves forward with ordinance banning AI data centers - Okaloosa County commissioners opt to regulate data centers, not ban them - Pensacola passes one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers as debate grows WEAR News spoke with the Crestview Mayor JB Whitten ahead of the meeting who describes the move as a precautionary effort. "Our city council is being very cautious," Whitten said. Crestview city council members unanimously voted to ban large-scale data centers from setting up shop in city limits. "I look at my own county," Whitten said. "[Okaloosa] County commissioners are talking about it and they're getting a lot of pushback on that. And I look over in Santa Rosa County and I look at Escambia County, all the other counties. And it could be because there's not a clear understanding of what they are." Whitten says while large scale data centers would bring money into the city, it wouldn't necessarily bring more jobs. "It can't always be about money," Whitten said. "One of the cons though is you think if you have a big data center, you have a lot of employees. You really don't. It's not a big workforce generator for the city." Whitten says while the ban passed, all it would take is another vote to revoke it. "I compared this very much to five or six years ago when they authorized medical marijuana," said Whitten. "We banned them the first year. There was not enough information to know what was going on. A year later, we authorized them." Whitten says if the city gets more information on the data centers, the ban could be revoked. "I think that what we have right now is the city council is taking a seat back, examining everything, determine where do we want to go with this," Whitten said. "So it could change in the future." For now, he says it's the council's job to listen to its residents. "We're seeing reactions of citizens right now don't want them," said Whitten. "They really don't. So I think the people [councilors] are trying to listen to the citizens." "So like I said, if it's not all that bad, maybe sometime in the future, it could be a change," he said. In 2025, Gov. Ron DeSantis passed a bill that allows local governments to decide where data centers can be built. artigo.texto: Governo teme que data centers puxem alta da conta de luz MME estuda alternativas para geração nos horários de pico de consumo como uso de gás natural e baterias para assegurar o fornecimento A expansão de data centers no Brasil abriu uma discussão sobre o risco de pressão na conta de luz. O governo federal avalia como atender ao consumo dessas cargas, aproveitando a oferta de energia renovável do país, sem elevar os custos para os demais consumidores, e discute alternativas como o uso de gás natural e de baterias para armazenar energia nos momentos de maior geração. No setor, há divergências, entretanto, sobre o impacto desses investimentos sobre as tarifas de energia. Nos Estados Unidos, onde esses empreendimentos avançaram em escala muito maior, os preços da energia estão entre os fatores que alimentam a resistência de comunidades. No Brasil, cálculos de agentes do setor apontam para um custo adicional de cerca de R$ 7 bilhões por ano na conta de luz. O cenário considera um crescimento de 3,5 mil megawatts no consumo de energia causado pelos data centers em 2026 e parte da premissa de que a demanda será atendida pela expansão da matriz, com novas usinas eólicas e solares. A regulamentação, porém, ainda não definiu se será exigida nova geração ou se poderá ser utilizada a oferta renovável que já atende ao sistema elétrico. Pelo critério de rateio da contratação considerado no cálculo, esses agentes estimam que 70% do custo seria bancado pelos consumidores do mercado regulado, como residências e pequenos comércios, e 30%, pelos consumidores do mercado livre, como grandes empresas. Na avaliação dessas fontes, o custo decorre da necessidade de garantir o fornecimento contínuo aos data centers. Como as fontes solar e eólica são intermitentes, é preciso assegurar energia também nos períodos em que não há geração, o que pode exigir capacidade adicional e pressionar as tarifas. Justamente por isso, integrantes do governo têm defendido o uso de baterias como alternativa para lidar com essa intermitência, armazenando a energia produzida nos períodos de maior geração. A avaliação é que a solução poderia mitigar a pressão sobre as tarifas e ainda evitar o uso de gás natural, que vai na contramão do esforço de descarbonização do setor elétrico. O Ministério da Fazenda é contra o uso do combustível e propõe soluções que permitam aproveitar a oferta de energia renovável disponível no país, enquanto o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) defende o gás como alternativa. A regulamentação definirá qual solução será adotada e se o gás natural poderá ser incluído entre as alternativas. Há ainda uma discussão sobre os custos de transmissão que podem recair sobre os consumidores, mas que não é exclusiva dos data centers. Como ocorre com outras grandes cargas, a conexão desses empreendimentos pode exigir reforços e ampliações da rede, a depender da localização e do volume de energia demandado. Existe, por outro lado, um potencial benefício para o sistema, segundo um técnico. O Brasil enfrenta excesso de geração em determinados períodos, especialmente de fonte solar, o que na prática obriga o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) a cortar a produção em alguns momentos do dia. Nesse cenário, os data centers poderiam criar demanda e estimular novos investimentos em geração e transmissão, movimentando a cadeia do setor elétrico, com criação de emprego e renda. O desafio, segundo um técnico do governo, é garantir que essas empresas arquem adequadamente com os custos adicionais gerados para o sistema. Segundo a fonte, a regulação pode ser desenhada para atribuir aos próprios data centers esses custos, evitando que sejam repassados aos demais consumidores. Segurança do suprimento devem orientar expansão do Sistema Interligado e atendimento a novos empreendimentos, defende ministério A Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais (Brasscom) avalia que a expansão dos data centers não representa um problema para a rede de energia no Brasil. Segundo o presidente-executivo da entidade, Affonso Nina, esses empreendimentos respondem hoje por cerca de 2% do consumo de eletricidade no país, e a estimativa é que a participação chegue a 4% ou 5% nos próximos cinco anos - parte ainda pequena diante do consumo total no país, segundo ele. “Temos excessos de energia de várias fontes, então a capacidade que já existe consegue atender essa demanda. Seria um problema se fosse algo na ordem de 10%, 20% do consumo”, disse. Nina concorda que um desafio está na transmissão, diante do excesso de geração, especialmente solar e eólica no Nordeste, e das limitações para levar essa energia aos maiores centros consumidores. Ele argumenta, porém, que a expansão da rede não se traduziria em aumento das tarifas. “As linhas de transmissão são construídas e pagas pelos usuários, mas, com a demanda crescendo, tem mais gente pagando por isso. Então esse equilíbrio dos custos acaba se mantendo”, afirma o presidente executivo da Brasscom. Nina destaca ainda que há casos em que os próprios data centers financiam subestações e trechos finais de transmissão. “Os data centers estão fazendo esse investimento por conta própria para viabilizar a chegada de energia”, diz. Ele ressalta que a realidade brasileira não é comparável à dos EUA, pois o Brasil tem, por exemplo, um sistema elétrico interligado e excedentes de energia renovável. “Não podemos de forma alguma afirmar que no Brasil vai haver um aumento de conta elétrica porque nos EUA está acontecendo”. Ethan Zindler, diretor de Pesquisa em Políticas Públicas e Países da BloombergNEF, afirmou em evento promovido pelo Valor e pela Amcham Brasil em Nova York, na semana passada, que a demanda de eletricidade nos Estados Unidos pode dobrar em cinco anos devido aos data centers. Segundo ele, o mercado de gás deve ficar mais restrito nos próximos 24 meses e uma alta do combustível pode elevar também o preço da eletricidade nos Estados Unidos e ter efeitos globa

artigo.texto: Five-Day Training on Solar Energy and Battery Storage Systems Begins in Nepal Kathmandu. A five-day training has started on promoting solar energy in Nepal's industries and making battery storage systems safe, effective, and sustainable. The training will provide participants with knowledge on the current status of solar and battery storage systems in Nepal, industrial carbon emission reduction, energy management, grid services, battery technology, safety standards, cyber security, environmental and social security, and other important topics. The training, organized by the Alternative Energy Promotion Center (AEPC) under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, has the participation of 45 engineers. The high-level training on 'Solar PV and Battery Energy Storage Systems for Industrial Sector: Design, Installation and Safety' is in collaboration with Practical Action and Ghampower Nepal. Representatives from the private sector, educational and research institutions, and related government and non-governmental agencies from across the country are participating in the training. The Alternative Energy Promotion Center has stated that in addition to theoretical knowledge, participants will be provided with practical experience through group exercises based on real industrial scenarios and field observation tours. In the context of Nepal prioritizing clean energy expansion, security, and green industrialization, the center expects to reduce overall energy consumption and make electricity supply reliable through the use of solar energy. In the context of climate-induced disasters exposing the risks to energy infrastructure, as highlighted by the Rusuwa flood, the center has pointed out the need to analyze the risks associated with monsoon-related events, as hydropower-based energy production, transmission, and distribution infrastructure are connected to river systems. Board member of the center, Ankita Shah, said that solar energy and battery storage systems can play a significant role in enhancing climate resilience if they can produce and store energy locally, given the risk of floods and landslides to electricity projects. According to her, promotion programs for energy production and storage will help create green employment and open up new entrepreneurial opportunities.
