artigo.texto: A handful of north Macomb County residents opposed to data centers in their communities voiced their concerns to county commissioners, and asked them to pass a moratorium on centers and help local communities fight them. “We need you guys to step into the fight. I need my commissioners to step into the fray,” said Tarra Samander, who owns a farm near I-94 and 26 Mile Road in Lenox Township and said she and her husband rejected an offer of $500,000 from a data-center developer as a 10% deposit to purchase their property. Residents spoke Thursday during the public-participation agenda item at the full county Board of Commissioners meeting in the Administration Building in Mount Clemens. Commissioner MIchael Howard of Warren said during commissioner comments that while the county can’t help them with a moratorium they can provide some expertise and assistance through county planners. “The county has very, very, very limited zoning and land authority” under state law,” Howard said. “This is truly a local municipality issue as well as a state issue.” There are currently three potential AI data center developments in the county in Lenox, and Washington and Richmond townships. Lenox is closest to development at this time. Also speaking was Arianna Welsh, who resides in Bruce Township but owns property in Lenox and Richmond, and runs a business in New Haven. Welsh asked commissioners to “expand and better coordinate technical assistance available to our 27 local communities when evaluating major and emerging developments.” “There is urgency to this request,” Welsh told the board. “Industry is not waiting for local governments to catch up. Communities are being approached now with increasingly large and complex projects.” The projects involve rezonings, master plan updates, development agreements, infrastructure commitments, environmental impacts, road-capacity considerations and tax implications on properties for “hundreds of acres” and “hundreds or millions or even billions of dollars,” Welsh said. “The window to obtain specialized expertise can become very short,” she said. “The county does not need to make decisions for communities, but it can give them better tools, though, to help themselves.” The assistance could be provided through the county planning department, Welsh said. Commissioner Phil Kraft of Chesterfield Township, located adjacent to Lenox, said he sent a letter many months ago to Lenox officials asking them to work with New Haven on a moratorium on data centers together but that didn’t happen.” “I think it would’ve been in our communities’ best interests for them to work together,” Kraft said at the meeting. “I have a lot of the same concerns that you do.” Lenox passed a 4-month moratorium last February that expired without renewal after attorney James R. Andary, representing a company called Lenox & Chesterfield Economic Development Alliance, a data-center developer, threatened a lawsuit in May. It was registered by Paul Reschke. “Our Client has expended substantial time, capital and professional resources to develop a large-scaled, phased technology infrastructure complex .. a proposed Data Center Campus would be generally located on the I-94 Development District,” Andary wrote In a May 4 letter to the township obtained by The Macomb Daily. “Under Michigan Law, Lenox Township cannot use zoning laws or a moratorium to ban or block either temporarily or permanently, a lawful land development use. I must emphasize the Campus and the Data Center is a lawful development use of the property that is owned or controlled by my Client. “We have been authorized to pursue legal action to not only seek injunctive relief, but also substantial economic damages from Lenox Township if the moratorium is extended.” According to another letter in May, the company again threatened a lawsuit if the township delayed efforts to draft the I-94 Development District ordinance, which has been subject of a first reading but was sent back by the township Board of Trustees to the township Planning Commission for more work. A web site has been created in support of the project, touting the benefits that would come to the area. State anti-data center forms Companies’ efforts to build data centers in Michigan spawned the creation of the Economic Development Responsibility Alliance of Michigan, which is helping local communities fight the centers and tracking close to three-dozen projects in the state, including in Lenox and Washington. “We’re pretty much across the board opposed to AI data centers,” said Marjorie Steele, executive director of the EDRA. “Based on what we are seeing … it’s become increasingly clear at this point that the purpose of these data centers is not the stated purpose they’re being marketed for. The reason that these data centers need such computing power and why they need such exponentially greater processing power than the standard internet and cloud-computering centers that we’ve had for decades is they’re trying to build a surveillance state.” Steele also pointed to the recent increased use of license-plate readers and AI software for surveillance. “We believe that local communities and local township can and should use any and all reasonable, legal means at their disposal to protect themselves, and that includes zoning and regulation,” she said. The organization says AI or “hyperscale” data cents consume large amount of water and energy; create only a minimal number of jobs post-construction; increase the risk of water contamination and “well depletion”; increase the number and level of power outages in the surrounding area; are “susceptible to toxic fires”; and receiving funds from the state and federal government. Of 34 potential sites in Michigan, the EDRA says it is “fighting” 13 projects, “winning” 12 and “won but vigilant” at nine sites, including Washington Township, where the developer withdrew the project last May. artigo.texto: Publicado em 28 de setembro de 2026 O segundo dia de ROG.e contou com a participação do presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, na mesa “Implementação das políticas públicas e regulamentos para diversidade energética e soluções de baixo carbono no Brasil". Um dos maiores eventos sobre óleo e gás da América Latina, a ROG.e foi realizada de 21 a 24 de setembro, no Riocentro, na Barra da Tijuca. A EPE participou da feira com um estande, apresentação de mais de 20 trabalhos e debates sobre o setor. Em sua participação, Prado dividiu o painel com o Subsecretário de Implementação da Sec. Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, Thiago Barral, e com o Diretor Executivo de Desenvolvimento de Negócios da Prumo Logística, Mauro Andrade. A discussão foi moderada pela fundadora e CEO da New Gaia Strategies Investments, Raphaella Gomes. O presidente da EPE destacou que o PDE 2035 e o PNE 2055 apontam uma matriz com bastante espaço para biometano, SAF, hidrogênio, captura e estocagem de carbono, entre outros. “Ambos os planos põem o hidrogênio como uma rota confirmada no longuíssimo prazo e com políticas concretas já aprovadas no Congresso. Temos o ProBioQAV (Programa Nacional de Combustível Sustentável de Aviação), a Lei do Combustível do Futuro, a questão dos mandatos de biometano e o Plano Nacional Integrado das Infraestruturas de Gás e Biometano (PNIIGB) que também tenta organizar um pouco esse mercado em relação à oferta e a demanda", enumerou. “Em comparação a todas as outras opções de recursos e aproveitamentos energéticos, eu colocaria a captura e estocagem de carbono como aquele aluno na sala que necessita de um pouquinho mais de atenção", avaliou. Em relação ao carbono biogênico, originado de matérias-primas renováveis, como a biomassa e os biocombustíveis, Prado enxerga uma “grande oportunidade". “Você pode ter combustíveis renováveis com pegadas negativas de carbono", afirmou. Neste sentido, ele destacou a necessidade de maior aproximação com os estados que possuem a maior produção de biocombustíveis. Thiago Prado falou ainda sobre a importância fundamental de avançar no detalhamento regulatório e sobre a atuação do Brasil na Global Coalition for Energy Planning (Coalizão Global para o Planejamento Energético), criada no âmbito do G20, e na Olade (Organização Latino-Americana de Energia). “A maior mensagem que o Brasil pode passar é de diversificação, mas principalmente de vocacionamento. A transição energética tem que respeitar as vocações. Esse desenho de mercado tem que ser suficientemente capaz de representar não só o Brasil como outros países para que isso faça sentido para todo mundo e não vire uma discussão de rotas tecnológicas". Plano Nacional Integrado das Infraestruturas de Gás e Biometano (PNIIGB) O Plano Nacional Integrado das Infraestruturas de Gás e Biometano (PNIIGB) foi tema da apresentação do analista de pesquisa energética Henrique Rangel, no painel Planejamento, Governança e Organização Institucional do Mercado. Ele apresentou o plano, a metodologia utilizada em sua elaboração, abordando etapas como os estudos de oferta e demanda, seleção de projetos, análise socioambiental, dimensionamento e Capex e estimativa de emprego e renda. A edição do PNIIGB apontou a necessidade de 15 projetos, com investimentos da ordem de R$ 35 bilhões e 2.200 km de dutos. “A análise integrada dos diversos elos do setor de gás natural demonstra que a expansão coordenada pode reduzir gargalos estruturais", concluiu. Rangel também destacou que a inclusão do biometano no planejamento reforça a convergência entre o setor e as metas nacionais de baixo carbono. A programação do segundo dia de ROG.e também contou com a participação do Superintendente Adjunto de Petróleo e Gás, Marcelo Alfradique, que mediou a mesa Distribuição, Regulação e Mercado Livre de Gás. Já no palco técnico, o analista de pesquisa energética Ederaldo Godoy apresentou trabalho sobre o estado da arte do BioGL no Brasil, com foco nas principais rotas tecnológicas e os insumos. O BioGL é sustentável e drop-in ao Gás Liquefeito de Petróleo (GLP), ou seja, quimicamente idêntico, sem necessidade de alteração nos equipamentos de queima, prometendo ser a molécula verde com potencial para ser adicionada na descarbonização do GLP. No estande da EPE, o analista de pesquisa energética Igor Veneroso apresentou o panorama dos investimentos em inovação no Brasil, enquanto a analista Pamela Vilela falou sobre o Zoneamento Nacional de Recursos de Óleo e Gás (ZNMT) 2023-2025.

artigo.texto: Vanderburgh County Commissioners approve $200 million battery storage facility EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Vanderburgh County Commissioners this week approved a series of agreements that clear the way for a new battery energy storage system, or BESS, next to the Elliott Station substation in Scott Township. Project details The developer, Elliot Battery Storage, an affiliate of RWE Clean Energy Development, plans to invest about $200 million in the project. The facility will store roughly 200 megawatts of power. This power could be used to help utilities manage high-demand periods. “So it’s a large station on the far east side of Vanderburgh County... they’re key to peak load... they’re a modern way of dealing with the peak load, and they need to be next to a substation, which this one is,” said Mike Schopmeyer, Vanderburgh County attorney. Zoning approval and neighbor notification The project already passed a Board of Zoning Appeals vote, 5-0. Schopmeyer said people living near the site off East Baseline Road were notified and briefed before that vote. “Everything’s approved now, so the petitioner... can move ahead with the construction. They’ve got to go through a building permit process,” Schopmeyer said. Payments to the county and timeline As part of the deal, the company will pay the county $250,000 for local development projects, plus cover the county’s legal costs for negotiating the agreements. The company must break ground by the end of 2029 or the deal falls apart. The facility is expected to be up and running no later than November 2031. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A DHL está a expandir a sua rede mundial de logística de baterias, que integra já mais de 20 instalações especializadas. A operação acompanha todo o ciclo de vida destes equipamentos, desde o apoio à produção e transporte até ao diagnóstico, reparação, logística inversa e preparação para reciclagem. A eletrificação dos setores automóvel, industrial e energético está a criar novas cadeias de abastecimento e a aumentar a procura de soluções logísticas especializadas. Para responder a esta transformação, a DHL está a desenvolver uma rede integrada de Centros de Excelência de Veículos Elétricos e Baterias nos principais mercados mundiais. A plataforma reúne competências da DHL Supply Chain, DHL Global Forwarding e DHL Express, combinando logística de produção, transporte, armazenagem, serviços pós-venda e gestão do ciclo de vida das baterias. A rede liga já mais de 20 instalações, estando prevista a abertura de novas localizações. A expansão surge num contexto em que as baterias deixaram de estar associadas apenas aos veículos elétricos. Os mesmos sistemas são cada vez mais utilizados em equipamentos industriais, operações mineiras, infraestruturas de rede elétrica e projetos de armazenamento de energia renovável. Algumas destas unidades ultrapassam as 50 toneladas, exigindo soluções de transporte pesado, equipamentos específicos e um planeamento logístico próprio. A classificação como mercadoria perigosa, as diferenças regulamentares entre mercados e modos de transporte e as exigências de documentação e controlo aduaneiro aumentam igualmente a complexidade das operações. “A logística de baterias é fundamentalmente diferente das cadeias de abastecimento tradicionais”, afirma Francisco Milián, Head of Inbound to Manufacturing da DHL Supply Chain EMEA. Segundo o responsável, os clientes necessitam de capacidades especializadas em todas as fases, desde a logística de entrada e o apoio à produção até ao armazenamento, distribuição, recondicionamento, devolução e reciclagem. As instalações especializadas da DHL combinam áreas de armazenagem preparadas para baterias com serviços técnicos, entre os quais diagnóstico, testes, carregamento, condicionamento, reparação, logística inversa e preparação dos equipamentos para reciclagem. Em Halle, na Alemanha, o operador disponibilizou recentemente 13 mil metros quadrados de espaço de armazém adaptado a este tipo de produto. Na Hungria, está a ser preparada uma nova instalação dedicada à logística de baterias, cuja entrada em funcionamento está prevista para 2027. A DHL está também a construir um hub europeu em Holtum, nos Países Baixos. A infraestrutura contará com 17 mil metros quadrados de armazenagem e serviços especializados para baterias de alta tensão e deverá iniciar atividade no princípio de 2027. A proximidade à operação automóvel já existente permitirá criar um campus integrado, dedicado à mobilidade elétrica e aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Muitas destas instalações integram transporte, serviços aduaneiros e operações transfronteiriças, procurando concentrar num único parceiro várias etapas da cadeia de valor. A proposta dirige-se a fabricantes de baterias e automóveis, mas também a empresas de energia, operadores industriais e projetos ligados à exploração de minerais críticos. Eletrificação cria novos corredores logísticos A concentração de uma parte significativa da produção de baterias na Ásia, conjugada com o crescimento da procura na Europa e noutras regiões, está a alterar os fluxos comerciais. Ao mesmo tempo, a instalação de novas gigafábricas gera movimentos de equipamentos produtivos, matérias-primas, produtos químicos, componentes e baterias acabadas. “A transição energética está a criar corredores comerciais e padrões de cadeias de abastecimento inteiramente novos”, sublinha Hendrik Venter, Global CEO da DHL Supply Chain. Para o responsável, as empresas estão a redesenhar as suas operações para apoiar a mobilidade elétrica, o armazenamento de energia e a expansão das fontes renováveis. A logística de baterias ganha ainda uma nova dimensão com o crescimento dos sistemas BESS – Battery Energy Storage Systems – utilizados para armazenar energia e apoiar a estabilidade das redes elétricas. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a DHL entregou mais de 1100 destas unidades em diferentes mercados. Estes projetos podem envolver sistemas de grandes dimensões, transporte multimodal, operações de elevação de cargas pesadas e entregas em locais remotos, além do cumprimento das regras aplicáveis às mercadorias perigosas. A área New Energy é um dos setores de crescimento definidos pelo DHL Group na sua Strategy 2030. O grupo desenvolve soluções logísticas para oito segmentos: energia eólica, solar, veículos elétricos e baterias, sistemas BESS, carregamento de veículos elétricos, infraestruturas de rede, hidrogénio e combustíveis alternativos.

artigo.texto: Digital Realty Plans Cable Landing Station at Los Angeles Data Center Digital Realty's first turnkey cable landing station is designed to bring subsea capacity directly into an established data center and interconnection environment. Digital Realty is planning to build a cable landing station (CLS) inside its LAX12 data center in El Segundo, Calif., adding a new on-ramp for subsea capacity into the Los Angeles metro area. The company announced the project on Sept. 22 in partnership with Assured Communications, a specialist in subsea infrastructure design and delivery. The CLS is aimed at routes between Asia-Pacific and North America and is expected to begin supporting cables in 2028. A cable landing station is where a subsea cable terminates on land and connects to terrestrial networks. Increasingly, hyperscale cloud and AI providers are bringing cables directly to specific data centers rather than terminating them at standalone landing stations. Assured is also a strategic partner to the landing operator for AWS’s Sta’O’Nuk cable. “Digital Realty sees cable landing infrastructure as an increasingly important part of the broader connectivity ecosystem,” said Craig Waldrop, vice president of strategy and business development at Digital Realty, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. “Subsea cables provide international capacity, but that capacity is most valuable when it can connect efficiently into the data centers, networks, cloud providers, and customers that need it.” Inside LAX12: Digital Realty’s First Turnkey Cable Landing Station The planned CLS is designed to provide subsea cable operators with a turnkey solution for landing and powering their systems. Assured is supporting the design, engineering, and construction, drawing on its experience with subsea cable systems and landing infrastructure. The project is currently in development. The station is a new type of project for Digital Realty. “LAX12 represents Digital Realty’s first turnkey cable landing solution and marks an important evolution in the company’s broader interconnection platform,” Waldrop said. The approach is intended to pull landing infrastructure and surrounding networks into a single location. “That simplifies the path from subsea infrastructure into terrestrial networks, while creating increased flexibility for cable owners in how they distribute capacity once it reaches the US,” he said. Why Put the Landing Station Inside the Data Center? The goal is to bring subsea capacity closer to the networks and clouds that consume it. “By bringing the landing point directly into an established interconnection environment, rather than treating the cable landing station as a standalone piece of infrastructure, the project creates a more direct bridge between subsea capacity arriving from Asia-Pacific and the broader digital ecosystem in Los Angeles,” Waldrop said. He noted that in El Segundo specifically, the proximity of the beach landing to Digital Realty’s existing infrastructure provides a more direct path from subsea systems into terrestrial networks. The connection will run through Digital Realty’s carrier-neutral model. “The value of a carrier-neutral model is that it gives cable operators a common landing environment that is not tied to a single network or cloud provider,” Waldrop said. What’s Fueling Investment in Subsea Connectivity? AI is a major driver of bandwidth demand, but not the only one. “AI is contributing to demand for high-capacity and resilient connectivity, but this extends beyond any single workload,” Waldrop said. “As traffic patterns evolve and infrastructure requirements grow, Digital Realty sees subsea infrastructure as an important part of the underlying infrastructure customers need to connect globally.” He added that demand for efficient, resilient connectivity continues to drive investment in greater capacity and route diversity. “While AI certainly contributes to that demand, it’s one of several factors shaping investment decisions,” he said. “Cloud adoption, content delivery, network expansion, and broader digital infrastructure growth are all driving continued investment in subsea connectivity.”

artigo.texto: A metodologia de acesso à rede de transmissão pode evoluir para incorporar mais flexibilidade no atendimento a grandes consumidores, como data centers, considerando alternativas como faixas de conexão, acesso sujeito a cortes previamente definidos e antecipação de reforços custeada pelo próprio interessado, segundo Rafael Kelman, diretor executivo da PSR. “Hoje, flexibilidade tem que ser pensada de uma forma mais ampla. E principalmente na decisão de investimento, através da criação de opcionalidades”, afirmou Kelman durante o AI Day, evento promovido pela PSR para discutir fundamentos, aplicações e perspectivas da inteligência artificial, além de debater desafios de infraestrutura e energia associados à expansão dos data centers. A discussão ocorre no momento em que o setor implementa a Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast), criada pelo Decreto 12.772, de dezembro de 2025. A política passou a organizar o acesso permanente à Rede Básica por meio de Temporadas de Acesso, nas quais os pedidos são analisados de forma conjunta pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). Antes de definir a necessidade de disputa, ONS e Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) calculam a capacidade remanescente da rede e comparam o espaço disponível com os montantes solicitados pelos agentes. Nos pontos em que a demanda supera a capacidade disponível, é realizado um processo competitivo. A Pnast também estabelece que a EPE deverá interagir com o ONS nos estudos de acesso, observado o critério de mínimo custo global, e permite que os resultados das temporadas sejam considerados no planejamento da expansão da transmissão. A primeira Temporada de Acesso de 2026 está em andamento e, de acordo com o cronograma do ONS, será concluída em 8 de outubro. Faixas de conexão Durante o evento, Kelman citou uma situação em que um consumidor solicita, por exemplo, 100 MW de acesso e os estudos indicam que esse montante não pode ser atendido. Esse mesmo consumidor poderia flexibilizar sua demanda para 98 MW, que poderia ser atendida. Porém, na configuração atual, segundo ele, uma eventual redução da demanda solicitada pode exigir que o interessado passe novamente pelo rito de análise. “Uma coisa que o mundo vem procurando é que os estudos de conexão comecem a dar faixas de conexão aceitáveis e faixas que você possa se conectar aceitando algum tipo de corte”, disse. Esse corte poderia ser limitado previamente, por exemplo, em número de horas por ano ou em volume de energia não atendida ao longo de determinado período. A discussão, segundo Kelman, ganha relevância no caso dos data centers porque parte dessas cargas pode ter algum grau de flexibilidade. Durante o evento, ele afirmou que os estudos atuais consideram a demanda necessária pelo empreendimento de forma contínua, o que pode restringir a capacidade indicada para conexão. “Se você precisar reduzir o meu consumo, talvez você tivesse mais cadeiras para os data centers do que estão sendo enxergadas”, afirmou. Segundo Kelman, isso exigiria “uma discussão, uma evolução até no acesso a essa rede”. Outra possibilidade levantada pelo executivo é permitir que o próprio consumidor arque com o custo adicional necessário para antecipar sua conexão. Kelman citou como exemplo um caso em que a solução de transmissão considerada de mínimo custo para atender determinada carga só pudesse ser concluída em 2035. Nesse cenário, o consumidor poderia optar por financiar uma alternativa que permitisse o acesso antes dessa data, pagando a diferença em relação à solução prevista pelo planejamento. “Por que não o data center pode chegar e dizer: tudo bem, a sua solução de mínimo custo fica pronta em 2035, mas eu pago do meu bolso para me conectar antes disso?”, questionou. Segundo ele, mecanismos desse tipo estão sendo discutidos também em outros países diante do aumento da demanda por conexão de grandes cargas. Geração atrás do medidor O CEO da PSR, Luiz Augusto Barroso, afirmou no mesmo evento que as dificuldades de conexão estão levando projetos de data centers em outros países a recorrer à geração de energia atrás do medidor, sem depender inicialmente da rede. Segundo Barroso, o aumento da escala desse tipo de solução também cria um desafio para o planejamento da transmissão, porque um empreendimento atendido inicialmente por geração própria pode decidir se conectar à rede posteriormente. “O que está acontecendo é que a escala da geração behind the meter está aumentando muito”, afirmou. “E se todo mundo fizer uma geração behind the meter, isso também muda completamente uma dinâmica para quem está planejando o sistema de transmissão.” A geração atrás do medidor pode ainda reduzir a utilização de uma infraestrutura de transmissão dimensionada para atender determinada carga, tornando a rede ociosa. No sentido inverso, se um grande consumidor inicialmente abastecido por geração própria decidir se conectar à rede no futuro, o sistema pode precisar de novos reforços para acomodar essa demanda. Barroso lembrou que a construção de infraestrutura de transmissão para atender cargas de vários gigawatts pode levar anos. A flexibilidade das soluções instaladas atrás do medidor é outro desafio. A geração precisa acompanhar as variações do consumo do data center, o que exige fontes ou recursos capazes de modular a oferta. Segundo Barroso, projetos de grande porte têm recorrido a contratos flexíveis de gás natural e baterias para fazer esse ajuste. “O que a gente tem visto, é que quem está fazendo geração behind the meter em escala trata a flexibilidade ou com contratos flexíveis de gás ou com bateria. Você não pode fazer behind the meter nuclear, carvão, coisas que são flats”, afirmou. Isso não significa, porém, que o aumento da demanda dos data centers esteja afastando a energia nuclear. Barroso avaliou que, nos Estados Unidos, essas cargas têm contribuído para uma retomada da fonte por meio do aproveitamento de usinas existentes, incluindo reativações e ampliações, em vez da const

artigo.texto: Politics Energy Benchmarks, Possible Moratorium Among the Topics Driving Chicago’s Data Center Discussion Large, resource-intensive data centers have drawn increased public attention in recent years as their construction ramped up around the country. But in an urban environment like Chicago, data centers of all sizes can have a big impact. Noise from cooling systems and air pollution from backup generators are two examples of data center impacts that can have an outsize effect in a densely populated city. Now, as a city task force explores the right guardrails on data centers, policymakers are shifting into gear as they work to catch up with the emerging industry. At last Wednesday’s City Council meeting, alderpeople voted to remove exemptions for data centers from the city’s Energy Benchmarking Ordinance. That move — a key recommendation from the city’s working group on sustainable data centers — is intended to provide transparency around data centers’ energy efficiency and water usage. But despite the support for benchmarking requirements, City Council members failed to get behind other proposed data center regulations — including a moratorium. In August, Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order addressing noise controls and air pollution permitting for data centers. Johnson’s order also called on alderpeople to enact a temporary moratorium on new data center development. That moratorium, introduced Wednesday, would have applied to data centers bigger than 1,000 square feet with more than 20% of their floor space dedicated to servers. But its fate is uncertain, after two alderpeople promptly routed it to the Rules committee upon its introduction. According to Angela Tovar, the commissioner of Chicago’s Department of Environment as well as the city’s chief sustainability officer, a temporary moratorium could give policymakers time to get the right guardrails in place. “The city was very transparent in saying, ‘The regulations we have in place today are not adequate for how we should regulate the modern data center,’” Tovar said. “This presents an opportunity for the city to course-correct.” But for Brad Tietz, the Midwest director of state government affairs at the Data Center Coalition, a pause on data center development isn’t necessary to work with the industry on regulations. “What (a moratorium) is doing is sending a signal to the industry that this might not be the best place to put forth a multibillion-dollar investment,” Tietz said. “We don’t believe you need a moratorium in place to spend all that time doing this. Quite frankly, we could have reached an agreement on these regulations pretty quickly.” While the Data Center Coalition opposes the moratorium, Tietz said the industry group did not oppose the mayor’s executive order, or the benchmarking requirements the City Council approved last week. Working quickly to bypass a moratorium was the goal of a separate ordinance introduced by Ald. Bill Conway (34th Ward), which was also sent to the Rules committee. That ordinance would have zoned data centers as planned developments, subjecting them to the public review process prior to approval. Currently, data centers are permitted by right in most commercial areas of the city. As data needs for business and personal use change, Tietz said he expects Chicago’s market for new development to shift toward smaller data centers that value proximity to end users. But Tovar said existing data centers in the city vary in their size and use. “From our perspective, I would say that all sizes of data centers matter here in the city because we’re in an urban area,” Tovar said. “We have data centers that are in mixed-use communities, that are existing right next to residential communities. … We can’t ignore some of the concerns we’ve heard from residents.” Heather Cherone contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Proteção para data centers: AXA apresenta sua solução integrada no INSUMMIT 26 O Brasil concentra 48% dos data centers da América Latina, segundo Arthur Mitke, vice-presidente de Subscrição e Sinistros da AXA no Brasil, e é a proteção dessas estruturas que o executivo leva ao INSUMMIT 26 na palestra "Data Center, nova solução integrada da AXA no Brasil". A conversa com a jornalista Thaís Ruco, da Insurtalks, acontece no dia 7 de outubro, às 10h, no evento online e gratuito de inovação no mercado de seguros promovido pela Segbox com apoio da Insurtalks. A solução dá sequência ao produto de Power & Energy, voltado a energias renováveis, que a AXA lançou no ano passado. Arthur vai explicar por que essas instalações, que sustentam bancos digitais, aplicativos, serviços públicos, ensino a distância e computação em nuvem, se tornaram infraestrutura crítica para a economia digital, e por que o país reúne as condições para atrair esse tipo de investimento, com matriz energética majoritariamente limpa, água em abundância e incentivos ao setor. Inteligência artificial e novos riscos O executivo vai explicar como o crescimento da inteligência artificial mudou o perfil de risco dessas instalações. A densidade computacional exigida pelos novos equipamentos gera um volume de calor muito superior ao da TI tradicional e impõe a migração para sistemas de refrigeração líquida, o que traz para a subscrição pontos de falha como o vazamento de fluidos. "Quando a escala muda, o risco muda", antecipa Arthur. A palestra também vai abordar os desafios de transportar e instalar equipamentos de alto valor, que podem pesar uma tonelada e ainda assim são extremamente sensíveis, e as interdependências entre riscos, como o ataque cibernético capaz de provocar superaquecimento e dano físico à estrutura. Da obra à operação Um dos pontos centrais da conversa será o desenho da solução, que acompanha o empreendimento desde o transporte dos equipamentos, com a central própria de gerenciamento de riscos da AXA e empresas especializadas em cargas sensíveis, até a fase de engenharia, com subscrição personalizada. Arthur vai detalhar as coberturas incorporadas à apólice de riscos operacionais, como os danos materiais causados por ataque cibernético e os danos ocorridos durante os testes de redundância, além do seguro cyber com cobertura de erros e omissões para danos a terceiros e do seguro garantia para diferentes fases da obra e para contratos de compra e venda de energia. O vice-presidente vai explicar por que faz sentido contratar engenharia e operação na mesma seguradora em projetos entregues por etapas, nos quais uma parte entra em funcionamento enquanto outra segue em construção, e como a AXA organizou a oferta de forma modular, sem obrigar o cliente a contratar o pacote completo. Prevenção e resposta rápida ao sinistro A palestra vai tratar dos riscos considerados mais críticos na operação, entre eles falhas em sistemas elétricos e de resfriamento, oscilações na rede, ataques cibernéticos e lucros cessantes por paradas não programadas, além do peso crescente dos eventos climáticos extremos. Arthur vai apresentar o trabalho da engenharia de riscos da AXA antes mesmo da contratação e o uso de sensores, termografia e monitoramento de vibração na calibragem da subscrição. "Evitar o sinistro é tão importante quanto estar pronto para indenizá-lo", afirma. Na frente de sinistros, o executivo vai explicar por que a regulação tradicional não atende um ambiente em que cada minuto de indisponibilidade pode gerar prejuízos milionários, e como a seguradora estruturou um protocolo de resposta pré-desenhado, com equipe multidisciplinar e acordos com reguladores. Ele também vai contar como a experiência da AXA XL em mercados como o da Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos, contribuiu para a construção do produto. O corretor como parceiro consultivo Na parte final, Arthur vai abordar o papel do corretor no atendimento a empresas do segmento e o apoio que a AXA oferece, com capacitação sobre as soluções, capacidade técnica e especialistas que acompanham o corretor em reuniões com clientes corporativos e investidores. O executivo vai revelar ainda como corretores especialistas participaram do desenho do produto e deixará uma mensagem para as empresas que investem em infraestrutura tecnológica. artigo.texto: The 200 GW Moment: Reinventing the Grid for the AI Economy As AI pushes rack densities into unprecedented territory, utilities, hyperscalers, and developers are rethinking how to deliver reliable, affordable power at massive scale. Global data center power demand is projected to exceed 200 gigawatts (GW) by 2030. AI workloads are driving typical rack densities from roughly 10-30 kW into 80-150 kW, with advanced deployments approaching 1 MW per rack. Individual campuses are scaling into the hundreds of megawatts and beyond. The pace of growth is unprecedented. At the Data Center World Power conference in Dallas, held Sept. 21-23, leaders from utilities, power producers, hyperscalers, data center developers, operators, and supply chain partners discussed how to scale capacity while safeguarding grid reliability, protecting ratepayers, and accelerating economic development. Bill Kleyman, executive chair of the Data Center World Power Advisory Board and CEO and co-founder of Apolo.us, opened an early session by laying out the realities of deploying Nvidia DGX-class servers. He noted that a standard rack can accommodate six such systems, each built around eight Nvidia H100 accelerators, with individual accelerator cards costing up to $40,000. “Sixty-nine percent of respondents to AFCOM’s State of the Data Center 2026 survey expect that rack density is going to increase like nothing we've seen in the past,” Kleyman said. “In parallel, we are seeing 36% growth in liquid cooling adoption in data centers, and that's continuing to expand.” Utilities Confront the Gigawatt-Scale Campus Scott Hart, executive vice president of NRG Business, a major provider of retail electricity, natural gas, and demand response in North America, described how customer requirements have escalated. “Traditionally, data centers would be a grid-connected, 20- to 40-MW facility,” he said. “Then we saw the cloud campuses in the 100 MW range, but now conversations have pivoted to a gigawatt and beyond.” With projects of that scale, it can be challenging for a utility to commit to constructing a power plant. Hart explained that there are two clocks running during data center development: a technology clock that operates on timelines of months or a few years, and a power infrastructure clock that operates on decades. That creates friction when customers want capacity on near-term timelines, but utilities must plan and finance assets over 15-30 years. “A utility needs a minimum 15-year time horizon and commitment with a secured [offtake agreement] that can pay for that entire period,” Hart said. Some sites will remain grid-only. Increasingly, however, projects are pursuing hybrid arrangements that combine grid supply with on-site generation and storage, Hart noted. That can involve mixing technologies such as geothermal, gas turbine plants, and renewables. Hart added that incorporating demand response – programs in which customers curtail load or shift to on-site resources during grid stress in exchange for incentives – is becoming more attractive. “Most of the data center projects we work on are excited about being part of a demand response program,” he said. Site Selection: Power and Community Alise Porto, vice president of sustainability and strategic initiatives at Switch, said the site selection calculus has changed. A few years ago, proximity to major metro areas and robust fiber connectivity often dominated decisions. Today, available and reliable power is paramount. “Everything now revolves around power,” Porto said. “And more recently, the scope has expanded to both power and community – it is those two together that now coordinate where you go, how big you go, and what you do.” “Everything now revolves around power.” – Alise Porto, vice president of sustainability and strategic initiatives, Switch Utilities, initially surprised by multi-hundred-megawatt and gigawatt-scale requests, are increasingly engaging earlier and collaborating on flexible solutions, Porto noted. That can include agreeing to reduce power draw during peak conditions or temporarily switching to batteries or backup generators to support local grid reliability when needed. To maintain optionality as chip roadmaps evolve, Switch is pursuing designs that accommodate both current and future cooling methods and densities. “Depending on the type of chips our customers have, they can deploy air cooling now and utilize liquid cooling later,” Porto said. She added that Switch’s “AI factory” design targets up to 2 MW per rack, with modularity to allow cabinet-level power draw to scale as denser server architectures enter the market. Developer and Operator Economics Dado Slezak, executive vice president of energy capital and strategy at QTS, emphasized the capital intensity of AI data centers, particularly when on-site power is part of the plan. “For every dollar you've got of generation, you've got multiple dollars of data center infrastructure,” he said. “With that scale of investment, there must be a decades-long financial return secured contractually.” Slezak also cautioned against rigid long-term prescriptions. “There is no point when you can look three or four years in advance and know what you should build,” he said. “A lot can change in that time, and decisions keep shifting, each with a downstream impact.” He urged deep collaboration among partners to manage evolving technology targets and interconnection realities.

artigo.texto: Os bastidores de ser rainha de bateria Para elas, a coroa exige mais do que samba no pé Atualizado Antes do samba-enredo começar, da bateria entrar e das câmeras se voltarem para ela, existe uma história que quase ninguém vê. O carnaval mostra apenas o fragmento mais luminoso da vida de uma rainha de bateria. Por trás dele, há mulheres para quem aquele posto não é vitrine, mas o reconhecimento de um laço construído com a escola, e a realização de um sonho. Tania Bisteka, Patricia Costa e Fabíola Andrade sabem bem o que é isso. Tânia, por exemplo, soube exatamente o que queria desde o dia em que a Mangueira anunciou um concurso para escolher a rainha de bateria em 1999. Não tratou como brincadeira, encarou como se concorresse a um cargo político. Espalhou faixas com o próprio nome pela quadra, abordava os integrantes da bateria para contar sua trajetória com a escola e, a quem estivesse por perto, defendia com convicção que merecia sair vencedora. Na época, o concurso reunia dez candidatas e um júri escolhido pela própria bateria, que avaliaria três entradas de cada uma. Durante o mês entre a inscrição e a disputa, Tânia lutou à sua maneira e sonhou com o que viria. Pôs em prática as ideias para viver o que define como uma festa: “Eu fiz blusas com a minha cara. Eu entrei, fiz uma roupa linda, fiz um biquíni lindo e ganhei. As pessoas desciam o morro para assistir! Só que você imagina, o morro todo lá embaixo gritando, berrando e falando.” A emoção foi grande quando descobriu que o que tanto queria se realizou. E deixa claro que ser rainha não é fácil. Estava o ano todo presente em ensaios, na academia e no boxe. Cuidava da alimentação, mesmo que reconheça que ter nutricionista não era tão acessível quanto hoje. E estava sempre na quadra, sem desculpas, para sambar até o fôlego acabar. Tudo na intenção de melhorar a resistência. Esse era seu preparo. Mas além da preparação em relação a exercícios e alimentação, Tania também se preparou psicologicamente e com a sua fé. A partir da espiritualidade, tomou uma atitude totalmente inusitada antes do desfile para que entrasse na avenida com energia boa. Conta que a Mangueira estava na concentração em um local que existia um valão, onde tirou sua roupa: “Eu fiquei pelada. Convoquei a todos, e quando as pessoas passavam e me viam diziam “meu Deus, a rainha está pelada!” E foi muito louco. Eu estava só com uma canga, eu arranquei a canga e comecei meu ritual.” Nascida no morro da Mangueira, foi muito bem recebida pela bateria. Algumas pessoas a chamam de rainha até hoje e, ao lembrar daquele ano, ela percebe que o processo é diferente para uma rainha cria. "É um trabalho árduo, mas que vale muito a pena. Principalmente quando você é da comunidade, uma rainha pé no chão. Quando eu digo pé no chão, quero dizer uma rainha do povo, né? Quando a rainha é cria da escola, ela é mais cobrada do que quando não é. Porque está ali para mostrar que realmente mereceu estar naquele lugar de rainha." Patrícia Costa, rainha de bateria da Viradouro de 1991 a 1998, também sentiu essa diferença. Ela conta que as pessoas famosas pareciam ter mais abertura para ocupar esse espaço. Quando foi chamada, já fazia balé, jazz e sapateado. O convite veio de forma surpreendente, quando foi prestigiar o mestre Maçal, com quem já havia feito um trabalho, e acabou sambando muito com os passistas. Foi um verdadeiro teste de fogo. Naquele dia, o então presidente da escola viu o movimento e ficou interessado em conhecê-la. No fim, a chamou ao camarote e fez o convite, quando teve que assumir uma postura: "Eu precisei me colocar assim, com muita responsabilidade e auto valorização da minha posição como uma artista do samba, uma artista, uma sambista que sabia o que estava fazendo ali à frente da bateria. Não foi fácil. Assim, fui conquistando a comunidade com a minha presença e dedicação." Patrícia explica que a relação com os mestres de bateria e os ritmistas é essencial. Durante os ensaios, a sintonia vai sendo construída. A partir das frases musicais e dos sons da bateria, surge uma criatividade que forma combinações capazes de ajudar a rainha a se movimentar em harmonia com os ritmistas. Nem tudo, porém, são flores. Sobre os perrengues, ela lembra de um ano em que desfilou com o sapato fechado e arrasou na avenida, mas terminou o desfile carregada no colo pelo namorado. Se sente neta da Águia da Portela, já que o avô foi um dos fundadores da escola. Cresceu ouvindo as histórias e foi ali que o amor pelo samba começou. Durante o desfile, essa paixão mantinha qualquer desconforto longe: “Nunca aconteceu de eu sentir alguma dor durante o desfile. O corpo fica quente, acontece uma troca de energia maravilhosa com o público, uma energia tão boa que não tem muito lugar para sentir dor. Para mim, naquele palco tem uma magia, o show acontece. Sem dor.” Energia essa também que também guia Fabíola Andrade. Foi rainha de bateria da Mocidade Independente de Padre Miguel de 2024 a 2026 e hoje é rainha da escola. Desde criança, já se encantava com a festa, o ritmo e a energia das escolas de samba. Para ela, ser rainha de bateria é fazer parte da história viva do carnaval carioca, levar alegria e garra a uma comunidade inteira. Pensando nas fantasias, diz que é um trabalho artesanal e demorado, feito em equipe com o carnavalesco e estilistas renomados do Carnaval. Segundo ela, os costeiros podem pesar de dez a vinte quilos e o salto alto exige estrutura. Então, garantir que nada saia do lugar é uma verdadeira engenharia. A rainha lembra que já precisou até de uma costura de última hora na fantasia, na concentração, com o coração aos pulos e frio na barriga. Assim como Patrícia, acredita que a adrenalina é um anestésico natural inacreditável, fazendo com que a garra da comunidade e a troca de energia impulsionem toda a animação: "É uma relação de puro amor, cumplicidade e respeito. artigo.texto: On September 12, 2026, CNBC reported that General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) is in the early stages of developing next-generation battery cells that it says can reduce U.S. dependence on China, days after Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) faced Trump administration criticism over its own Chinese battery-technology ties. GM has partnered with Denver-based startup Peak Energy to develop sodium-ion battery cells for stationary energy storage systems, using domestically available materials like sodium from soda ash instead of lithium and other inputs China dominates. GM vice president of battery and sustainability Kurt Kelty told CNBC the company is “developing a supply chain such that, two years from now, three years from now, it will be domestic.” Don’t Miss: Ford (F) Answers Washington’s China Criticism with a $1 Billion Kentucky Bet Bull Case General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) could strengthen its domestic battery position by developing U.S.-based technology rather than relying heavily on Chinese intellectual property. GM vice president of battery and sustainability Kurt Kelty said the company wants to establish a domestic battery supply chain within the next two to three years. Its work with Peak Energy focuses on sodium-ion technology developed for stationary energy storage. GM says sodium-ion cells can operate across a wider temperature range and endure more cycles than incumbent chemistries. It gives the strategy a potential technical advantage alongside its supply-chain benefits. Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) already has a more immediate path to U.S. battery production despite the political controversy surrounding its CATL relationship. Ford owns and controls its Marshall, Michigan battery plant and employs the American workforce there while licensing battery technology from CATL. Access to established technology could help Ford scale domestic battery manufacturing faster than companies that still need to develop and commercialize new chemistries. Ford retains operational control of the U.S. facility. Both GM and Ford could strengthen their competitive positions if they successfully localize more of their battery supply chains in the United States. Washington is scrutinizing dependence on Chinese automotive technology and materials. China still dominates several critical battery supply chains. GM is pursuing more domestic technology development, while Ford is bringing licensed battery technology into a U.S.-owned plant. Successful execution could give both automakers greater supply security and more control over strategically important battery production. Look Into: GM and Ford Take their Century-Old Rivalry to the Battlefield and the Power Grid Bear Case General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) still faces a long commercialization timeline, and its current sodium-ion program does not directly solve its near-term EV battery challenges. Kelty said GM needs another two to three years to establish the domestic supply chain it envisions, while GM designed its Peak Energy sodium-ion cells primarily for grid-scale stationary storage rather than electric vehicles. GM must still prove that its broader domestic battery investments can eventually improve EV costs, margins, and supply-chain independence. Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) faces much greater immediate political risk because its U.S. battery strategy still depends on licensed technology from China’s CATL. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Republican lawmakers have criticized Ford’s CATL relationship and other ties with Chinese companies, even though Ford owns and operates the Michigan plant itself. Additional restrictions on Chinese automotive technology could force Ford to modify its battery strategy, increase costs, or find alternative technology if political pressure intensifies. Both automakers still face a difficult and expensive path toward genuine battery independence from China. China controls large portions of global refining and battery-material processing, including about 98% of LFP cathode materials, so domestic cell production alone cannot eliminate supply-chain exposure. GM must commercialize new technologies at competitive costs, while Ford must manage political risk around licensed Chinese technology. Both companies ultimately need their localization strategies to lower costs and protect margins rather than simply shift where they assemble batteries. Hedge Fund Sentiment General Motors Company (NYSE:GM)’ hedge fund count fell to 75 in the second quarter from 77 in the first, with position value dropping to $4.87 billion from $6.08 billion, according to Insider Monkey’s database. Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F), the rival GM is implicitly contrasting itself against, held steady at 50 hedge fund holders, with position value slipping to $1.02 billion from $1.12 billion. Conclusion General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) and Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) are pursuing two distinct approaches to the same strategic challenge. GM is emphasizing domestic technology development and building expertise in sodium-ion batteries. Ford is using established CATL technology inside a battery plant that it owns and operates in Michigan. GM’s approach could reduce long-term political and technological dependence on China, while Ford’s approach could give it a faster route to large-scale U.S. battery production. Nonetheless, GM still faces a lengthy development timeline, Ford faces significant political scrutiny, and both companies remain exposed to Chinese-dominated battery-material supply chains. Investors should watch whether each automaker can turn its respective strategy into competitive battery costs, stronger margins, and greater supply security. artigo.texto: NH Investment & Securities will team up with Trinity Airline to cooperate on carbon finance spanning the supply of credits under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) and brokerage trading of domestic greenhouse gas emissions permits. NH Investment & Securities said on Sept. 28 it signed a memorandum of understanding with Trinity Airline on Sept. 21 for mutual cooperation on CORSIA and the greenhouse gas emissions trading scheme. CORSIA is an international carbon offset scheme designed to manage carbon emissions from international flights. Airlines must secure eligible carbon credits to offset emissions that exceed a certain standard. Under the agreement, Trinity Airline will use NH Investment & Securities' expertise in carbon markets and financial capabilities to procure the credits needed to meet CORSIA requirements. NH Investment & Securities will support efforts such as managing procurement timing and costs by providing market analysis and trading services. The company said this is the first time a domestic securities firm and an airline have built a cooperative relationship covering both CORSIA credit supply and brokerage trading of domestic greenhouse gas emissions permits. The two companies will first procure 20,000 tons of CORSIA credits through NH Investment & Securities. Trinity Airline plans to secure in stages by the end of this year more than 10 percent of the volume of credits it must offset ahead of the first-phase settlement deadline in January 2028. The companies will also expand cooperation under the domestic greenhouse gas emissions trading scheme (K-ETS). NH Investment & Securities plans to support Trinity Airline's domestic carbon credit trading through its own brokerage trading system and provide related information such as market analysis and policy trends. The airline industry faces a situation where, as international carbon emissions regulations tighten, it must secure the necessary credits in a stable manner while managing procurement costs stemming from fluctuations in market prices. Park Geon-hoo (박건후), head of Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities, said, "This agreement is meaningful in that it is a strategic cooperation model that connects a securities firm's expertise in carbon finance with an airline's demand for emissions permits." He added, "Based on the supply of CORSIA credits and brokerage trading of domestic emissions permits, we will expand tailored carbon finance services."

artigo.texto: BROKEN BOW, Neb.— The Custer County Board of Supervisors met in regular session for just short of two hours on Tuesday morning starting at 9 AM. Toward the end of the meeting, public hearings were held for the possible closure of road 351 outside of Sargent, data center regulations that were passed to the board from the planning commission, and a possible temporary moratorium on battery energy storage systems. Landowners alongside road 351 came before the board to express their support of the closure, saying the road hasn’t been graded since the floods that happened several years ago. They did express an interest in an easement agreement since a party would be land locked with the closure of the road. Ultimately the board decided to give the township its 120 days time to decide if they want to maintain the road. During that time, they will check to see if the county is to have involvement in the easement process or if the private parties handle it themselves. Ahead of the public hearing regarding data center regulations that were put in the hands of the supervisors from the planning commission last week, Zoning Administrator Darci Tibbs made a statement regarding the process. “The purpose of these regulations is to not encourage or attract data centers, but to make sure that if one is proposed in Custer County, we have appropriate standards and safeguards in place to protect the health, safety, and welfare of our citizens, and to protect the ag and rural character of the county,” said Tibbs. Hear the full statement from Tibbs here: No members of the public came forward to make a statement during the public hearing and a resolution will appear for consideration by the board at an upcoming meeting. Tibbs also made a statement expressing the planning commission’s desire for a 12 month moratorium on battery energy storage systems so that ample time could be given to researching them and working toward regulations. Tibbs explained that the systems typically include battery units or containers, inverters, transformers, cooling equipment, electrical controls, monitoring systems, and safety equipment. The facilities can range from small systems serving one property to large commercial or utility scale facilities that can occupy multiple acres and connect to the electrical grid. No members of the public came forward to speak and a resolution that would put the moratorium in place will be on an upcoming agenda. Other items from Tuesday’s meeting: - The Cozad Road and Dunning Road were approved for closure for next year’s Sandhills Open Road Challenge races that happen in Custer County. (August 13 and 14 respectively) - One parcel in the county was delinquent and on the report to the county, attached to two years worth of taxes at $327.11 and a utility assessment of $3,091.06 - It was reported by the treasurer that nine of the 43 distress warrants issued to the Sheriff remain uncollected and have been returned. The initial amount certified, including interest and fees was $52,611.63. The Sheriff’s office collected $36,314.60. Those not returned were for a variety of reasons including no property being found or bankruptcies. The $8,467.15 was approved to be stricken from the tax rolls. - A representative from Oak Creek Engineering came before the board with an amendment request for engineering services on the Anselmo south road project, stating that the quote given for service hours came in low and additional funds were needed. The original quote of $30,400 was eclipsed and the ask was for $15,250 worth of service hour dollars. artigo.texto: Russia hit the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile service provider, on Sunday, the company told local media, as Moscow continued a bombardment of Ukrainian data centers and communications infrastructure. Kyivstar told Interfax Ukraine news agency that its head office in Kyiv had been hit, but there were no casualties. Russia's Defense Ministry also said on Sunday it hit a data center belonging to Vodafone Ukraine, the country's second-largest cell network provider. Vodafone Ukraine did not respond to a request for comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russia struck a data center in Kyiv twice on Sunday morning, wounding two children and an adult. Moscow has also hit data centers belonging to Ukrainian internet providers over the past week, causing service outages to about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukraine's Digital Ministry. "Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential — they save lives," Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X on Wednesday. artigo.texto: The U.S. data center boom has entered a new, contradictory phase. On the one hand, both data center construction activity and credible forecasts for near-term capacity additions to the electric grid to serve data centers remain robust. The Electric Power Research Institute, for example, said in February that data centers will represent up to 17% of U.S. electricity demand in 2030 and as much as 20% in 2035. On the other hand, data center and utility infrastructure projects face a host of challenges. These include both physical constraints, such as equipment and labor shortages, as well as mounting public opposition driven by concerns about large-scale computing facilities’ impact on water supplies, the cost and reliability of power and natural gas supplies, and the quality of life in host communities. The upshot is that even some data center development projects advanced enough to appear in utility load forecasts with a named hyperscaler attached are not certain to move forward. Near Grand Rapids, Michigan, for example, a Microsoft data center touted by Consumers Energy faces an uncertain future amid local permitting delays. “[Data centers] are running into physical problems that are manifesting as market problems, political problems, regulatory problems and ultimately problems down on the ground." Blake Nixon President and CEO of Geronimo Power Another Microsoft-backed data center in Vineland, New Jersey, was recently hit with a $1 million fine for running dozens of gas-powered generators without the proper permits, and ordered to obtain them within 45 days or shut down. A proposed Google data center that would interconnect in Xcel Energy’s Minnesota territory faces a court-ordered work stoppage to allow time for environmental review. Even projects that sought to circumvent interconnection delays by building off-grid generation have seen setbacks. Last week, Oracle moved to protect itself financially from the delay or cancellation of Project Jupiter, a massive, 2.5-GW data center campus planned for Doña Ana County, New Mexico, after state regulators blocked a gas pipeline proposed to serve it. Data center opposition “has reached a pitch I have never seen before in my 20-plus years in development,” Blake Nixon, president and CEO of Geronimo Power, told Utility Dive in an interview. This spring, officials in Nobles County, Minnesota, shot down a proposal by Geronimo to build a 400 MW “data park” there, despite the company’s efforts at community outreach. Now, Nixon said his team is considering alternative sites in nearby communities. “[Data centers] are running into physical problems that are manifesting as market problems, political problems, regulatory problems and ultimately problems down on the ground,” he said. In May, Goldman Sachs said only 50%-60% of planned data center capacity will come online as expected in the next two years amid delays and cancellations. And while the 36 GW of capacity added to the development pipeline in the first quarter of 2026 sounds impressive, that’s down 19% from the last quarter of 2025 as developers “continue to shift their focus to existing … pipelines in the face of an increasingly challenging development and regulatory environment,” Caitlin Connelly, a senior analyst with Wood Mackenzie, said in a July note. Experts say these developments raise questions about just how much data center load will come online in the near term — injecting unwelcome uncertainty into utility planning cycles that must look years, even decades, into the future. Working around grid constraints with flexibility, BYO capacity It’s increasingly difficult for developers of large-scale data center campuses to find sites with the hundreds of megawatts, let alone gigawatts, of spare grid capacity they expect their projects to need at full build-out. In the PJM Interconnection, real or perceived power scarcity is a major driver of both local opposition and top-down political backlash to the industry. The independent market monitor in July blamed data centers for 38% of charges at the most recent capacity auction. The Democratic governors of Pennsylvania, Virginia and New Jersey have taken action in recent months to push regulators to require data centers to bring more generation and transmission capacity online. These moves are not only in PJM states with Democratic governors. Power scarcity and cost concerns have triggered organized opposition and political backlash to data centers in places developers until recently believed were sympathetic to their cause, like Texas and Utah. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, R, successfully pushed for a sweeping pause on data center grid interconnections that threatens up to 20% of the total U.S. development pipeline, BloombergNEF said earlier this month. Utilities and data centers are responding in several ways. The most straightforward is through “bring your own capacity” arrangements in which computing facilities colocate with new generation or finance local capacity additions. Some of these arrangements are massive: OpenAI agreed earlier this month to take 8 GW of the capacity from a planned 10 GW power generation project in Ohio that includes 9.2-GW gas assets. The facility, which is being pursued by Japan’s SoftBank Group and the U.S. Department of Energy, would be the country’s largest generation source if built. If not, that title would go to Amazon’s proposed 7.7-GW gas-fired power plant in West Texas, which would also be larger than the current titleholder, Washington state’s 6.8-GW Grand Coulee hydroelectric dam. Smaller-scale capacity procurements are also in the works, like Google’s “first-of-its-kind” deal with Voltus for 100 MW of virtual power plant capacity in PJM. Elsewhere, utilities and data centers are pursuing asset-light alternatives using software to find previously untapped headroom on the grid or to ramp down computing loads during periods of peak demand. artigo.texto: The Science Newswise — Battery materials called electrolytes allow ions (charged particles) to move from one end of a battery to the other. This process is necessary for charging and discharging. Superionic conductors (SICs) are materials that are solids, but some of their ions move like liquids. As a result, they conduct electricity very well. One SIC, lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride, is a promising type of solid-state battery material. Using neutron scattering and computer simulations, researchers gained a better understanding of this material’s atomic dynamics. By raising the material to more than 400 K (260 F), they put it in the superionic state where ions act like a liquid. In that state, the scientists found that lithium ions can hop quickly through the material’s crystal structure. The team also documented how specific types of vibrations in the crystal enable ions to jump through vibrating crystal bottlenecks. The scientists discovered that these vibrations enable long-range flow and significant improvements in conductivity. The Impact These findings show researchers how to improve ion flow inside a solid-state battery material, which would increase its performance. This information could enable a solid-state battery material that offers very high quantities of mobile ions as well as good chemical and thermal stability. This structure would enable a battery to use solid electrolytes that could perform as well as liquid ones. (Ions move more freely through liquid electrolytes than solid ones.) As such, this change could enable faster and safer battery charging. The ability to tailor SIC materials could also guide researchers in developing and improving other devices, such as fuel cells and computers. Summary One class of materials, superionic conductors (SICs), has the properties of both a crystalline and liquid electrolyte. When warmed above a specific temperature, the material remains partly crystalline, but also develops ion flow properties like those of liquids. This study combined machine-learning simulations with inelastic and quasielastic neutron scattering at the Spallation Neutron Source, a DOE Office of Science User Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The researchers investigated lithium-ion dynamics in the SIC lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride. The team found the crystalline framework facilitated fast, liquid-like hopping of lithium ions between stable crystalline lattice sites. Additionally, they documented significant enhancements in lithium-ion diffusion across a range of temperatures through the dynamic breathing (unified relaxation) of vibrating diffusion bottlenecks. They also observed how the vibrational spectra of mobile lithium ions in Li₆PS₅Cl evolve from a crystal-like to liquid-like phase. The research bridges conventional diffusive and lattice vibrational models. These findings offer important insights into the rapid ionic motion in SICs for potential use in solid electrolyte batteries, fuel cells, and computing systems. Funding The research was partially funded by the National Science Foundation (DMREF project); the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Basic Energy Sciences, Division of Materials Sciences and Engineering; and the German Research Foundation. This work used resources at the Spallation Neutron Source and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, both DOE Office of Science User Facilities.

artigo.texto: O que a guerra na Ucrânia e a guerra no Irã têm em comum? Ataque de Kiev a um navio iraniano no mar Cáspio expõe uma rede densa de inteligência militar circulando entre os dois conflitos. Maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, a Kyivstar foi alvo de um ataque da Rússia no domingo (27), em meio a bombardeios lançados por Moscou contra a infraestrutura de telecomunicações do país vizinho. A ofensiva não resultou em vítimas, como informou a empresa à agência de notícias Interfax. Além do ataque à sede da prestadora em Kiev, um data center da Vodafone também teria sido atingido, como divulgado pelo Ministério da Defesa da Rússia. No entanto, a empresa que possui a segunda maior rede celular da região optou por não comentar o assunto. Ucranianos sem acesso à internet Os ataques do domingo, que também incluíram outro data center na capital ucraniana, ferindo um adulto e duas crianças, segundo o presidente Volodymyr Zelensky, não são casos isolados. Na última semana, os sistemas de comunicação do país sofreram diversos bombardeios. - Como relata a Reuters, centros de dados utilizados por operadoras locais estavam entre os principais alvos; - Em um dos casos, as explosões teriam interrompido a conectividade para cerca de 100 mil residências ao longo da semana; - Os clientes que ficaram sem acesso à internet residem principalmente em Kiev e cidades próximas, de acordo com o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia; - Autoridades do país disseram que os bombardeios afetaram sistemas críticos para a segurança, aumentando os riscos de mortes durante os ataques. “A Rússia tem como alvo importantes centros de dados ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais, eles salvam vidas”, afirmou Andrii Sybha, Ministro das Relações Exteriores da Ucrânia, em mensagem compartilhada no X. Na rede social, ele também disse que alguns dos ataques russos incluem drones Shahed com propulsão a jato, uma nova variante da aeronave não tripulada. Essas versões se destacam pela capacidade de alcançar mais de 600 km/h de velocidade e operar em altitudes mais elevadas, dificultando as ações dos sistemas de defesa aérea. Um drone guiado por IA lançado pela Rússia matou três civis na Ucrânia no mês passado, em um dos primeiros ataques realizados por aeronaves autônomas. Relembre o caso. Com informações da Reuters.

artigo.texto: JANESVILLE — The Janesville City Council on Monday voted unanimously to enact a one-year moratorium on data centers within the city. The southern Wisconsin city is just the latest community to put the brakes on the rush of data center developments across the country. The ordinance comes as residents are preparing for a November referendum that if approved, would allow voters a say in any future major developments in the city, including data centers. According to a staff memo accompanying the ordinance, the moratorium would pause the acceptance, processing, review and approval of any application related to the development of a data center, including rezoning of property, permits, action taken on annexation requests, or other development approvals. During the moratorium, city staff would not solicit or actively encourage data center development, nor enter nondisclosure agreements related to such development projects. The purpose of the moratorium is to allow sufficient time to research environmental, economic, health, safety and land-use compatibility impacts; continue preparation of zoning code review, processes, and specific development standards for data center projects. It also would allow time for city staff to complete and the council to consider the Data Center Companion Ordinance.

artigo.texto: Archbald will hold back-to-back public hearings this week to gather testimony as council weighs developers’ applications for a power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road and seven data centers at a quarry. Council will convene at 5 p.m. Tuesday to continue to hear testimony on the 400-megawatt Essential Energy LLC natural gas power plant proposed near Staback Park and across from the same developer’s Project Boson data center. Then, the borough will hold a hearing Wednesday at 5 p.m. on Project Green Mountain’s proposal to build a data center campus across nearly 271 acres at the Stavola Quarry off the Casey Highway. Essential Energy Power plant representatives faced criticism and pushback during five preceding hearings over the conceptual nature of their plans as council considers Essential Energy’s March 12 application for a natural gas power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road. The debate over how much information is enough to satisfy Archbald’s zoning requirements has prevailed across data center and power plant hearings in the borough this year. Residents advocate for specific information during the hearings, while developers argue they can’t refine their plans until after they have approval. Developers’ representatives contend that permitting and regulations from agencies such as the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency will protect the community. Archbald has held hearings on Essential Energy’s plans April 27, May 21, June 22, July 21 and Aug. 18. The most recent hearing concluded with testimony from Andrew Markle, the technical lead of power generation for KCI Technologies of Mechanicsburg, which is the engineering firm representing Essential Energy. Markle spoke broadly about the operations and safety features designed into power plants, touting his experience overseeing power plant development both domestically and abroad. The hearing concluded before cross-examination, so Tuesday’s hearing will likely open with questions posed to Markle. Cross-examiners include attorney Justin Richards of Elliott Greenleaf PC in Wilkes-Barre, who represents Archbald residents opposing data centers; Stop Archbald Data Centers co-founder Tamara Misewicz-Healey; Highlands Archbald residents Karen Timmons and Meg Nudelman; Valley View School District Solicitor Kyle Callejas; and Archbald’s special counsel, attorney Brett C. Flower of Eckert Seamans in Harrisburg. Project Green Mountain Representatives for Project Green Mountain will return to Archbald on Wednesday after a three-month hiatus. Green Mountain 6 LLC, using a Pittsburgh law firm as its address, filed a conditional-use application Jan. 26, making Project Green Mountain Archbald’s sixth proposed data center project, with plans for seven two-story data centers, each 65 feet tall with 138,000-square-foot footprints. Project Green Mountain’s data centers would span an L-shaped campus at the Stavola Quarry. It is the only application so far in Archbald that sites data centers opposite the Casey Highway away from residential development. The data centers would use a projected 525 megawatts of electricity, divided into 75 megawatts per building, while using up to 14,000 gallons of water daily from Pennsylvania American Water for domestic uses like sinks and toilets. During an outage, Green Mountain would use 196 backup diesel generators, each storing up to 10,000 gallons of diesel fuel, totaling 1.96 million gallons stored on site. Project Green Mountain’s initial hearing March 19 largely discussed the campus’s utility demands and potential economic incentives. On May 11, it focused on air emissions from backup generators, as well as traffic from the data centers. The June 18 hearing focused on the noise of data centers and their generators. Though Project Green Mountain’s sound study found that the campus would remain below Archbald’s 55-decibel residential daytime limit, even with all 196 backup generators running, it was heavily scrutinized in cross-examination During the latest hearing, Project Green Mountain attorney Jeffrey Wilhelm of Reed Smith LLP in Pittsburgh responded to a question from Councilwoman Lisa Osborne asking if the developer had finished any other data center campuses with a post-construction sound study to give the borough additional insight. Wilhelm told Osborne they would come back with an answer to her question at another hearing. Both hearings will be at the Valley View High School auditorium, 1 Columbus Drive, Archbald. Borough Solicitor Jay O’Connor announced the Essential Energy hearing at the conclusion of the last hearing on the power plant in August, and the borough announced the Project Green Mountain hearing via a public notice published Sept. 15 in The Times-Tribune. Both Essential Energy, which is tied to Archbald-based Kriger Construction Inc. and its executive leadership, and Project Green Mountain seek conditional-use approval from Archbald council, which requires the developers to testify at public hearings to explain how their projects abide by the borough’s zoning regulations for data centers and power plants. Other companies tied to Kriger and its leadership also proposed four data centers and three power plants across Bell Mountain in Dickson City. Affected residents who received party status and their attorney, borough officials and the Valley View School District’s solicitor all have the opportunity to cross-examine each witness presented by the developers. Once they conclude their testimony, any of the opposing parties can then present their own evidence. Council will accept public comment prior to voting, though it is unclear exactly when any decisions will occur. There are currently 51 data centers formally proposed in the borough across half a dozen projects, although two other data center developers look to expand in Archbald around the Valley View Business Park.
