Proprietary iron & saltwater electrolyte According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Flow Battery Energy Storage market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global flow battery energy storage market is entering a decisive commercial phase as utilities and developers seek long-duration storage solutions that can economically shift renewable generation across four to twelve hours or more. Unlike lithium-ion systems, flow batteries separate power and energy, allowing independent scaling of duration and capacity, which makes them attractive for grid operators facing rising renewable curtailment and peak-shaving needs. As of 2026, deployment remains concentrated in utility-scale projects and selected industrial microgrids, but the pipeline is broadening as vanadium supply chains mature, project bankability improves, and grid interconnection standards become clearer. The market is supported by ambitious decarbonization targets, renewable portfolio standards, and the need for resilient grid infrastructure. However, growth is tempered by vanadium price volatility, competition from lithium-ion and other long-duration technologies, and the complexity of project financing. This report provides a structured analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, pricing logic, competitive positioning, and regional outlooks. It is designed for manufacturers, integrators, utilities, investors, and policymakers seeking a commercially grounded view of where flow battery energy storage is heading and which segments will lead adoption. The baseline scenario for the world flow battery energy storage market through 2035 assumes continued policy support for renewable integration and long-duration storage, steady improvement in vanadium electrolyte supply, and gradual cost reduction as manufacturing scale increases. Under this scenario, the market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 18.5% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 520 by 2035 (2025 = 100). Growth is expected to be front-loaded in Asia-Pacific, particularly China, where large-scale vanadium redox flow battery projects are already being deployed for grid balancing and renewable time-shifting. North America and Europe will follow, driven by utility procurement mandates and the need to replace retiring thermal peaking capacity. The baseline assumes no major breakthrough in alternative long-duration technologies that would displace flow batteries in the 4–12 hour duration range, but it also assumes that lithium-ion will continue to dominate shorter-duration applications. Key uncertainties include vanadium price spikes, delays in grid interconnection queues, and the pace of cost declines in competing technologies. The market outlook remains positive, with flow batteries carving out a durable niche in long-duration, high-cycle applications where safety, scalability, and longevity are paramount. Electric utilities and grid operators are the primary adopters of flow battery energy storage, driven by the need to integrate high shares of variable renewable generation and maintain grid reliability. Flow batteries are increasingly chosen for renewable time-shifting, peak shaving, and ancillary services where discharge durations of four to twelve hours are required. Utilities value the independent scalability of power and energy, which allows them to size systems precisely to grid needs, and the long cycle life that matches asset lifetimes. As of 2026, several large-scale projects are operational or under construction, particularly in China and the United States. Through 2035, demand will be supported by capacity auctions, clean energy standards, and the retirement of coal and gas peakers. Key demand-side indicators include renewable curtailment rates, peak demand growth, and the volume of storage capacity procured in utility integrated resource plans. The segment's growth is also tied to the increasing need for grid resilience amid extreme weather events. Current trend: Growing. Co-locating storage with renewables allows developers to shift generation to high-price periods, reduce curtailment, and provide firm capacity. artigo.texto: O edital para a segunda parte da concessão da Floresta Nacional do Bom Futuro, em Porto Velho (RO), foi publicado. A área de quase 40 mil hectares será usada para restaurar áreas degradadas, gerar empregos locais e produzir créditos de carbono, ajudando o Brasil a cumprir sua meta de restaurar 12 milhões de hectares até 2030. O Serviço Florestal Brasileiro (SFB) e o Ministério do Meio Ambiente (MMA) divulgaram as regras para a venda do segundo lote de gestão da Floresta Nacional (Flona) do Bom Futuro, localizada em Porto Velho, no estado de Rondônia. O processo foi preparado com ajuda técnica do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e tem como objetivo principal recuperar áreas que foram degradadas na região da Amazônia, permitindo que empresas privadas gerenciem o espaço de forma sustentável. O documento do edital mostra que a área disponível é muito grande, ultrapassando 39 mil hectares. Para dar uma noção do tamanho, isso equivale a quase 55 mil campos de futebol. Deste total, cerca de 6,4 mil hectares serão usados especificamente para plantar árvores e restaurar a floresta. As empresas interessadas devem entregar suas propostas na sede da bolsa de valores B3, em São Paulo, entre 10h e 12h do dia 4 de novembro. A abertura das propostas, para ver quem ganhou, está marcada para o dia 18 de novembro. - Área Gigante: São mais de 39 mil hectares, o que é maior que muitas cidades do interior. - Meta Climática: A ação ajuda o Brasil a cumprir a promessa de recuperar 12 milhões de hectares de vegetação até 2030. - Carro de Ouro: A empresa vencedora poderá vender créditos de carbono, o que ajuda a pagar pela restauração. - Empregos Locais: O projeto exige contratação de moradores da região e compra de sementes locais. - Primeiro Caso: O lote anterior foi ganhado pela empresa Re.Green, marcando a primeira concessão de restauração no Brasil. Modelo de concessão e impacto social Este é o segundo leilão para recuperar a floresta neste local. O primeiro lote foi arrematado pela empresa Re.Green em março. Naquela ocasião, foi a primeira vez no Brasil que uma empresa ganhou o direito de cuidar de uma floresta pública principalmente para gerar receita com a venda de créditos de carbono (prova de que a atividade removeu poluição do ar). Agora, com esse segundo lote, o governo espera repetir o sucesso e ampliar a restauração. O contrato da concessão não fala apenas de plantio. Ele exige que parte do dinheiro ganho com o projeto seja investida em pesquisa científica, educação ambiental e proteção da floresta. Além disso, o edital manda que a empresa ajude as comunidades que moram no entorno da reserva, incluindo a população indígena Karitiana. Há regras para garantir que mulheres tenham chances iguais, que povos indígenas sejam incluídos no processo e que a economia local seja fortalecida com a compra de insumos e contratação de mão de obra da região. Desafio nacional de recuperação da vegetação Esta concessão faz parte de um plano maior do Brasil para recuperar a mata nativa. De acordo com os dados divulgados, essa ação contribui diretamente para a meta de restaurar 12 milhões de hectares até o ano de 2030, estabelecida pelo Plano Nacional de Recuperação da Vegetação Nativa (Planaveg). Atualmente, o país já tem 3,4 milhões de hectares em processo de recuperação. Isso representa quase um terço da meta total. O novo lote da Flona do Bom Futuro vem justamente para impulsionar esse número, focando em uma das regiões mais importantes e frágeis da Amazônia.

artigo.texto: HSBC maintains bearish stance on Ola Electric despite battery manufacturing gains While acknowledging the electric vehicle maker's progress in cell localisation and gigafactory capacity, the brokerage cited weak financial performance and balance sheet concerns in maintaining a reduce rating. Global brokerage HSBC has maintained a bearish Reduce rating on Ola Electric Mobility Ltd., setting a target price that implies a nearly 38 per cent downside, despite acknowledging significant operational progress in the company's battery manufacturing and localisation efforts. The divergence between Ola Electric's technological advancements and its financial realities was laid bare in a recent brokerage note following visits to the company's manufacturing facilities. While HSBC praised the electric two-wheeler maker's vertical integration and proprietary cell technology, it cited weaker-than-expected recent financial performance and low confidence in management's near-term estimates as primary drivers of its cautious stance. Gigafactory milestones and technological optimism HSBC analysts recently conducted site visits to Ola Electric's Gigafactory and its future electric vehicle assembly plant. The brokerage noted that the Gigafactory's capacity has successfully reached 6 gigawatt-hours (GWh), a critical milestone in the company's strategy to reduce reliance on imported battery cells. The firm expects the facility's manufacturing yields to improve to approximately 90 per cent from the current 70 per cent over the next six to nine months. The brokerage specifically highlighted Ola's development of the 4680 cell utilizing proprietary dry-cathode technology. Management asserts that this innovation can reduce operating costs by 20 to 30 per cent compared to traditional wet-cathode processing. Furthermore, HSBC observed that the future factory reflects a high degree of automation and vertical integration, which supports management's claims of achieving better operating margins in the long term. On the retail front, the company is aggressively expanding its footprint. Ola Electric's dealer network is projected to jump from 30 to approximately 150 outlets by the Navratri festival, a crucial sales period for the Indian automotive sector. Notably, HSBC does not currently view the company's unsold inventory levels as a red flag, attributing them to the transitional phase of new product rollouts. Balance sheet realities and market reaction Despite the operational positives, HSBC's financial modeling remains deeply conservative. The brokerage set a target price of Rs 24 per share, implying a steep 37.6 per cent downside from recent closing levels. This bearish valuation reflects the firm's pricing of weaker-than-expected performance metrics and a fundamental lack of confidence in the company's aggressive forward estimates. The market reacted swiftly to the brokerage's assessment. Ola Electric's stock took a significant hit in Monday trade, falling as much as 3.5 per cent to Rs 36.53. This decline notably outperformed the broader market downturn, with the benchmark Nifty index falling 0.86 per cent and the overall auto sector slipping 0.7 per cent. The company's first-quarter results for the current fiscal year reflect the ongoing transition following a major operational reset undertaken previously. While the consolidated net loss narrowed to Rs 336 crore, revenue from operations fell sharply by 45 per cent year-on-year to Rs 455 crore. Management described the quarter as the first full period reflecting its restructuring efforts, emphasizing a sequential recovery in the automotive business. The road to operational restructuring For Ola Electric, the immediate challenge lies in reconciling its heavy capital expenditure on localisation with the need for near-term revenue growth. The company's diversification attempts beyond China for equipment sourcing and its focus on higher energy density cells are viewed positively as long-term strategic moats. However, rebuilding brand image and ensuring consistent delivery commitments remain key monitorables for investors. The broader electric two-wheeler sector in India is also navigating a period of moderated growth. Slower penetration rates and intense competition from legacy automakers and emerging startups have forced companies to prioritize unit economics over sheer volume accumulation. Until Ola Electric can demonstrate that its battery manufacturing prowess translates into sustained market share and improved cash flows, brokerages like HSBC remain cautious, advising investors to weigh the promise of vertical integration against the immediate realities of the balance sheet. artigo.texto: AURORA | Monday’s Aurora City Council meeting featured three hours of public comment opposing what would be Colorado’s largest data center. Around 100 residents of The Reserve, a local senior housing community, and the surrounding Windler and Green Valley Ranch neighborhoods attended the meeting to voice their concerns and disagreement with the planned Trident data center, located at 23001 East 48th Ave in northeast Aurora. Before public comment started, City Attorney Pete Schulte asked the audience to stand if they opposed the data center and nearly every attendee stood. No one stood in support of the data center. Speakers, who ranged in age from 16 to 86, were emphatic in their requests for council to impose regulations on data centers, including residential buffers, and require the Trident data center to have more safeguards for health and the environment. Dan Bergander, a resident of The Reserve, highlighted the potential health and quality of life impacts the data center will have on older and disabled neighbors. As he spoke, 50 or more people in the audience stood to support him while he spoke and then burst into applause when he finished. “I’m here speaking for the other at-risk neighbors in the audience and at home, and surprisingly enough, I’m also speaking for your future,” Bergander said. “You on city council will one day settle into retirement and I certainly hope you’re not betrayed by developers and government officials.” When the comments reached the typical hour limit, council voted 9-1 to hear all of the speakers who signed up, with Council member Curtis Gardner opposed. Other than some council members thanking the public for attending, the council did not respond to the wave of comments or address the Trident project at Monday’s meeting. Council did unanimously approve a ban on evaporative cooling, which is a more water intensive cooling system used by some data centers. Planning documents show the Trident data center will be around 860,000 square feet and located in Airport District zoning, which allows data centers as a use by right, which means the project can be approved administratively by the city without a public hearing, unless the project is requesting a variance. While Trident is not requesting a variance, city spokesperson Jennifer Soules said the city is working with the developer, Vantage Data Centers, to schedule a community meeting, but a date has not yet been set. A development application and site plan for the data center were first submitted in August 2025 and the project is on its third round of reviews, according to the city. Neighborhood opposition has grown swiftly, with a local town hall on Sept. 22 drawing about 150 people, while a Change.org petition against the project has more than 2,500 signatures. Ray Czaplewski, a resident of The Reserve whose home will be about a quarter-mile from the data center, said he found out about the project just two weeks ago from his neighbors. Czaplewski described feeling appalled and betrayed when he found out about the data center. “We were blindsided by it,” he said. “Never in our wildest dreams would we expect our city government to be complacent with putting in a hyperscale data center literally right next to residential areas.” Czaplewski said he has a lot of unanswered questions and he raised concerns about noise, air pollution and the toll of the facility on water and energy resources. He also disapproves of the city’s development process allowing data centers without public hearings or notification. “The use by right categorization in the airport district is designed to be opaque,” Czaplewski said. “If we had known a year ago and knew the magnitude of this, we could have started working with Vantage.” Czaplewski and other residents want the city to require a fourth review period to ensure all of the concerns are mitigated. Should they not be addressed, the group is considering legal action for possible damages to health and property values, Czaplewski said. Vantage’s Misty Allen, vice president of public policy for North America, said the company is planning more community outreach as the project moves into construction, including neighborhood meetings and a public website where construction updates will be shared. “It’s perfectly reasonable when people have questions of new developments coming into their community and it’s our commitment that we will be having open community conversations as the design for the project moves forward,” Allen said. “All of that engagement will start to kick off as the project moves forward, so we’re just at the beginning of this.” Allen said the meetings will include subject matter experts to answer questions and connect residents to company representatives. “We’re going to be here for the long-term, so it’s important for folks to get to know the new neighbor in town and to make sure that we have that relationship,” Allen said. In response to concerns from the community, Allen said the facility will have setbacks which will provide at least a 350-foot buffer from homes, as well as a brick wall and water-wise landscaping surrounding the property. Aurora also restricts the noise level at data centers to the same level as other businesses, with different allowances based on zoning and time. The data center is expected to use 334 megawatts of energy for computing capacity, which would be more than twice the state’s current largest data center — the 160 megawatt QTS facility, also in Aurora. The facility would use a closed-loop cooling system, which is less water intensive than other cooling systems, and it’s expected to have 28 emergency generators, as well as battery energy storage, Allen said. “(The generators are) far less than what you would see in a comparable size data center because we’re using the battery storage as well,” Allen said. “We definitely took into consideration how we can be most efficient in this environment.” Allen said Aurora attracted Vantage’s attenti

artigo.texto: ERS Energy Sdn Bhd has surpassed 1.5 GWh of cumulative utility-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity across Southeast Asia, with the company securing the majority of its portfolio over the past 12 months. The milestone includes a 520 MWh BESS project for ACEN in Zambales, Philippines, which ERS Energy described as a landmark project. The company has also secured two utility-scale projects under Malaysia’s inaugural Battery Energy Storage Programme (MyBeST), with the projects having a combined capacity of 800 MWh. ERS Energy said the latest project wins build on its expansion across strategic markets in Southeast Asia. The company combines project structuring, financing frameworks and energy storage system integration capabilities as part of its utility-scale BESS business. The company has expanded from its earlier focus as a solar engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) specialist into utility-scale energy storage development and system integration. Its growing BESS portfolio is aimed at supporting grid stability and addressing the intermittency associated with renewable energy generation. Jonathan Kan, Managing Director of ERS Energy, said the company’s 1.5 GWh milestone reflects its execution capabilities and the confidence of its partners, lenders and regional grid operators. ERS Energy said renewable energy expansion across Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Australia is increasing the need for grid flexibility and energy storage. The company’s BESS portfolio is intended to provide grid services and support the deployment of renewable energy across the region. The company said it works with technology partners and financial institutions to support utility-scale storage projects from design and project financing through to grid synchronisation. artigo.texto: Vena Energy has announced that its NRE Nakagawa 2 Battery Storage Project, with an awarded capacity of 46.828 MW, has been selected under Japan’s FY2025 Long-Term Decarbonised Power Source Auction (LTDA) conducted by the Organisation for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO). The battery storage project is currently under development in Japan and is designed as a grid-connected battery energy storage system (BESS) near Matsumoto City in Nagano Prefecture. The LTDA scheme was introduced in fiscal year 2023 to support Japan’s target of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. The programme provides long-term revenue certainty for selected decarbonised power projects, supporting investment and helping developers recover development and capital costs. The selection of the NRE Nakagawa 2 project expands Vena Energy’s battery storage portfolio in Japan. It follows the commencement of commercial operations at the company’s Hikone Battery Storage Project in 2025. According to Vena Energy, battery storage deployment is expected to play a role in managing the intermittency of renewable generation and improving the efficient utilisation of electricity as Japan increases its reliance on decarbonised power sources. Raul Rienda, Head of Japan at Vena Energy, said the selection of the project under the FY2025 LTDA would support efforts to strengthen the reliability and resilience of Japan’s power system. Vena Energy said it will continue to engage with local communities and consider environmental factors as it advances the NRE Nakagawa 2 project. The company is developing the project as part of its broader focus on battery storage and renewable energy infrastructure in Japan, supporting the country’s long-term decarbonisation objectives. artigo.texto: O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) definiu rodadas de dez minutos, com ofertas fechadas, para os processos competitivos da 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026. Os agentes vão disputar a capacidade disponível na rede de transmissão por meio da oferta de um prêmio, em R$/kW, com piso de R$ 0,38/kW. As regras constam das diretrizes operacionais publicadas nesta terça-feira, 29 de setembro, junto com o manual da plataforma que será usada nas disputas. O valor mínimo será o mesmo para todos os barramentos e produtos dos segmentos de geração e consumo. O piso corresponde a 10% da menor Tarifa de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão (Tust) identificada entre os barramentos candidatos associados aos cadastramentos admitidos na temporada. O processo competitivo é acionado quando a capacidade remanescente de transmissão não é suficiente para atender todos os agentes habilitados que disputam o mesmo recurso da rede. As ofertas de prêmio servirão como critério de classificação, respeitadas também as limitações de capacidade aplicáveis a cada empreendimento. Inicialmente, o ONS tinha identificado disputa para 2,94 GW, sendo 1,95 GW em cargas disputando espaço em São Paulo e 993 MW em geração disputando acesso no Rio Grande do Sul. Após as manifestações dos agentes confirmarem o interesse e a alocação sequencial da capacidade disponível, permaneceram na disputa quatro pontos de acesso de grandes consumidores em São Paulo. São 451 MW em cargas para 228 MW em capacidade de transmissão. Rodadas de dez minutos Pelas regras divulgadas hoje pelo ONS, em cada rodada, os participantes terão uma janela única de dez minutos para registrar a oferta. O valor poderá ser alterado enquanto o prazo estiver aberto, valendo o último registro confirmado na plataforma. Ofertas abaixo de R$ 0,38/kW não serão aceitas. O agente que deixar de apresentar uma oferta válida também poderá ter a Garantia de Participação executada, salvo nas situações de dispensa previstas nas regras, como quando o montante solicitado já tiver sido integralmente atendido em uma rodada anterior. Encerrada a janela, a plataforma fará a classificação em ordem decrescente do prêmio oferecido. A alocação, porém, também terá de respeitar simultaneamente a capacidade disponível no barramento e os limites aplicáveis à subárea e à área em que o empreendimento estiver inserido. Se a capacidade restante for menor que o montante solicitado por um agente, mas suficiente para atender o MUST mínimo declarado, poderá haver atendimento parcial. Empreendimentos sujeitos a uma mesma restrição de subárea ou área disputarão essa capacidade em uma ordem de mérito conjunta, ainda que estejam conectados a barramentos diferentes. As rodadas serão processadas de forma sequencial, por ordem crescente do ano de atendimento. A capacidade alocada em um produto será considerada nas rodadas seguintes do mesmo segmento. Geração e consumo, porém, serão processados separadamente. Desempate eleva prêmio Se houver empate em uma posição que interfira na alocação da capacidade, os agentes envolvidos terão cinco minutos para apresentar uma nova oferta. O valor deverá ser pelo menos 1% superior ao ofertado anteriormente. Poderão ocorrer até três rodadas de desempate. Uma nova rodada só será realizada se a igualdade continuar afetando a distribuição da capacidade. Caso o empate persista ao final da terceira rodada, terá precedência o agente que tiver registrado primeiro a oferta válida na primeira rodada de desempate. O agente que não apresentar uma nova oferta na primeira rodada de desempate será inabilitado. Nas segunda e terceira rodadas, a ausência de nova oferta não leva à inabilitação e mantém válido o último valor apresentado. As ofertas são sigilosas durante o processo competitivo. Assim, embora o piso de R$ 0,38/kW seja público, os participantes não terão acesso às ofertas apresentadas pelos concorrentes durante a disputa. Pagamento em dez dias úteis O resultado consolidado deverá ser disponibilizado até o fim do dia do certame, sujeito à homologação pelo ONS. O prêmio devido pelo vencedor será calculado a partir do valor ofertado e do Must efetivamente alocado. A quitação é condição para a emissão do Diagnóstico Prévio de Acesso (DPA) e para o prosseguimento nas demais etapas da temporada. Se o pagamento não for feito no prazo, ou for realizado em valor inferior ao devido sem complementação tempestiva, o agente perderá a capacidade alocada e terá a Garantia de Participação executada. Nesse caso, não haverá convocação dos demais participantes da disputa para ocupar a capacidade liberada. O montante poderá voltar a ser oferecido em temporadas de acesso posteriores. A Pnast foi estabelecida pelo Decreto 12.772/2025. Considerando a fase de transição das regras, o ONS informou ter analisado mais de 43 GW em solicitações de acesso, sendo que 19,7 GW foram viabilizados na fase de transição.

Ao fim da segunda etapa, prevista para ser concluída em 2030, a companhia terá capacidade global de fabricar cerca de 50 geradores por dia em suas fábricas no México, Estados Unidos, Brasil e China. Atualmente a empresa tem capacidade para produzir 10 geradores por dia, acrescentou.

artigo.texto: BYD says a long-awaited upgrade to electric vehicle batteries is finally getting close to real-world use. The world's largest EV maker is preparing to take solid-state technology out of the lab and put it into vehicles people can actually drive. BYD's Solid-State Battery For EV Is Nearly Ready BYD's executive vice president Stella Li said the company sits in the leading position in the solid-state battery race, with plans to introduce its first EV powered by the new technology in 2027. The company has been researching solid-state batteries since 2013, and by 2023 it had shown that mass production was feasible. Testing of prototype cells rated at 20 and 60 ampere-hours followed throughout 2024, laying the groundwork for the move from lab proof to commercial manufacturing. The batteries rely on sulfide-based electrolytes, which offer higher conductivity and better safety than the liquid setups found in most EVs today. BYD's battery business, FinDreams, aims to begin producing them in limited batches in 2027 before ramping up toward mass production by 2030 (via CarNewsChina). BYD Solid-State EV Battery For Open Roads The first vehicles to get the technology will likely come from BYD's premium brands, including Denza, Yangwang, and Fangchengbao, before it trickles down to higher volume models. According to Engadget, the first two years are expected to serve as a demonstration phase with limited production. Early estimates suggest cars using these batteries could reach roughly 800 kilometers, or nearly 500 miles, on a single charge, with some observers speculating the range could eventually pass 1,000 kilometers. Reports point to energy density targets of up to 400 watt-hours per kilogram, compared with roughly 160 to 180 for BYD's current lithium iron phosphate batteries and around 300 for the best nickel manganese cobalt cells. Charging times as short as 12 minutes have also been mentioned in early projections. Other Brands Have Been Working on the Tech BYD is not alone in chasing the technology. Chery has said its prototypes reach 400 watt-hours per kilogram and aims to push that to 500, while Toyota, Honda, and Mercedes Benz are also developing their own solid-state solutions. Even so, BYD executives describe the company as out in front, and its CTO has said scaled production could eventually bring solid-state costs down to parity with conventional liquid electrolyte batteries. BYD expects the technology to reach more affordable models between 2030 and 2032 as production costs come down. The company also does not see its Blade batteries, built on lithium iron phosphate, disappearing anytime soon, with its chief scientist projecting they will stay important for budget-friendly EVs for the next 15 to 20 years. Why Are Solid-State Batteries a Big Deal? Most EVs today run on lithium-ion batteries, where charged particles called ions move through a liquid medium. Solid-state batteries swap that liquid for a solid layer, which improves safety because EV batteries are known for catching fire, and the flammable liquid inside conventional cells is often part of the problem. A solid electrolyte offers better thermal stability, lowering the risk of fires and leaks. Solid-state cells also pack more energy into the same space, which means longer range and more compact battery packs. Sulfide electrolytes in particular are described as longer-lasting and more stable than liquid options, giving the batteries a more durable life and faster charging. The technology is difficult to build, since ions move through liquids more easily than solids and gaps between solid layers can raise electrical resistance.

artigo.texto: Oriana Power has completed the first tranche of its proposed divestment of a 74% equity stake in its subsidiary Truere Guj SPV Private Limited (T Guj) to Leo Energies Private Limited, formerly known as Helioact Power India 1 Private Limited, a group entity of Actis GP LLP. The subsidiary owns a solar project with an aggregate capacity of approximately 70 MWp, along with 30 MWh of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity. Oriana Power said it has received the consideration for the first tranche of the proposed divestment. The enterprise value of T Guj is approximately ₹325 crore, subject to closing adjustments in accordance with the Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) and subsequent amendments. The consideration has been determined after making the applicable adjustments to the enterprise value under the terms of the SPA. The first tranche has been completed in accordance with the agreed terms and conditions. The remaining tranches, where applicable, will be undertaken subject to the SPA, applicable approvals and other conditions. Oriana Power said the transaction supports its asset-recycling and monetisation strategy, while strengthening its balance sheet and liquidity position. The proceeds are expected to be redeployed into the company’s growing pipeline of solar, open-access and BESS projects. artigo.texto: Handwritten on pieces of cut-up poster paper, Amy Wright made her case that members of her city council have allegedly voted on issues they had a financial stake in and violated open meetings laws along the way. Tensions are ratcheting up in Carroll County, where two different data center developers are planning hyperscale projects in the rural community of 11,000 people. One project in particular, pitched by Louisville-based Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, has drawn the ire of local residents after the project went public a year after Carrollton city officials signed land deals with the company. Now, community members, including Wright, are filing ethics complaints saying several members of the city council who voted to move forward with that secret land deal should have abstained from the vote because they or an immediate family member works for Louisville Gas & Electric and Kentucky Utilities, which stands to profit from the energy-intensive data center. KPR obtained financial disclosures filed by each city council member via open records request — they are sparse, but at least two members noted LG&E-KU as a source of income for themselves or their spouse. Multiple Kentucky communities have been divided over hyperscale data center concerns, with opponents accusing officials of not keeping the community’s best interests in mind. Poe and PowerHouse are building a center in Louisville, where anti-data center activists have filed numerous complaints, including with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Office of Civil Rights. In Mercer County, activists uncovered emails showing an LG&E-KU employee in public office pushing other officials to support a controversial data center project. Proponents of data centers argue they would pay huge dividends to local governments through taxes to fund better schools, roads and more. The Carroll County Ethics Commission heard one set of complaints on Sept. 17 — several anti-data center activists and representatives of council members accused of violating the ethics code attended the hearing. After coming out of a lengthy closed discussion, Ethics Commission member Zach Spencer addressed the room of waiting community members. The commission voted to table the complaint over the financial conflicts, but moved forward with another complaint, and Spencer said they would open a formal investigation into “the alleged misconduct [and] required disclosure of withheld records.” “I want to air this out. I don’t want to keep coming back in for more and more complaints,” Spencer said. “I want everything. I want it out in the open.” Community concerns to be aired out Two days before the county ethics commissions met, the Carrollton City Council was scheduled to start the process of opting-out of those very ethics rules and “create its own ethics commission.” According to multiple people present at that public meeting, Mayor Robb Adams decided not to move forward with the reading and did not explain why it was on the agenda. Anastasia Coots, who lives in Carrollton and has previously clashed with Adams during her stint on the city’s Planning and Zoning Board, said she believes the council has violated multiple state and local ethics laws. “This is so much bigger than just a data center,” Coots said. “All of those people that voted and the mayor and the Carrollton Utilities Commission are beholden to the actual city to do anything in the best financial interest of the city, so when they went into executive session and signed an [agreement] with Poe, it actually only benefited Poe.” She has submitted complaints to various law enforcement agencies, including the commonwealth attorney’s office. She and Wright allege that multiple members of the Carrollton City Council have conflicts with LG&E-KU — they say one is a current employee, one is retired with a KU pension, and another has a son working with KU. Another council member’s husband got a job with the company after voting in favor of the land deal. Kentucky Public Radio asked for comment from the council’s lawyer, each council member allegedly tied to KU, but did not receive a response in time for publication. In a statement to KPR, LG&E-KU spokesperson Drew Gardner said the company has not reviewed the complaint. He said the company “has an obligation” to serve businesses seeking to locate in the area and have established procedures for doing so. “This project is no exception, and a connection to LG&E and KU gives no one special standing in that process,” Gardner said. “Because the review is ongoing, we won’t speculate about the allegations.” The Carroll County code of ethics specifically calls on officers with a prohibited financial interest to submit the “precise nature and value of the interest, in writing.” The code says that officers are prohibited from participating in public duties that present a “substantial conflict” to the business interests of themselves or “any immediate family member.” “The officer or employee shall refrain from taking any action with respect to the matter that is the subject of the disclosure,” the ethics code reads. As Wright showed me her handwritten complaints in the Carrollton Public Library, she explained that she isn’t trying to wage war against the city council, but she also doesn’t want this data center coming to her community. She said she’s glad the ethics commission is taking her complaints seriously and is interested in a “fair and impartial review.” “I'm glad that they're willing to just take a step back, look at all of the facts together, and make a determination on it,” Wright said. The ethics commission’s chair recused himself from the committee hearing — he too is a retired employee of KU. Spencer, who took his place to lead the meeting, read a lengthy open records request he was making to the city. It’s the start of the group's investigation into how the council came to enter a contract with Poe to sell hundreds of acres of land, near residential proper

artigo.texto: Trending Communities hosting hyperscale data centers are seeing benefits even while the protests grow. "New recreational spaces, water and wastewater infrastructure, traffic lights, build-outs of local roads and grants for schools were among the pluses for communities hosting them. "Our roads around our data centers are beautiful," said Etta Lockey, director of Commercial Energy Supply, Meta, also known as Facebook, Instagram, What's App and maker of novel hardware such as tech glasses. "Growth can pay for growth," she cited at the 16th annual Marcellus Shale Coalition INSIGHT 2026 in Erie. "My team is responsible for bringing the high voltage and electrons to our data centers in partnership with our utilities and energy development partners," she said. The goal, she said, is "not to shift costs onto the families in the communities where the data centers exist." Meta also has placed a priority on its commitment to the community and ongoing community engagement. "None of this is possible without our communities more than the jobs that data center development can support, we want to be good neighbors and good community partners," she said. This is done through hiring local contractors, boosting local tax revenue, paying for local infrastructure, and adding new energy to the grid, she added. This phenomena is where electrons and molecules are meeting the real economy. The workers, the townships, the utilities, the producers, a consortium of folks that have been powering the U.S. for generations are now having to address national AI dominance and meet demand. To do this right, developers need community partners who are seeing the upside and serving as home to some of the most innovative technology in the world. Meta, she noted, provides millions of dollars in grants year after year to support schools and nonprofits. In fact, Meta has given $94 million supporting over 3,700 grants and communities where it has data centers around the globe. One criteria screened for site selection is the availability of natural gas "We are also investing in partnerships and solutions that reduce the footprint over time," Lockey said. That includes support for U.S.-produced low methane natural gas. At Meta, energy innovation has become as important as software or chip innovation. The evolution of artificial intelligence is changing how thoughts are evolving on infrastructure, pushing innovation at every layer, Lockey said. For those in Appalachia, this presents an enormous opportunity. "We have the resources, we have the expertise and the workforce to help meet that demand," said Jim Welty, president of Marcellus Shale Coalition Meta is a company helping drive a new era of energy demand, he said. Lockey, an attorney by training, continues to lead efforts to secure the affordable, reliable energy needed to support the company's growing data infrastructure, he said.

artigo.texto: The next generation of data centers is changing more than how much electricity utilities must supply. It is also changing the speed, concentration and uncertainty of load growth. This demand is arriving amid transmission constraints, lengthy interconnection timelines and competition for grid capacity. Artificial intelligence is creating large, power-dense loads while also giving utilities tools to automate studies, analyze data and plan faster. That dual role was central to Siemens Grid Software’s webinar, Planning the grid at the speed of AI: From interconnection queues to grid readiness, featuring experts from Siemens, NVIDIA and Dominion Energy. Utilities need more infrastructure, but also smarter, faster and more collaborative planning. AI factories are changing the scale of demand Traditional data centers hosted enterprise applications and delivered computing and storage services. AI factories create value through model training and inference. As AI advances toward reasoning models and physical AI systems, its computing and electricity requirements are rising dramatically According to NVIDIA’s webinar remarks, traditional data center racks typically consume 15 to 25 kilowatts. Current AI infrastructure can require approximately 230 kilowatts per rack, while future systems could approach one megawatt per rack. For utilities, this is not incremental growth. Large loads may cluster geographically and seek service much faster than generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure can be planned, permitted and built. The grid is part of the AI technology stack As NVIDIA observed during the webinar, energy has become part of the AI technology stack. AI cannot operate without reliable electricity, making power availability a strategic factor in where AI infrastructure is developed. Utilities, regulators, system operators, developers, technology providers and customers must coordinate earlier on project certainty, ramp schedules, location, reliability and potential load flexibility. Dominion Energy’s Northern Virginia experience reinforced that integrating large loads is not solely a utility challenge. Stakeholders must align timelines and assumptions early. Planning must account for uncertainty Deterministic forecasts alone become less effective when planners face many possible futures. An AI facility may be delayed, resized, relocated, or phased. Its load profile may change as technology evolves, while renewable output, electrification, distributed resources and transmission constraints add variables. Utilities should complement deterministic studies with scenario-based and probabilistic planning. Key considerations include project probability and timing, load ramp rates, hourly and seasonal demand, generation and transmission availability, storage performance, flexible-load participation, behind-the-meter resources and permitting timelines. The goal is not to predict one future perfectly, but to identify decisions that remain sound across many futures. Flexibility could change the equation Some AI workloads may be more flexible than commonly assumed. Certain training processes could be shifted, throttled, or scheduled for different times or locations, although inference and other time-sensitive applications may have strict availability requirements. Even partial flexibility could reduce stress during constrained periods, improve use of existing assets and potentially defer selected investments. Options include workload scheduling, demand response, battery storage and phased energization. Utilities cannot assume flexibility. They need dependable information about which workloads can move, response speed, duration and operational limits. Behind-the-meter generation may accelerate projects, but it raises fuel, permitting, reliability, market and economic questions. AI can help utilities plan for AI Planning teams are evaluating more interconnection requests, operating conditions and investment scenarios, often without equivalent growth in engineering resources. Automation and AI-enabled workflows can expand analytical capacity by handling repeatable tasks, supporting data analysis and helping planners focus on higher-value engineering decisions. Faster simulation, improved data integration and interoperable platforms can shorten study cycles and create a consistent view of assumptions and results. Combined with probabilistic methods, AI can expand scenario analysis without compromising engineering rigor. The objective is not to replace engineers, but to give them the speed, scale and information to plan across more possible futures. Preparing for the AI factory era Utilities must preserve reliability, safety and affordability while becoming more agile and growth-oriented. Physical reinforcement will remain necessary, but building alone is not enough. Utilities must also use existing capacity more effectively, improve data quality, automate repeatable work and evaluate uncertainty systematically. AI factories make the urgency visible, but the implications extend beyond data centers. Electrification, renewable integration and distributed resources are increasing grid complexity. AI is creating part of the challenge, but it can also be part of the solution. Utilities that recognize both sides will be better positioned to support economic growth while maintaining reliable, resilient and affordable service. Watch Planning the grid at the speed of AI: From interconnection queues to grid readiness on demand to hear experts from Siemens, NVIDIA and Dominion Energy discuss how utilities can prepare for AI-driven load growth.

artigo.texto: Delta Electronics Unveils AI Modular Data Center with 800 VDC In-Row Power for NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Microgrid Solutions at Data Center World Asia 2026 SINGAPORE, Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Delta Electronics, a global leader in power management and smart green solutions, is attending Data Center World (DCW) Asia 2026 with its new AI Modular Data Center (AI MDC) and Microgrid Solutions to accelerate the deployment and enhance the energy efficiency and resilience of AI infrastructure. The prefabricated AI MDC integrates next-gen 800 VDC In-Row Power and liquid cooling systems for the fast deployment and scalability of AI data centers based on NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture. The Microgrid Solution integrates Delta's renewable energy, energy storage, and Solid Oxide Fuel Cell (SOFC) systems, as well as Solid State Transformers (SST), which are essential to directly convert medium voltage power to 800 VDC for the AI factories of the future. "AI workloads are scaling faster than most data centres were designed to handle, while their demands can be increasingly unpredictable. This means infrastructure planning must move from reactive to integrated and future-ready," said Jason Yuan, President, Southeast Asia & ANZ, Delta Electronics. "Our AI Modular Data Centers and Microgrids, both part of our Grid-to-Chip Solutions portfolio, are ideal to help our clients across Southeast Asia deploy and power their future-ready AI data centers. Moreover, Delta's solutions are engineered for energy efficiency, reliability and performance, while providing the flexibility to adapt to changing workloads and infrastructure demands." Visitors can expect interactive showcases spanning Delta Electronics' AI infrastructure portfolio, including its AI Modular Data Center designed for scalability, flexibility, and compatibility, high-voltage direct current (HVDC) 3.6MW in-row coolant distribution unit (CDU) technology to help manage the thermal demands of high-density AI workloads. The showcased 800 VDC In-Row Power architecture features 660kW output power, up to 98% AC-DC efficiency, 480kW capacity in battery backup units (BBU), and aluminium capacitors to optimize GPU workloads in next-generation AI data centres. In addition, Delta's prefabricated AI Containerized Data Center (CDC) Solutions deliver up to 60 kW per rack of AI compute within the footprint of a single parking space, as well as a seamlessly integrated Liquid-to-Air CDU system to achieve a PUE as low as 1.19. The unveiled Microgrid Solution demonstrates how on-site energy generation resources, energy storage, power conversion, and the new solid state transformer (SST) can support greater power resilience, efficiency and flexibility. Through real time coordination of multiple energy sources, uptime and power quality are maintained during grid connection delays or off-grid operation, with SOFC providing reliable on-site power 24/7. Its prefabricated DC coupled architecture combines SSTs, DC/DC converters and dynamic energy support to reduce conversion stages, enabling the system to respond to fluctuating AI loads while supporting scalable deployment. At the board-level, Delta's thermal management solutions include a dedicated state-of-the-art cold plate for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, with the latest microchannel and multi impinging flow design. See the Future of AI Infrastructure Live at DCW Asia 2026 Delta Electronics will showcase the In-Row Power at DCW Asia 2026, taking place from 29– 30 September at the Marina Bay Sands Convention Centre, Level 1, Singapore, at Booth D10. artigo.texto: CHINA unveiled a new five-year plan for its battery industry on Monday, aiming for the initial large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030 as the country accelerates the transition of next-generation battery technology from research to commercialization. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, together with six other government agencies, jointly issued the new development plan for the battery industry, outlining the sector’s development priorities over the 15th Five-Year plan (2026–2030) period. The plan comes as China continues to expand its role in the global battery supply chain and seeks to strengthen its leadership in the global energy transition, according to Chinese experts. The country already has strong battery manufacturing capacity, but industry experts said that it still needs to improve basic research and core technologies to maintain long-term competitiveness. To promote the high-quality development of the industry, efforts will be made to accelerate technological innovation, industrial transformation and upgrading, improve the industrial system, enhance the capacity of industrial science and technology services, and raise the quality and level of trade and investment cooperation, according to the document. China will seek steady growth in its new battery industry over the next five years, while making major breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials. It also called for significant progress in new battery systems, with all-solid-state batteries moving toward initial large-scale deployment by 2030. New batteries refer to energy storage and conversion devices built on new mechanisms, materials, structures and manufacturing processes. They include lithium batteries, sodium batteries and flow batteries, which analysts said are becoming key parts of China’s push to develop new industrial sectors, build a new energy system and strengthen its capabilities. China’s battery industry has strong manufacturing capabilities but still needs to strengthen fundamental research, Sun Xiaohong, former secretary-general of the automotive branch of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, told the Global Times on Monday. All-solid-state batteries are one of the plan’s key technological priorities. Compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries, which typically use flammable liquid electrolytes, solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes and are considered safer and potentially capable of offering higher energy density, according to Sun. The plan calls for faster breakthroughs in commercialization technologies, with a focus on improving ionic conductivity, cycle stability and cost efficiency. It also stresses the need to advance key materials and processes, including interface contact technology, high ionic conductivity, long life cycles and engineering pressure system design. China’s solid-state battery market is projected to grow from $42.5 million in 2025 to $384.8 million by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 44.4 percent, significantly outpacing the global average of 37.5 percent. Meanwhile, substantial research and development investments by domestic manufacturers such as CATL and BYD are accelerating solid-state battery commercialization and deployment, according to media reports. Sun said that solid-state battery technology worldwide is still in the research and testing stage, and has not yet entered large-scale commercial use. He noted that the main challenges remain manufacturing consistency and cost reduction. “Small-scale commercialization is already possible, but large-scale adoption still depends on lowering costs further and improving production processes,” Sun said.

artigo.texto: Sungrow has announced the successful grid connection and completion of full acceptance testing for the Cambodia EDC Kandal Stueng station (GS79), a 108.4 MW/215.6 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Takmao, Kandal Province. The project deploys grid-forming technology at utility scale and is designed to support grid stability, black-start capability, and coordination with hydroelectric and thermal generation. The facility is located at a key point in Cambodia’s central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. During system-restoration testing, 516 grid-forming power conversion system (PCS) units successfully energized the entire BESS plant from zero voltage while establishing stable voltage and frequency. The system also supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations as the network was progressively restored. As part of the testing, the BESS supported the startup and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant. The restored network was subsequently operated with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, the energy storage system, and connected loads. The project remained stable during five transformer energization events, including one involving a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stable operation while synchronizing different power sources with a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees. The BESS demonstrated extended islanded operation for 3.5 hours, allowing it to continue supporting the local network while separated from the main grid. The project also completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded modes, with voltage deviation maintained below 2% and transient frequency fluctuations within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. Sungrow said the project was delivered under strict testing requirements, a compressed construction schedule, and rainy-season conditions with ambient temperatures reaching 40°C. The commissioning and testing activities were completed within 20 days. The project team carried out hot commissioning and three rounds of performance testing during the commissioning period to support timely grid connection. Sungrow provided services covering storage and monitoring system design, equipment design, commissioning, EPC-related support, and operations and maintenance. The company said the integrated approach was intended to address the project’s grid-level requirements across design, delivery, and operation. The project adds a large-scale grid-forming BESS installation to Cambodia’s power system and demonstrates the use of energy storage for grid restoration, islanded operation, and coordination with multiple generation sources. artigo.texto: [DigitalToday Seung-ah Yoo, intern reporter] Hyundai Motor Group reaffirmed its position that it will continue pushing ahead with the development of all-solid-state batteries. From startups to major automakers, companies are continuing to invest in all-solid-state batteries, touted as a “dream technology” to deliver ultra-fast charging and longer driving range for electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, the performance of conventional lithium-ion batteries is improving quickly. Geely’s latest battery technology takes less than 9 minutes to charge from 10 percent to 97 percent. Even so, is there still a need to keep developing all-solid-state batteries? On Sept. 27 (local time), EV-focused outlet InsideEVs reported that Hyundai Motor Group R&D chief Manfred Harrer (만프레드 하러) gave a firm “yes” to that question. Harrer told reporters last week, “We cannot give up now. That is clear,” adding, “We must be part of this competition.” Current EV batteries use a liquid electrolyte to move lithium ions between the cell’s anode and cathode. All-solid-state batteries, by contrast, mainly replace that liquid electrolyte with a solid material such as ceramics or polymers. This could raise both safety and performance. But no company has yet succeeded in producing solid-state cells at a scale suitable for automobiles. Harrer cited smaller batteries, improved fast-charging performance and longer driving range as potential advantages of all-solid-state batteries. He forecast that a symbolic vehicle produced in small volumes with an all-solid-state battery would appear within the next 5 years. QuantumScape is also aiming to apply all-solid-state batteries to high-performance vehicles by the late 2020s. Raw material costs are expected to remain very high for years as the technology scales up. Harrer said this would make it difficult for all-solid-state batteries to enter the mass market. “In the end, you can solve everything, but it costs money. It comes at an enormous cost,” he said. Hyundai is developing all-solid-state batteries in-house while also working with partners such as Solid Power. Harrer described all-solid-state batteries as “the industry’s big bet right now.” Toyota has been developing all-solid-state batteries for at least 20 years and is targeting mass production within the next few years. Volkswagen is making large-scale investments in QuantumScape, while BMW is working with Solid Power. General Motors, Ford, Honda and Nissan are also moving into all-solid-state battery development. Some companies have already unveiled demonstration prototypes. Examples include a Ducati equipped with QuantumScape cells and a Mercedes vehicle using Factorial’s technology. But there are still no cases of all-solid-state batteries being fitted in mass-produced vehicles that consumers can actually buy. Harrer’s goal is for Hyundai to enter the market with its own supply chain and manufacturing capabilities once the technology matures. “We want to be the owner of this key technology,” he said. “That is why we are also investing in our own battery manufacturing.” Harrer explained that it is important to deeply understand battery manufacturing methods and the associated costs. Batteries are the most expensive component in EVs and are also used in other electrified vehicles. Hyundai plans to apply its in-house nickel·manganese·cobalt (NCM) cells to the extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) version of the Tafe, which is scheduled to launch early next year. In a recent announcement, Hyundai said it plans to launch the Tafe EREV in the first half of 2027. All-solid-state batteries are expected to take considerable time before reaching the mass market. “I do not think we can solve the raw material cost issue within 5 years from now,” Harrer said.

artigo.texto: INTERVIEW Hooxi Partners seeks to turn emissions cuts into revenue Climate fintech firm eyes expansion amid tighter carbon rules, targets 2028 Kosdaq listing Cutting greenhouse gas emissions does not automatically generate revenue. Companies must first measure and verify the reductions, then have them recognized as carbon credits before they can sell them. For smaller businesses with limited staff and capital, navigating those steps can be difficult. Hooxi Partners, a climate fintech company, was founded to help close that gap. Before establishing it in 2021, CEO Lee Haeng-youl saw an opportunity in the environmental, social and governance (ESG) market as environmental gains were difficult to measure, and businesses had few ways to turn them into financial value. He believed reliable emissions data could provide the basis for tradable carbon credits. “For carbon reduction to be sustainable, those making the cuts must receive an economic reward. Telling companies to do it because it is the right thing will not work for long,” Lee said in a recent interview with The Korea Times. That idea is reflected in the company’s slogan, “We make money from carbon credits.” Since founding the company, Lee has sought to change how businesses view carbon management. Many treat it as a compliance exercise, calculating emissions at year’s end, filing reports and purchasing credits to cover any shortfall. Under that approach, carbon remains a cost. “We want to move carbon from a cost item to a manageable asset on the balance sheet,” he said. “Rather than looking at greenhouse gas emissions data once a year or quarter, companies should manage it continuously, like sales or inventory, and calculate in advance how much value an investment in emissions reduction equipment could generate in carbon credits.” With that information, decisions to invest in equipment or upgrade existing facilities could move beyond the environmental team and become part of a company’s broader investment planning. Lee sees a particularly strong case for financial incentives among businesses that are not required to participate in Korea’s emissions trading system. Hooxi Partners consolidated its services this year under a platform called Carbon AI. Its NET-Z module calculates and reports corporate emissions. Measurement, reporting, verification and creditization (MRVC) helps companies develop emissions reduction projects and obtain verification and certification. Hooxi Connect links project operators with companies and financial institutions seeking carbon credits or verified reductions. The platform is designed to carry data through each stage, from measuring emissions to selling the carbon credits a project generates. “The synergy comes from continuity of data,” Lee said. “Emissions calculated in NET-Z become the baseline for assessing reduction potential in MRVC, and reductions certified through MRVC become volumes available for trading on Hooxi Connect. This eliminates the cost of reorganizing and verifying data each time a project moves to the next stage.” The company began in transport, focusing on electric buses. Lee noted that mileage and charging records make it possible to estimate emissions reductions compared with diesel vehicles, but individual bus operators often lack the resources to develop carbon credit projects on their own. Hooxi Partners has signed agreements with 272 bus operators and submitted electric bus projects representing about 1.8 million tons of potential emissions reductions. Projects covering 450,000 tons have received government approval. The company said it was the first operator in Korea’s transport sector to win approval for an electric vehicle emissions reduction program. “We demonstrated that the entire process works in practice by combining the reductions of small bus operators into one project, securing government approval and converting the results into carbon credits,” Lee said. The company is also seeking to address a funding problem that can prevent such projects from getting started. Emissions reduction investments such as introducing electric vehicles or upgrading facilities require upfront funding, while revenue from carbon credits may be years away. Under its “future carbon credits” model, a business can sell credits it expects to generate through a forward transaction and receive funding earlier. The firm said it has carried out a forward transaction with Hyundai Motor Securities. The arrangement was featured as a case of Environmental Progress Credit (EPC), an incentive mechanism developed by the Center for Social Value Enhancement Studies to reward climate technology developers early and encourage greater emissions reductions. “Small and midsize businesses with limited financial resources may give up on emissions reduction investments because they cannot bridge that time gap,” Lee said. “Future carbon credits use finance to address that delay.” Lee expects demand for emissions management to grow during the fourth phase of Korea’s emissions trading system, which began this year, and following the implementation of the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Companies covered by the trading system will need to secure credits, while exporters will need product-level emissions data. Lee said demand for such data is extending to suppliers. “We are working with Oriental Brewery and 15 of its suppliers to jointly measure and verify Scope 3 emissions, and demand for this kind of supply chain measurement, reporting and verification has been growing rapidly since CBAM,” Lee said. For its next stage of growth in Korea, Hooxi Partners is targeting solar installations and heat pumps. Although each project may produce relatively modest reductions, the company believes combining many projects could create volumes large enough for a carbon credit program. Overseas, Southeast Asia is its first priority. The company plans to work with local partners as the region adopts electric two

artigo.texto: The Chinese company Gotion buys 49% of Volkswagen's battery plant in Sagunto The Chinese manufacturer will invest €1,100M and will have 49% of the gigafactory - CAT - CAST BarcelonaThe Volkswagen Group, PowerCo and the Chinese company Gotion High-Tech have agreed to "deepen their strategic alliance" through a joint venture for the development and operation of the battery cell gigafactory currently under construction in the town of Sagunto (Valencian Community). In this way, the Chinese manufacturer is investing some 1.1 billion euros to obtain 49% of the gigafactory. The battery plant in Sagunto, which should start operating this year, had planned an investment of about 3 billion euros, with aid from the Spanish government within the PERTE for the electric and connected car. This plant should supply batteries to the Seat plant in Martorell and the Volkswagen plant in Landaben (Navarre). The German consortium is already manufacturing electric cars at both plants: the Cupra Raval and the ID Polo in Martorell, and the ID Cross and the Skoda Epiq in Navarre. The planned collaboration between the Volkswagen Group and the Chinese company Gotion "enhances the plant's technological capabilities, which represents a new milestone in the industrial development of the project and strengthens its role within the growing European battery value chain," company sources told Europa Press. The agreement signed this Monday maintains PowerCo (Volkswagen Group) with a majority stake of 51% in the Sagunto gigafactory, which guarantees "continuity in the governance, strategic direction and operational oversight of the project." In addition, the investment commitments and employment targets –3,000 jobs– previously announced "remain unchanged". The same sources point out that as the European automotive industry moves towards electrification, the demand for LFP battery technology (lithium iron phosphate batteries) is expected to grow significantly. According to market forecasts, LFP batteries will be dominant and could represent between 40% and 65% of total demand in Europe by 2030, driven by their competitiveness, safety, durability and suitability for high-volume electric vehicle segments. Currently, practically all LFP cells used in Europe are manufactured in China. With the joint venture, Volkswagen, PowerCo and Gotion are turning the Sagunto project into a key piece to establish a competitive European production base for this strategically important technology with cells destined for the European market. Its long-term competitiveness is reinforced thanks to a larger scale, manufacturing experience and supply chain resilience. First phase commitments The joint venture has been designed to "strengthen the long-term viability and competitiveness of the Sagunto project, while preserving the strategic commitments already made". The investment of more than 2.3 billion euros already in execution and the creation of more than 1,500 direct jobs in the initial phase –which includes the first two production blocks– remain unchanged, thus consolidating the gigafactory's position as one of the most relevant industrial projects currently under development in Europe. Sagunto will begin operations with two production blocks and a combined annual capacity of up to 30 GWh in a first phase.

artigo.texto: Note: Welcome To RCBJ’s “Your Voices” Column, an occasional column prompted by readers’ commentary. If you have something to say, in a well-reasoned essay of 500 to 700 words, email the editor at ttraster@rcbizjournal.com Battery Storage Projects Are Good For The Economy, Good For Reducing Energy Bills, And Safe By Justin Wilcox New York’s energy policy must be measured by more than the ambitions it sets. It must also deliver electricity that households and businesses can afford, a grid that remains reliable and an economy capable of supporting future growth. That requires practical investments in the infrastructure needed to meet the state’s energy needs. Battery energy storage is one of those investments. For years, batteries have held the promise of storing electricity when it is abundant and returning it to the grid when it is needed. Without substantial energy storage, the renewable mandates established by the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act become more difficult and more expensive to integrate reliably. They can also supplement dispatchable resources and displace generation from some of the least efficient and highest-emitting plants during certain hours. That is a legitimate grid function, and one that should not be overlooked simply because battery storage cannot solve every challenge facing the electric system. Upstate United has consistently argued that New York needs a diversified energy resource mix. Existing natural gas generation will remain necessary for years to maintain reliability, and the state should support strategic investments in generation and fuel supply that can reduce costs and emissions. Battery storage should be understood as part of that same practical approach. Yet as battery projects move from planning documents to individual communities, their promise is increasingly colliding with the public’s safety concerns. There are valid safety considerations associated with virtually every form of energy infrastructure. Natural gas pipelines, nuclear power plants and fuel storage facilities must all be engineered and operated with safety as a fundamental guiding principle. Battery storage should be held to the same standard. That principle was behind the creation of New York’s Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group in 2023. Following several battery fires, the state brought together fire safety experts and agencies to examine incidents, inspect operating facilities and identify improvements to safety standards and emergency response. The working group inspected 57 large, operating battery storage projects. Those inspections produced important lessons about fire code requirements, inspection procedures and coordination with local emergency responders. Many of the group’s recommendations were subsequently incorporated into New York’s updated Fire Code, which took effect in January 2026. The updated requirements address matters including emergency response planning, inspections, fire department coordination and independent review of project safety. These are not substitutes for careful local oversight. They are tools that can help communities evaluate proposed facilities with greater confidence and ensure that safety remains central to the process. New York’s Public Service Commission has approved a target of 6 gigawatts of energy storage by 2030. Meeting that target will require more than setting a number in Albany. It will require the state to provide communities with the technical resources, clear standards and support necessary to make informed decisions about proposed projects. Local governments should retain their authority to review land use and evaluate the impacts of development. At the same time, legitimate concerns should be addressed through rigorous standards, transparent information and meaningful engagement, rather than allowing uncertainty to become an indefinite barrier to investment. New York cannot afford an energy policy that encourages new resources in principle, while making it increasingly difficult to build the infrastructure necessary to support them. Battery storage is not a silver bullet. But it can help diversify our resource mix, improve grid efficiency and support a more orderly transition to lower emissions. Policymakers must acknowledge that new technologies can raise legitimate safety concerns, just as existing energy technologies carry risks of their own. But the answer should be to manage those risks, not to turn away from the benefits. New York needs to evaluate these investments on their merits, insist on strong safety standards and build the infrastructure that can deliver measurable benefits. If we are serious about an affordable, reliable and lower-emissions energy future, battery storage must be part of the solution. Justin Wilcox is executive director of Upstate United, a coalition of businesses, organizations and community leaders working to strengthen Upstate New York’s economy, improve affordability and create opportunities for growth.
